I played this on the PC back in 2012 and I don't understand why it's taken me this long to make a review for this game... but here it is. I've got 120 hours on L.A. Noire and that doesn't even include the 100 hours or so I've racked up on the Xbox 360. Before I praise the hell out of this game, I'd like to go over some issues with this game in general:
The main campaign's quite long (~20 hours) and at-times repetitive. This might not be a con for some people but it's worth mentioning regardless. Although there's a lot of variety, you won't shake off the feeling you've already done this x amount of times.
The city hasn't got much to do in it. Another game, Mafia II, similarly shared this issue but there are street crimes or sidequests to participate in, vehicles to find and collectibles to attain. The stunning recreation of a 1940's Los Angeles is worth exploring but unfortunately there's not a lot of reasons to do so.
The port is locked to 30 FPS. This is not a dealbreaker for people like me but again, I thought it was worth mentioning. There also exists several unofficial ways of unlocking this (and there's not a lot of negative side-effects which is neat).
Performance can be hit and miss for a few individuals. I recommend swapping from Direct X 9 to Direct X 11 and vice versa for those people, as well as changing the Threading mode from "single" to "multi" and vice versa.
With that out of the way, here's why you should get this game:
The atmosphere. This game oozes it and you'll be immersed right away. Set in the 1940s you are placed in the shoes of a bright star who is rising through the ranks of the Los Angeles Police Department. As you play as Cole Phelps and go from case to case: the voice acting and dialogue, the clothing, the cars... every little detail wants to convince you that you are in this setting. And to think an Australian team (Team Bondi) pulled this off. It's incredible and simply deserves to be mentioned.
The story. The story doesn't reveal itself until later in the game and until then, you're working your way from one case to the next with the occasional collectible newspaper acting as a "here's what's also going on" feature. What I liked most about the story is that it's subtle early on and then it all starts making sense. It's nothing super-amazing but I would be lying if I said I didn't think it was good. Bits and pieces of the game world also serve the story well in reinforcing issues and ideas that were present in the 1940s.
The characters. You've got a large roster with people of all different beliefs and personalities. Everyone feels unique, multi-layered and realistic. The characters further aid in immersing you in this wonderful game.
The gameplay. Most of the time the game's rather slow-paced. You'll be walking or driving to a crime scene while picking up clues, but at points in the game, all hell breaks loose. A man starts a brawl with you! A criminal starts making a run for it! A shootout occurs! Moments like these help break up the monotony, and while most of them are scripted, they really are exciting. Don't go in expecting an action game though. When you're not searching for clues or being a badass: you're doing interrogations. I'll talk about this in the next point.
The motion capture/interrogations. Never has a game utilized motion capture like this I reckon. When you're interrogating a suspect: you're not interrogating a NPC, you're interrogating someone that looks and acts like a real human being. It's something you'll simply have to witness for yourself. And this doesn't just apply to interrogations - the whole game uses motion capture for every character's face and I couldn't be more pleased with the result. Back to interrogations though... I love them. Some find difficulty with these but it's probably because the choices you have to make - Truth, Doubt or Lie - were originally called: Truth, Coax or Force. I have no idea why they were changed for the final product, as they make less sense. Still, interrogating is where you rely on this motion capture the most to see if the suspect is lying. Just like real life though: don't judge a person soley by their looks or behaviour though!
The soundtrack. I could go on and on in this section but let me just say this: Team Bondi killed it here. You might not be a fan of 1940s music but you'll be able to appreciate just how accurate the setting feels.
Everything else. The huge open city to explore. Being able to slap on a black and white filter in the options menu is just another thing that makes me love this game. Swapping between costumes for Cole Phelps is really nice too. Making different choices and the somewhat linear missions changing up a little to reflect this. The little conversations between Cole and his partners as you're driving in a car throughout the city. And if you don't want to drive? Being able to make your partner transport you to the destination in a few seconds or so. It's all small stuff in the end but it's the icing on the cake for me.
Hopefully you can see why this game is so special to me. I believe this game still doesn't get the recognition it deserves but it's great to see more and more people are experiencing this gem. It's definetly not perfect but I believe this is a game that needs to be placed in a "try this game before you die" list. Writing this review... I suddenly have the urge to revisit Los Angeles. Rating 9/10.

[Pros]

[Cons]
-Didi..........shut the f*ck up. At first you where ok girl, I really liked you, but after 1 hour, your voice become irritating to my nerves....I really wished the main character had a voice so I had a break from Didi's yapping.
-The shadows of the characters needed more work. This sound strange, but when you notice that the shadows don't move their lips [except Didi] and their hands movements sometimes are lifeless [except Didi again], you will understand my nitpick.
-The controls are ok.....but at some point if you are not precise with your movements, you will see yourself jump back and forth from a shadow without wanted to do it. At some point I wanted to pass a moving gear while I was a shadow, but every time I wanted to move, I became normal and fall down.........20 times I think.....f*ck.
-The story is ok, but not something very exciting. I was more interested in the extras, than the main story with the exception the ending.
-Very short game. I finished in less 3 hours.
-Very unsatisfying. Being a very short game, it let you with a desire to learn more about this world. I hope for a sequel to cover my curiosity for some details I wanted to learn.
[Final Thought]
I really liked this game, even with the some frustrations I had while playing it.
However because the game is very short and a not very interesting story, I suggest you buy it when it get cheaper.
With that said, I hope for a sequel for this game. Good work.

Im writing this review after finishing Metro 2033 and then Last Light, both on Survival and Ranger modes.
My initial impression of Last Light was it felt like little more than a stand alone expansion and right off the bat felt slighted in that my choice at the end of Metro 2033 in no way mattered in Last Light (at least if you got the Enlightend ending). I was quickly frustraited by a overall lack of improvement in the game itself, a few weapons were added and even fewer enemies were introduced, combined with inconsitant hit boxes and a infuriating abuse of invisible walls would have doomed a lesser game to the crapshoot department.
However Metro 2033 Last Light is not a lesser game, though I felt even on survival mode I wasnt lacking for supplies untill I reached the Swamp region, where filters became a issue and then the catacombs where bullets were in short supply (I killed the rhino with my last throwing knife) so as a result for me the game didnt really get interesting untill about midway through. It is suprisingly long, I did fewer chapter restarts in Last Light than I did in Metro 2033 but still took me about 23 hours to beat. If you enjoyed the first game, you'll probably enjoy this one as well even with its frustraiting issues so I recommend it.
Pros:
Longer than the original Metro 2033
More involving story, if cliche and moves at a breakneck speed sometimes
Throwing knives are still a enjoyable thing

Cons:

Breasteses, complete with nipples - bad for younger players
Arena style boss or wave fights hurt the already confined maps
Inexplicable appearence of objects that are easily shot through
Train fight with all (empty) cardboard box like objects for cover
Very low replay value

This is both a review for Halo Wars Definitive Edition, as well as what I think it means if more Halo games came to Steam.
Halo Wars. On PC. I freaked out when I found out - 20 bucks for the original game, improved graphics (...sorta), plus all the original DLCs.
I got chills when I opened the game. Hearing that amazing soundtrack - one of the best put into a Halo game to date - oh boy, it gave me the memories when I played it on the Xbox 360. The good old days, when you had games like this to play every now and again, and have a copy of Halo 3 or Halo Reach lying around to play splitscreen with your friends when they come over to your house. This game is without reasonable doubt worth the 20 bucks. Great value for a great game. Story is the same as it always is, with some of the - if not the best - cinematics put into a Halo game. Story lasts a good 6-7 hours. which is a nice lengthy campaign for a Real Time Strategy game. Overall, it's good to see a classic return.
8.5/10
And I would like to see me. Much. much more. *cough* Halo 3 Remastered *cough*
Now that I got that out of the way, what do I think about Halo games coming to Steam? Do I want to see more? Absolutely. But only certain games. To me, the games that feature The Master Chief, (Halo CE, Halo 2, Halo 3, Halo 4, Halo 5) should remain an Xbox Exclusive. That is because he is Microsofts FPS man. That deserves it to remain on console. But...for the games that don't feature The Master Chief? They would be a new revolution for Steam. Halo 3: ODST would make a warm welcome to Steam. Halo Wars 2 may even be welcomed. But I'm wanting the big Halo. The Best Halo. Halo Reach. A game with such good maps, gamemodes, customization, and creativity would become a new Bestseller. Halo Reach wouldn't be a Halo game on Steam. It would be THE Halo game on Steam. And if that day comes, which it could, but may not, then I will be the happiest person in the universe.

This is a floaty platformer, much like Trine or Limbo, though there were many times I either missed jumps or fell during platforming because the "Rush" move didn't work or over shot my jump. The game gives an impression of a simple indie platformer, and for the most part it is, but there were so many instant-death moments in the game that wore thin after the 20th time. I got to a point where I had to save "Fred the Knight" in a "shadow story telling" sequence and the game straight up crashed when the dragon's fire hit Fred. I'm not sure if it was supposed to Kill Fred or activate some sequence or cutscene, but the game immediately locked up my PC for a solid 15 seconds (I was sure to need a Hard reboot soon), then Windows came back up and shown that I was disconnected from Steam. Again, I don't know if that disconnect triggered some sort of glitch (maybe it was about to register an achievement, but I was offline and the game crashed),  but thanks to the irritating checkpoint system, the game took me back to the start of the level, requiring me to walk all the way back to the area and replay the entire sequence again. Mind you, there were two other story telling sequences I had to complete before then. Plus, earlier in the game, I got stuck in level geometry and had to restart from my last save. To my surprise, it damn near restarted the whole level and lost all my progress in the part of the circus that I was trying to repair. The death at the dragon was the final straw for me and I lost all interest in playing this.
I'm sure other, less demanding gamers can get enjoyment out of this, and honestly, I want to see more of the story, so I will watch the remainder on Youtube. Unless you absolutely adore what is going on here, I suggest you do the same. Value your time and money. I bought this on a deep discount for $3.74, but I could have done without doing so.

Lumino City is a game that instantly grabs the attention with its unique, imaginative art style. The price tag is undoubtedly steep, but it is attached to a rather long game with a plethora of surprisingly difficult puzzles.
In 2011, a game called Lume awed its audience with its fun and creative art design, filmed entirely at a hand-made paper and cardboard house. It took years for to finally get a sequel, but a single glance tells why: the game takes place in an entire city now, crafted with even more detail. Just building this set probably took years, and it’s a marvel of architectural design and crafting.
Great art style alone wouldn’t make a game though, as Lume painfully proved it. So we finally get a full-fledged puzzle adventure with a huge number of unique brain twisters. They share one fallacy of Lume, sadly: none of them are ever explained, so sometimes it is a task to figure out the basic mechanics before any attempt can be made at the solutions themselves.
This problem is present in the levels too. There are no hot spots, so most of the game time is spent clicking frantically to finally find that one interactive pixel that holds the key of progress. Sure, this turns Lumino City into an old-school puzzle game that doesn’t hold the player’s hand, but it also makes game mechanics feel dated and frustrating, preventing us from fully immersing ourselves in the magical atmosphere of the scenery.

Original, beautiful, seamless, fun. Contrast is everything you could want from an indie game. It breaks the mold of puzzle games and RPGs alike and blends them into a cohesive, immersive, fantastical world. There is never a dull moment in Contrast. This might be my favorite indie game of all time.

I bought this game back somewhere between late 2012 and the middle of 2013. The combat was excellent; probably one of the best melee systems I've seen in a game - and that was only bolstered by the fact that the gore was brutally fantastic.  It was ineffably satisfying to hack someone's arm off with a huge, heavy two-handed axe and then come back around with another swing while they're still clutching at their socket and take their head off. Combat was heavy and precise, the maps were cool, and the music was pretty good. So why am I not recommending it?
You'll remember I bought this game late 2012-mid 2013. Basically nothing has changed about this game since then; there's been a few miscellaneous tweaks and fixes, but there's nothing
. No new maps, no new weapons, no new music; they never fixed the fact that you can't change the time limit on your own dedicated server, so you have to deal with the map trying to switch itself every ten minutes. Also, something changed about the combat along the way; I can't exactly pinpoint it, but it doesn't feel as fluid and responsive as it used to.
At some point they decided to stop making big, important changes and additions to the game and start implementing new helmets, and new armors, and new weapons skins. Cool! So what's the catch? The catch is that you absolutely cannot acquire
of these by legitimately paying the game. See that fancy helmet? That'll be $5. See that cool skin for your zweihander? That'll be another $5. There's so many microtransactions in this game that I wouldn't be surprised if it was possible to drop over $100 on all this superfluous, superficial stuff that doesn't really make a difference to the overall experience. I understand TB has to make money, but there should be much more to every update than just more skins you can purchase and a few tweaks - it's pretty ridiculous at this point.
It's sad to see the game go this way, as I made some great memories with this game and enjoyed the experience, and I'd say I got my money's worth; but I'd probably unbuy it if I could. They even put out a Deadliest Warrior DLC, and I abstained from buying it since I knew it was just going to be abandoned as well.
If you're new and you're reading this review and you're considering purchasing this game, I'm not here to dissuade you. Chivalry is an excellent experience and still has some of the best melee combat I've ever seen in a game, and I've definitely had my fair share of good times with it. But if you're buying it and you expect the current core experience to grow and evolve, absolutely do not buy this. It hasn't changed in the past two years, and I suspect it never will.
Big improvement on the last game; just needs to sort out the myopic camera in battles and make the tech tree clearer to complete it.

Really great game.
+GUI is fantastic, the planets feel awesome, exploration feels cool, and findings unique planets with unique resources then colonizing them is fun and worthwhile.
+The space battles, while visually boring after a while, are interesting in the unique mechanics that go into them. The outcome is not always a sure thing, weapons and tactics matter, though not always in a predictable way that you can take advantage of.
+The economy system is solid.
+Diplomacy is unique
+There's events and lore to keep you interested.
+The factions all have unique playstyles
+The Vodyani
+Victory endings have cutscenes
-Some of the events aren't done. Specfically, the massive galaxy-wide conflict hinted at in the pathfinders trailer isn't done.
-Victory feels hollow. Its better than stellaris but still feels generic.
-The game is kind of easy on normal difficulty, and I personally hate giving the AI bonuses as a way to increase difficulty. You will be swimming in resources and have super-deathstar-destroyers and planetcrackers by halfway into the game, you will snowball hard, and you will snowball fast
-Balancing is not there
-While the factions are unique, the faction quests are all kind of samey.
-The game constantly gives you "choices,", but beyond flavor and role playing there is never any meaning to them. The story quests will never branch, and the minor quests are either balanced so it doesn't matter which choice you pick or unbalanced in which case you can only pick one.
-There isn't much to do with the diplomacy past a certain point, you don't need anything from the AI other than to declare war on them when you get bored
-The heroes feel less like people and more like stat containers. Its just an optimization game of which stats to pick and whether to make them governors or commanders
-There isn't a good way to predict how your fleet power actually compares to other player's based on tech. The predicted power balance the game gives you can be way off sometimes, and the AI doesn't understand that it needs to stop building more ships and research more tech instead
-The AI is not very good. Not only strategically, but optimization wise its builds leave it lagging behind you economically
-Government types feel hollow. Pick democracy if you dont need to change your leading party and want more laws, or dictatorship if you really need those laws from a group you don't have support for
-While the factions do play differently, at the end of the day, it doesn't matter since if you play peaceful by turn 100 you will have the most powerful and advanced fleet in the universe, which you can then use to walk over all the "militarist" empires that have no tech and all the "industrial" empires that have no pops (this could just be ecology being OP).
-There isn't a good justification for why I have heroes from different races willing to fight for me while I genocide their home planets
-Mercs are terrible and basically unusable
-Rebels spawn weird ships types since they pick from your templates
++This is a great company and they work really hard on their games. The updates are free, not DLC, and they're actively supporting their product. The endless universe is worth getting into.++

As you might notice from a lot of recent reviews, L.A. Noire is currently unplayable on Windows 10 64bit, and perhaps other operating systems too.
I tried all the fixes out there, checked the integrity of .NET framework (both 3.5 and 4), have latest upgrades and drivers installed. Compatibility modes, run game as administrator, run Steam as administrator, reinstall, check game cache, everything. Nothing worked.

Cute, short game. Lumino City is a point and click adventure with about 15 areas with about 30 puzzles. You can finish the game in about 5 to 10 hours.
Pro: The game is a work of art, in the literal sense: the world in which the adventure takes place, Lumino City, is hand-crafted from card board. It was filmed with motion control camera, and the main character was digitally added in the scenes. The world feels engaging and environment rich (many books in shelves can be examined and have actual content).
Pro: I enjoyed the puzzles, they were fun, and reasonably simple. I did use the Handyman book a few times, and the level of hints was good. The interface is intuitive and minimalistic, which works well for this game.
Con: As with most adventure games, the ending is pretty abrupt and slightly disappointing -- it's the journey that counts, and that's where Lumino City delivers. The linear storyline seems secondary to the puzzles.
I would recommend this game for it's engaging story, and well-executed puzzles. A few puzzles where too simple for me, some a bit frustrating, but the handybook proved helpful in those cases. Given the lenght of this game, I would expect a price point of about €10. I would recommend picking it up in a bundle or on sale.

Contrast is an enjoyable experience all around.

Wargame: EE is what RUSE should have been in the first place: a game that focuses on massive, accurate-to-scale battlefields, a diverse roster of units to choose from, and realistic tactics.  There's no basebuilding, no offsite artillery or airstrikes, no fancy RUSE cards - all you get are the units you spawn in and what you call in as reinforcements.  The units handle rather realistically too - many of the units have the strengths and weaknesses they have in real-life.
Keep in mind though, it's not completely realistic.  Some abstractions were made for the sake of balance, a good example being the supply units.  Any type of supply unit and repair, refuel, and rearm anything on the field, until it runs out of supply points.
Overall, if you're tired of the typical base-building RTSes or games that are more about your APM/ build orders, then you'd definately find the game to be a fun change of pace.

I will give you the too long didn't read right up front. This game is amazing, and it is definitely worth it even at the $60 value.
I purchased this game quite some time ago to play with some friends, and it is the first alpha game I can say did exactly what an alpha should do. Which is constantly update, add content, and actually become a full release title. After trying stomping lands, savage lands, dayz, the forest, and a few others, I can gladly say that ARK is leagues ahead of any alpha game I have seen in terms of content and gameplay.
Over the years this game has gone through it's ups and downs in essentially every aspect of the game. PVP and PVE have suffered and flourished throughout the life of ARK. There are plenty of reviews from people with hundreds of hours worth of gameplay that will shoot out a negative review at the first sight of any speed bump. The biggest ones were of course the DLC scorched earth, the fliers nerf, and the price hike.
When scorched earth came out, the game was still not technically released, but still had easily a couple hundred hours of gameplay for even the casual player. If you got into it, you put in a lot more. Content and patches were being released regularily (still is), but I guess players wanted a concrete point where the game was officially released. I am pretty sure around scorched earth that I had around 800 hours into the game at that point. Those hours include PVE, PVP, on official and non-official, with and without mods. I was against the DLC at first like everyone else seemed to be, but I held my reservations. I played scorched earth, and it was a fantastic addition to the game. We had the original map, a couple third party maps including the center, and now we had scorched earth, which was essentially hard mode. It's safe to say that the drama regarding those reviews should be ignored, but you should watch some gameplay videos and try the game for yourself.
Another hammer dropped was the fliers nerf. This absolutely sucked, but their reasoning behind it made sense. They slowed the speed of fliers to essentially aid in PVP and to reduce lag on servers from people speeding across maps. You are no longer able to put points into the movement speed of your fliers to make them go faster. Each flier will have it's own base speed and that is it. This can be turned off on non-official servers, but I am afraid on official you will have to make due. If you have never played the game before this nerf, it won't bother you, and it is not that bad as players made it out to be. In regards to PVP, people used to level speed on pteranodons and fly around in circles super fast to pick people off of other fliers and ground mounts in PVP. It was extremely difficult to shoot someone going that fast, and I believe it has made PVP a lot better.
Now for the final drama I will discuss the price hike. When officially released on consoles the price of the game jumped from $30 to $60. I got it for $30, so I am not one to complain on this regard but you have to understand why a company would do this. Manufacturing and distribution costs a lot of money, and a lot of the extra cost would go into that. People pay $30 for alpha games, but pay $60 for AAA full release titles that can get you 20 hours of gameplay if you pray a lot. I can tell you that if you remotely get into this game, you will enjoy it for as many hours as a AAA game could ever give you.
In conclusion, there are many pros and cons you can squeeze out this game, but when you read reviews, keep in mind how many hours someone ♥♥♥♥♥ing has in the game. For example, if you see someone saying, "my dinosaurs died because I don't know how to whistle them and developers never fixed it," and they have 500 hours in the game; you can assume they're full of♥♥♥♥♥♥ As always read reviews and watch some gameplay yourself to determine if you should spend $60 on this game or wait for a sale. In my opinion, it is worth every penny.

Contrast is a good game for people who are just starting out in the puzzle genre, but the more experienced puzzlers will not face any big challenges when playing this game.
The shadow mechanic is interesting and the puzzles are fun, but there aren't very many and they aren't hard either. I was expecting something more and a lot harder. The larger puzzles still only take a few minutes to solve. If you're looking for a real puzzle game, you will be dissapointed.
However, the atmosphere of the game is great: the puzzles tie in nicely with the story, the collectibles (documents and photos) are actually worth collecting, as they add some background to the story and the story is quite funny at times.
If you're looking for a challenge, this game probably isn't for you. If you're looking for a nice story with a bit of player interaction, you'll most likely enjoy this. However, I'd suggest you wait 'til the game is on sale, as you'll easily play through it in under 4 hours.
In short: Are you looking for a good story? Get this when it's on sale, it's very enjoyable but too short! Are you mainly interested in puzzles? Better look for a more dedicated puzzle game.

1 word: LOVELY.
This game truly is a piece of art, the most charming game I’ve ever played. The artwork is gorgeous and simulates a surreal, detailed world in an atmosphere similar to France in the 1920's. The soundtrack is also amazing and fits the game and environment perfectly. Contrast is overall quite original, from the shadow-shifting between two different worlds to the special artistic style.
It takes about 5 to 6 hours to complete. You could think this is rather short, but the delightful artwork really makes up for it. This game really is a story-driven experience, so if you're not into this, maybe this isn't really the kind of game for you.
I really like the story and the characters. They did a great job on the voice acting. The story is touching, lovely and well thought out, kind of mysterious due to the two different worlds. In the end, I still don’t really know which one’s “real” and which one isn’t.
The puzzles are special because of the shadow-shifting mechanism. Each puzzle is different, fun and challenging, not repetitive in my opinion.
Sometimes the game's a bit buggy, like the shadow-shifting mechanism between 3D and 2D at certain moments. The camera can also be a bit buggy and clumsy sometimes, but it doesn’t ruin the game.
Something you need to know: you can't change the controls. The game works with a QWERTY-setting, so keep this in mind. You can also play this with a controller, which I think suits the overall controls better. I still have to try this, though.
If it’s in sale, buy this immediately. Totally worth it.

This game is - just as pretty much any game in the Endless series - a rather unique gem. One of the things that always stood out as unique to me is how the races play out, instead of just giving you some numerical boni and mali like "Race has a X% higher ressource yield" the races here actually matter as each and everyone has a truly uinique feel to them, from the Vodyani, who are unable to colonize planets and instead reside on Arks to the Unfallen who have to entangle a system with galactic vines before being able to colonize it each race has some mechanic that makes it stand out from the rest.

From a gameplay perspective, Lumino City isn't all that unique. It's more-or-less your standard point-and-click adventure game. Get items, and then use them to solve puzzles. But visually, it is unlike anything I've ever seen. Every scene was carefully built and lighted, and the result is truly something to behold.
There is one gameplay element that bears mentioning, since it's the first of its kind I've seen in an adventure game. Right at the start, the solutions to all of the puzzles (or at the very least, some extremely helpful hints) are given to you in a book entitled "The Handymanual." The catch is that, despite there only being 30-or-so puzzles in the game, the book is about 1000 pages long. You can use the table of contents to find the page your looking for, but the page number is written as a simple arithmetic expression based on the scene the puzzle appears in (for example: 5+2*the number of flags on the boat). For those of us who are terrible at adventure games, this is a godsend, as it allows us to progress through the game without having to turn to outside walkthroughs, and the small amount of work required to get the solution from the Handymanual is enough to make us at least try to figure out the solution on our own first.
Additionally, the writeups for many of the solutions in the Handymanual contain little, charmingly-written bits of story that relate to the puzzle in question, so looking up a solution leads to a little bit of additional engagement with the world, rather than the feeling of stupidity over not being able to solve the puzzle one one's own.
If you hate adventure games, then this one probably isn't for you. But if you enjoy them at all, I'd highly reccomend picking it up - it's just so damn pretty.
Oh, and the music is great too.

If you're looking for a survival horror fps that is extremely realistic, and I REALLY mean it, then you'd love this game. Settings adjust well to run smoothly on your device. Awesome graphics, very realistic again: everything from having to wipe mud and blood off your mask to realistic stealth (true stealth in this game can only be acquired through, well, nothing... just as in real life). You can get pnumatic weapons that are fairly quiet, but hit something metal and shazam. You also have to manage your gas mask filters when in iradiated areas. You scavenge for supplies and are always looking for "extra" passages and side-tunnels to find new things, though you always have to fight hard for something good. Health does NOT regenerate, you must find first aid supplies. If you run out of filters and are in an iradiated area, you begin to suffocate. First heavy, labored breathing, then a little weezing, then choking and blurred vision. You get the picture. Uses choice-based progressively-developing gameplay... in other words, the choices you make in-game effect how you proceed, giving the game practically endless replayability. It runs very smoothly and the aesthitics are awesome. Back to the progressively-generated gameplay, nothing happens exactly the same twice. period. There is a little bit of a learning curve, but if you have played games like Halo or Elder Scrolls games, you will find the controls somewhat familiar. Definitely NOT like COD, though it does combine some Halo-esk aspects with the mask and the First-person view, though it's closer to Skyrim with the whole suvival and scavenge approach. It brings in the most elements from the Fallout games though, with regards to the survival aspect. And, due to the whole post-apocolyptic scenario, definitely sci-fi. Great game all-in-all, definitely most immersive I've ever played. Recommend 10/10, which is saying something from a guy who typically heavily criticizes FPS games. This is one of the only, if not the only, FPS I would outright recommend. AND BY THE WAY, IT'S 50% OFF ON STEAM RIGHT NOW... just sayin.

Pros:

Cons:
- The car driving system is mostly like GTA and its very hard to control. There's literally no FPS view and its hard to chase after another car, even if your partner is there and you cant switch.
- No jump feature which makes you hard to jump on small objects, like gta could easily does.
- No replay of investigation if you failed four interrogative questions. (you could exit and load the game again to restart, but its troublesome to do)

As with most reviews, this is steeped heavily in personal opinion and not much else, but here goes:
Today, this game is mediocre. But it was kinda good once.
48~ of my 56 some odd hours in this game were spent in 2012 when this game first hit Steam. It was fun back then; not great, but still entertaining. But most importantly, there was a huge opportunity for improvements in the coming years, which I was very keen to see (and still have yet to).
The most recent 8~ hours I've played have been far below the expecations I had for progress made in 3 whole years of development; really, if anything, the current state of the game is a straight
from the 2012 iteration. Hit detection issues have against all odds gotten worse, almost all the combat exploits are still here, the community has gotten
worse, and it seems like very little new content exists now that didn't exist 3 years ago. I mean, I guess the new menus and hats are nice, oh and you can change your armor color to confuse people by obscuring what was previously a clean "red vs blue" combat environment, but...
The array of weaponry, for example, seems identical. Sure, you have a bunch of reskins for real $$, but they're functionally identical to weapons which already existed 3 years ago. I can understand why adding more weapons just for the sake of more weapons is a recipe for disaster balance-wise, but really guys? Three whole trips around the sun and nothing?
The minority community of insular elitists has somehow blossomed since 2012, and what's worse is that it seems the developers only cater to this demographic when updating the game. This is why flat-out exploits like mouse dragging or bunny-hopping during sword fights still exist: long-time players have been using these as a crutch for so long that making the game work
hasn't even been considered.
Additionally, the populated servers all seem to suffer from high degrees of what I call "Garry's Mod-itis", where server admins go on power trips and break their own server rules pretty much constantly. A catastrophic lack of maturity is a recurring theme.
The most positive thing I can say about this game is that the tutorial is really well designed, probably one of the more content-rich tutorials I've encountered. It's too bad that the majority of the stuff you learn in it can be safely thrown out the window once you actually start playing multiplayer, because of the aforementioned exploits completely eclipsing all other strategies.
I guess what I'm trying to say is: if you want to play a melee-only TF2/Enemy Territory-style objective game that is completey mired in a cluster♥♥♥♥ of exploit-dominated playstyles, where new content drips in at a rate of 2-hats-per-year, and whose community of server mods/admins make Hitler look like a sensible and level-headed dude (come on, you know Godwin's Law had to fit in here somewhere), then dive right in.
But if you're looking for an even semi-realistic portrayal of medieval combat in a multiplayer videogame, with deep but rational gameplay and a mature community, and furthermore whose developers actively develop it to
its gameplay and appeal, rather than sheltering and encouraging a vocal minority of elitist shitheels who can't function without garbage exploits, then you'll need to look elsewhere.

The game?  Fantastic.
It's almost like Medieval: Total War without the battlefield maps, but with the world map politics/trade/alliances/plots on steroids.  Seriously near perfect.
If you are a fan of the "A Song of Ice and Fire" series by George R.R. Martin, the ASoIaF mod for this game is the absolute BEST thing you will probably ever get to play based on the series.
Political alliances, beneficial marriages, assassinations, wars, tournaments, adultary, family feuds, basically anything you could think of that would affect a family dynasty in medieval-type settings comes into play here.
Spend 10 years educating and training your first born son to be a perfect heir to your lands?  Sorry, one of your rivals just successfully arranged for a servant to poison him, leaving you with no male heirs to carry on your name.  Arrest him, fabricate evidence of treason, or set in motion plans to assassinate him in kind.  If you're really feeling devious, send agents to begin making false claims on his lands and titles, give it a few years, then go to war, take his lands, and banish him to the Wall, or even just let him rot in prison or execute him and his family (Lannister vs. Reyne style), and wipe his legacy from the world entirely.
So many things to do.  It's insane.
I don't think I've even played more than a few hours of the standard game, the mod is done so well.
They update CONSTANTLY, as well, so any game patches that are released result in at most a few days delay before the next hotfix.
Seriously, if you love the book series, pick up this game and the mod.  The sheer number of "what if" scenarious that you can come up with and play out are mind-boggling.
I give this game a 9.5/10 for that alone.

The game creator's obvious finesse for miniature models and photography is inevitably its most charming and rewarding element. Impeccable, colourful and highly stylized hand-made environments are a marvel to scrutinize and truly are the game's biggest appeal by far. The detail and quality of interior scenes is especially fascinating. An extremely pleasing and consistent art style, coupled with inspired and inspiring vintage graphic design make the presentation a positively successful accomplishment.
Lumino City presents itself as a puzzle adventure game, though its adventure elements are curtailed by filler dialogues and bland characters. The game's simplistic story briefly comes to life at the very end, where events are finally explained, but is otherwise almost entirely absent. Many characters exhibit a certain uneasiness or idiocy that fracture the lively mood created by the beautiful environments. As such, it is mostly a collection of puzzles strung together linearly without greater purpose.
Unfortunately, many of these puzzles overuse the same basic ideas: the photo booth switches, lightmill mirrors and garden balloon machine are all based on the same model. Likewise, the purposely awkward mechanical controls for the dome crane and fish tank pump are essentially the same puzzle with a different presentation. There are also two nearly identical gears puzzles at the moving city maintenance panel and at the mayor's house.
Though some of the puzzles are actually very enjoyable to solve, few exhibit the ingenuity of a comparable game like
and instead often feel derivative.
The game comes with a very clever hint system where the player must first decipher simple equations to get to the right page of a particularly detailed and well crafted book. However, hints are often ruined by offering straight out solutions instead of clever clues to sharpen the player's logic.
Lumino City seldom acknowledges attempts to interact with the environment unless it is scripted into the next puzzle. For instance, a hungry character is expecting a can opener to eat a meal, but offering him a perfectly delicious bun produces no reaction. The game literally ignores the player's proposed solution and simply sends the bun back into the inventory.
As such, there is little incentive to explore, except when it comes to perusing through dozens of finely detailed book excerpts, vibrant leaflets and posters that clearly demonstrate the creator's mastery of stylish vintage graphic design. That so much effort was invested into something that serves no actual purpose clearly illustrates the designers' focus on presentation over substance. The game is undeniably very pretty but feels a little hollow.
The game performs in buggy execution with the main character occasionally warping out of place unpredictably and frequent game crashes. Knowing which objects are interactive is sometimes only a guess.
The game's audio is serviceable though not especially memorable. Lack of spoken dialogue is sorely missed as there is no way to play back missed text. Bothersome typos can be spotted throughout.
Inventory mainly consists in picking up one or two items at a time, almost always immediately usable and just as soon disposed automatically. A single lemon carries over from start to finish to solve an easy final puzzle. There is thankfully no need to backtrack and nothing can be missed.
Ultimately, the game itself is nowhere as interesting as how it was made. It nevertheless is so spectacularly crafted that it still deserves to be played, or at the very least looked at, if not thoroughly enjoyed. Just be aware of its shortcomings to avoid disapointment, and make sure to get it on sale only.

6 Months after release....
So, I chose not to review this game immediately after release. It felt like it needed more time in Early Access, as it still had numerous bugs, some game breaking, and overall felt somewhat unpolished. I saw the core of a good game, and I did enjoy it, but decided to shelve it for a while.
Now, 6 months later, what is the state of the game?
Better. Much better, but by no means perfect. The game breaking bugs are gone, at least for me, the factions quests are more polished, and they have overhauled the Approval system and Diplomacy quite a bit. I've still had a few quest glitches, but they are mostly trivial.  And with those out of the way, I've had more fun than ever with the game. It's ambitious but flawed, but the unique factions provide a ton of replayability. The political system and random quests really make you feel like your empire is a collection of various groups and interests, which adds to the game. While I enjoyed the simplicity of the original Endless Space, ES2 adds on that enough to add more immersion and a new appreciation for the scale of your empire. Even the new Overcolonization system makes your choice of which systems to settle more meaningful.
Overall, the progress I've seen in the last 6 months of work on this game give me hope that it will continue to grow even better in the future. Highly recommended, especially for fans of the original.

Very fun and interesting game with a lot of depth. Not without issues, but it's a great idea executed well.
There are a variety of playstyles, and within those playstyles it's possible to further customize precise aspects with weapon choices. The weapon unlocking mechanic encourages experimentation and practice, giving you time to master the various weapons and playstyles.
Some balancing issues; weapons with long reach are very difficult to fight against. Dodging is a bit spotty, and the extreme deadliness of some weapons renders the extra health of tanky enemies frequently null.
But all in all, it's a great game that rewards skillful play, attention to detail, and patience. Highly recommended if you're looking for a new multiplayer fix.

Great game!  This game is a story-rich, highly stylized, puzzle platformer.  It's main mechanic is changing from 3D platforming and shadow shifting into 2D platforming (as well as using the shadows to move things like boxes and balls that you also shift into the 2D shadow world).  It tells the story of a little girl and her doting father and mother (as well as a quirky magician) as the doting father tries to win his way back into his mother's graces (with you and the daughter's help).
I really enjoyed the mechanics.  Although they are spotty and inconsistent sometimes (but they did this all with the Unreal Engine, which is amazing work in my opinion), but the vast majority of the time they work perfectly fine.  The music is great too!  If you like "video games as art," this is definitely one of them.

In comparison to the first game, I cannot recommend Endles Space 2. Get the first game instead.
While ES2 definitely has its good sides, it also comes with half a dozen of things it just doesn't have compared to the prdecessor, especially in regards to combat. For example:
You are severely limited in your ship designs. They only have a few slots in which you can fit some of the not exactly numerous options of this category. You want a tank-ship designed to take hits? It's not going to be any tougher than the rest and in order to make the ai target it, you have to put a special component into your already very few slots. Your options for tactics are extremely limited, you can split your fleet in combat into multiple battle groups, but there was no way to see what these actually do, because EVERY single battle ends already on long distance.
Smaller ship hulls have literally 0 advantages over bigger ones and their difference in power is far beyond extreme. It can't be that my fleet with 3 medium ships focused on damage with tech 3 modules got only one third of the defense and less than a fifth of the firepower of one large ship with the first modules in the game and only rockets - The weapon system with the second-lowest DPS!
Oh yeah, there are also only 3 hull sizes and 6 hulls in total...
A friend of mine also noticed some glitches with his dust-income. Without an active event or any other apparent cause, it went extremely low from one turn to another. Had he not been in this glorious and generous alliance named "Popopiraten", this may well have ended the game for him there.
But I like the new ground battle system.

Thanks for the free weekend.
That said, keep in mind this is a 'first impression' as I only got about 4 hours of game play (after deducting menus, loading and staggering).
----
The game is gorgeous... though dropping the settings didn't aleviate load times or chopping (previewing systems and such).
I admit though, my computer is old - though it was my RAM that gave me trouble. If your system has a total of 8GB RAM or less, you'll probably have trouble.
It also took my computer about 10 minutes to recover enough for me to be able to reboot it to clear the RAM so I could do anything else after playing.
One more note... the fancy hero system or whatever... I clicked on that without knowing. My whole computer froze up for over 30 minutes while trying to prepare to show the hero base thing. Total time before I could play again after clicking that was at least 45 minutes. Luckily, I am patient... and played on my DS while checking on it from time to time.
----
On to the game play. In the 6 hours (more like 5 after discounting menus, loading and chopping), I found that there is a lot of information... most of which I either didn't know what to do with or didn't think was needed.
The makeup of the planet (core, surface, atmosphere, gravity) was cool... but I didn't understand if I needed to know this stuff or if it was just flavour.
And then, while I was doing various things... I felt like information I wanted wasn't available. For example, does a leader assigned to a planet need their ship upgraded? Will they help in any combat?
----
As for the turorials... they felt a little random.
There were a couple times I opened a screen and did stuff, figuring it out... then a couple turns later it would tell me to open that screen and do stuff.
There were a few tutorials that had me open something to check it out and asked me to do something that I thought was a bad idea for my situation... or was something I couldn't do so there was no reason to be learning it yet.
----
Controls... well, I love using my keyboard. If I can hit a key instead of clicking an icon, I will. It would be nice if hovering over a button would tell me the key that will activate that. For example, the Num-Enter will end turn... but regular Enter wil open... um... chat? Not sure that that is... I should have tried saying hi or something in it.
And some other controls that would be great to include would be stuff like the arrow keys being able to scroll around the tech tree. Every time I opened the tech tree, I instinctively hit the arrow keys to try and move around to what I wanted to check... but nothing happened.
----
Summary.
While ES2 is gorgeous and looks like it might have some good story telling... I think it is easier to play ES1 (both for my computer and for the UI). It also made me want to play EL again... mainly because I knew what the equipment customization was actually doing for my heroes/units in EL.
If my gaming budget opens up again, I may actually get this game properly... but for now I don't have money to throw at lovely art that will take external research (wiki) to understand.

The differences  between Metro 2033 to Metro 2033 Redux are significant while the differences between Metro: Last Light and Metro: Last Light Redux are unfortunately miniscule and in some cases, non-noticeable. I personally purchased this game for some easy achievements but that's not to say I didn't enjoy what I experienced. However, I feel there's a bit to praise and criticise 4A Games on with this product.
● Enhanced lighting. This time around Metro: Last Light has been brightened and it now features lens flares! Whether it's for the better, that's up to you to decide!
● Many textures in Metro: Last Light Redux have been slightly enhanced. However, this enhancement will not be noticeable unless you're running the graphical settings on Very High.
● Enemies are now more responsive to light and sound. If you fall from a high place or turn off a light, expect an enemy to investigate.
● The addition of safes. Hidden throughout the game are safes with corresponding keys. These safes contain a variety of items including ammunition, military grade ammunition, grenades, throwing knives, etc.
● The ability to approach a combat situation in multiple ways. Sneaking, knock out kills, use of silencers, and using the darkness to sneak up on enemies. It may seem silly and common knowledge but many games in the current gaming industry fail to deliver anything more than just a watered down run and gun experience.
● The new A.I. combat subroutines are irritating yet innovative. If you're approaching a combat situation guns blazing be prepard for some jumpy, trigger happy enemies.
● The achievement progress saving system. In the original Metro: Last Light, progress was saved in a consecutive playthough. This time around you can reload checkpoints to accumulate kills, unlock safes, filter air time, burn cobwebs and unscrew light bulbs.
● No unsynced voice and facial animations. Although a little wonky, the facial animations and voice are never unsynced from start to finish. That's certainly saying something considering the majority of the games created today have the issue with unsynced facial animations.
● No 'in-game' store. The majority of developers feel the need to put a direct link to their game's downloadable content within the game itself. This angers some consumers while ruining the immersion they're trying to create.
● Non-existant NPC eye tracking. I never realized how important eye tracking was before I played the Metro series. Almost all of the NPCs in Metro: Last Light Redux feel as if they're staring off into space, unaware of their surroundings or the player.
● Copy and paste menus and user interface. The menu and user interface of Metro: Last Light Redux is the exact menu and user interface that Metro: Last Light used back in 2013.
● The watering down of achievements within the game. While they may have added 5 new achievements, they have completely gutted 28 from the game, including ones that were from once downloadable content.

Contrast is an exceptionally good game, if you enjoy what it does.
The sterotypical 12-year-old Call Of Duty player, or the stereotypical Madden-fanatic dudebro, are not going to like this game, nor are they going to understand what makes it so cool, or so fun to play.
But if you're the kind of gamer who can appreciate beautiful visuals, innovative gameplay, and a story-driven experience, Contrast is definitely worth a look.
First off, the artwork in this game is gorgeous. It's a stylized, animated style which summons up a surreal Jazz Age Paris (?). It's affecting and evocative and surprisingly detailed.
The game's shadow-shifting mechanic is novel, and the puzzles I've encountered thus far are unusual, but not frustratingly so. The story's the thing here, in the end, and the traversal puzzles and the jumping are just what you do while moving through -- and moviing forward -- the plot.
Ultimately, this is a game which tells a story. It's told mostly through cutscenes, but the voice acting is generally superior, and the writing is solid, which keeps it all interesting. As has been said, there's a vaguely Bioshock feeling to the storytelling -- there's a mystery unfolding, and a faint air of tragedy or melancholy surrounding events, as if something sad is about to occur, unless it can be outrun or outthought.
You play as the shadow-shifting "imaginary friend" of a little girl named DiDi, whose parents are on the edge of serious trouble. The game doesn't fully explain itself at the start. and certain events make you wonder if the often surreal landscape you move through is simply reality colored by a young girl's imagination or something ... else ... yet to be discovered.
The game isn't perfect, of course. The shadow-shifting mechanic doesn't always activate as intended, forcing retries of a jump puzzle sequence. Also, for Steam PC users, the controls for this game were clearly designed for consoles, so if you have a USB game controller hooked to your PC, you'll almost certainly have a better time using that.
And again, the puzzles and the narrative style of Contrast will not appeal to every gamer, but if you're intrigued, I'd say take a look.
Contrast may well be a flawed gem, in some ways, but it's still a gem. Gamers often say they want "something different" in their gaming. Here it is. Recommended.

A neat little indie with a cool gameplay hook, but Contrast falls short of its potential.  Contrast has a patchwerk story, which is incredibly unfortunate given the potential of the lore (it's visibly rushed despite a very interesting world).  I love the art style, and particularly love the 2D/3D platforming crossovers.  Contrast cleverly utilises intricate 3D world objects to affect the 2D world (to use a basic example that doesn't spoil the puzzles, dragging an item closer to the light to make the shadow on the wall bigger).  It has a 'cute' companion character and touches on some of the deeper issues surrounding families, but it only lasts about 2-3 hours on a slow playthrough.  I would say about 20-30 minutes of that focuses on the story, and the majority is spent trying to figure out the tricks for the puzzles.  Once you work them out, you could probably play from start to finish in less than an hour, without skipping.
There are two types of collectibles.  One type of collectible comes from exploring and overcoming optional puzzles, and is essentially useless outside of the few occasions you need them to progress (When you need them to progress, they're very easy to find).  The other works to build up the lore, and it's quite expansive.  These collectibles flesh out the story in much greater detail than the main storyline, but mostly they serve to highlight just how unfortunate it is that Contrast was cut short.
The pros:
An old-fashioned setting with a great accompanying visual style
Cool dynamics between 2D and 3D elements
Some deep themes around family
Clever use of mechanics in puzzles
Interesting lore
The cons:
Shallow and disjointed story, with a very rushed ending.
The majority of playtime and difficulty comes from initially working out puzzle styles
An irrelevant collection system (not referring to the lore collectibles)
The verdict:
Pick it up if you enjoy games with a sense of uniqueness, or the potential for depth (rather than depth itself).  Contrast will test your lateral thinking (though only on a few occasions), and it touches on some pretty cool concepts.

Long story short: This game is awesome. I, as a player, had a great time playing it. i enjoyed it, and don't regret for a single moment to have bought it. However for the purpouse of enlighting prospective buyers i will list the pros and cons:
-
i can't understate this enough. The kind of visuals that Tim Burton pioneered before he became a parody of himself. The music is the best the period has to offer. The world is abstract and yet historically accurate. The game portrays the feeling of the 20's like i've never seen before in fiction but also strangely a familiar, timeless story, perfectly relatable to the average player.
-The story is extremely engaging, interesting and believable despite the fantastic aspects of the game. You will love the characters, you will care and worry about them if they fall, and will feel a legitimately warm, fuzzy feeling if they succeed. The voice acting is also great, for all the characters wich are written in a way that, again, will make you remember them for a long time. Of special note is Didi: avoiding spoilers i can say that while children are hard to portray in fiction, both in building character and acting, they tend to be hit or miss (think Anakin Skywalker), she is not only very well acted but also very well written, being believable, helpful, and never annoying.
- The gameplay is great fun, engaging, the game mechanics are well developed, explained and exploited, making it fun and original, ESPECIALLY if you're a fan of old school plataformers.
-THE GAME IS SHORT. Is that simple. The collectables, tell a great story and are really cool, but they are easy to find in a single playthrough. The world is beautiful and intriguing but the game has a short lifespan, with no replay value whatsoever.
-On the gameplay point of view, the save system is kinda arbitrary. There are checkpoints wich work also as autosaves but there's no way of manually save the game, so it can be annoying if you wanna leave inmediatly and you're in the middle of a puzzle, but it is barely noticeable.
TOTALLY WORTH PLAYING, that being said, if you're strict on your wallet, and wanna make every single cent in it count, it would be wiser to wait until its lower than full price (a 25% discount would be spot on). But considering that is an indie game, made by a developer that is obviously on a budget i think the game deserves the price tag.

I played the free weekend and will be buying the game when its cheaper but thought I'd write a review incase someone finds it helpful. I'll start by saying that after an intial period of minor hatred, I did get into it. It was just a bit frustrating at the beginning and I'd say that I ended up after about 4 hours, knowing what to do and what was going on. It's probably worth saying that I'm not the largest fan of 4X, I dont dislike them by any means but I prefer RTS to turn based stratergy. It's for a bunch of little reasons but an example would be when I saw an enemy fleet hassling a star system of mine so I'd move in, only to have them move on their next turn. I understand you can retreat but we would pass each other on the star lanes and I'd not be able to do anything. Then they would start attacking another star system whilst I wait 3 turns to get to the first one, turn around and follow them. On the subject of the star lane system, I feel its a bit pointless considering that you can fly off them in a direction of any system.
So here are some of my thoughts on it:
I really like the concept, it reminded me of Star Trek (Warp drive, Federation political system, galaxy battles etc) and I think it was executed fairly well. There is a lot of variation that can be had by setting up matches and because of the way the systems work, the galaxy feels huge. I mean I have over 40 planets colonized in a relatively short space of time. My issue with that though was that the population on most will end up hating and rebelling against you despite giving them everything they want (assigning a hero can help). I think this is partly because you can't really develop much to improve their mood; I'd say something like 5% of construction and its all very early. So you will find they love you for the first 50-100 moves then begin to turn. And when they turn, its just a pain because they never win the revolt and they just keep trying. Also, the values of increased happiness mena nothing, it will say +25 for example and they will gain like 10% happiness; why use a metric that can't be accurately quantified? They also become♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥when you ask them to build anything so I just stopped building there and used infinte construction placers which would give you a perk basically, like convert industry to money or something as long as its applied on that system.
It kept me engaged and I really didn't want to get off when I got into it. There is a very strong focus on building and it does take a while. I did get to a point though where I would just focus on industry to build faster and money to avoid bankrupcy (more on that in a bit). You can focus on all these other areas but victory is done in battles and not really trade agreements. For example, I was losing forces so pulled back to defend and regain fleet numbers and the AI had blood lust in their hearts and just wanted to kill me and refused to discuss peace. I managed to form a treaty with another faction to halt nonsense assaults from that side and focus on the larger threat (btw, they offered no real benefit from the alliance except ruining my victory, but ill explain). I then started tearing through the galaxy when I could FINALLY get as many ships as them in my fleets. It was in the last upgrade in military that I could finally get some real sized fleets. They begged for a treaty 3 times but I refused because they wouldn't have it when I wanted peace and then!! my alliance partner signed it for us! So then I was in a truce with these ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s who kept telling me about how they wanted to destroy me. That was an alliance I made after they begged for peace and I took them for a bunch of their systems which was used just as a buffer incase they attacked... which they did.
Bankrupcy. Just sell the luxury items you don't need and you'll be rich. I found this was the best way to go about it otherwise the game will start selling your ships etc. You get little back from leaving a colony so I wouldn't recommend it, just leave it as a buffer for attacks.
Treaties. I found there was usually something in particular that a faction wanted, like a specific luxury that you could use to bargain. There were however people who just wanted to murder you and would do nothing but accept surrender. In this situation I did gift them 3 systems that were in their influence anyway and they came to a truce, so there are ways around.
Fleets. I didn't want to watch any battles and thankfully you can skip them. However, the battles were mainly numbers games, if you had a stronger fleet, you always win. You do have to pay attention to range of weapons and attack plans though in the later stages when you are dealing with fleet attack strengths of over 160k where it does get more tactical. Also, ground battles were so easy that they were borderline pointless, just remember that tanks will destroy infantry and planes for pre-emptive bombings are a god send (like you needed help anyway). I could have about 13 tanks absolutely decimate infantry regardless of how many, to the point where I would get tanks and have 0% infantry and only change the ratio to include air vehicles. Also, I had a massive population and conscription wasn't always available? I would have 1000s easily of people who were useless to me, just a value for no reason (at one point my max was about 15k).
Upgrades. This is where the game really drags. You can't get everything you need to win under 150 moves imo. That is unless you get the upgrade to buy out upgrades which I strongly recommend! Also, get weapons and hulls, a lot of other stuff is not really as important for victory in my experience. You could do with an upgrade to get 2 at the same time or something because my god, you just end up waiting for them and skipping so many turns because why not.
Pirates. Just please ♥♥♥♥ off. They just show up out of nowhere to annoy you. The problem is that they show up so early and theres no benefit to defeating them. They just waste turns really. Maybe they should add some bonus to victory or a gain in resources? If there is one, I didn't notice. Seems like there should be. I don't mid the idea because they would exist but execution needs to be improved.
Missions. Ha! theres no real point. You can play for missions sure, but they won't secure you victory in my experience. Just decimate everyone or be peaceful for free movement and then do them?

The differences  between Metro 2033 to Metro 2033 Redux are significant while the differences between Metro: Last Light and Metro: Last Light Redux are unfortunately miniscule and in some cases, non-noticeable. I personally purchased this game for some easy achievements but that's not to say I didn't enjoy what I experienced. However, I feel there's a bit to praise and criticise 4A Games on with this product.
● Enhanced lighting. This time around Metro: Last Light has been brightened and it now features lens flares! Whether it's for the better, that's up to you to decide!
● Many textures in Metro: Last Light Redux have been slightly enhanced. However, this enhancement will not be noticeable unless you're running the graphical settings on Very High.
● Enemies are now more responsive to light and sound. If you fall from a high place or turn off a light, expect an enemy to investigate.
● The addition of safes. Hidden throughout the game are safes with corresponding keys. These safes contain a variety of items including ammunition, military grade ammunition, grenades, throwing knives, etc.
● The ability to approach a combat situation in multiple ways. Sneaking, knock out kills, use of silencers, and using the darkness to sneak up on enemies. It may seem silly and common knowledge but many games in the current gaming industry fail to deliver anything more than just a watered down run and gun experience.
● The new A.I. combat subroutines are irritating yet innovative. If you're approaching a combat situation guns blazing be prepard for some jumpy, trigger happy enemies.
● The achievement progress saving system. In the original Metro: Last Light, progress was saved in a consecutive playthough. This time around you can reload checkpoints to accumulate kills, unlock safes, filter air time, burn cobwebs and unscrew light bulbs.
● No unsynced voice and facial animations. Although a little wonky, the facial animations and voice are never unsynced from start to finish. That's certainly saying something considering the majority of the games created today have the issue with unsynced facial animations.
● No 'in-game' store. The majority of developers feel the need to put a direct link to their game's downloadable content within the game itself. This angers some consumers while ruining the immersion they're trying to create.
● Non-existant NPC eye tracking. I never realized how important eye tracking was before I played the Metro series. Almost all of the NPCs in Metro: Last Light Redux feel as if they're staring off into space, unaware of their surroundings or the player.
● Copy and paste menus and user interface. The menu and user interface of Metro: Last Light Redux is the exact menu and user interface that Metro: Last Light used back in 2013.
● The watering down of achievements within the game. While they may have added 5 new achievements, they have completely gutted 28 from the game, including ones that were from once downloadable content.

Damn two way system...this would've been neither a thumbs up nor a thumbs down but a middle ground. It has some strong points, as well as some lesser ones. I'll see if I can post it without one to get around that pickle.
The strong points sort of sells itself on the store: the visuals and the ideas. Oh, and the voice-acting and the audio.
Theme-wise, this is a wonderful film noir kind of feel with the old stylish drama and some genuinely fitting soundtracks that perfectly fit the gameplay mechanics. Climbing the shadow of the musicians or the voice actors while they are acting their part is original to say the least. As well as having the far majority of the cast consist merely of shadows (which gives the game a strange atmosphere).
Unfortunately, while the gameplay is certainly fitting with the theme, the switching between 3rd person adventuring and 2d 'shadow' platforming doesn't quite mix that well. Despite the contrast in lighting, you sometimes have to guess where you can fade in the shadows, and sometimes you almost randomly drop out again. And rearranging lights in a 3D plane is a lot harder to properly 'aim' than in a 2D one (for those who are familiar with A shadow's tale: control was much tighter there).
I'm not so sure what to think of the plot. While the atmosphere, voices and visuals are all in place, I wasn't drawn into the game much. I partly blame the clunky controls and some glaring bugs (I encountered numerous invisible walls and pass-through walls), and partly because the far majority of the game you're just a nanny for Didi ("let's fix this! let's fix that!"), while your own role isn't explained until nearly the end (which is a shame. How am I supposed to care for the characters if I don't know what my own role in the play is to begin with?).
While contrast also has some platforming and puzzle segments, the only real meat is the storyline. It has those things, and they sort of work, but you'll push on through to get the next cutscene. And with that in mind, it should at the very least be labeled at "not bad at all". Awesome would be giving it too much credit, but it's certainly decent.
I just wish more was put into it. Bug testing. The conversations. Perhaps some extra thought for lip syncing (there is only one character who has all the monologues, but her lips seem to say something competely different).
But all in all, I'd say this is the sort of game I would give a 6.5 - 7. It's a good game. Not a great one. All in my opinion, of course. :-)

As coming from a background where I have many hours in MOO2, GAL Civ 2, 3, Endless Space 1 and Stellaris I can say with some surety that ES2 is not up to par in the 4X genre from my perspective.
BUT;
If you are someone who is new to 4X or doesn't mind the idea that you are not on an even playing field or playing a game with obtuse gameplay then ES2 is a worthy contender.
It's not a BAD game, per say. It's a disappointing game and a 'looks are deceiving' kind of game. ES2 starts off strong. It is interesting. Races are unique and give rich colour to the tapestry of space. It's pretty cool in a lot of different ways but where it faulters is in its execution. Poorly constructed AI who come out with annoying advantages, the mid-game slog of trying to get ahead while micromanagement becomes a chore and the failure of engaging the player in worthwhile diplomacy ultimately leaves me with giving ES2 a 6/10 and a not recommended.
If you like atmosphere over substance, as in immersion over engagement then ES2 is for you. Otherwise Stellaris is shaping up quite nicely to have great AI and gameplay and MOO2 is the ultimate turn based 4X game if you can get over the graphics. Gal Civ 2 offers colourful AI. Ultimately I find ES2 to be it's own creation but it only offers immersion which isn't what I am shopping for. Sorry Amplitude studios.

An excellent, fresh-feeling 4X TBS. Feels solid all around, from an expansion, military and tech perspective, but the standout features are population management and politics. Politics tend to be a secondary system in these games, providing passive boosts, with little in the way of interesting tradeoffs. Also, the politics of your empire are almost entirely under your control. In this game, the politics system feels like its own beast, with the player only able to influence the political leanings of the empire, not dictate it. The hardest, most interesting part of the one game I played was when a quest line made me pass a law from a party that was a distant fifth in my empire. I had to pull out all the stops to push them into a leading position, and it conflicted with other goals I had. It was fascinating. There's also some truly inspired sci-fi world building, with some truly wild ideas for factions. The cons I see for this game: a few minor bugs, I had one crash, and it doesn't quite escape the 4X trap of only officially winning long after you've taken control of the game. The UI is excellent overall, but there were some places where it was hard to find the information I needed.

Let me say before anything else, that this review comes as a
expert first, and a Halo fan second. Also, forgive me, but my reviews are long and exhaustive. I don’t like exposing my points too briefly, but I guess I can afford giving a TLDR:
With that in mind, I hope somebody finds the rest of my review useful.
I never played Halo Wars on Xbox before, and the PC edition here is my first experience with the game. From what I have seen so far, the game is really well made. Why? Because I’ve encountered too many RTS's which lacked a decent amount of factions, unit diversity, had few or poorly designed/not interesting technologies, etc... I have many examples I could name, but that would surely arise many debates, offend fans of said sagas and I don’t want to expose my review to a flame war. When I say RTS games often lack diversity and content I refer to games with only 3 total factions, games which have no or little unit upgrades, or games which boast only a dozen units per faction. I’ll make an exception, and mention Grey Goo as a vivid example of this. I would describe this RTS as a very classic one, comparable to what is for me the apex of this genre: the Age of Empires series(1). My reasoning is based on the following elements:
(1)I played many other strategy games, and I don’t consider the Cossacks or Battle for Middle Earth series, for instance, inferior. However AoE has some advantages over others such as the fact it has covered many historical periods and even a (historical) mythological scenario. Its engine has also allowed some franchise-based games such as that of Star Wars to come to life.
My brief conclusion is that of the TLDR you can read above.
This is a brief list of pros and cons I am adding progressively as I continue experiencing all of the game features. I tried to incorporate all of it in my original review but felt it would be confusing, and would alter the text too much.
Cons:
-There are no walls, or barricades, or trenches, or any other sort of additional defensive building that the player can construct to his liking. I believe walls would perhaps look stupid, but entrenchments and fencing items would seem appropriate especially as they were often seen in game. For humans jersey barriers are common in the campaigns, and so are "Covenant defense barriers".
-Technologies are a bunch like I previously stated, but I think there could have been a lot more, possibly giving the player a little bit more of strategy as in many other classic strategy games. Universities in historical RTS games I have in mind usually contain about a couple dozens of technologies to be researched - no, they are not all relevant or interesting as the ones in HW, but their quantity and diversity are vastly superior. A matter of taste I assume...
+The graphics are all in all beautiful, and all the effects pertaining the explosions, the bullets, or just the unit animations are amazing. I am extremely satisfied with the way the game looks, it makes the battles very enjoyable
+The campaign has a lot of cutscenes, is well designed and fun to play. I usually and categorically avoid campaigns in RTS games, never started any but a couple on AoE II. I made an exception here and I was not disappointed.
-I would have loved to be able to place not just barriers around my base, but also houses, farms, etc to give more immersion while looking at my base, and scenario around. Yes, I know this is not a historical setting with workshops and farmsteads, but in the halo universe the need for housing and a food replenishment system still exists. Again, a matter of taste, it would have added realism.
+The music is catchy and beautiful. I have always found that music is an important aspect of most games, but especially so in strategy ones due to the frequent moments of tranquillity.
