Let's be honest here: I bought this game for one reason only: To try to vote with my wallet and show Microsoft that we want ALL Halo-games to PC. I even paid the "full price", whereas I usually would have waited for some kind of sale for an old game like this.
Now, as I write this "review" I have only played the tutorial of the game. I have watched the cutscenes from this game many times over but never been able to play it as I have never owned an Xbox 360. So instead of giving a deep analysis of the game, here are a few things I have noticed in my first 60 minutes or so:
- The in-game cutscenes (not the pre-rendered ones) are stuck in some weird 30 fps interpolation. The game displays 60 fps (according to the fps counter), but it lags/jitters just like the game would at 30 fps. As soon as the cut-scene is over it is butter-smooth again.
- The game does NOT like if you run your system audio in 192 khz. It creates a lot of static noise and crackeling. Taking the quality down to 96 khz fixes these issues. Not a biggie, but I would prefer a fix for this. Annoying to have to change audio settings everytime I open this game
- People say this is an "excellent" port for PC and I highly have to disagree:
1) The UI-scaling is too big and the field of view is too narrow. It feels like I'm looking at a sub-FullHD game upscaled to 1440p, rather than actually looking at something that is 1440p. I kinda expect that for the game though, as it is a X360-port. But I think it should be mentioned. I just can't help the feeling that I would like to zoom the camera out more than is currently possible.
EDIT: I now found out how to zoom in/out with the camera. But I still feel it would be nice to be able to zoom out even further.
2) Keybinding is limited... Seriously! Whichever company that was responsible for porting this game; SHAME ON YOU! Why on Earth did you decide it would be a good idea to make some actions re-mappable, and some locked down? E.g. You have specific buttons for rotating the camera left/right, but they are locked to buttons "delete" and "insert". Like WTF???? There is NO - and I really mean it - NO reason for locking down key-bindings on a PC-port.
3) Camera-movement is way too aggressive. Clicking any of the WASD-buttons moves the camera way too agressively and quickly to either direction. This is a direct result of poorly ported controls from an analogue stick input to keyboard controls. On Xbox 360 you can easily decide how fast the camera moves with the joysticks, but on a keyboard it is 100 % speed from the get-go. The same goes for rotating the camera. Not only must you hold ALT + Mouse movement Left/right to rotate the camera, but also here it activates 100 % movement; like mouse input would be either ON or OFF, and not speed dependent. FIX THIS PLEASE! Lower the speed of the camera.
- When grouping units, why the frack is there no group-indicator or number indicator so I would know which key I binded which group to? This again feels like a rushed over-sight: "Yes, we must add grouping, because all RTS-games on PC has it! But don't bother adding any indicator. They won't need that!"
So is there anything good about this game? Probably YES. Probably everything that was great about it already on Xbox - I will see when I progress in the game. I'm mostly complaining about PC-port-specific issues. But the point is: Even if it was great on Xbox 360 with the mechanics it had there, it might not be up to snuff for PC as the mechanics we are used to on this platform is vastly different; RTS was born on PC, so we expect a bit more from an RTS title in terms of how to control things. On Xbox (or any console) I think this is one of the only RTS-games that has ever been released, so the stakes are also much lower. I've also seen other reviews complaining about localized/region locked multi-player. I don't know, but if those claims are true, then STOP IT MS! STOP IT! Global matchmaking please!
So why do I still recommend this game? Because even if it is filled with minor, yet somewhat annoying, flaws, most of the things I've listed above can (if the devs want to) be fixed with patches and updates. The game to its core is still solid, even if it is not a perfect experience on PC. But mostly, buy this game so we hopefully can get more Halo-games to PC. But if you are a hardcore PC-RTS-gamer, this game might put you off just because of those odd choices when it comes to controlling the game mechanics and the camera.

I'll review this in two parts. One is M:LL as a game, the other is Redux as an upgrade. M:LL first.
M:LL is the sequel to Metro 2033 (based on a fantastic book by Dmitry Glukhovsky) which was a decent but not great FPS. It did many things fantastically well, the oppressive atmosphere and incredible tension, while falling a bit flat on storytelling and shooter mechanics. It was still a shining example of amazing immersion and lack of hand-holding. Russian post-apocalyptica at it's finest.
M:LL picks up after the canon ending to 2033 (the one from the book) and delivers a vastly superior experience to 2033. Everything is far more polished. The combat, weapons and gunplay in general is more accurate, visceral and satisfying. The level design and various settings are far more varied and well designed and the pacing of both the action, the storytelling and the characters are far more polished this time around.
It's still very much a linear shooter, but I've found myself backtracking to where I started entirely by accident as I've explored and found various different paths to get to the same objective, which is fairly impressive for an underground tunnel setting. There's plenty of hidden nooks and crannies around the place, with goods and encounters you would otherwise miss.
I love the weapons. I really truly do. They give the impression of mostly cobbled together and improvised weaponry, further reinforced by the delightful customization system. Two barrel shotgun? Pfft, FOUR BARRELS! Have some of that, hah! There's quite a bit of variance within just a single weapon, with silencers, scopes and other mods and each weapon is fairly unique to start with. They all seem to have a very satisfying heft to them as well. Of course, four barrels at point blank most certainly should have that.
The characters are far better presented in this game than 2033. Voice acting has improved and so has the writing. This game really seems to shine now that the story has been written for presentation as a game, rather than how in 2033 they had to condense and adapt a book to an action/horror fps game. The story is well told and will take you all over the Metro system and let you see and incredible amount of gorgeous locations.
Speaking of gorgeous... this game is amazing in terms of visuals and graphics. I can't tell you how it performs on lower end systems, but except for during one particular level (full of fire and smoke) I never noticed frame drops on a GTX 780ti with everything but the in-game anti-aliasing option turned to max. I think one of the reasons M:LL is so amazingly immersive and delivers such a fantastic atmosphere is largely due to the lighting. It's flat out gorgeous. The lightbeams from friendly and hostile npcs and mounted lights, combined with the fantastic fog/smoke effects makes for an impressive sight. Especially when you take into account the moisture on your gas mask, the ambient lighting and the flares. This is truly an example of PC Graphics superiority.
The game effortlessly switches between action and stealth where you feel like a proper Stalker/Ranger in charge of the situation, and with breathless terror as you're just another prey animal in a horrifying world of predators. While LL didn't provide the same level of helpless pants-wetting terror as the Library did for me in 2033, there's no denying that it goes the distance and has nothing to be ashamed of in that regard.
So, judging it solely on its merits as a game I would easily give M:LL a 9 or 10 out of 10.
... however, I can't quite do that. There's serious technical issues and I suspect it's from the Redux upgrade so let's take a look at that.
2033 Redux and LL Redux is basically a GOTY pack including all the DLCs, slightly retuning some encounters and mechanics (and vastly upgrading the graphics in the case of 2033) and upgrading the entire graphics engine to 64bit. This has not been a painless transition, sadly. Quite a few of us initially couldn't even run either of the games, or couldn't get past intro sequences or crashed incessantly. The technical forums are to this day full of threads with issues and it's not entirely certain they'll all be resolved.
I've beaten both, but LL in particular had a tendency to crash my video driver and I've had to redo quite a few areas. At its worst, I could go so low as just 5-10 minutes of playtime and at its best I experienced 45 minutes before I had to start up again. Normally I'd attribute this to an issue on my end, but the technical forums show this is quite wide-spread.
As for the Redux itself, is it worth it? Should it just have been a free patch? I'd say it actually is worth it. It's quite similar to a GOTY edition as far as I'm concerned and the content, graphics and game updates are fairly priced as far as I'm concerned. This is giving one of the best FPS series/settings out there a new lease on life and I'm all for it.
So in conclusion, do I recommend this game? Oh yes, definitely.
Graphics: Top notch.
Gunplay: Top notch.
Writing/Storytelling: Good.
Length: I think I racked up about eight hours total for the campaign, without DLC missions.
Overall: 8/10, point subtracted for technical issues.
Buy it, but be aware that you may have technical issues.

Lumino City was gorgeous, and pretty entertaining, but it seemed quite rough around the edges. On top of the fact that the game was so short, some of the puzzles did not seem thought through very well. On about a third of the puzzles, I was basically looking up the answers in the book that the main character is given at the beginning of the game because I could not figure out what to do. There were several instances where the movement system would not move right, and various other bugs like your character (and other objects) not being able to stay flat on a surface while the camera was shifting around the scene, that led me to believe the developers weren't very committed to creating the very clean experience that the game portrays itself to be. And while I did think the hand-crafted set that the creators crafted was really neat, it was not actually that big in the end (leading to the game being shorter than I expected). Some of the craftsmanship of the set was a bit rough as well (improperly sanded edges, gaps between wood, and the pipes connecting the mailboxes look like they were thrown in without much care). Another thing that irritated me a bit was the lack of Steam achievements and trading cards, but I suppose I won't hold it against them. The soundtrack was entertaining, not really any complaints there. Overall, I would say it's fun, and I would recommend it, but certainly don't pay any more than $10 for it (that price even seems to be a bit much to me, to be honest).

The Good:

* Cutscenes are brilliantly incorporated
* A mature story that draws you in as it unfolds

The Bad:
* Some (rare) glitchy mechanics spoil the flow
* Gamespeed/movement feels too fast on high powered machines
* Too short (4 hours) and you want more
Impressions: I was strongly put in mind of the films of Jeunet (like a cross of 'City of Lost Children' with 'Amelie') and was impressed at the inventiveness of the puzzles and that the developer resisted repeating themselves just to pad out the game. That said 4 hours will be enough for a run through and another 1 to pickup missing achievements.
Some have criticised the game for not answering questions but the answers are all there if you listen, read the clues you collect and join the dots in your head.
Recommended for: Puzzle fans and those who like ingenious but forgiving platformers.
Conclusion: 9/10. Charmed me and tugged on my heartstrings from start to finish, just wanted more of it.

I found myself in the situation of looking through my Steam recommendations and found Lumino City, which directly got my interest.
Lumino City is a puzzle game which was build in the real world and digitalized in videos and pictures for the game. The people that live in this tower got animated and added to the scenes and deliver a really heart touching mini story and harmony between these.
What is the game about? We play the young woman Lumi who is trying to find her grandfather the handyman. He taught her everything about fixing things, solving problems and using different machines. This leads us to a great variety of puzzles and problems that we will solve in several hours, of course depending on how fast you can progress though these.
The graphics style is amazing and though the fps are capped to 25fps, it is fitting to the game and look. As I said, the tower was actually built and then captured in pictures and videos, then the people living in that tower got animated and added to the scenery. This is a great style to bring this game to live and the people have some really funny and heart touching interactions with each other and you too.
A fitting soundtrack supports the game and gives a great atmosphere for solving the puzzles. You will love the soundtrack!
I had no problems with the game in terms of bugs, but with the final chapter I was not able to progress on a ladder, if I don’t click immediatly on the next step. Restarting and clicking directly let me progress and see the end.
A truly memoriable game which you can purchase for 20€ on steam. I think the price is justified because of the great artstyle and the wide range of puzzles and problems to solve. It will be one of your special games to remember.

I'll review this in two parts. One is M:LL as a game, the other is Redux as an upgrade. M:LL first.
M:LL is the sequel to Metro 2033 (based on a fantastic book by Dmitry Glukhovsky) which was a decent but not great FPS. It did many things fantastically well, the oppressive atmosphere and incredible tension, while falling a bit flat on storytelling and shooter mechanics. It was still a shining example of amazing immersion and lack of hand-holding. Russian post-apocalyptica at it's finest.
M:LL picks up after the canon ending to 2033 (the one from the book) and delivers a vastly superior experience to 2033. Everything is far more polished. The combat, weapons and gunplay in general is more accurate, visceral and satisfying. The level design and various settings are far more varied and well designed and the pacing of both the action, the storytelling and the characters are far more polished this time around.
It's still very much a linear shooter, but I've found myself backtracking to where I started entirely by accident as I've explored and found various different paths to get to the same objective, which is fairly impressive for an underground tunnel setting. There's plenty of hidden nooks and crannies around the place, with goods and encounters you would otherwise miss.
I love the weapons. I really truly do. They give the impression of mostly cobbled together and improvised weaponry, further reinforced by the delightful customization system. Two barrel shotgun? Pfft, FOUR BARRELS! Have some of that, hah! There's quite a bit of variance within just a single weapon, with silencers, scopes and other mods and each weapon is fairly unique to start with. They all seem to have a very satisfying heft to them as well. Of course, four barrels at point blank most certainly should have that.
The characters are far better presented in this game than 2033. Voice acting has improved and so has the writing. This game really seems to shine now that the story has been written for presentation as a game, rather than how in 2033 they had to condense and adapt a book to an action/horror fps game. The story is well told and will take you all over the Metro system and let you see and incredible amount of gorgeous locations.
Speaking of gorgeous... this game is amazing in terms of visuals and graphics. I can't tell you how it performs on lower end systems, but except for during one particular level (full of fire and smoke) I never noticed frame drops on a GTX 780ti with everything but the in-game anti-aliasing option turned to max. I think one of the reasons M:LL is so amazingly immersive and delivers such a fantastic atmosphere is largely due to the lighting. It's flat out gorgeous. The lightbeams from friendly and hostile npcs and mounted lights, combined with the fantastic fog/smoke effects makes for an impressive sight. Especially when you take into account the moisture on your gas mask, the ambient lighting and the flares. This is truly an example of PC Graphics superiority.
The game effortlessly switches between action and stealth where you feel like a proper Stalker/Ranger in charge of the situation, and with breathless terror as you're just another prey animal in a horrifying world of predators. While LL didn't provide the same level of helpless pants-wetting terror as the Library did for me in 2033, there's no denying that it goes the distance and has nothing to be ashamed of in that regard.
So, judging it solely on its merits as a game I would easily give M:LL a 9 or 10 out of 10.
... however, I can't quite do that. There's serious technical issues and I suspect it's from the Redux upgrade so let's take a look at that.
2033 Redux and LL Redux is basically a GOTY pack including all the DLCs, slightly retuning some encounters and mechanics (and vastly upgrading the graphics in the case of 2033) and upgrading the entire graphics engine to 64bit. This has not been a painless transition, sadly. Quite a few of us initially couldn't even run either of the games, or couldn't get past intro sequences or crashed incessantly. The technical forums are to this day full of threads with issues and it's not entirely certain they'll all be resolved.
I've beaten both, but LL in particular had a tendency to crash my video driver and I've had to redo quite a few areas. At its worst, I could go so low as just 5-10 minutes of playtime and at its best I experienced 45 minutes before I had to start up again. Normally I'd attribute this to an issue on my end, but the technical forums show this is quite wide-spread.
As for the Redux itself, is it worth it? Should it just have been a free patch? I'd say it actually is worth it. It's quite similar to a GOTY edition as far as I'm concerned and the content, graphics and game updates are fairly priced as far as I'm concerned. This is giving one of the best FPS series/settings out there a new lease on life and I'm all for it.
So in conclusion, do I recommend this game? Oh yes, definitely.
Graphics: Top notch.
Gunplay: Top notch.
Writing/Storytelling: Good.
Length: I think I racked up about eight hours total for the campaign, without DLC missions.
Overall: 8/10, point subtracted for technical issues.
Buy it, but be aware that you may have technical issues.

There's also a fair amount of waiting involved as most weapons take 12 hours to build without paying and warframes (the word for classes or heroes in this game) take 72 hours. If repetitive content and waiting isn't really your thing, you might like the game less, maybe even not at all.
Now, I know that a lot of the stuff I said sounds like it'd be a negative review, as it mostly says "this game be grindy as ♥♥♥♥, yo" and yeah, it is, I'm not going to lie, there's a lot to grind for, espeically during your progression. But the game underneath the grind is so well-done and lovingly made, none of that matters for a lot of people, myself included. Once you actually get to hold that shiny new weapon in your hands and mod it so it cuts through♥♥♥♥♥♥like a knife cuts butter, or finish that cool new frame, each with unique powers and capabilities and roles they fill and quirks they have, it's so satisfying. and that's a big thing about the game: satisfaction. It's a huge F2P power fantasy with a weapon progression that genuinely feels like your stuff's getting stronger. Everything about the powers of the various frames you can build and use, the insane amount of weapons to choose and build, the fast pace and almost complete movement freedom and flow makes the game feel so fun to play, even if a lot of the missions aren't really that much to speak about.
I suppose I should address the elephant in the room of "how is its' F2P model"? Well, if you're worried that you'll eventually hit a roadblock where eventually the game soft forces you to pay in order to continue, or that all the super fun stuff is behind paywalls and F2P players only get the scraps, then I'm happy to say this is not the case. Every weapon in the game is obtainable without the need to spend money on it (barring a few extremely rare occurences like console/founders exclusives). Some are harder to grind for than others, to be sure, and sometimes grind will be necessary but eventually you can get any weapon your little heart desires, as long as you can deal with some repetitiveness every so often to make it happen. the only thing outright requiring the in game currency is Weapon and Warframe slots, which sounds like it'd be a massive red flag that you need to blow money on this game or you'll never enjoy it, but thankfully with the trading system, where you can trade things to others for other things, including platinum, you can build a healthy and sustainable amount of platinum without the need to spend a dime as long as you're willing to put the work into it and have an ear to the ground on what people want to buy or what can sell well.
Overall, I can't reccomend this game enough for everyone to at least try, see if you can get into it. It has some flaws, to be sure, and the dev's decisions aren't always the best (and are sometimes rather stupid), but the quality that the game has really shines through. Just be aware of what it demands from you, and I can surely say (for the most part) you won't be disappointed.

So this game turned out to be quite enjoyable even though it is unfortunately very short. You play Dawn a woman with the power   to shift from the 3D world into the 2D shadow world. The visual style of the game is great as well with a sort of 30's noir vibe to the world Dawn and Didi inhabit, as well as a decent soundtrack to match.
The biggest problem with this game is it's criminally short. I was left wanting more at the end and it really lets the game down.

- intersting mechanic of shifting from 3d to 2d to complete puzzles
- this game looks pretty good with a 30's Paris look to it

The Bad:
- Very short and i was left wanting more
-Little replay value

I took part in the free play weekend.
First, most of the reviews I’ve read on Stream by players have not helped me make a purchase decision, so was happy get the opportunity to sample the game itself.  In an effort to not repeat the same mistakes regarding a review, I’ll compare this games it to other games of what I consider to be a similar type.
The good:
Its depth of story and nuanced game play goes much farther than the latest “Masters of Orion” game in my opinion and as such, is more entertaining for me.  There are also game mechanics in place to curb / prevent “Doom Stack” vs “Doom Stack” combat game play which I find is also a relief.
The different races in the game, just don’t have difference abilities, but they been taken further so that they have their own race unique game mechanics to go along with them, i.e. they’re not just skinned differently with a +2 here and a -1 there to stat X and Y.  Race “A” actually accomplishes the same task leveraging a different game play mechanic / strategy from race “B.”  Planetary colonization is an example of this.
The not so good:
The game is a bit crippled from what I call the “Civilization Dilemma” which is having to start over and over again until you get game that gives a fair chance and worth continuing – especially if you do not disable the pirates.
There’s a bit too much game mechanic focus on empire happiness as well as punishment for playing with an expansionist play style, so be warned if that’s something you like to do.
All in all, I found it to be quite enjoyable game I’ve decided to add it to my library.

I am a strategy fan ever since. This game is time consuming and complex. Once you discovered how the game mechanics work (it takes approx. 20 hours) you are ready to lead your dynasty into glory, or complete extinction. Once a son of mine tried to kill the first born who I trained to become the next leader of the realm. I put the evil son into jail. Unfortunately, my first born died and the next heir was the guy in the prison! After 10 years rotting in a cell, he was crowned the first Emperor of the newly formed Empire of Scandinavia and was an excellent leader. Another time I was playing the merchant republic of Venice. My first character was Doge (leader of Venice) and died because of a plot of a rival family. But he had a son. He was very young, and my first jewish spymaster tried to kill him with poison. He failed to do so, and the young man became head of a dynasty with over one hundred members. He was a lunatic and howled to the moon in one event. Its funny to me to think about it that a head of a dynasty was a crazy guy. Its fantastic how stories are created in this game. It is the best Paradox game so far, as I have played Hearts of Iron to EU3 etc. I even like CK2 better than Europa Universalis 4 (at the moment) because I really like the roleplaying elements and different traits of a character. It is a lot of fun, but it is also very time consuming. If you play it for hours, your decisions get hasty and sloppy and its better to take a break and continue the next day. Concentration is important, but it's great fun if you like strategy games in a historical setting. Just make sure you get all DLC's because playing as a Viking (Old Gods) is completely different than playing Venice (Republic). If you play for hours you wish the map was even bigger.

Contrast is a strange beast. It's a platform-based puzzle game set in a surrealist, steampunk, early 20th century paris-like city. The player controls Dawn, the imaginary friend of the main character Didi, who has the titular power of being able to switch back and forth from the physical world to the shadow world. The player uses this ability to solve the many puzzles that are conviently wrapped around the story line. I don't want to delve too deep into the lore of this story, since most of its value comes from its twists (which is bad enough that I'm addressing), but it is something to witness. I wish that the game explored certain aspects that I felt needed developing, and the ending was a bit lackluster.
I have two main quips about this game. The first is its glitches. Sometimes when doing certain puzzles in the shadow world, the game will inexplicably pop you back into the physical world. Puzzles like these just require trial and error, but in a game where the main goal is to challenge the player's smarts and not their patience, it has no place. The second quip I have is the length of the game. It only took me three and a half hours to finish this game, and I usually consider myself as someone who plays through games very slowly. Since I actually got this game as a gift from a very generous friend (thanks BOT Mathew :3), I'm not that mad about it. However, if you plan on buying this game, ONLY GET IT ON SALE. It is definetely not worth a full $15. Other than that, I love this game. The controls are great, the visuals are engaging, and the collectibles give an excuse to marvel at such a beautifull world.
TL; DR: A very pretty game with an interesting story and even more interesting puzzles, yet can get a little buggy at times and is too much for its price considering its length. A must get game while its on sale. Can be considered one of those "art" games.

I didn't really know what to think of this game, due to all the negative reviews and downvotes this game got, most of them consisting of "it's not as good as it used to be" or " the developers have gone to♥♥♥♥♥♥recently". Nver having played the beat or any other version of this game before hand I can't confirm or deny these accusations but what I can say is that the game I played was a very fine experience. There are things that I love and things that I hate, as per usual with most games I play.
So, let's start this off with the thing that gets bashed the most, the community. Pretty much every review for this game is bashing the community, saying that "they're all ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s" or "none of them are chivelrous". I dont know if any patches have been removing any trolls or something, but i've only encountered a few rude people, the rest were very fun to talk to; I even made a few new friends in my time playing this game.
The character customization is also very linear, only having a few starting options for each class and the rest are either behind level locks or pay walls. This kind of took me out of the game for a bit, I was expecting a whole knight customization where I could make any kind of badass I wanted, but instead I got chump creator 2015. So customization is pretty bad, but I could create Solaire so i guess i'm cool with it.
Moving on to the gameplay, The game is a team based hack and slash taking place in the times of chivelry (duh), and I feel like the setting and weapons stay pretty true to the time period. The weapons have some real weight behind them, adding some strategic planning, and the games you participate in are very intense.
Some of the gameplay styles can either make you realise how much you hate the human race or make you feel like a badass when you come out on top.
Nothing about this game shouts "buy me now" to me, nor should it to you. It has a wealth of problems such as spherical hit boxes, some weapons are a tad op, sometimes whole teams will gang up on just you, the teams can become very unbalanced, and loading screens take too long.
This is a flawed game, yes. Should you buy it now? I don't think so. But if you're curious and you want to at least give it a try, then I think you'll be somewhat happy with your purchase. I give this game around a 6/10

The game has terrific possibilities but IT IS NOT FINISHED. It is easy to see the influence and parallels to Myer's CIVILIZATION. However, TOO much of the game seems a patchwork of ideas that are not linked together very well. Many of the features have very mysterious effects on one another.; some seem to have no relationship at all. At first I thought there were myriad "pop-ups" announcing some sort of event that wouls seem to be important but its effect, if there is one, was imperceptible. The "politics" is, to my mind, incomprehensible and its presence seems to be there because a developer thought something like politics should be in a game with such vast intentions. The UI suggested to me what an eight gear manual transmission car would be like if the gear selection linkages were VERY loose. This game looks like Ferari but drives like an old Chevy pickup. After many/several hours of play I became frustrated waiting for my facility with the game to improve. The 'learning curve' though steep would be acceptable if you were not forced to re-learn how to handle infrequent tasks or procedures. I am not at all convinced that 'Heroes' do anything useful for the game except to add another layer of complexity that (a) deloper(s) saw in another game. I think "fresh eyes" are needed to evaluate the playability of Endless Space. Methinks, the current "collective" is too close to the work to see the trees for the forest. Endless Space needs 20% less "stuff" and 20% more planning. More is NOT always better. The game does look terrific and, amazingly, I found no warez bugs. Keep going! I could really like this game when it is finished.

So let's get this out the way and say that both Bioshock 1 as well as it's sequel are incredible games, in my opinion they are maybe a few of the best games ever made, this review it's now about the games as much as it is about the "remastered status" of this games.
For starters both of this remasters have very few options, even less options than the original pc releases, there isn't a way to configure the fov of Bioshock 2 remastered, as of now, i've tried using the console (which you can open with tab) i've tried using "Flawless Widescreen" and i've tried to search for an option in pretty much every menu that the game offers, including the "gameplay options".
That being said the menu was locked to only using my gamepad when i started it, i had to navigate the menu using the arrows on my keyboard in order to disable the gamepad on the controller options and then configure a couple of the key bindings in order to actually get to play the game, after that i also had to recheck to have mouse acceleration disabled on the controller options given the fact that there's apparently a bug, or something strange happening with the mouse when it comes to the menus of the game, it feels as if my "dpi" or the sensitivity is separate from the in-game sensitivity, i've tried changing the sensitivity without luck.
The graphics while being good, are also not insanely improved, i'd expected to see more enhancements when it came to the textures and the lighting, but so far it's clear that they are pretty much just games with minor graphical enhancements.
This remastered, it's sadly the best option that you have to revisit this games, it's frankly a shame that they release this in this state, the whole point of remastering a game it's to make it better, the graphics, the menus, the bugs, fix things that affected the game in a negative way, this sadly doesn't do any of this, instead it just gives the game functionallity without going to hoops in getting the original ones started, something that should've been fixed since a very long time, something that's been bad enough that you have the first stickied post on the forums of Bioshock being how to get that game to run on windows 7/8.
This is simply a review to inform people as to what they're getting for Bioshock 2 Remastered, it's frankly a very good game, but not that much of a re-release, i wish steam had a "mixed" option so i could give the game the score or the recommendation that i think it deserves, it's not bad, it's not terrible, it just could have/should have, been better.

Metro Last Light is one of the best games ever made. Redux version updates the game to latest engine with new graphical effects, some new animations, better optimization and contains all released DLC's.
Now, I don't own the original version, so can't comment on that.
The game has great story, game play, characters, music and graphics. Everything you need from a great video game, and often metro feels like living, breathing real world. The game has system of choices, with consequences. Last Light got 2 different endings, both are done pretty well. although, I like good endings.
Game play is great. Once again, stealth is easy and so does gunplay. You can play this with the style you want in most parts. Rambo or Sam Fisher, your choice.
Game looks awesome, with good optimization. my 7770 can easily do 60fps on med/1080p(as with 2033 redux).
But the main great thing about this game is main story, mini-stories and mini-mini stores(weird). If you listen to NPC's, you will find some great small stories and some amusing ones. The main story is awesome and one of a kind, that I will never forget.
Music is the integral part of the game, and this game has some of the best soundtracks you will ever hear.
Update:
After 100% completing this game, I think this is best game I've played in 2014.
There are 9 different DLC chapters, and all of them are awesome.
Faction Pack contains three missions, where one is shoot everything up, second is stealth mission and last one is scavenging mission in The Library(best DLC IMO).
Tower Pack contains an AI challenge maps. really frustrating, but once you complete it, you'll feel victorious.
Developer Pack contains Shooting Gallery, Mutant Museum where you can observe NPCs and AI Arena, where you can make anything in game, fight each other. Really funny sometimes. It also contains the spider lair mission. where you get to burn spiders. yum.
Chronicles Pack contains little missions where you play as Anna, Pavel, Ulman and Khan. The mission involving Ulman and Khan has some of the most funny moments in Game.
Highly Recommended. 10/10

LA Noire is a unique and fun game in the aspect of how it plays. The main goals are to collect clues, interview witnesses and solve crimes with a cast of very real characters. I don't mean this lightly, having worked in security and talking with LEO, the different characters are people you will or have met before. The game is nearly six years old now, but still feels and looks pretty modern.
Casual and veteran players alike will enjoy most of the game. People living in LA will appreciate the games setting and take on a fictional 1940s. Don't come in expecting action like GTA, it's quite the opposite, but in a nice way. Think of it like listening to music from this time compared to modern tracks.
Where I feel the game lacks is namely it's pace after a certain point of the game and it's main character, Cole Phelps. Much like Zero Punctuations comments, Cole comes off as a robot and for me I don't see much change at all. It makes controlling him quite boring after a certain point. Yes, he is a straight as arrow cop wanting to redeem himself, but he's so detached for most of the game it feels a bit akward and the few times he does seem to show emotion or connect, it's almost like filler. Lastly is the ending, I won't spoil it, but to me it felt lackluster and as if the team inteded to make a sequel, but got canned before they could.
I still would recommend the game for it's unique approach to gameplay, but don't go in believing all the hype, because honestly, if they had made Cole develop as a character more, and the ending a bit more concluded, I felt the game would have overall been a fair bit better.

Where do I even begin with this game. First off ive been playing this game for about 7 years now and every playthrough ive had of it was exellent. There is alot of variety when it comes to builds. There is the obvious Light/Dark or Grey option for the game but there is also Force user builds, Ranged builds, Pure combat focused guardian, etc. I find the combat to be enjoyable (In my opinion) since its tactical and you can really plan attacks and things of that sort. Take DA:0 for example. Its pretty much the same system. You can start with 3 beginning classes: Guardian (Combat focused), Sentinel (Better skill progression), and Consular (Force powers). You then later in the game get different set of prestige classes depending on your allignment. Now, lets get to the writing of the game. This game has one of the best stories I have ever seen. You'll see once you play it for yourself. The reason I prefer this game slightly over the first is just because I prefer the darker, philosophical, grey aspects of the atmosphere and story a bit better (Kotor 1 is also one of my favorite games). Anyways, this game presents the idea that Dark is not necessarily evil and Light isnt nessesary good and you really get to see the Flaws of both sides. For example, you play as the Jedi Exile, who was exiled from the Jedi order for rusing to war to protect innocents. The Jedi were lazy and waited to "evaluate the threat". The dialouge and voice acting in this game is absolutely fantastic (Especially Kreia). For this game, you dont even need to be a fan of Star Wars. A non Star Wars fan would look at this game and just play an RPG. However a Star Wars fan would look at this and play an amazing Star Wars RPG. The reason for this is because the game is set in an era wayyy before the Movies. One flaw however, would be the cut content presented this game. Obsidian (The developers) were rushed to release this game by lucasarts, resulting in them needing to cut out content for the game. Luckily, a group of community modders managed to get into the games files and restore alot of the content that was cut. You can find the mod on the steam workshop. Anyways, hurry up and buy the game! You wont be dissapointed.

I've been a long time Civ fan and even tried other clones like Galactiv Civilization series.
But this game i found to be not that disappointing.
After a free weekend i decided to opt for the Deluxe Edition.
26 hours in now and i've drawn a couple of conclusions:
PROS:
The customizability brings memories of the Pax Imperia species and ship customizable options.
I've even gotten a basic understanding of how the deed system works, and is basically a hidden quest.
The curiosities system is interesting, allowing for it to be used as part of quests or have bonuses on their own. Either way it's wise to collect-them-all.
Actually, the whole quests system in a 4x game is interesting.
There is a lot of content and stories in this game.
The first time one explores a system, a nice vid presents all available planets with a nice camera angle. I found this to be very appealing.
The UI is slick, general GFX are great and music delivers a pretty nice atmosphere.
CONS:
Even though the diplomacy system is great (better than the civ series, at least) it would benefit from more options to influence the other faction positively. I found the influence messages confusing.
Like any well executed 4x can become quite addictive and you can find yourself playing this at 4am even though a work day follows.
There should be a way to have more custom appearances for custom species, if you're offering customizable species.
Popups tend to be obnoxious when you're in another window.
All in all, this is worth getting (not sure if the extra cash for the Deluxe is worth, though).
I'm waiting for more DLC stuff, but i'll probably go through what vanilla offers first. I estimate a couple of sleepless nights ahead...

I'm a sucker for engrossing environments, and poking around through Contrast's surroundings feels like perusing a Dali exhibit at times. While you're enjoying the ambience, there's a story about a little girl with family troubles that likes to sneak around at night. You play as her mute shadow-friend, swapping between 3Dspace and the 2D shadows cast upon the world.
The puzzles are fairly straightforward, although some will take a bit of experimentation. Solving them is less about flipping switches and more comparable to turning the hands on a clock to the correct time: it's difficult to get them in the precise orientation for success, but more often than not you'll get "close enough." As a result of this, a good number of the puzzles left me feeling like I'd somehow found an alternate, unintended solution from point A to B. This was actually the case once or twice, as I had found a way to sneak past a goal and into the next room with no way to continue since I didn't take the expected route. Reloading a previous save and checking online for the actual solution was my workaround that one time. I've uploaded a screenshot of this area so you don't get stuck like I did.
The shadow-swappy controls are fun, and the game doesn't overstay its welcome, being relatively short to complete (give or take if you go find the hidden locations of stuff). There aren't any badguys to shoot here, and it's a fairly comfy game despite its flaws.

About the game:
Metro Last light, like 2033, is a unique RPG in its own way. Level design is excellent with great atmosphere, and great story about life and moral. Metro Last Light is the only FPS that I considered to be worthy of best shooter of 2013.
About this Redux version:
However, Last Light Redux is more of a complete edition than a redux. It's pretty much the same game with full DLC that are either too short or uninteresting, and the changes to graphic are insignificant (even none at all to some people). The only improvement is, the game has been optimized and the performance is much better than the original version.
I'm not recommend this "Redux" for people who already owned original Last Light. But if you have trouble running the original version smoothly, you can in this one, but best get it when it's on sale.
So, thumbs-up for this amazing game, but thumbs-down for a Redux that should have been free for people who owned the original game.

This game is very atmospheric and charming. The art style is amazing and the audio/music is too. The puzzles are (sometimes convoluted but mostly) decent and have a very tactile feeling to them.
However it is frustrating to have to fight to get the game to do what I wanted it to. Expect input lag. Expect to misclick and have to wait upwards of 15 seconds to be able to do anything. Expect glichy areas where it takes upwards of 40 clicks just to get her to open the damned drawer. It took me forever to figure out why sometimes I couldn't open up my inventory. It's always hard to tell where exactly to click to get something done, making navigation difficult. At one point during the victory animation of a puzzle I clicked the back button to go progress in the game, but I apparently backed out too quickly and had to DO THE PUZZLE OVER. A brilliant game but you really have to fight with it.
Other complaints include the fact that all of their generated graphics (characters, speech bubbles(?)) are noticibly uglier than the rest of the game. There are also a few graphical errors (teleporting birds, boats rocking on a loop that isn't quite complete and then jerking back to the start of the animation loop). Another thing is that they say it should take about 10 hours to complete, but I'd say this number should be closer to 5. It took me just over 5 hours and that included the time it took for me to search around online to try to find a way to progress (it turned out that I just had to keep clicking the same spot over and over until the game finally decided that I had clicked the hitbox I needed to click).
Other than the frustration that comes with every minute of playing this game, it is a nice game and it does have interesting puzzle mechanics and a nice atmosphere. Wouldn't really recommend for the price.

Contrast: Endgame Review
(TL:DR Quick 'n' Dirty Version: Love it despite its faults. Worth supporting the developers even if just on sale)
I'll be honest - I went in prepared to love the sshit out of this game. The artwork was sublime, the music was orjazzmic and the concept was brilliant. Venturebeat had me at "It's as if Limbo and Bioshock Infinite had a baby while watching Pan's Labyrinth" - given that I'd just finished Limbo, and, well, I'm sure my avatar tells you all you need to know about Infinite.
Unfortunately, however, Contrast is not without its flaws, like the characters the game adeptly depicts. The story was well paced and engaging and there were some genuinely clever puzzles in the piece, but an overuse of cut-scenes and needlessly fiddly gameplay detracted from the overall satisfactory experience.
You play as Dawn, nine-year-old Didi's imaginary friend. Dawn helps Didi solve puzzles and navigate a troubled maze of family relationships by manipulating light and shadow in a sometimes third-person 3D puzzly, sometimes 2D-ish platformy, surreal depiction of the interwar era. The game marries the music of the Jazz Age with high-contrast film noir aesthetics and archetypes, and largely makes this work. It just looks and sounds beautiful, and the voice acting is realistic and moving, especially Didi.
There were lots of things the designers managed to get right - little things I really appreciated, like colour-coding the on-screen button prompts (Call me crap, but I'm still SO confused with the XBox buttons because they're the wrong way around from Super Nintendo!) or making it optional to collect everything, but easy to go back; this goes for Luminaries and collectibles. The final puzzles were immensely satisfying; I successfully put to use everything the game had taught me, which meant the learning curve was well thought out. Another thing was the inclusion of the soundtrack and a PDF of the collector's booklet.
And now for the whinge. The plot was engrossing, but I got sick to death of being interrupted by cut-scenes every few nanoseconds. The developers, again, got things right by making these skippable, but I felt I couldn't skip them anyway because I didn't want to miss the story. This and the way the camera kept getting yanked out of my control while trying to solve puzzles were some of the irritating aspects of the game: these interruptions kept breaking the flow so that things never really settled into a decent rhythm.
The consequence was that, when it came time to jump around, some of the puzzle-solving was quite hard to execute. I opted for a controller over keyboard and mouse, but wasn't entirely satisfied with either option. Shadow-world play is really fiddly; the camera doesn't neatly snap to a 2D view for this mode and I was forever accidentally leaping off into space and having to try again because of this. A lack of micro-save exacerbated the problem.
When not in shadow mode, the camera was at times so far up Dawn's bum it was nigh-on impossible to have a good look round for problem-solving, and at other times I'd solved the puzzle mentally but found the solution needlessly difficult to perform... Why have little bumps on the wall just to break you out of shadow mode and make it more difficult? For other puzzles, there was no intermediate feedback to show when the player was on the right track; the light had to be in exactly the right spot or things didn't work, and I had no idea whether I was right in theory or just all wrong. The game's physics also seemed inconsistent; there were loads of times when it looked like Dawn could easily make a certain jump, but wouldn't. I found all this incredibly frustrating to the point of controller-biting and rage-quitting, actually...
But Contrast wasn't all bad. As infuriating as the negatives were, the narrative was sustaining with its emphasis on family and dysfunctional relationships. I enjoyed the fact that the characters, though archetypal, were flawed individuals making the best of their respective situations -  a contemporary theme that will resonate with any mature, thinking player.
Add it to your wishlist and grab it next time it pops up on sale; you'll enjoy the cheap quickie.

This game is pure genius.
Well, maybe not so literally, but it's up there. It's a point and click adventure/puzzle game where you play the role of Lumi who is off to find out where her Granddad ended up. Your trek begins at the entrance to *drumroll...* Lumino City and immediately starts of with a rather tame puzzle (graph theory majors need not apply).
The game sports not too difficult of a challenge puzzle wise, but just enough to keep your brain sharp. It doesn't take long to figure out how to solve most of them, but even if you get stuck, your granddad was nice enough to leave you with a 1000 page handyman's guide, (which contains a whole lot of nonsense actually), but contains hints as to how to solve each puzzle, if you can decode what page number they are on. It's simple math formulas based on the puzzle you solve, but it's still pretty ingenious. "Going to the book" seems very 7th Guest style to me, so that's pretty neat.
The soundtrack is amazing. It's not over the top as to be annoying, just well suited for the puzzle you're solving and the area you happen to be in. Some catchy stuff here.
The visuals are awesome. Remember all those little carboard houses and things you used to make as a kid or would simply dream up and wish you had them? Well, albeit physically impossible, this game has brought a sort of quaint fantasy world that melds Pleasantville with Little Big Planet and managed to keep it from being hokey. It's almost like you're playing inside of a giant dollhouse, or something built out of tinker toys. The mixture of gadgets and propaganda you'd find in the 50's adds a nice touch.
The gameplay is pretty simple: you point- you go. That's pretty much it. There's no (very little) backtracking, so if you can manage to get to a new area, chances are, you found all that you need. The game limits the backtracking you have to do by making past areas inaccessible once you move on- preventing you from moving on until you have everything. It's a little linear in that regard because it's not true to the adventure games of yore, when you could legitimately break your game by forgetting something in the beginning (which is a♥♥♥♥♥♥move we all secretly loved). The puzzles are difficult, but not so difficult you just give up and resort to cheating, which is refreshing.
Give this game a try, you won't regret it.

I think this is a game I've wanted for a really long time and I didn't even know it. Just beautiful. The music, artstyle, overall atmosphere... it's even inspiring. It's all so overwhelming you get immersed and daydream about space exploration. I played 8 hours straight and tried 3 races - and bearing in mind Civilization, I didn't expect that they would actually play very differently. Wrong. Each almost feels like another game. In comparison to Stellaris, the game doesn't have nearly as much depth, which can be either a good thing, or a bad thing. It has way more personality though, and it doesn't take itself extremely seriously. Unlike the above mentioned, for this game, you don't need a university degree.
I also really like the politics and the random encounters & side quests. The latter for some obscure reason reminds me of Heroes of Might & Magic. Which is obviously awesome.
I was not convinced due to some of the issues, such as really frustrating pirates (something like barbarians in Civ, except it's a warship fleet instead of an elephant with a massive ballsack and a spearman riding it) and overall micromanagement (though compared to Stellaris... it's blissful - then again, so is flying an Airbus). But this game is really something. It's great to just chill out and explore, especially since you can turn the pirates off in the settings. It just all somehow fits together into one great piece of art.
So, after playing the whole Sunday and listening to the soundtrack at work the whole Monday... I have come to a decision.

Like another reviewer said, this game is like a cross between The Sims and Game Dev Tycoon.
You can customize your character, lead him or her into different social endeavors, while building yourself into a YouTube icon. You start off at your mom's house still going to school. You start off taking tests, but with some money you'll purchase new games and recording equipment. You put that back into your videos, and you rinse and repeat. That builds into new places to stay, and with enough persistence, you'll have your own YouTube team!
In my opinion it's a very fun game, but just be aware this is an Early Access game still. There are some balancing issues once you get into the Luxury stage and Network modes. For some people you'll probably find the game too repetitive in its current state. The "Sim" aspect isn't fully hashed out quite yet.
However I'm quite excited to see where this game goes. It seems the game will allow different types of YouTube channels in the future (currently you can only do a gaming channel). The developers seem to have clear direction on where this game is going as well, as opposed to other Early Access games.

You've seen your favorite youtube personalities play this and clucked "Hype! HYPE HYPE HYPE HYPE!" as you watched the videos and left a downvote (because you're bitter). Inspired by the claim this is like The Sims series, I decided to take a look.
It's certainly worthy of the claim. Not only is it like The Sims with balancing relations and a job (being a famous youtube personality), the mouse controls are similar to The Sims as well. If you're transitioning over, fear not. Easily done. The graphics are a bit cartoony which is charming in a way. You're walking around as your own customized character and they have an awfully large head, a terrible hairstyle, and they're hoping you're going to guide their way to a successful life.
It's a very nice start for Early Access. This is what I want to see for Early Access. Good job, devs. Keep up the good work. I'll keep playing.
I can understand if you're a little leery after seeing the hype and reading these reviews. Yes, the game has some bugs. I haven't encountered anything life ending right now other than some friends not recognizing that yes, I put up their videos in time. This seemed to stop once I moved to an apartment with a roommate. Now I'm rolling in cash.
The game isn't too hard to learn. There's some minor instructions and they don't hold your hand like you're a toddler. I found out most things on my own. What I would love to see in the future is a better explanation to the video editting. I'm still unsure how to do this. I caught on later that you can get higher scores with better arrangements, but this should probably be explained in gigantic letters for people who rush through.
Something that made me a little bit peeved (but otherwise still willing to play) were the ugly hairstyles. All of the women look like their hair has been cut by an angry lawnmower. That's probably an exaggeration, but this game is currently victim to "girls have long hair, pulled back hair, or fros". There's probably going to be more variety as time goes on, but as of right now, don't expect any ladies you create to look "pretty/to your liking/in your image/etc". A second thing is when you go to film vlogs, the text is as if you're filming a game video. Whoops. We're not gaming now. We're at a press release/party/con/movie!
Dating is a mysterious process in this game. My roommate seems to has the hots for me. That's great but like... She scares me. She comes on super strong and in real life, people who do that frighten me so I want to hide under those Space Invaders sheets and NEVER COME OUT. I haven't figured out how to flirt with other people. I do that and they stare at me, cringe, and just want me to go away. This is me in real life because I stare at romance then walk over to the macaroni art table, sit down, and start creating unicorns while talking about cartoons. Accurate. It's been about five different men and I haven't gone on a single date, but my roommate keeps trying to make awkward advances!
I'm not a fan of the meter that tells you went to leave an event. I feel like your needs for food/drink and sleep would be better indicators of that. I feel like those would probably drain faster being outside. Still, you do need something that says "hey, we need to leave and get back to work to make money off of youtube!" So this makes sense as something being there. It just doesn't seem realistic as a sims-style game to me. Usually your needs would tell you when it's time to go. Or maybe even the person you showed up with would tell you when they're leaving so it's leave now or have no ride back! We're splitting hairs here. Take this or leave this, it's just an incredibly stupid opinion!
Otherwise, there's not much else to say. It's a sim based on becoming youtube famous. It's still adding things (I can't wait to see cooking and fashion added because those are two other things I follow IRL) so keep looking.
It's up to you to get it now. The perks of doing early access means it's cheap. This game has the potential to become fairly big and whatever you saw your favorite youtube personality play? That's been fixed since you saw it. I\'m seeing fixes and additions since I was convinced to pick it up myself. You can also keep waiting.
If sim-style games are your niche in the gaming world, this is something to consider. Forget the whole "youtube personality" aspect of the game. It's a pretty nice sim alone. Adding the youtube concept makes it light hearted and gives it more fun. It's lovely.
As always, health warnings. The disco parties? I want to hurl. The lighting is offensive on the eyes and if you get migraines, you'll want to be away from those as far as possible. Oddly enough the Space Invaders-esque backgrounds at the release events you get invited to? Not as bad. Just beware the discos. They are very bad for your brain.
tl;dr, A very strong start. Keep it going. Keep revising. Us filthy sim lovers will sing your praises.

I am a strategy fan ever since. This game is time consuming and complex. Once you discovered how the game mechanics work (it takes approx. 20 hours) you are ready to lead your dynasty into glory, or complete extinction. Once a son of mine tried to kill the first born who I trained to become the next leader of the realm. I put the evil son into jail. Unfortunately, my first born died and the next heir was the guy in the prison! After 10 years rotting in a cell, he was crowned the first Emperor of the newly formed Empire of Scandinavia and was an excellent leader. Another time I was playing the merchant republic of Venice. My first character was Doge (leader of Venice) and died because of a plot of a rival family. But he had a son. He was very young, and my first jewish spymaster tried to kill him with poison. He failed to do so, and the young man became head of a dynasty with over one hundred members. He was a lunatic and howled to the moon in one event. Its funny to me to think about it that a head of a dynasty was a crazy guy. Its fantastic how stories are created in this game. It is the best Paradox game so far, as I have played Hearts of Iron to EU3 etc. I even like CK2 better than Europa Universalis 4 (at the moment) because I really like the roleplaying elements and different traits of a character. It is a lot of fun, but it is also very time consuming. If you play it for hours, your decisions get hasty and sloppy and its better to take a break and continue the next day. Concentration is important, but it's great fun if you like strategy games in a historical setting. Just make sure you get all DLC's because playing as a Viking (Old Gods) is completely different than playing Venice (Republic). If you play for hours you wish the map was even bigger.
Enjoyed the story and the jazz soundtrack, as well as the shadow-based elements.

(played during free weekend)
* The AI is very passive in general. On my very first playthrough, playing 2 difficulty levels above normal, the AI never so much as attacked me until what in Civilization would have been the modern age. To its credit, it at least managed to defeat me.
* Diplomacy is as good as not there. You can't get any AI player to agree on something as simple as a peace treaty (peace is not the default state; players start the game in a state of "Cold War" with each other). Even though they never actually escalate.
* The battle engine is unnecessarily complicated in ways that are opaque and impenetrable to the player. You can in theory watch battles, but it's more like you're watching a procedurally generated cutscene loosely based on what happened than a step-by-step, intelligible account of what happened, why and when.
The practical result is that you'll spend 95% of the game squashing everything because you outgun them grossly, and then you'll stumble upon a fleet that appears to you to be evenly matched with yours. Then they destroy your entire fleet without suffering a scratch; you can't explain why, and you lose.
* The tech tree and planet improvement design suffer from a quantity over quality approach. In something like Civilization 4, you agonize over your choice of what to research/build, because everything is enormously useful, even revolutionary (and the enemy is always at the gates). Here you browse a dozen techs struggling to find something that isn't completely useless. Almost everything has an upkeep cost that renders them circumstantial at best, completely unworkable at worst.
The game would have been much better if it had 1/3 as many assets, but super tightly balanced and interwoven into a cohesive whole.
* Too much micromanagement. Shuttling citizens back and forth so they synergize with their planet type. Verifying if you have a fertile, or a cold, or an oceanic planet in the same system to justify this or that improvement that costs 16 friggin gold a turn in upkeep, and barely gives anything back if conditions aren't right. Deciding whether you want your hero to have +5% evasion or +5% damage. The right promotion in Civ 4 was the difference between life and death, here they're busywork.
* This one is more of a pet peeve of mine, but all aliens in this game - with the exception of maybe the tree folk - are humanoid, with two sexes, their females happen to have two mammary glands, and those are located where you'd expect to find them on a primate. Even if the creature is like, an amphibian, or a being from another freaking dimension. I would have appreciated a little more creativity.

Halo Wars finally comes to the PC. It took it 8 years, but at long last it’s where RTS’ thrive and belong, Right? Well, mostly.
The short version of this review is simple. The game is good, plays very much like the original did on the Xbox 360 eight years ago. The game is very well balanced game play wise, and things generally flow very well from one combat to another. If your looking for a toned down, casual RTS that’s good starting point to jump into, then this is your game. But be advised, there are some hang ups.
It bears repeating that this game was built for Xbox 360, and playing it shows. While the game has been ported with drag box system for your mouse curser, which allows you to accurately select units, and double clicking allows you to select all your units of one type, which was not in the original game, a lot of features not common to RTS’s are present. Namely scrolling to zoom out the map is not supported here, as it was in the original title. In addition there appears to be no way to group units threw normal Ctrl+ number groupings, though the game does support a “jump to army” feature, or bases, which might be a hurdle for some RTS players.
Also be prepared to learn the hot keys to this game. Selecting local units, all units, using your armies abilities, and your global abilities (Such as Mac rounds or ODST drops) are a must to learn quite rapidly. Precision is not this games strong suit having been designed for consoles, and while mobbing your enemy and using army group abilities on a single target like a base or super unit is viable, when you want hero units like Spartans to steal vehicles, you’re going to have to be meticulous and very quick to select your Spartan and get to that enemy before your army blows it up. The game “fixes” this by tying one unit group in an army to your scroll wheel, which again, is a bit of a stretch to learn and adapt too.
But again the game is extremely well balanced. Limiting resources to two (Research level, and supplies) allows for quicker tactical planning since both can be effectively either managed at your base(s), or found around the map at strategic locations. Various areas of the map have special resource nodes, defensive structures, or even light bridges or light walls to block troop movement. Which ultimately for people playing competitively is a massive plus and helps to allow for a better experience overall.
So while the game has some fumblings with the port, I don’t think it’s flawed in any way. Fans of halo will like the game, even if the story is a bit barebones and filled with sarcastic wit, and fans of RTS’ and competitive games will like it for the balanced game play. I don’t play multiplayer for halo wars, so I can’t speak for the matchmaking system. Overall though, for 20 bucks, it’s definitely a game you should at least look at and maybe add to your collection.

If you ever played Game Dev Tycoon (or the original Game Dev Story) you played this.
Visually, it feels like Game Dev with improved graphics, but gameplay and mechanics are not just similar, they are exactly the same. Both use the same basic formula to make their products (games/youtube videos), and the way you use that formula will tell if they'll be good or bad.
The main difference (well, the only difference, really) is that Youtubers Life throws some social elements from The Sims into the mix. So, while you need to make more and better videos to get more subscribers, money and fame, you also need to eat, sleep, study, socialize with people, go to parties and events, find other jobs while your videos are not making enough money and so on.
So, you have a game that is basically a mix between Game Dev and a simplified version of The Sims. Is it worth it?
First, remember this is EA, so expect bugs, framerate issues even with high end computers. The game is far from being optmized. If stuff like that bothers you, don't get anywhere near it for now.
That being said, as long as you understand what EA is, if you like Game Dev and The Sims, chances are you'll like this. If you never played those, you can give it a try, it's not like you'll waste a lot of money anyway. It feels repetitive after a while, the social elements are just that, elements, so don't expect too much veriety on that department. However, even when you realize you're doing the same stuff over and over again, the gameplay is interesting enough to keep you going to get more subscribers and all the fame and money that comes with that. The rewarding "rags to riches" feeling you get in (good) tycoon games is there, although I have to say in it's current state is not very challenging once you start to figure out how it works, so keep that in mind.

Contrast is a short, sweet, stylized adventure with an intriguing story and a fascinating concept. It only took me about 6 hours to finish the game with all achievements, so don't come looking for an exceptionally long playthrough. The story it tells is worth experiencing nonetheless.
The story follows a little girl named Didi and her mysteriously invisible friend Dawn, who you play. The girl's mother is a singer at one of the local clubs, giving Didi a chance to sneak out at night and try to learn more about her father, her family, and ultimately, the origin of Dawn. As Dawn, you have the special ability to enter the walls around you, walking atop shadows to help Didi during her strange and dream-like adventure.
As you can imagine, there are quite a few puzzles to keep you occupied, but not as many as I would have liked with such a fascinating concept. The music is fantastic, as is the stylized atmosphere, but what really ties things together are the story. Almost the entire story is told through the shadows and the things people leave behind, and they still manage to craft an interesting arch for it all. If I had to complain, though, harder puzzles would have really made this game a lot more fun, and the occasional frustrating glitches shaved off a point in my book.
Still, for this kind of price tag, it's a crime not to pick it up.

Is Crusader Kings II worth your attention and money?
I like to think so, even though the dlc is getting a little out of hand. But if you like grand strategy it should be a must buy, regardless of the abundance of dlc. I've gotten all of them apart from Sons of Abraham and I must say they were worth every penny, though if you are just starting out with the series, I'd just recommend getting the standard version (or just try the demo). My reasoning for this is that the dlc adds to the learning curve of the game and if your new it could be a little overwhelming.
The Base Game:
So you start the game by picking a nation and family of your choice or creating one with the creator, which tends to sometimes make the game more difficult because you have no existing relations and family when you begin. Once you've chosen your nation you're thrown into the game's main screen, the map. From there almost everything will happen, so don't expect any fancy battles like in the total war series. Though CKII makes it up by putting so much thought into the strategic mode, like for instance diplomacy. It's one of the only games where I've seen diplomacy count as a valid strategy for actually winning the game.  The reason why is because your family will be the most important thing to manage in the game and one diplomatic mistake could even cost you the game and your lineage, be it to a civil war or a marriage.
I remember one multiplayer game where I was playing Lombardy and a friend of mine was trying out the vikings. He just kept harassing me which drove me to the point where I would start a plot. Plots are “diplomatic” ways of achieving something, like killing someone. (you can see where this is going). So after the millionth raid on my lands (and stealing my daughter and only heir) I started the plot to kill of their leader and I succeeded rather rapidly. My friend was left wondering who could have killed him. Now his nation was ruled by a nine year old and a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ uncle as his regent who wanted to kill the boy as well. I effectively knocked him out of the game with the use of “diplomacy” and greasing some palms as he tried to regain stability inside his own country.
So, is the game just a diplomatic simulator? Heck no. If you want to crush your enemies with the power of your armies, be my guest, but be wary of the unrest. Your military consists of different brigades of units who are raised in their home province. So for instance, I raise the London army and I'd get all units from the London province in a stack. You can do this for every province you own, thus raising your army. But beware of raising them to long because your vassals could get upset at you or you could go bankrupt.
And lastly, let's not forgot this one: Religion. In the base game it's pretty dull if you compare it with the dlc but it's still better then most other games. Ever wanted to set up an anti-pope, dethrone the existing pope and be the papal controller? Now you can. Or you could just ignore the church overall but beware their dangerous sting in the form of excommunication. Each religion also has their own bonuses and modifiers attached to them as well as a special something like for instance the ability to ask the pope for a crusade on your preferred target or to reform the Orthodox Christian faith.
And last but not least: The decisions! The base game has quite a few events that tend to pop up every now and again, which can make you life sweeter or a living hell. You can also, for instance, pass a no-alcohol law to boost the productivity of your people but at the same time you make them less happy. Almost every choice has a good and bad thing that'll happen. And lastly you've got the mayor decisions which are highlighted in the decisions menu, like form Great Britain with england, once you've conquered the isles.
The expansions:
Sword of Islam:
For starters it makes the Islam factions playable. Once you start a game with them you'll notice a few new things, like the decadence meter. This meter is quite important to manage unless you want a civil war to tear apart your empire. As a Muslim you'll have to manage your family very carefully since you can take up to four wives, which produces a whole lot of offspring and managing a large family is quite hard in CKII. And lastly they also added combat traits for your generals, like an extra bonus to hill defense or he might be a good infantry leader, which opens up a whole new level of military strategy in the game.
Legacy of Rome:
A must buy if you love roman/byzantine history. This expansion has a mayor focus on the Byzantine empire but changes a few base things as well. You can now have factions within your nation, like the court faction or the religious faction. These factions represent different aspects of your civilization and they all like and hate different things, so I usually end up trying to balance favor between the factions as to anger none. Secondly you've got the addition of standing armies, which are armies that don't need to be disbanded in times of peace. This is quite handy if you get surprise attacked, but I find them less useful then just your normal army, because eventually the standing armies will get too small and insignificant to matter, even though they grow throughout the game. But my most liked feature of this expansion is the possibility to re-create the roman empire in all it's glory. Imagine the glory...
Sunset Invasion:
Not much to say about this one... If you like alternate history it's a must-buy. The expansions is centered around the Aztec empire invading Europe, instead of the other way around, which usually provides some interesting and hilarious scenarios. Like for instance The Isles being taken by the Aztecs and them building a giant temple on the banks of the Thames after sacrificing most of it's people. It's also quite challenging to try and beat them back because they have gargantuan armies, so if you like a challenge, you should get this dlc as well.
The Republic:
Ah the republic... I had some great times with this one. The republic adds the trading civilizations as playable nations, like Venice, Genoa and The Hansa. Your task here is to accumulate the most money possible by building trading posts all around Europe and trying to stay the dominant family within your nation. There will be elections, feuds and wars between the traders to be able to establish the greatest trade empire there ever was and ofcourse don't forget the counts, dukes and kings around you trying to snatch your gold away.
The Old Gods:
This expansion is centered around the viking raiders but it also makes every pagan playable (including the Mongols and Aztecs) and the Zoroastrians. In this expansions they also added a new date to start from to the game: 867 AD, which is a whole lot earlier then the base game. As a viking you'll be able to plunder cities without any mayor reprimand from the nation you're pillaging, since it counts as a temporary war or you could call for an invasion against a nation which, over time, bolsters the amount of troops you can muster. But if that wasn't enough and you'd like a challenge, try playing the Zoroastrian faction and rebuilding the old faith.
So this was my review and thoughts on CKII and it's dlc, I hope you enjoyed it!
