I really want to like this game, believe me, I do.
I adore the music and the unique art style and the story is interesting, but the gameplay is so infuriatingly difficult at times that it breaks the immersion and makes me not want to play it.
The shadow shift ability is very sensitive. If you run into something, or if you're crushed by something, you'll shift out of the walls and you'll have to try again or you just might die altogether. Not only that, but it's very easy to miss jumps when you're trying to jump over certain gaps (most are easy to scale, but there are a few that are just mind boggling). And there are also some puzzles in which you have to reach a platform in a small amount of time - and those kinds of challenges in games are always maddening.
I'll play and I'll be mesmerized by the details and I'll want to find out what happens next in the story but then I reach a roadblock of a challenge and - after being pushed out of the walls, failing to jump over gaps and dying repeatedly - I get increasingly frustrated and then it's not about the story or the gameplay anymore, all the focus has shifted to that one piece that just doesn't seem to give if you don't get it just right. And after all is said and done and I can move on, I just can't relax and enjoy the game anymore and have to shut it off. A game is something that you should be able to enjoy and crave, but if it's frustrating - there's no point in trying; and that's a real shame.
It's a good game if you're a big fan of challenging puzzles; but if you're looking for a fun game with a sense of ease and flow, you might want to find something else to try.

Contrast is a very well-done and innovative Indie game. It falls into the puzzle genre, but utilizes first-person character control and does require a bit of speed.
Like all games, Contrast has its merits and pitfalls. Some things I really liked about the game are:
- A very well-thought-out and touching story
- Beautiful soundtrack (especially "Kat's Song". Youtube it!)
- A unique gameplay mechanic
- Some decently challenging puzzles
- Beautifully done art. Many noir games and movies nowadays are just creepy and Sin City-like. This is a much more refreshing take on the noir theme.
And some things that weren't so great:
- I don't know anyone who has clocked more than 10 hours to beat this
- Some minor bugs
- a reference to Albert Einstein in an earlier time period (learn your history, people!)
Simply put, Contrast is very well-done and a must-buy for any Indie fan. People who liked story-intensive games such as Bastion will definitely enjoy Contrast more than most. Of course $15 for a game this short may pinch wallets, so do wait for a sale. And of course, we hope to hear of a second game from Compulsion Studios soon. =D

(played during free weekend)
* The AI is very passive in general. On my very first playthrough, playing 2 difficulty levels above normal, the AI never so much as attacked me until what in Civilization would have been the modern age. To its credit, it at least managed to defeat me.
* Diplomacy is as good as not there. You can't get any AI player to agree on something as simple as a peace treaty (peace is not the default state; players start the game in a state of "Cold War" with each other). Even though they never actually escalate.
* The battle engine is unnecessarily complicated in ways that are opaque and impenetrable to the player. You can in theory watch battles, but it's more like you're watching a procedurally generated cutscene loosely based on what happened than a step-by-step, intelligible account of what happened, why and when.
The practical result is that you'll spend 95% of the game squashing everything because you outgun them grossly, and then you'll stumble upon a fleet that appears to you to be evenly matched with yours. Then they destroy your entire fleet without suffering a scratch; you can't explain why, and you lose.
* The tech tree and planet improvement design suffer from a quantity over quality approach. In something like Civilization 4, you agonize over your choice of what to research/build, because everything is enormously useful, even revolutionary (and the enemy is always at the gates). Here you browse a dozen techs struggling to find something that isn't completely useless. Almost everything has an upkeep cost that renders them circumstantial at best, completely unworkable at worst.
The game would have been much better if it had 1/3 as many assets, but super tightly balanced and interwoven into a cohesive whole.
* Too much micromanagement. Shuttling citizens back and forth so they synergize with their planet type. Verifying if you have a fertile, or a cold, or an oceanic planet in the same system to justify this or that improvement that costs 16 friggin gold a turn in upkeep, and barely gives anything back if conditions aren't right. Deciding whether you want your hero to have +5% evasion or +5% damage. The right promotion in Civ 4 was the difference between life and death, here they're busywork.
* This one is more of a pet peeve of mine, but all aliens in this game - with the exception of maybe the tree folk - are humanoid, with two sexes, their females happen to have two mammary glands, and those are located where you'd expect to find them on a primate. Even if the creature is like, an amphibian, or a being from another freaking dimension. I would have appreciated a little more creativity.

In the distant future of Warframe, you are a space ninja who has woken from a long slumber to find the solar system in disarray. Armed with a variety of exciting powers, you must fight an army of decaying clones, tech-minded science jerks, mutant freaks and other awesome enemies. The entire game is free to play, but it’s so good that I spent a hundred bucks on it and don’t regret a cent.
For me, it’s a point of pride that I don’t spend money on free to play games. Spending money means giving in to systems designed to manipulate me; it feels like losing. That constant reminder on players to buy, buy, buy is like a movie theatre interrupting a movie every few seconds to remind people that they can buy popcorn and soda any time they’d like. Not giving in to the ads feels like winning against an intrusive and unpleasant experience.
Digital Extremes’ Warframe is different–different enough that I actually bought Prime Access and some platinum. In all, I’ve spent about $100 on the game, something I’ve never done for a free to play game before. I felt like Warframe was worth it.
You don’t have to pay, though, and the game does not constantly dangle the option to pay in your face. The only reminders that you should spend money are located deep within customization menus or in the store, which is a console in your ship that you can easily ignore.
Warframe doesn’t care about balance. You’re a badass space ninja, after all! ... What’s great about being overpowered is that, since everyone is overpowered, no one is.
The multiplatform free-to-play game is an action shooter with some of the trappings of an MMO. It launched in 2013 and is available now on PC, PS4 and Xbox One, where it is regularly updated. As a recently-awoken space ninja called a Tenno, your job is to fly around the solar system doing space ninja stuff like assassinations, spying on people, stealing information, and performing sabotage. Each mission location and type remains the same, but the missions themselves are somewhat randomized. The game relies on a random tile system to keep things fresh. Your base of operations–and your main menu–is your ship.
When you log in, you’re sitting in front of your command console, which lets you select where you want to go in the solar system. To your right is the store. To your left is the codex. Behind you, deeper in the ship, are other stations, like the foundry that lets you build weapons or the armory that allows you to outfit and modify your frames.
Ah, right, frames. The eponymous warframes operate like character classes, except instead of being locked into one class per character, you can swap frames at will, with each frame having four unique powers. For one mission, you might feel like running the supportive frame Trinity, who can mass heal the entire team or provide energy vampire abilities to ensure quick regeneration. On the next mission, you might want to play as Ember, whose incredible World on Fire ability burns every enemy within a massive radius.
You obtain warframes by defeating bosses and getting their parts or by completing some of the game’s great quests. Warframes are not just some cool gimmick or branding idea, but a cool design choice. Two good ideas make them great: first, they’re all overpowered, and second, you have to hunt them down.
Warframe doesn’t care about balance. You’re a badass space ninja, after all! Rather than pushing players through a lengthy and meaningless grind, Warframe provides players tons of awesome and incredibly destructive powers. I love running Frost, a frame that launches a massive blast of ice, freezing everything around it, killing most low-level enemies. Playing like Frost feels like running around as a tactical nuke. The sheer destructive power being wielded is awe-inspiring, but that’s true of every frame. Valkyr’s power is invulnerability. It comes at the expense of ranged weapons, but that’s fine, because as a space ninja, your swords are just as cool, if not cooler, than your guns.
What’s great about being overpowered is that, since everyone is overpowered, no one is. The power you wield makes you feel like you’re actually a badass space ninja, because you’re killing lots of enemies quickly and efficiently. Other sci-fi games, like Mass Effect 2, force you into cover through a lack of health and a focus on small groups of enemies. There’s no sense of lethality or badassery going on when your character feels like they’re made of soggy toilet paper while enemies can last through an entire magazine of gunfire. Warframe understands this, so every frame feels fun to play, because every frame has powerful, over-the-top capabilities.
A friend of mine recently picked up one of the harder-to-obtain warframes, Ivara. He didn’t like her at first, until he realized that, among other things, he could use her abilities to create ziplines anywhere on the map. Ivara drastically altered his mobility and our fireteam’s damage capabilities, allowing us to breeze through content that had previously been too challenging.
I’ve played a lot of games over the years, and it seems like most developers’ idea of balance is that everything should feel equally underpowered. The player generally has to play with caution, staying back, even occasionally bunching up, letting enemies come to them as they cheese their way through fights. Warframe’s “you should feel like a ninja” approach encourages more proactive players who slice, dice, and explode their way through hundreds of enemies. I’ve seen builds that kill every enemy on the field at a given time. I’ve watched players one-hit kill a boss and continue onwards as if nothing happened. Warframe’s lethality doesn’t just make you feel effective. It gets you through content quickly, too.
Most online games require massive amounts of player time but lack sufficient content to actually demand that time. They rely on heavy amounts of repetition and luck. Players have to play a lot to get a little. Warframe instead allows you to pass through content quickly and always guarantees something interesting at the end of the journey.
As a ninja, you can “bullet jump” through most of the maps. Bullet jumping is a way to bypass lots of enemies by zipping past most enemies faster than they can respond. This means that you can get through missions quickly. That works well with another of the game’s better-implemented elements: timed content. Every few minutes, a new challenge pops up. Sometimes, the reward is credits. Other times, it’s crafting materials. I follow a Twitter feed that alerts me any time a blueprint is available. Combined with the speed at which I can complete content, I can catch a Twitter alert, pop into the game, grab the loot I want, and get back to whatever I was doing without a problem.
I recently got an alert for an item I wanted, logged in, played through the mission, and obtained the item within about 10 minutes. The result is a game that can be played in brief 10 to 15 minute spurts, as opposed to a game like The Division, which has a tiny handful of missions that require daily grinding if you want to be able to get enough credits to buy good gear.
Warframe’s speed means that it doesn’t doesn’t demand your commitment, but if you’re looking for something more in your relationship, the game’s got you covered.
A traditional loot game sends you into an encounter with the expectation of randomized loot. Take Borderlands, for instance. The game claims to have about 87 bazillion guns, but how many of those are meaningful or interesting guns? Most of the guns I’ve encountered in the Borderlands series are samey, even unremarkable, with the exception of a few gag guns. The same is true of The Division; I can’t tell you how many Vectors I’ve located, but I can tell you that they all play the same, just doing more or less damage depending on their stats.
I wish more games were like Warframe.

Por ahora solo he jugado una partida en el fin de semana gratuito, mis primeras 27 horas y lo he disfrutado como hacía mucho que no lo pasaba, me ha recordado a noches hasta las tantas jugando "un turno más" con el Civilization.
El juego es visualmente precioso, una música que no molesta y cuando las notas es que ha dado un giro para llamar tu atención y un juego muy completo que parece sencillo... El truco está en el "parece".
Con la primera partida puedes ir aprendiendo bien como funciona el juego e ir adquiriendo conocimiento para ver la profundidad que tiene, aunque al principio intimida un poco. Tras tanto tiempo de juego aún hay cosas que no sé como se hace y he visto fallos gordos. Es un acierto por ejemplo que cuando te falta una tecnología para hacer algo al ver la descripción puedas pulsar con ctrl e ir a ver que tecnología es, pero hay muchos quests que o bien son imposibles por la situación en que te encuentras o que simplemente están mal explicados, perdí mucho tiempo buscando como detener una nave que huía que supuestamente tenías que capturar sin matarla pero mis flotas solo tenía 4 opciones de acción invadir un planeta, atacar a un enemigo y las 2 de usar sondas... No sé si me quitaron acciones por ser el tutorial, si depende del tipo de naves o de tecnologías pero a día de hoy sé que por lo que he visto en internet hay la opción de dormir (esperar) y defender que era la que necesitaba para ese quest. Y busqué como un loco, dentro del juego y fuera, contruí naves específicas y busqué tecnologías (lo que me supuso algún problema) y no lo tengo claro a día de hoy (agradecería a quién lo sepa que me lo aclare).
Creo que he encontrado algún bug menor, pero me he quedado con la duda de si habré tocado algo que no debo o ha pasado algo que no entendía. Y el juego puede ser llegar a ser realmente molesto con los anuncios de que estás apunto de ganar, a mi empezó a ponérmelos 10 horas antes de acabar y los últimos turnos eran casi avanzar turno y apenas un par de acciones y se me hizo muy de madrugada (un clásico en este tipo de juego).
Pero no puedo negar que me ha encantado, y me ha enganchado como pocos. Al principio todo lo que descubres es nuevo y sorprendente y con el tiempo los anuncios siempre con las mismas imágenes se vuelven repetitivos y molestos, creo que debería ir variando dependiendo de la raza/colonia a la que se refiere o al nivel en ese momento. Los eventos le dan mucho juego y convierten el juego en una gymkana aparte del clásico sabor de los 4X. Al parecer hay muchos logros y se pueden jugar con diferentes razas lo que le de mucha rejugabilidad, aunque he echado de menos el logro de mejorar todas las unidades de tierra con lo que me costó.
No sé si dentro del género será un referente o si los habrá mejores o peores, tampoco lo puedo comparar con el anterior. Pero con el miedo que le tenía cuando me salió el logo de SEGA al principio (admito que le tengo manía y miro sus productos con recelo porque me suelen liar alguna que otra: por ejemplo la mayoría de las imágenes que acompañan al juego en la tienda son una engañifa porque son concept arts que se ven de fondo o son pantallazos muy bien cogidos de la parte del combate de naves que es un coñazo de animación que fue de lo primero que desactive ya que normalmente siempre te pegas con naves similares y ves como disparan sin mucho más y a veces sin enterarte de lo pasa hasta que no miras como sube o baja el marcador y el primer vídeo -y el tercero que es el mismo con publicidad encima y la lista de los funders- otro tanto porque apenas hay animaciones de ese tipo en el juego y es poco más que un mapa interactivo con imágenes superchulas, como se ve en el segundo.)
Me ha gustado que los DLCs sean gratuitos y aunque el juego me parece un poco caro aún para el tiempo que yo puedo dedicarle lo marcaré para tenerlo en cuenta si aparece en algún bundle, porque creo que me merece la pena pagar algo por él por la diversión que me ha dado este fin de semana.
Me ha gustado mucho el community challenge del que me acabo de enterar y me alegro de haber colaborado y que se puedan añadir mods y tenga workshop.

A dark noir atmospheric tale set in the 1920s that is reminiscent of the Dark Horse graphic novel "Misty Circus" or many other tales of this genre inspired by Neil Gaiman or the "Beautiful Stories for Ugly Children" series. Every aspect about the game is wonderfully enchanting, from the sad storyline of a broken family and child neglect, the beautifully rendered graphics, to the melodic soundtrack. This game successfully transports you to and immerses you in a world of wonder.
The mechanics are simple, crossing between a 3d world to a 2d platformer by using light and shadows. This is a decent 4X game with good visual and musical content. However, I found three weak points in the course of a few hours of gameplay.
The combat is very basic, you can't really manage it, just throw in your ships and hope they will win. You should be the better equipped/stronger to achieve it, but even in this case the outcome  could be unpredictable. This area should be developed further in my opinion.
The pirates are a major nuisance, most of my empire-building was hindered by them and I had to fight with them constantly, even when I set their frequency to the minimum at the start. The other civilisations were just supporting actors in the drama.
The strangest thing was diplomacy. I never engaged in any such activities during the game. Yet I saw in the diplomacy screen that I suddenly became allied to another civilisation (two rounds earlier "worried" about me) and I happened to be at war with another, but I never attacked them or entered their territory. How? Why?
Also there was an instance when the game notified me that I will be victorious in 4 turns. Never happened.
All in all, as I've said, this game is a decent effort, I recommend it, but it definitely needs a little more development here and there, mainly in the area of combat.

Contrast left me wanting more. I loved the shadow world you get to explore with Dawn and Didi. Its style and story is the kind of thing you best see in foreign films and the magic realism of Neil Gaiman (Mirrormask in particular kept cropping up as I played).
Didi has a friend no one else can see named Dawn, who looks like she's an acrobat of some kind. What is her story? How did she gain her powers? Is she real or a figment of Didi's imagination? None of this is ever truly explained over the game's short running time (I finished it with all the achievements in a little over 3 hours), but what does happen is Dawn getting involved in the story of Didi and her parents. Her mom is a lounge singer and her father is a shiftless dreamer in debt to the mob. Jonny has one more scheme up his sleeve to get back in Didi's mom's good graces, and Didi will do everything in her power to help make it happen (with Dawn's help, naturally).
It's hard not to get excited as you run and jump through Contrast's levels. The music and art design sell the world well, and the voice acting draws you into the struggles of its inhabitants, told enough enough as shadow plays. These are just for story design either; oftentimes you'll have to make use of the shadows you see to reach a switch or a puzzle piece. Collectibles take the form of either documents that reveal the game's backstory or glowing globes also used to power some of the game's puzzles.
A lot has been said about the game's controls. I found them as tight as could be expected with the mechanics, with a handheld controller the best way to go. A keyboard and mouse setup could work but the best experience I think would be found with a controller if able.
Contrast decides not to overstay its welcome, but I hope that the game devs do come back for an encore performance.

TLDR:
The game is great, especially if you're a lover of survival games and dinos/prehistoric creatures. Definitely worth playing, just be prepared to have a PC/laptop that can handle it.
FULL:
I've been playing ARK: Survival Evolved for a while now and have been playing well before it's official release. I've watched this game grow from only having just The Island to play from to patiently awaiting the release of the Aberation expansion and o far all I really have to say are good things about this game. That being said, there are some downsides to this game, but I feel everything good about the game far outweights that.
First off the gameplay itself is excelent; a player wakes up in an unknown world where prehistoric creatures from all ages roam and enough of them from the largest all the way down to some of the smallest are pretty much out to kill you, while others just go about their dailey meandering ignoring you. Upon waking up you need to find ways to keep yourself alive; find food, make tools, build shelter, and then thrive. You'll get to tame dinos/creatures and build your own home/base/fort/town/castel/etc, run around practically naked or make yourself some clothes (we don't judge here....too much), grow some crops, and wage all out war on other tribes or make alliances or completely ignore everyone (online play of course, as single player you're on your own).
The graphics are wonderful but can take a toll on some PC's/laptops, even on it's lowest settings. I have a custome built higher-end gaming PC and this game can give even me some trouble if I get too crazy with way too many dinos or structures in an area, especially with the game set to Epic settings, but mostly it runs fine for me. A few crashes here and there and a few bugs but nothing major that I've encountered so far that hasn't either been fixed at some point or is able to be worked around/managed fairly easily, so no complaints from me.
There isn't too much music to the game aside from time-based music (sunrise, noon, sunset, etc) and some battle music, so most of the time it's just you and all the noises nature can make around you. But when the music does kick in it's always good and doesn't take away from the game at all and just adds to the experience.
Probably one of my favorite parts of the game is Workshop for the game. There are so many creative people who have made their own contributions to the workshop with amazing mods that add to the game in so many ways (gotta give credit where it is due and these people need some serious thanks and applause). So many new maps, overhauls, creatures, additional items, decor, etc, they've just outdone themselves with everything. So if you love Ark, but you want to shake things up a bit there is always something in the Workshop that can just make the game even better or just change it up a little or a lot.
Now, finally, we get to the price. A lot of people lately have been up in arms over the recent change in the price once the game was fully released and it is understandable as it was quite a jump in price. Personally, I feel the higher price is ok (though I am a bit biased as I do have a great love for this game), but want to remind people that Ark does go on sale from time to time so if the price is an issue I would suggest waiting until it goes on sale. Endless Space 2 - A very good game with a few rough patches.
Endless Space 1 was the game that brought me back from the oblivion of 4X gaming. I was tired of 4X. I was disappointed in 4X. I was just bored of it. Then ES1 came, and all of that changed. It wasn't a perfect game, but it was the right game at the right time. Then Endless Legend was released a couple of years later, and I can honestly say that it is one of the best games I have ever played.
Fine, what do either of these games have to do with Endless Space 2? Well, Endless Space 2 is the natural progression of both of those games. Did it learn anything from its predecessors? Yes, but read on.
Endless Space 2 came out a little too early. It had a lot of good ideas that weren't realized, and the fanbase let Amplitude know with their reviews and the "lower than expected" sales, but, Amplitude did not quit. With each free update and patch, Endless Space 2 improved. Then fans gave further feedback, and Amplitude made further changes. That is how thngs go.
With the release of the recent free update, Galactic Statecraft, Endless Space 2 is finally where it should be. A solid 4X, with a lot of interesting and interconnected systems that make the experience very compelling.
As usual, Amplitude makes a beautiful game. The lore is fantastic. The music is stellar. All of it is out of this world. So, is that it? No, here comes the areas that still need improvement.
1. The User Interface. Yes, you read this right. The UI is stuningly beautiful, but some functionality is missing. I wish it conveyed information better which in turn would make it fully functional. I know Amplitude will keep refining it. So, no problem there.
2. Build everything mentality. Right now, we are stuck in a limbo. About half way through the game, we need to be selective of what we build and where so as to not wreck the economy and drain it of crucial strategic resources. But in the late game, this isn't a concern. I think that this is an area that Amplitude needs to focus on.
3. Combat is... Improving, but not satisfying. I don't know how to fix this completely without a total redo, but if Amplitude keeps tweeking it like they have been, I think combat will continue to improve. But they should consider redoing it completely in the future.
Having said all of that, I think the game is amazing. Certainly a Game of the Year contender.
Anyways, I absolutely recommend this title. Amplitude has shown in the past that it listens to its community. It adds the content that we want and brings its own flair to it along the way.

Halo Wars was my first introduction to the RTS genre, and it was probably one of my most played Halo and Xbox 360 games. I love this game so much, so seeing it get a proper Steam release is great.
: (6/10)
Halo Wars story is decent for both a Halo and RTS game. The game takes place 20 years before the events of Halo: Reach and the original trilogy. While some of it's characters aren't very memorable and it does have some cheesy moments, it also has some pretty awesome scenes involving the SPARTANS. The missions themselves are fun to play through, though on Legendary difficulty they can be a bit challenging.
: (9/10)
As an RTS game, Halo Wars is pretty simple. Since it was designed for consoles, it has watered-down RTS mechanics (no free base building, small unit cap and only one resource type). But this doesn't detract from the gameplay at all. The slower gameplay is a plus for me, since I'm not good at the multi-tasking other RTS games demand from you. While it's not nearly as intensive as other strategy games such as Starcraft or WH40k, there's still a good amount of strategy involved and micro/macro is still important. You get to play as both the UNSC and Covenant in multiplayer, both of them having 3 leaders. The UNSC gets access to leader abilities, while the Covenant gets to control hero units. All of the units are fun to play around with, and they are generally balanced.
: (9/10)
For being an 8 year old game, the game's graphics still hold up nicely. The unit models/textures and resolution are improved from the original game. The audio has also been significantly been improved. The game runs smoothly on my PC, and I haven't encountered any issues yet. A nice addition 343 included with the Definitive Edition, was unlocking the pre-order unit skins for both the Warthog and the Wraith for everyone.
: (8/10)
While the original game was very playable on a controller, being able to use a mouse and keyboard is much nicer.
The controls are mostly great, though some things such as using leader abilities do feel pretty sluggish. The hot keys are pretty standard for an RTS game. Another nice addition is the ability to create command groups with your units, which was missing in the original game.
: (8/10):
While there are no dedicated servers as it uses P2P connection, it does a feature a server browser where you can search games on. The multiplayer set-up system is very nice, allowing you to host both multiplayer games and campaign missions, with several option such as skulls being able to be toggled.
:
Overall, the Steam version of Halo Wars: Definitive Edition is a good port with some small issues. No doubt that you should buy this over the Windows 10/Windows Store version, as it has a much smaller playerbase. If you are looking for a simple but yet fun RTS, or wanting an interesting take on the Halo universe, pick it up!
I'm happy to see that 343 Industries is interested in bringing more Halo games to Steam, and I hope this a good sign of things to come. My hopes are that they bring Halo Wars 2 and most importantly, the original trilogy and Reach to Steam aswell (though I wouldn't mind Halo 4 or even Halo 5 aswell!)

Endless Space 2 - A very good game with a few rough patches.
Endless Space 1 was the game that brought me back from the oblivion of 4X gaming. I was tired of 4X. I was disappointed in 4X. I was just bored of it. Then ES1 came, and all of that changed. It wasn't a perfect game, but it was the right game at the right time. Then Endless Legend was released a couple of years later, and I can honestly say that it is one of the best games I have ever played.
Fine, what do either of these games have to do with Endless Space 2? Well, Endless Space 2 is the natural progression of both of those games. Did it learn anything from its predecessors? Yes, but read on.
Endless Space 2 came out a little too early. It had a lot of good ideas that weren't realized, and the fanbase let Amplitude know with their reviews and the "lower than expected" sales, but, Amplitude did not quit. With each free update and patch, Endless Space 2 improved. Then fans gave further feedback, and Amplitude made further changes. That is how thngs go.
With the release of the recent free update, Galactic Statecraft, Endless Space 2 is finally where it should be. A solid 4X, with a lot of interesting and interconnected systems that make the experience very compelling.
As usual, Amplitude makes a beautiful game. The lore is fantastic. The music is stellar. All of it is out of this world. So, is that it? No, here comes the areas that still need improvement.
1. The User Interface. Yes, you read this right. The UI is stuningly beautiful, but some functionality is missing. I wish it conveyed information better which in turn would make it fully functional. I know Amplitude will keep refining it. So, no problem there.
2. Build everything mentality. Right now, we are stuck in a limbo. About half way through the game, we need to be selective of what we build and where so as to not wreck the economy and drain it of crucial strategic resources. But in the late game, this isn't a concern. I think that this is an area that Amplitude needs to focus on.
3. Combat is... Improving, but not satisfying. I don't know how to fix this completely without a total redo, but if Amplitude keeps tweeking it like they have been, I think combat will continue to improve. But they should consider redoing it completely in the future.
Having said all of that, I think the game is amazing. Certainly a Game of the Year contender.
Anyways, I absolutely recommend this title. Amplitude has shown in the past that it listens to its community. It adds the content that we want and brings its own flair to it along the way.

Is Crusader Kings II worth your attention and money?
I like to think so, even though the dlc is getting a little out of hand. But if you like grand strategy it should be a must buy, regardless of the abundance of dlc. I've gotten all of them apart from Sons of Abraham and I must say they were worth every penny, though if you are just starting out with the series, I'd just recommend getting the standard version (or just try the demo). My reasoning for this is that the dlc adds to the learning curve of the game and if your new it could be a little overwhelming.
The Base Game:
So you start the game by picking a nation and family of your choice or creating one with the creator, which tends to sometimes make the game more difficult because you have no existing relations and family when you begin. Once you've chosen your nation you're thrown into the game's main screen, the map. From there almost everything will happen, so don't expect any fancy battles like in the total war series. Though CKII makes it up by putting so much thought into the strategic mode, like for instance diplomacy. It's one of the only games where I've seen diplomacy count as a valid strategy for actually winning the game.  The reason why is because your family will be the most important thing to manage in the game and one diplomatic mistake could even cost you the game and your lineage, be it to a civil war or a marriage.
I remember one multiplayer game where I was playing Lombardy and a friend of mine was trying out the vikings. He just kept harassing me which drove me to the point where I would start a plot. Plots are “diplomatic” ways of achieving something, like killing someone. (you can see where this is going). So after the millionth raid on my lands (and stealing my daughter and only heir) I started the plot to kill of their leader and I succeeded rather rapidly. My friend was left wondering who could have killed him. Now his nation was ruled by a nine year old and a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ uncle as his regent who wanted to kill the boy as well. I effectively knocked him out of the game with the use of “diplomacy” and greasing some palms as he tried to regain stability inside his own country.
So, is the game just a diplomatic simulator? Heck no. If you want to crush your enemies with the power of your armies, be my guest, but be wary of the unrest. Your military consists of different brigades of units who are raised in their home province. So for instance, I raise the London army and I'd get all units from the London province in a stack. You can do this for every province you own, thus raising your army. But beware of raising them to long because your vassals could get upset at you or you could go bankrupt.
And lastly, let's not forgot this one: Religion. In the base game it's pretty dull if you compare it with the dlc but it's still better then most other games. Ever wanted to set up an anti-pope, dethrone the existing pope and be the papal controller? Now you can. Or you could just ignore the church overall but beware their dangerous sting in the form of excommunication. Each religion also has their own bonuses and modifiers attached to them as well as a special something like for instance the ability to ask the pope for a crusade on your preferred target or to reform the Orthodox Christian faith.
And last but not least: The decisions! The base game has quite a few events that tend to pop up every now and again, which can make you life sweeter or a living hell. You can also, for instance, pass a no-alcohol law to boost the productivity of your people but at the same time you make them less happy. Almost every choice has a good and bad thing that'll happen. And lastly you've got the mayor decisions which are highlighted in the decisions menu, like form Great Britain with england, once you've conquered the isles.
The expansions:
Sword of Islam:
For starters it makes the Islam factions playable. Once you start a game with them you'll notice a few new things, like the decadence meter. This meter is quite important to manage unless you want a civil war to tear apart your empire. As a Muslim you'll have to manage your family very carefully since you can take up to four wives, which produces a whole lot of offspring and managing a large family is quite hard in CKII. And lastly they also added combat traits for your generals, like an extra bonus to hill defense or he might be a good infantry leader, which opens up a whole new level of military strategy in the game.
Legacy of Rome:
A must buy if you love roman/byzantine history. This expansion has a mayor focus on the Byzantine empire but changes a few base things as well. You can now have factions within your nation, like the court faction or the religious faction. These factions represent different aspects of your civilization and they all like and hate different things, so I usually end up trying to balance favor between the factions as to anger none. Secondly you've got the addition of standing armies, which are armies that don't need to be disbanded in times of peace. This is quite handy if you get surprise attacked, but I find them less useful then just your normal army, because eventually the standing armies will get too small and insignificant to matter, even though they grow throughout the game. But my most liked feature of this expansion is the possibility to re-create the roman empire in all it's glory. Imagine the glory...
Sunset Invasion:
Not much to say about this one... If you like alternate history it's a must-buy. The expansions is centered around the Aztec empire invading Europe, instead of the other way around, which usually provides some interesting and hilarious scenarios. Like for instance The Isles being taken by the Aztecs and them building a giant temple on the banks of the Thames after sacrificing most of it's people. It's also quite challenging to try and beat them back because they have gargantuan armies, so if you like a challenge, you should get this dlc as well.
The Republic:
Ah the republic... I had some great times with this one. The republic adds the trading civilizations as playable nations, like Venice, Genoa and The Hansa. Your task here is to accumulate the most money possible by building trading posts all around Europe and trying to stay the dominant family within your nation. There will be elections, feuds and wars between the traders to be able to establish the greatest trade empire there ever was and ofcourse don't forget the counts, dukes and kings around you trying to snatch your gold away.
The Old Gods:
This expansion is centered around the viking raiders but it also makes every pagan playable (including the Mongols and Aztecs) and the Zoroastrians. In this expansions they also added a new date to start from to the game: 867 AD, which is a whole lot earlier then the base game. As a viking you'll be able to plunder cities without any mayor reprimand from the nation you're pillaging, since it counts as a temporary war or you could call for an invasion against a nation which, over time, bolsters the amount of troops you can muster. But if that wasn't enough and you'd like a challenge, try playing the Zoroastrian faction and rebuilding the old faith.
So this was my review and thoughts on CKII and it's dlc, I hope you enjoyed it!

"Contrast" - Review
Gameplay:  6/10
It has a game console feel to the gameplay that, as a PC person, I'm not into. However i can appreciate it is the easiest way to achieve playability for Vol 1 of the concept of this game and quite possibly console gamers were the target audience. More camera control would have been nice (such as zooming with the mouse wheel) and i wish the game was a little longer.
Game ambiance: 6/10
There isn't all that much sound going on around the character which does make the world feel a little empty.... or is it?
The visuals, lighting, area design, overall feel and style are enough to keep me well entertained. Set at night with a little dust here, some falling leaves there, limpid pools of sporadic puddles, fog around the corner, it's enchanting.
Reliability/Stability: 10/10
This game is based on the Unreal Engine and I've experience No problems with game stability. No CTD.
Story/Plot: 7/10
The story was fun however maybe a little schizophrenic, at times i couldn't tell if it is aimed at kids or adults (maybe both?). Some parts seemed a little simple, then there are parts that could be questionable content for young ones (like violence and a recurring silhouette featuring some BIG boobs). Set in what seems to be a dream in the 1920's-1930's era, there are many enjoyable throwbacks to behold (jitter bug lolz). All in all the plot blends well with the concept and makes me wonder; is it all just a trip into the psyche of the main character, Dawn?
Concept: 10/10
This is a great concept for a game. Right away you can tell the game creators think outside the box. It's great to see people expanding the possibilities of gaming and i hope it doesn't end here.
Concept execution: 8/10
Featuring dynamic and changing gameplay this concept is a great introduction to what i hope will be a whole series of Contrast games. Given the challenge of creating something this different, and how the game production is creatively performed, it's hard to score this less than 8. I'm looking forward to buying Contrast 2.
Textures: 7/10
The textures were a little simple in places and not all that detailed (compared to some other titles available), that being said it suited the atmosphere and visual styling of this game to a tee. I think any over done attempt at realism would have detracted from the fairy-tail style charm this game delivers in spades.
Modelling: 6/10
I wish there was more detail to the characters. Yes, I understand that using low polygon objects gives better frames per second, and yes I understand that detailed modeling is challenging. That being said i felt as if they were just a little too low poly. I Don't want sacrifice the low res option; maybe add a selectable check box in game settings to increase the detail of the models.
Graphics: 6/10
Easily enjoyable and pleasant to look at, this game oozes dream-time, misty-eyed scenery, that inspires the imagination. HDR is pretty in the Contrast world and given this is a game based on shadows... using it is a no-brainer.
Sound: 7/10
There aren't all that many sounds in this game although the sounds it does have are of a good quality. does it need more? Maybe, maybe not, but a little more ambiance would have been nice.
Music: 9/10
Taste in music is subjective, personally i thought the music is great. A real treat for anyone new to the style, or into the genre. With good production and a light focus on environmental dynamics the music defiantly entertains and adds a very nice sense of immersion. I am thankful that the soundtrack accompanied the game on-disk as I can enjoy it at my leisure.
Adjustable shadow mapping: No
Bonus/Extras: Soundtrack

With the free weekend that allowed players to try out Endless Space 2, players like me who loved Endless Space 1 had to try this one out for themselves. And I must say that I'm impressed.
The game has changed a lot since it's early access release, and in a good way. At first I was kind of lost in the new interface, tech tree and all of these new changes I thought weren't so good.
They actually are excellent, bringing more choice and decisions to the player, for example there are now researches that you can't have simultaneously, like an upgrade for your missiles and an upgrade for your lasers, but the upgrades being independent, you can always research the higher tier for your missiles and still keep the previous tier of lasers you researched, which I think is better than just bulk research like in Endless Space 1 where you could just research everything without even thinking about "Is this going to work against that faction I'm at war with ?".
I also love the fact that the devs are really taking care of the community's opinion, the forums being very active and the devs asking the players "what could be in our game" or "what quest could we add" and make contests out of that is simply awesome.
This and the brand new graphics, which look absolutely gorgeous, and runs pretty well on beautiful even for a medium tier PC like mine with a GTX 750M and an i5 late gen core.
Though the price is kinda high for me atm, It's an absolute must buy for anyone who loves 4X type of games, with turn based strategy which spices things up as you have to plan what you are going to do (missing a turn could prove fatal to you on higher difficulties).
That's pretty much all I have to say from my free trial, which I ended up really enjoying.
P.S : For the OST, I fell in love with it in less than an hour of gameplay, and it really stood up to my expectations of an Endless Space game, which are really high. For the nostalgia, there is even a remix of "Flawless Theory" by FlyByNo (the original composer, pretty much outmatching his own skill), if that can convince you.
Edit : I thought to myself it would be a reasonable choice to ignore the -50% and wait for a bigger sale, probably a christmas sale.
Guess what ? I couldn't resist. I'm a huge fan of Endless Space 1 and this addition to my library was a no brainer, though I really tried to fight off the "need" to buy it. This game was so good and fun to play during the free weekend that I couldn't even resist ONE. SINGLE. WEEK. to buy it.
You can make your own conclusion out of this little commentary, but I'm certainly happy with my purchase.

Stunning visuals. Beautiful soundtrack. Challenging puzzles. 1920s noir ambiance. A bit of carnival, a bit of burlesque. This game is full of art, music and beauty. There is no daylight – only streetlights that bathe the cobblestone streets and alleyways. You are in a dreamlike world. Straddling the physical world and the shadow world, you must use various light sources to carve your path in the shadows to the other side. Though all but two characters are mere shadows upon the walls, their voices echoing around you, the game manages to pull together an interesting and captivating story… a story that becomes an adventure for you, Dawn, and Didi - the only one who can see you. Didi wants her family back together, and you are here to aid her using your unique abilities.
At times, the gameplay mechanics are frustrating and glitchy. But overall, the game is challenging without being impossible. The puzzles are creative and clever, and they carry the shadow play throughout the entire game and encourage you to use it intelligently to either continue on your path or obtain necessary elements or optional collectibles. The immersion is consistent and flawless - you do not leave the world the developers have created until you quit the game. And even then, you may find yourself humming the theme song...
Though it will only take you a handful of hours to finish, it would be well worth your while to give this puzzle-platformer a try. This game has heart.

I played ES2 as part of the free weekend, and have played both ES1 and Endless Legend before. For players new to the franchise, it might be worth a play; the graphics are OK, the factions are rather cool and there's a lot of little quests and activities.
But, really, would  I recommend you pay money to pay this? No. Nor would I recommend you spend any time playing it.
TLDR; it's ok but not worth the time, more like Master of Orion 2 than say, Stellaris.
More depth below.
The UI is rather clumsy and unintuitive. Coming from other games it just seems...off. Plus a lot of the fleet control is done by this holographic displays that don't feel immersive.
The tutorials are extremely spotty. They will tell you how to do something, but not always in advance (like you might want) and sometimes not at all.
The diplomacy system is also shallow and extrmely annoying. I was allied to another race and they could negotiate peace independently of me and I would then have to spend influence to re-start a war, a war that we were winning to begin with and my allies seemed bent on peacing out.
Fleet design is extremly limited, you have a selection of pre-set hulls that you have to unlock and you also must unlock technologies for more 'command points' allowing larger fleets. In all fairness, there's a limited degree of customisation possible in outfitting your ships with shields, armour, a range of weapons or utility modules but to me it falls short of other games such as Stellaris or Sword of the Stars. The command point system in particular feels weak, because it means big, decisive epic battles are being fought with 'fleets' which are more like squadrons of less than a dozen ships. It also seems rather bizzare that such fleets could even support enough manpower to launch ground invasions.
On the upside, there's some detail to fighting ground invasions and you can unlock technologies and alter the composition of your armies to include both air power and armour.
For all battles, the game uses selections of 'tactics' which are sort of like buffs you can apply. For instance one might increase experience gained at the end of battle, another might boost shield strength at the cost of damage output.
However, the battles are entirely out of your control and often you have little say in how a fleet performs. It's doubly frustrating because it's very hard to dodge defending fleets or avoid attacking fleets with your own fleets (for instance, of scouts and explorers) and this seems entirely immersion breaking from the perspective of space combat. Retreating from combat is also troublesome, and can't even be done with ships that are at less than 50% health (which is an oversight).
Each faction has their own quest lines, a returning feature from Endless Legend, and this is a good thing that keeps the game interesting. Rewards may range from technologieis to resources and heroes, but the criteria for these technologies are all over the place and don't seem to be related in any way to high strong your empire is.
A lot of planets have unique modifiers, returning from ES1, and this adds some much-needed depth. But it doesn't seem to have added anything which is a big let down. Indeed, coming from ES1 it appears a lot of races are missing or demoted to 'minor' races.
Long story short, it's not really an improvement over ES1. I'd recommend Stellaris over this any day of the week, and dobuly so if you're looking for a game that seems like you're in control of a star empire.

Don't get me wrong, it's a fantastic game concept, both visually and gameplay, and while survival games are still very much in their infancy, this is absolutely the next generation.
You play through a level system of crafting, on a complex and diverse map/s, and depending on what sort of server you play on, you can find yourself either enjoying perhaps one of the most immersive adventures, and I truly do mean adventure of your gaming life, or find yourself frustrated that you are not accessing the content or experience that you want, and that is a big part of how this game lets you down.
Because of the nature of so many multiplayer survival games, it is very easy to be griefed by other players, so getting onto a good, supported server is nigh impossible, and seems to be reserved for only the most prestiegious content creators. Much of this game is very much in that sense of elitism, which is understandable facing the barberous alternatives, but it does also show itself in the massive graphical and processor requirements, not aided by the second greatest flaw in this game, and perhaps the issue that lets it down the most; bugs.
This is a momumental game, and naturally, a very ambitious project, as all great games must be, and as such, is consistently crippled by it's own strange and persistent bugs, or coding issues. Wait times are long, even for the sorts of modded server experiences we've come to expect, servers are sometimes impossible to find without outside help, and large graphical and interface glitches plague it right down to the basic level.
But all this aside, it is the most ultimate game I am yet to see. For me, it reaches something higher than a mere art form, it has the heavy, rich feeling of a real world, but charged with the electric buzz of oppurtunity - you could find just as much enjoyment in rearing a tiny outpost, or careening down into the depths of unknown oppurtunity, and that's just what the base game has to offer, without player interaction.
So it might come as a strange review, that I spend so much time speaking about what lets the game down, though I am very optimistic it will deal with those challenges as it continues to be a relevant game.

I played ES2 as part of the free weekend, and have played both ES1 and Endless Legend before. For players new to the franchise, it might be worth a play; the graphics are OK, the factions are rather cool and there's a lot of little quests and activities.
But, really, would  I recommend you pay money to pay this? No. Nor would I recommend you spend any time playing it.
TLDR; it's ok but not worth the time, more like Master of Orion 2 than say, Stellaris.
More depth below.
The UI is rather clumsy and unintuitive. Coming from other games it just seems...off. Plus a lot of the fleet control is done by this holographic displays that don't feel immersive.
The tutorials are extremely spotty. They will tell you how to do something, but not always in advance (like you might want) and sometimes not at all.
The diplomacy system is also shallow and extrmely annoying. I was allied to another race and they could negotiate peace independently of me and I would then have to spend influence to re-start a war, a war that we were winning to begin with and my allies seemed bent on peacing out.
Fleet design is extremly limited, you have a selection of pre-set hulls that you have to unlock and you also must unlock technologies for more 'command points' allowing larger fleets. In all fairness, there's a limited degree of customisation possible in outfitting your ships with shields, armour, a range of weapons or utility modules but to me it falls short of other games such as Stellaris or Sword of the Stars. The command point system in particular feels weak, because it means big, decisive epic battles are being fought with 'fleets' which are more like squadrons of less than a dozen ships. It also seems rather bizzare that such fleets could even support enough manpower to launch ground invasions.
On the upside, there's some detail to fighting ground invasions and you can unlock technologies and alter the composition of your armies to include both air power and armour.
For all battles, the game uses selections of 'tactics' which are sort of like buffs you can apply. For instance one might increase experience gained at the end of battle, another might boost shield strength at the cost of damage output.
However, the battles are entirely out of your control and often you have little say in how a fleet performs. It's doubly frustrating because it's very hard to dodge defending fleets or avoid attacking fleets with your own fleets (for instance, of scouts and explorers) and this seems entirely immersion breaking from the perspective of space combat. Retreating from combat is also troublesome, and can't even be done with ships that are at less than 50% health (which is an oversight).
Each faction has their own quest lines, a returning feature from Endless Legend, and this is a good thing that keeps the game interesting. Rewards may range from technologieis to resources and heroes, but the criteria for these technologies are all over the place and don't seem to be related in any way to high strong your empire is.
A lot of planets have unique modifiers, returning from ES1, and this adds some much-needed depth. But it doesn't seem to have added anything which is a big let down. Indeed, coming from ES1 it appears a lot of races are missing or demoted to 'minor' races.
Long story short, it's not really an improvement over ES1. I'd recommend Stellaris over this any day of the week, and dobuly so if you're looking for a game that seems like you're in control of a star empire.

As someone who followed the development of Contrast with much anticipation, going as far as preordering it on steam, it pains me to say that the game is not good. What looked like a fascinating premise in a fantasical world intermixed with an amazing sound selection turned out to be only one of those things. Being a shadow becomes very boring very quickly, as the puzzles all end up revolving around a convulted system of controls that will leave you very very frustrasted. You will be afraid to enter walls. You will be afraid of messing up a button press. And you will be very afraid when you realize this puzzle will just continue to drag on with more complicated situations that faulty controls will only make worst. The only puzzle game I can think of right now that followed the same tune as Contrast is Braid, and by Jove does Braid make this game look like a joke. In Braid you can rely on your platforming abilities to carry you through a series of increasing difficult puzzles, which will truly reward the player for their abilities to think intuitively as well as perform proper platforming practices. In Contrast, you will struggle about a world with frustrating controls, little variation in puzzles, and little reward from solving the them. Little reward as in you will not care at all about the story because your willful suspension of disbelief will begin right at the start. The game takes place in France, and it makes a point to say so. What it doesn't explain, unless I understood world history entirely incorrectly, is that the world is floating in a vacuum of space. No explanation ever. No explanation as to why Didi, the girl you are escorting most of the game, sees the pit once but never comments on it again, as well as no one else commenting on it. Hell, in my opinion, the characters stopping to talk about the fact they live in a void would be more interesting than any plot point presented in this game. The story is weak, from the first moment of blackmail to the ending scene. The ending won't make you feel anything. You will be annoyed by Didi. You will hate every character that pops their ugly mug in this game. So what do you have so far? A messy universe with messy controls, a cast of completely unlikable characters, a character that is a young annoying child most of the game (Trust me, Didi is no Clementine, and you will go back to hating video game children after playing this,) in a story that is riddled in plot holes and does nothing to keep you interested in it. Oh, but the music is pretty at parts. I think I heard some of it over my continued groans over having to do another jump dash puzzle that would randomly throw me out of the wall to my death. Do yourself a favor, and skip out on this one.

I played Halo Wars extensively on the Xbox 360, and I loved it. It was a big part of my childhood and I was extremely excited to see it come to PC, and for such a reasonable price. The game is ported exactly as I remember it, however there are two fairly major problems I'd like to see fixed in future patches. Now, I know this game came out on Steam pretty recently - so I'm giving it some slack but as with any new games there are problems.
First, anyone whose familiar with the Halo franchise will know that one of the things it's famous for is terrible AI drivers. In the first person Halo games this is more just something funny to watch, but in this game it's borderline game breaking. The units have no idea how to interact with eachother, or the environment. Entire armies can get stuck because of one bad move by one unit, it can take your units what seems like years to reach the front lines as they keep running into each other. It's not so bad in the campaign, but in multiplayer it's the difference between winning and loosing the game. In maps with especially narrow cooridors this can really restrict the game play experience, and the user's enjoyment in general. I would really like to see this as the first thing fixed in the patches.
Second, in a multiplayer game we are all subject to the whims of the character with the worst connectivity. In most games, if a player has a bad connection, only they have to deal with lagging out. In Halo Wars, the entire game slows down and freezes at the drop of the slightest ping, even if everyone in the lobby has amazing connection, all it takes is one to ruin the game. And I'm not saying just a little laggy, I mean the game could freeze for 10, 20, even 30 seconds at a time. This gets especially worse as people amas bigger armies.
I do love Halo Wars, and I will certainly continue to play it, but these absolutley have to be fixed to be considered a valid stragety game - especially for those who have never played it.

This is by far the most accessible of the Grand Strategy Games that Paradox has made. A wonderfully convoluted game, where you define your goals and the means to achieve them. Be warned, you learn this game by playing it, gradually blooming into one of the most magnificent machiavellian meanies (darn you, profanity filter) the world has ever seen. Rewrite history as you see fit, Scheme and plot, command armies and then laugh at your demise at the hands of your subjects, your enemies, your supposed friends, your children and the wonderfully cruel winds of change and chance.
But be warned, this game does not provide you with a goal aside from survival of your dynasty. Do you wish to unite Ireland and then subjugate the heathens that currently hold Jerusalem? How about bringing forth the downfall of the Holy Roman Empire as just a lowly Count of France? Or maybe you really just want to make that one guy pay who plotted the death of your insane, crippled and infirm Court Jester? Do what you want and suffer the consequences.
All in all, this game is ripe with dark humour and seems to be easy at first. But it deceives you, sucking you in and suddenly gripping you by the balls, as you die from consumption, your son gets killed in a crusade and your remaining heir turns out to be gay, possessed and a complete lackwit, all while your allies drag you into wars and your vassals rise up in arms against you.
So, laugh at the cruel twists of fate, or grow mad from the revelation. Or maybe just enjoy a quiet, uneventful life as a lowly vassal to better lords.

I feel like I should have liked this more. I like open world games. I like police procedurals. I love noir. But LA Noire is just kinda meh.
I think you can sum up the issues with two statements--it fails as open world game, and it fails as a narrative game. On a lesser note, it fails as a technical achievement.
As an open world game, it's very meh. You have a handful of crime scenes per case, where you march around in a very small area and look at tiny little objects, many of which are only put there to pad out the gameplay (you don't necessarily know which clues are valid clues until you've picked them up and Cole has either told you what the importance of the clue is or said he doesn't see why this is important). In between crime scenes you usually just drive around uneventfully. It's not like GTA or Prototype or Saints Row. You won't come across any minigames or collectibles or random streakers getting run down by ambulances. You will have exactly one conversation with your partner per driving segment, and if you're lucky you might come across a smaller beat crime where you drop in, tackle a criminal, and watch them get loaded into the paddywagon. Periodically there are chase segments, wherein you must  drive after an escaping suspect. You do not get to ride shotgun in these segments. I guess your partner enjoys picking at tires with his peashooter and complaining that you drive too slow.
And as a narrative, the game is a mess. The overarching plot is part Caine Mutiny, part Donald Goines cautionary dug tale, and part boring. There was a nice twist in the military story, but the drug story ended rather predictably, and Cole himself did nothing to endear himself to me. His entire arc seemed to be driven by an affair with a german lounge singer, but we never see his family and only see his wife once toward the tail end of the arc, so why should I care if he's cheating on them? We also never really see why it is he's so enamoured with the singer. He sees her sing once with his cop buddies, comes back to watch her sing a few times, and then bam, instant oatmeal love story. I'm not much of a romance person, but I tolerate it in games like Dragon Age/Mass Effect because you actually have agency. You can romance whomever you want, however you want, or you can romance no one. In this, you're just watching a dorky guy carry out a series of half-baked ideas.
Finally, I know there are people who love realism in games, but these graphics are just boring. Cole and his partners are bland generic white guys, the commanding officers all kind of blend together, and there's just no style to anything. There's a reason people love games like Borderlands and Saints Row, game.
I read that the production of this game was a hot mess and I believe it. Non-managerial developers got worked until they burned out and employee turnover was supposed to be absurdly high. It looks it, and it plays like it. I had assumed this game had the basic framework of the GTA games underneath it, but there were so many weird bugs I'm starting to doubt that. Sometimes your partner stops responding no matter how you yell at him, so you drive all the way across LA, check your map, and your partner's still standing on the same sidewalk beside the same gas station you left him at. Sometimes entire buildings vanish during cutscenes and characters are just floating in mid-air. Once I was in a chase scene with Bekowsky, and we drove so fast the textures didn't have time to load, and we were driving down a big red blob through a sea of white blobs. Eventually the game stuttered, and then suddenly Bekowsky and Cole were standing on this ledge on the side of a building and then they fell forty feet and died. I really don't know what the hell happened, but I've never been able to reproduce the bug. Shame, really. That was the most interesting thing to happen that day.
Oh, and the DLC isn't much to write home about. It looks like a couple of different suits for Cole (none of which seemed to change the gameplay in any meaningful way) and a handful of cases that probably got cut for time on the first go-round.

Chivalry: Medieval Warfare. Oh, what can I say about it that hasn't been said before? Probably not a damn thing, so I'm not going to try, I'm just going to put things in my own words and ♥♥♥♥ trying to differentiate myself.
Chivalry: Medieval Warfare is a game that can best be described as a first-person gratuitous medieval murder simulator(fpgmms). There is a third-person mode available, but hardly anyone ever uses it, and with good reason. But, I digress. You're pretty much a member of one of two armies locked in
a war to determine the fate of the nation and who will be king, and there's really not much more to the story than that, which is good as this game is primarily multiplayer. You furthermore have four classes you can choose from, which I shall attempt to describe below.
-Knight
The preferred class of many a new player, knights are heavily armored warriors with high damage weapons, often accompanied by large shields. Knights are extremely versatile warriors, able to wield a myriad of weapons of varying sorts. They can wield large swords in one hand or two, often using a shield in the former case. Their primary weapons are often long-reaching, high damaging, but extremely slow. This is made up for with their secondary weapons, many of which are primary weapons in the Man at Arms' arsenal. A knight's secondary weapons are generally fast, but with relatively low damage and poor reach. A knight's secondary weapons are also exclusively one-handed, and as such are usually paired with a shield. For tertiary weapons knights have a few options. They have three types of shields, two of which are fairly large and one of which is smaller and can only be used with flails. These shields can be used or left on the back. Leaving a shield on the back provides passive protection from arrows, bolts, stones, and javelins fired at the back. Knights also have access to throwing axes, giving them a degree of ranged capability, though not much.
In short the knight is an extremely tanky, but often slow class good for beginners to use to get a feel for the game's mechanics.
-Vanguard
Masters of crowd control, vanguards are warriors clad in mail, wielding various sorts of spears, polearms, and greatswords. With extremely long reach and high damage, vanguards can sweep across multiple enemies with their swings, and are equally good in single combat. Vanguards are furthermore able to produce an extremely damaging lunge attack after sprinting for a certain period, though this attack is fairly easy to predict and avoid. On top of their normal weapons, vanguards have a secondary loadout much like that of the knight, and their tertiary weapons are smoke bombs, throwing knives, and throwing axes.
Overall the vanguard class is a jack of all trades on the battlefield, and are definitely an important part of any team. It should be noted, however, that you may want to stand back from a friendly vanguard in combat, as the less considerate players may wind up hitting you with slashes meant for the enemy.
-Man At Arms
Fast and agile, men at arms are lightly armored soldiers with one-handed weapons, often bearing smaller shields. The man at arms is most notable for the ability to do a sort of dashing dodge, allowing them to move out of the way of certain attacks, and also position themselves away from an enemy's guard. However they are not especially durable, and only archers are weaker in that regard. Their primary weapons consist of a variety of one-handed swords, axes, and maces, as well as a quarterstaff(the man at arms' only two-handed weapon). For secondary weapons, a man at arms can use a couple of even faster swords, some daggers, and a cudgel. Their tertiary weapons are two smaller shields, throwing knives, and oil pots(essentially incendiary grenades).
Overall the man at arms is an extremely fast, but vulnerable class that takes some time and study to master.
-Archer
Using bows, crossbows, slings, or javelins/throwing spears coupled with bucklers, the archer is an extraordinarily flimsy class designed less for melee combat and more for raining death from a distance. Though the archer can survive melee engagements, the best philosophy for them is to not let the enemy get that close. When using throwing spears, the buckler can increase survivability somewhat, however you still don't want to take a hit from the heavier classes, especially to the head. For secondary weapons the archer has access to the same extremely fast shortswords and such as the man at arms. Their tertiary arsenal is unique in that it always serves as an enhancement to the selected primary. For bows you can choose between broadhead or bodkin arrows. Broadheads do best against other archers and men at arms, and bodkins do better against knights and vanguards. For crossbows you get either a pavise shield or extra ammo. The pavise shield can be carried on the back and later placed to give the crossbow archer cover, and later be picked back up and re-used. As for extra ammo... You can carry more bolts. That's it. For slings you have access to stones and lead balls. Stones are extremely weak, but fire quickly and you have unlimited ammo with them. Lead balls are limited and slower to fire, but do more damage. Finally, with any sort of throwing spear you automatically get the buckler as your tertiary weapon. This greatly increases the melee capability of the archer, however it still does not compare to any of the pure melee classes.
Archers are extremely flimsy, but their ranged effectiveness is unparalleled and they are extremely valuable to any team.

Noire.

Contrast tells the story of a little girl named Didi and her seemingly invisible friend Dawn, who is literally living in the world of shadows. The story is set sometime in the 1920s and takes place in a wonderfully crafted and stylistically consistent world that looks like a mix between reality and dream.
You as player take on the role of Dawn, who is not only invisible to everyone but Didi, but can also shift between the 3-dimensional realm of reality and the 2-dimensional plane of shadows, where ever there is a bright light on any large enough surface. The feature is well-implemented, and most of the puzzles are cleverly built around this feature; the way it forces  the player to view things and think about them differently reminded me of Portal 1 and 2 - in a good way.
The story, surprisingly, is far from being a fairy tale for children as there are some very dark tones to it. On the other hand however, Contrast is a fantastic example for a compelling experience that does not need unnecessary violence in order to work. Both gameplay and story work well together, and neither falls short.
Speaking of short, the only short thing about the game is the time it takes to complete the story; for me, this was less than four hours. This is not to say the game is too short, however, as I found it to be just the right duration for the story to unfold. Any longer and it would've fallen into the same trap as so many other games that try to stretch the length of a decent story by diluting it with repetitive gameplay segments.
So can I recommend this game? Yes, the story, gameplay and presentation (both visuals and audio) are definitely worth it. However, if you are unsure because of the short length you may wish to wait until it is on sale again.

Having very much enjoyed ES the first and Endless Legend (also the first?), ES2 is one of the rare sequels that I was looking forward to- and was not disappointed by.
The biggest change in my first playthrough was that exploring the galaxy suddenly became an exciting, at times breathtakingly beautiful undertaking- diving into the system view of a newly discovered star system a welcome reminder of the scale of universe and the objects that clutter it.
The second change was the tone of the game. In the past games, I've enjoyed that the "Endless" titles take themselves seriously, but not too seriously, with campy humour intermingling with dramatic, even tragic moments, making for entertaining, though pragmatic storytelling and interactions in the game. But hitherto the ingame characters had lacked voice. They speak here.
The third was the much more present quest system, which, to me, is a mixed blessing. Although the questing part of the game can be ignored if you wish to focus on your personal emergent narrative, attempting to combine the overarching storylines intended to guide the player through this world with the story you are developing in each playthrough can be a challenge. Essentially, the way the quest system is implemented is that you can play two entirely different games in two different playthroughs (without taking the gameplay changes caused by races into account): One playthough might be a relatively straightforward 4X experience, while the next might be much closer to a linear RPG, following the narrative breadcrumbs that make up a races' ongoing story. Additionally, co-op quests are an interesting addition that could be better integrated into diplomatic systems.
On the topic of diplomacy and politics: It felt mostly organic, though at times almost too chatty, almost as if all the leaders in the galaxy are interacting on some interplanetary version of Twitter. The much- lauded politics systems are at times intransparent, with the occasional unattributable revolution unfolding, but that may be a reflection of real life, right down to the propaganda and disinformation you, as the administration, can disseminate to your populace and watch them react to it. There is a part of me that wishes for a deeper exploration of the relationship that develops between a ruling body and the factions that make up a "nation" in this game, but I wonder how this would impact the carefully balanced flow of the game. What would be interesting, though would be to experience a stronger reaction to the outcome of quests.
The combat remains the weakest part of the game (though the battles are very pretty to watch). To their credit, Amplitude seem to have learned that this is one gameplay system that, unless innovated heavily upon, is difficult to implement satisfyingly in a 4X type of game. Though repetitive, the battles are streamlined enough to not feel like a chore. That is not to say the occasional "BSG: Deadlock" style confrontation would not be very welcome, but those would have to be used sparingly, considering how many scraps you will inevitably get into.
And finally, victory. With a cutscene. And glorious STATS. Very satisfying and a tremendous step up form the "You have won!" Pop-up from Endless Legend.
In addition, the game runs mostly smoothly on a system that is almost ten years old, which either says something about said system, or about the optimisation that went into the Mac edition of the the game. As it does run, I am tending towards the latter.

I always saw Halo Wars as a crappy, and unnecessary console version of Command and Conquer 3 (You know, like the crappy Console Port of Command and Conquer 3), all joking aside, I was wrong. The game does have it's own identity and truly does feel like a Halo game. Resource Management is fairly simple, and the amount of units you can control is tiny compared to what I'm used too, but it all makes up for it with the combat and building.
The Campaign is probably the best part about the game. The CGI cutscenes still look outstanding by today's standards, and the characters are pretty decent if a little generic, (Sergeant Forge is the wisecracking macho Marine stereotype, Anders is the stuck-up Doctor/professor), yeah it does get a little tiresome. But those cutscenes and the storyline hook them all together perfectly.
The combat is a runner-up in the best features. You need to have a good mix of Power/Supplies, and Heavy/Light troops in order to find that sweet spot in the battle. You can't send in twenty Scorpions and expect to bring down a base, as you'll most likely be countered by Banshees or Hunters which can take you out fairly quickly. All in all, the game is decently balanced unless the enemy has saved up enough supplies and just spams ODST drops at you.
