Not a full review, just a free weekend review. Based on my experiences learning about the game mechanics in sandbox mode. I own and have played Endless Space and Legends and some of their DLC but it's been a little while since I've played through them.
Endless Space 2 feels like the Endless Space core with better graphics and some of Endless Legend's systems added on (most notably the quest system, shared marketplace, and a variant of the government policy/influence system - which I'm fine with).
There are a lot of new simple mechanics/upgrades to keep track of that you do alongside the Endless Space 1 actions. As you unlock the relevant technologies you have to deal with government elections & laws, trading companies (and buying trade routes), system development upgrades (effects based on your selected luxury), the resource/unit/hero shared marketplace, choosing ground unit composition (and buying upgrades), and building reputation with minor factions.
Worth a look if you like Endless Space/Legends or 4X games. The unhappiness penalty seems pretty tough (and there are not enough approval technologies/buildings unlike in Endless Space) so you may be disappointed if you don't like non-domination victories.

Story's Achilles heel is the Homicide desk. A desk which one would think be the most engaging and interesting is the most boring and repetitive. Removing the Homicide desk would significantly improve the overall pacing and quality of the game. Most people who leave the game unfinished will do so during Homicide or just after completing it. Also, don't forget the romance subplot later in the game which comes out of the left field.
As for the gameplay. What they were going for was basically Phoenix Wright, but they couldn't pull it off - quite often forces you to jump to conclusions and focuses too much on facial animations instead of deduction. In addition, splitting the game up into cases just didn't help the story at all. What could have been a coherent and compelling film noir was made confusing and ultimately unsatisfying.

I wanted to get my money's worth out of L.A. Noire and I can say I did for the 5 bucks I spent, but I don't feel like it was worth more than that.
Pros:
- Great voice acting except when Cole is yelling for no good reason
- Love the 1940s setting and music
- Fun car chases
Cons:
- AWFUL port.  Texture pop-in, rough edges, lag, and even an occasional crash.  This was a lazy port.
- Driving is pointless; just get your partner to drive you everywhere.  In fact, you can only cause harm by driving around since you get deducted when you hit something.
- The brawling gets stupid after the first time you do it.
- Completely random "Truth, Doubt, Lie" system that seemingly is irrelevant because you're going to solve the case and advance the story whether or not you get the questions right.
- Extraordinarily uninteresting side missions.
- The face/mouth/voice technology is need but often looks really weird against a face which is animated completely differently.
- The phone calls to "R&I" take FOREVER and go through the same speech line every time
The whole game just feels so drawn out.  It's a moving point-and-click, basically.  Not one of the better products to come out of Rockstar.

Endless Space_2 is a pretty fun game! I got to play it for about a day during its free weekend. It's like a mix between Civilization V and Starlink. It's a turn-based game where you build an empire, colonize planets, and take over the galaxy. Each system has a certain number of planets, and each planet is unique, and may hold secrets for you to find.
One thing I love about this game is that the primary resources, like food and stuff, is not stockpiled, so you can't save them up. Instead, you have to spend whatever resources you earn each turn, and you can get more resources from each system by buying upgrades. If there's an upgrade that costs more resources then you earn each turn, that upgrade will take as many turns as it needs to complete.
Another thing I like about the game is the detail in everything. If you like reading lore, this is the game for you. I love reading lore, but there is a LOT of reading in this game, I eventuially came to the point were I had to skip the reading. There's a lof of it, as every single planet, upgrade, character, and resource has a description to read. The quests have a lot of reading as well.
One thing I didn't like while playing is that my planets were filling up with lots of people, and it was getting hard to manage my populations, and it was taking too long to colonize more planets to move them to. Maybe I'm just not strategic enough to figure out population control.
It's complex, but the tutorial guy explains everything pretty well, and is not annoying. Anyway, it's a really great and detailed game, and is basically Civilization V in space. Thanks, and #BBlessed!

This is one of the most well-imagined games I have ever played. The art style, the concept, the characters, the storyline, the soundtrack; everything is phenomenal. I was drawn in instantly. Unfortunately, I found it a bit difficult to stay immersed at times. The gameplay is quite buggy. I'll admit, it has gotten better than it was the month after release, but I still feel like it could be better. Interacting with items is difficult to initiate and rather imprecise once you do, making some puzzles a bit more difficult, not to mention frustrating, than they otherwise would be. Another minorly infuriating aspect was the save system. You cannot manually save. The game saves automatically after solving certain puzzles or reaching a crucial plot point. The problem is, you never know which puzzles it saves after unless you're paying close attention to the corner of your screen. I was so fed up with having to do certain parts over that I abandoned the game for weeks at a time several times. All of that being said, I still truly enjoyed the game. The positives definitely outweigh the minor glitches and I am recommending this game to everyone. And who knows, they may fix the save system and wonky item interaction at a later point.

Setting: nailed

Story's Achilles heel is the Homicide desk. A desk which one would think be the most engaging and interesting is the most boring and repetitive. It contributes literally nothing to the overarching plot and causes it to grind to a screeching halt. Removing the Homicide desk would significantly improve the overall pacing and quality of the game. Most people who leave the game unfinished will do so during Homicide or just after completing it. Also, don't forget the romance subplot later in the game which comes out of the left field.
As for the gameplay. What they were going for was basically Phoenix Wright, but they couldn't pull it off - quite often forces you to jump to conclusions and focuses too much on facial animations instead of deduction. In addition, splitting the game up into cases just didn't help the story at all. What could have been a coherent and compelling film noir was made confusing and ultimately unsatisfying.

I wanted to get my money's worth out of L.A. Noire and I can say I did for the 5 bucks I spent, but I don't feel like it was worth more than that.
Pros:
- Great voice acting except when Cole is yelling for no good reason
- Love the 1940s setting and music
- Fun car chases
Cons:
- AWFUL port.  Texture pop-in, rough edges, lag, and even an occasional crash.  This was a lazy port.
- Driving is pointless; just get your partner to drive you everywhere.  In fact, you can only cause harm by driving around since you get deducted when you hit something.
- The brawling gets stupid after the first time you do it.
- Completely random "Truth, Doubt, Lie" system that seemingly is irrelevant because you're going to solve the case and advance the story whether or not you get the questions right.
- Extraordinarily uninteresting side missions.
- The face/mouth/voice technology is need but often looks really weird against a face which is animated completely differently.
- The phone calls to "R&I" take FOREVER and go through the same speech line every time
The whole game just feels so drawn out.  It's a moving point-and-click, basically.  Not one of the better products to come out of Rockstar.

Personally, I don't count this as a flaw of the game. Battles are fought using tactic cards, and the outcome depends on fleet composition and its synergy with the selected tactic. Since you can retroactively watch finished battles, it's used primarily to determine why the hell you won or lost. This can be used to improve your tactics, fleet composition, and ship fitting decisions.
I have to say that I hated the first endless space. With options like the complex Paradox games and Wargaming's
simpler Master of Orion, it never really had a place. The battles were underwhelming and (in my opinion) not fun, since the tactic (card) system didn't appeal to me at the time.
Despite this, I love the work that Amplitude has done, especially when tying the games together and using the diverse cast in multiple settings. I've always been a fan of their UI design and art direction, which makes up entirely for the relatively low fidelity of most assets (although this game is an exception).
I started playing as the cravers, despite the game advising otherwise. I really ♥♥♥♥ed up there. Their playstyle requires fast expansion, which requires a knowledge of the combat and ship fitting system - something I didn't have.
When I encountered my first pirates, I went straight to battle. I selected my tactic, turned on the "watch" switch, and clicked ready.
While loading the battle, the game used 14 gigs of ram (I have 16). Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ this is a huge issue. Every battle after, I had the same issue - at least until I stopped bothering to watch them.
My empire starved as I clicked through the text-based (although relatively well-done) tutorial and tried to get a grasp on what I was doing. At turn 50 I was confident that I had an understanding of the unique mechanics to abandon the train wreck I had created and start a new game.
I created a new game playing as the United
Empire, and I had a blast. By turn 30, I had rushed early combat tech and wiped out the pirates, replacing them as the nuisance to my neighbors. At this point the Militarist party stole the election from the Industrialists, which turned my empire upside down.
The major law I'd put into place to boost my approval had been replaced, and half of my systems were munitous due to expansion disapproval. I rushed production of approval-boosting structures and resource upgrades, and eventually pulled out of the dive.
I really enjoyed this dynamic, even if it became just as calculable as the other mechanics after some more play time.
Turn 100. I applied heavy pressure to my neighbors and basically forced them into an alliance, then declared war on the single Craver faction next door. The AI, while pretty dumb in peacetime and during cooperative quests, reacted surprisingly well to this. Their units moved in on enemy systems (unlike in Civ, where they behave nromally when called into a war) and attacked fleets. Again, I was fairly impressed.
While on the diplomacy screen with another target, the game hard crashed - presumably due to the game's consistently-high memory usage. Thankfully load times are relatively short (for a 4X game).
Rince and repeat, war after war, until the whole map is controlled by my overpowered alliance. At around turn 250, the game resulted in an allied spuremacy victory.
Endless Space 2 improves massively on the formula from the original. The visual presentation is hugely improved. Characters have more - well - character, and the ships look distinctive and overall pretty badass. The effects of political parties and the tactics system bring new twists to amplitude's 4X formula, which really is a breath of fresh air. Each race has its own unique playstyle (as meaningless as that may sound), and their ships favor certain tactics and fittings. In my opinion, a very well-executed 4X game.
After almost 20 hours, I've experienced a flawed but fresh experience. Learning the mechanics alone made me grin in excitement. I was not disappointed.

Disclaimer: I played this during a free weekend.
I'm a 4X veteran (Alpha Centauri, various Civ games) but not a megafan. I'm rating this thumbs-down because this game, despite being relatively new, still keeps many of the failings of 4X games from decades past (ending fatigue, randomness, overcomplicated-but-unspoken rules) and is altogether littered with small and annoying issues.
First the good:
- The presentation and user interface are very good. The artists, musicians, sound engineers, and writers should all be proud of themselves. I appreciate the satire and random humor sprinkled throughout, that while many parts of the game are serious (the tech and planet descriptions painting how brutal life would be on some of these planets), it still knows it's a video game (you can find a mushroom that causes "craving for pastries".)
- The races are mostly unique. There are are couple with mostly standard gameplay, like the Empire and Lumeris. But everyone has some weird race-specific attributes you have to play around.
- None of the planet types are outright "bad" or "useless". Barren planets may not be very good at supporting life, but their science output is excellent.
- The diplomacy mechanics are one of the better I've seen, incorporating influence (political pull), and allowing demands or forced truces when they'd make sense. War and peace are means to an end -- though you can still aim at wiping your enemies off the map.
But I have a lot of complaints too:
- Early on, you can only colonize reasonably nice planets (anything sunny and green), and these serve as the drivers of population growth. With unfavorable RNG, you might not find many of these nearby and be stuck on very few systems or have your empire spread out too much. The tech to colonize other planet types is low in the tree, but they'll grow slowly without a "food planet" or more technology.
- Many of the enhancements are geared toward certain planet configurations (e.g. this improvement gives "more food on Hot planets"). Unless you're really powering through research for system improvements, you'll soon reach a point where remaining improvements won't have much impact if built. So either you sit idle, or build lots of and lots of military (which is discouraged through upkeep and the manpower mechanic, but not discouraged *enough*).
- You aren't allowed to colonize many systems before you start taking an increasing happiness penalty empire-wide, encouraging you to grow "tall" rather than "wide". But the maps in general are pretty big, and conquered enemy systems become yours, easily putting you over the limit as you go for a military victory. For some reason the option to abandon a system was greyed out on many of my systems, and the game did not explain why.
- Maximum population in a system is only shown in one place, which is inconvenient if you want to see at a glance who is nearing max pop, or who has room to receive immigrants.
- The random quests are a neat idea, but not always achievable. I understand that they're meant to be inconvenient and you won't succeed at every one, but some were just impossible. When playing as the Lumeris, the main storyline wanted me to increase political support for Industrialists. That's very hard for a race that naturally favors Pacifists, and when my otherwise idle systems are pumping out military vessels (increasing Militarism).
-Huge ending fatigue, where once you pull ahead there's no mechanic for others to catch up. Granted I played on Normal as I learned the game. Certainly the harder difficulties offer more challenge across all turns.

This game is targeted at a very niche group of people. Best to describe it as "inspiring" After finishing it you will feel like putting on a record of some old french chanson, grab "Mario and the Magician" by Thomas Mann and spend the rest of the evening reading and thinking about the lost world of circuses, magicians, and cabarets.
If you have the slighest doubt about the world shown in the trailers, or you find yourself not interested in the world of the 1920s cabaret-world at all then my advice is to stay away from this game. You will simply not enjoy it based only on the gameplay or story because it has it's flaws (quite a few unfortunately). I made a pros and cons list just to show it in detail.
Pros:
- absolutely amazing, beautiful world. a true artistic masterpiece.
- brilliant soundtrack, there are a very few games that come close in quality and execution.
- great sound design (I'm talking about the fade-outs, reverbs and use of filters)
- an interesting (but poorly executed) content.
- tons of potential
- interesting characters
- puzzles requiring "out of the box" thinking.
Cons:
- horrendous glitchy gameplay with a tons of bugs (rage inducing at times)
- glitchy and shaky camera movement
- unresponsive controls (I played with mouse+keyboard)
- mediocre story
- a small game world, invisible walls not really meant for exploring (except for a few collectibles)
- relatively short game time (3-4 hours including collectibles)
As you can see I personally enjoyed my journey with "Contrast" but I'm sure it's not going to be a mainstream success. If you still feel like buying it after reading this review then I'm sure you will love the game (knowing what to expect)

Is there anything more sublime than a round of minigolf with your buddies? Some of my fondest childhood memories were of birthday parties at the putt-putt course, and even as an adult I sometimes cajole my co-workers into a round or two. Like the name suggests, Golf With Your Friends aims to capture that same simple joy, and does so with an ever-growing list of content and features.
When I first jumped into GWYF there were but three courses to choose from, Forest, Oasis, and Twilight, at 18 holes apiece. Forest hews closest to what you remember of minigolf, with the classic windmill, Plinko drop, and river jump holes. Oasis is an Egyptian-themed course with longer, more elaborate holes that cross over and send the ball flying through the clear desert sky. Twilight is a significant jump in difficulty, with unforgiving ramps and pits that might require half a dozen or more strokes to get just right. Added to those now are Haunted, Candyland, and Ancient, which vary even more in challenge and variety of scenery.
Navigating these courses is as easy as click, drag, and release. Your mouse aims your shot and you pull back to fill the four-part power bar, which gives you a wide range of control over the ball. Everything from feather-light taps to line drives are possible, and the holes you encounter will require them all. There's definitely a learning curve to the courses, a large part of that being no preview or free camera to scout your shots so learning the courses is expected. Once you have the lay of the land, the challenge becomes learning just the right finesse to put on the ball to overcome the traps. I could come close to par on all the courses after just a round or two, but it does require come patience to learn the more insidious holes.
That's probably going to be the biggest hangup for anyone looking for a casual golfing experience, honestly. GWYF isn't really here to simulate a real-world putt-putt outing, but rather a fanciful, hectic, arcadey approximation of the sport. Holes can be huge, sprawling, and require you to carom balls off of statuary, comestibles, and levitating decor. Getting some of the gimmick holes right can take dozens of shots and while replicating that success isn't too hard, having the patience to suss it out might be an uphill battle. Especially with the uphill holes.
At least the interface is simple enough to get you into a game almost immediately. Since this golf is intended to be enjoyed with (your) friends, every game is set up as a hosted server. Choosing to join gives you a handy browser with all the filters you could want, and hosting plops you down with name, password, and custom game options. One nice touch is that the lobby itself is a practice hole where you can putt around different obstacles while waiting for the match proper. And then there are loads of alternate modes and silly options to enable if you just want to fool around with your balls. The player base seems pretty chill as well and it's always easy to find a match, even if it's not necessarily the course or options I might want at the moment.
The graphics have been improving along with the content, taking ever-fuller advantage of the Unity engine to render its hazards and accouterments in excellent detail. The sound design is less ambitious, featuring a peppy, looping soundtrack and only the most basic effects. Obviously you're going to have more fun if you have the titular Your Friends to play with, but even going in solo there's plenty of fun to be had. Even in its early state, Golf With Your Friends contains enough fun and adventures to make it worth your time.

DISCLAIMER: IF YOU WISH TO PLAY ON 60FPS, USE WIDESCREENFIXER SINCE THIS GAME IS LOCKED IN 30FPS. FOR FOV, USE FLAWLESS WIDESCREEN AND PRESS EITHER + OR - TO CHANGE THE VIEW. THE PORT FOR THIS GAME ISN'T REALLY THAT GOOD BUT THE GAME ITSELF IS.
LA Noire is an open world detective game set in the 1940s after WWII. You play as a Cole Phelps, a marine turned police officer then detective. You solve cases from traffic to homicide to vice and then arson.
PORT
This game was ported by Rockstar Seeds who were known for porting other pc games either developed or published by Rockstar such as GTA 4. Team Bondi developed this game for Xbox 360 and Ps3 and a year later, Rockstar Seeds brought it to PC. Like GTA 4, LA Noire isn't really that a good a port, maybe worst if you ask me. There's no mod support so there's nothing anybody can do fix the issues this game has. The PC controls aren't that well so you need a controller. The framerate is capped at 30fps, unless you use the tool I mentioned above, it's easy to use. However some of the physics in the game will be messed up when playing at 60fps, there are videos on Youtube that shows it. But just cap it back to 30fps for a minute and you'll be fine. Also there are plenty of texture pop-ins everywhere you look especially driving. It's obvious how much they truly cared from this console port.
GRAPHICS
As stated there are a ton of texture and assets popping up in the screen but you can handle after a little while. The amount of detail in this game is amazing. As a guy who lives in Los Angeles, I actually recognized a lot of buildings in the game, the amount of work put into the interior, and exterior design of the city is beautiful. As you may know, this game utilizes what's called MotionScan, where the developers used 32 high definition cameras to capture actors faces. While it looks great, less attention I believed was put into the bodies since it was done separately.
STORY
You start as a cop, then rise to becoming a detective. The story is told by the cases you solve, however the actual story to the game does start later near the end when you're in vice. You can pick up the pieces to the story by picking up newspapers as you're doing the earlier cases. The dialogue in this game is well written but there were some times when I felt that the actors where overdoing it. Above all, the story is really good and dark since that's what you would expect from the noire type of entertainment.
GAMEPLAY
Rockstar may have published this game but it doesn't mean you blast gas stations up with a rocket launcher. To simply put, the gameplay is extremely limiting. You can browse the open world detail of LA Noire but there isn't much to do in this game when not doing the cases. There are mini side quests where help people out but they're really short (Lasts about 1-3 minutes). Interrogation in this game consists of asking a question and wondering if that person's telling a truth or lieing and expose them with evidence, or doubt them if you don't believe them. Like other Rockstar games, there are gunplay but in my honest opinion the gunplay in this game feels like an arcade game. It's not the same as GTA or Red Dead Redemption's gunplay which I think is amazing (Rockstar please bring to PC).
CONCLUSION
I believe you will enjoy this game especially when getting the Complete Edition which has every case the game has to offer. I know I haven't said much about your character Cole Phelps but to honest he has no personality at all. You don't know much about him in a personal level.
1.) Port isn't that good (30fps lock)
2.) Environment is really well detailed and amazing
3,) Don't know much about the character you play as.
If on sale, get this game and have fun, it's a long game.

This game was quite odd. As a game its nothing special; it would even be fair to say its gameplay is just bad. I often felt as though I tricked trough some levels by takng advantage of the hit-and-miss gameplay like making jumps that would avoid the puzzles. The stories execution is equally questionable, with a protagonist who serves to guide you through the game without any real finesse. And by that I don't mean your character; you seem to serve more as a tool for her tasks but that is the point.
TO THE GOOD!
This game had a very specific feel about it which I felt made it worth playing. The art style and music marry so well together that I forgave the shaky gameplay (at least for the most part). Depite its dodgy execution, I got what it was trying to show and it made for an enjoyable experience. The story wasn't as linear as what I've come to expect; whether thats a good or bad thing, im not entirely sure. Its fair to say Didi (the young girl) was a bit 'pushy' in trying to force you into the story, but I didnt really mind as my character is there to help her and the interactions of the character felt right for the situation.
Theres plenty to find out beyond the game through exploration. I actually think these bits were what made the game as it added another level of story beyond Didi's life to something more personal for the character Dawn (who never speaks IIRC), also - great name without being something cheesy. I would throughly recommend you endevour to find the 20(I think?) hidden media snippets! It reminded me of Bioshock in that the information you find explains the situation youre in; but in a modest way.
This game however is by no means difficult! I did the entire story in a single 2 hour sitting and found everything in that time. This wasn't even deliberately to finish it, I just felt like the game never lost traction and felt so, almost, calm to play that I kept casually playing. This isnt to say the story was good; it was weak with the hidden snippets making it interesting but it was solid enough in terms of character and situation.
Overall, as someone who does try to game as much as possible, I can't honestly say its a great game. But for me, it was incredibly playable and I will revisit it again gladly. It was like listening to music, I did indeed just easily loose track of time and do it. I found it quite charming if I'm being honest.
I played it with a controller if that means anything? You wont need the precision or focus of a kb+m but thats just my preference for this game. I would also say if youre on the fence about it, its probably best you wait till a sale comes around. I don't think I paid full price and despite enjoying it, don't know if its worth it. Definately feels like it should be £6.99 or similarly priced. Wouldn't be upset if I did pay retail though.

If you are into Jazz, Contrast is worth playing just for the sake of the soundtrack.
If the premise of a bluesy, gloomy, artsy, early 1900's Paris atmosphere - which this game reflects brilliantly - doesn't particularly appeal to you, you might want to think twice.
Contrast's gameplay is entirely based around blending 2D and 3D, a good idea; fits well with the semi-magical atmosphere, but unfortunately doesn't feel like it's been used to the full potential. The biggest challenges lie in the 2D platformers, whilst the 3D part feels underexploited (and the keyboard controls clunky - this was clearly designed for a controller). The 3D world just serves as an aid to model the 2D world, or as a link to reach the next 2D surface. At some moments, you feel like it's almost there and regret what the game could have become if the 2D and 3D had been made to blend in a bit more crazily.
Some of the puzzles are brilliant, some of them just about mediocre, but it all ends too soon. The game is extremely short (only 3 levels, count about an hour each). WIth no extra difficulty or challenge, with all collectible lying out in plain sight of the linear path, the replay value relies on just one thing: the really compelling atmosphere, characters, and the excellent voice acting.

I've had my eye on this game for a while, so naturally I dove into the free weekend. The graphics are something truly beautiful and special, and that's on my crappy i5 HP laptop. After completing the tutorial, here's my second game save.
-Started with the Riftborn
-Began my civilization like normal
-Encounter a single Reaver ship
-Wondering where they're hiding, I explore to find the local Reaver base
-I find it and ignore it until I get my military tech up
-Maybe 10 turns later, 12 Reaver ships start besieging my homeworld
-Trying to stop them, I realize the Reavers have ridiculously advanced fleets (compared to my next to 0 military tech)
-Their full army, 40+ ships, invades my territories and, being Riftborn, I put production to manpower to keep them alive
-After realizing I can't win, I send a colony ship beyond a nebula to create a new colony
-Pulling back my remaining ships to the colony, I leave my territories and develop my new colony
-After about 50 turns, I take my massive fleet (22 CP) and flank the ships and invasions
-I swiftly destroy a couple fleets on the way, realizing I can now win
-My ground invasion lasts a mere 3 turns, and I destroyed the Reaver base
-Later, after going to war with another empire, I bring the same fleet to invade one of their systems
-It disappears without a trace
I had such a fun time and while others may find Reavers a ruining factor, they forced me to grow and improve my overall strategy, and I can't imagine playing without them. This game is definitely worth the money even if you're bad at strategy games like me.

This was an all time classic on the 360, back in the good old days. They even got the price tag right with this title, 15.99 seems pretty reasonable for a "remastered" classic. This title is also a personal all time favourite in terms of Real time strategy.
I'm going to start with the pros:
- Wide variety in units, as well as generals to play as
- Each general is different, having their own special ability as well as their own special unit which makes them feel unique
- Being an RTS game the tensions are high, as you will need to plan your style of play accordingly, choosing either a defensive or offensive position(or both) in order to win the game
- The story was surprisingly interesting for me, with some pretty decent story telling in terms of characters and dialogue along with a wide variety of objectives
- The campaign on the 360 takes about 5 - 8 hours to beat, depending on your playstyle, I am currently half way through so far on the PC steam version
Cons (While I struggle to find anything wrong with this title, these cons are more like nitpicks if anything)
- Modding could be added, imagine being able to mod a game in the Halo series
- Sometimes the camera has movement issues on the mini map when I try jumping from one area to another
Overrall, if your a fan of the Halo series or RTS games in general, you should pick this up. It's safe to assume that we might be getting other games in the Halo series ported onto Steam so if we can show as much support as we can maybe this will be a dream come true for many of us :)

From a design perspective, there is nothing wrong with this game. Control is spectacularly fluid, and there's enough depth within the mechanics to give you a staggering amount of lasting power for a free to play game. With those two things in mind, it's very easy to see why many people have sunk so much time into Warframe. Yet, in spite of how well-made this game is, I can't recommend it in good conscience.
77 hours in, there was a moment where I realized that I was only playing to unlock new items, and had long since forgotten the stilmulations of fun and personal engagement. The mere act of booting up the game was akin to stepping onto a treadmill that you only ever use out of a sense of emptiness and boredom.
Just stay away; all you can do is keep going until you eventually burn yourself out with nothing substantial to show for it. And no, the ability to drain yourself of all human emotion without spending a dime is not something that justifies subjecting yourself to this game. Unless you want to experience some hardcore existential dread, look anywhere else.
Edit: I wrote this review directly after that moment of self-realization, so I probably went a little overboard there. Point being, the game itself isn't rewarding to play, and the only reason I stuck with it for so long was rather blatant usage of skinner-box techniques. Plently of other games are grindy, but still have some clear end-goal to give the game a better sense of purpose (which in my opinion this game sorely lacks despite the system of progression).

INTRODUCTION:
YouTubers Life is an interesting game, in the sense that I've always wanted this kind of game to exist, but I never knew how someone was going to make it. YouTubers Life is a mix of similar games such as The Sims and many Tycoon-style games. You're given a character creator, you make your YouTuber, and you're set out to complete various actions and goals to build your channel, network, friendships, and more, while also taking care of your YouTuber's basic necessities (hunger, sleep, etc.) While this game is a lot of fun, quite addicting, and has a lot of -promise-, this game isn't perfect. Early Access is a tag slapped onto the front page of this game, and that makes us wonder, will the developer(s) run with our money or follow through with their promises? We can only hope it's the latter.
PROS:
- Despite being Early Access, YouTubers Life has more content than the current price tag. ($1 = 1 Hour of Gameplay)
- Graphic style is silly, yet I believe that adds to the game's colorful personality.
- Character customization is fairly good for being Early Access, in physical appearance and clothing options.
- There are many things to collect in the game. House items, computer upgrades, personal clothing, and more.
- Always saving (however, this could be a -con- as well.)
- Tugs at your strings to think strategically, as producing and editing your video requires some patience and proper placement of cards, clips and effects for the best possible video.
- Provides a good sense of character development. You'll begin in your mother's house, eventually move out into an apartment with a friend, and more. You will always be upgrading something in this game, from your computer to your personal life.
- Good tutorial. If there's something new put into the game, you can guarantee the game is going to tell you all about it. You're often forced to go along with the tutorial as well. However, I found that I could get ahead of the tutorial sometimes and I'd get explanation about things I already knew.
- Ripping off company, video game, and brand names was quite funny to me. You could argue that this doesn't push creativity, but I think it adds to the game's personality.
CONS:
- Music is severely lacking. As far as I could tell, only one single song repeatedly loops while you're at home. You're given a single song based off of your area. There needs to be more variety.
- Sound effects could be improved on. The developer(s) have a good idea of what they're going for with voices, it's very -Sims- like, in the sense that there's a mix of words you can't understand while they speak. Voice actors and sounds could have a better overall quality.
- There are some translation errors that still exist in the game, as well as grammar mistakes that make certain dialogue weird to read. I believe the developer(s) should hire a translator ASAP, this task shouldn't be very hard.
- No option to "speed up" the gameplay for specific things. Features such as your character studying to learn certain skills, this takes a long time and it's quite boring to watch them stare at a book for so long. When waiting on a video, you could sleep or do something else. With studying? That isn't an option.
- RNG cards can be fairly annoying while producing a video. Sometimes you're forced to use copyrighted material in a video, or you don't get a matching card, which ruins the production and can stab you in the back. I enjoy that there's a struggle, but sometimes it's too harsh.
- There should be several saves that you can make, instead of being locked to a constant auto-saving feature. I've read that if you don't pay your rent, the game will end on you. I've never had this issue, but that just sounds terrible.
- Receiving items you've purchased can be repetitive. Each individual item will appear in a box next to your door that you have to click on. Imagine waiting on each item if you buy many things at once. I'm not easily annoyed by this, but I can see how others would complain about it.
- Repetition in dialogue, video game covers, YouTube video comments, everything. There needs to be a larger variety with everything to make the experience feel unique.
- Channel subscribers, views and ratings seem a little unrealistic to me. I think that you should start off A LOT smaller after your first few videos. Success is not found that easily.
CONCLUSION:
The YouTubers Life developer(s) seem to have recognized the popularity that has been brought to their game, and hopefully that is enough motivation for them to finish their game and listen to their community. In it's current state, if you enjoy this genre of game, I'd recommend buying it and supporting the developer(s) for creating what they have so far. I'd like to note that this game won't appeal to everyone, so I'd recommend doing your research beforehand. Also, the golden rule of $1 = 1 Hour of Entertainment looks like it'll be met, so I'm very happy about that.
RATING:
YouTubers Life receives a 9/10 for me, and I can see this game being a 10/10 for if the developer(s) follow through with their promises, finish the game, and add/fix the content that people are talking about.
NOTES:
- I've read about people crashing while playing this game, but I haven't once ever experienced that before.
Yes, I want my life spent on this game back. But I regret nothing!

First, The Multiplayer:
Great game, and it was revolutionary, it showed that an RTS can work perfectly on console. Now yes it may be simplistic, nothing near Hearts of Iron, Sins of A solar Empire, Stellaris, or Supreme Commander in terms of complexity.. But that is where it shines. It is easy to learn and get into but it takes time to know the strategies, especially in multiplayer! Yes, you may have seen people win with rushes like a warthog rush, a simple and effective strategy, but it can be easily countered with a Scorpion or two (Or Wraiths) and some air units. Another good covenant strategy is the Hunter-Jackal combination, but in its own regard, is garbage against air units such has Hornet's and Hawks, if you play as forge you can even use Grizzly's to wipe them out.Those are only a few of the strategy's to Halo Wars multiplayer, there are TONS of ways to play and counter your enemies, and it makes the game "complex" in its own use of simplicity. Can be super casual or super competitive depending on how you play. (The only downside I have seen to Halo Wars in multiplayer is people quitting early because the enemy has the ever-so-slightest advantage and is too lazy to counter it) Also not to forget that the Definitive Edition includes all the DLC from console meaning that there are more gamemodes to be played too over the base game!
Now the Campaign:
It has a wonderful campaign! It shows the Halo universe from a different standpoint just like Halo: Reach and Halo 3 ODST but in an RTS style. The campaign has pleased me greatly and even more so in Legendary Co-op with a friend. The cutscenes in the game still look amazing and they were made in 2009 (With a few revamps just like the actual game itself in the Definitive Edition) there are a few flaws though mostly when it comes to the setup of the missions. Nothing too large, just a few personal tics such as the Covenants spam of useless units sometimes which in its own regard is fun to mow them down, but doesn't offer the biggest challenge. Other than minor things like that, its great overall

Is there anything more sublime than a round of minigolf with your buddies? Some of my fondest childhood memories were of birthday parties at the putt-putt course, and even as an adult I sometimes cajole my co-workers into a round or two. Like the name suggests, Golf With Your Friends aims to capture that same simple joy, and does so with an ever-growing list of content and features.
When I first jumped into GWYF there were but three courses to choose from, Forest, Oasis, and Twilight, at 18 holes apiece. Forest hews closest to what you remember of minigolf, with the classic windmill, Plinko drop, and river jump holes. Oasis is an Egyptian-themed course with longer, more elaborate holes that cross over and send the ball flying through the clear desert sky. Twilight is a significant jump in difficulty, with unforgiving ramps and pits that might require half a dozen or more strokes to get just right. Added to those now are Haunted, Candyland, and Ancient, which vary even more in challenge and variety of scenery.
Navigating these courses is as easy as click, drag, and release. Your mouse aims your shot and you pull back to fill the four-part power bar, which gives you a wide range of control over the ball. Everything from feather-light taps to line drives are possible, and the holes you encounter will require them all. There's definitely a learning curve to the courses, a large part of that being no preview or free camera to scout your shots so learning the courses is expected. Once you have the lay of the land, the challenge becomes learning just the right finesse to put on the ball to overcome the traps. I could come close to par on all the courses after just a round or two, but it does require come patience to learn the more insidious holes.
That's probably going to be the biggest hangup for anyone looking for a casual golfing experience, honestly. GWYF isn't really here to simulate a real-world putt-putt outing, but rather a fanciful, hectic, arcadey approximation of the sport. Holes can be huge, sprawling, and require you to carom balls off of statuary, comestibles, and levitating decor. Getting some of the gimmick holes right can take dozens of shots and while replicating that success isn't too hard, having the patience to suss it out might be an uphill battle. Especially with the uphill holes.
At least the interface is simple enough to get you into a game almost immediately. Since this golf is intended to be enjoyed with (your) friends, every game is set up as a hosted server. Choosing to join gives you a handy browser with all the filters you could want, and hosting plops you down with name, password, and custom game options. One nice touch is that the lobby itself is a practice hole where you can putt around different obstacles while waiting for the match proper. And then there are loads of alternate modes and silly options to enable if you just want to fool around with your balls. The player base seems pretty chill as well and it's always easy to find a match, even if it's not necessarily the course or options I might want at the moment.
The graphics have been improving along with the content, taking ever-fuller advantage of the Unity engine to render its hazards and accouterments in excellent detail. The sound design is less ambitious, featuring a peppy, looping soundtrack and only the most basic effects. Obviously you're going to have more fun if you have the titular Your Friends to play with, but even going in solo there's plenty of fun to be had. Even in its early state, Golf With Your Friends contains enough fun and adventures to make it worth your time.

I've played Chivalry for awhile, I'm not sure why I haven't written a review for it.
Chivalry is a first to third person medieval combat game. Although it is far from realistic, it is entertaining in the gameplay aspect, with certain /heavy/ flaws to it. Being able to combo overheads, lunges and horizontal swings fluently with only a break if the enemy is capable of parrying in time is astounding. Getting struck during the wind-up phase can make you flinch, which will lose the wind-up, a good idea not a lot of games impliment. If the enemy is a capable man of parrying, you can feint to trip him up, although the feint is capable of being countered by timing your parries to be at the exact moment.
Combat is fast and lethal, with a variety of weapons that suit your interests, with multiple classes that function better in certain ways, such as the Man-At-Arm's ability to dodge back, the Vanguard's ability to leap into the enemy and the Knight's ability to one hand a two handed weapon, and couple it with a large shield. They've recently added the ability to customize your character for each class, as well as purchase special cosmetic items that in no way give the buyer an advantage in combat. Mods are regularly released and community content is sometimes permitted to be official.
The voice-acting is entertaining and very well done. There's even a war-cry button handy while you're sprinting.
Unfortunately, Chivalry suffers from a very extreme problem. Sword dragging is an exploit in which the user will tilt their camera at an angle so as to do a overhead swing on you, while their backs are turned to you, or stabbing into you well after your parry is over. It has become a common trend and used by the players that have played for a long while and rather than taking the chance of upsetting this small number of would-be customers, or perhaps being too lazy to fix it themselves, Torn Banner has simply allowed it to carry on for the time being.
If you are a new player in this game, do not leave the low rank servers until you can't play in there anymore. If you are interested in getting into Chivalry, you shouldn't buy it at full price, because I personally believe laziness shouldn't be rewarded. It is, at its core, a good game, and at the very least you should buy it on sale. s

You join the game with romanticized expectations of this great adventure in a world full of extinct, mildly fantastic and overall amazing creatures. And this may persist, as long as you play without other players or on a PVE server. To me playing in a player-wise peaceful environment would rob the game off a lot of spectacle and in the long run ruin the experience, because the focus shifts toward the game's PVE mechanics. With so many bugs, on laggy servers in particular, ARK does not have the same longevity as it has with PVP involved.
PVP in ARK makes it a sandbox experience akin to games like EVE Online, even though mechanically it lacks a lot that these kinds of spreadsheet simulators have. Because players are a constant, everlasting and game-changing threat, everything soon evolves around establishing friendly relationships, optimizing your game (settings-wise), your base and your general playstyle to fit the lurking horror, that is a complete wipe of everything (or depending on how well you hid things or what allies you shared your accomplishments with) you built, tamed and did for the past hours, days, weeks or even months. In that sense, the game is quickly losing a lot of its dino romance and turns into a continuous grind of rebuilding and learning from your mistakes to eventually adapt to this hostile environment and meta-game.
Both the PVE and the PVP experience have their flaws, because the game is far from perfect and more than once will you shake your head, how the developer Studio Wildcard was able to even release the game with such a seemingly easily fixable, but annoying bug. And naturally, they're both not for everyone.
Do I recommend this game though? Yes, I do, to both PVE and PVP players. While I think PVE outlasts itself rather fast, it will still get you well over a hundred great hours of gameplay in, and for some it may easily cross the 1000 hours mark. Either way, it's worth the price. PVP is recommendable to anybody, who is accepting of the fact, that none of their efforts will last forever, and that every base will be taken down eventually. Every. Base. Even the largest megatribes with hundreds of people working on them lose their bases to raids, that last days and days on end. In the beginning you will lose everything over and over again until you learn how to adapt and how to at least save your most precious assets: For example animals. Animals you may have been breeding for months and even years to optimize their statistics and make them compete with bloodlines all over the world. Or just PVP trophies from killing newbies or attacking large tribes and taking something away from them. Or rare materials. Or structures helping you rebuild an equally suitable base in no time. Or...
Either way, PVP easily offers you thousands of hours of grief and joy in an alternating fashion. I personally love the game and was able to overlook most of the shortcomings very quickly in the face of the overall, greater picture unfolding behind them. That does not mean I stopped shaking my head - trust me, I still do - but I am also grateful for one of the most fulfilling gaming experiences I ever had. I racked up nearly 1100 hours in less than three months, at times playing 12h+ daily. But because the game is so consuming, especially since it's a real time race against all other players on your server cluster, I eventually decided to live outside of the game's world and tend to the love of my life, which I have been unjustly neglecting for way too long.
To everybody else: Have a great time hunting, taming and breeding dinos, delving into small- or large-scale politics, battling other players with or without dinos, blowing up people's essence of their time and throwing insults in bad English at each other (really one of my favorite parts of the human interaction, always had something to laugh). Just make sure you are prepared for some really annoying bugs (which you will eventually learn to work around for the most part) and losing everything you worked for over and over again, each time learning more and more about the game as a result.

In L.A. Noire you play as Cole Phelps and begin with him joining the LAPD. During your game he rises through the ranks in the force. However don’t expect to see Cole react to his amazing progress in the police with anything other than a blank expression. This is indicative of on overarching problem the game has. While the story tries to make Phelps a compelling character there is a glaring disconnect between him and the player. You never see his family despite their existence being important to the plot. While you see moments from his time at war they never feel overly impactful. I didn’t care about Phelps which in a story like this is a deal breaker.
The game focuses far too much on the technology that went into making it. While the facial recognition technology used is amazing that isn’t what makes a good game. The facial expressions are often laughably over the top (which is understandable when you think that it is actors being told to ‘look like your lying’) and destroy the immersive experience the game is trying to present. It often ends up with characters being too far inside the uncanny valley for them to be truly relatable
However the game world is beautiful and represents 1940s Los Angeles very well. It’s obvious that a lot of time and research went into creating this world. It is full of landmarks, street crime and collectables to find. Yet the game lets you skip every driving section where you would have a chance at finding them. This feels like two games squashed together. One a detective based drama and one a GTA style action game in 40s LA. My issue is these two styles don’t fit as well together as they could and so the game feels split with neither mechanic living up to its potential.
This game can be buggy and sometimes you don't know what the truth or doubt mean in a situation but it is an amazing game with an deep question asking story. It is worth buying!

What you probably don’t know is that Halo Wars was the final release of Ensemble Studios (Age of Empires). Sadly, even prior to the release of Halo Wars they had been marked for closure. Despite strong sales and a good reception, the writing was on the wall and even the game seemed to be a one-off.
Pros
+Game has aged very well and transferred well over to the PC
+Very smooth and visual upgrades are well made
+Game is easy to understand and play
+Strips down Real Time Strategy for use on a controller
+Lots of love for the Halo Universe
+Multiplayer has lots of modes
+Online Co-op for Campaign
Cons
-Reuse of Assets can be a bit obvious
-Not a game for experienced RTS players
-Limitations from the original release are needlessly kept in the game where removing them would improve it
-Not a real definitive edition, more of a graphical remaster
-limited options available
I feel it’s important to get this information out at the beginning, as sort of a disclaimer. Especially, for those that may have played the original Xbox 360 version. Since there could be some that wonder if it’s worth picking up a Steam VersionOther than running at a smooth 1080p and 60 FPS and including all the DLC, which is mainly multiplayer maps. It also runs up to 4K on PC. Everything about Halo: Wars Definitive Edition is exactly the same, as its Xbox 360 counterpart.
Personally, I’m not someone that plays RTS games. Give me a Strategy Role-Playing Game and I’d probably give it a shot. RTS games just have too much going on for me to understand. The draw to the original, like for many others, was probably the Halo tie-in. Being a huge fan of the Halo universe, it gave me a reason to want to play the game. Ensemble and Microsoft absolutely honored that by showing some major love and affection to the Halo lore. From the moment a player starts the game, they are treated to familiar looking menus. Music akin to what’s in the other games. Not to mention, campaign and multiplayer modes.
what I enjoyed is how easy it was to setup a base and get units rolling quickly. I wasn’t bogged down with minutia of selecting through so many kinds of units. It was easy to see where the upgrades were and the game explained them. So, I could decide if I wanted to use medics or instead use the healing ability. Then, the focus could go on something else. This goes even further, once there are missions where you are tasked with multiple bases.
However, this may be where the game falters a bit. The over simplification can create situations where you just keep pumping out the same units every mission. Controlling multiple bases on the later missions at higher difficulties does add some chaos and variety though. Ultimately, the campaign is more preparation for the multiplayer. Regardless of difficulty, the campaign is fun. But there’s not many situations where your base will get overrun. Especially, if you figure out how to keep bases protected,
Conclusion:
Halo Wars: Definitive Edition acts as a good remaster of what has shown itself to be a game that stands the test of time fairly well. Still inhibited by restrictions implemented due to its Xbox 360 origins, it still manages to be fairly enjoyable and look pretty decent while doing it.
My verdict: 8/10 play it if you are a big HALO fan.

Disclaimer: I played this during a free weekend.
I'm a 4X veteran (Alpha Centauri, various Civ games) but not a megafan. I'm rating this thumbs-down because this game, despite being relatively new, still keeps many of the failings of 4X games from decades past (ending fatigue, randomness, overcomplicated-but-unspoken rules) and is altogether littered with small and annoying issues.
First the good:
- The presentation and user interface are very good. The artists, musicians, sound engineers, and writers should all be proud of themselves. I appreciate the satire and random humor sprinkled throughout, that while many parts of the game are serious (the tech and planet descriptions painting how brutal life would be on some of these planets), it still knows it's a video game (you can find a mushroom that causes "craving for pastries".)
- The races are mostly unique. There are are couple with mostly standard gameplay, like the Empire and Lumeris. But everyone has some weird race-specific attributes you have to play around.
- None of the planet types are outright "bad" or "useless". Barren planets may not be very good at supporting life, but their science output is excellent.
- The diplomacy mechanics are one of the better I've seen, incorporating influence (political pull), and allowing demands or forced truces when they'd make sense. War and peace are means to an end -- though you can still aim at wiping your enemies off the map.
But I have a lot of complaints too:
- Early on, you can only colonize reasonably nice planets (anything sunny and green), and these serve as the drivers of population growth. With unfavorable RNG, you might not find many of these nearby and be stuck on very few systems or have your empire spread out too much. The tech to colonize other planet types is low in the tree, but they'll grow slowly without a "food planet" or more technology.
- Many of the enhancements are geared toward certain planet configurations (e.g. this improvement gives "more food on Hot planets"). Unless you're really powering through research for system improvements, you'll soon reach a point where remaining improvements won't have much impact if built. So either you sit idle, or build lots of and lots of military (which is discouraged through upkeep and the manpower mechanic, but not discouraged *enough*).
- You aren't allowed to colonize many systems before you start taking an increasing happiness penalty empire-wide, encouraging you to grow "tall" rather than "wide". But the maps in general are pretty big, and conquered enemy systems become yours, easily putting you over the limit as you go for a military victory. For some reason the option to abandon a system was greyed out on many of my systems, and the game did not explain why.
- Maximum population in a system is only shown in one place, which is inconvenient if you want to see at a glance who is nearing max pop, or who has room to receive immigrants.
- The random quests are a neat idea, but not always achievable. I understand that they're meant to be inconvenient and you won't succeed at every one, but some were just impossible. When playing as the Lumeris, the main storyline wanted me to increase political support for Industrialists. That's very hard for a race that naturally favors Pacifists, and when my otherwise idle systems are pumping out military vessels (increasing Militarism).
-Huge ending fatigue, where once you pull ahead there's no mechanic for others to catch up. Granted I played on Normal as I learned the game. Certainly the harder difficulties offer more challenge across all turns.

This game may seem like a RTS game, but it's more of an RPG.  You play as a dynasty, all characters in your bloodline.  The game can get really tense, or actually quite funny.  There's a learning curve, but other than that, it's easy to get into once you know how to play.  It's only just about a gigabyte, and I couldn't recommend a Paradox game more.  Seriously, you can SEX someone to death.  WHAT MORE DO YOU WANT.

If you like games with emergent story (That is, the story is created through your gameplay rather than pre-written), than this is an excellent game for you.  I'm on about my 4th or so dynasty, and I love the drama that comes out of pulling off some clever tricks of politics or military strategy.
For example: In my most recent game, I started as the to-be-King of Sweden.  I united Sweden before the end of my first character (when you die, you switch to playing your heir), and spent my second generation adding Norway and pieces of Ireland and Holland to the mix.  I was having some problems in the heir department though, even with 3 young concubines all I was producing was daughters (about 6 of them).   Worried about how the Norse would react to a female ruler, I sighed with relief when I finally got a son... only to have him murdered in his crib by his eldest sister.  I banished her from my kingdom and then fortunately had another son... and then a third.   This was a problem, because as the King of Norway and of Sweden, my sons would each inherit a different country, dividing my empire in half right as I prepared to go to war with Denmark to unite Scandanavia.  Unfortunately, I died of old age before I could come up with a solution (like murdering one of the sons, or finding some other way to disinherit them).
So now I was the 5 year old king of Sweden, and my 4 year old brother was king of Norway.  Within a week, both kingdoms were in open rebellion.   I was able to help my little brother keep his throne initially, but when a section of the Sumonesko to the north declared their independence, I wasn't able to hold off the wars and I had to surrender the Throne.  Deciding the best solution would be to get myself killed and pass my titles to my little brother, I placed myself under the mentor ship of a 21 Intrigue vassal who hated me.  This surprisingly did not result in my death, but instead I hit 16 with a 21 in Intrigue myself.  I murdered the king who had overthrown me, and then his oldest daughter, mostly out of spite (but also to keep the realm in chaos while I finished the war with the Sumonesko).  Finally, I was ready, and declared war on the child-Queen-usurper and found about 3/4ths of the nation willing to join me (the same ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s who threw me off the throne 15 years ago, mostly).  I retook the throne and I'm recovering Norway and the north from the barbarians who moved in, and preparing once more to move on Denmark.  Long live Sweden!

I've played Chivalry for awhile, I'm not sure why I haven't written a review for it.
Chivalry is a first to third person medieval combat game. Although it is far from realistic, it is entertaining in the gameplay aspect, with certain /heavy/ flaws to it. Being able to combo overheads, lunges and horizontal swings fluently with only a break if the enemy is capable of parrying in time is astounding. Getting struck during the wind-up phase can make you flinch, which will lose the wind-up, a good idea not a lot of games impliment. If the enemy is a capable man of parrying, you can feint to trip him up, although the feint is capable of being countered by timing your parries to be at the exact moment.
Combat is fast and lethal, with a variety of weapons that suit your interests, with multiple classes that function better in certain ways, such as the Man-At-Arm's ability to dodge back, the Vanguard's ability to leap into the enemy and the Knight's ability to one hand a two handed weapon, and couple it with a large shield. They've recently added the ability to customize your character for each class, as well as purchase special cosmetic items that in no way give the buyer an advantage in combat. Mods are regularly released and community content is sometimes permitted to be official.
The voice-acting is entertaining and very well done. There's even a war-cry button handy while you're sprinting.
Unfortunately, Chivalry suffers from a very extreme problem. Sword dragging is an exploit in which the user will tilt their camera at an angle so as to do a overhead swing on you, while their backs are turned to you, or stabbing into you well after your parry is over. It has become a common trend and used by the players that have played for a long while and rather than taking the chance of upsetting this small number of would-be customers, or perhaps being too lazy to fix it themselves, Torn Banner has simply allowed it to carry on for the time being.
If you are a new player in this game, do not leave the low rank servers until you can't play in there anymore. If you are interested in getting into Chivalry, you shouldn't buy it at full price, because I personally believe laziness shouldn't be rewarded. It is, at its core, a good game, and at the very least you should buy it on sale. s

Well, what can I say? L.A. Noire is a pretty good game, and definitely one of the most unique ones I've ever played.
Where do I begin... well... (I hope I'm not accidentally spoiling anything here)
So there isn't that much of a 'story.' It's a series of *mostly* unrelated missions, broken up into an intro, four 'desks' and a side story that ties in near the very end of the game. The intro begins with the main character discovering his talent of investigation, while patrolling as a police officer. Then, he is assigned as a detective, working in four different departments, known as 'desks.' Then, in the last two desks, the main 'story' begins to take shape, and a second playable protagonist is introduced.
L.A. Noire is definitely one of the most unique games I can remember playing. Most of the gameplay is the investigation of many (and sometimes painfully hard) crimes, with some shootouts and chase scenes thrown in.
Unfortunately, this is a really LONG game. I spent so many hours playing through, and, near the end of the third desk, I became bored and took a month-long break from the game.
Nevertheless, the detective work in this game is quite interesting, even though it can be repetitive at times. Start a case, go to a crime scene, look around, find a lead, hunt someone down, find something that incrimidates them, yell at them, and throw them in jail. It's a bit of an oversimplification, but some missions boil down to that. However, there are plenty of interesting missions that don't. One of my favorites was the hunt for a serial killer, who left a series of clues around the city.
TL:DR, L.A. Noire is a good game for anyone who wants to take a break from 360 no-scoping and do some good old fashioned detective work.

I cannot stop playing this game, for it's one of the most refined blends of RPG and strategy I've ever been able to play. The strategy elements are interesting, but what truly makes Crusader Kings II unique is how it features characters that are, despite their titles and prestige, human beings who make mistakes, with their own desires, fears and failures. You actually get to play the lords that are part of your dynasty, to see their triumphs and failures happen before your very eyes. Few games offer the possibility of actually taking on the role of a lecherous duke, a king's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child, a widowed queen who had her husband assassinated, a multitude of characters that will make decisions that will shape the future of the game world, and these games are never as unpredictable, vast or complex as Crusader Kings II is.
It's a story generator, a huge sandbox full of random events and variables, a game in which even defeat and utter failure can become fun. You never know what'll happen when you start a game. You don't know which of your dynasty's members will end up killing his children for the good of the kingdom or accidentally giving birth to a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child that will be the cause of many problems for the entire nation. The game's complexity might intimidate most players at first, but after five hours, I had a good understanding of the game and I had tons of fun from then onwards. For history freaks, fans of sandboxes and people who like games that feature actual "role playing" in which you take on the role of a character and make meaningful decisions instead of simply playing as a soulless avatar, Crusader Kings II is a must-have. Consider buying the expansions if you really like the base game, as they add content to a game that is already extremely deep.

I've been a Halo fan for as long as I can remember, and Halo Wars was my first Halo game. My father was rather strict about M games when I was a child, so when he saw a T rated Halo game that required strategy he thought it would be a great learning experience. It took me years to realize it, but he's one hundred percent right. When I first played this I thought it was boring and had "no action", but as I've aged so has my realization that flashy set pieces and epic guns aren't the things that make games great. This game is a simplified rts, but that doesn't mean it's easy. One must understand the rock paper scissor system in place to take full advantage of their enemy, and find a play style which leads them to victory. Good game. The music is FANTASTIC. It fits the game like a glove, and the vocals are amazing. The whole concept of the game (the ability to morph into and out of shadows) is genius. The graphics are good, but the system requirements for max graphics are very high, so I had to play on less than max. The story is good but not fleshed out very much as there isn't much time to do so. I recommend it to anyone who enjoys fairly simple puzzles, but mostly enjoy story and just having a good time.

The gameplay should have been kept in "2D" (wrapping around the walls, but 2D control wise). Instead, it tries to keep you in 3D (without the shadow puppet stuff) most of the time.
The intriguing part of the game, using the shadows to move around, seemed like a lot of fun. Unfortunately, the main part of the gameplay seems to consist of moving lights or boxes to create those shadows where you want (without much in the way of real solving). The actual platforming across them, is only difficult by it being nearly broken. A lot of the time, I wasn't sure if I had glitched my way through, or solved the "puzzle". Really, the only puzzle is that you have to place the box so that it's shadow forms a super easy platform jump. This is made harder because the "targetting" system makes it hard to actual lock onto the object you want to carry. When there is any actual puzzle that isn't an immediate solve, it's only really difficult because of the trial and error of moving the light as well as shadow generators. But there isn't really any lateral thinking about it, just move a few things around.
The platforming, as a I mentioned is nearly trivial, made difficult only by the 3D controls being near broken, and the 2D having awkward physics (made worse by the fact that modern analog controls don't adapt well to it).
When not in the shadows (which is most of the game) it is all the broken camera and awkward controls (made worse when the camera suddenly changes the perspective forcing a control direction correction) of poor late 90's platformers. You are always wasting time either because the controls messed you up and you need to recover, or because you need to keep running back to the objects to manipulate into position yet again.
It is a shame, because the moments when you are using shadows made by things other than your own dragging boxes around (such as a sequence early on where characters are having an animated conversation, movbing their limbs all over the place), it is a hell of a lot of fun. If the game had been entirely this, moving from shadow to shadow as the scene plays out around you, I would have really enjoyed it.

I bought this for cheap and thought I'd give it a shot.  I was immediately disappointed.   The idea behind the game is great and the combat system is actually pretty well done too.  All of the different melee attack angles make for a fairly intricate duels and battles.  The game looks reasonably good too, so there are good things about it but...
It's VERY bad in terms of physics and collision detection.  Even simple stuff like units walking isn't done right.  The characters sort of glide along the ground while their legs move.  Melee combat, while really well done in theory, fails in a practical sense because of confusing collision detection and latency problems along with a screwy camera.  Whether you kill someone with a giant two-handed swing or miss them completely feels more like a dice-roll where you hope your latency, camera angle and timing combined properly.
Ultimately, the problem with this game comes down to how primitive the physics are.  Supposedly it's just a small indie dev and it shows.  Look up a video of Chivalry archery to see how pathetic the ranged mechanics are.  It will tell you all you need to know.

I am unsure what that balance should be but I am no longer enjoying what use to be an entertaining game. I witness creative tactics that have been progressively hardcoded out of the game. The high stakes nature of PVP means that a successful tribe needs a near 24 hour presence to fend off against offline raiding. Developers has on many occasions rolled out fixes that appears to wipe out alot of player's hundreds of hours of work. At this stage, you are better off purchasing another game and entertain yourself there. ARK has been balanced into mediocrity.

My friend plays the game like a geneticist, trying to breed the perfect ruler. I play the game constantly trying to spread whatever religion I'm playing, because it's obviously the only true religion.
With hundreds of playable characters and hundreds of different ways to play, I can see myself playing this for thousands and thousands of hours before I get bored of it. Heck, look at how much I've played already. Download this game, download the six important expansions (Ruler Designer, Sword of Islam, Legacy of Rome, The Republic, The Old Gods, Sons of Abraham) and then decide how you want to play! Conquer the world? Have one of your children elected Pope? Mend the Great Schism in the Christian Church? Establish the Jewish nation of Israel? That's just a tiny little bit of what you can do in Crusader Kings, and I can't recommend this enough!

I can recommend this game - with reservations.

Having said that - it's something of a masterclass in world building. It's a game world I wanted to explore and know more about. The voice acting is all terrific (though having the voice of Adam Jensen as the doting father unnerved me - I was waiting for him to start snapping necks any second), and the game looks sharp despite a complete and noticeable lack of anti-aliasing.
Worth it for a sale price. You can power through it in about three hours and I think it's worth it to see the intoxicating world this small 7-person team has built.

Contrast is one of those games that has a good premise - the idea of use light and shadows to create a separate bit of 2D puzzle gameplay from the normal 3D world, but the implementation from a story and setting as well as design is a bit disconnected.  The technical approach is good in how you can shift in an our of shadows, but the problem is that the areas you can do this in are very limited and separated from each other, making each puzzle its own microcosm.   The puzzles that use this aren't that difficult as well, with the most difficult ones being where you can either move objects to change shadows or the location of the light source. Again, with the puzzles being separate entities, these are one-stop problems as opposed to part of a larger difficult mechanism to figure out.
The story is interesting but it's hard to get into and leaves some questions on getting into the characters. Whether this is a fantasy, a dream, or something else isn't clear, and whether it is a flashback or the like.  As such, the game quickly devolves into just moving from puzzle to puzzle with story getting in the way.
It is still a decent game, but it's one I'd wait for a sale for, getting about 3 hrs of playtime from it.

-Memorable heroes: Cpt. Cutter, Dr. Anders, Sgt. Forge. Some of 'em we will meet again in the sequel.
-Decent AI to play against.
-The soundtrack.
-The kb/m controls feel solid, though they're not like the bulk of RTS's out there. Keep in mind that this game handles better with a gamepad.
Cons (so far):
-Gameplay locked at 60 fps.
-Cinematics locked at 30 fps.
-Haven't been able to find any matches in multiplayer (I'll update this as soon as this changes for me).

Go do it, but be wary, your vassals may start an independence war against you, or a jealous king may start plotting to murder you or your son, in which case your infidel, wroth and slothful sister will become your heir. While fighting wars is important, the core elements of this game is intrigue and diplomacy. Even the smallest county can become an empire if you have enough allies and a good spymaster who won't stab you in the back ...

I would extremely recommend this game. I adore history. The Middle Ages of Europe are definitely a great time to learn and know about. My favorite aspect of this game is the freedom. You basically can set your own goals, and I believe that is what makes it so replay-able for me. I also absolutely love the concept of lineage, and dealing with people. I love civilization, but Crusader Kings is so much more fun in my opinion.
I love dealing with mortal people instead of rulers who live forever. I love the interpersonal dealings with your character and others. Marriage, murder, and other things like dealing with depression and killing off numerous amounts of your children to achieve the desired heir. It's just a extremely great game. Dealing with famlies, and people is much more fun than just dealing with the kingdom, or whatever title you have.
I mean, I say things I never thought I would say after playing this game! I have to murder three of my children, kill my wife so I stop having children, castrate men to stop their family from producing, killing an entire family out of revenge. It feels so Shakespearean. I love it! Nothing feels better than murdering a whole family off after one member kills your son.
Let's not even talk about the multitudes of DLC for this game. Now, I'm normally against so much DLC but if it's done well I will give it credit. Pretty much every huge DLC pack for CK2 has expanded everything I thought this game could be. It's utterly amazing. I'm speechless.
So, 10/10 I would definitely recommend this game for strategy lovers, and people who like dealing with more than just basic politics, or crazy violence.
