A 2D/3D platformer where you can merge with walls to become a shadow. Utilize this to explore new possibilities in platforming.
The game is divided up into chapters and acts, which you can select from the main screen if you wish. However, the game is really short. I clocked in with about 4 hours on my first playthrough, an hour of which I don't think I was playing. In addition, some mechanic frustrations also prolonged my playthrough.
You play as a character named Dawn, whom only Didi can see. Didi is a child of a broken family who is trying to get back together leading to the different levels you encounter. Sometimes this leads to some interesting levels.
The game also tries to induce a little mystery of if Dawn is real or not and what exactly is she. However, the game doesn't go too far along that route that it doesn't really matter, especially at the end.
The graphics are okay. I had to run this on low settings so I cannot testify how great it can be besides online videos and pictures. I also wonder if the lack of some environment is a result of my computer or design. It does lead to some cool views. The shadow style is a pretty nifty idea that helps distract the player. As I was watching the cutscenes, I was wondering if people can be charmed by simply a shadow on the wall and a voice.
The game has a Jazz music style. It fits with the setting, and the vocals aren't bad in that respect.
The vocals are actually fairly good too. Didi can get annoying sometimes, but sometimes her actions actually brought a smile. It's interesting that Dawn is voiceless but I guess that's to keep the player guessing what she is exactly and if she's real.
This game had a lot of promise. The idea of manipulating shadows to create solid platforming makes it a small thinking game as well. When I was little, I used to contemplate how interesting it would be if you can become a shadow. This game allows me to play with that idea a little bit, but not as much as I would have liked.
You are given 5 basic controls for most of the game. Movement, Interaction, Shifting, Jump, and Dash. You also have control of the camera, which leads me to controller preferences. You do not want to play this game with a mouse and keyboard if you can avoid it. The camera is controlled with the mouse, which you also use for Dash and Shifting. This becomes a problem when you accidently move the camera while meaning to shift or dash. It has led me to many frustrations. The camera setting with the mouse is also too sensitive even after I adjusted it to get it right. When I switched to a 360 controller, the experience improved greatly. The camera was fine and my hands were less confused with which button was shift and which was dash.
This game has no action in it, which is good for this style. Since there are no enemies to fight, you can focus on the platforming and puzzles you are given. The promise of the game expands with the different mechanics you find in the different chapters. There is some room for exploration, but not too much freedom. ONe time when I wanted to wander, Didi would interfere and force me to continue.
Speaking of Didi, this game started to make me think about useless companions in video games; Didi is one of them. While you need to follow her to know what you next mission is, she never really helps you out. There is one occasion where she helps you out in the story and that is it. It's a shame because the image I posted near the top seemed to promise that you can use Didi to create an environment for you. There is one particular scene where I wish I could have controlled Didi to use something she was right next to instead of me doing something more complex than it needed.
One of the things that could use some fine tuning is the mechanics. I resorted to Gamefaqs for one thing only to find that I was doing it right all along, but the game mechanics would screw it up.  The glitch I'm referring to is the game forcing you or an object to shift out where it shouldn't. Eventually I got it to work, but I was still upset over the whole thing. Unfortunately, the mechanics would still be glitchy every now and then, forcing me to restart multiple times when I should have easily progressed. It's a shame too, because if it wasn't for the occasional glitchy mechanics, it would have been a solid platformer. The game does have some redemption on the matter by giving you multiple checkpoints to restart from when you die and it doesn't take too long to reload.
As mentioned before, the game is short and you can select specific chapters to play again. However, with the frustrations I encountered with the mechanics, and the story not being so grand, I probably would stay away from it for a while before trying to play again.
This is one of those little disappointments for me. The game has promise and it shows it in sparks throughout the game. Unfortunately, it never completely capitalizes on it's potential. It can give you an interesting experience, but I think I would have more faith if they did a sequel with solid mechanics. This is a game where you might want to wait for a good sale before you buy it (maybe $5-7).
My recommendation is for platforming fans who want to try something a little different. If you play with a controller and on a computer that can run it smoothly, then it is less frustrating and possible to enjoy.

Contrast, to put into a single word, is marvelous. Its graphics are well detailed, and the way that light is used in this game is borderline genius. The voicework is well done for all characters. The music is excellent, being very rythmic and jazzy. And the story is quite interesting. The collection of collectable that you can obtain is both expansive and impactful for the length of the game. The Bioshock-esque way of using collectables to explain plot points was well done. It was always interesting to read an article about a missing person, or seeing a picture of the "scientific" explainations of the shadow world. The light puzzles that are used are especially interesting because the game mechanic of switching between two worlds is wonderfully unique and fun. All of these factors really combine to create an incredible atmosphere.
However no game is without its imperfections. Though I do, in fact, recommend this game to anyone who wants a interesting experience, I must also explain the game's faults. Contrast has 2 major flaws which both fall into the gameplay category. The main problem is that Dawn, the main character, is incredibly floaty. She's a tad hard to control because her jump arc seems a tad unnatural. The second would probably be the camera. See the having the camera be controlled by the mouse is fine in third person, but when you enter the shadow world the camera tends to be kinda random, causing you to have to adjust your mouse in odd ways.
The small gameplay flaws that Contrast has pales in comparison to the experience of playing it though. Playing through the game is honestly just a marvelous experience, because of it's brilliant atmosphere, as well as its unique concept.

Crusader Kings II is an unbelievable game that I would recommend to anyone who has an interest in Medieval history. It's a slower game, and it takes a long time to really figure out how to play the game and maximize its full potential. This game focuses less on economy and warfare, and more on political decisions and your house (family dynasty). This is "Game of Throne" the videogame, it's a must-play, but very niche.
One of the best sratagy games I hae ever played

A definite must for those of you that want a good strategy game.
Paradox Interactive has a history of gems like Crusader Kings II that blends turn-based stretegy and some role playing elements. For instance, you can create a character that you can play in a historically accurate world and make decisions based on how you (or your character) would react.
So, let me discuss the strategy part of Crusader Kings II. Firstly, this is a must for those of you who like history. Secondly, for those of you that wish they could change things in history (like the Battle of Hastings) this is also a must. This embodies strategy because you must manage finances, wage war, secure the dominance of your dynasty, and conduct diplomacy all at once. This may sound a little overwhelming but it really isn't once you learn the mechanics. You can play as any King, Emperor, Count, Duke, Earl, Caliph, Emir, or Chief (assuming you have the corrent DLC) you see on the map. This allows for a great expanse of experiences without being terribly repetitive.
The role play aspect (albeit small) does make an appearance in thie game. Your character could be proud and greedy (both actual traits in the game) and could play the character accordingly. If your character is an ambitious count you could aim to become king or on the other hand remain static under a contented and slothful character. This is also why I reccomend the ruler creator because you can put yourself in history.
One awesome thing I find is the modding community (with my favorite mod being A Game of Thrones mod). It adds even more replayability to the game.
I have thusly spoken of the "pros" of the game and I now have inevitably come to the "cons". Firstly, combat is going to happen and you as the player have no control over it except when choosing certain modifiers like terrain or generals. Secondly, the music can be a bit repetitive so after playing for awhile, I recommend lowering the volume and putting on something in the background to counter it. Finally, and I find this to be the most annoying, is the constant civil strife once you become large and powerful. Your most loyal vassals will plot to lower crown authority or plant a pretender on the throne shortly after you give them a title in the first place, which I find to be a little rediculous. The most dangerous time to play the game is not during a war with a foreign power, but shortly after the death of your ruler.
So I really do recommend this game for you history buffs and strategists out there. It really is a must buy.

I had much higher hopes for this game. The premise is neat - you control Dawn who can literally "shrink into the shadows." However, the execution is poor; the controls are clunky; the story is cliche; the writing is atrocious; and the voice acting is grating.
The game is broken (intentional pun) into three acts and tells the story of Didi who is the only one that sees Dawn. While you can shrink into the shadows, the lights only light up in the areas where there is a puzzle. Everywhere else, there are no shadows. Given some of the platform jumping needed for the puzzles, the controls are wonky. They are extremely loose and the camera wanders which makes the POV confusing. Sometimes you will do a puzzle and the camera is in one location. The next time (because you fell) it is located differently and can't be moved to a better location because it is stuck or something.
There are collectables in the game that are easy to collect. They are usually in your path and have blue sparkles swirling around them. In addition, there are several luminaires in the level. These are balls of lights that can be used to power equipment. These are spread through the level - some in your path (enough to finish the level) others in harder to reach areas. However, in many cases if you don't get them you can't get them later. In order to get full completion, you have to start over. I did this several times. Frustrating...
There are no people in the game, other than Didi. Key story points are told through shadow figures. (My wife saw Didi's mom and made a comment that she wouldn't be able to stand and likely would end up on her face she was so top heavy.) This is interesting enough, but the shadows clip through the environment. Along with the voice acting, I was pressing the "Y" button to skip them. Some special swirling items activate "special" shadow show puzzles to flesh out the story.
Its not
bad. Some of the puzzles are clever. Act II is pretty neat. Didi needs to fix a circus for her dad. And as I said, the idea has potential, just poorly executed in my opinion. It is hard to recommend this game, especially at full price. Wait for a sale. A good sale and don't expect too much.

This game has been out long enough for you to find plenty of reviews and video gameplays (my favorite person to watch right now is Arumba at
- if you are reading this: multiplayer match?). There isn’t much I can say that hasn’t been mentioned before, so these are just my “two-cents.”
As to why I've spent a good part of my life playing this game: it has everything I liked from the Civilization and Total War series and what I missed from them. I was never really fond of the battles from Total War (I tended to just build unstoppable armies and quick-finish battles), but I loved the idea of managing an empire; there were elements of micromanagement missing that kept me from feeling like I truly ruled my kingdom and vassals. Civilization just felt too much like a board game and I’ve grown wearing of 4x games like it; empires run on gold, not finding where the iron is.
The game is complex in that there are a lot of moving parts that go into creating your future empire or reducing you to one county in another NPC's kingdom; it took me roughly two weeks before I hit the "I got it!" phase. However, I never felt like it was because the game was out to beat me since my downfalls were typically the result of my ignorance of the intricacies of running your own fiefdom. Who knew letting your brother rule some of your lands would lead to him having enough men to lead a revolt against you? Who knew that following anything but Catholicism would lead to the Pope granting invasions of your lands? Who knew that marrying a close relative to join two empires would lead to horrible heirs with inbred traits? Definitely not me at first!
There are also elements of humor sprinkled about that deserve a good laugh. I once had a reagent that kept trying to kill me and that last incident (these come up as pop-up windows) had him trying to stab me while yelling “Why won’t you die!?” There is also an assassination incident which makes note of a lone archer on a grassy knoll. While these are infrequent, they add something to give a chuckle at while to go from feeling king of the (western European) world to crying in shame that you lost it all to an inbred cousin.
I've bought all the expansions and DLCs because I truly enjoy this game! I have yet to find another strategy game (or any other game) that has be a joy to play even after several hundred hours.
PS - There is a multiplayer element, but I have yet to find a ruler-buddy to try that with.

L.A. Noire is about a detective named Cole Phelps that worked in post-WW2 late 1940s Los Angeles. Gameplay is open world and consists entirely of interviewing/interrogating people, chasing suspects with cars/on foot, shootouts with criminals, and walking around crime scenes or area of interest to find clues and evidence. This is a pretty unique game since it's made by Rockstar, which is well-known as the creator of GTA. You get to be the good guy this time, including chasing & ramming cars that will be ended with you busting the suspect GTA-Style (remember Busted scene in GTA? you're the cop here).  Even with obvious low-budget graphics, the story was very well made and the characters expressions (face and voice) are EXTREMELY 'alive' compared to other games. This is because you get to judge whether someone is lying or not by facial expression/voice tone. Ah, if you're a classic car lover, this game paid a lot of attention to them. In short, L.A. Noire is a very out-of-the-box interesting detective game that is definitely worth the price.
Now let's talk about the good things first. I'm no policeman and I have no experience in any police work, but I dare to say that with a huge amount of available cases and side missions, the game will definitely satisfy your thirst of 'problem solving' or 'mystery' or straight out 'detective work'. I definitely can't say it's realistic (apparently, shooting someone in the leg made fatal chest wounds) but it's...well-designed. The cases are all realistic with carefully designed motives and chain of events. You'll find the thrill of being in a crime scene looking for clues like footprints, shoe sizes, blood traces, injury marks, and other 'detective stuff'. You also get to judge whether someone is telling the truth or lying by looking into their faces and voice tone. Facial expression is carefully designed to show real-life 'lying' or 'truth' or 'holding out' expression (e.g. eyes looking left when lying). Bored of the same routine? Whenever you're driving, you'll receive dispatch calls that will give you side-missions. So yeah, the main advantage of this game is its well-designed gameplay.
The bad parts of the game is really not that much and does not affect the gameplay. Graphics looks very low-budget, it's as if they put all of the graphics money into character's facial expression realism. But in my opinion, it's still in the acceptable level. The weapon choice is also very limited, only Colt 45, Thompson, M1 Garand, and BAR. Since the game is not focused on the gun fights, this issue has miniscule effect.  And as a good guy, you don't get to do the legendary GTA reckless driving. You don't have to follow traffic rules and all but you can't run over pedestrians or ram cars that cut you off if you don't  want your case report to be ruined. Some of the cases are also pretty complicated, giving you a long list of person of interest and clues. This particular mission gave me the 'What am I doing? Who the heck is this guy? Whoa, now who are you? What's their connection to the case?' moment. But that's the fun part, right?
In conclusion, the gameplay is very unique and I don't think there are many open-world detective games out there. This advantage makes this game a 'must-play' for me and it's worth every cent. I spent over 13 hours and I'm not even a quarter finished of the whole game. The cons of the game is almost meaningless and it will not ruin the gameplay. I definitely recommend this game, it's worth it.

If you are a fan of strategy games, and more specifically, grand strategy ganes (ig. Civ) crusader kings 2 is a must have game. The game begins in the year 867, or 1066 depending on if you own the "The Old Gods" expansion or not, and you must guide a noble family through the medievel era. This may seem bland to someone without experience with paradox interactive grand strategies, but it is certainly not. This game is very similar  to Game of Thrones(there is a Game of Thrones mod also) imagine playing as the lannisters, starks or any family in westeros of signifigance. As in Game of Thrones, intrigue is paramount. I have countless times murdered my children and siblings in the name of preserving my realm and i have been assassinated by my siblings and brothers countless times also. Intrigue however is not the only component of CKII, military, religious, and economic gameplay is as rewarding as Intrigue. When all of these elements work together, the Game is damn good. Imagine you are the king of Sweden. Your younger brother is the King of Norway and your uncle is your vassel, duke of Lappland with a measly 4 holdings(counties, castles, cities, and temples/churches/mosques). Your spymaster is unskilled and your uncles plot to claim your kingdom for himself has gone unnoticed. Even if the kingdom of Sweden is the most powerful of nations, you can still lose a war to revolting vassles. Especially if a foreign king like your afformentioned brother helps the rebels. It is gameplay like this that you experience in crusader kings but so much more dynamic than i could ever hope to explain on paper.
In my opinion Crusader Kings II is the best grand strategy game ever, fans of the genre and newcomers alike can appreciate it: 9.5/10

Well, where do I begin? Halo Wars: the first RTS I played back on Xbox 360. It's highly underrated and has kept us waiting for eight years and finally it has been released on Steam. The wait was worth it as there are major graphical improvements, a resolution boost as well as all the DLC from the original game added. You should not hesitate to buy this game as it is cheap, highly addictive and always has you thinking of new strategies to defeat your opponents; whether AI or human.

The main mechanic of the game is very unique and quite fun to wrap your head around. Music is both haunting and enchanting all at once and the visual style is beautiful in an artistic- rather than purely technical, polygonal county way.
Controls are responsive though edge detection could use a little polish. There were times when a jump looks like it should've landed but the character 'bumps' the edge and falls. Luckily, the checkpoint system is very forgiving and no more than 5 minutes of progress was ever lost through multitudes of jumping off edges.
Level design Is a little inconsistent with a lot of levels containing linear solutions while others allow solutions that skip the entirety of the puzzles via jumping on objects in the 'real world' and dashing into the 'shadow world'. However, this is hard to fault as the shadow mechanics are very complex melding 2D and 3D puzzles across the levels.
The way the story is told is very unique as well. Since pretty much all the story is told in the 'shadow world', each scene feels like a snapshot of what's happening with a slight time leap in between each one. The pacing of the story is well enough that it never feels like a drag. There is a drive to see what's next. This is all backed up by some pretty fantastic voice acting with moments of melancholy, angst, and anger delivered with emotion.
The developers have left the ending a bit open for interpretation so those who are looking for a clear cut finish where everything is answered will be a bit irked. However, those who enjoy discussing interpretations with others will find a nice conversation with others in the same boat.
Though it might be a bit short time-wise, it doesn't artificially inflate the time to beat. So it's enjoyable from start to end.

What hasn't changed, for those of you who never played the 360 game, is how you can play the campaign (both solo or in co-op) and enjoy a rather unique experience from what you get in MP, while still learning the ropes of its core RTS designs (what units are good against what, etc).
343i and friends have done, and are doing, a great job on remastering this game. Which was made with an engine that never even ran on the PC, even in development. It was strictly a 360 game engine.
Whether you like RTSes, or don't. Whether you played the original or didn't. For $20, or even less in sale, there's no reason not to pick this game up. Especially if you want to vote with your wallet and show Microsoft that Steam is a good place to release all their games on as well.

Contrast's charm is evident from the moment you start the game. As soon as the first title screen comes up and you hear the stylings of 1920's blues, you know you're in for something different. Contrast takes place in an atmospheric France, 1923. You're a mute acrobat that can merge with shadows and you're followed by a little girl named Didi. Didi is the star of the game, her perfectly casted voice actor and her adorable lines will have you thinking "Who the hell is Ellie?". The noir aesthetic is reminiscent of Dishonored meets Bioshock meets Boardwalk Empire. The acting, story and scenery feel authentic to the era. The gameplay is perfectly simple, though the puzzle aren't much of a challenge. The past three years have been landmark years for the downloadble/indie game scene. The quality of absolutely great and relatively cheap titles rivals that of their AAA counterparts. Contrast is, without a doubt, a legend among it's peers; Bastion, Braid, Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons, Castle Crashers, Guacamelee, Insanely Twisted Shadow Planet, Journey, Magicka, Mega Man 9, rain, Shadow Complex, Skullgirls, Stacking, Super Meat Boy, Terraria, Torchlight II, Trine and more. In my opinion, the game tops most of those. There isn't much to say about the game's flaws. It's unfairly short; I collected every collectible, completed all of the achievements and still clocked in at 4 hours. A gem like this deserves to be a lengthened experience. Aside from the game's length, there is a clear lack of polish. Had Compulsion Games taking more time to test the game, we wouldn't have to be putting up with invisible walls or floors. While they weren't too frequent, they were uncomfortably noticable. At one point I left a building, turned around to go back into the open door and couldn't because of an invisible wall. I walked forward a bit and came back and was able to go back into the building. Though I am convinced these blemishes are related to an overbearing publisher wanting to rush their investment out,  small details like these and the game's length are the only thing that keep it from being a perfect game in my book. Anyone looking for a unique experience, pick Contrast up. It will definitely continue to go on sale, so do yourself a favor when you see it marked below it's normal price of $15.99. Games like this, from independent developers are on the rise, and as gamers it's up to us to support their new ideas in an effort to show the multi-million dollar publishers/developers that bigger isn't always better.

Crusader Kings II is an exceptional game in that no other title will make you feel like a ruler as well as it. You're not just a country, like in other grand strategy games. You are a ruler with qualities, flaws, vices and virtues. You can be a Duke who is a brilliant diplomat with a hunchback, an ugly, stuttering dimwit count, or a mastermind plotter/lesbian queen. (I'm NOT making it up). And you can be all that within in a single playthrough, as you re-incarnate into your heir when you die. You have to be good at managing your realm, but you've got to be even better at managing your dynasty by arranging favourable marriages, assassinate pretenders... It's all very involving and requires a lot of micro-management (which you may or may not like).
It's not without flaws: the interface could see much improvement and the game starts to slow down when you become powerful. By slow down, I don't mean that your computer has a hard time coping, I mean that there are many more events that require your constant attention, making things move at a slower pace. To be honest, after several hundred hours, I think I'm a bit burned with the game. And that, even though there are entire DLCs I haven't really explored yet: I have only really played as a Catholic or Muslim ruler, but DLCs let you play as pagans, Orthodoxes, republics...
And then there are a couple of Mods that are probably worth exploring as well: "Game of Thrones" and "Tamriel" (from the Elder scrolls series)
Still, with so much content and the unbeatable feeling of being an actual Middle-Ages ruler, it's hard to rate CKII anything lower than a 9 out of 10.

This is a solid puzzle platformer, if a little short and rough around the edges. Primary mechanics feature the protagonist moving into and back from the wall, as a shadow. There is an interesting motif associated with this which ties into the story of the game which I'll leave for the user to find out, but it's done in a way that I've not seen in a game before.
The controls are a *little* loose, and there seems to be a little edge detection problems when it comes to the shadow movement. However, it's rarely overly frustrating. I will say that (with one or two exceptions), the puzzles seem rather straightforward, and even devolve into box puzzles despite the short length of the game - so some folks might find that a little disappointing.
The one thing that the player should probably be aware of going in, though, is that the story is rather weighty, dealing with some rather serious topics (abandonment issues, deadbeat parents, etc). When I first booted up the game I was looking for something a little more whimsical, so it caught me off guard. Please note that this is not a mark against the game - simply something that I was not expecting, and which other players might want to know going in.
Overall, I'd recommend it for folks who are looking for a short, stylistic puzzle platformer.

This is one of my favourite games, ever. It has a charm to it that won't let me go, I play it with my friends both online and playing swapsies couch multiplayer and every loves it, even if we do suck at this game, we thoroughly enjoy it. Of course it has its obvious drawbacks so check out my first 'proper' review below.
Here is a pros and cons list from my point of view.
GAMEPLAY
Pros:
- Fun.
- Simple to grasp the basics - Left mouse button, scroll up, scroll down (attacks). Right mouse button (block).
- Difficult to master, but SATISFYING when you do (attacks, blocks, timing, situational awareness, reflexes and movement incorporated together).
- 4 DISTINCT classes, allowing for varied styles of play. (Archer, Man at Arms, Vanguard and Knight).
- A large number of weapons varying in: Speed, reach and damage (you can also purchase cosmetic weapons skins from the in-game customisation (real money micro-transactions).
-  Removable limbs.
- Horrifying glitches.
- Siege weaponry.
- Grab a controller, some beers and link up to a TV, it is fun played with friends as a swapsies couch multiplayer game as well as on your own.
- Not pay-to-win, unless you are willing to pay with your blood, sweat, tears and sanity.
- The voice overs are hilarious and so overused that they only get funnier.
Cons:
- 'Exploits' which allow people to painstakingly wrench their puny wrists across the desk with mouse in tow, the middle button scrolled upwards parallel to their throbbing erection as they gleefully murder you in a crouched poise with such an unnecessary amount of effort that it almost tires you out to the point where you are passed out in your own naked, sweating lap.
- People can be bothered to exploit.
Overall: Very positive. This game is challenging but even when death drags you down to the crustiest depths of hell, your (most-likely) amusing demise will take the edge off the rage. Just enjoy yourself, its what we're here for!
GRAPHICS and ANIMATIONS:
Pros:
- Yeah they're not bad at all, if you're a graphics buff then it isn't the best, but it'll do. The gameplay compensates for the lack of next gen graphics and I don't even play on full settings.
- Animations are overall pretty nice.
- Dependent on the map, environments are usually very nice and distinct from map to map. The workshop and community creation incorporation has allowed for numerous more new, creative and fun maps.
Cons:
- The graphics aren't amazing, but they're good enough, stop complaining.
- Animations glitch sometimes, especially death animations, but who cares we're having so much fun.
Overall: Very positive.
COMMUNITY:
Pros:
- Some people are very amusing.
- Very well-integrated user generated content, many interesting maps, armour and weapon skins.
- Mods, mods, mods! Everywhere! Thank you creatives!
Cons:
- So much butt hurt you'll think you are playing the Sodomy Simulator 2015.
- Team killing is rife, do not go afk unless you wish to be either slain or kicked within roughly 15 seconds of you leaving your computer to grab a bag of quavers.
- Keep your quavers or other such crisp snacks nearby.
Overall: Mixed. A lot of really very lame people about but oh well, there is a fair share of decent guys and gals though. Death isn't as fun to deliver when it doesn't result in butt ache anyway, right? And anyway, who else is going to create sweet mods?!
CUSTOMISATION
Pros:
- It exists.
- It has fair depth, enough to make clear variations in players, especially in free-for-all where your colours cloth and shield patterns are entirely of your choosing.
- There are micro-transactions, but only for cosmetic features which do not change gameplay mechanics, makes you look pretty rad though. (Reasonably priced in my opinion too).
- You can make your own distinct look without having to purchase in-game skins.
- User crafted weapon skins and helmets are heavily incorporated here. 3D artists come join in the fun!
Cons:
- Micro-transactions, but it helps keep Torn Banner developing so its kind of a plus-minus.
Overall: Yeah!
DEVELOPERS (TORN BANNER):
Pros:
- Responsive.
- Fairly regular updates.
- They encourage community creativity.
- They have a sense of humour.
Cons:
- They need to fix a vast number of balance issues in the game such as team balancing and hitboxes were apparently changed for the worse a while back. Then again I'm happy with the hitboxes, they seem reasonable to me.
- The updates don't often do a huge amount to fix faulted mechanics, historically it has made it worse at times! However the community is speaking up about it more and so hopefully changes will occur.
Overall: Not bad, they made a good, fun game and are engaged with their following. They also haven't ran off with all our money, not yet anyway.
CONCLUSION: Yeah it is a great game, it has obvious downfalls but a lot of them are in the community itself! This is a shame because its kind of making what could be one of the most FUN and SATISFYING games on the market seem a bit less... fun ...
But please, consider buying this game, I'm not great at it and rarely end with a K/D ratio above 1.00, but who cares? Its genuinely an amusing and pleasing game to play, its about showcasing your skills and helping your team. Just enjoy yourself and immerse yourself in a low-fantasy, gritty, humorous, gory and glorifying realm of melee combat (♥♥♥♥ off archers).
------
Hopefully this was helpful, it is my first 'actual' review, so feedback is appreciated.
Feel free to add me, I play this a fair bit with my friends and missus so do come and join us!

To keep this review short and simple, since I'm terrible at writing reviews, but I feel like I really need to express how much I love this game, eventhough it has quite a few of problems.
The world in this game, the environment, the feel, I absolutely
it. Driving around in a car, seeing all the other traffic, the people on the sidewalk, the things the people say, the whole atmosphere in Los Angeles, maybe it is far off from reality, but to me it feels very real.
The cars, I love how this game is filled with branded cars, I love these old american cars, and I love the effort put in to have the cars done properly in this game.
The world/environment/city. It is huge, and I love it. Maybe there is little to do, but I still love it. Combined with the whole 40s feel and all, it still is a great experience to just go drive around and explore stuff. I just had this first case where a car full of blood is on the tracks. Well, afterwards I took my Military car I took from the military base before, and drove around the train tracks, and it just amazes me how much detail there is in a place you never really are going to visit otherwise. I just parked the car on the train yard and walked around abit. Then I drove around the city abit, getting out of the car at some places admiring some places, seeing a boy at a fruit stand shouting, seeing the magazines on a shelf at a theatre. I LOVE how this game is filled with details that serve no real purpose to the story themself. How the developers went out of their way to create this huge world, absolutely FILLED with streets, a world full of places the story itself doesn't use. Unlike games like GTA, also big worlds, but they don't compare to this. GTA V is a big world, but it's stuffed full of different things, none of which come close to the scale of LA Noire. There is this desert in GTA V, I was looking forward to exploring it, but turns out it was just a few streets, a small yellow splotch in the middle of the map. But in LA noire, it is absolutely huge, it really adds something combined with the detail put in and the fact that it's set in the late 40s.
All in all, this is a very rare gem of a game to me personally. I am very sad to see no LA Noire 2 coming out, or any other game like this. No games that have such huge worlds to explore, experience, worlds filled with detail, worlds build on a real size scale. Sure it was still pretty empty, but still, the detail, the fact that it's set in the 40s, I still want to call this a proper game, though I'm afraid this only appeals to a rather niche part of the gaming community :(
And not to forget, ofcourse, the game itself, Cole Phelps. I loved it, maybe it's rather simple, but i love the detective game. Always wanting to advance the story, see what's next. Though it sadly isn't very replayable. After having played it once, the curiosity is gone, because you know in each mission what the real story is. You already know the answer to the puzzle, which is a bit of a bummer. But the world itself still hasn't gotten old though.

Allow me to preface this review by noting that this playing this game has made Skyrim's combat seem trivial at best. That coming from someone who has played Skyrim for over 700 hours across PC and Xbox 360, and considers it one of the finest 1st person combat games.
Chivalry: Medieval Warfare is an online-only competitive game where two teams (the blue Agatha Knights and the red Masonic Order) battle in a variety of maps and gamemodes. Player limits vary per server; the most common caps are at 24 and 32 for Team Deathmatch and Team Objective, but there are also 36, 40, 64, and even 70 person servers.
Team Objective focuses on, in most cases, one faction besieging the other in some sort of scenario, whether it be the Masonic Order sacking an Agatha keep or the Agatha Knights freeing their king, Feydrid (who is played by Agatha's best player) from a Masonic prison (there are many more objective scenarios I won't list here). Players can interact with trebuchets, ballistas, pots of boiling oil, and more to decimate their enemies, defend their positions, and conquer their goals.
Team Deathmatch and Free-For-All are self explanatory.
Duel is a 1-on-1 gametype where two people fight to the death while the rest of the server watches in delight, preparing for their turn at combat. The rounds are cyclical, so everyone will get a chance to fight.
Where this game truly shines and stands out from the rest is its combat. As stated in the beginning of this review, the combat for Chivalry: Medieval Warfare is the most engaging, adrenaline-inducing mechanic I've ever experienced in a video game. You can chop off limbs, decapitate your foes, and deflect their hits in real time. LMB slashes, RMB blocks, scrolling the mouse wheel up stabs, and scrolling the mouse wheel down does an overhead chop. It is essential to know when to use which attack, as you can kill your allies just as easily as you can kill your foes. Do a wide slash in a tight space and you may very well have just accidentally decapitated the buddy to your left.
Combat is focused on hitting only when you know you'll do damage; miss an attack and you'll lose vital stamina used to recover from attacks and successfully parry/block. Many 1-on-1 fights are epically drawn out because of this, rather than the "button-mash 'til their dead" tactic of games like Call of Duty, Skyrim, Dragon Age, etc.
The combat of Chivalry obviously has a pretty decent learning curve; while I have only played the game for around 10 hours or so, 4 of them were spent wholeheartedly learning the tactics and methods of each class.
Speaking of classes, you can play as an Archer who can use bows, crossbows, javelins, and throwing spears, a Man-at-Arms who can use mid-range swords and axes, a Vanguard who can use polearms and halberds, and and a Knight who can use mauls, heavy swords, and double-headed axes. Each class has their own advantages and disadvantages.
Archers are fast and nimble, as they should be, but are incredibly vulnerable at any distance that isn't long range. They are to be played with patience and mainly as a support and defensive role.
Man-at-Arms are your general fighter. They can hold their own in most situations, and can use shields to act as a frontal line while charging. They're a strong balance between speed and defense.
Vanguards, with their longer-ranged melee weapons, are best played defensively. Keep the enemy from reaching their objective by poking and lunging and they won't stand a chance. Use faster weapons like the Bilhook and you'll be quite formidable.
Knights are the tanks of Chivalry. With their heavy armor and even heavier weapons a single slash can rip you apart. They're the intimidation factor and are best taken on in groups.
Chivalry stands as a pillar upon which all other first person games should measure. However, not every aspect of this game is glorious. The community for Chivalry is atrocious. New players are battered with insults and kicking, and team killing is off the charts. People will team kill for not getting the seige equipment they want (which players vote for in the beginning of some objective matches), or will kill you just so they can steal the ballista out from under your corpse. Know that homophobia, racism, sexism, and the like are not blocked from chat (as is the case with most games, to be fair) so interacting with players via chat isn't for the faint of heart.
If you can get passed the terrible community, though, then Chivalry: Medieval Warfare is absolutely a game you should purchase. It will change your view of multiplayer games entirely, as well as every game that involves a bow or blade.

I figured I'd write a review for this since I've played the literal♥♥♥♥♥♥out of Halo Wars on Xbox 360 and later Xbox One.
First off I'll begin addressing the state of the PC-port. Surprisingly I've had very few issues with it. Halo Wars on PC features both mouse and controller support, the former works very well considering that the original game had no mouse support and the former also works just as well as it originally did.
PC controls (mouse & keyboard) are a bit un-orthodox when compared to other PC RTS games such as Starcraft II, Company of Heroes, etc.
Most of the keyboard hotkeys can be rebinded and while the controls are a bit ~funky~ at first they are easy to get used to.
My only problem right now with the keyboard controls is the lack of a proper multitask command (commonly shift) so as of now you can't units multiple commands.
Graphics-wise the game holds up well IMO and despite the requirements most machines should be able to play this on maximum with little to none impact on FPS and other performance. The game looks considerably better than the old 360 classic and you can't count the individual polygons on a model anymore.
Sound and visual effects are all on-point. As with the graphics the FX have also been updated (they look less cartoony too IMO).
As for the rest of the game it still hold sup if you ask me. I've always been a fan of Halo and I'm probably one of the few who loved the original game on Xbox.
The story, characters and environments are all interesting and I definitely recommend Halo Wars for fans of Halo or for people new to the RTS genre looking for a good introduction into strategy games.

TL;DR
I have first played Endless Space before Stellaris even existed. Than the game seemed to be quite complicated, and I didn't stick around for long. But when I saw the hype over Stellaris and played it, my first though was: "Ehm, it's 'Endless Space', but RTS(sort of) instead of turn-based". The game has so many similarities, that it is definitely not coincidence, considering that Enless Space was released 4 years earlier. Of course many 4X games take roots from "Masters of Orion" after all, but that's my impression.
TL;DR Endless Space 2 rating: 9/10 + unusual 'Endless Space' type of space combat.
Medium-length story:
I find second part much more friendly toward the new players, and the GUI is impressively convenient. That's an example all strategy games should take. I don't even know what to say to the players who say that it's difficult or inconvenient, IMHO, it's as good as it can be. The game is complex, thus requires basic patience, thus maybe play tutorial? The idea of tutorial is common with Stellaris - "adivisor" that gives suggestions and instructions as you play.
It has some specifics, especially regarding space combat and the maximum size of the fleet (e.g. 5 ships in fleet, but as many fleets as you want) - it's a controversial idea (Explanation: fleet fights one other fleet at a time. Meaning that if your fleet has capacity of 8 ships and enemy has 2 fleets 5 ships each - you fight 2 battles against 5 enemies each, instead of one against 10), as if it is a turn-based part within a turn-based game with a turn-based combat. Wow. But thinking of it, chess are much more stupid in that regard: they don't have damage system at all and also do not allow playing in defence (meaning the figure is attacked, but destroy the attacker).

The game mechanics is a little unusual in the combat part, but not bad, since all players are subject to the rules applied. At some point it's also better than Stellaris - there you actually choose battle tactics, but do not to have to agree with the standard one about small ships in front, heavy behind. Also, due to specialization of armor, weapons, range and tactics, you cannot build a fleet that's better than any else - there is alway an alternative set of parts that can defeat you. Imagine multidimentional rock-paper-scissors. It makes it more real to fight much more powerful invador, but also allows to create a decent force out of nothing (if you have researched needed tech, of course).

Multiple races with different benefits and targets. Same standard planetary resources produces by population: money("dust"), food(for population growth), industry (to produce stuff per turn) and science. Only dust is accumulatable. Also several "strategic resources" that randomly appear on different planets to use in advanced technologies, but also rare "luxury" resources that give bonuses to the planets and can be used to upgrade system level. Guys from Stellaris copied it quite straightforward. Except that you can store both "strategic" and "luxory" resources.
A large diference in gameplay between ES2 and Stellaris is that everything happens on the star system level: all planets of a system contribute resources into one "pool". Upgrades are applied on the system, affect all the planets at once, even though planet type (lots of them) has a large role in that.
There is no playable map within the system - if your and enemy fleets are in the same system - they can interfere. It is not possible for them to be on the different sides of the map like in Stellaris. The idea is that with interstellar drive the distances within a star system are insignificant. It reduces the amount of headache putting mining station on each asteroid in the system, uninhabited planets and so on. Also, population is assigned to the planet, there is no need to assign grids or build factories for each one.That's where Stellaris went further, but I cannot say that I miss building  mining stations on each damn asteroid and hunting enemy fleet across the system. Looking backward, it is very time consuming part of Stellaris. Eventually, I always had only 5 core systems and the rest gave to AI. The approach of ES2 allows player to concentate on more important stuff and make turns pretty fast with less manual checks.
As for checks - if user click End Turn and one of the planets doesn't have anything in the construction queue or Hero has not assigned a skill point - you have a chance to do it. Like in Total War series, I'd say.
On the normal difficulty AI is developing effectively to some extent (making you feel that it's damn strong), but after some treshold (turn 80 or so) starts backing up. Some complained about overpowered pirates - well, that's kind of true. Pirates are not as dangerous for the system as in Stellaris (rarely make sieges and only for a short time), but their fleet is much more powerful and gets updated with time. Meaning, they are not such a pain, but more difficult to get rid of.
Technology tree is not randomized and is known from the very beginning. It allows better planning and you don't have to rely on luck. It's quite flexible, though.
Market is common for all the players, thus if you sell some resource - it can be bought even by your enemy. Abundant resources on the market decrease price, rare - increase. Sort of stock market.
Heroes are immortal, but after defeat it takes ~20 turns until they can be used again.
Politics, law, government types are also part of the game. The special part is that there is a political party for each of main development directions: e.g. Insustry, Religion, Pacifist, Militarists, Ecologists, etc. Depending on your actions (what you constructed, what decisions taken in event) these parties gain votes. The winning party, as long as it rules, issues one law that gives some specific benefits. Of course, if you have sort of democracy, in dictatorship there are no elections. Plus, you can issue additional laws, they depend on the elected factions and how experienced these factions are (e.g. if you elect Industrialists a few times - you can use some advanced laws/edicts that cost "influence" most of the time).
Despite always having good reviews, I think Endless Space franchise is unfortunately often overlooked by the players who could otherwice like it. I encourage you to try it. Different races provide different ways to achieve victory.
PS: I didn't face any bugs or crashes in these 23+ hours of gameplay, but some people complain about it, though the number of these complaints decrease in time - bugs are truly getting fixed.

Crusader Kings II is an exceptional game in that no other title will make you feel like a ruler as well as it. You're not just a country, like in other grand strategy games. You are a ruler with qualities, flaws, vices and virtues. You can be a Duke who is a brilliant diplomat with a hunchback, an ugly, stuttering dimwit count, or a mastermind plotter/lesbian queen. (I'm NOT making it up). And you can be all that within in a single playthrough, as you re-incarnate into your heir when you die. You have to be good at managing your realm, but you've got to be even better at managing your dynasty by arranging favourable marriages, assassinate pretenders... It's all very involving and requires a lot of micro-management (which you may or may not like).
It's not without flaws: the interface could see much improvement and the game starts to slow down when you become powerful. By slow down, I don't mean that your computer has a hard time coping, I mean that there are many more events that require your constant attention, making things move at a slower pace. To be honest, after several hundred hours, I think I'm a bit burned with the game. And that, even though there are entire DLCs I haven't really explored yet: I have only really played as a Catholic or Muslim ruler, but DLCs let you play as pagans, Orthodoxes, republics...
And then there are a couple of Mods that are probably worth exploring as well: "Game of Thrones" and "Tamriel" (from the Elder scrolls series)
Still, with so much content and the unbeatable feeling of being an actual Middle-Ages ruler, it's hard to rate CKII anything lower than a 9 out of 10.

Half is played collecting clues and questioning people (which is hard!), the other half is chasing bad guys in cars or on foot and having shoot outs.   It got dings from me for being unable to skip cut scenes when you fail/replay, the sudden Tomb Raideresque climb/balance/mazes plopped in the middle of the game, and half a point for a personal dislike of specific behavior from the main character three-quarters of the way through the game.  The story was still solid and well worth playing, and has a murky ending that's realistic.  Stick around after the credits for a final flashback scene.

Halo Wars is very simplistic when you compare it to other RTS games, but it definitely gets the job done.
For anyone who hasn't played Halo Wars:
The very first time playing through the campaign is worth the cost of the game itself, then there's also multiplayer, for PvP or just PvAi, for all you people who don't like playing against players.
Although there is PvP, it can be very frustrating for new players, as most of the people (at least, as far as I've seen) are players coming from Xbox, and know the game very well, crushing, and humiliating you.
If you stick through it, you learn stratagies very fast, and can start challenging the same players who were previously crushing you.
Playing through the Campaign could take you 10~ hours, or maybe even 20+ hours depending on how skilled you are/what difficulty you play on.
All in all, if you want to play a new RTS game, Halo Wars is for you.
For the people who HAVE played Halo Wars, and are wishing to play on PC:
It's a great port, the controls feel very nice, and are all customizable.
If you're looking to play the Campaign, it's basically the same. Just playing on PC instead of Xbox so you may have a better experience.
Now as for Multiplayer Gameplay, I find it much more fun than Halo Wars on the Xbox, because you can communicate to your allies/enemies.
It's also a lot faster to play, and gives it a more competetive feel, now that you have so many hotkeys to use.
Now on to the most discussed topic, the way in which you find games.
In my honest opinion, it's WAY, WAAY better. Instead of match making for a game, waiting in queue for 10+ minutes, you can search for games and join in less than a minute.
It also allows you to search for multiple modes, and number of players. Ex: Search for 3v3,2v2, and 1v1 matches at the same time.
It's a lot easier to find games. You can launch HW, and be in a game within 2 minutes.
There is a downside to lobby games, though. Eventually you get to know the players, and learn who is good/bad.
This is bad for multiple reasons, If you're a good player, it *can* be very hard to start a game, because the enemy might just leave the lobby once they see you're on the enemy team.
It's also bad because good players can lobby hop untill they find players they know are bad, and beat them to improve their ranking.
This is all possible, but I wouldn't say there's a definite chance it would happen.
(ignore the console fanboys saying the new search system is broken)
ALSO, THERE'S MOD SUPPORT. THERE. IS. MOD. SUPPORT. THINK OF THE POSSIBILITES!!!!! (although it will probably take a bit for the good mods to come out)
For me, buying this was obvious. I love Halo Wars, and I will get so many hours out of this game playing Online.
If you've already experienced the campaign, have multiple hours in multiplayer, and just want to buy the game for a couple hours of casual PvAi, I personally wouldn't buy it. Unless it goes on sale, it's not worth the $22 for 5~ hours of already experienced gameplay.

Wow. Okay, wait, let's get the bad out of the way first.
1) It's optimized poorly. The game seemingly started fine, or perhaps I was too enamored with the city to notice, but DX9 or DX11, highest settings or lowest, nothing mattered. The camera would stutter, the engine would slow, and otherwise damage the otherwise breathtaking aesthetics of L.A. Noire.
2) The driver and pedestrian A.I. is atrocious. For a game that forces you to spend the majority of your time driving, expect to laugh at the ridiculous decisions made by the NPCs in this game. Then, when chasing down suspects or trying to avoid... well, I won't spoil anything, but let's just say at certain points, you will yell at the television for these dummies to get out of the way.
3) The action sequences aren't as interesting as the investigation ones. Basic action, such as the street crimes, or even a moderate shootout, aren't too bad but the above complaints tend to ruin any tension Team Bondi attempted to create.
I think that's about it. So what did I like?
1) The city. Sorry, Sleeping Dogs, you've been knocked off the top spot (previously owned by Saints Row 2) for best video game city. It's no wonder Team Bondi went bankrupt after this game. The amount of time and resources it must have taken to recreate Los Angeles is staggering.
2) The characters. Thanks to stellar voice acting and the well-publicized facial animation engine, it's easy to forget you're playing a game and not watching a movie. Tip: Play L.A. Noire in black and white and the effect is even more staggering.
3) The story. I'm a sucker for noir in general, and this is a pretty good tribute to the genre. That pretty much every single element is tied to the main story, no matter how minor it seems, is a nice touch.
4) The investigation. Whether you're screaming at a widower -- er, I mean 'doubting' a widower -- or trying to figure out how a torn letter fits with the case, I enjoyed poking around the city's seedy underbelly and solving the (many!) mysteries.
Note that I keep writing "the city" instead of "the game." Yes, it's that realistic.
I loved L.A. Noire, and if you like mysteries and history at all, please don't hesitate picking up this game. Just be warned that even at 30 FPS, a computer that laughs at the recommended specs of the latest games will (probably) not run this smoothly. Fortunately, you'll probably be too engrossed to care. I know I was.

Consider this just a "first impressions" type review as I did not play for very long and merely tried the game on a free weekend.  This is definitely not a 4X game for a casual sesh.  It's got a lot of depth and thus a steep learning curve.  The interface is very polished, but seems to err on the side of style rather than ease of use.  It takes a while to get used to how things are organized.  And there is a lot of information thrown at you.  The tutorials are helpful but have very basic triggers (the upshot of this is that they'll appear automatically but you'll have to close them manually).  From someone used to playing MOO or galciv, the tech tree seems much busier, there are new considerations such as hero units and luxuries, and certainly different approaches to many areas including space combat and mini-quests.  There's a lot of hands-on and micro-management and since I prefer my games more play than work, I could only recommend this to a very particular type of thinking gamer.

A clever but underachieving adventure / puzzle game elevated at times by an interesting setting and story.
For those of you that don't know, your character can blend between 3d person and 2d projected platforming by stepping into the light projected onto walls. Shadows become walls, floors and even lifts to new areas. At its best it feels like a mix of fez and portal, but at its worst the shadow stepping can be awkward and unreliable.
The pacing is acceptable and there seem to be multiple ways to approach some puzzles, but there's no serious challenge here.
The setting falls somewhere between Bugsy Malone and Alice in Wonderland, but doesn't fully deliver on either. The noir story is a nice touch, but not gritty enough for my tastes, and whilst the worlds warp and float like a fever dream this fact is entirely ignored by the characters. I would not have been shocked to see: "But it was all a dream. The End"
There were some beautiful moments towards the end of the game where a deeper meaning is hinted, but it arrived a little late.
If you're curious, pick it up on a good sale day, but you're looking for puzzle, platforming or story, this game hits under average on all accounts. [5.0]
Once you learn how the game works, it'll be one of the most addictive and fun you'll ever play.

Impressive tech combined with an interesting story and solid gameplay.
Its similiar to the point and click police games of the past but in real time instead. The main thing here is the story where action segments are really just a way to break up the investigations and keep the game from being monotanous. The shooting, driving, and open world are really more of a secondary aspect where the investigations are the main thing you do in the game. The action isn't anything new or hugely interesting but the shooting and driving are solid enough and fun enough to not become annoying especially when broken up in between investigating.
What you do alot of is talk to people and figure out if they are lying or telling the truth essentially. This can be very hard and in some contexts I found that the game didn't make logical sense in what I was allowed to use as evidence of a lie in a conversation. Usually though it is logical and there is alot of help mechanics in the game ranging from intuition points that literally remove wrong answers or show you what the community has choosen statistically, to suspects using questions to tell the player what evidence would be applicable in a given situation. Its really fun to actually do but can be extremely frustrating at points.
The story is also very good. Very gritty and unfortunately realistic. I don't want to spoil anything but just know that the story and cases are very intertwined and can be hard to connect the dots at first. The story goes places and is diffrent and not always predictable. I really like it... even if I don't always like what happens.
The setting is lovely. This is when the USA was at its epitome in most ways.  Its lovely to see all the classic cars (which are actual Ford or Chevy vehicles) and buildings aswell as clothes and everything in this game fits in the time period as far as I can tell.
The big downside is that this PC version is very messed up. Its very glitchy at times and loads much slower on the fly than I remember the PS3 version. Having things pop in very close to you is pretty common aswell as having sound cues not work right or animations of characters faces wig the heck out in scary ways. First thing to say is LA Noire in 2016 now seems to work perfectly on the PC. I am certain this is not really because of my system power which is an I7 4790K and GTX 970  graphics, but because they fixed the problems the game had originally.  I also have the habit of buying games in sales on Steam and leaving them for ages, and this time I wish I had played this sooner.
The atmosphere of the game is superb you can even play it in black and white if you want the game to make it look more like an old film noire movie.  You play a cop in 1948 Los Angeles, a decorated war veteran you begin as a beat officer then work through traffic, homicide, vice, and arson.  Although it is possible to solve cases without finding all the clues the more you find the safer the conviction is which makes for a happy captain.
Interviews of characters are vital and their faces are properly motion captured in the hope that you can spot the truth, a part truth, or a lie.  It is not easy and is always a challenge.
I liked the action sequences I have seen so far especially the car chase of a suspect who was involved in a street race.  Only part way through the game at the moment the game seems to be building towards something, flashbacks suggest Phelps (you) maybe has guilt issues, and newspapers that show past events suggest characters in the game.  I have no idea how they fit together but the game leaves me wanting to find out.
As stated earlier I love the atmosphere of the game.  As an old rock fan I was genuinely surprised to find myself enjoying listening to Louis Armstrong on the car radio for example while laughing at my terrible driving.  The feel of the game leaves you not knowing if any of your partners are corrupt, and I definitely enjoy the banter between you and them in car on route.
Parents be warned this game does use 1948 attitudes to women, domestic violence at times, and race and people talk accordingly.  The dead body of the murder victim in my current case was naked, and the case before it involved a fifteen year old girl being sexually abused by people in power.  You do not see it happen but the subject matter is there so parents be aware.  Although as far as I know some or possibly all of the cases are based on real crimes of the period.
To sum up to me at least LA Noire provides a facinating world and it makes you be patient and think which makes a change.  Yes the game is linear and not open world but it also has side missions so it has plenty of options, and I have not tried any dlc missions yet.  Often the game is in the sales on Steam including the dlc's and I have loved it so far so I think it is worth a buy.

TL;DR
I have first played Endless Space before Stellaris even existed. Than the game seemed to be quite complicated, and I didn't stick around for long. But when I saw the hype over Stellaris and played it, my first though was: "Ehm, it's 'Endless Space', but RTS(sort of) instead of turn-based". The game has so many similarities, that it is definitely not coincidence, considering that Enless Space was released 4 years earlier. Of course many 4X games take roots from "Masters of Orion" after all, but that's my impression.
TL;DR Endless Space 2 rating: 9/10 + unusual 'Endless Space' type of space combat.
Medium-length story:
I find second part much more friendly toward the new players, and the GUI is impressively convenient. That's an example all strategy games should take. I don't even know what to say to the players who say that it's difficult or inconvenient, IMHO, it's as good as it can be. The game is complex, thus requires basic patience, thus maybe play tutorial? The idea of tutorial is common with Stellaris - "adivisor" that gives suggestions and instructions as you play.
It has some specifics, especially regarding space combat and the maximum size of the fleet (e.g. 5 ships in fleet, but as many fleets as you want) - it's a controversial idea (Explanation: fleet fights one other fleet at a time. Meaning that if your fleet has capacity of 8 ships and enemy has 2 fleets 5 ships each - you fight 2 battles against 5 enemies each, instead of one against 10), as if it is a turn-based part within a turn-based game with a turn-based combat. Wow. But thinking of it, chess are much more stupid in that regard: they don't have damage system at all and also do not allow playing in defence (meaning the figure is attacked, but destroy the attacker).

The game mechanics is a little unusual in the combat part, but not bad, since all players are subject to the rules applied. At some point it's also better than Stellaris - there you actually choose battle tactics, but do not to have to agree with the standard one about small ships in front, heavy behind. Also, due to specialization of armor, weapons, range and tactics, you cannot build a fleet that's better than any else - there is alway an alternative set of parts that can defeat you. Imagine multidimentional rock-paper-scissors. It makes it more real to fight much more powerful invador, but also allows to create a decent force out of nothing (if you have researched needed tech, of course).

Multiple races with different benefits and targets. Same standard planetary resources produces by population: money("dust"), food(for population growth), industry (to produce stuff per turn) and science. Only dust is accumulatable. Also several "strategic resources" that randomly appear on different planets to use in advanced technologies, but also rare "luxury" resources that give bonuses to the planets and can be used to upgrade system level. Guys from Stellaris copied it quite straightforward. Except that you can store both "strategic" and "luxory" resources.
A large diference in gameplay between ES2 and Stellaris is that everything happens on the star system level: all planets of a system contribute resources into one "pool". Upgrades are applied on the system, affect all the planets at once, even though planet type (lots of them) has a large role in that.
There is no playable map within the system - if your and enemy fleets are in the same system - they can interfere. It is not possible for them to be on the different sides of the map like in Stellaris. The idea is that with interstellar drive the distances within a star system are insignificant. It reduces the amount of headache putting mining station on each asteroid in the system, uninhabited planets and so on. Also, population is assigned to the planet, there is no need to assign grids or build factories for each one.That's where Stellaris went further, but I cannot say that I miss building  mining stations on each damn asteroid and hunting enemy fleet across the system. Looking backward, it is very time consuming part of Stellaris. Eventually, I always had only 5 core systems and the rest gave to AI. The approach of ES2 allows player to concentate on more important stuff and make turns pretty fast with less manual checks.
As for checks - if user click End Turn and one of the planets doesn't have anything in the construction queue or Hero has not assigned a skill point - you have a chance to do it. Like in Total War series, I'd say.
On the normal difficulty AI is developing effectively to some extent (making you feel that it's damn strong), but after some treshold (turn 80 or so) starts backing up. Some complained about overpowered pirates - well, that's kind of true. Pirates are not as dangerous for the system as in Stellaris (rarely make sieges and only for a short time), but their fleet is much more powerful and gets updated with time. Meaning, they are not such a pain, but more difficult to get rid of.
Technology tree is not randomized and is known from the very beginning. It allows better planning and you don't have to rely on luck. It's quite flexible, though.
Market is common for all the players, thus if you sell some resource - it can be bought even by your enemy. Abundant resources on the market decrease price, rare - increase. Sort of stock market.
Heroes are immortal, but after defeat it takes ~20 turns until they can be used again.
Politics, law, government types are also part of the game. The special part is that there is a political party for each of main development directions: e.g. Insustry, Religion, Pacifist, Militarists, Ecologists, etc. Depending on your actions (what you constructed, what decisions taken in event) these parties gain votes. The winning party, as long as it rules, issues one law that gives some specific benefits. Of course, if you have sort of democracy, in dictatorship there are no elections. Plus, you can issue additional laws, they depend on the elected factions and how experienced these factions are (e.g. if you elect Industrialists a few times - you can use some advanced laws/edicts that cost "influence" most of the time).
Despite always having good reviews, I think Endless Space franchise is unfortunately often overlooked by the players who could otherwice like it. I encourage you to try it. Different races provide different ways to achieve victory.
PS: I didn't face any bugs or crashes in these 23+ hours of gameplay, but some people complain about it, though the number of these complaints decrease in time - bugs are truly getting fixed.

This is probably one of the best puzzle games I've played. If you have any liking for French jazz culture, this is the game for you. It is all about using light in creative ways to solve puzzles, most of which are platforming.
My favorite pieces are the music which was put together with care. The vocalist they hired to sing a couple songs has the perfect voice for this type of jazz. All of the voice acting is quite solid. The other piece that drew me in was the use of shadows to represent characters rather than physical beings. I think that is explained through collectibles, but I haven't spent much time with it. Contrast also manages to portray a sense of innocence surrounding Didi while giving some very adult conflicts when she's not around.
The only real issue I had was with either the controls or the design, I'm not sure. Sometimes when something seemed easy to accomplish, like a jump, you'd be force off the wall for some reason and have to start over. Basically I think some of the shadows in the environment were unintentional and created surprise blocks for you to avoid. It could also just be I'm not very practiced at platformers. The puzzles seem well designed and not too challenging to figure out. After figuring out what needs to be done, you may still need to take a few tries at it before succeeding, but it isn't usually too frustrating.
It is quite a short game if you figure out the puzzles quickly, it took me maybe 6 hours. So I probably wouldn't buy it for full price just because of the length, but I would definitely buy it on sale. Also, the soundtrack is a great jazz compilation.
One last note: at I believe the end of the first act, there are two endings depending on if you just stand and watch, or actively do something (I don't want to give spoilers) If you don't do anything, you'll fail the level and be put back to the beginning of the dialogue, so I recommend just listening first, then actually doing what you're supposed to.

Consider this just a "first impressions" type review as I did not play for very long and merely tried the game on a free weekend.  This is definitely not a 4X game for a casual sesh.  It's got a lot of depth and thus a steep learning curve.  The interface is very polished, but seems to err on the side of style rather than ease of use.  It takes a while to get used to how things are organized.  And there is a lot of information thrown at you.  The tutorials are helpful but have very basic triggers (the upshot of this is that they'll appear automatically but you'll have to close them manually).  From someone used to playing MOO or galciv, the tech tree seems much busier, there are new considerations such as hero units and luxuries, and certainly different approaches to many areas including space combat and mini-quests.  There's a lot of hands-on and micro-management and since I prefer my games more play than work, I could only recommend this to a very particular type of thinking gamer.

Forget Dungeon Keeper and its many clones. Forget Overlord. Forget Evil Genius. If you want to know what it's like to be evil, to be the bad guy, then you have to play Crusader Kings 2. This is a game where you have your eldest son murdered so that your second son can inherit in his place. This is a game where you find that your heir has decided to marry some baron's daughter, matrilinially no less, after you gave him a duchy to look after; then have her killed so that you can marry him to someone more suitable. Marry the princess of Scotland, and then have all of her brothers killed so that she inherits the crown. If you can keep her on it, then when she kicks the bucket your children will have two kingdoms to toy with.
Crusader Kings 2 is a solid strategy game, but unlike other strategy games of its ilk its focus on individual characters makes it generate stories almost as well as Dwarf Fortress. I cannot recommend this game highly enough.

Ark: Survival Evolved really immerses you in a world of wonder, though that usually will be followed by confusion and rage, however, as you progress, you'll find it quite exciting to play this game.
PVE servers usually host the friendliest of people, whilst PVP can get you that extra bit of challenge.
If you love learning about a lot of extinct animals, then you'll like this game. It's in-game models do give a sense of what it would have looked like, whilst the dossiers address any sort of alterations the game made to them, allowing you to get a pretty safe and well-researched idea of the dinosaurs.
Its DLC, Scorched Earth, adds another layer of difficulty on it, and will certainly put even the best of veterans to the test of survival, whilst also expanding on it with all new fictional creatures.
What also is a major pro point of this game is the developer's non-greedy attitude. Whilst there are timers (sometimes huge) on taming dinosaurs, there's no way to artificially speed this up with in-game purchases, and when they decided to make a steam community map into a full-on DLC, they decided not to ask payment for it, as it was developed by the community.
With another DLC coming up, I'm looking forward to it and the new exciting monstrosities it will bring.
On the con-side though, the game doesn't explain much, and dino levelling is a bit arbitrary for when a dino spawns, it's given a random level, no matter where it spawns, meaning that you can spawn and run directly into a level 90 dilophosaurus, then into a level 120 Carnotaurus. Without proper explanation how the game works, this can lead to new players being left confused on how to survive and stay that way. This game, through the fact that most of your time you need dinosaurs to get materials effectively, puts more advanced players directly at an advantage, which can severely inhibit your PVP experience as you can be wiped overnight with no way of protecting yourself.
TL:DR;
pro's: -Good gameplay
-Great dino diversity
-can teach you a thing or two.
- Devs aren't greedy
- Still content upcoming
- Good community
Cons: -PVP offers zero protection
-Areas do not mark difficulty, dinosaurs with different levels spawn randomly
- No explanation on how to do things in the beginning, best you have are hints on how to tame dino's in the Dossiers.
So much fun to play with friends online... or without friends, if that's your preference.
