This is one amazing game. And for me, as of writing this review, a person who only has 112 hours in, I can easily say it's only going to get better as I progress.
Starting this game, I had not the slightest clue of what the heck I was doing. But I stuck with it because it was fun.
The fluidity of this game is *mwah* noice. The playstyle is incredibly adaptable, too - you can be a Naruto all the way to being Rambo. There are no bad frames, only bad players... to a degree, at least. And don't get me started on fashion framing (you'll find out, if you play long enough).
But then... then... my god. The story. The story, the lore... it all comes into place. And it's wonderful. It doesn't throw its best at you right away; but if you hang in there, and just keep playing, by golly the story and lore just begin to get mind blowing.
This part may not be for everyone, but this game gives a great sense of satisfaction. Like, you WORKED for your weapons and armor. No instant gratification, but it still feels soooo good. Speaking of, everything, and I mean EVERYTHING, can be achieved with just some work. Weapons and frames kind of just come to you. And platinum, the in-game currency, can also be achieved without using hard earned paper. Just learn the trading system and trade Prime items and mods for platinum! Of course it takes lots of time, but many RPGs tend to take lots of time, especially a free to play MMO. So expect some grinding; but somehow, it's not wearisome.
The community is also one of the nicest I've ever met. So many helpful veterans and non-toxic newbs. Of course, you're bound to meet some toxic players, but you're also going to 100% meet someone who is willing to hold your hand through some missions and give you tips on how to play the game.
For new players wondering if they should play this, I'd say give it a try. Especially if you liked *cough* Destiny *cough*. Destiny is kind of a bad word in the Warframe community, haha - but you'll be soon to see why, if you keep playing. I'd recommend you spend your beginning 50 platinum on just getting slots in your inventory for weapons and warframes. At low level you won't see why you need so many slots for weapons but as you get higher level those slots get filled real fast. Oh, and never throw away a weapon until they are max rank - leveling up weapons gives Mastery points and helps to increase your mastery rank faster. I made this mistake as a newb.
And for your sake, join a clan. You're likely to find some chill clans, and being in clans will give you weapons you could not get otherwise (clans have research facilities that have weapons that you can't get by building or playing.)
Have fun, Tenno!

From someone used to playing MOO or galciv, the tech tree seems much busier, there are new considerations such as hero units and luxuries, and certainly different approaches to many areas including space combat and mini-quests.  There's a lot of hands-on and micro-management and since I prefer my games more play than work, I could only recommend this to a very particular type of thinking gamer.

I heartily recommend this game. While I love EU4, this is a much more newbie friendly game in my opinion. With no real research (what I did at first) you can probably create the empire of britania after a weeks worth of attempts (not an easy feat) but if you want to actually get good at the game the wiki is very helpful.
I recomend you do not buy dlc immediately, and instead start off as a vanilla catholic. Ireland is great for your first few playthroughs, as it is really hard to absolutely. That said, after you get your feet under you I suggest buying old gods and then the new sons of abraham. I have not been able to bring myself to play much of the muslim rulers (I love the christians to much), so I can not recommend the sword of Islam DLC either way. I will say that the republic dlc, while not bad, is not nearly as compelling as the vanilla gameplay, so I would give it a miss.
While I love the Byzantines and the Legacy of Rome DLC, I have found it extremely difficult with the latest patch. I recommend it for when you know what you are doing, because it is really demoralizing to be destroyed by the  muslims repeatedly. It is an extremely rewarding playthrough if you can actually reform the Roman empire, so if you think you can do it, YOU SHOULD.
I do have some warnings though. This game does not believe in fairness or coddling. You could be amazngly lucky and have a genius strong heir only to have him die at the age of 3, leaving you with an inbred female cousin about to inherit your hard won empire. That is unlucky, and probably then end of your playthrough. That said, the same could happen to your enemies. The skill really lies in minimizing risk and learning how the dynasty system works. If you want to get good, you Need the wiki. It can be immensely frusterating to have everything slip through your fingers like so many grains of sand, but it only makes that moment when you survive the Islamic Jihad and create your own KIngdom of Jerusalem all the more sweater.
I have heard the Multiplayer has improved tremendously recently, but I do not play multiplayer so I can not recommend it. It would probably be amazingly fun with friends though.
The new achievments are actually pretty well chosen for this game, although a few are utter bull that I can not even theorize a way of getting (How do you go from count to emperor in one lifetime? HOW!)
They are mostly actually challenging, or hilarious, and a good guide of what to try to do next when you just finish building the wendish empire.
This game is spectacular, and for the price I would say it is a must buy if you have even a passing interest in grand strategy.

Contrast is one of those story driven games, but it has enough platformer to be a bit challenging. Its more of a beginner platformer than an advanced platformer so if you are looking for hard puzzles you won't find them here.
Its got a pretty unique game play style, and as the game is story driven, the plot is just amazing, and the whole feel of the world (as well as a few bugs) keep you on your toes the entire time. Its got that deep otherworldly feel to it while you are tackling pretty everyday(ish) problems in extraordinary ways. The voice acting is pretty amazing as long as you don't mind a LOT of it, you get attached to all the characters. And, I have to iterate, to enjoy this game fully, you MUST try to pick up the collectables and read through them as you go, as they are an integral part of the plot, especially later in the game, and you will get very lost very quickly plot wise if you don't.
All in all, its a little rough around the edges but its got a passionate heart that will move you in story and in some really cleverly disguised, if not a bit easy, puzzles. Its very much an open to interpretation game, like Journey, and with art I think is pretty influential and amazing to the atmosphere in a cartoony yet gritty style with fantasy splashed on it in the most fascinating ways.

This review is based more so on the ending of the game & the story, but includes information about other aspects of the game too.
*Spoilers*
Just replayed the game. Have to say there is a valid point to Jack being the new primary character at the end. The ending in the sewers offers the segmentation needed to have a potential sequel. Cole was expendable at the end. His character had changed, and his story was told. Jack offered a character that had seemed antagonistic throughout the game, as the true hero of the story for the audience at the end. I support the chain of events in that Jack be the new focus, I do however think the final mission being a drawn out back and forth hurts the finale for the game. The transition of clue sleuthing, to car chase, to sewer shoot out, all seemed rushed. The ending seemed less dramatic than it could have been, outside of the scene with Courtney it lack any real emotion at all. Even the small dialog with Ira seemed half♥♥♥♥♥d. One could make the case about Cole's death being the emotional aspect, but the issue lies in the chain of events after his passing; in addition to the aforementioned lead up in the last mission. The only thing we have to go on in the ending is that the Assistant DA cut a deal to become DA. The audience is left to assume that the Chief of Police, the Mayor, and even Earle were left untouched by what the player has discovered during the last 10h or more of game play. Therein lies my issue with the game, yes it does leave it open for a potential sequel, but it gives no closure for the player. The ending with the Eulogy makes the player question if anything that they've done been worth it in this universe; when the real villains walk scott-free. I feel the events set the game up for a sequel, but as Rockstar has indicated there will most likely never be one. As such the player at the end is left with a bitter taste, one could compare the ending to realistic politics, but in gaming the point is to escape reality; not experience it. If Rockstar could do one thing, I believe it would be doing a short OAV describing how the real villains met their ends, outside of that I believe the ending to be the worst part of the game; they should have just cut to the boat scene and not have a funeral at all. Even when the Police chief says "want to make a deal?" the player can get the hint that its all downhill from here. L.A. Noire isn't meant to be a happy story, but the funeral takes what could have been a great story, and turns it into a lead up for another tale that may never be told. Having replayed it, I found myself saying "why did I waste my time?" I enjoy the nostalgia of the 1940s, much the same way I enjoyed Mad Men. Nostalgia aside, looking back on the story, the roadblocking superiors, corrupt politics, I genuinely felt that I had wasted my own time. Sure the game itself is fun, outside of the AI mechanics for driving/walking, the game is very impressive; but the issue is the story. The story as I stated offers little to nothing  in the end, the real Villains escape, and even the entirety of the Homicide case ending is nonexistent. I would propose the only accomplishing and rewarding cases in the game are the patrol, and traffic ones. Some of the DLC cases are enjoyable sidetracks, but they're sad excuses to repair an already pathetic story.

One of my favorite games. This is a strategy/history game, based on Medieval Europe. Unlike other grand strategy games, you don't  control a country, but a single character, in control of a county, duchy, kingdom, or empire, between 1066 and 1453 AD. You don't directly control much, and must manage your court, and your demesne (counties you rule), for prestige. The game is primarily spent telling armies where to go (battles are automatic; you do not control them!), engaging in diplomacy with other leaders, constant conspiracy, and marrying your sons and daughters to wealthy nobles. Balanced production has been removed (why?!) from the Empire Summary screen, meaning you must micromanage all of your systems by flicking through "prioritise food/science/production" etc, or going to the system screen and picking individual buildings.
Modding is as dense as ever, leading to few mods in the Workshop and a learning curve like Everest if you want to make one yourself. Any customisation requires digging through reams of incomprehensible code in XML files. They couldn't have just included an in-game editor?
Turn duration can be limited (to 30-180 seconds, etc) but elections aren't affected, so a slow or AFK player can hold up the game indefinitely every 40 turns.
Graphics when you watch a battle are worse than Endless Space 1. Pressing H doesn't hide the ugly UI to give a cinematic feel anymore. Windows pop up demanding your attention even during these scenes. Tactics are very poorly explained.
Expansion penalties to happiness are rampant, which are basically a punishment for being good at the game.
AI will attack you if you have a higher score than them, even if you're as nice as possible, which breaks immersion. Weak nations would not realistically start a suicidal war against strong nations just because the strong nations are strong. The AI doesn't even attempt to form alliances to beat me, they just kamikaze into my dreadnoughts.
I bought the Standard Edition and feel ripped off. Two heroes are locked behind the Digital Deluxe Edition paywall. They're just cosmetic but it feels like I'm playing an incomplete game. Paying an extra £5 per hero skin is ludicrous though.
It also feels like certain popular factions have been left out of the game so they can be re-sold as DLC at a late date.
Higher difficulties don't improve AI, they just cheat more.
That's all I can think of for now.

A lot of multiplayer servers can be nauseatingly hostile and troll-heavy, but there are good ones out there so I will leave it to you to find them if you choose to get this game. What I CAN tell you after playing a good 378 hours of single player, is this: ARK is a game with a lot of potential, plenty of replay value, a variety of interesting mechanics, and more than anything, it has charm. It will make you laugh until your stomach hurts and it will make you yell rageful profanties so loud that you scare your neighbours at 4am. It will even make you care for your dinos/creatures as if they were real in some cases, but even if it doesn't, it WILL make you feel a range of emotions just from the sheer fact that your position, be it good or bad, can change in an instant due to a brilliant move, a tiny fumble, or in some cases, pure, unadulterated luck.
It has it's flaws, such as Ichthys (Dolphins) instantly dying if they surface (and I mean really, devs, FIX IT already! It's been like that for ages and it makes no sense!) or the occasional bizarre glitch, and sadly, it barely runs on anything short of a beastly gaming PC, but all in all, it's a beautiful game that is very much worth playing if you enjoy Survival, Crafting, or Open World games.
Also, if you ever come across a crazy naked lady with a rifle chasing wild rexes down the beach screaming angrily, yeah, that's me.

As a long-time fan of Amplitude my review may be biased, but I really like this game and developers making it better with every update actually listening to the community.
ES2 improved its eXploration element over the first installment, you absolutely have to explore galaxy for there are systems out there, chances of great loot and exploration bonuses.
Battles for eXtermination are  simple yet more strategical than tactical: you have to be prepared for the enemy with the right ship loadouts and fleet composotion before you hit the attack button, and there are some choices of tactics and ship behaviour once the battle starts.
As for eXpand and eXploit there are a new nice political system, minor faction relations (improved over Endless Legend), overall system management is close to ES1 with little touches of Endless Legend.
Diplomacy was not really great but improved in last update, I still need to look at all the new options.
The quest system is also from Endless Legend but improved. Each faction has its own playstyle and faction quests are branching now with 2-3 options in each chapter.
UI, music and artstyle is phenomenal, as always for Amplitude.
AI still needs some work, they improving it but it is not on par even with Endless Legend now.

My memories.
This was literally my first RTS game I ever played, I used to only ever play the Original Xbox, and then the Xbox 360. I remember when I used to play Halo every other day, and when this game came out for the 360 my heart raced, I used to even watch the E3 trailer and presentation, I was so excited...
I bet some people expect me to say it wasn't worth it, it was though, it was so worth it. This game taught me that you don't always need to be the low down tough and gruff guy doing all the shooting, you could see the action from a top down view and feel just as good as you would up close in the blood. And personally, this game hasn't lost it's touch, with mouse and keyboard controls, it's as if this game aged with me and I love it, now there's still the stupid control scheme for camera zoom (page up and page down) which I despise, I wish it was just the mouse wheel like every other RTS but I can forgive them for that seeing as they gave us the DLC reskins of the warthog and wraith, (which to be honest should never have been sold for actual money in the first place, it's two skins for five bucks..) but other than that they bumped up the graphics a bit and it really does look good, now it's not a remaster, far from it, but it certainly holds up for PC standards at least in my eyes.
Gameplay?, you wanna know about gameplay? What's there to know, it's an RTS, you build the resource strcutures, raid resource areas, build up a ton of infantry at first then spit out mad amounts of vehicles towards the end with some special powers here and there.
One issue I really have with this is the special powers, for example, the UNSC feel perfect, calling in MAC rounds to be fired from orbit, dropping carpet bombs etc. But the Covenant, on the Xbox 360 you controlled them, their hero unit was their special power, it felt like you were playing as that unit, something I never thought was possible at the time. But in this it feels a bit.. off, but it's minor at best. Few more tweaks and we've got us a propah smash em' brawl ere' lads!
What would I rate this game AT LEAST 7/10 because blinded Nostalgia. and of COURSE 9/10 Because why not.
I'm not the technical person who gets into the nitty gritty of these types of reviews, I just say it how I like it. You want technical stuff scroll up or down. For me?, this is a game I recommend and that's all I got.

L.A Noire is one of the most innovative and mature games I've played in a long time. It takes a lot of risks and attempts to tell a thoughtful and engaging story. And it's safe to say it was perfectly executed.  It sets a new standard of the mystery and noir genre for future games to come.
In L.A Noire, you play as Cole Phelps,  a former war lieutenant now serving the LAPD. As the game progresses, you get promoted to 4 sqauds, Traffic, Homicide (My favorite), Vice, and Arson. With traffic, you experience car theft, hit and runs, and vehicle fraud. With homicide, you investigate a series of murders that are linked to a certain serial killer. In Vice, you investigate the overwelming flow of morphine circulating the streets of L.A, and interact/investigate the prime criminal underworld that call the shots in Hollywood. And in Arson, you investigate a series of fires linked to a serial arsonist and a highly corrupted company. Each case brings a mature and mysterious tone to the game, engaging you to investigate further.
PROS
-Great story
-Exellent acting (some of the best I've ever seen)
-Great visuals
-Fluid gunplay
-Great driving
-Most of the cases are engaging and interesting
-Amazing music
-Great atmosphere
CONS:
-Near the end of the game, the last 3 cases (excluding Nicholson Electroplating) require no thinking whatsoever and is mostly just combat.
-The game had a stuttering problem because of the 30fps lock. Its nothing game breaking, but it is annoying
-Some cases just end in a firefight, leaves me disappointed
-Some questions can be confusing and when you get them wrong, it can lead to a "What?! That makes no sense."
FInal Verdict: 9/10

After playing Endless Legend for many hours and deeply enjoying that games simple but very satisfying combat system I am totally dissapointed in ES2. Its basically like some American footbal simulator where you choose formation and press play to see a lame animation showing how your flotilla flies in a stright line or maybe takes a slight turn at some point while firing all of its weapons at equally boring enemy fleet. I think chess can be more exciting then this game.
I understand that this if a 4X game and not a new Homeworld but then why try and make it look like one on all of the store screen shots? And the strategy portion is boring as well, unlike Endless Legend you dont see how your planets grow and prosper cause they always look the same. All of the projects you build apply to all planets in a system which is lazy but I guess it makes the game less micromanage prone. The story seemed interesting as always but the gameplay is just so boring, I literally spent tens of turns just clicking "next turn", the thrill of exploring ancient ruins was supposed to be replaced with exploring new planets but the probe system is even worse then Mass Effect 2 and the dreaded "probe launched"... I have had more fun playing Galactic Civilizations way back when over ES2.

This game will provide countless hours of gameplay, exploration, and strategy formations, in a variety of venues.
- Building: while initially challanging, once understood, this becomes a test of skill and asthetics.
- Taming: exploring the world and taming (in a variety of ways) various creatures of various forms is immensely satisfying.
- Exploring: conquering the various biomes, realms, and various dangers (including caves) is incredibly challanging and satifying once completed.
- Maximizing: once the mechanics of the game are learned and understood, a certain level of efficiency can be achieved by performing tasks and necessary processes in various ways. Finding a way that works for you to gain what you need within the game can be quite fulfilling.
- Always on edge: This game, omitting and ignoring bugs (which there are), is constantly challenging even at the highest levels. There are always new things to explore and perform, and there is always a fairly large element of danger (of losing hours, materials, creatures, or all of these). If you don't enjoy an underlying level of stress, don't buy this game.
For the menial amount of money I paid for this game, it has been extremely gratifying, along with times of complete frustration and fulfillment, with infinite replayability. What else could you ask for in a game?

While I did not enjoy my playtime, I am fully aware that the first three times I downloaded Stellaris, I hated it.
So, it is with hope that I endure the painful process of uninstalling, and awaiting the slumber until the next time I give Endless Space 2 a try.
Things that turned me off in the game were the progression system, feeling of lostness, and lack of consequence. The game felt flowy, almost as if I, the player, had little to no interaction with the ingame world. On the opposite side of that coin, there is a very heavily scripted interaction system between the already created races. It feels rigid and storylike, which plays well for a first time. However after completing one story, you are left feeling like that is it, and disturbiting it plays poorly.
I absolutely loved the art style, music, and aesthetics the game had to offer.
I enjoyed the politics, but felt that intergalactic relations severely lacking, although I am told the DLC adds much needed fluff.
I did not enjoy fleet battles. It felt more like scripted rail shooters mixed with football, than actual fights. I am also led to believe that these tussels get more interesting as bigger ships are introduced, but I lacked the ability to wait that long in my level of play. I simply did not enjoy the game enough to progress to anything meaningful I suppose.
While I do rate the game rather high for something I wouldn't recommend, (85/100) I must stress that it simply is not my style of game yet. I said that once about Stellaris, now I clock hours regularly on it. Times change I guess.
If you take anything out of this review, please understand that this is a good game with excellent ideas and nice creative touches, not to even mention free DLC. It just is not interesting to me in the slightest.

Set in the final years of 1940s, L.A Noire perfectly captures the golden Hollywood era feeling and puts you in the boots of rookie detective, who has fought in the second world war and is now trying to succeed as a detective in the glamorous post war Los Angeles.
Game uses animation technology which makes it possible to tell if a person is lying, telling the truth or hiding something, and this is the part of the game that really stands out from the games you have played, it gives the game a whole new dimension, that other games havent been able to capture yet.
Post war Los Angeles and Hollywood are beautifully captured and recreated to the smallest detail, which makes exploring and driving around much more interesting.
Voice acting and movement of the characters are movie like, and the game really captures the feeling of being part of old Film Noir movie, and being an actual detective.
If you are interested and attracted to the Glamour of classic Hollywood, great actors and excellent cases to solve, this game is definetly for you. And even if you are not that interested of those things, you should still buy the game, you might be suprised how good it is.

I heartily recommend this game. While I love EU4, this is a much more newbie friendly game in my opinion. With no real research (what I did at first) you can probably create the empire of britania after a weeks worth of attempts (not an easy feat) but if you want to actually get good at the game the wiki is very helpful.
I recomend you do not buy dlc immediately, and instead start off as a vanilla catholic. Ireland is great for your first few playthroughs, as it is really hard to absolutely. That said, after you get your feet under you I suggest buying old gods and then the new sons of abraham. I have not been able to bring myself to play much of the muslim rulers (I love the christians to much), so I can not recommend the sword of Islam DLC either way. I will say that the republic dlc, while not bad, is not nearly as compelling as the vanilla gameplay, so I would give it a miss.
While I love the Byzantines and the Legacy of Rome DLC, I have found it extremely difficult with the latest patch. I recommend it for when you know what you are doing, because it is really demoralizing to be destroyed by the  muslims repeatedly. It is an extremely rewarding playthrough if you can actually reform the Roman empire, so if you think you can do it, YOU SHOULD.
I do have some warnings though. This game does not believe in fairness or coddling. You could be amazngly lucky and have a genius strong heir only to have him die at the age of 3, leaving you with an inbred female cousin about to inherit your hard won empire. That is unlucky, and probably then end of your playthrough. That said, the same could happen to your enemies. The skill really lies in minimizing risk and learning how the dynasty system works. If you want to get good, you Need the wiki. It can be immensely frusterating to have everything slip through your fingers like so many grains of sand, but it only makes that moment when you survive the Islamic Jihad and create your own KIngdom of Jerusalem all the more sweater.
I have heard the Multiplayer has improved tremendously recently, but I do not play multiplayer so I can not recommend it. It would probably be amazingly fun with friends though.
The new achievments are actually pretty well chosen for this game, although a few are utter bull that I can not even theorize a way of getting (How do you go from count to emperor in one lifetime? HOW!)
They are mostly actually challenging, or hilarious, and a good guide of what to try to do next when you just finish building the wendish empire.
This game is spectacular, and for the price I would say it is a must buy if you have even a passing interest in grand strategy.

I have a hard time recommending Contrast, but an equally hard time not recommending it. It's based on a really interesting concept, is set in a cool environment with great art direction, and it has a killer soundtrack. It also has a fairly decent story (or at least the beginning of one).
However, despite these things, much is left to be desired. Character animation and control is
stiff. Most times you'll know exactly what you need to do, but the game's temperamental controls will prevent you from actually accomplishing it. A major frustration was the game randomly deciding to pop the character out of the "shadow realm" for no apparent reason. Even running along an even surface sometimes resulted in the character popping out and falling either to her death or back to the beginning of a platforming section. Another frustration was the fact that, despite controlling a character who's supposed to be an agile acrobat, you often feel like you're controlling a much larger character who's invisible bounding-box is always bumping into things and preventing seemingly simple jumps from being accomplished.
Sadly, I have to go with "not recommended." It's just too short, and too glitchy. It seems like there's definitely a lot of potential for a really great game hidden underneath Contrast's annoyances. Hopefully, we'll see a sequel with these issues ironed out.

is certainly not for action junkies, nor for gamers who aren't all that interested in storytelling, but for me this little gem from Compulsive Games makes for an excellent puzzle-platformer.
The big mechanic here is the ability to shift into silhouette form and solve problems with shadows.  It's remarkably adept at holding player interest because
gives us so much to do, from simple platforming to complex object manipulation.  The 3D platforming elements are minimal, though there is a fair bit of 2D-3D shifting in certain sections to keep players on their toes.
Our intrepid developers have done very well with the Unreal Engine, bringing a dreamscape 1920s world to life with a unique art style that makes full use of a specially commissioned Jazz n' Blues soundtrack.  This game treats us the way a lot of independent titles should: like intelligent people who don't need a compass pointing towards every objective, or a full explanation for every plot point.
It isn't
or
by any stretch of the imagination, but it is an indie game that has been built with careful attention to detail and a clear love for simple ideas that lead into complexity.  A potential downside is that it's too short.  That said, I paid full price for the Special Edition and I'm not regretting it.
So, action-seekers stay away.  Thoughtful types who enjoy their puzzles with a twist of atmosphere - welcome!

Check elsewhere for the nuts and bolts reviews - by March 2016 most people will know enough about the game to understand it.  This is more a lament for the sequel that may now not be made.
What makes the game so special ?
The story and chracterisation are amazingly good.  Arguably not just the best, but clear blue water   in front of its nearest challenger.  Compared to even high end police procedurals - "Blue Bloods", "Hawaii 5-0" - L.A. Noire is streets ahead in its storylines and characterisation.  This is "L.A. Confidential" the video game and whilst I'd still rate that film a smidgen higher there's not one character here who is a poorly drawn cliche.  Phelps himself we learn is another Rockstar character seeking redemption.
The game mechanics are both unique and highly workable.  It's rare for the game to expect you or your characters to do something stupid and contrary to their personalities.
And it's easy to forget - Rockstar effectively recreated 1940s L.A. just as a backdrop.  The entire god damn city.
It's not perfect.  Too many of the missions involve travelling half way across the city to each destination which can be a chore.  Sometimes it doesn't even hang with the story.  Would the bar where a woman drunk regularly really be a twenty minute car ride from her home ?  Eventually you "get your partner to drive" going from crime scene to crime scene without driving.
The mini missions annoy at times because they are often completely the other side of the city from your location - also unrealistic as well as discouraging driving.  These tend to fall into one of three categories - foot chase, car chase, shoot out.
The game can get a bit repetitive and some of the clues in later missions can be ridiculously difficult to find - thank goodness for walkthroughs although you can use intuition points.
If your effects for wet clothing aren't that good it probably isn't a good idea to have your character spend most of the final level wading through waist high water.
There was room for a sequel to be even better than the first - maybe consider Mass Effect style dialogue trees, perhaps consider story making like that series which does stories based on Game of Thrones, Walking Dead etc.
I've played many computer games.  But only a few genuinely amazed and delighted me: - Elite, X Com Apocalypse, Baldur's Gate, Freedom Force.  L.A. Noire stands alongside them - perhaps even above them for of the games named only Elite (and with far less confidence Baldur's Gate) could be described as changing what people thought was possible with gaming the way L.A. Noire does.
It's noteworthy that L.A. Noire's review rating is higher than GTA V.  If they were movies the GTA series would definitely have the bigger gross.  But it's L.A. Noire that would win the Oscars.

How do I put it?.. Well, in short - this game is magnificent. It truly is that good. How good is 'that good'?
I bought it to play with my wife on the first sale I've caught it, 11/17/2017 and
Usually she can't sit around more than two hours because games aren't captivating enough but this one is!..
I'd say in total this game is a perfect way to pass your time playing with your friends, your loved ones, and, ofc, solo. Playing this game solo is faster, btw - because it's just you making long turns ;)
1. UI, aka user interface. It's marvelously well-put together. It's beatiful and thoroughly designed. so you won't have trouble navigating the many features of the game once you learn what's what. Many kudos to those who made the UI, you're the best folks!
2. Government managing. It's quite a visual one, where you can see what every your decision will have influence on. Tho i miss some of the viewpoints like custom governments and fanatical purifier civs from Stellaris, this is a huge user-friendly success.
3. Space battles. New stratagems are amazing, and all of the issues I had with the camera in ES1 are finally gone. You can watch your victories in action from any angle you want, including tactical map one.
4. Space exploring. Nice, understandable, reliable, one easy to enjoy.
5. Race creation system with two scales now: people and traits (traits we got in ES1). Hands down I liked it even more that Stellaris'es one, which is great in it's own way.
6. AI diplomacy. While some of the AI reactions go against the lore (like, Cravers asking to join your alliance) even these opportunities are well-done. Those Cravers, for example, are asking you to join the alliance to feast on the galaxy together.
7. Easy aliied victory conditions. You can easily join your forces with any player and still have an opportunity for supremacy victory, while in ES1 (and some other notable games on the market) you had to turn your arms against a friend in the end.
1. Race creation could be not that tightly tied to existing races and their racial quests. While I understand the technical difficulties that can come up with that it's a real thing to do (give me the possibility to become crusading fanatical purifier scientists, please - my favourite choice in Stellaris).
2. Ground battles are a little bit ... odd. I mean, looking odd. Maybe, improve those animations and make them looking serious?..
3. I really don't get why heroes should always have their ships. I say we need fleet commanders to stay on the deck of the ship we choose (or a fleet in total, like in the ES1), not bouncing around in some ... space yaht or something.
All of those 'bad things' aren't really bad, it's just feels like things the devs could improve to make the game perfect.

Halo Wars was released in 2008 as an xbox 360 exclusive. To appeal to a console audience, the gameplay and RTS elements remained relatively simplistic and facile. It's also important to note that this game was not meant to be released on the PC by the original developers, Ensemble Studios.
If you're looking for an in-depth RTS, then it's recommended to skip this title. However, the story and fast-paced skirmish gameplay makes this a good buy for anyone looking for a competitive game, and for sure, is a must-have for any Halo fan. Sure to bring nostalgia to any Halo fan, Halo Wars: DE will likely have you replaying the countless hours of campaign and multiplayer with a new community and platform.
In short, this isn't another mobile top-down shooter like the Spartan Assaults. It's an RTS that, in my opinion, adopts the quick and competitve nature of the earlier Halo fps titles, while retaining a comforting level of simplicity.

My boyfriend grabbed this for me because he knew I'd been anticipating this game since it was announced. Contrast is a noir-mystery that's filled with creativity, empowering messages, and gorgeous graphics. You play Dawn, a picturesque, fashionable, speech-impaired woman who can fade into the shadows, unseen by the colorful characters that walk among your partner in crime. You're there to aid Didi, a brave, optimistic, imaginative young girl trying to pick up the pieces her broken family leaves behind. The still life of everything around Didi and Dawn are metaphorical in that it makes the situation seem dark and bleak until you play through the puzzles and breathe life into everything.
I would have had a problem with the length had the story not been executed as well as it was. The mechanics are unique and unlike anything I'd seen before and it seems like they've fixed all the glitches fans mentioned. I also used a controller so shifting from 2D to 3D and vice versa was done with ease. About midway, I started wondering who Dawn was and how she spawned from Didi's mind and was left with a treat in the end when all of my questions were answered.
This game has a lot to offer and if you ever get a chance to pick it up, do it.

Been playing this game outside Steam for quite a long time, so thats all i have to point out:
Concept: You are a guy that hires heroes, that help you progress the game in exchange for gold. You get gold for beating levels, full of monsters. Almost every hero gives you a DPS ( Damage Per Second ) bonus, that helps you move forward in game. After progressing some levels and unlocking some heroes, you will have to Ascend. Ascension is a process inside the game that resets your game progress and gets you back to the very beginning. Idiotic though it may seem, when you ascend over and over again, it gets easier and easier to get back to your peak level. The bonuses are immense, no bullsh*t. No specific goal is set at the game, but if you are aiming to get some achievements, you want to reach the higher level you can. There are much more stuff to mention, but no point if you are not going to play the game, so lets move on to some pros and cons.
Pros:
- Simple ( at beginning ) , yet addictive -> great time killer.
- You can play this game in 2 ways: actively or passively. When you are active, you help the game progress by clicking yourself. When playing passively, the game progresses itself and you do not have much to do after progressing to the first few ascensions.
- Fun graphics, animated.
- Maths included at a very latter part of the game, yet you can find lots of calculators online.
- Clans. In cooperation with your clanmates you try to get down some bosses, involving fair rewards ( Co-Op Mode, accessible later in game ).
- The game progresses even when your PC is shut down. All you have to do is save your game and it will progress as you are offline.
- Low spec mode. Sacrifice part of the graphics and animations, in order to gain performance.
Cons:
- Some people do not like the idea of starting over and over again, doing the same thing. ( Because doing the same thing actually happens in this game, but when it does its for good. )
- Needs much dedication at times.
- There is no competition, if that's what you are looking for. ( You could come up with challenges with your friends though... )
In my opinion, if the cons disappoint you, you should definitely NOT give this game a try, as it will result in a waste of your time. All in all, the game is great, but be sure that if you like it, you will lose a lot of time in it.

While I did not enjoy my playtime, I am fully aware that the first three times I downloaded Stellaris, I hated it.
So, it is with hope that I endure the painful process of uninstalling, and awaiting the slumber until the next time I give Endless Space 2 a try.
Things that turned me off in the game were the progression system, feeling of lostness, and lack of consequence. The game felt flowy, almost as if I, the player, had little to no interaction with the ingame world. On the opposite side of that coin, there is a very heavily scripted interaction system between the already created races. It feels rigid and storylike, which plays well for a first time. However after completing one story, you are left feeling like that is it, and disturbiting it plays poorly.
I absolutely loved the art style, music, and aesthetics the game had to offer.
I enjoyed the politics, but felt that intergalactic relations severely lacking, although I am told the DLC adds much needed fluff.
I did not enjoy fleet battles. It felt more like scripted rail shooters mixed with football, than actual fights. I am also led to believe that these tussels get more interesting as bigger ships are introduced, but I lacked the ability to wait that long in my level of play. I simply did not enjoy the game enough to progress to anything meaningful I suppose.
While I do rate the game rather high for something I wouldn't recommend, (85/100) I must stress that it simply is not my style of game yet. I said that once about Stellaris, now I clock hours regularly on it. Times change I guess.
If you take anything out of this review, please understand that this is a good game with excellent ideas and nice creative touches, not to even mention free DLC. It just is not interesting to me in the slightest.

One of the singularly best games to come out for PC since 2010, Crusader Kings II is a grand strategy game developed by Paradox. In CK2, you play as head of your dynasty through the ages. The goal of the game, unlike most strategy games where you expand your lands, is to ensure the survival and expansion of your family. Warmongers may find something they like in CK2; however, the heart of the game is in its politics.
Combat has improved since release, with various traits for your generals and the occasional reworking of how levies work, but battles often comes down to who has the bigger stacks. It's not a bad system, but it can be frustrating at times.
What the game lacks in combat, it makes up for it in the raw emotions it can invoke without you realizing until it's too late. You invest money and time mentoring your genius eldest son to a brilliant strategist to ensure that your heir (the future king) is a great leader, only to have the boy die the year after he comes of age, before he has produced a son of his own. Now his younger brother, the detached priest is next in line. Ugh.
The game lacks a good tutorial, but there are plenty of strong tutorial "Let's Plays" series to be found on Youtube. In the end, however, the best way to learn CK2 is to play it. To suffer, to lose, and to learn from your mistakes. It's a challenging game, but it is immensely rewarding.

Maybe I'm just too quick to be critical of games, but sometimes you have to be in a world with hundreds of thousands of video games and lots of Triple A titles.
For me, Contrast is the type of game that delivers a game mechanic that promises to be innovative and amazing, but fails to really deliver where it matters - namely, being able to use shadows as though they were tangible things. You start off as an unnamed woman walking around in a little girl's bedroom, and it is quickly conveyed that all living creatures (with the exception of one special little girl) appear only as shadows and you are invisible to one-another.
Unfortunately, after establishing that you are this little girl's friend (by way of picking up a drawing she made with you in it), that's all the reason you are given to follow her off on a boring adventure of interacting with objects, collecting objects, and being pestered to do things and go places in order to watch cutscenes. It really feels like it's being forced upon me when I don't even want to follow this little stranger and watch her parents fight; I want to explore the world and be given my own reason for doing things instead - not because a child tells me to.
So that was storytelling ruined within the first 5 minutes.
Then there was the shadow mechanic - it seems cool in theory, but you end up using it to do very rudimentary platforming straight off the bat. Exciting stuff. Maybe throwing a few shadow balls would be nice, or knocking over a bottle, or knocking over a bottle's shadow using a ball's shadow! The first few minutes are where you really have to give OOMPH to this new mechanic, and sadly it's used only to run up shadow ramps (some of which are inaccessible until you have tagged along with your new friend so she can push a simple object for you and progress the story). Again - I'm feeling like this is off to a bad start. I hear the game eventually progresses to pushing boxes around, but manipulating an object to reach a high place is hardly an innovative improvement.
And finally there's my last gripe - atmosphere. At one point within the first 5 minutes you also walk into a cabaret restaurant which is completely devoid of people and life. "BUT WAIT," you say, "people are invisible and appear as shadows!" Well yes, this is true, but there is nothing to make this restaurant feel LIVELY. There are glasses of alcohol on tables and cigars smouldering away in ashtrays, and there is ambient audience music playing, but there is nothing to make it feel ALIVE. No swaying and sliding of chairs, no sloshing of alcohol, no strange poltergeist-esque atmosphere replete with drinks trays floating around the room; bartenders shaking tumblers and pouring them out, no cats in alleyways knocking over trashcans and yowling, certain conversations that dim and fall as you wander the room - there is nothing - and that is where this game really falls flat on its face. You walk into a dead room and your only objective is to interact with the flashing objects scattered around the room so you can progress the plot because an invisible woman keeps nagging you to turn on the lights.
I'm sorry, I wanted to like this game, but it took 5 minutes to convince me that I hated it - all because there was nothing to try and persuade me into staying a while, looking around and really enjoying myself.
Maybe somebody somewhere else will do it better one day - because this game isn't there by a long shot.

CKII is a title from Paradox, a company with a great reputation for grand strategy games, and Crusader Kings lives up to this. Though the game has been called a "kill your brother and steal his stuff simulator," it incorporates elements from medieval cultures, religions, dynasties, and above all - wars. The game is primarily one of expansion and consolidation more than role-playing, though it does have elements of both.
Controls: Not very good. The game is vastly centered around the mouse; I'm pretty sure the only vanilla keyboard control is space, for advancing time. It is perfectly playable with a trackpad. There is a mod by Arumba07 which adds many useful keyboard shortcuts; I'd recommend picking it up.
DLC: Paradox has a huge amount of DLCs, but most are for sprites or music. Nearly essential are The Old Gods and Sword of Islam, allowing you to play as pagans and Muslims respectively. I would also recommend Legacy of Rome, allowing the reunification of the Catholic Church and the Roman Empire, as well as retinues - standing armies, as well as Ruler Designer, doing exactly what it says on the tin. They are somewhat overpriced. The newest, Sons of Abraham, adds Jews. It is also recommended.
Mods: Somewhat More Historical Map adds massive amounts of provinces and reworks de jure titles, Umbra Spherae adds the rest of Eurasia, VIET adds more traits and events, and Immortality Revised adds...what do you think. Those are my favourites and I recommend them.

To put it simply, Contrast is a game that follows a little girl through her beautiful, broken world.
In Contrast we take on the role of Dawn, the imaginary friend of the character Didi- we go on an adventure with this little girl who is trying ever so hard to just put her family back together.
Contrast features a wonderful Jazz soundtrack that really brings a lot to the game as a whole. The voice acting is full of emotions in both the English and French translations of the game. The voice acting is well recorded and well cut. 5/5
The visuals in Contrast are some of the best to come out of Greenlight. This near unique art style really gives the game some flavor. Contrast has top quality visuals both in it's 3D, and 2D worlds. I have yet to encounter fuzzy or broken models/textures. 5/5
The story is brilliant and the execution is just as wonderful. Though many complain that the story is "too short" we need to remember that length does not dictate the quality of the story. Contrast's story is about bringing a broken family back together. The story has all elements of a story, a great intro, tense climax, and an interesting conclusion. Watching the world change as the story progresses is simply fantastic. 4.5/5
Mechanically, Contrast has a few issues- though the game does contain a brilliant feature where the character has to work through both 2D and 3D worlds, this proves to cause some of the major problems in the game. In the shadow(2D) world, the gameplay is relatively choppy- whether the character will execute commands correctly in this state is hit or miss. We can regularly see the character pop out of the shadow world for no apparent reason what so ever. This is not game breaking, but does cause some frustration when attempting more complex or multi-step puzzles. 3.5/5
I believe that this game could also use some optimization with the keyboard/mouse. For me, it was a little tasking making the settings work with my hardware. This has no impact on the final rating.
Final rating – 18/20 or 90%   - I would suggest getting this game.

REVIEWED ON FREE WEEK END
I just spent 7 hours in a row playing and discovering this excellent title, and as far as I'm concerned, I am definitely seduced by the deep, deep, DEEP level of complexity of that very peculiar 4X game.
And I'm not a 4X player, at all !
My favorite aspect so far for me is the political aspect of it. Each action on each planetary system have an influence on different ''parties'' [industrials, militarists, scientists, ecologists, pacifists, independant, religious] which will influence the VOTE each voting cycle [20 turns i believe].
Each system votes independantly, and according to LOCAL actions [the more you build INDUSTRY producing buildings there, the more inclined they'll be to vote for INDUSTRY ; each system having a number of ''seats'' equal to their local population number].
Then comes the vote, which defines who will seat and lead at the governement.
But that's not all ! Because there are different types of governement possible !
Federation : 2 parties are leading
Dictatorship : 1 party is leading
Democracy : 3 parties are leading
and some others [republic and something else i don't remember]
That's pretty important, because each party leader allows you to choose from different LAWS to pass for the entire empire, which will drastically change the course its evolution.
And for sure, all the rest of the game seems just incredible , exploration is awesome, the narrative/writting is close to perfection, the replayability seems... endless !
I thought to myself this afternoon ''yeah... why not trying ? I'm bored of Rocket League anyway... and Fallout 4 just breaks my balls...''
7 hours later, I force myself to stop playing it just for the sake of having some sleep !
Game2gether, you made my day ! [and my whole week end]

This rts game was the rts game that got me into rts gaming. My first ever rts game. I was a console player, and this was the top selling rts for the xbox 360. So I picked it up and boy did I enjoy it. I am a huge fan of halo (having read some of the books and have played every single halo game), and too anyone who hasn't experienced the story of halo. You are missing out. Now I may be a bit biased, however I am not alone when I say that the halo universe is quite exciting. You won't be playing with the Master Chief in this game, but instead you will be taking command of the Spirit of Fire, a modified colony ship, and help fight the losing battle against the Covenant. This game captures the universe at it's grittiest, especially with the opening cut scene.
For those who have had no experience with halo, you can still pick it up and enjoy the story. The best thing about Halo War's story is that it is set at the very beginning of the human-covenant war, on the planet Harvest. All the backstory you need is that negotiations went south (there is a reason for this I won't spoil, but it has something to do with the religon of the Covenant) and the United Nations Space Command are fighting for survival against the genocidal campaign of the aliens.
The gameplay, I'm going to be honest, is not the greatest. This was a game made for the xbox 360. It is very dumb-downed and should not be compared to some of the RTS greats like starcraft and SupCom. However, it is very good for a first RTS game and casual RTS players looking for some fun. However, every hero is unique. The game play is still very fun, and is based on a 'rock, paper scissors' system (which imho I never found to have a strong presence, they are more soft counters).
However, Halo Wars is still very fun to play, and is a good introduction to the halo universe for new players.

After all these years, reaching level 54, I cannot recommend the game. I have 500+ hours on this, and all I can think of is remembering the good times. I hate this game so much because I used to love it to the point it became my most played game for almost one year. I'm gonna tell you why you should avoid this game that has become deteriorated over time (and has become less valuable than it was at release):
The good times, that was when this game didn't have regular crashes (it had none in fact). Now it crashes EVERY FIRST TIME you join the game, you Alt+F4 and then you have to again load the game. THEN it's very likely the server you wanted to join is full. You have to wait. Then it's possible that it crashes at the character screen etc... It's also possible to simply crash mid-game. I once had over 16 crashes while waiting for the server list to load. This never happened at the start.
Secondly, the networking is riddled with problems. It's laggy, choppy and after a certain amount of players it's going to skip registrations of animations, hits and more. Even on 32 player server this happens from time to time. I can live with it occasionally but now it happens so frequently, most servers crash like every 30mins.
Thirdly, bugs, bugs and bugs. In the level design, in the combat, in the animations and the graphics. It's unbelievable how many collision problems there are in the game. The parrying is completely inconsistent, you can even block attacks coming from the back where there is no shielding whatsoever. Catapults disappear, send you to other realms, dragging is imprecise and in general the abuse of the animation movement that can happen at any time is just ridiculous.
I don't want to spend much effort into the XP as it's just a gimmick, but it's funny to see how they fixed THAT particular thing that offers nothing new in the gameplay experience at all.
I haven't talked about the spawnbug, but it happens... ALL the time. Players don't spawn anymore from one team and the Pings start to skyrocket. The only way is for an admin to force win or mapvote. This has been happening so many times and it's still, not, fixed, after ALL the updates in the mean time.
One of the most terrible things in Chiv is the chase system where you gain over 4 times as much speed as your opponent you're chasing to prevent endless cat and mouse. However, it's SO fast it's literally baffling. I have literally seen admins KICK players because they thought they were speedhacking, while they were simply being speed up by the game... Unbelievable. You sometimes see an enemy well out of range that faces you from the FRONT, and OFTEN (not sometimes, not occasionally, but very OFTEN) the game just dupes like always and SPEEDS HIM UP. IN FRONT OF YOU. WTF. This problem has been known forever, never fixed so far.
Lastly, the performance. The performance is (except for LODS) inexistant. The larger the new community maps become, the worse the performance. One big bubble of rendering all mashed together and hoping for the best.... It's what makes battle sometimes impossible. I'm running a rig that should run Chiv with ease. Crysis 1 runs almost twice as good as chiv. On top of that, the game has become a product for DLC. I appreciate the community made content and the extra stuff, and I WAS glad to support chivalry, but these updates from the last months are nothing but updates to milk out of the game. Literally, I saw update reasons listed that represented fixes for most of the maps, and NOTHING was changed. It was coördinated with the release of new DLC coupled with free weekend to make sure they could get as much as possible, without fixing any of the massively gamebreaking bugs.
The way I see it, the image of TornBanner I had when I watched their videos at the start of release and when I followed before release, it was amazing. I felt as if TornBanner was one of the rarer companies who really cared about the player base and what we wanted. I was so happy at one point that community made content would arise and would reward everyone, but I would never have though the game would still be slumbering in day-1 problems in addition to the extra problems added with each and every update. It's breaking, it's collapsing under the chaos in their code, and each new adaption just kills the game more. I thought I could go through it, but essentially, this is the line. THIS version of Chiv, I cannot recommend.
Rewind time 1 year and a half back, and we will meet again. As it stands now, move onto more optimised games that offer you a reliable experience without crashes, go to games that when you enter the game, at least you know what's going to happen. Not like in Chiv now.

I love Amplitude, and I love the Endless games, and this game looks like it's going to be amazing, but it's just not finished yet.
The Good: The economic system is pretty nifty, and the inflation mechanic keeps it from being a game of "generate billions every turn and just buy every improvement the minute it's available." It incorporates the resource systems from Legend, and introduces a few new development level mechanics.
The Very Good: This game has incorporated the quest structure and story structure from Legend, and the writing is awesome. Also, Exploration is now a more active venture, and gives you a feeling of charting out the unknown. (Plus: Random Anomaly generation is an awesome Skinner box.)
The Dealbreaker: Combat in ES1 was a chore because it was so hands off. Amplitude saw this and implemented some changes that ought to keep the "Grand Strategist" vibe they're going for without making it a game of "Line up 5 battleships and hope your mil-tech is higher." The task force, range, and battle card mechanics that they've implemented all look like they'll be great. In the future. Unfortunately, combat is currently unworkable. Although AI can set target priorities, players cannot. AI can maximize ship disposition by assigning the best ships to their best task forces, players cannot. I'm sure that these fixes are coming in future patches, but they're not there yet, and it makes combat both boring AND unfun.
Verdict: Buy the livid daylights out of it in 4 months when Amplitude fixes the combat, and you'll be set for a sold few hundred hours of awesome.

Intro:
Well I first noticed this game shortly after I started playing Bioshock Infinite. It cought my eye because of it's art style. After watching the trailers, I added this to my wishlist and purchased it during Winter Sale.
Well I'm not sure how to rate this game. It's really well done in the visual and aural departments. The atmosphere really transports that 20s France feeling. But there are some things to be improved.
Graphics:
Not much to rant about. Maybe that's because im easy to plese with graphics, as long as they just fit together. But there are some glitches, especially on movable objects (crates and balls). The puddles on the streets look more like ice than water. That's because there is no added effect if you walk through them.
Audio:
Also nothing to really complain. The music is well done and fits the scenery. I really like the track that runs during the menu screen. The voice acting is okay except for Didi. Her lines just sound "strange" every now and then.
Controls:
My main complaint. It just feels like one of those early cheap 3D games. I often had problems judging how far I could jump. It just doesn't feel right. But I got used to it after a while.
Gameplay:
You spend a lot of time shifting into the shadows to acomplish your tasks. Sometimes the engine seems to have problems if the surface you are moving on is not even. If there is a corner, that's also a problem sometimes. But at least once the game forces you to go around a corner (which is evenly lit), so it cannot be intentional that the game throws you out of the shadow realm.
Sometimes there are new things to consider when solving puzzles. Unlike in many other games you are not shown that those concepts are there. Like shifting certain objects with you or moving objects using spotlights. I'm not really sure if this is a good thing or not. But I really liked finding those things out by myself. Maybe some optional hints would solve this "problem" for both sides.
Story:
To make it short: No epicness, no world rescue, no over the top characters, no "only he/she can do it". But nothing that special either... but as there hasn't been a story one could call "groundbreaking" or "has never been done before" in the recent past, I really like that simplicity.
Conclusion:
An artistically nice game with a few control hiccups that doesn't do handholding and is solvable without the use of walkthroughs or FAQs. Tells a down to earth fantasy story without uneccesary epicness. Buy it if you like artistically interesting games that don't neccessarily appeal to the masses.
EDIT:
What I really forgot:
It would've been nice if there was some more interaction with Didi. She often just stands there and does nothing. It only was about two times that she assisted you in one way or the other. For example: the screenshot where she lights the way with a lamp? Never happened.

Contrast is a 3rd person platforming puzzle game that uses the shadows cast on walls as its primary medium. The artwork is reminiscent of the 1920's and the rest of the game follows suit.
There are some incredibly good songs in this one but the overall music is just decent.
The controls and actual implementation of game mechanics can feel awkward and unpolished at times. The game makes up for this though...by limiting when you actually get to use any that. Level design feels incredibly linear at points, and some of the dialog and writing could have been done better.
It's a very short game and the difficulty isn't really there to prolong the length. There are some very obvious and often angering bugs that appear in game, mostly when using your shadows, which happens to be the primary game mechanic..
The culmination of all these factors led me to believe that the game was not ready for release. It had a very rushed and unpolished feel to it.
It was still an enjoyable play and I would recommend it for most people. When its on sale again.

What a surprise. This game feels like all the fun parts of other games that they gate behind energy, stamina and cooldown mechanics but without those barriers. You don't play this game because it's fun sometimes, or because it looks like the end-game is fun - the combat is just damned good right out of the gate. The movement is fast and the animations are good and you feel like a badass. Then on top that there is a deep system of warframes, weapons, moves, with collecting crafting and modding and plenty of aesthetic customization as well. The environments are varied and look great; sometimes creepy sometimes beautiful. As far as the genre, thinking of it as a looter like Diablo is a good place to start, except with badass 3rd-person action fighting (roughly Mass Effect on hyper-steroids) instead of boring clicking.
If someone told you this was a AAA $65 game and you watched them play it, you'd never doubt it. Probably the most surprisingly good free-to-play game I've ever come across. Definitely worth checking out.

---- Halo Wars: Definitive Edition ----
----              Day One                 ----
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
This game feels exactly the same as it was back in 09 when I played it on my Xbox 360.
For a PC edition, so far there are no complications I can see or anything wrong with it for that matter, the controls are smooth and feels nice and fluid.
The soundtrack as always is hella comfy, just like the rest of the Halo series having a very cozy
soundtrack.
Cutscenes for this game are very well done and, again the functionality of it both gameplay wise and menu's are perfect, there are no complications as of yet.
With the Definitive Edition, you have access to all of the downloadable content that was originally offered with Halo Wars, including the Pre-Order bonus Fireball Warthog skin and the Honor Guard Wraith available in the Limited Edition of the game.
If you are a big fan of the Halo Universe, Halo Wars actually has a timeline within the game, that allows players to go back and view different parts of the storyline and key moments in the games history. Including the events of Reach. (Most of these are obtained via finding 'Black Boxes'  throughout the story.
If you are seeking a little bit more of a challenge in the campaign apart from the Legendary Difficulty, you have the choice of obtaining 'Skulls', these skulls can be added to different missions to either at a challenge, or in some cases an advantage to your gameplay. And can even be something fun to use, for example 'The Grunt Birthday Party Skull', which in Halo 3 was a skull that if used, when a grunt was shot in the face, would spray confetti all over the place.
Of course it being on Steam, means that there is none of that use of Windows Live etc, so there is that as a massive plus.
Overall, it's great to get back into the fight and enjoy one of my all time favourite RTS' on the PC, bring back a hell of a lot of memories and is quite a nostalgic experience for those who played it back in the day!

I really do like this game, I like the concepts and everything for it. I wish they would introduce positional blocking (similar to what they have done for attacks) to keep it interesting.
I have some very large complaints about the game however, firstly, the keybinds are fairly complex and should vary from character to character. I enjoy setting things up so that the origin side of the swing comes from the same side as the button I am pressing (to keep it logical). However since all keybinds are set together as "offside swing" or "mainside swing" some characters will swing from the opposite side when you use the same button. I really wish that you could have profiles for character archetype to change that.
The second large issue has to do with what I see "good" players doing. I enjoy parrying and poking and fighting with people and enjoy that kind of engagements. However, what the good players do is more a fault of how the hit detection works. Basically "if a sword on a swing touches you, you take damage", so what do good players do to upgrade their chances to land hits? They abuse the system, they literally spin backwards to block and then overhead swing because it instantly throws the sword overhead scoring a hit, or they grab a two handed sword, after a block they look flat at the ground and crouch and it insta-hits the people in front of you. These types of game mechanics make me not want to play the game at all because you cannot block fast enough to deal with it.
The game IS still pretty fun regardless of the glaring issues, in fact the new player introduction stuff and the first 10/15 levels (whatever new player games a limited to in levels) were great! The problem is that beyond that there are at least 2 people abusing the broken mechanics in each game. If you still want to continue playing I would recommend playing in a server that disables third person view, as from my experience the people using instant hit abilities have a harder time with that disabled (especially the 1h sword ones where you have to block backwards).

I really liked L.A. Noire as a game, not really as a story though. People will say the acting is complete♥♥♥♥♥♥*cough* YourMovieSucks *cough*, but I can easily defend the game's acting because of how it was directed.
Man, was this one hell of a game to direct, people were using a certain type of motion capture to detect facial expressions. That sounds so wierd on paper, but they do it incredibly well. The actors do an astonishing job in making the game seem lively and immersive with their actions and responses. Now, maybe some aren't entirely good, but the majority are doing a bad reaction either on purpose or trying to trick the player. Unfortunately, I don't think the budget was well with the company considering they filed for bankrupcy only a few months after release.
The game is great with it's gameplay, as I said before, the idea is innovative and it carries out well. Even though this review is about 4 years late, the game does hold up and still is as innovative as it can be. In those years, this game uses motion capture to expand past immersion and into facial recognition. I'm stating this in here because you need to understand this game uses the motion capture incredibly well and that you need to be reading people's expressions to figure out if they are lying or not. For example, a man is going to try to say he's telling the truth but says it with a very sarcastic, dragged out "Nooo..." along with a shaking head. If you read the man carefully, it's obvious he's lying. This may not be the case for others though, as people throughout the game can get difficult as you try to figure out cases.
Alright, as the game has this incredible thing going for it in the whole motion capture thing, it's story really brings it down. Since you are a detective, you'd think you'd learn this actual backstory on Cole and his partners, but really you get a few crumby flashbacks and that's it for Cole. Cole's partners are pretty crap too, cause all they are are just really uninteresting characters who are only there for a chapter until you get promoted. *The only thing they have going for them are these personalities which I guess makes up for it, but it still doesn't help the end game in anyway.
*Something to note is that I haven't completed this game before, and thus, I have not a clue what happens in the last few cases.

This is one amazing game. And for me, as of writing this review, a person who only has 112 hours in, I can easily say it's only going to get better as I progress.
Starting this game, I had not the slightest clue of what the heck I was doing. But I stuck with it because it was fun.
The fluidity of this game is *mwah* noice. The playstyle is incredibly adaptable, too - you can be a Naruto all the way to being Rambo. There are no bad frames, only bad players... to a degree, at least. And don't get me started on fashion framing (you'll find out, if you play long enough).
But then... then... my god. The story. The story, the lore... it all comes into place. And it's wonderful. It doesn't throw its best at you right away; but if you hang in there, and just keep playing, by golly the story and lore just begin to get mind blowing.
This part may not be for everyone, but this game gives a great sense of satisfaction. Like, you WORKED for your weapons and armor. No instant gratification, but it still feels soooo good. Speaking of, everything, and I mean EVERYTHING, can be achieved with just some work. Weapons and frames kind of just come to you. And platinum, the in-game currency, can also be achieved without using hard earned paper. Just learn the trading system and trade Prime items and mods for platinum! Of course it takes lots of time, but many RPGs tend to take lots of time, especially a free to play MMO. So expect some grinding; but somehow, it's not wearisome.
The community is also one of the nicest I've ever met. So many helpful veterans and non-toxic newbs. Of course, you're bound to meet some toxic players, but you're also going to 100% meet someone who is willing to hold your hand through some missions and give you tips on how to play the game.
For new players wondering if they should play this, I'd say give it a try. Especially if you liked *cough* Destiny *cough*. Destiny is kind of a bad word in the Warframe community, haha - but you'll be soon to see why, if you keep playing. I'd recommend you spend your beginning 50 platinum on just getting slots in your inventory for weapons and warframes. At low level you won't see why you need so many slots for weapons but as you get higher level those slots get filled real fast. Oh, and never throw away a weapon until they are max rank - leveling up weapons gives Mastery points and helps to increase your mastery rank faster. I made this mistake as a newb.
And for your sake, join a clan. You're likely to find some chill clans, and being in clans will give you weapons you could not get otherwise (clans have research facilities that have weapons that you can't get by building or playing.)
Have fun, Tenno!

CKII is a title from Paradox, a company with a great reputation for grand strategy games, and Crusader Kings lives up to this. Though the game has been called a "kill your brother and steal his stuff simulator," it incorporates elements from medieval cultures, religions, dynasties, and above all - wars. The game is primarily one of expansion and consolidation more than role-playing, though it does have elements of both.
Controls: Not very good. The game is vastly centered around the mouse; I'm pretty sure the only vanilla keyboard control is space, for advancing time. It is perfectly playable with a trackpad. There is a mod by Arumba07 which adds many useful keyboard shortcuts; I'd recommend picking it up.
DLC: Paradox has a huge amount of DLCs, but most are for sprites or music. Nearly essential are The Old Gods and Sword of Islam, allowing you to play as pagans and Muslims respectively. I would also recommend Legacy of Rome, allowing the reunification of the Catholic Church and the Roman Empire, as well as retinues - standing armies, as well as Ruler Designer, doing exactly what it says on the tin. They are somewhat overpriced. The newest, Sons of Abraham, adds Jews. It is also recommended.
Mods: Somewhat More Historical Map adds massive amounts of provinces and reworks de jure titles, Umbra Spherae adds the rest of Eurasia, VIET adds more traits and events, and Immortality Revised adds...what do you think. Those are my favourites and I recommend them.
Experience: Understanding the concepts is slightly challenging but once you get the hang of it the difficulty curve drops to the floor. I'd recommend playing as smaller nations or vassals to increase the challenge.
OVERALL: A great game with infinite replayability. It is well-maintained and has a great (if dispersed, but now it has Workshop) modding community. A great bonus is that the soundtrack is included in the files, so you can have it for free.
Buy: If you like the brand, wait for a sale. If you like the genre, buy it now.

With 96 hours into this game, I can tell you that this game is quite the gem.  I've been playing it off and on throughout its development.  There have been bugs, and there are still probably bugs, but that is because underlying a incredible user interface (the best UI in every strategy and 4x game that I have ever seen), there is a very deep and very complex game.  Each race is completely different and plays different, unlike many games where each race is pretty much just a re-skin of others.  This is a beautiful game, and it definitely has that "one more turn" kind of feel to it.  The tech "pie" is incredible, with the vast majority of the techs being interesting, adding interesting strategic decisions along the way.  The only thing I thought used to be really weak was the diplomacy, but I see that they have made a lot of recent changes to resolve this.  I haven't tested that part really yet as that update just released, but I greatly look forward to exploring that over the next weeks.
Bottom line, this game is great, it's much better than all of the other 4x strategy games that have been released so far, and it has developers that really take in feedback and update and resolve the issues.  This game has changed a lot since release, and always for the better in my opinion.

This game was not what I was expecting, but in this case that turned out to be a gaming experience I will never forget and will continue to come back to for years to come.
If you're a major European history buff, or want to get into those really complicated grand-strategy games, this is a great game for you. It looks as if it's one of those map-staring strategy games, but it's actually a map-staring RPG. You play the invisible hand which guides a noble family's dynasty through the ages, rather than a king or emperor attempting to take over/save the world. While you may end up playing the part of a king attempting to take over/save the world at times, your ultimate goal is to see your family do good for itself. I know it's a hard idea to understand, and it's even harder to try to explain to someone, but essentially this is a RPG first and a strategy game second.

I think as a player who bought this game right when it came out and played for hundreds of hours on Official Servers it's time for me to give my review on this game.
