Ark in general is very fun and interactive. I've spent many hours doing one of the hundreds of things that can be done in this game. This survival game requires a lot of heart and dedication if you are planning on playing on an official pve or pvp server.
Im sure most people who have thousands of hours on Ark can relate that the PvP aspect of this game is the best part in the game and without it, it is boring and meaningless. Atleast for me it was, as I felt there was no point in spending hours into a game if there was no type of hierarchy and fear of being attacked by others. A lot of my hours on ark were spent mass taming dinosaurs and this was the time without kibble(makes taming extremely fast). Then when I logged off at night and got back the next day everything would be dead. Thats 12 hours of my real life time gone in mere minutes. Anyone thats played on a PvP server knows the struggle and the grind and YES thats what PvP is and it's fun.
In conclusion, if you think this game is for you as I once did, then be ready to treat this game as a full time job because thats the type of effort and hours you need to put in to survive on Official PVP Servers. Contrast is an interesting game. 3D in the main world, 2D in the shadow world. Puzzles are built around the concept of traversing shadows to get to places you could not otherwise reach. Unfortunately the execution is lacking. The game is VERY finicky when it comes to where you can enter the shadows and if you get even the slightest bit off while in shadow you'll pop back into the 3D world and have to begin what you were doing from the beginning.
Further, there's no educating the player going on at ALL. Studying Half-Life 2 and Portal's puzzle education should be mandatory for all aspiring puzzle game developers. On several occaisions Contrast throws some new concept at you and forces you to realize it's there. The end result is a game that you're fighting with in order to play instead of one you're figuring out. Frustration abounds, not because you cannot figure out what to do, but because the execution has to be pixel perfect or you have to start over.
I would LOVE to be able to recommend Contrast. I really would. The music, the art style, the gameplay concept, the story of a kid with a troubled home life seeking to fix her world in any way she can. It's all great, but the core mechanics are just not there. Perhaps with some polish Contrast can become a game that I can recommend. Until then, only buy it if you reall love platformers AND it's cheap.

First thing's First. If you never played the console version, it might seem a little jarring to you because of all the wheels and simple mechanics.
The second thing, The Publisher NAILED the price perfectly, not because it's a bad game but because they know its age, and its quirks are going to be intimidating at higher prices...that and it's no longer worth a full $40-60.
The UI is extremely responsive, the loading is very quick, and there are some minor speed problems which I have to assume is tied to the FPS which might be why V-Sync was enabled.
The graphics aren't super crysis levels, and that's fine. But they are definitely better than the original version on the Xbox 360.
I loved the old game years ago when I still had a working copy for my 360, to see it released now on Steam is a dream come true, and hopefully an indicator of things to come.
There are some minor visual problems, mostly the UI scaling hasn't taken into effect yet, so you're going to have a UI designed for max 720p, though the game resolution is much better overall.
The gameplay is still awesome, and it has Co-Op campaign as well. This is how you do games, this is how good ports are made. I can fault 343 for many many attrocities, but this is not an attrocity and it is definitely a good game. It's not a ground breaking RTS but it is a good one none the less. Made by (still around at the time) Ensemble Studios which made excellent RTS's in the past, this port was so far, well done.
For $20 I say get it, let's show Microsoft why Steam is prefered over the windows store, and let's let them know there is a vast and viable market waiting for more.
*EDIT, I should note, I am hoping the game is moddable. The community can do wonders for this game and might even increase its value ten fold.

Best game I've ever played hands down. There were a few minor flaws in the game at launch, but the dev team releases patches and expansions so regularly, that the game is all but perfect now. Very difficult to get into at first, but once you get it, you're hooked. The official forum community is the best I've ever experienced, and they happily guided me to being almost an expert on how the game works. Great Linux support, and part of IMO the best dev studio in existence. The game is also extremely moddable, and there are many improvement mods as well as overhaul mods that change the entire game. The most popular is probably the Game of Thrones mod, but my favorite is the Middle Earth mod that while still in development, is already great. The best thing about this game is that there is no set way to win, no goals or pathways, just your own willpower. If you aim to convert Europe to the Norse faith, go ahead. If you want to unite Europe under the banner of Dublin, go ahead. If you want to reunite the Roman Empire then plunge it into turmoil, go ahead. Anything is possible in this game, and that's why it never gets boring. Just look at how many hours I've spent on it.

There's a reason why Warframe is so highly reviewed, and it's because it may be the only F2P game in the world that does it right. Oh, AND it's a fantastic game.
Pros
- Really slick movement/parkour, feels really nice
- Great mix of abilities (tied to Warframes) and gunplay
- Huge variety of playstyles through different guns and Warframes
- Leveling doesn't feel as grindy because every item you level up caps at 30
- AMAZING COMMUNITY - in a world of toxic multiplayer games (DOTA2, LUL, other MMOs), this community is an oasis
- Great crafting system and resource-based loot system
- Earn real money currency in-game via trading
- Constantly updated and added content
- Haven't had to deal with Customer Service yet, but on the subreddit I've only heard good things about them
Cons
- Third person may turn off some people
- The actual total grind in this game is
; grind to 30, grind for mods, grind said mods to max level, grind for more gear to grind to 30, grind old gear to 30 again after upgrading them, grind Warframes to 30, etc...
- Because of the grind, earning new Warframes and weapons is going to be  slow for newer players
- The game is pretty dense, so learning all the systems will take you a while. The complexity helps the game in the end, but learning it is painful.
As for the F2P, while you can technically buy most the Prime Frames and weapons via trading and buying resources (regular Frames and weapons can be unlocked with Platinum, the real-money currency), some will require resources that cannot be bought for real money. Therefore you're forced to grind for it anyway. On top of this, you can actually trade your own drops for Plat from other players, so you actually don't need to spend any money on the game. There are players end-game that have thousands of Plat from this system (for reference, a non-Prime Warframe costs around 250-300 Plat)
Many players that spend money do so to suppport the company, which is something I've never seen people do in a F2P game (in other games they P2W or pay to unlock new stuff). It's kind of incredible that their F2P system is as unscummy as it is, considering the sheer amount of companies releasing LOOT BOXES or end-game content locked behind paywalls.
Honestly I would give this game a try. It's FREE anyway, and if you enjoy it you can continue to unlock all the content in the game for free as well (assuming you have the patience for the grind). I find this game insanely fun because I love MMO shooters, and whenever you do a mission it feels like you're actually progressing, instead of filling an EXP bar that goes up 10%/hour.

Early Review: Vaguely Frustrating Game.
There seems to be a misconception with the design of this game, and that is that everything is focused mainly around combat, or that it should be focused around combat. In the first game I played, my level 1 scout encountered a pirate, and I was pretty much railroaded into a fight by the tutorial. No time to learn about ships, or weapon design or tactics or anything. 'Oh, you found a planet! Look, it's another person! QUICK SHOOT EM BEFORE THEY GET AWAY!!!'
Later in the game, as everything was going well and I'm doing research and planetary development... suddenly I'm told I don't have enough money, and the game tells me to 'do something about it'. ... what exactly? The marketplace wasn't unlocked yet, so I couldn't trade for anything, and I had no other means of suddenly making money. Next thing I know, the game auto-sells most of my ships, unassigned my heros and cancels a bunch of research on various planets, basically screwing my game beyond recovery.
After several turns of this, with still no idea what I can do to stop it, THEN the marketplace opens up and I'm able to sell a few resources. Of course by then planets are in full rebellion, and I still have no real way to do anything about the negative income...
Again, this was a first time attempt at playing, and I'm hoping for a different result next time through. We'll see what happens. As of now though, I'm kinda annoyed at how the game just seemed to throw me a curve ball without any means of countering it.

Disclaimer: Marking as if I got this for free since I played this on a free play weekend.
tl;dr: Although this game looks great, it suffers from a UI that needs work, AI that does not feel competent, and the game just doesn't feel complete. 5/10.
I was a pretty big fan of the first one and the Endless Space franchise was definitely in need of a sequel. Well, this is it, but unfortunately it feels more cluttered than the first while also having less content. It might be my imagination, and maybe there was more added in DLC's to ES1 that I mark as the "full game" but this game feels like an Early Access game that got stopped when it was "good enough."
Although the game looks beautiful, the UI system is clunky and worse than the first game. In some cases the game got better, like with ship design, but in others the game got much worse, like with upgrading planets. There is a fair amount of micromanaging required in a 4X game that I feel that it's ok to be overwhelmed from time to time. But that's not what I get from this game. I've been stumbling to remember where all the buttons are, or how to get to screen X or edit feature Y on one planet. The game controls are counter intuitive and lacking the basic industry accepted controls. For example, you can't scroll around the galaxy map with wasd, you have to go into the menu and manually key bind it. Not a big deal, but come on, really? This isn't some duke nukem game from the 90s ported over to a modern PC, this is a modern game and things like wasd scrolling should already be here.
The graphics and ship battles got a huge boost in the wow factor in terms of visual appeal. There's still the wonky camera angles that show you a piece of a ship getting hit and other than some nice looking textures and a few floating particles, there isn't much in the way of shown battle damage. I was really hoping for a chase cam on my missiles from my long distance ships, but nope. Just the same old over-zoomed camera angles.
The battles themselves are just like in the first one where you watch what is essentially a cut scene of "what happened" after the strategy round. Unfortunately the strategy round changed in an inventive but detracting way. Now you can select your long range, mid range, and short range ships into groups, But those groups don't move out of their initial area (at least in my experience). In that regard I was blasting away at the AI with a long range and mid range squad, and beat them even though I have crappy weapons and was shown to be at a disadvantage in the preview screen. It could just be my play through, but I feel the AI was crap at ship design/tactics, which is a shame.
The diplomacy, from what I played with it, was pretty much the computer taunting you or telling you something like "I'm coming to get you rawr".. but they didn't come to get me when they said they were going to, and when they did come, they sieged a system for 3 turns, which I ignored because there is no lasting effect to a siege, and they left on their own. I don't think that was a clever AI being programmed with a personality. I think that was more one of those well we wanted to make the AI appear aggressive and most players would defend their territory so we never thought of programming an AI that actually does anything other than blockade a system for 3 turns... It's pretty clear that there was little work done on the AI and by default there was likely no QA done on this game. I think I remember seeing this game on Early Access, but I can't imagine they listened to people because things like that and others that I've found wouldn't pass the sniff test. And mistakes like that glaringly show that this game is really only a pretty looking game. I find it's much like a girl who wears too much makeup, but she's still kinda pretty, and when I try to get to know her better, I ask who her favorite actor is and she says, "Rob Schneider." And as soon as I've seen that deep into her mind, I'm turned off by the whole experience and have to walk away.
Despite all of the issues, in a lot of ways this game is better than the first, but in its current state, I don't see this as a complete game. It looks good, it feels good to boot it up and look at your growing empire, but it doesn't play fun and it's a bit confusing where it shouldn't be. Right now I think the devs need to take another run at things like the AI with a bit more complexity and think about the UI with this in mind, "how can the players manage their civ with the most amount of fun and the least amount of clicks?" I'm not saying simplify the game, but the UI is disjointed with some buttons that don't look like buttons, when the UI should be streamlined and uniform across the board. If this game had a bit more complexity, usability, and depth it would be a pass for me, but unfortunately it does not. 5/10.

Early Access review for Version 0.7.5
Long things short: Would definitely recommend this game, however given its current state with some bugs, better to wait until for a few versions of updates.
The gameplay of this game reminds me of Game Dev Tycoon, but I think this game does excel in terms of fun. There are more than just uploading the game to Youtube (Date, Work, Shopping, etc) which gives a better immersion for this type of business simulation game. You are not just looking at numbers and play chess, you are more of playing "yourself" now.
Issues: Every once a while, the issued command will not be executed. Observed causes include path finding (the character needs to walk to the play to execute the command, which gets stuck if there are body collision with another character), overlapping action (a constant bug, when I try to edit the recorded video/interview, if I try to check my staus or click somewhere else, the "editing video" command is gone and there's no way to retrieve it), delayed scheduling (not sure if this is caused by the poor optimization of the engine, but some actions will be delayed for so long).
Suggestions: Despite the bugs I faced, there are still some features I hope to change/add. During recordings, the cards we are given can only be replaced if you use one, this sometimes gets annoying. For example, I once got three copyrighted cards which I don't want to use, but there's no way to get rid of them. I would suggest adding an option to swap some of the unused cards to increase recording mini-game experience. One possible way could be the total number of times you can swap cards will depend on your character's skillset or other factors.
Another suggestion is regarding the time progress in game. The game time constantly progresses even when no actions are made, and the rate of progress is very fast. I understand if this feature is a design choice, but I'm really against such fast pace of time progression during idle moves. After all this game is mostly for casual purposes, if we have to race against time (such as to meet the deadline). Possible improvements are slowing down or stop the time if the player is just idling and maybe add some time skip option if player choose to idle the time purposely, this also speedsup the game for those who want it to.
Overall I really enjoyed playing this game, but I'll comeback when the game is (completely) published.

Take a moment here to remember your childhood. Remember how afternoons after school could be filled with fantastical worlds brought forth from the trees, the rocks, the tall grasses in the backyard or the field near your neighborhood: all you needed was your imagination. Remember as you went to sleep at night and stared at the shadows in your room, sometimes in wonder, and sometimes in fear of the shapes they made. Remember how life could be magical in the most ordinary of things and how, as you grew older, you longed for the days when reality didn't have to be so damned
all the time: homework, bills, politics, relationships, family...
That longing is at the heart of Compulsion Games' lavishly realized and gorgeous platformer adventure
. Set in 1920s Paris, it paints a dreamlike world of cobblestone roads, nightclubs, and carnivals, all of which will at once remind you of
art deco atmosphere, the simple drama of Hollywood's Golden Age, and with perhaps a helping of the musical
. Didi is the young daughter of a quarreling nightclub singer mother and a sometimes-there father who is trying to strike it rich with some shady investors but, as often is the case with shadiness, never quite seems to get a break. Didi copes with all of this with the help of the player in the form of Dawn, Didi's tall, waifish, silent imaginary friend, and the game leads Didi and Dawn through the nighttime town trying to help her family with their woes. To say any more of the plot would be a disservice to you, so let's move on to the gameplay.
Anyone who recalls making shadow puppets on the wall as a kid will instantly feel in tune with the core mechanic here which involves Dawn's singular ability to become a shadow on the wall, quite literally. There is a sense of astonishment every time the game opens up a new platforming section because it is all done with light sources: streetlights and spotlights are switched on and suddenly and quite beautifully make the most ordinary setting, like the facade of a storefront or the walls of a hotel, into a visually striking obstacle course for Dawn to traverse. While sometimes the gameplay could occasionally be a tiny bit tighter, it never gets old to "shift" into shadow, and you will be challenged to think in some strange ways to solve some of the puzzles in your path. This is a mechanic as new and different as Portal's portal gun and it's something you will remember long after Didi and Dawn's story has concluded.
That conclusion, unfortunately, comes much too soon as this game is quite short on the order of four or five hours, although you could spend a long time marveling at the charming art style of the characters and the setting of the moonlit Paris suburb, not to mention looking for and gathering each of the areas' collectibles, which add little distinctly artful flairs to the main story here and there. Normally I would find this too short of a game, but I can't bring myself to complain and here's why. A lot of story-driven games want to say and do a tremendous amount of things in the course of their stories, because, understandably enough, the developers want to have as many opportunities as they can to wow the pants off you with crazy setpieces and wild spectacle. The trouble with that is they almost always seem to get off course somewhere along the line and it can feel like a total sensory overload that in the end leaves you reeling, and not always in a good way. (I'm looking at you, Bioshock Infinite.) But
has a single story to tell through Didi's young eyes and, without distracting you with twenty different characters and eight bizarre environments and thirty different weapons, Compulsion Games excels at telling it, a very ordinary, touching, human and absolutely enchanting story. One of my top games of 2013 and I very much hope it receives the wide recognition it deserves in 2014.

Endless Space 2 is a deep, immersive, beautiful space strategy simulation that I highly recommend.
With the latest large, free update provided I felt I should finally write a review since I have been enjoying the game since the launch.
The gameplay is similar to many other space strategy games but what make it stand out are the details:
Beautiful artwork which is everwhere from system anomalies to techs to quest popups. It really helps immerse you into the universe.
Unique and interesting factions to both play as and compete against. From the terrifying Cravers (what do you sound like when you scream?) to the haughty United Empire.
A wonderfully clean and elegant interface which makes the game a pleasure to play no matter what is happening.
A quest system that will give you different story events to take place in and nice rewards if you are able to complete them.  Again it really sucks you into the universe.
Hereos that you can acquire  that add much flavor and character to the game. You can either use them as system governors or fleet admirals. They are also part of a very interesting quest line about an academy they come from.
Amazing space battles that occur when opposing fleets meet. All the factions have interesting and varied ships designs which you can equip with various weapon and defense modules that are researched.  Multicolored energy beams and pulse lasers strike out at enemy ships, missles race towards targets and  bombers make their attack runs, both which can be knocked out by point defense flak weapons. Destroyed ships explode spectacularly (which I would like to see even more of).  All against the backdrop of many varied different and beautiful types of star systems.
The game also has great music.
There are many other different parts to the game to mention them all. While there is a learning curve it is a game that is fun to learn and explore how all the different parts work together.
The developers provide constant support and regular free updates to the game which include many additional features.

This game won my heart. Few games can be considered a visual and audio delight such as Contrast is. It is definitely not for everyone, not action packed or with potential cliffhangers but it’s by far a star.
It’s the result mix between the 20's- 30's atmosphere, the vintage representation of the decadent circus life, the dream shards of a Parisian street, and the film-noir instrumentals. It has clever and most importantly aesthetic puzzles, playing with memories and shadows.
It does however have its disappointments: few bugs and glitches that may at times annoy the player a bit. I also heard that people have problems playing the game itself because it freezes (it happened to me as well but only on short period of times) and crashes; and of course, the biggest problem of the game is that it’s too short. I would have adored to spend more hours of gameplay; not only that but because the game is too short we have to take the characters as they are, with few information about them and we have to adjust to the ‘momentary’ feeling of the plot.
In what concerned the characters and the story telling: it’s a great plus. Until the end it makes you wonder what is reality and what not, what is fantasy and what is science. You get to see all these interesting side characters and discover that, in truth, the story is about them.
It’s a game perfect to play during the evening and I encourage anyone with a bit of taste for the aesthetics to try it.

Quite simply one of the greatest strategy games ever made.
From the outset - Crusader Kings is not for everyone.
It will be best enjoyed by people who are interested in deep systems and the interplay between them. Those seeking a way to crack the "optimal" way to play, and those seeking to "win" will be disappointed, whereas those seeking emergent systems and effects will enjoy hundreds of hours of discovery.
It is therein that lies CK2's greatest strength - creating a narrative through emergent systems.
Crusader Kings II relies largely on the player setting their own goals and then working towards them. Be they immediate goals, medium term aspirations, or long term dreams, a large part of CK2's appeal lies in pondering how best to "exploit the code" to reach your ends. In fact, the best way to play CK2 is not to play to win, but to let the game "happen"; to let your dynasty's fortune ebb and flow with the passage of time, creating a narrative of a family streching across the centuries.
Crusader Kings 2 is a game that you can sink literally hundreds of hours into and still find out new and exciting things to do. CK2 isn't a perfect game; the learning curve can be steep, particularly for those new to the genre, and the presentation is a little short of the cutting edge. But, with a fantastic level of developer support, continual free and paid content additions, hundreds of mods, and a lively, friendly and supportive community, it is fair to say that CK2 is one of the greatest strategy games of all time and, for strategy fans, possibly one of the greatest games of all time. For this writer with over 30 years of gaming behind him and hundreds of hours on the game (mostly on the Gamersgate version), it's certainly cracked the Top Ten!

Crusader Kings II is a grand strategy game that will suck you in. There is a lot going on, which is overwhelming at first, but allows you to play the game exactly how you want to. However, he joined the Scottish court and ended up plotting to assassinate me, and was successful. I then had his younger brother, as the new family ruler, fighting a war against his rotten brother to keep Ireland secured in the family.
That's what makes this game great. If you like history, even a little bit, and you like the idea of playing the role of a leader in Medieval Europe, then this game WILL take many hours from you. Oh, and I want to mention that it keeps getting better with each patch and expansion. Have fun, and good luck with making your family name truly great!

You know you’ve been playing too much Crusader Kings II when you start arranging betrothals between your and your friend’s children and spend the rest of your time musing on heraldry. Crusader Kings II is an ambitious strategy masterpiece full of intrigue, diplomacy, and war. The player controls a single noble dynasty through the European middle ages in a world as changeable as it is engaging.
One word I would definitely not use to describe Crusader Kings II is ‘accessible’. When I first started the game, I had to sort through dozens of menu screens and tabs trying to figure out to do. I can’t be sure, but at one point I think I accidentally attempted to abdicate the Duchy of Kent in favor of my Norwegian half-brother. There certainly were helpful messages and tips in great abundance, but if I really wanted to spend an hour reading, I would be downloading O. Henry short stories, not starting up a new game.
Once you do get the hang of the controls, though, Crusader Kings II opens up to almost endless possibilities. You can expand your dynasty by clever power play, strategic marriages, or through military force alone. If you work hard as an impoverished count, your grandchildren could be kings and queens. In a game revolving around diplomacy, however, the AI can be a little off-putting in its lack of complexity. While computer players are reasonably clever, they always make the most rational choice, which makes you feel a bit out of place as you attempt to coerce an Arabian sheikh to help you to invade Sweden.
The graphics are nothing to write home about, unless you wanted to let your folks know that games can be released in 2012 and still run on any computer more advanced than an abacus. The Crusader Kings II interface is basically a detailed map surrounded by different menus. If you weren’t wearing your glasses, it would look a lot like Total War, only you can’t zoom in for battles- all physical conflict is resolved off-screen as you watch the number of troops still alive decrease. The constant music definitely helps to distract from the less-than-interesting graphics. The same tracks are played over and over, but they’re epic enough to make it worth it.
The beautiful thing about Crusader Kings II is the way it generates stories through emergent gameplay. Take King Tudwal the Great, who loved gardening but would occasionally fly off the handle and kill his own family members, or Count Oberto, who despairingly turned to a scholarly life after failing to find a bride for his homosexual nephew. These aren’t characters you find in most Triple-A games.
If you only want to relax for a few minutes, you would probably be best served playing Plants vs Zombies, but if you want to spend a challenging 400 years taking over medieval Europe through vilest treachery, Crusader Kings II is without rival. Now if you’ll excuse me, my uncle just raised the banners of Scotland in rebellion against his Welsh overlords.

Early Review: Vaguely Frustrating Game.
There seems to be a misconception with the design of this game, and that is that everything is focused mainly around combat, or that it should be focused around combat. In the first game I played, my level 1 scout encountered a pirate, and I was pretty much railroaded into a fight by the tutorial. No time to learn about ships, or weapon design or tactics or anything. 'Oh, you found a planet! Look, it's another person! QUICK SHOOT EM BEFORE THEY GET AWAY!!!'
Later in the game, as everything was going well and I'm doing research and planetary development... suddenly I'm told I don't have enough money, and the game tells me to 'do something about it'. ... what exactly? The marketplace wasn't unlocked yet, so I couldn't trade for anything, and I had no other means of suddenly making money. Next thing I know, the game auto-sells most of my ships, unassigned my heros and cancels a bunch of research on various planets, basically screwing my game beyond recovery.
After several turns of this, with still no idea what I can do to stop it, THEN the marketplace opens up and I'm able to sell a few resources. Of course by then planets are in full rebellion, and I still have no real way to do anything about the negative income...
Again, this was a first time attempt at playing, and I'm hoping for a different result next time through. We'll see what happens. As of now though, I'm kinda annoyed at how the game just seemed to throw me a curve ball without any means of countering it.

I was a pretty big fan of the first one and the Endless Space franchise was definitely in need of a sequel. Well, this is it, but unfortunately it feels more cluttered than the first while also having less content. It might be my imagination, and maybe there was more added in DLC's to ES1 that I mark as the "full game" but this game feels like an Early Access game that got stopped when it was "good enough."
Although the game looks beautiful, the UI system is clunky and worse than the first game. In some cases the game got better, like with ship design, but in others the game got much worse, like with upgrading planets. There is a fair amount of micromanaging required in a 4X game that I feel that it's ok to be overwhelmed from time to time. But that's not what I get from this game. I've been stumbling to remember where all the buttons are, or how to get to screen X or edit feature Y on one planet. The game controls are counter intuitive and lacking the basic industry accepted controls. For example, you can't scroll around the galaxy map with wasd, you have to go into the menu and manually key bind it. Not a big deal, but come on, really? This isn't some duke nukem game from the 90s ported over to a modern PC, this is a modern game and things like wasd scrolling should already be here.
The graphics and ship battles got a huge boost in the wow factor in terms of visual appeal. There's still the wonky camera angles that show you a piece of a ship getting hit and other than some nice looking textures and a few floating particles, there isn't much in the way of shown battle damage. I was really hoping for a chase cam on my missiles from my long distance ships, but nope. Just the same old over-zoomed camera angles.
The battles themselves are just like in the first one where you watch what is essentially a cut scene of "what happened" after the strategy round. Unfortunately the strategy round changed in an inventive but detracting way. Now you can select your long range, mid range, and short range ships into groups, But those groups don't move out of their initial area (at least in my experience). In that regard I was blasting away at the AI with a long range and mid range squad, and beat them even though I have crappy weapons and was shown to be at a disadvantage in the preview screen. It could just be my play through, but I feel the AI was crap at ship design/tactics, which is a shame.
The diplomacy, from what I played with it, was pretty much the computer taunting you or telling you something like "I'm coming to get you rawr".. but they didn't come to get me when they said they were going to, and when they did come, they sieged a system for 3 turns, which I ignored because there is no lasting effect to a siege, and they left on their own. I don't think that was a clever AI being programmed with a personality. I think that was more one of those well we wanted to make the AI appear aggressive and most players would defend their territory so we never thought of programming an AI that actually does anything other than blockade a system for 3 turns... It's pretty clear that there was little work done on the AI and by default there was likely no QA done on this game. I think I remember seeing this game on Early Access, but I can't imagine they listened to people because things like that and others that I've found wouldn't pass the sniff test. And mistakes like that glaringly show that this game is really only a pretty looking game. I find it's much like a girl who wears too much makeup, but she's still kinda pretty, and when I try to get to know her better, I ask who her favorite actor is and she says, "Rob Schneider." And as soon as I've seen that deep into her mind, I'm turned off by the whole experience and have to walk away.
Despite all of the issues, in a lot of ways this game is better than the first, but in its current state, I don't see this as a complete game. It looks good, it feels good to boot it up and look at your growing empire, but it doesn't play fun and it's a bit confusing where it shouldn't be. Right now I think the devs need to take another run at things like the AI with a bit more complexity and think about the UI with this in mind, "how can the players manage their civ with the most amount of fun and the least amount of clicks?" I'm not saying simplify the game, but the UI is disjointed with some buttons that don't look like buttons, when the UI should be streamlined and uniform across the board. If this game had a bit more complexity, usability, and depth it would be a pass for me, but unfortunately it does not. 5/10.

Quite simply one of the greatest strategy games ever made.
From the outset - Crusader Kings is not for everyone.
It will be best enjoyed by people who are interested in deep systems and the interplay between them. Those seeking a way to crack the "optimal" way to play, and those seeking to "win" will be disappointed, whereas those seeking emergent systems and effects will enjoy hundreds of hours of discovery.
It is therein that lies CK2's greatest strength - creating a narrative through emergent systems.
Crusader Kings II relies largely on the player setting their own goals and then working towards them. Be they immediate goals, medium term aspirations, or long term dreams, a large part of CK2's appeal lies in pondering how best to "exploit the code" to reach your ends. In fact, the best way to play CK2 is not to play to win, but to let the game "happen"; to let your dynasty's fortune ebb and flow with the passage of time, creating a narrative of a family streching across the centuries.
Crusader Kings 2 is a game that you can sink literally hundreds of hours into and still find out new and exciting things to do. CK2 isn't a perfect game; the learning curve can be steep, particularly for those new to the genre, and the presentation is a little short of the cutting edge. But, with a fantastic level of developer support, continual free and paid content additions, hundreds of mods, and a lively, friendly and supportive community, it is fair to say that CK2 is one of the greatest strategy games of all time and, for strategy fans, possibly one of the greatest games of all time. For this writer with over 30 years of gaming behind him and hundreds of hours on the game (mostly on the Gamersgate version), it's certainly cracked the Top Ten!

Crusader Kings II is a grand strategy game that will suck you in. There is a lot going on, which is overwhelming at first, but allows you to play the game exactly how you want to. You'll be able to steer your own story in medieval Europe, and that's what makes it so great. It's not just a strategy game, but a role playing game, too. You'll be drawn to your ruler from the start of his rule, and death will impact you. If you read other reviews, you'll see people mention stories, and it's true. You'll have the urge to jot down all the events and create a story of your dynasty. My most memorable was exiling my oldest son from Ireland because he was a rotten kid and was not a fit ruler. However, he joined the Scottish court and ended up plotting to assassinate me, and was successful. I then had his younger brother, as the new family ruler, fighting a war against his rotten brother to keep Ireland secured in the family.
That's what makes this game great. If you like history, even a little bit, and you like the idea of playing the role of a leader in Medieval Europe, then this game WILL take many hours from you. Oh, and I want to mention that it keeps getting better with each patch and expansion. Have fun, and good luck with making your family name truly great!

Endless Space 2 is a deep, immersive, beautiful space strategy simulation that I highly recommend.
With the latest large, free update provided I felt I should finally write a review since I have been enjoying the game since the launch.
The gameplay is similar to many other space strategy games but what make it stand out are the details:
Beautiful artwork which is everwhere from system anomalies to techs to quest popups. It really helps immerse you into the universe.
Unique and interesting factions to both play as and compete against. From the terrifying Cravers (what do you sound like when you scream?) to the haughty United Empire.
A wonderfully clean and elegant interface which makes the game a pleasure to play no matter what is happening.
A quest system that will give you different story events to take place in and nice rewards if you are able to complete them.  Again it really sucks you into the universe.
Hereos that you can acquire  that add much flavor and character to the game. You can either use them as system governors or fleet admirals. They are also part of a very interesting quest line about an academy they come from.
Amazing space battles that occur when opposing fleets meet. All the factions have interesting and varied ships designs which you can equip with various weapon and defense modules that are researched.  Multicolored energy beams and pulse lasers strike out at enemy ships, missles race towards targets and  bombers make their attack runs, both which can be knocked out by point defense flak weapons. Destroyed ships explode spectacularly (which I would like to see even more of).  All against the backdrop of many varied different and beautiful types of star systems.
The game also has great music.
There are many other different parts to the game to mention them all. While there is a learning curve it is a game that is fun to learn and explore how all the different parts work together.
The developers provide constant support and regular free updates to the game which include many additional features.
Despite it's mixed reviews, definitely a game that keeps you going for hours, if not even days, on end

Contrast is a rather simple indie, platform/puzzle game about a young girl, Didi, and her (apparently) imaginary friend Dawn trying to help out Didi's father figure, Johnny, over one single night in a 1920's, jazz-themed city.
You take control of Dawn and are given the power to switch between a normal world and a shadow world in order to advance in the city, solve some puzzles and collect bonus items, like luminaries and plot documents. The premise is simple enough, but the game, while being worth just 2-3 hours of platforming and puzzle solving, is able to offer you a decent but fair challenge, introducing new mechanics and gimmicks as the story progresses that manage to keep you on your toes. Furthermore, failing a jump or anything of the kind won't inconvenence you at all, given you have pretty much infinite lives/tries.
The  strongest points of Contrast are a very charming art style, which heavily borrows from the 20s and jazz music, and an interesting story, which is able to engage the player even if not exactly long or overcomplex. As mentioned above, there are some collectables to be found, but hunting them doesn't extend the game's lenght substantially.
It's also worth mentioning that Didi, the young protagonist, is one of the most berable, cute and useful child I've ever met in a videogame

I like the idea of the game:  by using footwork, feinting, choosing one of the 3 attacks, ducking, or blocking you do combat with another player.  This *should* play as a reasonable rock-paper-scissors game,  where you land hits by psyching out your opponent, or closely watch his wind-up animations and react to them.
When it does play like this, it's mostly a battle of wits and it's stupidly fun.  This is why I have like 160 hours in.
HOWEVER, by moving in very specific patterns, your opponent's character will display corrupted animations, and wildly shorten the timing of his attacks, or in one case, have two chances to hit you in a single attack (not even joking).  At this point, you panic because this contorting, flying, spinning thing is buzz-sawing you to death and you can't predict when the hits come in.  In my opinion, this breaks the contract of the game.  In this game, if you're looking at the opponent, you should be able to tell what he's doing.  But the animations get so ♥♥♥♥ed that isn't possible anymore.  People have got these insane buggy, unfair moves down to a science.  High level players WILL DO THIS TO YOU EVERY CHANCE THEY HAVE.  They think "this is how you're supposed to play!"  This is true, and it's why I don't play this flying, crumpled-up knight backwards-hitting exploit-fest.  This game is just a couple of bug-fixes away from perfection, but it ain't happening.

Due to the relative simplicity of this game, it seemed more fitting to do a quick overview to cover the important highlights.
For $5.99 you get 3 maps with 18 holes each. All three maps sport a unique location with holes ranging from realistic to unpractical. Luck is a factor with some of the holes and due mostly to the abstract layout. Expecting to get a hole in one for most of these maps is unrealistic. Boredom can be a possibility too based on repetition alone. This is why it is more of a party game than a stand-alone venture, benefiting almost entirely on the use of friends. If you plan to play this game alone (as I did for most of it), expect this lack of variety to be a factor.
Visually the game relies on simple design, but it is rather fitting. It is decent on the eyes with some nice lighting effects. Music could use more variety as the few tracks that are available can become mundane after awhile. Balls can also be customized using the RBG system of sliders. You cannot equip fancy hats or anything, but it helps when you are trying to tell your ball apart from one of your friends.
Gameplay is regulated entirely to the mouse and for the most part works. I have experienced issues when shooting (Hold left button, scroll the mouse up for power, release left button to shoot) determining a simple 1 bar shot to be a full power shot. Other times it wouldn’t shoot at all or an additional shot would be added to the stroke total. The game also supports a couple of features that add some more competitive attributes such as ball bouncing, jumping, allowing harsher treatment to the laws of gravity and even the ball’s shape. It helps to keep things interesting when playing with other people, but dull and frustrating when playing solo.
There are a couple of issues that can be detrimental to a game, but only effects you during the current hole. On occasion, I have experienced my ball rolling and not stopping. Once or twice on Twilight I have had the unfortunate luck to get a ball stuck out of bounds with no reset. In the long run, your score will take a big hit, but thanks to the games forced time limit the match can continue. It doesn’t excuse it, but the timer is a helpful feature.
Multiplayer lobbies are generally hit and miss, often resulting in plenty of open rooms with AFK owners. The amount of people playing can also range from desolate to overblown. This game is centered around playing with friends more so than strangers for this reason alone.
Due to the limited amount of courses present, the issue concerning crashes/freezes and the problems associated with finding games, I have to recommend waiting on this title. There are some neat features being brought up for future releases, but until then it would be money best spent elsewhere. I will revisit this game again in six months as per the quota.

It's 2016, and this game still runs like an absolute pig on a capable gaming rig.
This same set up (with an r9 380 GPU) runs games like Shadow of Mordor at a rock solid 60 fps+.  Yet LA Noire - from 2011 no less - still runs like a slideshow.  Specifically, any situation where you can see more than 4 feet from your character drops the frame rate down into the teens or low 20s, making movement jerky and the visuals distracting and unpleasant.  Unfortunately very little of the gameplay takes place in phone boxes or toilet cubicles, meaning that most of the game runs badly.
This, along with Episodes from Liberty City, marked the low point in Rockstar's dismissive treatment of PC gaming.  It is obviously a problem with incredibly shoddy coding in the PC port - do a web search for "LA Noire framerate issues" or similar to see thousands of others just like me.  It's never a good sign when there are dozens of potential hacks or command line tricks available to try to get a game to work properly.  Oddly, you will also find people with inferior systems having no problems, confirming that the game is not demanding, just badly written.
There's probably a great game in here somewhere.  But if you buy this, you're risking horrible, game breaking performance problems.

This game is a different kind of game than most that I play, even with respect to other strategy games. It's realtime event driven strategy, with battles in between.
What this game is about is building your dynasty. Your family. Garnering power for yourself and your children, backstabbing and assassinating competition (including your family and subjects), partaking in intrigue and schemes to annex land, marrying the right people together, imprisoning the right enemies, and so on. It really opens up when you realize that it will allow you to play as devilish or angelic as you so wish.
For instance, your wife might be plotting to kill you because you murdered some of her family in your campaign to annex their lands. Do you start a plot to murder her? Throw her in prison and behead her? Banish her from your lands and risk her making a claim against you later? Have the pope declare her a heretic and kill her without incurring any penalties? make her your spymaster and place her somewhere where she is bound to be caught and imprisoned (and thus making her someone else's problem)? OR let her kill you so your son takes power, which you want anyways?
The choice is yours. All are possible and more still.
If you are devious and politically minded, or perhaps the kind of person who enjoys RISK or a nice paced game that you can take your time with, you will like this.

I like the idea of the game:  by using footwork, feinting, choosing one of the 3 attacks, ducking, or blocking you do combat with another player.  This *should* play as a reasonable rock-paper-scissors game,  where you land hits by psyching out your opponent, or closely watch his wind-up animations and react to them.
When it does play like this, it's mostly a battle of wits and it's stupidly fun.  This is why I have like 160 hours in.
HOWEVER, by moving in very specific patterns, your opponent's character will display corrupted animations, and wildly shorten the timing of his attacks, or in one case, have two chances to hit you in a single attack (not even joking).  At this point, you panic because this contorting, flying, spinning thing is buzz-sawing you to death and you can't predict when the hits come in.  In my opinion, this breaks the contract of the game.  In this game, if you're looking at the opponent, you should be able to tell what he's doing.  But the animations get so ♥♥♥♥ed that isn't possible anymore.  People have got these insane buggy, unfair moves down to a science.  High level players WILL DO THIS TO YOU EVERY CHANCE THEY HAVE.  They think "this is how you're supposed to play!"  This is true, and it's why I don't play this flying, crumpled-up knight backwards-hitting exploit-fest.  This game is just a couple of bug-fixes away from perfection, but it ain't happening.

As a sci-fi nerd I find the detail and depth to this game to be stunning, I love the soundtrack and my dreams of galactic domination have been well satisfied. However if you're just looking for cool space battles this probably isn't for you. A long, hard and often slow grind. It can take me over a week to finish a single match. If you can overlook a lack of depth to the non-military actions and enjoy micromanaging a galactic empire then this is certainly for you.

I do recommend Contrast, but just barely.  It's yet another puzzle platformer. The hook in this one is the main character can turn into a 2D shadow on the wall to overcome environmental puzzles. It's not that original of a mechanic, but it goes well with the noir look of the game. Objects and light sources get moved around to create the perfect shadow that the player can use to proceed. Unfortunately, this game is pretty easy and the 2D shadow puzzles aren't nearly as creative as they could have been. There's also a melodramatic story about bad things happening to poor people in 1920's France. Another thing too, is the world is all but empty. The game looks fantastic, but it is devoid of any life as only the main character and little girl are depicted as more than shadows on the wall. There's a kind of weird motif in the game where the player is jumping across the bodies of shadow characters acting out scenes on the sides of buildings. The game took around five hours to finish. The voice acting was good. Almost good enough to make me care about the corn ball story that throws every cliché in the book at you to manipulate your emotions. Some of the puzzles were fun and generally exploring the world of Contrast was enjoyable. The best way to summarize this game is that it had a lot of potential that was never fully realized. The actual game is just the 2D shadow projection on the wall from the game that could have been. The people that made this game are obviously talented. I'm looking forward to the next thing they do and hope they learn from their mistakes.

Hello Gamers! PET here with my Crusader Kings II review!
First of all this is a hard game to pick up but once you do it will create one of the best and unique experiences you ever encounter (in video games lol).
If you follow my video at the end of the review I guarantee you will be able to pick up the game. If not...
CK2 is a Grand Strategy Game. You will start around year 1100 and play until around 1300 (don't remember the exact dates. You can change the start year but the end year will be the same).
CK2 is a game about your dynasty, about politics, about your vassals and about surviving your dynasty. One of the reasons why this game is hard is that it does not give you a purpose. You can do whatever you want and this might be confusing to some people. You will get that "now what?" experience. Not only that but you will be able to play with any king/duke/count in Europe. As you see I wrote a person title and not a country. Why? Because in CK2 you play with a person from a dynasty. Your purpose is to expand your dynasty, marry your sons so they can create children, marry your daughters to other powerful rulers so you will have a claim on that territory... oh yes yes...
CK2 follows the feudal system and that's one of the reasons why people find this game hard. For example you can not declare war on another person without having a De Jure claim. What does that mean? Well it means that you are entitle to that territory because you might have a title that contains that territory. Oh yes, you have titles.
Really, I think it's much easier to just watch my review & tutorial here:
But trust me guys, this game is simply amazing. Once you learn the basics you will be able to have an amazing time.

Amplitude has always been good about post-release support,  but even if they stopped development today the game would still be an excellent buy.

This is one amazing game. And for me, as of writing this review, a person who only has 112 hours in, I can easily say it's only going to get better as I progress.
Starting this game, I had not the slightest clue of what the heck I was doing. But I stuck with it because it was fun.
The fluidity of this game is *mwah* noice. The playstyle is incredibly adaptable, too - you can be a Naruto all the way to being Rambo. There are no bad frames, only bad players... to a degree, at least. And don't get me started on fashion framing (you'll find out, if you play long enough).
But then... then... my god. The story. The story, the lore... it all comes into place. And it's wonderful. It doesn't throw its best at you right away; but if you hang in there, and just keep playing, by golly the story and lore just begin to get mind blowing.
This part may not be for everyone, but this game gives a great sense of satisfaction. Like, you WORKED for your weapons and armor. No instant gratification, but it still feels soooo good. Speaking of, everything, and I mean EVERYTHING, can be achieved with just some work. Weapons and frames kind of just come to you. And platinum, the in-game currency, can also be achieved without using hard earned paper. Just learn the trading system and trade Prime items and mods for platinum! Of course it takes lots of time, but many RPGs tend to take lots of time, especially a free to play MMO. So expect some grinding; but somehow, it's not wearisome.
The community is also one of the nicest I've ever met. So many helpful veterans and non-toxic newbs. Of course, you're bound to meet some toxic players, but you're also going to 100% meet someone who is willing to hold your hand through some missions and give you tips on how to play the game.
For new players wondering if they should play this, I'd say give it a try. Especially if you liked *cough* Destiny *cough*. Destiny is kind of a bad word in the Warframe community, haha - but you'll be soon to see why, if you keep playing. I'd recommend you spend your beginning 50 platinum on just getting slots in your inventory for weapons and warframes. At low level you won't see why you need so many slots for weapons but as you get higher level those slots get filled real fast. Oh, and never throw away a weapon until they are max rank - leveling up weapons gives Mastery points and helps to increase your mastery rank faster. I made this mistake as a newb.
And for your sake, join a clan. You're likely to find some chill clans, and being in clans will give you weapons you could not get otherwise (clans have research facilities that have weapons that you can't get by building or playing.)
Have fun, Tenno!

Pro:
distinct look, sane controller layout, puzzle game without fights, charming story, good flow, quite enjoyable
Con:
Fixed (and questionable) keyboard layout, no proper saving, no choice of character/avatar (liked the one you get though)
In a nutshell:
Casual game I replayed pretty much immediately after finishing the first time around. Would buy a second part.
The details:
Contrast has the good taste to let you think its riddles through, without pushing fight or flight at you while you're working it out. The puzzles of course for the most part aren't too hard, so the game develops a nice flow, all the while looking distinct and neat -- rare enough for a game that will also please the casual player. (In fact if you're stuck, you've probably either overthought things, or run into a bug. The latter are rare, but in the last act, I twice had to restart from a savepoint when vital items became impossible to interact with (one got stuck for no apparent reason, the other became intangible). Given that savepoints can be a good while apart, this is a bit annoying. (There is never a good reason not to have "saving any time, as many times as you like".)
The story starts off as inoffensive -- somewhat basic, but not bad, and not getting in the way of the game's flow --, and gains charm with some minor twists as it goes along. Very "children's book", in a good way. (I'm not quite sure what earned the game the "sexual themes" label, by the way.)
Act I and the endgame are the strongest parts of the game; Act II has (amongst other bits) a fairy tale segment that tells a nice enough story, but outlives its welcome -- rather than capitalize on Contrast's strengths, that segment looks a good deal like Limbo, and incorporates that game's trial-and-die gameplay. The actual tale told is amusing enough, but a bit repetitive. Less would've been more.
Act III would have been fair enough, although the rare bug soured the experience a bit; there are also two moments where the game should've been more forgiving, or the controls more precise. I'm also still not sure why sometimes when I seem to do the exact same things, Dawn suddenly unshifts, while at other times she doesn't. Is it a bug? Is it an intended feature of the game world that wasn't properly communicated? All I know is it's frustrating -- and fortunately somewhat rare.
The verdict:
The game isn't too long (which I tend to consider a feature) and can be finished in a session or two (but "an act a day" might be best). Due to the short length, the verdict is,
Ignore if you think you'd hate it;
buy when it drops below 10,- if you think you might love it;
buy if it drops below 5,- if unsure. ;)

This is by far, hands down, the most immersive 4x game I've ever played.  Gameplay is largely intuitive, reasonably complex to master, and extremely fun.  The audio and visual experience is pure candy.  The UI systems are well layed out, and (this may seem a bit petty) the font is easy to read.  I don't see why every damn strategy game out there makes things hard to read or unpleasant to look at.  Endless Space 2 is the rare exception.  Every bit of information is displayed in a large and easy to read font.  This is especially helpful given all the resources, races, governments and planet types you'll be managing.
Although combat lacks true tactical combat, at least there's mechanisms in the game to strategize ahead of time (moreso for ship combat).  It's not Stars in Shadow good, but it is not Stellaris/Galactic Civilizations bad either.
This is not to say this game hasn't had some rough edges.  Performance, albeit improving with patches, can be a bit slow or non-responsive at times.  Not so much in turn time, but sometimes the UI just stops responding to clicks and you have to tab out and kill the process.  Thankfully autosaves every turn keep you from losing time.  Victory turns can take a few minutes before displaying, giving you that dread of "ugh did my win die with a bug or what?"  Minor nuisances really.
All in all, this is a very, very solid 4x game, quite arguably the best on the market right now.  Where Stellaris and Galactic Civilizations 3 are very Sandboxy and open, this game is tight.  Its unique lore, factions, and systems are what really make it shine.

This is the first Steam review I've done, and I'm only doing it because Endless Space 2 is really that fun to me. Lately, it feels like the trend of developers seems to be all about the profits and less about the true enjoyment of the game. As Amplitude Studios seems to be one of the few exceptions to that trend, I felt I owed it to them to leave a review.
About the game:
I stumbled on Endless Space 2 out of the blue several months ago and decided to give it a shot as it was only $40 and seemed interesting enough. There are very few games that I truly feel have paid off as much as this one has for me. I find the game to have a great deal of depth and replayability. I have a huge amount of hours on this game and find myself still discovering new features and fun combinations (regarding things like research, expansion methods, etc.) I hadn't thought of before. Moreover, the game has an amazing soundtrack that really adds to the overall atmosphere and feel of the game.
About the developers:
Since I have been playing, the developers have released two big (free) updates and have a new big (free) update coming tomorrow. I recently started to follow the game's website (Games2Gether) and noticed a lot of the changes they have implemented come directly from player feedback, which I feel is very rare now days. If you don't believe me, checkout the "Trending Ideas" section of the website and you'll find various ideas that players have suggested with the status of "Implemented" tagged to them by Devs.
TL;DR: Great game, great atmosphere, great replayability, great devs. Highly recommend.

There's a lot that's great and engrossing about this game, which is both to its credit and oddly enough to its fault (as a dad with a full time job who can't afford to be too engrossed).
When you first start, Crusader Kings II is big and intimidating.  Tutorials introduce you to many aspects of the game, but ultimately the best route is to learn by doing.  One of the things that immediately sets Crusader Kings II apart from many strategy games is its low-action pace.  Your goal is to play the long game, over the course of your play your character will die (from treachery, accidents, disease, or old age) and your heir will pick up where you left off.  Attachments are not to your avatar, but to your lineage and legacy.

The low-action pace is reinforced by the fact that you cannot just invade your neighbor at will, you must have casus belli (case for war) to enter into conflict and expand through military force.  Building relationships and alliances are at the heart of the game, not pure muscle.

It's definitely a meticulous, thinking man's game, and the pace can feel pretty slow.  I know I've had hours melt away while I stared slack-jawed micro-managing all things big and small in my realm.  It's rewarding, but I ultimately quit playing it because the immersion was too deep.
Overall I heartily endorse the game, but only if you've got nothing better to do.

YT-L is a fun game. Time-management, keeping up appearances, social engineering, a puzzle-minigame in the form of video-editing and empire-building. The game is really good in appearing to be casual, but it is actually reasonably hard to master.
Moreover, the game gets awesome-points from me for avoiding to include RL-youtubers, so there's no Pew-die-pie in there. Even more awesome-points for the game because it avoids namedropping meme-games, minecraft or FNaF. It makes the game, apart from the title, a timeless management game that explores a new industry.
But there are some major bug-bears. A PC-setup that's nothing but top of the line components shouldn't break every five minutes of real gameplay time. It's annoying and it actually broke my current playthrough of the campaign as my sci-fi PC got stuck in a perpetual loop of breaking, getting repaired and then breaking before I could do anything with it afterwards. The frequency in which the PC breaks is unrealistic, irritating, annoying and as far as I'm concerned a FU from the developer to their player-base.
The player should not be the only one keeping up friendships. A cell-phone is not a one-way only gadget. Also, why can't I order stuff through the cell-phone? My youtuber had the best cellphone money could buy, a cellphone that obviously had Internet, because it could access the 'Wall' (their version of Facebook, I guess). Yet, when my PC is broken again or it is rendering a video, my cellphone is totally useless to order stuff online, to chat with my friends or do other things that RL-cellphones can do.
I have the feeling that this is a contrivance to make the game 'harder'. It's just extremely irritating that only through the PC the internet can be used, even to stock up the fridge.
The game has many things right. There are many options to costumize your youtuber's looks and appearance and the style of clothes they wear are important for events and gatherings. You can also buy many items for your house, though you have no control over where things that you buy go. I have also not found any indication that buying stuff for the house makes your youtuber's life better or easier. It's merely a money-sink.
Editing videos is minigame that's a rudimentary deckbuilder; you enhance video-clips with post-production cards that you earn for different things that your youtuber does. There's depth there as the cards have different strengths and can be positive or negative. It's up to the player to guess the right card for a given video-clip.
After selecting the 'powers' for all the clips, the player must puzzle the clips together in the best possible way. The more clips that have the right powers, the easier that will be.
However, there were many instances where I canned a video because the choices I had were mostly negative including being forced to select powers that would result in copyright infringement. The fines on those prohibit uploading the video. While probably realistic, it's wasted time and I believe that a game should always respect the player's time.
At this time YT-L is allright, being held back by instances of being caught in a unescapable fail-loop that basically ends your run, a one-way friendship system and a mini-game that can screw you over through no fault of your own. It gets compounded by nagging NPCs that only seem to be there to be annoying.
But there's also a lot of good things going on that I enjoy and I look forward to see how the game grows over the coming months towards 1.0.
At this moment, this game isn't worth a positive recommendation, as the awesome-points I give it are being undone by the game's insistance of being an annoying piece of crap. I hope that the developer adjusts those instances in the future to make YT-L a truly fun and enjoyable product!

If you`ve been looking for that gem that lets you play a career on the other side of the GTA fence, then this is certainly the one and not only that, its a masterpiece.
Highly stylized and cinematic this game tips it`s hat to the Hollywood of the 1930 and 1940s taking after films like L.A. Confidential (one of my favorites).
There is so much more to this than a game like GTA in the way of storyline and character interaction that it is beyond comparison. As you`ve probably read on other reviews, pain staking detail was paid to facial animation for this title giving it one of the most realistic in terms of facial rendering allowing you to look for facial and body language to determine whether someone that you`re questioning is lying or not and the subtle nuances of their mood, all of which affect your questioning and your case. Sure there`s shootouts, foot chases, car chases and stakeouts but the real heart of this game lies in the career of your character and his interactions with potential witnesses and crime scene evidence.
Be prepared for an involved commitment or if you`d rather just run around on patrol, you can play with the Free Roam mode. You'll play from four desks: Traffic, Patrol, Homocide and Vice. Each has a series of cases that take you through your character's career which plays out like a classic movie with modern drama and writing. There's top notch voice and motion performance and some of the greatest moments in the game will come from your interactions with the various partners you have at each desk. Highly recommended if you like Rockstar's style and attention to detail. This title shines in its attention to storyline and the details of working in that line of work and of course if you've tired on running with one side of the law in the various virtual worlds out there, this one will give it to you in glorious detail that experience from the other side.
It does require a bit of horsepower to fun smoothly though a fast dual core 2 Ghz with a half decent video card (Geforce 210 w/512Mb) should do sufficiently with the graphics options turned down which still looks great. I'm running at about 3/4 of full graphics and it looks and feels awesome with a machine a fair bit faster than what I've recommended.
For the price this one sells it is a gem for certain. Keep in mind that this title is definitely for a mature audience as you will be solving cases accurately modeled from actual crime scenes. Viewer discretion is definitely advised.
This title really gives you the experience from the other side of the fence to so many other titles out there and its an honest and hard hitting title for certain. A great experience and Rockstar has pulled all the stops to tell this police story.
Highly recommended

One of the best Space 4X games I've ever played.
Absolutely overflowing with personality and interesting mechanics, Endless Space 2 is game that takes what is familiar to the genre and puts it's own spin on it and introducing solutions to problems that have long existd in the 4X space.
Not all of them work mind you. Diplomacy is weak (EDIT: The latest patch has completely overhauled Diplomacy AND IT IS MUCH, MUCH BETTER! It is a literal "Game Changer" The only thing missing now is a proper Espionage system which Amplitude said will be coming in the future. Amplitude is an amazing studio and has already gone above and beyond in terms of updating their game with free content that vastly improve an already amazing game. If you're a fan of amazing 4X Space Games, this is definitely one to add to your library.

Reviewing Chivalry will not be an easy task, so make yourself comfortable while I attempt to give as legible a testimony as possible. I warn you that this is going to be a long read.
Chivalry as a standalone product was released in September 2012, five years after its' initial debut. It had been known beforehand as "Age of Chivalry" - one of many Half Life 2 mods. Being officially accepted into the Steam market must have been an incredible experience for the developers, which really shows in the early builds of the game. The tutorial is one of the only things that remain untouched since the release, and I could really feel the enthusiasm. It's easily one of the best tutorials I've ever seen. The voice acting is phenomenal and the early maps look & play perfectly. The level of immersion was unreal, and I've yet to see anyone come close. I'd go as far as saying that the first few weeks one of the best experiences in my entire gaming career. Everyone was amazed at the fact that the combat system played so well, and that it actually worked in an online environment with up to 32 players. The developers' enthusiasm carried on to make a few important patches, as well as new weapons. Unfortunately, however, all good things must come to an end.
At some point, Torn Banner decided to completely redo the hitbox system, into what is now known as the "bubble". They decided to fix something that wasn't broken - the hit detection. A crucial selling point of the game. Everyone opposed the change, everyone still hates it to this day, but the new system remains. You wouldn't think that changing cubic to spherical would make that much of a difference, but it did. Things were so bad that the developers decided to implement FAKE DISTANCE between the players, in a game that's very much about spacing. I can't help but compare this move governments subsidizing things that don't work. Fake distance, multiplied by your ping, means that if an enemy is moving away from you, you cannot hit them with fists or daggers, and short weapons are worse in general. Longer weapons are completely unaffected.
The next decision was to make the claymore (the sword in the game's logo) stronger. Everyone preferred the slower, more damaging weapons to the faster but weaker claymore. Despite being one of the longest weapons in the game, they also made it one of the fastest, while still being able to kill anyone in 4 hits. This instantly promoted it from slightly below average to a game-breaking absurdity, and votekicked on sight. I'm sure Torn Banner will patch this.
Next up: customization. A very neat idea and executed quite well. One tiny little problem - both red and blue teams can wear a black uniform, they look almost identical. Are they going to patch it?
Somewhere around this time, Vanguards (the class with the longest weapons) became glitched, because their charge attack catapulted them forwards at least three times the distance, as if they had a jetpack. These rocket Vanguards were funny at first, though they did lose their charm after a month or two. When they finally fixed the issue, it turned out that the patch broke the audio, the graphics and toggle sprint. This took another few weeks to revert back to normal.
Introduction of microtransaction hats. Great! More revenue means more patches, right?
Introduction of microtransaction weapon reskins. Guys, can you fix the claymore?
Introduction of microtransatction character reskins. Guys?
Introduction of even more hats... I think I've seen this happen before.
In the meantime, people had discovered a bunch of exploits. Instantly striking with gigantic, slow weapons, feinting without any stamina cost, shrinking their hitbox to the size of a football or just about anything you can think of that defies both physics and proper game design. Most of the community have enough decency not to use the claymore (they don't want to be votekicked), but by now they've figured out what works best. As a result, you see very few of the 40+ weapons ingame.
This was the rise of incredibly arrogant "pro" players, who are on a mission to have the highest K/D ratio possible, and throwing tantrums if they take any team damage. It is enough to google "what's the best sword" or "how to glitch through blocks", and turn Chivalry into a game of lucky hit, because no honest man can defend against that in an online environment. These players can be overwhelmed due to their lack of fundamentals, but it just isn't worth it. At this point, the fun has been completely sucked out of the game.
You may have also heard about a game called Chivalry: Deadliest Warrior. A flawless concept, and the beta was tons of fun... only it remained a beta forever. It was released as DLC for 20$ and abandoned by the devs, because they couldn't get the netcode to work.
I find myself wondering what happened to this once fantastic, once indie game studio, and how they drove a perfectly good game into the ground, as well as failing to deliver such a promising sequel.
Hopefully, Torn Banner will attempt to improve the situation, but we all know that's not going to happen. Maybe a competent modder will do all the heavy lifting for them (for free).
You may see me ingame every now and then, but it's more for sentimental value than anything else. The new maps and other content is nice, but I'd much rather have 2012 Chivalry again.
