Crusader Kings 2 is a complex grand strategy game.  The most complicated game I've ever played. Be prepared to spend hours and I mean hours confused as hell, looking at youtube, the wiki and forums.   Once it clicks though, it's awesome.  Not for everyone, but its kinda like playing through 'real life' Game of Thrones (there's a game of thrones mod too).
You control a land owning character starting on any date between 1066 and 1453 AD (The Old Gods DLC will push this starting date back to 867 if you wish).  You can start as a powerful emperor or a lowly count.  The map you play on is more or less Europe stretching into parts of Asia and Africa.  Your sole goal in the game is to keep your bloodline going (and I believe holding land).  Other than that, there isn't a win screen, there aren't defined goals, its open ended, you play until 1453AD and then the game ends (save exportable to Europa Universalis 4 to continue your game with the purchase of a DLC).  You get a 'score', but that is just a rough estimate on how prestigious and pious your bloodline was.  It's quite possible to have 400 years of super rewarding gameplay without getting a high score.  This is a trend you will see me developing on and is a big part of what makes CKII so awesome.
That's kinda hard to grasp, but it is less awkward than it sounds.  The goals sort of present themselves naturally.  You don't often sit there with no idea what to do (again, once you understand the game), you kind of always have something you're working towards.  For a first time player this is usually just become as powerful as possible, i.e. aquire land, become a king, then become an emperor and expand your empire.  If you're an advanced player you can set your own crazy goals, roleplay, or do other things to spice up the game.
The game runs in 'real time', with a day going by a few times a minute on normal speed.  You can fast forward and pause.  Most of the time you will indeed be going through various menus.  Arranging marriages, keeping tabs on powerful families, plotting assinations, acquiring territory through political shennigans, keeping your subjects happy, bringing in powerful characters to tutor the children of the realm and hold office, and much more.  You can micromanage to your hearts content, play a more hands off style, or switch between the two.
When combat breaks out, it is done by moving stacks of armys around the campaign map, meeting an opposing army will cause a battle.  These really just compose of watching numbers go down, and kills go up, so if you're looking for Total War style combat you arent going to get it here.  Don't be fooled though, many times I've been on the edge of my seat watching these numbers change.  The combat system is quiet nuanced as well. To be the most effective you have many things to consider. Terrain bonuses, attrition penalties, appointing competant commanders from your realm, and more add depth.
In all I highly recommend this game to anyone who has played something like Civ or Total War and fancy themself a strategy gamer, is looking for a challenege, and has a lot of patience.  This is kinda the next step you can take into something quite a bit more complicated.  That is the path I took into the game am loving it.
The game is still actively having expansions and patches developed for it as of the writing of this review 11/25/2013.
Full disclosure:  Your reviewer has not quite finished a playthrough yet but am close.  I have 120 hours playtime. I own the dlcs The Old Gods, Legacy of Rome, and the Europa Universalis 4 save converter.  I solely purchased EU4 because of how much I enjoyed my crusader kings 2 game and wanted to continue playing my empire, I haven't even played it yet.
Also: Don't buy for full price.  Even though it is worth it, getting the game and all the dlc all at full price is pretty expensive. The base game is often on sale or in bundles.
This is my first steam review so if you think this is helpful give the thumbs up and I'll do some more reviews.  Hope you enjoyed reading.

Contrast is a beautiful third-person puzzle platformer revolving around the little girl Didi and her imaginary friend Dawn, who can freely shift between the real and the shadow world. The game takes place in a Paris-like city in the 1920's and is also the debut for Canadian developer Compulsion Games.
Didi's mother dumped her father a long time ago and since she is a singer at a night club, nobody is watching after Didi at night. Naturally, little Didi takes this as an opportunity to take her imaginary friend Dawn with her on a night-time scouting expedition throughout the city to discover that her father came back and tries to win the heart of her mother again. But something stands in the way...
I'm not sure if I just didn't get the reason for this during my play or of this was a story element deliberately chosen by the developer to create a certain experience, but apart from Didi and Dawn, all characters in the game are shadows, so you never see them in 3D. This works out okay, but makes the city look fairly empty and liveless most of the time. Considering the beautifully designed enviroments, this is a bit of a shame.
The game is based on the Unreal Engine, so visually the game looks really beautiful. The overall art deco style of the game, the level design and the lighting effects fit together perfectly and create an immersive atmosphere. Quite frankly, a lot of the visual elements remind of of Bioshock: Infinte which, funnily enough, is also based on the Unreal Engine.
Unfortunately, as with many UE-based console games being released on PC, the game doesn't really offer a vast amount of graphics options. Apart from gamma, graphics quality, resolution and fullscreen there's nothing else to adjust through the game directly. Don't get me wrong: The game looks great regardless but definitely could've used a bit of Anti-Aliasing. This could probably be tweaked through the config files or external tools such as SweetFX or your graphics drivers directly, but personally that wasn't really worth the hassle for me, so I decided to stick with the options that were available.
The voice acting is surprisingly good for a non-AAA game like this. Didi's voice actor has that cute little girl's touch to her and really fits great to that character. Her imaginary friend Dawn, though, doesn't say a single word throughout the entire game, so whenever Didi talks to her (you), it always feels kind of weird that she never really answers. Might be one of those imaginary-friend-drawbacks, though. Who knows, heh.
Didi's father is voiced by Elias Toufexis, who also voiced Adam Jensen in Deus Ex: Human Revolution. I was definitely surprised to hear him in this game but recognized him right away because of his distinctive voice. Voice acting for the side characters, which often tends to be poor because of limited budget, is also pretty decent, so nothing to complain on that side.
The game being set sometime in the 1920's, it is accompanied by a fitting and relaxing Jazz-y soundtrack which fits the overall atmosphere of the game perfectly. Not exactly my musical taste, but then again, a Death Metal soundtrack wouldn't quite work in a game like this. Heh.
You control Dawn, the imaginary friend, and Didi effectively becomes your sidekick. Throughout the game, she will assist you with a couple puzzles but most of the time you will have to solve them on your own to clear the way for her, so you both can progress on your journey.
The main gameplay mechanic is the shadow shifting, which you will use to solve puzzles and overcome obstacles such as huge gaps and so on. How this works is, that you basically approach a shadow that is cast by certain objects in the level, hit the shadow shift key/button and Dawn transforms from a 3D character into a 2D shadow, allowing her to climb around on those shadows. Together with the dash ability, that you unlock relatively early into the game, this makes for some partially challenging platforming as often the shadows will move (because the objects that cast them move) and thus require you to time your actions.
While this mechanic is pretty cool and unique and works out quite good, it often suffers from imprecision and the fact that you often get shifted back into 3D for no apparent reason. You can't die in the game and if you fall down into the void, you will simply respawn at the puzzle again. This makes failing not that much of a big deal, but keeps you wishing the developer had put a bit more fine-tuning into the gameplay mechanics to reduce or eliminite those annoyances alltogether.
For some puzzles, you have to move objects around such as wooden crates, serving carts or cardboard stand-ups, so they cast shadows in the right size and angle for you to be able to jump and move on them. This adds a bit of variety to the puzzles and demonstrates the impressive lighting effects the Unreal Engine is capable of.
The puzzles as such generally are farily obvious and easy. The challenge often lies in the platforming or the object manipulation that comes with them, so often you have figured out how the puzzles work but will eventually struggle with the right shadow setup or the right timing during the platforming itself.
All in all, it's definitely a cool mechanic but could've been pushed a bit further with a bit more extensive and varying puzzle design to actually test your combination rather than your platforming skills.
With roughly 4 hours of playtime, which included collecting all collectibles and getting 100% of the achievements, the game is relatively short and could probably be beaten in around 3 hours if you just rush through it. There aren't any additional game modes, so, apart from replaying the story for the collectibles/achievements, there's nothing else to do in the game once you've beaten it.
Contrast is a short but beautiful and charming puzzle platformer with a fairly unique gameplay mechanic.
The game undoubtedly has some minor flaws and annoyances, but if developer Compulsion Games is able to deliver such a debut, I'm definitely looking forward to see more of them - and more of Contrast.

The game is not the newest anymore and probably got plenty of reviews so I will try to be brief:
The game is set in 1947 Los Angeles and I do really enjoy the setting and the story of the main charakter as well as the story of the cases you have to solve are quite deep and interesting. ( I wont say much about it because I dont intent to spoiler).
The Missions are very well developed. You have to question suspects and pay attention for example in which order you ask questions or which evidences you provide. You have to check if you can dig up more evidence by visiting different people or points of interest, find information on places murderes happend or find information in letters, written orders or other types of papers. You often question people and either decide if they lie, tell the trueth or seem suspicious which you can tell by their facial expressions. (If they hide something they will often try to avoid looking at your or into your face and search the room with their eyes).
There are shootings happening frequently. The side missions are often based on catching someone escaping from a crime scene or even shooting down all oponents. You can use their guns. Aiming and taking cover is similiar to  GTAV.
So action is present in the game as too and balances it very well.
It is very fun even if you fail in most cases you still will move on with the story but get less points by setting up wrong evidence or accuse them of a lie while they spoke the trueth to you. There arent many games that combine those features with an open world and an interesting story.
The open world is interesting too since all the cars and environments are set in the last century. Do not expect a GTA V of course, The game is made in 2011 and the traffic AI is horrible in fact you can try to drive perfectly and the AI will simply ram you off if they want to switch the lanes.
The environment is set in LA only and you cannot really leave the city. You can visit some real life landmarks, especially the train station is very nice as you can see incomming and leaving trains but sadly its also a bit glitched.
There are no different radio stations which is a bit of a downer too. The city is very alive and you in fact are able to look into the different shops and even enter many houses and buildings.
The pedestrians however act funny too. You should avoid to run them over since you are a cop you get a message you shall protect civillians and not bring them into danger. In fact you even can lose points if you do continue bad behavior.
Another thing I personally dislike is the social club login. You always have to keep signing in but in LA Noire it simply wont save my account data and I regularyly have to retype it to be able to start the game.
I payed 5 Euroes and 99 cents but the game was completely worth it. I enjoy it a lot and since you can handle the missions very differently, there is quite some replay value as well if you wanna keep puzzling on a perfect score.

It took me 15 hours of gameplay to realize that you shouldn't watch Netflix while playing this game. You see, I'm a veteran of the original Endless Space. So I wasn't really expecting immersion or story.
Boy was I wrong.
The creators of this game have patched up the gaps in the experience. No longer do you feel like Civilization #3 in galaxy seed 233544. Instead, its so very easy to slip into the role of the Riftborn, fleeing the horrors of their dimension. You feel their plight and you wonder what will happen next. In fact, I was bummed when I completed the storyline.
The gameplay has interesting complexity. Only recently have I gotten a hand on combat, though my best fleets will sometimes still lose to my vexation. No longer is the formula to overload enemy defenses with all missile pods or all laser beams.
Despite these things, the game is about 8% away from being *the* perfect game for me. I'll wait to see if they can make the story a tad bit more immersive and random.

By all means try the demo, but don't be scared off by the amount of information. Whilst great, the interface is certainly intimidating at first, but the tool tips are excellently written for just about every button. Just take your time and don't worry about losing to much at first, just mess around and it will soon come to you.

(My first review, yay!)
I have only played this for one night, so I don't know how long this game can last for, but I certainly enjoyed it.
Moreover, I was mainly playing as an archer, while the game is supposed to focus on melee combat. I won't say much about the blocking / melee attacking mechanics, because I feel I'm too new (and so were my enemies) to have a solid opinion. So far it feels OK.
Other reviewers said the community is bad and they get kicked and stuff.
Some folks were kicked indeed (like 3-4 players in 6-7 hours), but they had indeed hurt their teammates a lot, some of them most probably on purpose.
The game itself can be partially blamed for this, because they allow "custom" armor sets that have minimal colored areas, which make it hard to tell friends from foes. Also some guys can be covered in so much blood that they look "red", haha.
The game can be currently played for free, which means there were many new players in the games I played. When this offer ends, things will most likely change (I guess they'll get worse for new players).
The game has many flaws:
-some textures can get blurry for a split second,
-shadows change depending on your point of view,
-the game ran out of video memory once (GTX 460 1GB) without warning (then I lowered some settings),
-the controls are unfriendly (for example, you have to wait for your bow to be "fully" equipped before pressing the attack hotkey, otherwise your attack never happens),
-my bow crosshair disappeared twice,
-mouse sensitivity could have been more open to customization,
-you can opt to toggle "sprint" (instead of keeping the hotkey pressed) but you can't do it for "crouch",
-the keyboard can't handle "sprint" (shift), "forward" (w) and "switch weapon" (2) simultaneously, but you get used to it...
-(I think) the net code makes the game stutter sometimes, especially when you're near the edge of high ground (and you can also fall down, without pressing any movement hotkey),
-it uses all your mouse buttons (a different button for every action), instead of using mouse gestures, which worked better IMO in similar games,
I could say more, but I think you get the point already.
There is MUCH, MUCH room for improvement.
But I AM recommending the game,
so here are some notable positive features:
-Great voice acting,
-Heads are chopped off like no problem,
-Teamwork pays well,
-The gameplay is enjoyable overall.
I believe it has enough value for its money (2.45 EU per person, 4-pack, -80%).
Many of my friends are getting it too; a big reason I got the game is to play it with them. I don't know if I'd get it if I wouldn't play it without them.

Crusader Kings 2 is a complex grand strategy game.  The most complicated game I've ever played. Be prepared to spend hours and I mean hours confused as hell, looking at youtube, the wiki and forums.   Once it clicks though, it's awesome.  Not for everyone, but its kinda like playing through 'real life' Game of Thrones (there's a game of thrones mod too).
You control a land owning character starting on any date between 1066 and 1453 AD (The Old Gods DLC will push this starting date back to 867 if you wish).  You can start as a powerful emperor or a lowly count.  The map you play on is more or less Europe stretching into parts of Asia and Africa.  Your sole goal in the game is to keep your bloodline going (and I believe holding land).  Other than that, there isn't a win screen, there aren't defined goals, its open ended, you play until 1453AD and then the game ends (save exportable to Europa Universalis 4 to continue your game with the purchase of a DLC).  You get a 'score', but that is just a rough estimate on how prestigious and pious your bloodline was.  It's quite possible to have 400 years of super rewarding gameplay without getting a high score.  This is a trend you will see me developing on and is a big part of what makes CKII so awesome.
That's kinda hard to grasp, but it is less awkward than it sounds.  The goals sort of present themselves naturally.  You don't often sit there with no idea what to do (again, once you understand the game), you kind of always have something you're working towards.  For a first time player this is usually just become as powerful as possible, i.e. aquire land, become a king, then become an emperor and expand your empire.  If you're an advanced player you can set your own crazy goals, roleplay, or do other things to spice up the game.
The game runs in 'real time', with a day going by a few times a minute on normal speed.  You can fast forward and pause.  Most of the time you will indeed be going through various menus.  Arranging marriages, keeping tabs on powerful families, plotting assinations, acquiring territory through political shennigans, keeping your subjects happy, bringing in powerful characters to tutor the children of the realm and hold office, and much more.  You can micromanage to your hearts content, play a more hands off style, or switch between the two.
When combat breaks out, it is done by moving stacks of armys around the campaign map, meeting an opposing army will cause a battle.  These really just compose of watching numbers go down, and kills go up, so if you're looking for Total War style combat you arent going to get it here.  Don't be fooled though, many times I've been on the edge of my seat watching these numbers change.  The combat system is quiet nuanced as well. To be the most effective you have many things to consider. Terrain bonuses, attrition penalties, appointing competant commanders from your realm, and more add depth.
In all I highly recommend this game to anyone who has played something like Civ or Total War and fancy themself a strategy gamer, is looking for a challenege, and has a lot of patience.  This is kinda the next step you can take into something quite a bit more complicated.  That is the path I took into the game am loving it.
The game is still actively having expansions and patches developed for it as of the writing of this review 11/25/2013.
Full disclosure:  Your reviewer has not quite finished a playthrough yet but am close.  I have 120 hours playtime. I own the dlcs The Old Gods, Legacy of Rome, and the Europa Universalis 4 save converter.  I solely purchased EU4 because of how much I enjoyed my crusader kings 2 game and wanted to continue playing my empire, I haven't even played it yet.
Also: Don't buy for full price.  Even though it is worth it, getting the game and all the dlc all at full price is pretty expensive. The base game is often on sale or in bundles.
This is my first steam review so if you think this is helpful give the thumbs up and I'll do some more reviews.  Hope you enjoyed reading.

UPDATED: As I suspected, they will continue to enhance and add things to the game. I have improved the score and given it a positive review, but until they address them some of those negatives may turn off players after a while.
As a parent, my reviews are always my experience only on a game for other parents and young gamers to review. Endless Space 2 is simply a beautiful version of Endless Legend, but in space. The mechanics are extremely similar with a few non-controlling factors. Civilization 5 did a sort space mod that works very similar to ES2. It has wonderful plusses and some strong minuses. I always give a positive rating to any developer that puts in tremendous time and effort on any game. Gameplay I find always to be the most important factor of any game. For those who never played Civilization or Endless games. Endless Space 2 is a turn-based strategy, science fiction 4X game, that simple
PROS
•	A: It is refined and a beautiful cinematic game, each object, planet, minion, leaders, all of it. Done with high fantasy result looks and feels. Gorgeous
•	B: The Tutorial and mechanics to the game are easy to pick up. There is a learning curve, but its support makes the game extremely easy to follow and understand. My 10-year-old is in awe.
•	C: It has smooth controls and wonderful fantasy faction’s representation. Each faction has its plusses and minuses and truly can be fun to try.
•	D: The ships are wonderful to view and easy to move around the system. If you like micro managing your empires resources, customizing ship weaponry, and civilization tasks. It has it all...but (See Cons 2-4)
•	E: Very easy multi player set up and outcomes. You can play alone, with friends or enemies.
CONS
•	This is Endless Legend, but with streamlined functions that hurt its overall concept. It's diplomacy, system and the fact that it really becomes a race of tech and building more than strategy. You still micro manage, but it becomes more about correct selecting than actual strategy. Matching the correct buildings to the planet's strengths become a factor.
•	The Battle system is beautiful to watch, but that is all you do. Is watch. You make pre-selective choices and watch the results. It is like Birth of the Federations battle system were u make a choice, and then watch. This is crippling to those who like to be part of the battle action. Make choices in battles to change outcomes. It is a cinema. You sit back and watch and go, cool, but wish I could do more. The massive fleet battles are cool to see, but after time you will want to do much more.  That could possibly change with additions to the game. In multiplayer this cinema function will not be used since I doubt in massive multi-player games they select seeing them.
•	Diplomacy and AI seem to be so redundant and useless that it takes away from the strategy and tactics of the game. This has been a huge issue since Diplomacy in game functions were created. How do you make Diplomacy a game in itself instead of "You're in my way" war? It becomes more about just building up and defeating a faction then actual diplomacy tactics. This function of the game will need the most upgrading to down the line.
•	Ships- (Pro and Con) All u can do is create the model and then altering the weapons. A huge reason why many previous Space strategy games fail. There is no difference between ES2 and Endless Legends custom building. You do not get to create your own looks and feel. So, no real ship customizations, but replacing. Now there are specifics to each ship type. Some may enjoy the matching of skills and bonuses, but some may not. This I do think will change in time.
•	Again, not sure Political affiliations matter in game. A function to me that had no real end game purpose. You must monitor this because ignoring it could lead to rebellion and an internal mess, but a function of the AI deterring you. Again, may turn off players or it may not.
Nuetral-Ground Battles: The lack of definition makes the ground battles look under developed. They come off cheap in appearance as a fast outcome. All the effort in the space battles but the ground battles are underwhelming. This should be more defined to the races, have better effects, graphics and feel to make it two solid combat systems -space and ground, instead of one. The execution is fine for number percentage outcomes, but it distances the player not drawn him in.
I do think this will get updated in time.
OVERALL
UPDATE: I am giving Endless Space 2 a positive review simply because I don't think they are near to being done. You may see more updates and events to improve the base game enough. I reviewed the base game at the time. I can see a lot added to their base template. The stream line functions are so well done that it takes away from you being drawn in and involved. It is a game off obstacles than strategy. You click and sit back and watch. That to me takes away from a lot of the gameplay in action that you may be used to in grand strategic games. You could have a massive battle fleet with a friend, both pick your selections and go do the laundry while the battle plays out. Not quite what you want in turn base battles. Those who love Endless Legend, will love Endless Space, but may feel that functions they got used to in Endless Legend, do not offer anything further, and the fact that they do less, may hurt the overall take of ES2 It is a stunning gorgeous game, but beautiful is not gameplay. It will keep you invested, but at the end. You may feel not fully satisfied. I strongly advice you look at the computer specs to playing this, low end machines may have difficulties with the high-quality cinematics of Endless Space 2. I can see conflicts, bugs being an issue, but they are constantly updating so this is an evolving game. Always See the VIDEO above discussions to preview the game prior to buying and look for free tries of the game. I would also advice getting this during sale events. If you love Civilizations, Masters of Orion and Galactic Empires, then you will enjoy Endless Space 2.  I think it will grow and get better as it goes along with added DLC content. it is a wonderful template to build on. My GRADE 3.7 stars out of 5.

A very charming puzzle-platformer with a very impressive motif and soundtrack. The story of the game largely revolves around a broken family trying to piece itself together and is at its best when it focuses on their trials and tribulations. (It takes a weird turn near the end trying to answer questions I never asked about the broken shadow dimension that protagonist Dawn inhabits that just end up raising even more questions, but that treads into spoiler territory.) Manipulating shadows so that Dawn can become a shadow and platform across them proved to be an interesting challenge that had me scratching my head more than a few times, and they were never afraid of introducing new elements (even if some of those elements involved box-switch puzzles seen in many games before). The game is definitely a bit on the short side, however, and the only thing that kept me from clearing it 100% on my first run was a few collectibles and one item that was only available for a short time frame and ended up being lost forever. It's also very story-focused, and relies heavily on cutscenes to tell its tale. Overall, it's definitely flawed (probably rushed a bit to be a PS4 launch title), but it's an enjoyable game that should be tried.

Compared to Endless Space (the first of the series), two of the few things that I would consider improvements are graphics and UI (... at least when the UI isn't overlapping separate components).
I've only played this three times, two times during alpha, and once after it was "released."
My experience during the alpha was playing with a friend and desyncing every turn after an hour or two of gameplay. I'm glad they have fixed that.
More recently, I played as a custom Unfallen (basically space-trees) civilization. The civilization is kind of neat, requiring the player to "branch" out from their starting system. However, it comes with two MAJOR disadvantages. As far as I know (and I played till the mid-end game):
2.
branch across large expanses. And lucky for me, since I was in an alliance with my friend (playing multiplayer), I was effectively system-locked. I could not expand *anywhere.* I even tried trading with one of the AI's to get a system elsewhere. However, the trade ended with them getting a bunch of techs from me, and
the system they were supposed to trade.
Yeah, these seem like major gameplay oversights. But that's just my opinion.
Building ships in this game is more simplistic and the strategic resource system
. After absorbing the two nearest AI empires next to my space-tree empire, increasing the resource production to its maximum, and gathering for 100 turns, I was able to make 3 fleets worth (each with a size of ~20CP). I hit the resource cap for Titanium, which is apparently 999. Honestly, I don't really care about doing the math at this point... just don't expect to make many fleets with top-notch ship designs. I had to use my entire strategic resource stock to build those 3 fleets.
The different population types really is quite awful. If you want to min-max your empire, you're gonna have a very bad time balancing your different populations using space docks. Seriously, boring to all hell and takes a significant amount of time. I didn't bother with it... Even though I knew that my empire would get a significant boost overall.
The economic system with dust is awful. On the marketplace, goods that are stocked in the thousands (because the supply is MUCH higher than the demand), can have prices on par with goods stocked in the hundreds. Using "buyout" for ships and improvements ended up being around 19-20 times their production costs late-game. It would essentially cost 100x my empire's budget to produce a single ship. In my experience, dust also seemed to be an almost useless commodity when trading with the AI.
I could point out more mechanics I dislike about this game, but I'm too lazy at this point (and the post is getting kind of long). Personally, I enjoyed the first game more. Though, this is coming from the perspective of a player who disables all victory types except conquest. I personally find science, economic, and religious victories to be boring.
A comment on my review has pointed out that it is possible to increase the speed of vining. The player has to stack vineships in a fleet if they want to increase their rate of expansion. I had tried stacking them as separate fleets, but it had not occured to me to try this after combining them into a single fleet. Guess that one is my fault. Though it certainly couldn't be bad to include this information in the description in-game.
Apparently it's also possible to increase the vining range as well. The empire has to increase their influence to do so.
, I don't think I could have increased my influence enough to cross the huge expanse I mentioned. If I were to guess, I at least would have been locked from expanding until end-game.

I would not recommend es2 at least as it is now, it is a micro nightmare and not in a good way, it has a lot of the same problems for me as stellaris.  you can't choose the things you would like to be able to, and you have to micro things that could easily be programmed into the game.  movement for example, exploration is often the most fun part of a 4x game but here you are lucky to have 3 options of where to go, more likely 2 or 1 at the start, because you have to research a tier 2 technology to be able to move freely, otherwise you're stuck moving along these predetermined lines.
The exploration rewards (i forget what they're called) require you to manually click on every planet in each system, often multiple times, with a dedicated ship type that only has a certain number of exploration charges per turn, if you want to get them.  ruins were one of my favorite parts of endless legend but these exploration things are just a pain to deal with.
Another thing is population types, there are different types of population giving unique bonuses which sounds cool until you realize you can't even choose which population type grows in a system, and they only give bonuses on certain planet types but they're placed randomly so you would have to go in and move them around if you really wanted to get the small bonus, and it would be so easy to have it done automatically, like this guy likes to be on a cold planet so he will go to the cold planet.
Combat is pretty disappointing coming from endless legend, you can customize your guys but the damage systems are pretty poorly explained and you can't control the actual combat, everything is autoresolved, plus the actual combat ships are a tier 2 technology for some reason even though there are hostile neutrals roaming aroud from tier 1.

Contrast was one of the few games that geniunely stayed in my mind when I saw it at PAX Prime last August. It looked like a seductive Film Noir platform adventure game with the capitivating aesthetics of the 1920's and the bold design ideas of an Indie studio. But despite all that I think my experience with Contrast was a little conflicted.
The gameplay revolves around using the environment to wink in and out of reality and into the world of light and shadow. Its makes for a fun time bouncing about on the shadows that are canvased on the side of buildings by conveniently placed flood lights, street lamps and Chandeliers; its made even more interesting in the sections where you must navigate moving shadows in the games multiple shadowy puzzles. Its pretty good, but when you build a game around traversing light and shadows, you often find yourself trying to fruitlessly jump into a lite wall only to realise its not one you can jump into. And its actually a little more buggy than I'd like in a type of a game that requires precision. Often you are in shadow and you clip until something that causes you to pop out from the wall and be forced to restart the platforming sequence.
Its visuals are in same the boat. The envorinments that you travel through are simply marvelous and diligently detailed to suck you into its unearthly 20's world almost completely. But than you get thrown off by the less than great animation of the characters. I mean most of the voice acting and music is rather good along with the delivery of the story is well done. But the moments when a character lefts theirs arms and exposed an empty gap in the model's armpit or back of the knees because there's no polygon just makes you raise an eyebrow (this is routinely compounded by the fact that most of the characters and indeed the story is delivered in silhouette).
So its really charming and fun, but its doesn't totally come together. As if the designers should've spent just a little more time ironing out the wrinkles in the game. But at the end of the day I am but disappointed in Contrast. These kind of platformers in my opinion are meant to be a little imperfect. Growing up on the 3D platformers from the N64 days, half the fun was wierd and wonderful quirks of this pioneering era. And although game design has vastly improved over the years, games like Contrast, albeit a little flawed, are very special.

Huĺnia vyjšla ŭ śviet jašče ŭ 2011. U mianie tak i nie atrymalasia uspryniać hetuju historyju i sklaści niejkija ŭradžańni dziciačym rozumam u tyj čas. I dobra, bo ja, chutčej za ŭsio, i nie zrazumieŭ by šmat rečaŭ niepasredna ŭ siužecie.
Pačaŭšy karystacca Steam, piĺna sačyŭ za huĺnioj. I voś, kaliści, padčas zimovaha rasprodažu naprykancy 2015 ad naradžeńnia Chrystova, huĺnia apynulasia ŭ maim košyku, i za niekaĺki amierykanskich prezidentaŭ adna ź biaskonkoncych ličbovych kopijaŭ pieratvarylasia ŭ maju ŭlasnuju. I ja nievymoŭna rad.
Zaraz pra samu huĺniu:
1. Atmasfiera -u čas, kali ty prajazdžaješ pa vulicach dy buĺvarach Los-Andželiesu, bačna što ŭsio vykanana z ducham tych časoŭ i na heta byŭ zroblieny vialiki ŭpor. Jašče dźvuma huĺniami z padobnaj atmasfieraj dlia mianie zjaŭliajucca Mafia I (1930-ja, "suchi zakon" i "Vialikaja depresija" i Mafia II (1945 - pasliavajennaja žyccio ŭ ZŠA i pieršaja palova 1950-ch, zaradžennie epochi rok-n-rolu) ,
Taksama aŭtamabili zjaŭliajucca niezamiennaj častkaj atmasfiery, boĺš za toje, tut ich vielizarnaja koĺkasć i ŭsie reaĺna isnavali ŭ 40-je z ich reaĺnymi nazvami, a nie vydumanymi, čaho ja nie bačyŭ ni ŭ adnoj huĺni.
2. Siužet - zaviazvajecca ŭ 1947 hodzie, pasliavajennaja žyccio, alie ŭ adroznienni ad huĺniaŭ sieryi "Mafija" užo na zachodnim uzbiarežžy. Vy huliajecie za patruĺnaha Koŭla Fielpsa. Ŭvažlivasć da detaliaŭ i kiemlivasć dapamahaje jamu raskryć paračku drobnych zlačynstvaŭ. Daliej idzie pavyšennie - ciapier vy detektyŭ Fielps. Siužetnaja linija pabudavanaje davoli cikava, tut ja nie chaču raskryvać karty i razžoŭvać, treba pahuliać, kab zrazumieć pra što ja.
3.Piersanaži - kožny piersanaž, niachaj heta budzie spravy abo siužetu, zroblieny jakasna. Mimika, reakcyja padčas dopytu, razmovy - vydatna!
Niedachopy ŭ huĺni josć, jany nie zanadta značnyja. Ja b vylučyŭ prymityŭnuju straĺbu i fiziku aŭtamabiliaŭ, alie heta Havok i vycisnuć z jaho što-niebudź liepiej naŭrad ci ŭjaŭlialasia mahčymym. Heta nijak nie ŭplyvaje na ahuĺnaje ŭražannie.
Mabyć adziny na sionnia sapraŭdny nuarnyj detektyŭ. Za amaĺ 5 hadoŭ z momantu zjaŭliennia huĺni analahaŭ nie vyjšla. Rekamienduju dadzieny pradukt ŭsim prychiĺnikam detektyvaŭ i nuara kupić sa znižkaj i adrazu z DLC.

Judging by the "Mostly Positive" reviews i'm playing the game wrong. But I can only go by what i've experienced. Early days, but not a fan so far. TL:DR, information overload and it feels completely aimless and inconsequential.
First we got the tech tree, it's friggin huge. Something like 120 techs all with something like three different unlocks each. It's organised into 4 quadrants, but they all cross over to a certain extent. It has a search bar, but getting round it is still a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ It really needs something like a filter button that literally removes every tech other than ones to do with a certain topic, say colonising planet types. Small and easy to look at, rather than search for "planet" and individually search the tree for each match. Right now I have like 50 possible tech choices and although the game says 4 or 5 techs are recommended I have absolutely no idea why. It doesn't say, and for a newbie like me that would at least give me SOME direction. But right now i'm just sort of aimlessly clicking techs depending on how I feel at the moment.
Second, the diplomacy is crap. Minor factions you can give the equivalent of a thumbs up every now and then and your influence with them will slowly increase. Thats about it for minor faction diplomacy, until you reach a certain threshold at which point you can do a quest. Major factions meanwhile, if they are aggressive are just friggin worthless. Every so often they'll say "gimme some cash" or whatever, and then when you give it to them they'll be like "thanks" and that's the end of the diplomacy. They aren't like "huh, these guys are actually alright, maybe we can be friends" after you do it a couple of times. No, they just do that every 10 or so turns and that will be it unless you want to give them literally all your stuff to get them to ally with you. And you don't know what your resources are worth until you offer them, so right now i'd have to click through like 20 resources types to work out what they actually care about. Hell right now a faction I know has like 50 dust (gold) and even if I offer them a thousand they still won't make peace with me, and they are FRIENDLY with me. That is non-sensical. Make it obvious what factions want in diplomacy.
At least in endless legends minor factions were a bit interesting, each one you met gave you a quest straight away and you'd have a bit of direction for your army. Here though? Absolutely nothing until you give them like 5 rounds of diplomatic thumbs up.
Third is my biggest problem, there is too much of everything and you can put them everywhere. Y'know that giant tech tree? I'm at turn 60 and I can build something like 40 buildings in any star system. The buildings are usually tailored towards certain planet types or planets with resources on them, so most of them are just going to be wastes of time. Buildings should be restricted im some way, either by having buildings depend on other buildings existing, or needing a certain amount of resrouces/planet types in the system to be built. Right now any system I colonise I have to sift through the 40 or so buildings I have unlocked and work out which ones are actually optimal for any given system. That's dull.
The systems themselves are a bit of a problem for me, for each system I can see a whole bunch of numbers telling me how much of the resources it's generating, but those number mean nothing to me. Are these high? Low? Should this system be making a crap load of population and sending it to other systems? Should it just focus on money? I dunno. All i've got are these numbers. There are no recommended buildings, you can say "auto-build and focus on X" but I don't even know what X should be.
Right now i'm playing the scientist race, and the game just feels pointless. I'm just researching the endless amount of tech and building the endless amounts of building waiting for something to happen. Nothing I do feels like it matters in the slightest. I have enough money none of the other races are going to attack me, but they sure as hell aren't going to be friends either. So what do I do? Am I just meant to research until the game ends? I have no idea how strong everyone else is compared to me in economy, military or whatever, so I don't know what I should be focusing on.
I'm going to keep playing, but just to see if i'm wrong and maybe turn 100 is where it gets good. I enjoyed Endless Legend enough to try.

I've been playing 4x games since the original Master of Orion and Master of Magic. I don't think I've played one this good in a really long time. This probably knocks Distant Universe off it's throne for me.
The game is wholistically perfectly put-together. It all works incredibly well together. The sub systems on their own might not be the best in the genre - for example, the combat is totally hands off and a bit hard to make sense of, but with all the other systems, the graphical polish and other presentation aspects, it works. The diplomacy is not the deepest, but it is innovative (the pressure meter, for example), and it just works. It's a pleasure to use as well.
I am continually getting the feeling that I could dig even further into the game to tweak my empire on an even futher level. Managing the population, for example, is something I don't do (much), but can have a huge impact. Managing planetary specializations is another example of how deep you can go with the management (though I don't do that either).
I haven't been able to pull myself away from the game - the "one more turn" syndrome is strong with this one. And I'm very deep into my second campaign and I haven't passed that threshold where no one else can stand up to me - the game stays challenging. New events pop up that add a level of complexity and diffuclty as well.
The game is incredibly deep, but intuitive. I only had to check a wiki for an answer once so far. The tutorial is very good - it doesn't invade your game or make you play through a scenario, it just gives tips in the top right of the screen which you can read or ignore (like Total War). There were a couple I skimmed and later I had to figure out something I should have already known, but that's fine.
I really love this game. I'm glad I waited a few months after it's release to jump in - this thing is beautifully polished. I'm looking at the patch log and they're hitting the AI every update. Right now the AI does some tricky stuff, though hasn't been incredibly difficult in combat yet (occassionaly yes though). It looks like they're hitting that hard.

L.A. Noire is an enjoyable and interesting crime thriller that puts you in the shoes of LAPD Detective Cole Phelps, and later a fire and life investigator Jack Kelso (But only for a few missions). The game has an interesting and rather different way of going about completing missions (solving cases). The gunplay is fluid and intense, the graphics are a bit outdated, but this game could run well on really any system, and the story is nearly impeccable. The game in and of itself has a few minor flaws, some are immersion-breaking, but they're very easy to overlook. I would buy this game at full price, on sale it's definately worth it.
It's different, it really is. The detective work is interesting and enjoyable, the gunplay is fun and works very similar to GTA and/or Mafia II. There's an intoxicating sense of style in this game that makes it seem authentically 1940's, and the way it goes about missions and investigations are fresh and innovative. The game feels like an interactive movie, but not like the PS4 exclusives, one where you actually have choices and more gameplay than just QTEs. Driving is a bit of an annoyance, and if you aren't a great driver with the keyboard and mouse, the game punishes you for hitting civilians or running into things, which isn't really a big deal, just incentive to drive more safely.
Graphics aren't bad, but they aren't great either. The 30 FPS lock depreciates the graphics, however, there are guides to increase the lock to 60, provided you know what you're doing and are willing to go into the files. It's not that much of a hassle, and it's worth it for the graphic elitists. The black-and-white mode also makes the film-noir vibe shine through, and is definately better than playing the game in color. The motion-scan technology is very innovative, causing L.A. Noire to take a step towards next-gen gaming, and shine out among.
The story is very well written, and the characters (with the exception of a few) are effectively developed throughout the game. There are several flaws with some of the missions, and there is a point where the game feels tedious and the story doesn't pick up. The first two departments, Patrol and Traffic, are essentially tutorials, ones that get boring really fast. From Homicide on, the noir vibe picks up, and you are drawn into an enticing story of murder, mystery, and intrigue.
I found myself saying "I love this game" as well as "I hate this game" throughout certain points. I'd definately recommend buying it, as it's a fresh and sleek take on the open-world action genre, mature in a sense that means more than just the rating on the box. I'd give it a 9/10.

I have never played this game as a straight up, real life mini golf experience. I think the game is meant to be played with low grav, bouncy ground, and especially with random ball shapes. I think you're missing out if you do not frustrate yourself and your friends to the point of friendship-ending rage that comes with this game. Conceptually, it's genius. Also, when typing in a password, you have to erase the word password before typing. It's something small but incredibly annoying after the first four or five times you do it. The option to create a lobby through Steam would be nice.

Sometimes it will stop when the turn is over, but sometimes it will just keep jumping forever and the only thing you can do to stop it is end the game. However, this is still an early access game and I've heard the developers are already on top of it.
Overall, it's a great game, it's hilarious, and the bugs are being worked out. I highly recommend it.

I know this game has received a ton of grief but lets be honest... Most of the people complaining have hundreds of hours in the game.  Don't expect the ETA's to be correct for patches, DLC's or anything else.  The developers are not good at time lines and the game has some bugs.  I will admit that I don't really play it that much any more but is it worth the price?  I think so.  People have complained about performance issues, I personally haven't had any.  I have had some clipping issues but never any major technical glitches.
With all this doubt and negativity, why do I recommend it?  Because I remember what it was like when I first started.  This game will frustrate you and drive you up a wall, but it has moments that are not like anything you have experienced in any other game.  When you first start the game, you will wake up to a beautifully rendered world.  Everything is soo much bigger than you.  This game has soo much beauty in it.  When you are first starting out, you are going to have those "Whoah!! Did you see that!?" moments.  You will have those heart beating "Oh gawd RUN!" moments.  It will have those "I just wasted all that time on this!?" moments as well.
This game will give you both the drastic ups as well as the downs and I highly recommend it to anyone (especially if it is on sale) to at least give it a shot.  I don't highly recommend the Official servers.  I started there and had a rough time learning.  It has your normal griefers and the time it takes to get anything done feels like a second job but if you find a good Unofficial server, it can make the game drastically easier to learn.
Try it and experience those moments, I promise you will easily get your money's worth of entertainment.

I love EVERYTHING about this game: the plot, the gameplay, the location, the dialogues, the characters, Phelps' suits, EVERYTHING. This game focuses on thinking, observing and analyzing, yet it never gets boring.
So basically you're this badass cop who climbs the ranks of the LAPD as fast as Road Runner on cocaine, your suits are still classy and on fleek even when you've been shot multiple times, you work so well that God himself decides to help you and makes music play when you're near the clues you're supposed to find (you can always choose to ask him to give you some space, anyway), your partners basically live their life hidden behind the shadow of your sassiness. When it comes to interrogate someone you take out your faithful notebook whose pages never end, and questions magically appears on it without you even writing them!!! And you're so smart that all you have to do is to observe people's face while they're talking to state if they're good people or filthy liars and therefore decide whether you should leave them alone or put them in jail. Everytime you have to look for clues, ask the rights questions and solve the various mysteries you can feel the tension from head to toe, but YOU'RE SO COOL YOU DON'T GIVE A SINGLE FLYING DAMN ABOUT IT.
You rise like a damn phoenix and end up working for the Vice department (after the Traffic and Homicide ones), but then something goes wrong aaaaaaaaaaand now you're demoted to the Arson department. Sorry 'bout that. Anyway you're still a good guy.
In the meanwhile, you remember the time when you were Lieutenant in Okinawa during WWII, making us discover a past you still don't get along with.
This is basically what happens in L.A. Noire; I didn't write a "serious" review because it would take me days to express how much I loved this game and what's it like in detail. I have never played this game as a straight up, real life mini golf experience. I think the game is meant to be played with low grav, bouncy ground, and especially with random ball shapes. I think you're missing out if you do not frustrate yourself and your friends to the point of friendship-ending rage that comes with this game. Conceptually, it's genius. I don't know who thought it would be a good idea to put a cone on a mini golf course, but it makes for an interesting game.
As of right now, there are only three maps. But the game is still in early access, and I can forgive that because of the replay value that comes with this game, especially in multiplayer. There are so many ways to customize games that each game could have an entirely different spin.
The lobbies are pretty annoying as of right now. You can't search a lobby name, so you have to flip through pages. Right now, that's not a huge problem since there are maybe 30 pages at max at any given time, but when this game becomes more popular, that's not gonna fly. Also, when typing in a password, you have to erase the word password before typing. It's something small but incredibly annoying after the first four or five times you do it. The option to create a lobby through Steam would be nice.
I think the music kind of sucks, which is a little disappointing but not a dealbreaker. There is, however, one game-breaking bug I've encountered a few times where your golf ball begins to jump in place on its own without stopping. Sometimes it will stop when the turn is over, but sometimes it will just keep jumping forever and the only thing you can do to stop it is end the game. However, this is still an early access game and I've heard the developers are already on top of it.
Overall, it's a great game, it's hilarious, and the bugs are being worked out. I highly recommend it.

L.A. Noire is one of those games that can really surprise you with how good it is.
While it has some open world aspects to it, the game is actually quite linear as far as mission structure and story are concerned. This is not a bad thing. It's like watching an old mystery movie, combined with point-and-click game concepts, and GTA mechanics and gameplay. It all fuses together to form a unique game that is very interesting to play through.
The visuals are quite good, and even today could be mistaken for next-gen quality. The faces are very expressive, much more so than most games in general. This is because part of the game is about reading your subject when interrogating them to see if they are lying or not.
While the different elements of this game are derivative from many games you've probably played before, the experience and setting make this a game feel unique. It is certainly worth the playthrough for just about any gamer.

Endless Space 2 is to Endless Space 1 what Mass Effect 2 was to Mass Effect 1. They took the original game and just made every thing better. The combat, the immersion, the AI, the balance, the graphics, the UI, and even the music. But what sets Endless Space 2 apart from other 4x game is the immersion. The dynamic ways you can change your empire and how the population actually repsonds to your gameplay choices makes it feel almost RPG-like. Not to mention the storyllines each empire and each minor civilization has. This kind of immersion is sorely lacking in almost every other 4X game I know (and I've played almost every 4X game out there). That said, there are some minor nitpicks but they are being rapidly patched out and I expect huge expansions in the future - like E.S.1: Disharmony.
Some Cautions and why they are perfectly acceptable:
Like all grand 4X games... late game performance is an issue.
My machine:
CPU: Ryzen 5 1600X (6 core, 12 thread) OC to 4.3 GHz
GPU: MSI GTX 1070 Gaming X 8GB
RAM: Corsair 3200MHz DDr3 16GB
Around turn 200 when I have discovered 90% of the map and every other empire, the frames tank to 35-40FPS when I zoom out all the way in the galaxy view. (But what other 4X game doesn't LOL). BUT Turn times stay consistently in the 3 second range when playing against AI, which is how it should be (I'm ♥♥♥♥ing looking at you, CIV V >_<)
And in space battles with 15+ ships total, I am lucky to get above 45FPS. This issue will be most likely fixed with patches and drivers BUT hey... when they have modeled and rendered every single weapon hard point (complete with the turrets deploying and turning to engage enemies)... it is worth it. Every battle feels like the awesome opening battle of the Revenge of the Sith. And at 1/4 speed, I can see each slug fired either shatter on my shield, or pass through a broken shield and impact on my armor, and a different fx if it penetrates the armor. No other space 4x does that kind of detail.
The AI is a bit of a pushover? Nah not really. Compared to the paethtic likes of MoO4 or the OP Roflstompfest that was Endless Space 1's AI, the AI in this is actually pretty competent and balanced. Joining an alliance actually feels like an alliance. Countless times, I joined forces with the Lumeris and Vodyanni to stop the Craver menace and time and time again they saved my♥♥♥♥♥by defending my systems and me theirs. An AI you can actually count on and shows appreciation when you help them? When is the last time we saw that? MoO2?

A fantastic 4x game set in space. A great sequel to Endless Space, and a great game on it's own. The customization options for creating custom factions is fantasticly done. The mod community is providing excellent extra content/changes. Endless playability, and you can make this as easy or as hard as your want. Go for ultimate hardcore mode with tons of enemies, difficult smaller factions, chaotic start, and a custom faction that has only negative traits! It's a doozy. Or go for an easier method with fewer enemies, easier small factions, and a hyper-focused custom faction.
The variations of potential factions is crazy fantastic. Unlike other games that provide some trait differences to production of food or materials, or a slightly different start bonus, you can have factions that don't even use food, and can warp time. Or you can have a faction that has gigantic motherships that can move between systems to claim ownership, leaving the other system open to colonization in the process. Or a faction that buys out production with influence. Or another faction that buys out smaller faction favor and settles new systems with dust (gold equivalent). The possibilities are endless, and are a great example of how to do a very varied faction/race system.
The research trees are well done, and are being well tweaked for balance and gameplay fun as the updates roll out. This is a beta game for purchase done right. They handle broken stuff quickly with little mini updates, and have rolled out a few new factions and gameplay features since they started. I loved their endless series from before (legend, space, dungeon, etc.) and this is a good follow up to their previous games.

After playing this game for 3 days straight, I must conclude that the game is much better than Galactic Civilizations III (with expansions for that game).
1) Better tactics: unlike GCIII, this game has many more tactics and tweaking and customizability for both space and ground invasions.
2) Better streamlining: unlike GCIII, where you can easily get overwhelmed by having to manage every tile on each planet, or worry if your enemies can slip past your systems through each individual space grid, ES2 is more streamlined, requiring far less micromanagement - ideal for large maps. Micromanagement hell on GCIII drew me away.
3) Better lore: Each civ has their own unique quests and stories. More minor races and lore.
4) AI is more loyal: Alliances on EL2 actually works better than GCIII - they are less likely to backstab you - in fact, they are extremely loyal, making alliance-based victories very viable.
The only problems with ES2 are:
1) Quite a few interface bugs: occasionally, my ship grouping malfunctions, and I get flickering on some of the cutscenes. Not a huge issue though, since resetting the game resolves it. I only get this problem like 3 hours into a gaming session.
2) Empire disappearing bug: perhaps the most gamebreaking was how a single empire suddenly collapsed in a single turn and disappeared (anarchy perhaps?).
(EDIT: as of 3 Oct 2017, I heard that the 1.0.57 patch fixed problem (2) )
Overall:
8/10 rating
I would give it 9 out of 10, if not for the 2 bugs that I have just mentioned.

First of all, I'll start with the positive things:
- The vibe and atmosphere/Setting: They did an AWESOME job at setting up the right setting and getting into the spirit of LA in 1947, at least IMO. I do like this period a lot, and the look of the game (if you like, you can play this in b/w as well), the music/radio broadcasts (unfortunately, no way to switch radio stations manually, apparently. No custom music either, but then again, listening to modern music in the car would kinda ruin the immersion), the cars, fashion, lingo etc... just GREAT.
Also, since this is based on old thrillers and stories by guys like Raymond Chandler, they went for that vibe, and did it VERY well... this does feel a lot like a that noire crime fiction Chandler was famous for.
- The general idea is very cool and, IMO, refreshing - interrogating people and, based on the clues you found and their facial expressions (done with actors and motion capture) figuring out whether they're lying or not... great job there! The IGN review says that sometimes, it is too easy to tell when someone is telling a lie or getting nervous - but doesn't that add even more realism? After all, not everyone is a good liar irl!
- The gameplay. The cars DO feel a bit... odd, chases can get a tiny bit frustrating, the shooting mechanics are far from perfect, but between examining crime scenes, searching for clues, interrogating witnesses and suspects, using your notebook to find clues, car chases, shootouts and some interludes to deepen the story, there is some variety.
- The characters. I really like the main protagonist, and some of his fellow policemen. Sure, there is quite a bit of clichè to be found here, but that again fits well, as this is a tribute to the noire-genre, which never was deep literature anyway.
Now for the less than positive or even negative parts:
- On rails. To a certain degree, the game takes away your freedom. An example: In one case, I apparently missed a clue at one of the places I visited. I was doing interrogations at the police station, and was not able to go back to those places and pick up the thing I missed, which would have made solving the case easier and unlocked some additional questions/accusations.
- Evidence. Basically, if you think a person is not telling the truth, you wanna choose "doubt". If you pick "lie", you have to prove the person is a liar with a piece of evidence/clue from your notebook. And sometimes that doesn't work right. Not a bug, it's the writing. The abbreviated details of the clue or piece of evidence might make you think that it is clear evidence the guy is a liar, but when you choose it, the game says it's wrong or not enough.
- Some frame rate issues. This game is by no means recent. I don't have a killer gaming pc (i7, 16 gigs of ram, Nvidia GTX 960 with 4 GB of ram), but I would think that it should be able to run this game well... and still, there are frame rate issues, the game sometimes slows down. Odd, when games like Unity, Mad Max, GTA V, Witcher III or even Arkham Knight perform much better on my system. YMMV.
- Repetition. Sometimes, the cases are TOO alike, or at least the procedure you do is. There is a bigger storyline with a certain series of murders, and at one point, it was like "OK, another murder like those other ones. Check for clues. Interrogate. Visit a bar. Visit another place. Interrogate. Done". Of course, those steps should be part of it in a crime/police-game, but I think there should have been more variety in the cases or the activities that are involved in them.
I did enjoy the homicide cases (after the first or second promotion), but didn't enjoy the drug-related cases I was given after my next promotion
- Mechanics. As I said, driving feels...wonky. Mind you, you are not driving a very recent sports car or something like that, but the controls feel a bit clunky sometimes, and so do the physics. I did play the game with an Xbox controller.
Verdict: The idea was refreshing, and they really nailed it with the setting and vibe. Unfortunately, there are flaws to the whole Lie/truth/doubt/clues/notebook-system. Sometimes it's misleading, not elaborate enough, and sometimes it's too much "on rails".
However, the story, vibe and the idea itself are great, and even though it's not perfect, I'd give this a 7.5/10. I got this while it was on sale and do not regret it at all, I do enjoy the game. Check out some gameplay videos maybe, and if you can get it on sale and dig crime/police-games and the era this is set in, check it out!

Contrast is short, has a few minor bugs and flaws. There was actually a lot that erked me. For example, the game screwed with my mouse sensitivity in game, so i had to tweak it so the camera wasn't making me dizzy. Also, it was a bit more demanding on my pc then i thought it would (but my pc is old. Any up to date pc should do fine). Fixed camera angles when interecting with objects can also be a bit obnoxious.
However... for the flaws, this game was really enjoyable. It's a bit of soul food, makes you think and ask questions. It feels substantial as far as the story and the world is concerned (Some say gameplay is lacking challange, but for me it lacked a lot of the frustration that can come with some puzzle games with obtuse solutions. For example, the secret star solutions in Braid, one of which requires you to do nothing but wait for nearly 40 minutes or so). The art is fantastic, definitely different from what i've played recently. The Music and overal sound design is wonderful, though the voice acting isn't the best.
Contrast is one of those examples of "Games are Art" while still being a game, as opposed to a tour with some narration over top. If you don't mind a short, but fufilling experiance or some so so gameplay, and you want a great story, world, and overall aesthetic then pick up contrast. If you want something challanging, lengthy, and a bit shallower (i.e. good dumb fun such as Painkiller) then look elsewhere. A game for when you're in the mood, and a damn good one if you end up playing it in that mood.

This game. This effin' game has inflicted unforeseenly severe addiction spikes on me. No other game has done it quite like this one. Spending hours and hours on building and managing your ever growing medieval kingdom in the medieval world. Ruling your kingdom with a sim-like feel on the game with character traits gives the game experience a nice touch of livelyhood and fun choice options. Will you be a kind ruler who tries to win his subjects' favor through justice and being rational or be a cruel and sadistic ruler who shamelessly stomps on everyone's requests and demands, and who particurarly likes to throw little children in prison and execute them, or even blind and castrate them? The large amount of possibilities and events are bound to keep you entertained for quite some time.
Medieval history haters and those passive towards it must step aside or risk invoking deep hatred towards this game for being too "complicated" and "boring". This game finds its juice in its historical aspects of how the world worked during the medieval period. Family and Dynasties being the key to all forms of ruling and inheriting. You play from 1066 to 1453, during which your dynasty must survive all different kinds of odds and historical events (Black Death can be a mean ♥♥♥♥♥). World domination is not the objective, surprisingly, although that is the most fun thing to try to accomplish. However, the bigger your kingdom gets, the harder it becomes to manage it. Internal affairs and greedy usurpers are often a bigger threat than foreign kingdoms. There will always be people wanting to undermine your rule and reign. When your ruler dies, you take up control of his chosen heir to continue the game. Without getting too deep into the game mechanics, I'll break it down more simply.
This game is Medieval 2 Total War's campaign map gameplay on steroids.
Those who liked the campaign map play of M2TW are bound to like this game. For those who didn't play M2TW, prepare for a difficult learning curve. It's definitely not a casual game. You must think of everything all the time, otherwise you might as well start lubing up that Ainis and wait for the Painis. It really helps if you have someone to explain the game to you. The tutorial sucks big time, though I learned to play the game in about five days without help (plenty of rageful quits included). If you're ready and willing to give the game a chance despite its cold grace, I can highly recommend it.
WARNING: I am not joking about the addictiveness of the game. There were times for me when I could hardly even sleep without wanting to play the game. I'm sure this is no issue to most people, but if you're a history buff and an empire builder like me, you're most likely in the danger zone.

I'm right on the border for how to rate this game and since we only have the choice of Recommend or Not, I'm going to have to lean towards not.
To me, this plays just like civilization in space.  I love the graphics and animations, extremely well done, along with options that allow me to turn them off when I'm tired of watching them.
The turn off for me is the imbalance of politics and resources in the game.  The pirate element of the game is a constant and significant challenge to your resources.  They are an endless and continues drain on your military operations to defend your space, popping up over and over again as spawning as quickly as you dispatch them only with no time to repair your own vessels.
Because you have to develop ships to combat the pirates, all the other AI players think you're aggressive and take wary and aggressive stances towards you, don't expect to find many friends unless you're neighbors with an inferior race who's only playing nice to survive (watch that back).
The "Dust" is needed for everything, building, repairing, and especially maintaining ships, buildings, and is also the payroll of your hero's.  You can't produce this stuff fast enough and if you develop your planets with industry you drain dust even faster on maintenance so it makes little sense to develop your industry as it quickly becomes self defeating.
Enemy AI does not suffer from your limitations to resources, easily spewing out warships heck-of-a-lot faster than you can with less than half the systems you do.
Multi-player is probably the best option for this game as all the players suffer from the same growing pains, the AI option for a single player game is simply waaaaaay out of balance on resources and political views and is the straw that throws my thumb on the downward side.

Pros: The visuals for this game are great, and I have enjoyed the story telling elelments of the game a lot.  Exploration is pretty satisfying, and other races feel distinct from you.  SOund track is nice and helps with emmersion.  You have a lot of choice when it comes to your empires political scene but micromanagement is not necessary.  Game manages a nice blance of micro control versus time saving mechanics.
Cons: Ship building and combat is very rock paper scissors, which would be ok if you got to actually make impactful choices.  You dont though.  Your not given any "real" tactical options, and the "strategy" side of combat is very unsatisfying. Weapons etc work best in particular "ranges", and a range category will beat another range category.  IE Long beats Short.  So you cant make a fleet of ships designed to close rapidly with heavy short range fire power and expect that fleet to do well against a fleet with all long range weaponry who have 0% effectiveness at short range. I bounced off the original Endless Space but loved Endlesss Legend. Endless Space 2 is already shaping up to be one of the best 4X games I've played and Amplitude tend to really invest in and continue to add to their games over time so it's only going to gain more depth. Already they've added additional quests and some features that didn't make it in prior to release. You know they're doing something right with Civ devs start stealing design and mechanics stuff from them (tech web in Beyond Earth and city districts in Civ VI for example).
The Good
- Their art team has always been outstanding and this is no exception - it really adds a lot to the flavour and immersiveness.
- UI is another of their strong points
- Factions are all unique with their own mechanics and quest story lines
-  Early game exploration is interesting (probes for loot, early quests, etc.)
- Wide variety of planet types, anomalies and galactic features
- Empire management offers a lot of depth
- A variety of playstyles and strategies based on your use of heroes, your faction choice, goals for win condition, plan for teching, etc.
- Ship design is fun and easy to understand with drag and drop modules for weapons, armour and support
The Bad/So-So
- AI diplomacy is often tough to emulate in these games and feels a little wonky sometimes
- Combat is not bad per se, just mainly hands-off other than picking a pre-battle plan and designing your ships weaponry
- Ground combat needs a little something more to it, not sure what though - it's much more bare bones visually and tactically than space combat
- The end game is not as interesting as the rest. Most of the quests have finished up, usually a victor is already well-ahead and it's just a matter of end turn/mopping up. Definitely an area that got added to in Endless Legend with more content to flesh it out, so likely same will happen here.
- Still has the occasional crash or lock up in the game processing something but much rarer than it used to be and with auto-save on every turn, it's just a matter of initializing the game again.
- The government/senate aspect I have mixed feelings about. I like the new concept of passing laws. Representatives of parties throughout your systems I find a little confusing still and harder to factor in when it comes to wanting to have a certain party in power. Your research and construction choices also strongly influence which party will be in power.
Overall, it's the game atmosphere, quests, art, fun learning curve of many moving parts in your empire, and variety embedded in the different factions that I like - plus knowing Amplitude is only going to add more to it with time, based on their track record.

The good: Who can say "no" to the idea of riding around on a raptor and shooting an assault rifle at a T rex or flying around on an Quetz loaded with turrets as you raid an enemy base. It's a tropical wonderland filled with all sorts of toothy creatures looking to just make you their lunch.
The bad: The AI still sucks. The material grind is still endless. The spawning behavior still cheats through walls. And Multiplayer on public servers is still cancer.
*edit* Let me clarify.
The AI sucks. Dinosaurs will frequently get caught on trees, rocks, terrain, walk off ledges, and generally be unable to follow you for more than a few meters at a time without you suddenly losing your tames and having to backtrack. They have shown that they can program more detailed AI with some dinos in the Ark having special behavior when wild (mostly lost as soon as tamed), but they were too interested in just churning out content instead of making that content look and behave right. And similarly the tactics people have put into place for dealing with the AI is also lazy; standing on a higher ledge and shooting at alphas who just stand there and take it, using stone pillars and doorways to block movement and shoot from safety, ect.
The Material Grind is still endless. Metal is only available in reasonable quantities in certain areas of the map which can be a long and dangerous route to bring it back. Specialty resources like crystal, obsidian, silica can only be obtained from certain places on the map which can be a good distance away and due to the AI problem makes running a land convoy impractical.Tek tier stuff cannot be legitimately obtained by a solo player unless you have months of your life to devote to breeding hundreds of Rexes to see most of them die in a single attack from a boss. You can increase resource collection rates, download mods to affect stack size and weight, but that is all cheating and covering up what is still at its core, bad design and balancing.
Spawning behavior still cheats through walls. Just building walls around an area doesn't stop things from just magically appearing inside. Instead you have to place dozens of pillars or foundations everywhere to block respawning. You also don't know the radius that a single foundation prevents respawning by anything visible ingame so if you don't cover everything in a single layer of pillars, ceilings, and foundations hostile dinos can still magically appear in your base. Even with all this, things can still clip through walls or floors whenever that area gets loaded back into active memory so there is no solution other than lots of excess structure, turrets, and having a sizable number of dinos on aggressive.
Servers being cancer is mostly just a requisite disclaimer. Official servers are run by mega tribes that pillar off and wall off starting areas to prevent anyone unaffiliated with that tribe from doing anything. They have to do this to prevent other tribes from getting a foothold and destroying their things, but it also makes it impossible as a solo player or small tribe.
Unofficial servers and Non-dedicated servers are about the only realistic option, but come with their own challenges and limitations.

Endless Space 2 is a real spectacle. It's gorgeous, the UI manages a nice balance between giving you a good overview and allowing you to request full details, the storylines mesh nicely with the mechanics and each civ feels highly distinctive. The strategic side is good; I find myself working out nice synergies and routines but also having to readjust them to face new challenges or exploit new opportunities.
The caution I would give is that it's still glitchy, and it is somewhat obtuse.
Glitches in such a large and complex game take time to solve, but the community team is reactive and present over on their official forums. Problems of balance and AI are fundamentally hard problems, but again, the game sees constant active development which is what a modern 4X needs.
This is unfortunately a game which needs a well-designed, live manual, not word of mouth, fan wikis and superficial tutorials. Combat is difficult to understand, made even more difficult by outdated information still being passed on. However, between the tutorials, tooltips and looking things up, I feel like one-and-two-halves of a game in I've fundamentally understood how it all works without too much trouble. New 4X players might be better served with a slightly more rigid 4X like Civilization.
