Contrast is a sometimes...frustrating game. But ultimately rewarding.
The pros? Where to begin! Absolutely top-rate storytelling (this could almost be a film), often ingeniously clever puzzles (though none so hard that one just throws in the towel), gorgeous graphics, wonderful sound, and a genuine sense of child-like wonder which seamlessly blends with the harsher realities of the adult world. Think Tomb Raider meets Limbo - that is to say, both 3D and 2D platforming elements, effortlessly combined - with a story and direction worthy of old-school Tim Burton. Oh, and it's nowhere near as painfully LLLOOOONNNGG as all games seem to feel the obligation to be these days (or in other words, it doesn't "overstay its welcome").
Now the cons. Some of the platforming elements are PAINFULLY pedantic...one teeny, tiny miscalculation in where you place a lighting rig (this game is all about shadows), and you could very well waste the next forty seconds running and jumping to a point just to realise you ain't gonna make that final jump. And then it's ALL the way back to the start of the puzzle again. And there's some reflex-based moments of timing which become frustrating thanks to the occasionally ill-responsive controls, though these bits are at least few and far between.
Honestly, though, none of what I've just said would be all THAT much to grumble about, if it wasn't for the POSITIVELY DIABOLICAL SAVE SYSTEM. Why does nearly every modern game have to insist that if someone switches it on, they'd better be ready to sit there non-stop for HOURS? Do they not know that some of us have JOBS? LIVES?! That we CAN'T necessarily invest two hours at a time into conquering A WHOLE FREAKING CHAPTER before switching off and going to bloody BED???
But as I said earlier...sigh...at least this is one recent game which doesn't feel the need to give us a non-linear plot full of extreme repetition, constant backtracking, and an "open world" which takes 180+ hours to explore. Short, and on the whole, very sweet. But man oh man, do these game designers EVER test their own games, or better yet...give them to NORMAL people to try out before commercial release? It's a good thing I don't have a "life" to spend precious time on, or I'd just about give away this whole "gaming" lark altogether!
Verdict: 9/10.

Multi-player is probably the best option for this game as all the players suffer from the same growing pains, the AI option for a single player game is simply waaaaaay out of balance on resources and political views and is the straw that throws my thumb on the downward side.

This game. This effin' game has inflicted unforeseenly severe addiction spikes on me. No other game has done it quite like this one. Spending hours and hours on building and managing your ever growing medieval kingdom in the medieval world. Ruling your kingdom with a sim-like feel on the game with character traits gives the game experience a nice touch of livelyhood and fun choice options. Will you be a kind ruler who tries to win his subjects' favor through justice and being rational or be a cruel and sadistic ruler who shamelessly stomps on everyone's requests and demands, and who particurarly likes to throw little children in prison and execute them, or even blind and castrate them? The large amount of possibilities and events are bound to keep you entertained for quite some time.
Medieval history haters and those passive towards it must step aside or risk invoking deep hatred towards this game for being too "complicated" and "boring". This game finds its juice in its historical aspects of how the world worked during the medieval period. Family and Dynasties being the key to all forms of ruling and inheriting. You play from 1066 to 1453, during which your dynasty must survive all different kinds of odds and historical events (Black Death can be a mean ♥♥♥♥♥). World domination is not the objective, surprisingly, although that is the most fun thing to try to accomplish. However, the bigger your kingdom gets, the harder it becomes to manage it. Internal affairs and greedy usurpers are often a bigger threat than foreign kingdoms. There will always be people wanting to undermine your rule and reign. When your ruler dies, you take up control of his chosen heir to continue the game. Without getting too deep into the game mechanics, I'll break it down more simply.
This game is Medieval 2 Total War's campaign map gameplay on steroids.
Those who liked the campaign map play of M2TW are bound to like this game. For those who didn't play M2TW, prepare for a difficult learning curve. It's definitely not a casual game. You must think of everything all the time, otherwise you might as well start lubing up that Ainis and wait for the Painis. It really helps if you have someone to explain the game to you. The tutorial sucks big time, though I learned to play the game in about five days without help (plenty of rageful quits included). If you're ready and willing to give the game a chance despite its cold grace, I can highly recommend it.
WARNING: I am not joking about the addictiveness of the game. There were times for me when I could hardly even sleep without wanting to play the game. I'm sure this is no issue to most people, but if you're a history buff and an empire builder like me, you're most likely in the danger zone.

Contrast:  This is a game of light and shadow. A simple three-dimensional platformer where a flick of the wrist turns into a two-dimensional platformer. Such a decision we have already seen in several projects, unlike Contrast - to use lights and shadows to create and manipulate level elements.
Contrast short game: Three acts can run for 2.5-3 hours, even with search collectibles and secrets. The final stories are so predictable that they are even insulting. The visual style and mood of the game promises some mystery , detective story or drama, and as a result we get some banal family history, a place that in some lowly daytime drama. A pity.
Gameplay:  This puzzling platformer built around the ability to turn into a two-dimensional character shadow. You press the button, the camera hangs somewhere on the side, and Dawn leaves from himself only a shadow in the form which overcomes obstacles and chasms . Depending on the shape you need to change the situation: a break in the wall will not go through the shadows, but to circumvent it in bodily form can be easily. On the other hand, the flesh will not leak, for example, through the glass, but the light (and shadow) will penetrate through it without any problems.
Emotional Impact:  The emotional impact that you receive from the story is the jewel of Contrast.  This leaves you with a very memorable performance throughout the three acts.
Visuals:  Incredibly stylish and beautiful thing. Almost every game screenshot can be long and enthusiastically regarded as if considering - a jazz fan, retro, cabaret and burlesque - the pleasure is doubled.
Story:  The whole essence of Contrast - in the plot. Didi not the happiest child in the world : the parents at odds , mother rambles in the entertainment business , his father trying to deal with their problems , but even more breaks in them. But meanwhile, the sly little Didi goes into his inner world - a natural reaction of protection against the constant attacks of the vernal world. And the inner world in turn leads you, purely friendly shadow named Dawn
Summary:  Contrast is a game full of heart, beauty, and at least a few excellent puzzles. It’s at its best when it marries its poignant story to its platforming, and at its weakest when it’s about moving boxes, but it rarely goes very long without showing us something worth playing.

I want to like the game, but I just don't.  I'm a fan of previous Endless games, the game is beautiful (like others in this line), the pieces look promising, but...things just don't fit.  Decisions are offered, but some options seem too obviously weak while others are too obviously better.  Some game elements look important but have no real impact on play; an example is Luxury goods, and a marketplace to buy and sell them:  out of over a dozen goods (I think I saw a tutorial note saying there are sixteen), you get to define one or two that will be marginally useful to your empire, and the others can be ignored.  A similar system in Endless Legend is a sought-after boost to your development;  here it is a weak afterthought.
The most critical problem, though, is the incredible randomness of the game setup, and the feeling that the game is won or lost when you first venture out and see your neighboring systems.  I had one game--the very first I played--where I was literally trapped in my home system, hemmed in by minor races and one system containing no colonizable planets.  I have found myself starting the game three or four times looking for just one playable starting position, and even then losing interest too quickly when I am assaulted by a pirate fleet stronger than any ships I've so far been able to build, or discovering that nearly all the planets around me will require mid-game tech to colonize (and with poor development prospects even then), or just meeting my first neighboring AI opponent and realizing they already have five planets to my two.
The game does not present an interesting, approachable challenge and I find myself losing interest in learning the tech tree, the special abilities of the various races, or even the core dynamics of the game, because none of it seems to make any sense.  There are a lot of other 4X games that are more enjoyable.

This game was an absolute pleasure to play. It's a short indie game telling a mature story of a young girl and her broken family trying to come back together as they make painful choices, solve difficult situations, and all the while unraveling a mysterious tale of science & intrigue closer to the heart than expected.
I understand this may not be for everyone... but the deciding factor I believe we should all consider is this is a very affordable, small-team, indie game worth experiencing. That said, the amount of storytelling I experienced was amazing.
If it is worth anything, I have a background in animation as a storyboard artist... I am especially keen to stories that feel "thought through" from start to finish, and not merely trying to get to certain moments or even the climactic finale just for the sake of it. Surprisingly the story has quite a few sad & heavy scenes that really tug at the heart.  Stay for the end... it's incredible.
The difficulty is quite easy, and that may throw some people off... in my opinion however I enjoy story over challenge, so making all the collectibles glaringly obvious throughout only made me focus on their content and how it intertwined with the story rather than the pursuit. This is very subjective, so those looking for a hard time may be turned off. I've read here & there some having troubles with the shadow puzzles; this again is a tough one, as I got through all of them pretty easy... the most I spent was maybe 20-25 minutes on the last act's few big ones... still, the visuals and little rewards you are given with wonderful voice acting or visual design was well worth it.
Speaking of voices, the acting was tremendous. I especially enjoyed the voice of Didi, as child voice overs can sometimes be a hit or miss.
Visually the game is an absolute joy to experience. Didi and Dawn are interesting, and I even grew to love the wonderful silhouettes of the characters around them. The soundtrack is very well thought out and you can clearly see the sound & visuals were designed hand in hand to compliment each other.
I know reviews can be a subjective mess for some, but I hope this helps in whatever way it can! I'm a pretty level-headed, patient man who really appreciates good art & story. If this isn't your cup of tea, I again remind you it was a fifteen dollar purchase that definitely wouldn't make you regret the experience.
I'm not a hardcore "anti-big publisher / developer" gamer, but I do want to say, humbly, that games like this make me so hopeful and excited about indie games. They provide an intimacy and patience in story I don't see often enough in the AAA titles.
Warm regards,
DDCP

resume L.A. Noire quickly, it's the story of a LAPD cop named Cole Phelps and his rise & fall in the police system, all while questioning a bunch of people about various crimes. This game manages to immerse you into the past, in the late 40's as a LA police officer trying to climb the ladder.
I like alot of things about this game: The ambience, the music, the facial system, the captivating storyline, the relevance of almost everything placed in the decor, the dialogue, etc, and the list goes on. Rockstar/Team Bondi (R.I.P.) have done an amazing job on this game, making sure to create a different feel than in their previous games (such as Bully or GTA). There is no other game like this one, and that's a quality I love when it comes to good games.
The story will run you at the very minimum at least 26 hours (DLC included) and you can then retry past cases individually to try and get better. I like to play through L.A. Noire about once every 1/1,5 years (it's kinda like a movie, where it's as enjoyable as the first time once you let some time pass and come back to it).
I would recommend getting the complete edition of this game to any fan of Noire TV series or movies, and fans of well scripted detective games. DO NOT come into L.A. Noire expecting exactly the same as GTA but as a cop in the 40's because you will be very dissapointed. That being said, the game is amazing, probably the most immersive game i've played.

I have mixed feelings (giving an upvote to support indie developers). The game seems to have a lot of potential. Below I list quite a lot of cons, but it's only to let the developers know what (in my opinion) could use some improvement. The game is really fun to play, and given that it's early access, I hope the developers will keep on improving it.
PRO's
- great art style
- good idea
- fun gameplay (see some fun-limiting cons listed below)
- some realism, which is nice (having to study when living with your parents, having to buy your food when living on your own, etc).
CON's
- Buggy. As others have stated, some ordered items never get delivered. It's especially frustrating when you accept a paid review mission and have a tight deadline to make a video and the game doesn't arrive. Then you get the message from a frustrating publisher: "you were supposed to deliver it and you did nothing!" - well, of course I did nothing, because I didn't have the freaking game! :-|
- Editing part of the game is a fun concept, but it also gets frustrating later in the game when it gets noticeably unfavorable for the player (getting more and more cards with copyrighted content that forces the player to pay the fine or cards that don't fit a given scene). I wish editing was based on actual skill, not complete randomness (the cards you get to choose from are chosen randomly, but become more and more punishing as the game progresses).
- The social aspect of the game (meeting people, partying, etc.) is not interesting enough. Every party event is exactly the same: clicking "talk" button and staring at the screen for 5 minutes. Highly repetitive music makes this experience quite annoying.
- After about 3-4 hours of play I ran out of things to buy / improve. The game quickly turned into watching my money and subscribers grow with nothing else to do (except attending parties and getting a girlfriend, which, as stated before, quickly starts feeling repetitive). Randomly generated titles of new releases and their repeating covers make further gameplay not exciting enough. Feels like the game needs more content to live up to its full potential.
- Taking a course seems like a cool idea, but later you realize it does exactly the same thing as making a video. Taking an advanced course takes so much time that you start loosing subscribers. I didn't see a reason to ever take a course - making another video always seemed like a better idea
- It was frustrating that the game doesn't pause when you get a pop-up message or enter any statistic window of any sort. I wish the game didn't punish the player (losing time = losing subscribers) for trying to read all the information that needs to be read. Also, the lack of ability to speed up time while taking a course or talking to somebody at a party made those activities uninteresting. It's because of that I decided not to attend any events and not to take any courses.
If those issues are fixed (especially bugs), this could be a very good game!

What is so amazing about a 2011 game and a love letter to old noire movies like "The Untouchables" and "The Black Dahlia" from rockstar and team bondi that puts you into the shoes of a rookie detective Cole Phelps? Everything.
L.A. Noire is all about amazing you with its crisp gameplay, groundbreaking facial capture technology (at the time), and great atmosphere and setting.
Set in 1946 Los Angeles, the second world war has come to a close and living soldiers have to make a living somehow. Cole Phelps decides to go into law enforcement, and the story ramps up from there, no spoilers at all from me, you just have to trust me. I bought this game on my xbox360, ps3, and now my tablet, (surface 3), and the game still manages to feel new to me.
The controls on PC are great, I love the default control, but you can easily adjust and edit those controls in the options. You can use any game controller as well. One thing for tablets though, using the right click if you have no mouse gets troublesome pretty fast, but for desktop users it is fluid, no doubt.
The graphics are beautiful, but the game is capped at 30FPS (I believe) and that might bug people, but you can always tinker with the graphics in  game anytime. ANYTIME. No more launcher people!
Facial capture technology is what really shines here though, as it displays the emotions and "tells", (which you need for interrogations and questioning people at the crime scene). perfectly.
The gameplay is fun if you like puzzle games, third person games, story rich games, or even just noire like games. The feeling and atmosphere as stated above is just incredible. Just incredible! It has...
. Puzzle solving and deducing
. Gunplay
. Car chases and on foot chases
. Hand to Hand combat
. Tough decision making
. Driving
and more.
The length of this game is also fantastic, though near the end, I began to lose track of the story as I didn't like something that happens. I won't spoil it completely, but you'll know what I mean. Why was that necessary? Stick with the ideas you had. Not to mention, I didn't entirely get the ending, it is a bit underwhelming, and very unexpected.
All in all though, this game is definitely worth a buy, even more if you can pick it up on sale.
Here's to hoping for L.A. Noire 2 folks :)

I was annoyed to find that I was unable to get a refund because I had logged 8 hours of game time. 5 1/1 of that was spent waiting for turns to complete and googling " (insert game mechanic here) , Endless Space 2". The other half was in a single player game that essentially played out exactly the same as the multiplayer game. So, because I gave this game a decent shot, learned how to play it, tried it as multiplayer and single player I am rewarded with a big "NO YOU WILL NOT GET YOUR MONEY BACK" message from Steam. Thank you for reminding me why I prefer other platforms.
So here's your negative review and why I want my money back.
I bought this game along with two friends who I have played many games with. We were looking for a multiplayer space game and thought we found it. We each snatched up for about thirty bucks and set to play on a huge map with the maximum number of races. I chose the Horatio (because their back story is awesome of course), one buddy was the toke white-guys and another the tree people. Long story short -- White Guys OP -- not that any of us actually interacted in any meaningful way while playing. He just got to "get" more stuff in the game and we had to hear about it.
After quitting the tutorial after 10 minutes (which is fine because apparently it is less than helpful anyway), we created a multiplayer game, excited to conquer the galaxy. The beautiful graphics were engaging at first, but after 50 turns they already begin to lose their appeal. Things like cut-scenes of battles are useless and boring. I don't need to see a useless closeup of the planets for each new system I "explore" (aka, moved my ship into). It is as if the developers created a bunch of pretty things, then tried to justify their existence within the game. Form certainly doesn't follow function. A lot of wasted clicks were used to skip the pretty thing I'm sure took a long time to make.
After 50 turns, which took us about 3 hours (yes, we were still learning the game, but even basic stuff is so hidden and hard to fine or not at all explained that much of that was spent looking things up) we had colonized a few planets. Found a few minor races and a bunch of the other empires. We had discovered the Academy and one of us (the white guys of course) was racing to colonize it. But, that's it. We hadn't interacted in any way out side of asking each other how to do something. I had negotiated with minor races, which seem all to willing to give up their sovereignty, freedom, and planets for some purple stars. I interacted with the other major empires, who have a "warm opinion" of me, while we are locked in a "cold war" who will constantly decline the ONLY diplomatic thing I can do (which is offer peace or declare war). Oh, and another piece of candy forced down your through every other turn. A computer empires with insult you, or make a insignificant and unexplained demand, to which you cannot reply. I'm looking at the ill-designed tech-tree BOOM something about a church and their people not hating me but not liking me either. My reply options: Give Map, Offer Peace, Declare War...
Throughout the game there were exciting quests that popped up, challenges to try and complete. Although playing with my friends was nice, we simply didn't interact at all. yes, the galaxy was big, but we made a point to find each other and we didn't start very far apart. There was just simply nothing to do together. We can attack a common enemy because of how you move units and the fact that battles are team a vs team b. We can't trade because we haven't researched the appropriate tech yet (after 50+ turns, come on I can't send you some trees? That's beyond me?) Why is this game multiplayer?
To say the least, the multiplayer aspect was a disappointment. We couldn't team up to take down an enemy. In fact, my "mighty empire" could barely handle the pirates that "randomly" appear in systems with minor races. I mean, despite all of my industrial might, these 2-population (that's not a lot) minor races pump out pirates with better tech and bigger ships. WTF am I doing ruling this empire? I should be submitting to them over the course of 10 turns with no interaction from me except clicking the "influence" button one or two times. What is going on here?
That's a constant thing in the game. There is little to no feedback throughout the many mechanics you will have to navigate through. A galaxy-wide quest is going on. Poof, team "unknown" won after 3 turns. Of course "unknown" won, their races is set up to generate Dust (basically $). My Horatios do one things well: colonize planets and make more Horatios. We do it almost as well as the other race that is Horatio, just a few systems away. It took me forever to find out how combat works. Even the sites that explain the game don't explain combat. I had to find a forum post by the Dev himself to find out how they changed it (due to the glorified rock-paper-scissors game enraging people and being utterly terrible).
I don't hate the combat system, it's just pointless like much of the other mechanics in the game. The only rule is Stronger Fleet = Win. The "Battle Tactic" you "pick" is pre-determined because there is simply one beneficial action to pick. You COULD pick something else, but that's like intentionally tying one hand behind your back. Again, the illusion of depth and choice is lost.
The next day, after our marathon multiplayer session that left us saying "ok, maybe it get's better," I tried a single player game. This is where I truly realized that this game has no depth and no soul. The first 50 turns played out EXACTLY the same as the multiplayer game. THE SAME QUESTS popped up. I mean, exactly the same. In the same order. The only change was the system that I had to move a unit to or the name of the player that I had to "investigate." And this wasn't just the first quest, it was ALL of the quests. Matter of fact, many of the quest challenges are in the tech tree and will always be there. Again, I was sent looking for The Academy. Again, I had to kill a group of pirates. Again my Horatios got mad that I had other races on my planets.
Every action played out the same. The ship designs were the same, because you are left with no choice. You design a ship to be effective or useless. Or, somewhere in-between. You can enact some laws that might take advantage of the planets you've colonized, but it's best just to NOT do this. Forget diplomacy. You're going to click the first minor race you see (which is pretty, but who's looking at this point anyway. IDK what your race is called you were in the last game foo!) You're going to explore the anomalies and find a whole bunch of stuff that you just can't do anything with. There are no resources to manage. You either have it or you don't. There is no managing, or seeking out more, or modifying your planets to make more. You're going to build all the improvements anyway. I thought research was where it got fun, plenty of options to choose from. No, not really. You HAVE to research in a particular way to be efficient and get some of the basic stuff you need. Must get shielding, must get autonomyous build, must get armor because the pirate fleet that popped up from that SAME QUEST all use projectiles. Plenty of buttons to click. No real choice.

Contrast is a puzzle platformer in a 1920’s themed setting, featuring a young girl named Didi and her friend Dawn.The game starts with Didi sneaking out of bed and into a nightclub where she finds that her family life is not quite as perfect as she hoped. You play as Didi’s mysterious friend Dawn, and must help with her journey to repair her broken family and get her parents back together.
From the title screen, the scene is set wonderfully with a jazz soundtrack and noir design looks great. I have always loved the style in games such as Bioshock and the individual locations ooze of it, from jazz clubs, to cinemas and hotels, they all look the part.

Your character, Dawn, can move between three-dimensional reality and into the shadows where the game becomes almost like a 2D platform game as she is limited by the shadows on the walls. Light sources create shadows and can found placed in areas to reach a platform that is too high to reach. So for example, if Dawn needed to get to an outside balcony in reality, she could enter the shadows, and now reach it by traversing shadows of a nearby café tables and chairs. that are on the wall.
It is a clever idea and on the whole it does work very well but I found that despite learning new abilities along the way such as being able to dash through shadows, the gameplay mechanics start to feel samey and predictable. It usually involves reaching an area which is inaccessible in reality, reach it in the shadows, and then activating a switch or cutscene to progress. One puzzle which stood out was the final level which involved some great use of lighting and platform/puzzle elements that offered a bit of thought. There were one or two occasions where I was not even sure I completed the puzzles as the developers intended, as it felt to me like I had taken a shortcut to completing what I imagined a more difficult puzzle.
The story is told well and without spoiling it, the game follows Didi’s mother and her troubles with her husband. The husband gets himself mixed up with the mob, and while his intentions are good, things do not go well for him and he lands himself in to more trouble the harder he tries to fix things. If you explore the world a little, you can find snippets of story which act as mini-puzzles while you listen and in ways interact with as you jump over the shadows of the characters or events.
The gameplay can be a little clunky at times. I was reviewing the PC version and played the game with both keyboard and controller. The controller felt very sensitive to small amounts of input and it occasionally made me fall off platforms or do something I did not want to do. The camera can occasionally give you trouble but it is free-aiming and can be fixed. The most annoying aspect is that I managed to get stuck in walls and scenery on a few occasions, with no option other than to restart from the last save position.
The length of the game should also be put into question. It took me just over three hours to complete the game which I found was very short. There are collectible items to find over the course of the game but you will find many of them on your first playthrough. There is little to keep you coming back after completing the game. I would have liked some more puzzles or side quests to add some lifespan and replayability.
Don’t get me wrong, I enjoyed the game a lot. The characters are likeable, especially Didi who reminds me of Clementine from The Walking Dead game. The story is interesting to watch unfold and interact with. But there was simply not enough puzzle content to get really stuck in to. It is worth pointing out that Contrast is free on PlayStation+ and in this case it is a must play. If you are a fan of the era or platform/puzzle games then you will enjoy the game, I would wait for a sale otherwise as it is a little too pricey.
Gameplay - 7/10
Clever use of reality 3D and shadowy 2D platform elements, but is let down by occasional clunky controls and finding yourself stuck in walls.
Graphics - 8/10
Lovely 1920's noir style locations and design set the scene perfectly.
Sound - 8/10
The main theme tune is perfect for the game but there is not much else to listen to that is memorable. Character dialogue is done well.
Final Score - 7/10

The atmosphere in the game is great. Music, cars, scenery, clothing, you really get a feel for the time period. The start of each new chapter gives the feel of a new episode of a crime drama on TV. This is a good fit, as the game is quite a bit like an interactive movie.
The game controls are a bit like Bully (also from Rockstar). Grand Theft Auto controls would have been better, but the game plays perfectly fine with a controller.
The graphics are quite good. The latest and greatest lighting and textures may not be present, but the game does a great job with facial expressions. This is a good thing, as most of the game revolves around your ability as a detective to identify when someone is not telling the truth.
Gameplay has youin the role of a detective. You look for evidence, question suspects and in your "off time" run down street criminals as sort of little mini missions.
The evidence searches are quite easy if you set the controller to vibrate when they are nearby. Without the aid of vibration, it would be very easy to miss a clue without clicking every shred of paper you walk close to.
Suspect interviews are a little tougher. You ask a question and get an answer. Then you have to  decide on facial expressions (shifting eyes, a smile, looking away...etc. if the suspect if not giving the full story, or if they are flatout lying. If you choose correctly, you are rewarded with more information and some points. Choose wrong, and you will fail to be promoted.
There are intuition points you earn that can help to find evidence and determine if someone is lying, but you can burn though these quickly and will need to solve more crimes to refill your suply.
There are fight scenes with guns and fists, and chase scenes in vehicles. If you fail these smaller missions several times in a row, the game shows you merry and allows skipping the mission without penalty.
As I said, the game is very much a story that you are taking part in. Gameplay is not very difficult, and while you can replay missions to do better, the story and cutscenes do not really make for interesting replay value.
I'm enjoying the story, and am intrigued enough to keep going. Overall the game is good. I think the only downside is a low replay value.
There is some type of online social component to the game, but I've not been able to connect to it, The game is a few years old, so maybe the servers have been shutdown?

Contrast is a game that seems like it should be amazing, based purely on the premise, mechanics, and art direction alone. And while I do still recommend it (to a point), the final package ended up being a tad underwhelming. But let's start at he beginning. There is a lot of good to the game, specifically the elements I just mentioned. The setting (early 20th century Paris) and art direction are very interesting, and there are lots of cool things to see throughout the journey. You play as Dawn, the acrobat "imaginary friend" of a young girl named Didi. The game revolves around Dawn's ability to transform from a 3D person into a 2D shadow. As a shadow, you can maneuver along any other shadow, as if it were a normal platform. Puzzles generally involve manipulating light sources to create navigable shadows, and then platforming your way through those shadows to reach new areas. The story, without revealing much, is just OK. It involves Didi's lounge-singer mother, her loser father, and a mysterious magician named Vincenzo. There's nothing wrong with the story, but it's also nothing mind-blowing, for the most part. And that sort of sums up the game as a whole - merely adequate. The main gameplay hook of transforming into a shadow, while cool, just isn't enough to sustain a whole game in its own. Don't get me wrong, there are plenty of neat segments and cool applications of the idea. But after a while, you'll start to get the feeling of "been there done that", only in a new location. Not to mention, most of the puzzles (such as they are) are very simple anyways, there's not all that much meat on the bone in terms of challenge or completely fresh ideas. I am not sure they even could have added anything more to improve the game. As I said, it's perfectly adequate as-is, and definitely doesn't overstay its welcome. I just have this nagging feeling that there were missed opportunities for additional puzzles or ways the shadow mechanic could have been used. Maybe that's unfair, but so be it. Despite all this, I actually did enjoy and have fun with the game overall. I just feel that maybe with a bit more development time, it could have been better. But what's here is definitely an interesting experience, and worth checking out if the atmosphere or shadow mechanic intrigues you, as it did for me. The entire experience lasts around 5 hours or so, so also keep that in mind when considering your purchase. I would say hold off for a sale, unless you really feel the need to check it out right away.
My only real complaints would be for technical issues. Specifically, the game lacks many of the customization settings one would expect in PC games, such as video options and the like. Personally, I had an issue with the lack of an option for x-axis inversion for the camera controls. And while there is still no solution patched directly in game (at least as of the time of this review), for the record, I wanted to note that the developers actually responded to my request within minutes and provided a configuration file fix that could be changed manually to implement that feature. While it wasn't the ideal solution, I really appreciated their responsiveness, as it allowed me to play the game the way I wanted. So kudos to the developers for that. Which reminds me - I definitely recommend a gamepad for this one.

I really do love this game, though I know for sure it has flaws.
I've almost exclusively played network games or single player, so this is a review of those aspects. This also is going to be a fairly mediocre review most likely.
I will be doing this review in a category by category style.
Categories:
Aesthetics & Graphics
Pro
-It is aesthetically beautiful, even on low-moderate settings. On higher settings it's a work of art.
Con
-To run it above moderate settings you have to have a pretty beastly computer. I think that RAM plays in almost as much as video card though, given that lots of people with better video cards than me are having more trouble.
GAMEPLAY (this has a lot of subaspects so bear with me here)
Customizability
Pros
-You can customize your experience in singleplayer/local games quite readily both through the sliders on the game hosting menu and editing the Game.ini (basically a blank .ini that allows you to put in overrides for spawn codes, engram points per level, and many similar things)
Cons
-You have to tweak it a LOT and it's often difficult to tell how much to tweak it and what to tweak.
Character Model
Pros
-controls well
-your character's physicaly size has a degree of effect in the game. Taller characters seem to have better sightlines while shorter characters seem to be able to fit more places without ducking
-You have a lot of control over your character creation
-you can save your character presets to use again later
Cons
-It is hard to make the male character not look like a brick with a brick for a head
-too tall and you can have to duck under sloped roofs
-it is easy to mess up with your character design
Leveling
Pros
-Your bonuses definitely have an impact on how your character plays
Cons
-The bonuses are often too small per level to make much of a difference (you can now rectify this with the sliders when you launch a singleplayer/local game)
-You do not get enough engram points (used to learn how to make items) to make all of the items you will need/want in the course of the game (this can be rectified in your Game.ini)
Taming
Pros
-seriously, all kinds of extinct and mythical creatures to tame
-most tames have ample usefulness
Cons
-Often extremely difficult to do in single player (this can be partially rectified in the game settings for single/local play)
-Rectifying the difficulty in higher difficulty tames makes other tames too easy
Gathering/crafting
Pros
-Plenty to gather
-getting to things to gather is an adventure in itself
-Gathering and crafting give XP
Cons
-Some things way too much to be easy to get in quantity in singleplayer
-Some items take a LOT of resources to build when you consider it's one person gathering all that *cough metal structures cough*. Good news is that most of those are unnecessary in singleplayer since no one is trying to blow you up.
-Many crafted items are obnoxiously heavy to transport with you
Exploring
Pros
-Lots of cool places to explore
-A definite sense of thrilling danger much of the time while exploring, at least early on
-There is always a new community made map to explore
-Big XP rewards and sometimes gear rewards for it
Cons

The game's title perfectly encapsulates my play experience, which alternated between delight and frustration. The story follows a young girl named Didi, and so do we. We step into the shoes of a mysterious young woman called Dawn, who assists Didi on her quest to mend her broken home. The story is generally well executed and the art style and music help sell it beautifully. Steeped in early 20th century vaudeville aesthetics, the game's mood is warm and magical, but the over-the-top theatricality often seeps into the dialogue, at times causing it to come of as trite rather than impactful.
The main conceit of the game is that Dawn exists in a sort of parallel world, and her only connection to the real world are Didi, who seems to exists in both worlds, and the shadows. Dawn has the ability to literally become a shadow on the wall, and most of the gameplay revolves around using this mechanic to solve puzzles and execute jumping challenges. Shadows are also the only way in which Dawn can see people besides Didi, and the game's most inspired moments combine moments of shadow-puppet storytelling with actual gameplay. Unfortunately, these moments are far and few between, and most of the challenges are fairly mediocre, with the shadow-shift mechanic adding little but a bit of flavor. My biggest disappointment is how often the game interrupts the flow of gameplay with little cutscenes, sometimes wresting away control of your character simply to execute a camera pan and deliver a line from Didi.
The game shows great potential, but falls short in execution. Aside from the issues already discussed, there are the occasional technical issues, such as graphical glitches, erratic collision detection and at times wonky controls. A more rigorous synthesis of gameplay and storytelling could have elevated this game out of its mediocrity. However, its charming style and rare moments of inspiration make it worth a look should you find it for cheap (e.g. during on of Steam's many sales).

I bounced off the original Endless Space but loved Endlesss Legend. Endless Space 2 is already shaping up to be one of the best 4X games I've played and Amplitude tend to really invest in and continue to add to their games over time so it's only going to gain more depth. Already they've added additional quests and some features that didn't make it in prior to release. You know they're doing something right with Civ devs start stealing design and mechanics stuff from them (tech web in Beyond Earth and city districts in Civ VI for example).
The Good
- Their art team has always been outstanding and this is no exception - it really adds a lot to the flavour and immersiveness.
- UI is another of their strong points
- Factions are all unique with their own mechanics and quest story lines
-  Early game exploration is interesting (probes for loot, early quests, etc.)
- Wide variety of planet types, anomalies and galactic features
- Empire management offers a lot of depth
- A variety of playstyles and strategies based on your use of heroes, your faction choice, goals for win condition, plan for teching, etc.
- Ship design is fun and easy to understand with drag and drop modules for weapons, armour and support
The Bad/So-So
- AI diplomacy is often tough to emulate in these games and feels a little wonky sometimes
- Combat is not bad per se, just mainly hands-off other than picking a pre-battle plan and designing your ships weaponry
- Ground combat needs a little something more to it, not sure what though - it's much more bare bones visually and tactically than space combat
- The end game is not as interesting as the rest. Most of the quests have finished up, usually a victor is already well-ahead and it's just a matter of end turn/mopping up. Definitely an area that got added to in Endless Legend with more content to flesh it out, so likely same will happen here.
- Still has the occasional crash or lock up in the game processing something but much rarer than it used to be and with auto-save on every turn, it's just a matter of initializing the game again.
- The government/senate aspect I have mixed feelings about. I like the new concept of passing laws. Representatives of parties throughout your systems I find a little confusing still and harder to factor in when it comes to wanting to have a certain party in power. Your research and construction choices also strongly influence which party will be in power.
Overall, it's the game atmosphere, quests, art, fun learning curve of many moving parts in your empire, and variety embedded in the different factions that I like - plus knowing Amplitude is only going to add more to it with time, based on their track record.

On paper Contrast seems like a really cool game: a puzzle platformer where you can switch between being a physical person and being a shadow on the wall, using the shadows of other objects to get where you need to go. Couple that with a jazzy nightlife setting, and you can't go wrong, right?
Unfortunately that is not the case. The platforming was often really frustrating and the game was fairly buggy. I found a few places where I could melt with a wall or I would have to jump three or four times to make it onto a ledge that was well within reach.
The story was alright. You play as Dawn, the imaginary friend of a little girl named Didi. Didi's parents are separated and she sneaks out in the night on a regular basis to watch her mother sing at a club. Dawn helps Didi to progress past obstacles and fix things, and hopefully eventually to reunite her family. Dawn and Didi are the only ones who appear as three dimensional people in the world; everyone else appear as shadows on the walls, and are often parts of the platforming that the player has to perform.
In a lot of ways I am glad that the game only took three hours. I wish I could recommend Contrast because it has the makings of a cool, unique indie game. But it just wasn't made well at all. Don't buy it.

So I've played quite a few hours of Endless Space 2 and I'm completely on the fence and whether to give it a thumbs up or thumbs down.  Quite literally at 50%.  I had a lot of fun playing it and I think it deserves a little more attention so I'll give it the thumbs up.  There are a few things that need polishing like the AI, tech tree, interface and some bugs.  It feels like a game on open access ... jussst before it is ready for release.
I'll start with the good.  It a beautiful looking game and runs smooth on my GTX 1080.  No crashes, lag or hiccups in the graphics department except maybe at the end of a space battle.
I love the exploration part of the game.  Sending out probes to planets or even the far reaches of the galaxy it cool and a fun new mechanic to space 4x games.
The different species in the game are well designed and fun to play.  Each has it's own new mechanic that makes it different to play than any of the others.  They all seem have a lot more personality than other simlar games.
Onto the bad.  The first glaring issue in my opinion is that the game moves way too fast.  Even at standard settings it can be very easy to completing researching techs in one turn very early in the game.  After building just a production building or 2 your systems can be churning out buildings every other turn.  The problem with that is that they all have a substantial upkeep and you can start running low on dust (gold quickly).  So sometimes you have systems with the ability to build but can't afford to build.
Part of the game moving too fast is that you get slammed with quests quickly and they can pile up where you have a handful at a time, plus the tech tree bonuses you might want to achieve, plus the minor race aquisistion quests... this can lead to easily a half dozen quests or more you can have on your radar.  Some may be counter intuitive from one another and therefor may be impossible to complete.  I guess that's hard for a OCD completionist like me.
The tech tree bonus achievements seem pretty hard to get:  I've had another civ achieve 100 gold per turn in one system on turn 16. what? I've had another civ have 8 colonized systems by turn 40ish. huh?  I don't understand how this is possible unless the AI is very lucky with random quests or bonuses.  Not really a fun "race" if a random boost catapults someone to victory.
Another of the biggest issues with this game is that there is just too... much.  Too many quests.  Too much going one.
Too many bonuses and penalties.  And yes too many bonuses from completing these quests can be a problem when you have so many bonuses piled up and ending in different turns you begin to lose an idea of what your base empire is capable of without all of those bonuses.  I went from +335 dust a turn to -3 after losing one bonus.  The same can happen to your science, influence, happiness where you think it is going great until a bonus or 2 suddenly end and you are in a major deficit.
Also, though I love the techs and the idea of an open tech tree.  It is overwhelming, especially on the first few playthroughs.  Techs radiate out from the center of core techs so can literally go in any direction and rush to certain powerful techs.  I was on a turn count in the early 100s in one game, I was far in the lead in point score and though I had a pretty balanced and powerful navy.  At least it seemed so compared to my immediate neighbrs.  Well, I discovered warp lanes and found another new neighbor..  They were equipped with giant star-destroyer sized ships where one ship protecting each system had 20,000 hitpts where one of my command point maxxed groups were around 15,000.  Their attack and defense was far superior to any other races in the game as well.  I guess that race rushed research and military and built themselves quite the powerful armade.  Luckily, I gifted them maps, dust and resoruces to keep them happy with me.  If they were aggressive, however, I don't think I had a chance.
Other issues:  For some reason pirates spawn one ship nearly every turn in the systems of minor species.  Don't know if this is a bug or purposeful but it creates so many pirates you have to keep a navy on these system constantly unless you want pirates knocking at your door every couple turns. So you are basically sending navies to systems other than your own to stop the pirate spawning.  Only absorbing that system into your empire will stop the pirates completly.
Factions are very unbalanced in that the military factions will always gain more support than the others because you are constantly building militaries to protect yourself from potential rivals and pirates.  I don't think there is a way to play this game peacefully.  Even when I was rich with 4k dust, I didn't have enough resources to appease the the Reaver race from making threats and eventually coming for me.  If I defend myself and build the military for protection than the military factions end up controlling my government.
Overall, a fun game with a lot ot offer, but a lot needs ironed before it joins the ranks of space games like Masters of Orion 2 or Stellaris.

This game. This effin' game has inflicted unforeseenly severe addiction spikes on me. No other game has done it quite like this one. Spending hours and hours on building and managing your ever growing medieval kingdom in the medieval world. Ruling your kingdom with a sim-like feel on the game with character traits gives the game experience a nice touch of livelyhood and fun choice options. Will you be a kind ruler who tries to win his subjects' favor through justice and being rational or be a cruel and sadistic ruler who shamelessly stomps on everyone's requests and demands, and who particurarly likes to throw little children in prison and execute them, or even blind and castrate them? The large amount of possibilities and events are bound to keep you entertained for quite some time.
Medieval history haters and those passive towards it must step aside or risk invoking deep hatred towards this game for being too "complicated" and "boring". This game finds its juice in its historical aspects of how the world worked during the medieval period. Family and Dynasties being the key to all forms of ruling and inheriting. You play from 1066 to 1453, during which your dynasty must survive all different kinds of odds and historical events (Black Death can be a mean ♥♥♥♥♥). World domination is not the objective, surprisingly, although that is the most fun thing to try to accomplish. However, the bigger your kingdom gets, the harder it becomes to manage it. Internal affairs and greedy usurpers are often a bigger threat than foreign kingdoms. There will always be people wanting to undermine your rule and reign. When your ruler dies, you take up control of his chosen heir to continue the game. Without getting too deep into the game mechanics, I'll break it down more simply.
This game is Medieval 2 Total War's campaign map gameplay on steroids.
Those who liked the campaign map play of M2TW are bound to like this game. For those who didn't play M2TW, prepare for a difficult learning curve. It's definitely not a casual game. You must think of everything all the time, otherwise you might as well start lubing up that Ainis and wait for the Painis. It really helps if you have someone to explain the game to you. The tutorial sucks big time, though I learned to play the game in about five days without help (plenty of rageful quits included). If you're ready and willing to give the game a chance despite its cold grace, I can highly recommend it.
WARNING: I am not joking about the addictiveness of the game. There were times for me when I could hardly even sleep without wanting to play the game. I'm sure this is no issue to most people, but if you're a history buff and an empire builder like me, you're most likely in the danger zone.

It's hard to say that I don't like this game. I've had so much fun with it, even though I've owned it since earlier this morning. Multiplayer is the ONLY option in this game,
. On that note, the multiplayer netcode is amazing and the game has a very thriving community.
The gameplay is very solid and works very well, actually. Swordplay feels VERY powerful and slow- like how a real swordfight would be. Archery, on the other hand, isn't as great in my opinion. Player's movement is usually jagged and all over the place, so archery is hard to learn. Hitboxes have been reported as an issue, but when I was playing, the hitboxes seemed as they should have- normal. There are 4 classes to choose from- Archer, a Run and Kill class, Vanguard, and Knight. All these classes have their own set speed and set armor. Classes such as the run and kill offer little to no armor, but very fast paced moving speeds.  There is lots of customization to your character as well- you can choose your helmet, armor, emblem, weapon, and also color your armor, helmet, etc. You may also buy helmets with your native currency as well.
Multiplayer is the only real option in this game, so if you get a very high ping or don't have internet, this is NOT the game for you. On that note, I've never experienced lag at all. Yes the servers I connected to gave me around 5-18 ping, but still, the only lag I had was from unoptimized settings (which I toned down to a playable framerate) instead of connection.
There are LOTS of different ways to play. There is your average free-for-all, TDM (team death match), and then you also have your "Medieval modes" where you must stop the enemies from doing certain objective (burning down food markets, infecting water supply, etc). So if you like to play casual and do a TDM or FFA match, you can, but if you like to explore new modes and such, you also have that option.
Playing with friends is just as easy as inviting them to your own personal match. No use for Hamachi or any 3rd party applications. As for Online Mulitplayer, the community is (like I said before) very thriving and is populated fairly well. You can filter out matches that do not have players currently in them and you can also filter out games that are full. Either way, you will almost ALWAYS have a server with people in it. Oh, and did I also mention that there are dedicated servers for newcomers? VERY helpful for newbies. You rarely find higher ranked people in those servers- mainly levels 0-5.

Contrast is a highly ambitious game which just falls short of being amazing. The gameplay is unique and interesting given that the game allows you traverse between the real realm and the shadow realm which greatly changes how the player would interact within the world compared to a game which is just in the third dimension or just in the second dimension. While the puzzles are integrated nicely within the world you are placed in, the game is rather short taking me just under four hours to complete the entire game.
The aesthetics and charm of this game brings back the feeling of a platformer back from the Playstation One era, however the game often has issues explaining the story and world to the player which is mainly due to the game being so short. However if the player is keen on collectable hunting, collecting as many as possible can give some very interesting and subtle insight onto details the story does not wish to make obvious.
The voice acting feels stiff sometimes and often repeats itself, more often than not having the child explain to you where to go despite you already knowing where you have to go. However the voice actors in themselves are believable and well done, each reflecting the character nicely.
Despite being a short game, 15USD is not a steep asking price for what this game offers if you are looking into a unique platformer. That being said, I would recommend waiting until a sale since 15USD can buy games with a lot more gameplay.

So... Contrast.
The short version is this: great soundtrack, decent game, decent story, way too short and the ending is a bit rushed and predictable.
The longer version is this: I personally really enjoyed the game.  The style of the game was really well done.  Some of the mechanics were interesting, such as using the shadows of people in conversation to reach a new location.  That said, the ending really did feel a bit rushed, and, assuming you find a few of the (extremely easy to find) collectibles, extremely easy to predict.  Would I recommend it?  For $15, definitely; I think I paid $20 for the pre-order + soundtrack, which I'm still okay with, considering I'm a sucker for this style of music and atmosphere.
Anyway, if you've got $15 to spare, support some indie devs and give it a shot.

A competent 4X game with enjoyable single player campaigns.
Endless Space 2, a year and a half out from release, is a mature and mechanically solid game. The 4X components are strong and relatively standard, with a few new spins. Exploring is extended with the probe mechanic and interesting encounters. There are options in expansion, building tall or spreading wide. It is not overly easy or too painful to grow new colonies. This and other map-based gameplay like resources can be adjusted in map generation. Combat is robust, and works on a solid system in combination with the ship designer. The game's score is especially good in my opinion, with inspiring brass for a space opera setting.

The game was enjoyable, so enjoyable I got everything thus far. But it isn't perfect. The controls are noticably stiff at times, but one can argue that this is purposly design because your character is walking around in heels. Not much opened endedness, which seems like it should but you are stuck on a one way path. But, the good things about this game is the platforming sections and it's unique "shadow" mechanic. The platforming feels like it wasn't just a another "ok, let's just put this here, that there, and this over there" kinda platforming. I honestly felt like I was playing in a Banjo and Kazooie style platforming, something crafted over time and really thought about, not just something crafted in a few minutes. The story is kinda there, and not. Your character is utlimately ignored in the main story, only a few people will talk about your character. But they never provide much information about you, and your character never talks either...so that doesn't help with this mystery about your character. The game can be done in a matter of minutes, or a few hours, it all matters on your skill level and how fast you are capable of beating platformer games. But, I will tell you this, you won't regret this experiance if you liked banjo and kazooie.

Contrast is one hell of a buggy game but what I got out of it was something more. I was frustrated all the time when I played Contrast. I was always stuck in walls, lost in the geometry, and always felt out of control when I played.

When I saw Contrast at Steam Greenlight I knew that was a title I was going to play.
Those who know me will easily understand why: Contrast has female protagonists, something I'm always looking forward to,  beautiful character and environment design, with an aesthetic close to my heart, an interesting mechanic and was non-violent, which is something I'm beginning to appreciate, even though I love to hack and slash things.
So, as soon as it was available for pre-order, I decided to buy it, even if I was not at my best financially. It was worth it.
First, the whole game was translated to brazilian portuguese, with the exception of the audio (which would've been really costly). Although I have no problem understanding english, this was a nice touch, specially when most people at my country don't have easy access to english lessons. Second, the game is beautiful, entertaining and interesting. I almost gasped at the final revelation: something I thought to be just an aesthetic choice, in the end, had much more meaning within the story.
The puzzles were difficult enough to keep me interested, not hard to the point of making me want to give up nor easy to the point of leaving me bored. I once or twice thought of looking through a walkthrough, 'cause I'm lazy and always craving for more pieces of information surrounding a game's story, but I'd always close the window and decide to solve the puzzle myself. I loved when you activated some sort of "memory" and interacted with the shadows.
There were glitches and bugs, like getting stuck between shadow-world and "real-world", but nothing really troubling.
The controls were a bit weird at the beginning, I felt like Dawn walked too fast or something, but I got used to it quickly.  I could complain that the game is short. It is, really, but I honestly think it's worth it. It's an engaging experience and I think it lasts enough.  My only true complaint is that sometimes the cut-scenes would break the pace of the game. You'd walk a bit or solve one short puzzle and have a cut-scene right after it in a way that felt a tiny bit out of place. In the beginning of the game I felt there were too many short cut-scenes happening all the time.
Still, it's not something that takes anything out of this wonderful game. This is a game you can show your non-gamer friends and family members too and I think would grab their attention. If you are open to it, you could ask them to help solving some puzzles, to make them engage more with the game.
Visuals are lovely, gameplay is nice and the story is interesting.
I'd recommend it for sure.

Contrast is a stylish platformer that doesn't entirely manage to convince.
Let's start with the graphics. They\re quite stylish, '30-'40's style, but they're also a bit dark sometimes. As a result fine details aren't sometimes clear enough. Nothing gamebreaking but a bit disappointing. And while the game makes you think the world is open there's usually only one correct path to follow. You can run around a bit and try to collect orbs or collectibles, but it's nothing fancy. Where Contrast shines, however, is the fact that it allows the main character to use shadows in order to solve puzzles. It's unique and usually works quite well, but there were a few times where the game got glitchy, getting the character stuck in the environment or switching to your 3D form while still using these shadows.
There's also a story which is actually fine, just not very well realized. There's a connection with the little, physical girl but whenever there's a shadow conversation it's hard to connect with these characters, because they're just that; shadows.
The music is actually well done, with some nice jazzy tunes in it. The voice acting is also done extremely well for a game of this caliber.
The game ended after about 3 hours, which gave me mixed feelings. I kinda wished it was longer, but, you know, bigger and better. But because it's not I was actually glad it was over. It felt a little bit too gimmicky. Which is a shame, because you can clearly see the game was created with passion.

Visit the 1940s Los Angeles and help the young LAPD detective Cole Phelps solve crimes ranging from arson to serial murder. L.A. Noire is a third person open world adventure with great graphics, amazing soundtrack and fantastic voice acting.
PROS:
- very good storyline
- amazing graphics
- huge world to explore with infinite details
- 90 car types you can drive and driving around is a lot of fun, there are some really cool car chases
- character depth and development
- great old-timey jazz soundtrack
- voice acting and facial expression detail
- overall noir atmosphere
- if you like drainpipe climbing, this game is a perfect choice
MEH:
- it's quite easy when you come to think of it: most clues are right there and you can miss some of them, you can make some wrong accusations during interrogation and still successfully solve the case
- some action sequences are rigged: you are not allowed to catch the criminal too quickly, so that you have to run/drive all the fun locations developers have prepared for you (and the locations are great, so I forgave that easily)
CONS:
- the game saves only at certain points, so there are moments where you may lose 10 minutes of gameplay if you suddenly quit
- some cutscenes are quite long
To sum up: one of the greatest games I've ever played. Masterpiece!

GRAPHICS 10/10
AUDIO 10/10
STORY 10/10

Wonderful grand strategy game. Not as complex as Europa Universalis but still has great depth. Unlike other Paradox GS games you don't control a notion but rather a medieval noble dynasty (you only ever directly control you dynasties patron/matron, other family members have to be influenced via diplomacy) with the goal of amassing as much glory/piety as possible (alternatively you can just try an take over the world). Great care has been taken in regards to historical accuracy, the feudal lord/vassal structure has been mapped precisely and is one of the main game mechanics, nations and faction are (at the beginning) historically accurate and you even encounter several historical figures (with ingame Wikipedia-links)
All-in-all one of my favorite strategy games in the last years. Must buy for any fan of grand strategy!

This game is basically EvE online but with dinosaurs. Ark will give you some  of the most serious highs of any videogame you wil ever play.  The first time you club out a raptor, tame it and then ride it around exploring is a feeling of wonder and exploration that no modern game has given.  The last time I felt the smae sense was when I hit lvl 40 in vanilla World of Warcraft (over a decade ago) and was able to buy my first mount.  The massive world became jsut a bit smaller and you felt like taking in every sight you can.  Ark rekindeled that feeling of accomplishment.
That isnt ot say the game is all happy fun time.  I would suggest starting out in PvE in order to learn the game.  PvP can, and will, devastate you.  When you log in to find your entire base is a smoldering crater and your hard  earned dinos are rotting around you, you will never feel so hopeless.  But, you will also never feel so motivated to enact revenge.  You needto be ready, mentally, emotionally and economically to handle that situation.
Take some time, play Offical PvE or even join the vast numbers of UnOffical servers. When you feel ready for the real game though, its all about offical PvP.
The risk of official is what makes the rewards so much better. Its like gambling, winning all the time is not what makes it fun. The fun is its having everything on the line as the card is being dealt--all the meticulous planning you have done, the building, the farming, the alliances you forged -- all of it coalescing in the one moment someone calls out into the alliance chat that foreign server invaders have just spawned in a wyvern. You make a mad break for your dinos, dropping everything you have. You go into the one vault you have set aside just for this moment, suit up and grab that mastercraft fab rifle you managed to snag from the sea cave after losing your favored Basilo (that took hours to tame). You hop on a prize bred Pteradon you bought from the south shore alliance for 5000 ingots (spent the weekend farming that) and rocket away to red ob to join up with the other alliances. Its in the moment that the the real game begins.

Pros:

I have owned ark since the day it was released, and I have been playing it off and on ever since I bought it. At times, the game consumes my every waking moment, and I literally dream about a weird diamond thing in my forearm and dinosaurs eating my face off. Other times, I can't bear to look at the stupid game, and would willingly jump into oncoming traffic rather than play another minute of it's ridiculousness.
I have been through the rise and fall of Survival of the Fittest (SOTF), I bought Scorched Earth the day it was released, and I now own the season pass, and am anxiously awaiting the release of Abberation, which I'm sure will spark another of my "Ark-consumes-my-life-phases." at least until the Nameless jump me one too many times, or that giant Naked Mole Rat looking thing decides that my time on this Ark has come to an end, and eats my face repeatedly. Then I will probably go back to hating Ark's guts.
As I'm sure you can tell, Ark and I have a bit of a love hate relationship. I was a huge fan of SOTF, and I played the crap out of that game mode. My rig was never good enough to let me compete with the pro players, but me and my friend still had a blast playing the normal games, and we even got into one or two of the qualifiers for the old competitions. We loved that version of the game, and spent hours perfecting our strategies and trying to get better. But then it died.
The base game is fun and enjoyable, but it is so time consuming that the normal, average college student just cant devote the amount of time necessary to truly exxperience the full game on an official server. Unofficial is ok, but I would love to be able to get to full tek tier on an official server.
That is what I loved about SOTF. Maximum, my friend and I would be able to put an hour into tames, building, and crafting, and then we had to sprint for the center, trying to keep ourselves, and our ridiculously idiotic, horrible-at-pathing Rexes and Spinos, ahead of the ring of death. Then, there were a few intense minutes of adrenaline and hunting down the other players, and then its over. No slaving for days to get stone teir, and then having it wiped out by someone on a tek armored rex. Just an hour and a half of hunting, crafting, taming, and finally dying and restarting.

I first played this game with its newest patch of 1.06x. This happened due to not having access to a computer that was resourceful enough to run the game. After it has been released, both performance and content have been vastly improved.
This game is very giid, it looks promising with further content added, but some things really buged me while testing it.
1.: Random pirate attacks ruin you in early game - and you have no idea how to defend with just a single patrol ship at your dispose. Really makes you want to quit. (And nooo, this is balanced comments, please, it was not!) Hence, even as a peaceful nation, you MUST muster some ships with some reasonable equipment. Do not build laser frigates with ballistic shields against missile and kinetic armament ships with strong deflectors.... really, do not do it.
2.: Techtree looks great, but I, as a new player, have no idea what technology allows me to do what. The recommendation tags are really not helpful - I miss the old Endless Space research screen. (Working search function now - still overwhelming but you can search even for components and get highlighted results.)
3.: Sudden bankruptcy - really sudden. No idea what or why, and when I managed to buy a dust generation improvement, the game still scrapped an improvement despite generating enough cash. (More cash-generating buildings, better knowledge of the techs and upkeep costs makes it far easier to have a well balanced economy. Search for endlessly repetable constructions in the techtree... )
4. Vast galaxy, 10 players, and yet in turn 5 I got visitors that started colonising right infront of my core world. Plus, you are stuck if they block you. Normal AI, so again really makes you want to quit. Hard AI+, that is ok, but not on the standard AI and difficulty setting. - This has also been dealt with, with proper map positioning for example.
I give the game a thumbs up, not just because I see great promise, even with new content, but I really tested it and can say: good game, great time.
After a long time, with access only to decade old hardware, I started the game anew, and I was truly astonished how much since the old beta I had played had been done. More content, FREE, heroes, talents, fighters, systems, improvements, technologies, tech-tree search function, and many more bigger and smaller issues were all fixed.
My recommendation: play one or two games on easy with your desired faction before you start playing them against more capable AI or human enemies, so you get to know how to deal with threats both economically and hostile, be it rebels, enemies or pirates.
