I honestly cannot recommend this game for a few reasons (Buckle your seatbeats cause it's a long one)... So I'll do a quick list of pros and cons...
Pros:
- The graphics are pretty nice
- You can make some really good friends (Who do sometimes also play other games with you outside of ARK)
- If you take out the fact that some people are♥♥♥♥♥♥♥(Referring to Raiders) then this isn't that bad of a survival game.
Cons:
- Alpha Tribes
- Grindy AF
- Taming takes ♥♥♥♥ing forever
- Breeding also ♥♥♥♥ing takes forever
- Pretty much everything takes ♥♥♥♥ing forever
- Raiders/griefers
- You can lose 600+ hours of grinding in a few hours (even while offline)
This game has so much potential to be great, but the developers choose to be ignorant to certain key issues mainly in regards to the griefing (which from what I've read is for a scummy practice that earns them more money) that honestly ruins the experience for so many people.
---Griefing (Raiders/Alpha Tribes/♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s)---
So to start, I played this game for 622 hours (which was all consolidated to one server) and I lost it all overnight when the Alpha tribe (I'll describe that at the bottom), it honestly killed the game for me because I sunk multiple months into the game to have it destroyed in under a day. Furthermore, the raiding and griefing aspect of the game sounds really fun in theory but sucks♥♥♥♥♥in practice. When you log off your body doesn't disappear, you actually just fall asleep which I mean as long as you have a base you'll be fine right? WRONG, I'd say the part of somebody killing you and taking your stuff actually isn't the worst part... the worst part is that they can take everything in your inventory, handcuff you, throw a bunch of crap inventory so you can't move due to encumberance (and no you can't drop anything when you're handcuffed) and then throw you into a jail cell, where you have no chance of escaping and probably will take more than a few days to starve and die to escape through respawn (Assuming they don't feed you in your sleep, which yes they can do that to stop you from starving).
---Grinding (Part 1: Leveling)---
This game is far too grindy, and I mean it has it's ups and downs and can be appealing to some people, but with what I mentioned above, it really just doesn't make any sense. The Levels, essentially lock all the crafting behind the levels, which honestly isn't bad I actually quite enjoy that, however, unless you either 1) Really know what your doing from hundreds of hours of experience, or 2) joined a large tribe that allow you to use their tames for lvling, then leveling up is gonna take forever, and you'll be sinking in weeks, possibly even months before getting the higher tier tames to be able to at the very least hold your ground against similarly sized tribes.
---Grinding (Part 2: Taming)---
Taming honestly in my opinion needs to be taken down a notch time wise (Resources are fine), some of the most basic tames such as the triceratops can take upwards of 1 hour to tame early game when you don't have the kibble for it, like when you tame with berries or meat. Now you may think oh well just make the kibble for it, how hard could it be? For some not too difficult, for others it can be extremely time consuming, why because you get the eggs of another dinosaur to make that kibble (1 egg = 1 kibble), where sometimes you can require upwards of 50 or more pieces of kibble just for one tame, and believe me most dinos don't♥♥♥♥♥♥eggs out very often, not to mention you have to be in the area of your base for them to do it,I think it takes about 15-20 minutes per egg, and if you go too far even for just a second, that timer gets reset. Anyways, now lets say you ground to get a higher tier Dino, for certain dinos, it can still take you upwards of 1-3+ hours of taming for things like T-Rexes and Brontosaurs, even more for a quetz (Essentially a huge pteranadon) a lot of which have to be babysat. Now, something that I did was I sat nearby, and I watched YouTube videos while I tamed checking up on progress from time to time, but lets say you do that however, you lose track of time in the last 10% of the taming process and the dino wakes up.... welp say goodbye to all your progress, because everything you stored inside the dino while taming is gone, even if you knock it asleep again all your items cease to exist, also any of your taming progress is also gone, so not only do you have to grind your narcotics (what you use to keep the dino asleep) and your kibble, but you also have to start from scratch, no matter how quickly you KO it after waking up.
---Grinding (Part 3: Breeding)---
Very similarly to Taming, I also think breeding needs to be taken down time wise (resources are fine). So first of all, You have to get 2 dinos together for smexy time, which is when they'll poop out a fertilized egg, afterwhich, you need to incubate the egg, now if your really late game this isn't too big of an issue when you have air conditioning units which will keep the egg at the right temperature, however, if you do this mid game you have to use fires and continously monitor the egg's temp and move it around so it won't die before hatching this alone can take upwards of 3 hours... So you hatched it... congratz! but your not done yet, ohhhhhoho no, you then have to feed the baby pretty much every 5 seconds early on and a few minutes a bit later as it grows, and you have to do this until it reaches adolesence which is when it can start automatically using a feeder for the rest of the way, but that takes anywhere between 1.5 to 3 times the duration of the incubation period, so break out your gamer grub and make dinner early because you're going to be doing nothing for your whole afternoon. Now that's done, your almost out of the woods, the last foot of the process while somewhat automated isn't done yet, depending on which dino, you can be waiting a few hours to up to a week real time for it to finish growing up, and during that time you have to make sure the feeder is stocked, and that your food won't spoil. Mess up here and once again you have to start from scratch.
---Summary---
As I mentioned earlier this game has soooo much potential, heck it's still one of my top 3 longest played games, but between the massive grind and the griefing that the devs seem to be encouraging at this point, the game just isn't feasable if you want to have a life outside of gaming or even to keep your sanity. This is one of those games that isn't for players who like to take it slow and to have an experience of playing the game, rather than a sprint to the finish line. I would practically have to say if you really want to enjoy the game either play on a private server with just your friends but you'd have to pay to have that, play on ones with strict rules for griefing, or play on PvE (But I feel like that ruins the point of the game) or play on singleplayer (which frankly with all I mentioned above, is going to be incredibly boring, not to mention is going to eat up every shread of free time you have, and you defeat the purpose of the game, which is to play with others). As for some of the grindy elements there are modifiers for that on private servers but they are super limited and don't just reduce to time that things take, they also reduce how much kibble it takes (can't do one without the other, cause the time is tied into the quantity of food required for taming), which honestly then makes elements of the game that I think are balanced just far too easy, and it just isn't a challenge anymore which ruins the fun of the game for me. Overall, I would give this game a 3/10, great concept, fun to play with others, but is just♥♥♥♥♥♥and underdevelopped in every other way.

It's been almost a year since I wrote something up here. But well, everybody is at some point back, where he started, so I figure it out, why just don't write up the review for a game, which is in my personal TOP 10. Right?
When I look back, and check all the products, that Rockstar Games has put out, I'm not even sure if I'm able to name at least one, which was average or even under that. They even made a fantastic movies, didn't they?
When they try to make open world game, it's understandable that comparision with Grand Theft Auto is not anything bad.  Red Dead Redemption v. GTA. / Bully v. GTA. / The Warriors v. GTA (My lord, The Warriors are even better than GTA in some way) / and also Midnight Club for some reason. And there comes the L.A. Noire. New genre that R* step a foot in, and got out as a king again and again and again.
L.A. Noire is as you of course know the detective game set in 40s Los Angeles. You can compare this to Sherlock Holmes games, and Cole Phelps will be still better detective. Story is so gripping that one case might drives you crazy, and then you realize that Rockstar is just master of art in the gaming world.
There is one thing, that I also realized during the exploration of LA which is really huge and more realistic than GTA V would ever be. However, the developer itself pretty doesn't give a flying f*ck if people discover beautifulness inside. I am talking about hidden spots and interesting places all over the Los Angeles. It's pretty usual that some devs puts spots out to player to see them. R* is not doing that way. They put tons of spots, and hide them even more than usually.
This game is filled with landmarks, and especially golden film reels which are pretty difficult to spot. Thing is, that even after discovering 30 of various world-famous places and 50 hidden golden films, you can go further, explore on your own, and discover spots that wasn't made for casual player, but for true explorer. I've been to LA this year, and I must say, that a lot of places that are shown in this game, looks practically same (not just landmarks, also the standard streets at some point) no matter the time game is set was more than 70 years ago.
I've talked a lot about the town, but I have to be honest with you, but town is most enjoyable thing for me personally in the game. More than the characters, more than Cole and more than the story and cases.
More than 20 cases ready for you (which lenght of the one might be easily above 40 mins) 40 side street crimes, and enormous spots to discover for you. Great thing was, that besides the main story line, there was a lot of different stories going all way along and meet each other in the end.
I've got to tell you much more, but I will leave it. I don't want this review to be another Saints Row 3 review of mine :X

I'm giving this a thumbs-up because I like Amplitude and feel that I have gotten my money's worth from this game, but wow - Endless Space 2 is a real disappointment. It's a beautiful game that suffers from very poorly thought-out mechanics and a lack of real substance. Amplitude need to shake things up and just start over with their next title - if ES2 is the epitome of where they are headed from a mechanics standpoint, they are in trouble.
Pros
- Fantastic production values - great graphics, music, etc.
- Interesting factions, as usual with Amplitude games
Cons
- The writing is mind-bogglingly puerile. Seriously, who wrote the text for this game? A twelve year old? The comically juvenile writing completely clashes with the otherwise serious tone. It reminds me of the best man speech at a recent wedding - funny, but in an embarrassing, groan-inducing way.
- The tech tree is, quite frankly, incredibly boring. In good 4x games, the tech tree forces the player to make interesting, difficult decisions and trade offs. Here, it just felt incredibly bland, and a great deal of it is simply unlocking the ability to actully utilize planets in systems you've already colonized.  Boring.
- The tactical combat elements are really bad.  Like the first Endless Space, the player has no real control - battles are basically cinematics with no player interaction. Yet somehow, the devs have managed to make space (and ground) combat even less interesting than in Endless Space 1.  Very disappointing.
- The new political aspects of the game (elections, factions, etc.) are a complete train wreck. They add very little and are simply annoying.
- The interface is very slick-looking, but at the same time rather obtuse.  At several points I stared at it and just scratched my head wondering how the devs intended the information presented to be useful.

There's no doubt that this game truly excels at recreating 40's Los Angeles post WWII. The city feels alive, there's plenty of classic cars, and a great sense of fashion. But i think that the map is unnecessarily big. This game is also unique in the sense that is really acted, with the best facial movements in a videogame to this date (and with a great cast too). Gameplay-wise, it's average, collecting clues, driving and chasing suspects. But it truly puts you in the role of a detective, working together with your partner and getting info from the rest of the LAPD staff, like the coroner or the R&I lady. But the biggest innovation was interrogating suspects and witness. It sounds cool, but it's a bit disappointing, and i'll explain. For each question you must first tell if the person is telling the truth or lying. However, most of the time it's pretty obvious (but there's some exceptions). The challenging part is knowing if you have or not the evidence to prove a lie. However, there's a flaw. When given the option to chose between Doubt (lying without evidence) or Lie (with evidence), many times the game isn't clear about what evidence is needed. Chosing Lie will give additional and crucial information that should be there before, and if you think you don't have the evidence, you can backtrack and choose Doubt without penalty. So, most of the interrogations goes like this: 1- Truth or not, which is almost always easy to tell; 2- If lying, choose Lie to get all the information; 3- If you don't have evidence, go back and choose Doubt. And it's a bit sad because the interrogations were supposed to be mostly about reading faces with real acting and motion capturing with incredible detail, but instead it's mostly about if you have the evidence to prove a lie, which is nothing new in the genre. But still, i think that it's a great game with a great story and very interesting cases. But the extra stuff is kinda boring and dull, except for the street crimes. Also, replaying cases to get a better ranking can get repetitive.

Similar to all of Paradox's other grand strategy titles, Crusader Kings 2 places you in the boots of one of the rulers of a medieval Duchy, kingdom or empire and playing from 1066 to 1453.  The large difference between this grand strategy and Paradox's others, is that you actually play as a character, instead of the embodiment of a nation.  Whenever you die, you play as whoever is in your line of succession.  If someone who is not part of your dynasty is your heir and you die, it's game over.  Along with this feature, you must also manage your family as well as your vassals, keeping them happy.  Nothing is more annoying than having to open up the vassal tab, sort them by the lowest opinion and then having to funnel money to 6 people to keep them happy, only to have them send you a message, labeling you a pretender of the throne a few minutes later.  Something in the game is still appealing however, and is making me reccomend it.

Endless Space 2. The Science Fiction turn based 4x strategy game. 'Civilisation' if you will but set in Space. For the newcomer; what is 4X? It stands for Explore, Expand, Exploit and Exterminate. Start from your Homesystem, send out explorers to explore new resource rich star systems and send out your population to colonise these new worlds and harvest the resources to develop these colonies into fully fledged active civilisations within your empire. Build up and watch your interstellar empire grow to become the superpower civilisation of the galaxy, Do this through various means; Religious, Economic, Military and Science or maybe a mixture of some or all but it won't come easy. Be prepared to compete with other alien civilisations with the same goal. Some will come in peace and will be prepared to share the galaxies vast territories but others will stop at nothing to achieve total domination. Make money, collect resources, influence the masses or create a warfaring campaign to eliminate your competition. Watching space battles between your ships, the pirates and rival civilisations is nothing short of breathtaking. The choice is yours. Choose your fate. The whole galaxy awaits you.
Endless Space 2 is both an easy game to get into for the newcomer (don't be daunted by the multitude of actions you can execute) and quite challenging for the experienced 4X Gamer depending on the game settings you set and the stragegies you decide to use. It stands out with the best of the Turn Based 4X science fiction strategy games. I highly reccommend Endless Space 2. Immerse yourself in hours, days, weeks or months of nailbiting fun. Enjoy!

Fantastic role-playing strategy game which is extremely satisfying and very fun to play. Steep learning curve but totally worth investing the time as when it clicks it is so enjoyable. I recommend watching YouTube videos by the likes of Quill18, Tekkor, Arumba and/or Northernlion to help you find your feet. I'm enjoying it so much because the game creates some great stories and provides a lot of fun role-playing opportunities. I can see myself continuing to put a lot of hours into this amazing game.
CKII is not a typical strategy game as it has heavy role-playing aspects and is about managing a dynasty and acting on behalf of characters rather than countries. The game creates some great scenarios and you can get really involved in the stories that it generates. It might be that you start as some petty little count trying to amass power through whatever cunning and devious means that you can, much like playing out an episode of Blackadder!  Or it could be that you are a powerful king ready to destroy those who might attempt to dethrone you. You easily become engrossed in the stories and the petty squabbles with your vassals or your overlords.
It seems worth mentioning the DLC here as it can seem somewhat overwhelming to a new player. I regularly get asked which DLCs I recommend and if any add vital things to the game experience. Ultimately, a great deal of the DLC is cosmetic (portraits, shields, units and extra music) so none of these are needed at all but you might feel it is nice to freshen up the game later on with some new music or portraits after you've been playing for 100s of hours. I must mention the music here, which is absolutely excellent (it is composed by Andreas Waldetoft who has also produced high quality music for EUIV and other Paradox titles). Anyway, regarding these minor DLCs, you can always wait for another sale on Steam for this kind of thing and pick them up at a super cheap price. CKII tends to go on sale a lot.
The DLC that is actually significant in terms of game play is as follows:
- The Old Gods (one of the best DLCs because it adds a new start date in 867 and the opportunity to play various pagan rulers, with an emphasis on the Vikings, which is an absolute blast)
- The Republic (ability to play Merchant Republics such as Venice, Genoa, Pisa etc. so only really needed if you want to do that in the game)
- Legacy of Rome (this is definitely worth picking up as it adds some useful stuff, not least the ability to use retinues to have standing armies. It's one of the cheaper of the main DLCs)
- Sword of Islam (makes Muslim rulers playable and adds a whole bunch of events and mechanics specific to them - so only needed if you want to get into playing a Muslim ruler)
- Sons of Abraham which adds more depth to the Abrahamic religions (Christianity, Islam and Judaism).
- Sunset Invasion (this is a fictional and non-historical add-on that I've never used - bit of a strange release from Paradox for this game - you don't need this at all unless it strikes you as being interesting)
- A smaller DLC worth mentioning is the Ruler Designer, which is quite fun too, allowing you to create your own ruler with traits etc. I mostly play as the historical characters but it can be nice to throw together a custom character for a bit of fun.
- Recently, they have added the Rajas of India (making Indian characters playable), Charlemagne (with a new start date of 769) and Way of Life (a role-play DLC).
Ultimately, you can pick and choose what you are interested in with the DLC. It might be that you have a certain interest in one of the DLCs but ultimately a huge amount of hours can be put into the base game with the vanilla 1066 start. You don't desperately need any of the DLC but I think the only thing that it would be nice (not essential) to have is The Legacy of Rome, in my opinion, for the reasons I outlined above.
My favourite DLCs are Legacy of Rome and The Old Gods. The latter is probably one of the best DLCs I have bought for a game. I've had such a blast with all of The Old Gods content. So much fun!

I'm not someone who plays any games for very long.  60 hours is a pretty long time for me, and I've put 80+ hours on only  a few games in my entire lifetime.  I just passed 90 hours this week on Endless Space 2.  I'm definitely not done playing it either.  There are still other races I want to play through, and I'm not quite finished with my Sophon science victory.
What I like best about the game is how different each race plays/feels.  I also really like how different each game feels depending on the galaxy map that is created, and what resources I have access to.  I think the combat is fine.  Generally after seeing a couple of battles with new ships or weapons, I auto-battle the rest.  Ground combat is always auto.  If those things are super important to you, then you'll be much better of with a total war title.  I personally don't like the total war games as much, because there is too much emphasis on battles with too little emphasis on strategy.
My biggest gripe is diplomacy.  I don't like diplomacy very much in any game, so it's not really any different here.  I don't think diplomacy works remotely intelligently in any game.  I find the diplomacy in this game to be boring, and a negative distraction from the very many things that I enjoy.
I can't say this is the best game I've ever played, but it is definitely one of the better space simulation games I've played lately. It's not so in depth that you can't enjoy it for 20 hours, but it's got enough meat on it's bones to enjoy dozens if not hundreds of hours of gameplay.
If you're a fan of strategy games, especially 4x space strategy, then I believe this game is an absolute must-have.  You won't regret it.  Enjoy!

I've played games from this company since the beginning.  Endless Space, Endless Legend, Dungeon of the Endless and all the various expansions and optional purchase content that they provided.  I've even purchased copies of the games for friends and family over the years.  But the simple fact is, that this game does not by any means live up to their previous standard of quality they have held themselves to.  It has been around 2 months since the game came out, and it came out in a poor and buggy state.  Since then there have been repeated attempts to quick fix the problems, some that have been successful such as reducing time between turns, but ultimately for every fix two bugs seem to take their place.  As of this moment I can finally play the game for more than a couple of hours without hitting a game crash bug, but otherwise almost every other aspect of the game has problems.
Diplomacy is completely broken, basically the ai accepts deals while the game says they ignored them; this means that you are in a peace or alliance you have no way out of but the enemy can repeatedly attack you.
The economy of the game is also unworkable as several of the factions are just leaps and bounds above others technologically and special ability wise; and although this is the case often the computer has no idea how to manage a faction and still manages to mess it up.
Technology is kinda irrelevant as well due to the fact that very few of the technolodgies are worth anything and nothing has pre-reqs.  Thus you hyper focus economy and population, just waiting to flood nothing but capital ships which can be done fairly early in the game.  Ironically this also destroys one of the features they worked so hard on (the cinematic battles) because the computer is at least smart enough to recognize a losing battle and simply auto retreats.  Meaning you rarely get to see the battles.
So if one is to simply judge it based on the 4X mentality, explore, expand, exploit, and exterminate, then technically you can do all the above; but it is kinda like killing a baby seal while drunk.  Honestly far too easy, as long as you can manage to avoid random blackouts or other self inflicted wounds.
In comparison to their latest game, Endless Legend.  Heroes are more unique in EL, Factions are more balanced in EL, quests and random events are somewhat more interesting in EL, and most importantly EL has very very very few bugs even since day one because at that time they apparently thought that putting out a completed game was important.  Strange I know, but awful nice.  About the only things going for it are the faction quests which are better, and the extra bits of lore they put in.  But... I can't really say that simply adding in extra flavor text can make up for what is a very poor example of what they are capable of.
TLDR:  I've got around 1500-2000hrs on Amplitude Studios games, but I will likely not be buying another game from this company as they have decided that allowing an unfinished game onto the market is good for their customers.  Since day one I've spent hours playing matches only to have one game breaking glitch or another stand in the way of a decent experience.  Until they finally get around to fixing all the bugs, or this game starts selling for about $10-$15, I'd advise avoiding it and any other new games this company may produce in the immediate future.

I must say that this is a beautiful game with some interesting mechanics that easily triggers the “just one more turn”-mentality. Performance wise the early game is fine but in the later stages it becomes sluggish and starts to crash.
Sometimes ships become invisible and it is impossible to issue commands. Avoid ANY special characters in any names, even you steam nick, as it may corrupt the save files. Fleet names cannot be longer than a handful of characters, hardly even a third of the auto generated ones. Luxuries become more or less pointless in the late game and it is tedious to sell of all (~14) of them every turn. Most negotiation options, apart from the very basic ones, are to be found deep in the tech tree. Ships lack features. Even one year after release, carries carry nothing, except guns like all the other cruisers and battleships.
This game lacks features, has performance issues, and has a sometimes more tedious than fun late game.
In conclusion, I cannot recommend this game, but I hope it improves and becomes worth its asking price.

This is one of the best game I've ever played so far.
It's a strategy game in real time with the pause button :-)
It's a sandbox game though there aren't specific targets, but you have to set your own goals, but you'll find yourself reviewing them continously adapting your strategy to either planned or unexpected events.
In the game it's well represented the feudal system of the middle age, though you can start playing as Count, Duke, King or Emperor and therefore ramp up and grow your domain size caring about relationships within your own realm, your vassals and the court members, but also building alliances with other rulers via weddings.
When you start a new campaign, you pick a ruler between 1066 and 1421 (Christians in vanilla, other rulers unlockable via DLCs like muslims, sea republics and pagans) and the target is to make your dinasty becoming more and more powerful. It's possible to start from 867 with "The Old Gods" DLC.
You're noble then you should manage only castles or county having a castle in the capital (you could play as mayor if you have The Republics DLC).
There are 3 types of character in the game nobles, religious and mayors which manage different types of holding and contribute to their liege's economy and armies in different ways. You can't have under your direct control all your lands, because any ruler has a limited number of holdings (demesne limit), beyond that you get huge penalty in relationships.
You can earn other titles in many ways:
you can inherit some lands if you're the heir of the relative title;
you can speed up when this happens via plotting or assassination of the title holder or why not all the line of succesion before of you;
you can push claim raising war, or even fabricate some or use claims of your vassals or relatives to raise the war and expand your realm;
or why not decide to have your own antipope, which you can install, therefore having a really thankful pope, and in some conditions it will be even your vassals.
For catholics the pope plays an important role, because it can excomunicate you or others, call for crusades, conceding divorces or granting you possibility to invade and therefore seize some other title.
The game has also elements from RPGs, indeed any characters has 5 skills: diplomacy, martial, stewardship, intrigue and learning. And many traits either phisical traits or behaviour ones.  You can try to change skills and traits via proactive actions (ambition and plotting) or via casual events.
Each ruler has a council of 5 people which helps them with specific matters: chancellor for diplomacy, marshall for armies, steward for the finance, spymaster for the intrigues and court chapelan for religious issues.
There are other aspects in the game like buildings, technology research and ...
All of these can be done either in single player or mutiplayer!
So I've just tried to mention the most important to give an idea of what game you'll play, you're advised that this game has a steep learning curve.
I warmly suggest to read the manual, see some let's play and then expirementing, and look for advices, but once you start mastering the game you'll get all the satisfaction and you'll find yourself sinking hours playing without even notice it.
Perfect, when you're mad at a friend and you just want to chop him into pieces, this is the game for you!

This game is definitely fun, when it works. As of 1.0.25 preview, it's too buggy for me to go the distance at 10,000 turns played, so I'm walking away with 99% of the achievements done.
Pro:
- Turn-based play where players take turns simultaneously. I like this, and it's why I played as much as I did.
- The achievements are thoughtfully designed, offering a comprehensive overview of the single player game.
- Quests (think MMO-style fetch/do quests) occur, somewhat predictably, to enhance your strategy and planning. They offer some story, too, but I only care about outcomes and don't chase story in games like this.
- Pretty game, decent music.
Con:
- The company who financed this game appears to have taken a risky gamble, which is releasing a game that you can barely play, even when the stars align. It's so good that I want to keep trying, but I'm thinking about what the game might be as opposed to what is.
- More bugs than features as of July 2017.
If you like a game that's fun even when it crashes every time, this is it.
Caveat emptor.

L.A. Noire is a noir detective action adventure video game developed by Team Bondi and published by Rockstar Games released as a Microsoft Windows port on 8 November 2011. It is set in Los Angeles in 1947 and tells the story of a LAPD officer solving a range of cases across five divisions.
This game draws heavily from both the plot and aesthetic elements of film noir which are stylistic films made popular in the 1940s and 1950s. Because this is a game about 1940s detective work, it doesn't shy away from adult themes such as gruesome multilations on a full frontal nudity victim, racial bigotry, paedophillia and even necrophillia. Definitely not a suitable game for the young.
Graphics wise, I am most impressed with the character face renderings which till this date (2015), no other game I have seen comes close to replicating how realistic the faces are. That said, while the faces were realistic, their body animations look rather stiff and it can look quite jarring at times.
Gameplay wise, while there is an open-world of Los Angeles for you to explore, there really isn't any point in doing so other then solving minor crimes and finding several point of interests which contributes to an achievement score. The game even allows you to completely skip driving to locations if you so wish.
With a total game time of about 25 hours, it is spread over a total of 26 cases and they are all played out in a very linear fashion, not unlike a graphic adventure game.
To break down the gameplay at its basics, almost every case is basically
1) Go to Location.
2) Look for a bunch of clues.
3) Question some people.
And thats it. There are sometimes action sequences and gunfights inserted along the way to break the cycle. But thats basically it. Rinse and repeat until every case is solved. I actually recommend following a walkthrough to get the correct answers when questioning people so there is a nice flow to the story with no disruptions.
Overall Rating: 8.0 / 10
Well worth playing for its story and character development despite its very linear approach at storytelling. Don't go into this game expecting it to be a Grand Theft Auto or Mafia clone. Definitely well worth a purchase when on a sale.

While this game is truly the most gorgeous 4x game I've ever seen, stay away. Stay far away.
First off, the game often corrupts saved games. You may be able to play a game and even save it, however if you try to load that game you may be unable to. Your game may be corrupted and the game will lock up every time you try to load it. As 4x games tend to take more than one session to play, I'd consider this to be a gamebreaking bug. The game should never have gone retail without the ability to load a saved game, and we're long past it going retail.
The AI is quite poor when carrying out a war. At high difficulty levels the AI gets massive industry, science, and money bonuses. While this is standard fare for high difficulty modes on 4x games, all it means is that the AI will immediately begin producing vast quantities of really big ships. However the AI appears to be incapable of using them. You may be woefully outmatched by the AI with their fleets of dreadnoughts, but thats okay. The AI is happy to declare war on you at the drop of a hat, but seems unable to follow up with its declaration of war and actually attack. The end result is that the AI feels extremely passive. The entire game, even on maximum difficulty level, feels like a mop-up operation where the game has already been decided and you're already the victor, but you need to clean up the map anyways.
Another bug, though not gamebreaking is also quite annoying. The auto-build function does not work. Most 4x games have some sort of auto-build function. If you have a lot of settlements it can be a chore to manage them all. Auto-manage comes to the rescue. It should over time build all available improvements so a low priority settlement can take care of itself. The build order might not be ideal, but thats fine, you're only using it for the low priority ones. Unfortunately in Endless Space 2 this simple function does not work. The auto-build queue stops working and stops building improvements for no rhyme or reason. It just stops. You end up having to micro-manage every single star system every single turn. On large maps this can be quite a chore indeed.
Gameplay itself is almost entirely obfuscated. 4x games are really just spreadsheets with a lot of window dressing, but as part of that the player must have clear feedback. Players cannot be left in the dark as to why something happened, or what the result of a player decision are. Unfortunately Endless Space 2 gives close to zero player feedback in multiple areas;
* Diplomacy with AI players is baffling. The AI will routinely accuse you of making hostile gestures at them even when your fleet is orbiting your own homeworld. The AI may also accuse you of blockading their systems while your fleet is orbiting your own homeworld. There is often no indication as to why the AI suddenly hates you. You don't have to do anything and sometimes the AI gives you messages saying its hates you, sometimes the AI sends you messages saying it loves you. There's no feedback between cause and effect.
* Combat is mystifying. Weapons have long/medium/short engagement ranges. You can deploy at long/medium/short range, but so can your enemy. If you pick short range and they pick long range, at what range do your weapons actually engage at? Is one flotilla shooting at another a short range attack? Long range attack? There's no feedback, so all you can do is build lots of defenses, lots of weapons, and hope for the best. Expensive ships with all of the upgrades beat less expensive ships. The actual mechanics of combat are entirely unclear.
* Icons aren't explained in tool tips. You may eventually figure out what luxury goods boost what stats, but this will require a great deal of trial and error. The tooltip will happily explain what something does, but it uses an icon to explain what the thing does. Unfortunately at no point is that icon explained, so you're left with a tooltip that may as well be in hieroglyphics.
Overall verdict:
Major game features are broken or poorly implemented. The ability to save/load a game successfully is dubious at best. AI is passive. Expect a lot of tedious micromanagement for no benefit. The game provides little to no feedback to player actions, leading to a lot of guesswork from the player.
But its a really, really, really pretty game. Its downright gorgeous.
Pick it up if its on sale, but wait until it hits $15 or so. It sure is pretty as an art project, but its not a good game.

Overall Endless Space 2 is an excellent 4x game that continues the stellar record from Amplitudes other offerings.
For a more indepth statement: I have played both Endless Space I and Endless Legends, but most of my 4x time recently has gone to Stellaris, a game on offer from Paradox Interactive. While I have given Stellaris more hours, I found the experience ultimately lacking. This is not a review of that game, but there are issues in Stellaris ranging from empire management (sectors) to the tedium induced in the midgame (building all the little space stations). Stellaris's biggest weakness, however, is its warfare. Paradox games have always had pains in modeling armed conflict and the shift to space did the game no favors.
In short Stellaris warfare boils down to not just building the biggest fleet, but the biggest fleet of basic vessels that you start the game with, a strategy called "Naked Corvette" spam. In multiplayer it's either forbidden or something everyone has to do to compete. It made the game a tedious choir and unfortunately I see no sign Paradox is willing to address it instead opting to pump out yet more DLC while the game has some fundamental problems.
But on to Endless Space 2. I've been overjoyed at how Endless Space and indeed Amplitude at large continue to push the boundaries of the 4x genre while adding their own unique twists. The factions in the game are diverse and offer radically different playstyles from each other while still feeling suitable to persue multiple paths to victories. The ship design is a simple module system that still allows customization (and it's important to mix and match your vessels strengths against your foes), and warfare is a smooth yet still deep and tactical endeavor (the mixture of star lanes with fairly early free travel tech means you can approach your foe from different angles, literally, and hit and run is a valid strategy). The game also features a "CP" or command point cap on fleets, which can be expanded with technology but also does away with the flat and 1-dimensional "death ball" from Stellaris.
While Endless Space 2 is not a flawless game (there are some balance concerns like the Voidyani having high variance based on their starting conditions and their heroes being absurdly powerful once they reach a high level) Amplitude have already made patches and they have a proven and demonstarted track record of supporting their games. I look forward to what they have planned.

Great core mechanics and absolute aesthetic beauty are plagued by bugs, questionable controls and misdirected design.
-----------------------------------------
Pros:
-Basic swinging, blocking, kicking, shield attacks, etc. are well thought out and, for the most part, control well.
-From the graphics to the map lighting to the physics to the sound design to the un-intrusive but excellent background music, this game is a tasty treat.
I was psyched after I played the training... however...
Cons:
Bugs:
-Forget about playing with bots.  The AI pathfinding frequently doesn't work at all.
-I saw a couple instances online of players stuck in walls
Questionable controls:
-Even on LAN, there seems to be some delay and sluggishness to the controls, particularly their responsiveness.  If this is a way of simulating the weight of weapons & armor, it feels artificial and is more of a frustrating immersion-breaker.  I never could confidently tell whether I was going to perform a combo attack or two regular attacks.
Misdirected design:
-This is the killer for me.  Individual players progress through ranks and unlock gear which significantly impacts their play, and they can match with players who have not unlocked that gear.  The archer is completely underpowered, and doesn't have his portable cover unlocked by default.  The leveling system essentially kills any true competitive aspect of the game.  There is a nagging prompt on the character customization screen that keeps you from making certain changes until you follow the game's community page (yes, really).  Many DLC weapons cost something like $3.00 EACH.  Most of the maps I played were either too tiny or a little too sprawly and meandering.  Very few strike a balance that feels right for each class and for the movement scale without also being oversimplistic.  Certain modes and servers remove the crosshair which makes the game exponentially more frustrating to play.

I approached this game from a couple of different angles since the first time I played it a couple years ago. The first time I played it was on an official PVP server. This gives you the survival genre experience you expect. You wake up on a beach, immediately get eaten, respawn, get stabbed by another player, spend the rest of the time cowering under a rock afraid to play the game. Playing on official PVE servers give you the option to advance at your leisure in a more unified environment. In my opinion PVE is the way to play this game, but certain timers are a bit abusive if you don't want to hop in and do regular maintenance to everything you built. I wasn't willing to make that sacrifice so I took a long time away from the game.
Most of my play time is from relatively recently actually. A group of my friends from work began playing ark again, just tethered to one of our local servers. This wasn't a GREAT way to play, because you find yourself tethered to the host, only being able to travel so far away from them before being dragged to who knows where because they ran off to chase a dodo just slightly outside of the tether distance. The tether distance IS adjustable, so if you plan on playing relatively close together the whole time, this may work for some players.
Instead we decided to take advantage of a server hosting sites trial period, and in doing so, we found the sweet spot on this game. We are able to move forward at our own pace, we all help each other out. We have been building our own bases on different parts of the island and plan on building dino armies to take out the world bosses when the time is right.
There are people reviewing this game with over 6000 hours of play time saying that it's not worth it for the price. This has blown me away, especially seeing as just going to a movie these days costs 20 dollars for 2 hours of possible entertainment. There are a lot of ways to move forward with this game, and I'd encourage people to definitely give it a shot if you've played similar games of this nature before. I grew up loving dinosaurs and this game has an amazing world to learn about and explore. Try it out and know that, unless you just don't like the core mechanics, there are probably ways to get around your least favorite aspects of the gameplay.

Chivalry: Medieval Warfare is a fun hack-and-slash game that you can enjoy with friends during a LAN party or other social event. Or if you're in a guild and like to join games en masse, you can do it in this one and it works out nicely.
The things about Chivalry: Medieval Warfare that drive me simply bat♥♥♥♥♥♥crazy, and the reasons why I won't recommend it even though I had lots of fun with the game, are four-fold.
Chivalry: Medieval Warfare was the ONLY game to ever give me the dreaded blue screen of death. My graphics card, the card that had run the game well over 300+ hours, decided it had had enough and just refused to work... er, rather, refused to run Chivalry without crashing itself. That made me PERMANENTLY uninstall the game altogether and has put a really bad taste in my mouth about it. Call me biased, but whatever.
Being a small-time game developer, Chivalry Medieval Warfare appears to me to be a poorly-coded game in general. The menus, at one point, were BARELY functional. Most of the buttons didn't work, and it took the developer MONTHS to make them halfway functional again. Animations bugs are still everywhere. Players can exploit the game in obvious ways that the developer has to know about but don't actively fix. Hell, it took them close to 5 months to release the game's first patch that ultimately broke combat forever. (If you have been playing since a few months after it released, you know exactly what I mean)
The devs seem to have a very difficult grasp on what the word balance means. I don't mean to directly bash them here, but for a time, spears were the end-all. Vanguards literally ruled the entire game room (even today they do) because of their strengths against ALL other classes. Then the devs saw that this was happening and completely destroyed spears, to the point where they were no longer useful. One extreme to another. Hit boxes weren't fixed, merely modified to make them almost worse than they were before. Man At Arms, at one point, could reach around a tower shield staring them straight in the face, and if you get caught in that, it's game over.
Since the game has been out a long time, and many people still play it, it is really, really difficult for newer players to have any fun. I remember joining every single lobby and going 34/6 or 28/4 every free-for-all round (check my screenshots, it's legit). Fun for me, but discouraging for the new players. There is no incentive to play other than getting ultimately trashed by a rank 50 person who camps on the game all day. And don't even get me started on how freaking awful the community is with the little thing called "swing manipulation". You can literally feint using your mouse speed. You can literally slice someone in half by twirling around like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ballerina and slice them through yourself (I guess). I never, ever feinted and still won most FFA matches. I never, ever manipulated my swing unless my opponent did so. And none of those walking jokes could EVER beat me in a 1v1 without using the manipulation tricks; not even feinting worked. They always had to resort to underhanded, idiotic flippy-doos and curtsy-flips to get a cheap shot.
All of this said, you can buy the game if you want to just have low-stress fun. But if you hate losing to game camps that live on this thing to train their mouse-speed button skills, don't even bother.

Another fun 4X from Amplitude.
Despite others claiming it feels unfinished or unpolished, I don't see it. The game feels really solid to me. There's probably room for improvement here or there, but we can say that about anything, can't we? Personally, I love the look and feel of ES2.
There are / have been some bugs I've noticed since launch, but one of which got fixed very quickly. The other, the multiplayer desync, has gotten much better, but is still there. However, I personally haven't found it to be much of an issue. It often resolves itself on the next turn, or within the next few. Even if it doesn't, I haven't had problems just playing through it and ignoring it. Saving and reloading the game will resync everyone, if you're worried. It also happens very infrequently now, at least to me and my friends. To the best of my understanding, it's usually triggered by players trying to input commands while the turn is ending/starting.
I don't think we've had the game crash on us, and I can't think of any performance issues we've run into. No lag. It's really easy to invite your Steam friends to play with you. Loading a multiplayer game hasn't caused any problems. We've had a friend get DCed once, due to his own internet problems, and he reconnected without any problems. And one of these friends has a pretty trash computer that can't run a lot of stuff; I often hear him complaining about lag or frames in most games we play, but he doesn't seem to have problems with ES2, at least not after he lowered the graphics settings.
I feel like Amplitude didn't let us down with ES2. I've had a lot of fun with it so far, and I personally think it's worth the price.

This is my first review and I want to start off by saying that I am highly recommending this game if it is on sale! Right now the game is just over $5 Canadian, which is a steal! If you have some friends make sure they buy it with you!
So I will start off with what is great with the game, which is quite a bit, then I will move on to why this game went downhill.
So my friend and I got this game when it was on sale last time. The tutorial system is fantastic, if not the best tutorial system I have ever seen. Heck it was fun and interesting! The voice acting and everything was superb. After that we both ended up joining a server and playing together. Thankfully they implemented a server for beginners. Level 1 to 15 I believe.
We both started off doing pretty well and maintaining an average K/D ratio and it improved with time; we ended up usually being the top people on our team. Everything seemed balance whether you were defending or attacking, and even all 4 classes. They all had their strengths and weaknesses. The maps were incredible and were playable over and over. The game modes were great too (make sure to try the lightsaber mod!).
One of the great things was the community in the beginner servers. Everyone was understanding when you hit a team mate or killed one; they all had a good sense of humour. Heck some people even honoured when 2 people were battling so it was a 1 vs 1.
Ex: There was this one battle where we had 3 team mates alive and they had 1 guy left. It was a 1 vs 1. One of our team mates went to jump in and kill the guy from behind and the other bystander on our team chopped his head off so he wouldn't interrupt their duel. Priceless. And respectable.
Another great thing about the community in those servers was how some people role played and their comments. It really did improve the gameplay and made it a lot more exciting when your team is shouting: Kill the Agatha inbreds!
Eventually my friend and I reached level 16 and we could no longer play in those servers, which is understandable, but that is where everything went downhill. I will now explain why this game is not worth the full price.
Once you can no longer player in the servers with the new people you have to join the more experienced people. Makes sense. But almost every server we joined we didnt see anyone below level 30 and it's probably because most people stop playing the game once they reach 16. The community is awful! One of the worst I have ever seen. You hit your team mate once (heaven forbid you kill them by accident) and you get kicked, sworn at, and even killed yourself.
It is as if all kindness disappeared. If you did crappy on you team and had a crap K/D or got the lowest amount of objective points people would kick you, and once again swear at you and tell you how much you suck. Your team and the other team. But this isnt even the worst of it.
The worst part is the gameplay! Every single person has mastered not just the normal moves, but every cheap ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t move out there. No joke, people do moves that look like the funky chicken and kill people. It is hard to explain but you can google these techniques and try to master them. It is people who know how to manipulate the mouse so you aim one way then swing it back, with a different speed and such and they perform weird moves which work really well. It actually looks hilarious and we be even funnier if people did not do it all the time.
So along with everyone who would cheat, you would have people who play this game so much that they bought the game three times and would have all their accounts maxed out (along with them cheating). It went hand in hand with their attitude and how they took the game. Everyone would take it seriously. As I stated before you would be kicked for doing less than average.
So my conclusion: If this game is on sale for AT LEAST half price I would recommend buying it because you can get about 30 hours of gameplay that will never be forgotten. One of the best multiplayer experiences I have ever had (up to lvl 15). Having a friend doubles the value as well! But if you are looking for a long time commitment to this game and you are an average skilled gamer or less than average I would not recommend playing it if you are thinking of playing it regularly. Of course if you put time into it and practice the moves everyone else does once you reach the pro servers then maybe it is worth it but the battles no longer look or feel as "cool" and "fun". It is hard to explain but when you battle normally it feels as if you are someone in a medieval movie. When you start using the cheap moves it is more a battle of luck and ping if both opponents are using those moves.
The choice is yours but at $5 this game is definitely worth a buy to get those 30 incredible hours of gaming in!

The gameplay is great, definitely still the best detective game out there. Another fun 4X from Amplitude.
Despite others claiming it feels unfinished or unpolished, I don't see it. The game feels really solid to me. There's probably room for improvement here or there, but we can say that about anything, can't we? Personally, I love the look and feel of ES2.
There are / have been some bugs I've noticed since launch, but one of which got fixed very quickly. The other, the multiplayer desync, has gotten much better, but is still there. However, I personally haven't found it to be much of an issue. It often resolves itself on the next turn, or within the next few. Even if it doesn't, I haven't had problems just playing through it and ignoring it. Saving and reloading the game will resync everyone, if you're worried. It also happens very infrequently now, at least to me and my friends. To the best of my understanding, it's usually triggered by players trying to input commands while the turn is ending/starting.
I don't think we've had the game crash on us, and I can't think of any performance issues we've run into. No lag. It's really easy to invite your Steam friends to play with you. Loading a multiplayer game hasn't caused any problems. We've had a friend get DCed once, due to his own internet problems, and he reconnected without any problems. And one of these friends has a pretty trash computer that can't run a lot of stuff; I often hear him complaining about lag or frames in most games we play, but he doesn't seem to have problems with ES2, at least not after he lowered the graphics settings.
I feel like Amplitude didn't let us down with ES2. I've had a lot of fun with it so far, and I personally think it's worth the price.

This game is as the title says. It's a game where you start as a succesful Youtuber, and explain how you got there. You start off as an aspiring youtuber, and slowly progress your way through levels, granting further ways to produce higher quality videos.
The idea of the game is interesting , and one you can easily spend time playing; however I felt after a couple of hours that the game play had become repetative and stale. I found myself repeating the same things every day: Sleep, eat and create a video. At the start of the game you do also have to juggle studying as well, though your mother never seems happy when you study.
The game does offer things to do outside of your room; however I found little use to these, other than meeting new people, and even that didn't seem to make much difference to my day to day life.
If you are a fan of other sims, where you slowly become a better gamer, games creator etc, then you will surely find this game fun. However I was personally hoping for a bit more.

My list for the best 4x space strategy looks currently like this:
1. Stars in Shadow (best mix of style and working mechanics)
2. Galciv 3  (best in mechanics=best challenge)
3. Endless Space 2 (best in style)
Stellaris and MoO do not contest as both have horrible style and mechanics
Style is considered not as a subjective rating of the feel of the game but rather how systematically Music, Art and GUI are integrated, their coverage and if they get in the way of the gameplay or support it

This is the ultimate medieval dynasty simulator. You rule over realms in Europe, North Africa, the Middle East and India and have many different cultures and all christian faiths at your disposal and yes, you can change both during the game.
You play one character at a time, a person with skills, virtues and flaws which has inherited titles, prestige, money and also claims on titles from his parents. You can wage war, but only when you have a proper (medieval) reason to do so.
Holy War, assassination plots, cheating on your spouse and inheritance of land just through succession will be part of your daily routine if you play this game. You can work your way up from a low Count title to becoming an Emperor, become a heretic, annihilate cultures and religions and make your dynasty the most powerful one in the world of CKII, dominating the world from Portugal to India and from Norway to Ethiopia for centuries.
The expansions allow you to try different religions (Norse Pagans, Muslims, Buddhists, Jews...), different governmental systems (Eastern Rome, Trade Republics...) or expand the gameplay in other directions (deeper focus on roleplaying or certain religions, earlier start dates etc).
Buy this game. But be warned, it's about characters, not about optimizing economy or developing technology. Another warning: It will eat up your time...

ARK is not without its faults. Official servers are a grindfest, some portions of the community can be toxic, the building mechanics could be improved, and the game is not well optomized. However, despite all this, I love this game. I've played it for two years fairly consistently, and have spent more hours on this game than all other games in my library combined.
Some advice that helped me enjoy this game to the greatest extent:
1) Find a good server. Some communities can be toxic, some alpha tribes abuse their power and don't treat new players well. Other servers have awesome players, everyone is friendly, and even PvP feels less heartbreaking because you have other tribes who are willing to help you rebuild. I personally love playing on unofficial servers because the official server gather/XP/etc rates are not fast enough for me. So find a server with a good community (you'll know within the first week or so), rates that feel good to you, and an active playerbase. Then, stick with it!
2) Play with friends. I love this game because I play in a tribe with a bunch of friends. Going it alone means you won't be able to progress as fast, tame larger dinos, or build cooler bases. Endgame progression is nearly impossible unless you work in a team or spend 8 hours a day playing.
3) Understand that PvP means you probably will get raided, and you probably lose most of your stuff. If you have found a good community, people wil help you rebuild, and you will learn techniques to defend yourself. Just don't ragequit! It's a fact of the game, and there are ways to mitigate the pain of getting raided.

The performances by the actors are really good.
Los Angeles is huge and beautiful (for the graphics of the time), and its really hard to tell the repetitive use of various buildings.
The game elements themselves are varied being a combination of puzzler (clue finding and determining truth in POI questioning), third-person cover shooter, and (less common) foot chases, car chases, tailing a suspect unseen, and (rarely) unique mini-games involving evidence reconstruction. All of this is broken up into chunks that can be played a case or two at a time.
The car-driving mechanic of the game is clunky and handles poorly. It's easy with barely any key pressure to send your vehicle careening to either side, making even simple turns at intersections overly difficult. It greatly increases the likelihood of crashing into something, particularly during critical game sequences involving chases (of which there are many).
The cover mechanism is clunky as well, particularly when you have to break cover and run.
The story structure and length. The game is big and ambitious, and really deserved to work. Driving around 1947 Los Angeles you can see where Rockstar is headed with open world settings, though the game doesn't quite fall into that category because most of the city is cosmetic. Fortunately enough does work to recommend the game, but it comes with some heavy caveats.
First, the length. While you can't claim you aren't getting your money's worth, you have to work your way every case, 21 + 5 DLC (they aren't optional either if you bought the extended edition). This isn't counting all the street crime cases (40 total) which are small but add up quickly. Rumor has it that Team Bondi had two other desks (Burglary and Fraud) that didn't make it into the game because Rockstar said it was already long enough.
The length immediately sets up a problem with pacing for the main narrative comprised of two non-overlapping arcs, one that encompasses the entire homicide desk (the middle third of the game) and the other that covers the vice and arson desks (the final third). The problem is that the Patrol plus Traffic desks (first third) already take a long time to get through, and by then the witness-questioning game element that is repeated in every case has already lost its novelty and become relatively easy to get a high score.
And that's a shame because Homicide is where the story begins to get interesting, even though the Vice/Arson arc is the better story. Furthermore, the split arc means the majority of major characters aren't even introduced until you reach Vice/Arson. And the Arson desk is really more focused on resolving the final arc than investigating arson cases.
What this all amounts to is that the story design should have been geared to be much tighter (combine Patrol and Traffic) with elements that tied into both arcs, and each desk having maybe 3-4 cases that drove the story with the others cases being more like side quests. Try as they might, the street crime cases are too small to be full side quests.

I definitely think the game has tons of issues that need to be fixed, including localization issues, some rather tedious aspects of gameplay, a better explanation of the mechanics, an improved social system, and perhaps the removal of the clothing system for anything but aesthetic reasons, or maybe if clothes affect your video in some way.  But there is the kernel of something interesting here.
Anyone familiar with Game Dev Tycoon is aware of this kind of game, but there's more control while also more randomized elements in the making of each product.  You have to produce videos with varying sorts of clips in them, such as an intro, a transition, a comment, and a close.  It isn't always the same.  You get new cards by ranking up.  Each time you are deal three cards and must use one to satisfy the need of the video at a particular time.  Sometimes you have perfect cards dealt to you to make a great video and other times you don't get more than one or two to align.
I like this system because it makes it so there is some randomization to the success and failure while still leaving the ultimate quality up to the player.  In addition to this, there's a lot of Sims type stuff in the game and I think these are my least favorite parts of the game.
Overall it's an interesting game that needs a lot of work but can be pretty good eventually.  I'd pick it up now if you like this style of game, like I do.

I may or may not come back in a few months / years / etc. to play this again & see if things have improved, but until then, if it's not a yes, it's a no.
For now, Stellaris is the gold standard, and this falls short of that standard on most fronts. Here's what it does better than Stellaris :
GRAPHICS : ES2 is pretty. So pretty. It's so pretty the awkward skeletal icons for fleets really stand out and make you think they didn't finish the game (it's just the same style they used in the first game), but the planets, fights, etc. are purrrrty. IMO strategy & gameplay are what strategy games are about, not graphics, but at the same time I don't want to play an ASCII strategy game either. Amplitude leans more towards the prettiness in their strategy games, and they do it rather well, so that's nice. Contrast with Stellaris, where the graphics seem low-res in some cases.
RACIAL DIFFERENTIATION : I'm talking gameplay-wise, because ES2 has fallen into the old Star Trek trap of "aliens are just humans with different foreheads." Gameplay-wise, Amplitude has always done a good job of really making races different from one another. I'm talking about how a Vodyani does different "stuff" to colonize & manage planets than a Riftborn. In Stellaris you can play a mushroom with no arms or legs, but racial qualities are little more than pleasant nudges in certain directions, and while the "build your own government type" is waaaaaaaaaay more robust, it too doesn't do much to make your race "unique."
GROUND COMBAT : This isn't saying much. Ground combat in Stellaris is literally "land troops, watch them punch each other until one loses," so it's not tough to be better. ES2 gives options - orbital bombardment, guerilla, or blitz, and even the defender gets to choose their own strategy. You also get to determine how much of your army will be infantry, armor, or air, and can spend resources to give them permanent buffs. I'm continually confused at how a "grand strategy" game like Stellaris can have such bland ground combat. Probably because they excel at literally everything else, but whatevs.
To be fair, there's a little bit of "apples to oranges" comparison here, because ES2 incorporates a lot more fantasy into its sci-fi, and Stellaris is more "grand strategy" / "run your entire economy while dealing with unrest and alien wars". ES2 isn't grand strategy, nor does it try to be. Still, there are some basics I expect in a strategy game, and as-is, I don't feel like they were met. I'm hoping future DLC doesn't just add races, but also adds content, like more neutral factions, more robust diplomacy, more "stuff to do" in the late game, etc.
My issues were mostly bugs (which I'm betting they'll fix in the future, but seriously, so. many. bugs. Do you even test, bro?), the terrible, terrible AI (which plagues most Amplitude games), the rinse & repeat of beating up alien empires in generally the same way, really long waits while the computer decides if it's gonna fight or retreat (dude you have two small frigates and I have an entire battleship group led by a hero. Why does it take you 30 seconds to decide to run away?) really long end of turn processing, and the terrible (but pretty) space combat.
And before people get all "well you only have 60 hours blah blah," I actually played another 50-80 offline, so that people on my friends list wouldn't message me and ask me to go play Starcraft 2 or Diablo 3 or some other nonsense (they still found me).
It's good to be the king ... sometimes ...

This is the ultimate medieval dynasty simulator. You rule over realms in Europe, North Africa, the Middle East and India and have many different cultures and all christian faiths at your disposal and yes, you can change both during the game.
You play one character at a time, a person with skills, virtues and flaws which has inherited titles, prestige, money and also claims on titles from his parents. You can wage war, but only when you have a proper (medieval) reason to do so.
Holy War, assassination plots, cheating on your spouse and inheritance of land just through succession will be part of your daily routine if you play this game. You can work your way up from a low Count title to becoming an Emperor, become a heretic, annihilate cultures and religions and make your dynasty the most powerful one in the world of CKII, dominating the world from Portugal to India and from Norway to Ethiopia for centuries.
The expansions allow you to try different religions (Norse Pagans, Muslims, Buddhists, Jews...), different governmental systems (Eastern Rome, Trade Republics...) or expand the gameplay in other directions (deeper focus on roleplaying or certain religions, earlier start dates etc).
Buy this game. But be warned, it's about characters, not about optimizing economy or developing technology. Another warning: It will eat up your time...

We are living in wonderful times as a sci-fi strategy gamer. Between "Stellaris" and "Endless Space 2" there isn't much difference in the 4X formula. Instead, both excel in the pace and grandness of their design. I find "Stelleris" to be the epitome of "grand strategy" and more of a macro-type of play. "Endless Space 1 and 2" have a faster more manageable pace akin to "arcade-mode". Both are great in my opinion, and I bounce between the two games in my spare time. What they both excel at is story-telling. It is easy to get immersed into both games. Even when first playing, "losing" just made me want to start another game.  I however have to give credit to "Endless Space 2" in their portrayal of space battles--very unique and very beautiful graphics.
I hope Amplitude keeps it coming.

No idea what the mixed reviews is all about.
First of I'll say (and I say this about every other game they've made), but amplitude and the endless series has some of the best dev support of any franchise ever. The devs are active in the discussions (they've responded to, helped, and fixed multiple bugs I've posted about) they update the game with new bugfixes often, admit when they make mistakes, and overall just have amazing support for their games. That alone is reason enough to support them, but you're not here for that, you're here to see if the game is worth buying.
Endless space (original) was my favourite 4x strategy game of all time, almsot my favourite strategy game in general (only just beaten by sup com) So when I heard a sequel was in the works, I jumped at it. Unfortunately, money was tight, and I was not able to buy into the beta, or the full release, and only got it at the start of the summer sale (gift from a friend), this means I missed a lot of the games "teething" problems, and more importantly, the (since patched) bug that the mixed reviews come from.
Endless space 2 is an amazing game. It's beautiful, it's detailed, it's complex, yet simple, catering to a wide range of players and skill levels. The factions are unique, the gameplay interesting no matter how long you play, and with great lore. I personally do not think it is as good as the original (maybe thats just because of how much I love the original), but it is definitely a worthy successor, with improvements across the board, as well as taking and adding the best parts from endless legend (another fantastic game) and adding them seamlessely. If you're a fan of 4x strategy games, or strategy games in general, it's definitely one of the best out there, and well worth double the price they ask for it.
Keep up the great work Amplitude.

You can have a blast with this game within the first minute of playing.  The controls are pretty simple and familiar to that of other fps games.  I remember the first game I ever played.  It was 'free for all' on the stonehill map and within 20 seconds my head got chopped off.  There is a startling and satisfying level of violence and all too familiar amounts of dismemberment.  All around you arms and legs are being detached, someones head explodes like a suicidal extremist cantaloupe, from an arrow,  bone and tendons being exposed from a blade raking against skin, the clashing of shields and mace/sword/rock on a stick while you get stabbed in the back from a stalking man at arms as he runs away laughing with his head held high in the air.
Point is: this game is fun even if you suck/are new.
The reason you see so many players with 500+ hours is due to the depth of combat.  You initiate a swing with a mouse click or scroll of the mouse wheel and the weapon will follow a general path of its swing.  However, you have the ability to move your body and pivot your torso in order to alter that general path.  This allows you to swing your weapon in so many different ways (reverse attacks, accelerated swings, delayed attacks, attacking from a particular direction)  PLUS: there are 4 different soldiers to pick from all with unique attributes and weapons.  Each weapon makes for a different playstyle. Example: You can play as knight and either charge into several people with a heavy weapon and hope to 1 shot someone, or be a tank with a shield and absorb attacks while dealing medium damage and assist the rest of the group.
Once you get the basics of the game down there is so much to experiment with and new skills to learn that it makes for an amazing game to invest time into, because you will eventually be a mini boss.  However there is no advantageous weapons/attributes once you get higher level, like explosive slugs etc.  You have to unlock certain weapons by killing peeps but that can be done in less than 10 hours.

Endless Space II is a game you happily play through once per faction or so but probably not much more. It is really enjoyable at first, but its relative lack of replayability is a major downside.
GOOD:
-The look and feel puts a lot of other turn-based strategy games to shame. The music is good. The writing is good. And with a couple notable exceptions, the graphics are great. The hand-painted art panels compare well to non-digital tabletop games. And the strategic map is attractive, informative, even dynamic. The planets orbit their stars and moons orbit their planets.
-There is a good amount of detail to manage, no micromanagement. The star system is the basic unit of galactic development, rather than individual planets. Still, individual planets each have their own properties that contribute to their systems.
-Each race or faction is truly unique with its own story and often a significant modification to the game mechanics, not just a little bonus here and there, like other games.
-Exploration ships launch expeditions on planetside “curiosities” as well as launch probes into deep space to discover unknown systems. The rewards gained from searching goodie huts are just about right.
-Technology is laid out in concentric circles, leaving a lot of freedom to prioritize and differentiate. It always feels like any one technology is pretty achievable but getting all the techs is nearly impossible.
-There is a good balance between moving along established “star lanes” and (later) free movement of ships.
-Strategy really matters in a satisfying way. There are meaningful long-term consequences for turn-by-turn decisions.
MIXED:
-Fleet battles are non-tactical. Players do not control ships at all during combat, but rather choose from a list of predefined battle tactics that typically revolve around staying in optimal weapons range or boosting the right type of defense. Space battles are shown in cinematic quality, but most players will probably not watch them much.
-Population management is clearly intended, as certain races have bonuses on certain types of planets. However, population movement between systems is so slow as to frustrate any thorough attempt to manage this aspect of the empire.
-Population and food movement, as well as trade, are handled automatically, but it would be nice if the player could upgrade the merchant fleet to make it faster, more resistant to blockade.
-The politics mechanic is interesting but not really powerful enough to matter much. Some laws become potent in certain situations, but most are pretty so-so. Anarchy has very little effect. Ultimately the elections become an almost meaningless distraction.
-Heroes are a big part of the Endless franchise, and choosing their promotions as they level up is both enjoyable and strategic. However, while heroes level up quickly governing systems, they barely level up at all as fleet admirals.
-Quests are good at first but get very repetitive later. Many quests are easy, but some are too difficult. The late-game Academy questline seems especially pointless, strategically speaking, because it requires such a huge investment of time and resources (i.e. heroes).
-The AI is decent--at least not terrible--but slow.
BAD:
-Lack of replayability is a huge issue. There should be an optional random quest generator.
-Ship movement is not user-friendly. It is sometimes hard to select a fleet and choose its destination. Worse, the pathfinding for fleet movements gives little control to the player. Fleets will often walk straight into unnecessary conflict, even when other paths are theoretically available.
-From a technical standpoint, the game is unreasonably slow and resource-hungry. This seems to be mostly for the sake of AI processing.
-Economic victory is a little too easy to achieve accidentally.
-Ground battle animations and fleet representations on the strategic map view are the two notable exceptions to the otherwise excellent graphics.
-Outpost growth predictions are not accurate.
-Certain aspects of the game are unnecessarily opaque, such as how combat is resolved, what happens to leftover production and research points, and how ship experience works.
