This is the most complex, deep, and surprising strategy game I have ever come across.  Crusader Kings 2 has an extremely high learning curve and it takes many hours to pick up on what is happening in the game, but once you get past the initial hump there is a bottomless well of rewarding experiences.
The game is a turn based feudal lineage simulator.  You control a character with the goal of continuing your dynasty through the centuries, once you die you play as your heir.  You must attempt to expand your family’s holdings, keep your vassals happy, and increase your prestige.  Choose to start out as a lowly count and work your way up to being a king, or start as a lofty emperor and try and expand and maintain your empire...or play as anything in between.  You are able to plot against your enemies, arrange marriages for powerful alliances, and go to war for more land.
The game also has more than 30 DLC options to purchase and the list can be daunting at first, but the DLC fall into 2 main categories: cosmetic additions and gameplay expansions.  The cosmetic additions are the vast majority and include extra portrait options for characters from various regions, extra music tracks when playing as certain countries, and extra options for the dynasty shields that represent your family.  All of these add extra flavor to the game, but do not affect the gameplay mechanics at all.
The gameplay expansions are the larger and gameplay changing DLC.  These include: The Ruler Designer which allows you to customize your character, The Legacy of Rome which introduces retinues, The Sword of Islam that allows you to play as a Muslim character, The Republic which gives you access to playing as one of the trading oriented countries, and The Old Gods which opens up the option to play as a pagan.  All of these add a great deal of additional depth and replayability to the game, I would highly suggest picking these up.
If you are looking for a grand turn based strategy game with depth beyond compare you are looking in the right place.

Prequel to Call of Duty: Modern Warfare, Chivalry: Medieval Warfare is a great game in which you play as a rookie soldier who gets instantly killed by many things including crossbows, zweihanders, daggers being wielded by underweight archers, 600 ping teleportation wizards, javelins, swords, and more. It takes forever to build (or get the parts/resources for) anything in this game, but you get used to it. It takes forever to level up your gear to Rank 30 (to then sell it and get new gear), which is required to progress your Mastery rank in the game, but you get used to it. The entire dang game is a grindfest, with a period maybe 50-150 hours in where it's actually legitimately fun, before you fall victim to the Affinity grind. I've spent all 1000+ hours of my playtime doing the same thing, making gear (warframes, weapons and sentinels/companions) and playing various but usually the same missions to level them up before selling them and continuing the process. But, you get used to it.
Obviously there's some inherent satisfaction to leveling things up and increasing your Mastery rank, or no one would do it. But I wouldn't call that fun. If you want to have fun in Warframe, you have to remember to have fun, which usually people don't. But if you get some good gear and good friends together and play some challenging missions (or just screw around looking for secret areas or something), you can have fun no matter how far into the game you are. And if you're in that transition-to-the-grind period, getting new Warframes and weapons that don't suck can be a ton of fun too.
Absolutely recommend playing with a friend that's ahead of you, unless you're a trailblazer. The game can be pretty hard to newbies who don't have decent gear, or know how to get it. But if you can remember to just have fun, you'll be used to the grinding before you know it.
Also, if you don't have someone willing to give you Platinum, the premium currency, and you're not willing to tough it out and sit in Trade chat for hours on end attempting to sell things for Plat (which is what most people do), be prepared to spend money. Wait until you get a 50% or 75% off Plat daily login reward, then buy whatever you're comfortable with. You can play the game without spending plat later on, but at first you are REQUIRED to spend some plat on slots for warframes and weapons. You CAN play with only two warframes and like eight total weapons, but at that point you're better off playing like, RuneScape. Buy some warframe slots, a few weapon slots, and a single color palette, and you're set for a very long time, long enough to know if you're willing to spend more money on the game. You do start with 50... Enough to buy a few slots with no color palette, I guess. But it won't be enough; DE wants your money.

This game has potential, but I cannot recommend it in its current form. I've played since early access started, and it's definitely addictive, however, there are some game breaking flaws for me.
Firstly, the AI is far too aggressive. Everyone but the Lumeris will literally delcare war on you a few turns after you meet them, for absolutely no reason, while the Lumeris are the opposite and will never become aggressive. It's a bit absurd.
Secondly, playing a huge map is basically useless, as there is an expansion mechanic, that even with advanced techs ruins the game. You can't expand past X systems or the penalites will bankrupt you in 2-3 turns and every system in your empire will revolt. Game over. It's profoundly annoying, luckily I was able to easily mod the file which controlled the expansion limit and set it to 9999 to make sure I can actually play large maps.
Third, the AI is annoying in other ways. If you even remotely outmatch it (this includes pirates which run around attacking your systems with one ship) they will just retreat. Now you take damage when you retreat, but by late game the problem is ships reapair within 2-3 turns because of tech, so what ends up happening is the computer will just build a massive fleet, attack your system, you respond. Since you can only attack one stack of ships per turn, the AI just retreats, leaving another 4-5 stacks left to invade your planets, the fleet that retreats comes back in 2 turns fully repaired from the previous retreat, with a full compliment of troops, rinse repeat. this causes you to never be able to destroy their fleets and they run amok invading all your systems. I have about 10 super fleets and I simply cannot destroy anything. It makes war totally pointless, and infuriating. A simple fix would be to implement a chance that a fleet wont be able to retreat, or if it's recently retreated it can't retreat. Problem sovled.
Combat suffers from the same problems as Endless Space 1. There's a few more mechanics, but basically its a back and forth cinematic with little to no control. If the enemy even slightly outmatches you in technology you will lose the battle, period. Essentially it comes down to, who has the next tier of tech first, or numbers. No tactics or strategy. Eventually, even if you're ahead in tech, the computer catches up, and once that happens combat becomes a useless back and forth of who has more ships. Endless Space 1 suffered from this same problem, and I have no idea why they didn't address this in the sequel.
Last, performance late game is awful (I have an inkling this has something to do with the Riftborn, as everytime I take one of their systems or destroy one of their fleets performance drastically improves). It's a massive lag fest, and I have a very good system. I'm fairly certain the program is riddled with memory leaks, which is what's causing the progressive slow down that eventually forces you to exit and boot the game back up (which then gets you perfect performance for a few turns before the leaks start screwing your system again).
It's a good game, but it has lots of problems. Wait for some patches.

THis game is great - but... There always is a but in here.
1. The ships looking great - but: The shipbuilding is bland and easy going, Energy or balistic, that is it. Just 4 weapon types, repeating themselves.

3. The different factions are cool - but the AI housing them is lousy. Declares wars for one system and leaves them, gets themselves beaten to death before even thinking about a proposal for peace. ES2 could have learned so much here from Stellaris.
4. The population mechanics are cool - but: you can't just purge unwanted or harmfull population, kill them, or push them out, no you have to go trough some SJW tier Culling or find a way to work around.
5. The late game would be epic. - But there are so huge lags it can even be a problem to assemble a fleet with the UI hanging back. Really, it's nearly unplayable, and only SotSII is beating it in this regard, but(!) even that just by a little bit difference. Suddenly a faction controlling about 10% of the galaxy beats your empire by completing a wonder. Well, nice of you to sit through the 250 turns to get beaten by a random small empire. Still this is the one thing that ESII makes better than Stellaris
6. The Heroes are cool - but: They all come out of a cloning tube and get a different number. Human Hero#22 or Tree Hero #3? It really doesn't matter. Most heroes have only lack luster Skill sets that often have benefits in a layout making me uncertain if the devs realy want you to develop tem? Why do I have to skill my combat hero hero for population controll to advance into the next tier of combat skills? ES I did a much better job in this, making it easy to get the Hero you wanted. The cloning tube hero syndrom also permits that you get attachted to any of them. They all feature the same look and appearence, the same 3 classes and responding skill tress and ships. Really boring.
7. Diplomatic... - but: You can't bargain for systems you invade currently while leading in war and trying to get a peace going. Why? Why can' I take a planet that I already controll to 90%? So if you go to peace the invasion is stopped. Bamm. Also the AI gives you plantes as a price for peace that are inside their influence sphere and are autocaptured by them without even one ship asap, because this game has some nasty bugs and influence is certainly one of them.
Tl;Dr
This game has many flaws. Also it is buggy. If you want better combat, play SotS, if you want better Diplomatic, play Stellaris. If you want to stick with these guys, do so, this game has potential, but do so on your own risk.

This is an extremely intricate and impressive Grand Strategy game. While daunting, since it can make Civilization look like a casual game, there are plenty of rewards waiting for those willing to devote time and energy to learning the game. It is more than just a game of conquest, as every important character in the world has their character fleshed out and politics and interpersonal relations are important. Religion and economics, bloodlines and personality, all these will impact how you interact with others.
It should also be noted that the game is very much alive. It was released almost two years ago, by which point the average game is long dead and forgotten, but CK2 is still having regular content updates. The team has said that the game will be supported with new content, both free and DLC, for another two years. If you want a Grand Strategy game, this is rapidly becoming the gold standard.
Even after all these years, this game is still getting updates and is still getting better. This game ages like fine wine, becoming fuller, more complex, and ultimately better.

I was really late to the party on L.A. Noire, but if you're somehow arriving even later than me, it's worth giving this a look. The game does an extraordinary job of immersing you in the role of a detective, searching crime scenes for clues and trying to determing the right time to bring them up during the conversations, which, due to the facial-capture technology used in the game, are the true selling point of L.A. Noire. The game's story is surprisingly long (which I'll cynically attribute to its age), and is well worth the price of admission.
Although the game is open world, that's really more of a gimmick than an actual selling feature - likely a vestige of a shared engine with previous Rockstar titles. As you can't even draw your gun outside of the combat sequences scripted into the game's missions, you won't find the aimless rampages of GTA here, and I found myself passing the opportunity to drive through the city in favor of making my partner do it after awhile.
All in all this is a great game though, and if you somehow missed it, you should really try it out.

Would I recommend this game? I wish I could say yes..
On the plus side; It's original content with the same charming gameplay with nice, meaningfull additions, such as new features, balancing and even pretty decent remakes of the original music, which were very good. Singleplayer is very stable ( for me, at least)
On the downside;
1) What really, really, really dissappoints me is that this game is virtually unplayable on multiplayer. The level of instability is a disgrace. First 30 rounds will go some-what smoothly but after that, all hell breaks loose. Currupt save games, sudden client crashes, unsyncronized clients, linearly increasing time for battles to be concluded, etc. On turn 100, we, a group of 5, have had to re-host the game 7 times, and the time it took us to get through an average turn was 30 - 45 minutes. All because of the huge increase in time it takes for the game to respond to your commands in multiplayer.
Note: Slowest internet connection between the 5 of us were 10mb up and down, fastest was 100/100. All 5 players tried hosting, most of us with I5's and I7's. It had absolutely no effect on the stability.
2) I was hoping Endless Space 2 would implement a more detailed combat system. The combat system is too simplified. You can choose a 'Battlecard' for an engagement that dictates the range + some special bonus that your ships/troops will enjoy. By the end of the day, it's more or less about numbers, leaving actual strategy in combat almost non-existant.
3) Game needs balancing on the economical/resource side of things as well.
Conlusion:
This game is not finished. It's remarkable it would be released with such short comings. If you want to play with your friends, don't buy this game. If you can live with not playing with any other than yourself, go ahead.
Don't play if you don't have any friends. Tsunami like waves of depression will ensue.

First impressions after 10 hours. I say it again, FIRST INPRESSION. Not my final opinion I'm sure. :)
Not too impressed. The game wasn't nearly as deep or as complex as I first thought. At least it doesn't feel that way from my 10 hours. I have played three games that have spanned beyond turn 200 with three diferent races. The Empire, The Cravers and the Trader faction whos name I cannot recall. The races play pretty simillar to one another. The cravers played more differently than the other two but I think they're the big exception. In short, there doesn't seem to be that big of a difference for the different races. Though the other races may end up being different. I wouldn't know just yet.
They have strengths and weaknesses. Some unique mechanic usually but nothing game changing.
The games tutorial did a good enough job of teaching me the game, to be honest, I exited it after an hour because I felt I had learned what I needed. The UI is very nice and good looking. I found a few menus hard to find but that might just be me.
The game itself is very nice looking with a really neat artstyle. Love the art in ther game as well as the loading screens and events. Gives some really nice immersion.
I didn't come across any major bugs. Small UI glitches was the worst I got. No crashes and pretty solid framerate in battles.
So yes, the game can be enjoyable, when it works. Escpecially in a big galaxy with 4+ empires. In fact I had a great time with the game at first. However, here we come to the games worst failure.
I see this is so many turn based games. And it ticked me off when I realized it was the same here.
The longer you go on. The slower the game gets. And I'm not talking super late-game. I'm talking after turn 200 you will have to wait from half a minute to a minute for the turn to pass. Even after that the game will lag horribly. If you make it to turn 300 you will know a new level of lag. I made it to around turn 360 before it got so bad it was basically unplayable.
It's really gamebreaking. I can't "finish" a game because at the end the Ai has so many fleets going around slowing the whole game to a halt. It's really quite crushing when you've played for hours on end just to end up in a bog, so to speak.
I tried in a smaller galaxy as well with only two AI empires but it remained the same.
My rig has nothing to do with these problems. The game is on an SSD and I'm playing on a 1080ti with a 7700k.
If they could make the late game work I'd recommend this game. But since you can't play after a certain point I can't give it a recommendation at this moment.
I will update this review when I've played more.

This is definetely a good game, assuming you don't end up with one of the technical issues some people seem to be having. I have not run into any of these issues myself, so I can review this game as a functional one.
I'm familiar with MoO and Stellaris, as well as the older MoO games and the original Endless Space. Also, I am somewhat familiar with Galactic Civ 3 and Civ 6. That being said, I would classify this game as more of a MoO style game with a few notable differences. The biggest being the addition of heroes to use as a boost to systems and fleets.
Expect games to take longer than MoO overall as it has a bit more to it, so it tends to consume a bit more time. The different races you can play are varied and interesting and lend each to a fundamentally different style of play. The AI does tend to be a bit passive, but I think there's a big reason for that. The main one being that taking any political action uses a resource called "Influence". Most empires only generate a small amount of this (with United Empire being the exception as they generate extra)... meaning that if other empires were to be doing a lot you would be forced to spend, and potentially run out of, this resource as you responded to their actions. Possibly leaving you unable to interact with these other factions until you accumulated more.
While I do think it's a good game it has its flaws. Even though there's starlanes, you can't effectively block a fleet from passing through a system even if you have it set to "block". Sometimes it will work, depending on if the fleet ends its turn in the system, otherwise pirates just end up blowing past your borders and go off and pillage your planets and there's nothing you can do. It's a hassle defending your core systems when you are completely unable to engage a fleet unless it stops in a system. Yes, you can use this to your advantage. But when you do the same with your fleets then the other races get mad and like to declare war. So it basically punishes you for doing it while encouraging the AI to do the same thing it gets mad at you for doing. Also, you can't stop a planetary invasion even if you regain control of the system... you have to wait however many turns until the invasion concludes and then if the other faction won you have to re-invade the same planet. Even though your fleet was 1 turn too late in coming to their aid. They just drop all their troops in that 1 turn. Even though you destroyed their orbiting fleet and have troops of your own in your ships, you can't invade or assist your own planet. They just get to wage ground war on you while you watch from orbit. The technology tree is a bit off, as well. While the techs are powerful and helpful, the planatary improvements are prohibitavely expensive and take extreme amounts of time to build on non-productive worlds. Even high-production lava planet systems will spend several turn to make a single building. So while you can improve your high-production planets in a reasonable amount of time, that just means the rest of your empire is sad. When games are expected to take like 200-300 turns and you don't really have a decent number of systems colonized until turn 70 and then it tells you that a single t1 building is going to take 15 turns to build it's just like... what's the point? By the time you get the planet up to having decent production the game is over and it contributed nothing... other that sucking up dust on maintenance cost for those buildings. So you primarily end up using the domestic research trees to unlock strategic resources so you can build a few things on your core planets and bigger lasers on your ships... which is a problem for some governements becuase that forces you to go militaristic... when you really just want to be industrial/pacifist.
Overall, if you're looking for a MoO experience that's a bit more complicated than the new one then you may want to give this a shot. You get to explore and plan out how to grab the best planets with the resources you want to build the empire you want. If you're a stellaris fan, then stay away as this is not a broken economy simulator where you just spam your starting unit to win.

TL;DR: This game has breadth but is ultimately shallow. It's a decent 4X game with too many features, too many dynamics, many of which become a chore to take care of. The story elemets of the game are over-done and undercut the overall experience.
------------
Endless Space 2 is a well-polished game. It works well, runs smooth and doesn't crash. But these are never sufficient reasons to play a game over and over. The two major flaws are writing and game mechanics.
Let's look at the writing. I'll leave it for others to focus on the mechanics.
The first thing you notice when you play your first game -- after the reassuring 4X game setup options -- is the cutscene video for your faction. The problem with these "faction introductions" is that each faction has an obvious glaring flaw which the faction leader is oblivious to.
Both the flaws and the lack of self-knowledge on the part of the leaders prevent you from identifying with the faction. You wouldn't want to live under any of these factions, you don't think the leader would treat you well if you worked for him, and it feels wrong to expand their malign influence to other star-systems.
Yes, this is an empire building game in which the writers invite you to feel guilt about the core mechanic of the game AT THE OUTSET!
In Civilization 5, one feels that extending the influence of one's faction over the world is unquestionably NOT a bad thing. The faction introductions in Civ are sincere in their praise for the both the leader and the faction. If you play as Shaka Zulu, then you are 100% behind your Impi warriors. Spreading your Zulu religion over nearby City States is good for those City States. City States will often ASK you to do just that. If you had to work for Shaka, you feel that he'd treat you well.
Endless Space 2 has writing which is more subversive.
The "United Empire" faction for example is clearly a malign influence on its own people. They remind you of the "Advent" leadership in the XCOM series, all propaganda and disqueiting turns-of-phrase which hint at gross injustice behind the scenes. Similar stories have been written for each faction.
As a result, you can never really get behind your faction. A war between your faction and another becomes NOT "a war between you and these aggressive ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s who declared war on you", but "a war between the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s you represent and some other ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, neither of whom will deliver a better life."
Endless Space 2 imparts a dystopian, despairing feeling to the gamer, in which your leader is a highly questionable individual. For example, the Horatio faction leader exhorts you to help "Make Horatio Great Again". The writers must feel very clever for having put this in -- you can imagine them all laughing in the office.
However by writing this in, the writers broke the "fourth wall" -- the dramatic device which separates actors (in-game) from audience (you the player). They burst the bubble of fiction that you want to be immersed in. This is the antithesis of what you want from a Space Sim -- escape from the real world, into another world in a different time, with a sense of purpose, where you have a clear mission.
By sticking in references to politics in 2017, the writers show that they're just NOT sincere in their world-building. The writing says more about the writers -- who are basically showing off, virtue-signalling and attention-seeking -- than it does about the gamer.
These writers have badly let down what could have been a great game, by undercutting its core mechanic with superior-than-thou commentary, inviting you to doubt your faction and despair of your leader.
Attempts to shunt "plot twists" into the factions end up giving the story a "light-hearted" feel which is totally at odds with the core game concept.
The overall effect of writing in this game is dissonance between what you want as a gamer (immersion which fulfils your desire to escape from the real world), what the game promised (the same as what you wanted), and what the game actually delivers (a disappointing hollow feeling that you've wasted your time).

Played this game a lot on PS3, but bought it on Steam because I love it so much. Graphics are great, especially with the motion capture of the faces, which not only make the character models look more realistic, but also play a part in interrogation, where you will have to see a character's expression and decide if they are lying or not (like the show Lie To Me). This is not only extremely unique and keeps the game fresh, it also is surprisingly challenging. The story is effing fantastic; not only are a lot of the individual cases themselves compelling, there are times where they show Cole's (the main character) past or when he's off duty, and these scenes are equally as interesting, even downright jaw-dropping at times. I also have to add how immersive this is, from the city of LA that is actually modelled after 1940s LA, to the fact that you can walk around a crime scene and examine clues. I really felt like a detective in 1940s LA. You even get to meet real people like Mickey Cohen, how awesome is that? However, this game has issues. tl;dr: Best space 4x since Master of Orion 2.
-----------------------------------------------------
I very rarely write reviews, the main reason being that I'm not very good at doing so. Most of the time I couldn't tell you why exactly I like one game while another one doesn't click with me.
It is much the same with Endless Space 2. I'm enjoying it immensely and have already completed three games in my limited spare time since it came out.
I love the asymmetric race design. Every single one of them has something unique that draws me in (some more so than others, but that's simply a matter of preference). I love the stories, told through the factions quests, the minor civilizations (although they could be fleshed out a little more) and the Academy (that's where the in-game heroes come from).
I like the sense of exploration, which is mainly driven through the ability to explore curiosities on planets which might reveal any kind of goody (or not so goody, watch out for pirates!). That is further helped by the need to secure strategic resources, and the hunt for luxury resources that provide welcome benefits to your empire.
I even like the battles and the accompanying ship design. Although I undoubtedly still have much to learn, they are far more "deep" than they might seem at first glance. Designing the right ships for the right circumstance and choosing the right tactic against the enemy fleet's strengths and weaknesses does provide room for serious decision making. And they do look fantastic indeed!
There are a few minor gripes. Some mechanics are a little opaque and could be explained better. Performance worsens with game length, although that is far from uncommon in 4x games. So far, I did not run into any crippling performance issues, and my PC is a good few years old by now.
Overall, for me it's at this point (39 hours in) the best space 4x since Master of Orion II - a game which has never been surpassed so far in my eyes. Endless Space 2 just might do the trick, or at least prove equally engaging as that old classic.

Played this game a lot on PS3, but bought it on Steam because I love it so much. Graphics are great, especially with the motion capture of the faces, which not only make the character models look more realistic, but also play a part in interrogation, where you will have to see a character's expression and decide if they are lying or not (like the show Lie To Me). This is not only extremely unique and keeps the game fresh, it also is surprisingly challenging. The story is effing fantastic; not only are a lot of the individual cases themselves compelling, there are times where they show Cole's (the main character) past or when he's off duty, and these scenes are equally as interesting, even downright jaw-dropping at times. I also have to add how immersive this is, from the city of LA that is actually modelled after 1940s LA, to the fact that you can walk around a crime scene and examine clues. I really felt like a detective in 1940s LA. You even get to meet real people like Mickey Cohen, how awesome is that? However, this game has issues. Firstly, on the PC version, it suffers from texture pop-in when driving around the city, and I don't think there's a fix for this. Next, while I did say a lot of cases are interesting, there are a couple that are slow and boring. In addition, there really isn't much to do off-duty; you can't run over people because you play as a cop and that wouldn't make sense, there are side missions but they eventually get repetitive (usually involves shooting a few baddies, you can finish these in 5 minutes), there are landmarks to check out (which is actually pretty cool because like I said, it's modelled after 1940s LA) but it's not something most people would honestly bother about, and you can collect vehicles scattered about LA. Don't get excited, you can't actually ride the cars after you collect them. All that happens is that you can visit them in a showroom, and that's it. Riveting. However, these points aside, I still think this game is fantastic, and easily one of the most underrated games ever.

Overall, I reccomend the game for the price if you can find it on sale for £5 or less. It is a really long game and the entire charm and unique-ness of the game wears off a few hours in. Personally, I find myself too stupid to be able to solve some of the later cases and it didn't help that by that point I just wanted the game to end. The game, at least for me, got rather dull about 15 hours in which is roughly around the 1/3 - halfway point in the game. The only reason I carried on with the game was because I heard that the story towards the end start's getting really good. But 10 hours later I was more bored than I could be and I just decided I couldn't be bothered to finish it. So I watched the ending on YouTube.
The game is pretty much a detective game where you have to walk around crime scenes to find clues and then interview people for information. On the interviews you have to ask questions and then you get the choice to say whether they are telling the truth, to doubt what they are saying or to show evidence (from the clues you found at the crime scenes) that they are lying. You determine whether they are telling the truth or not by how they react. The game used clever face scanning technology to scan people's faces and movements so they look realistic which, while cool, does look a little strange, isn't the best quality and also is the reason the game is locked to 30fps on the PC with no simple way to unlock it. Also, for someone who suffer's from minor autism, I personally have a hard time reading the people's faces to tell whether they are lying or not! You also have shooting and driving sections, but these are rather generic and get dull fast. The shooting sections are fun but are always really short and thankfully the driving sections can be skippable (hold down the button you use to enter the car and your partner will drive instead of you).
The game is fun at first. The first few levels in the game are great fun and you feel very clever. However the game starts to get rather confusing and difficult towards the end and the games charm does slowly start to fade so I never finished the game. However I bought the game on sale and I have enjoyed my time with it. However I never finished it and I am done with it. But I don't feel like I was ripped off so I still reccomend the game.
P.S. The PC port is not that great. The game is locked to 30fps due to the face animation technology used in the game. the graphics are a little dated and there is a lot of pop up. However, if you play the game just for the actual detective parts and don't really care about the shooting or driving sections (which thankfully are skippable if you fail them a few times) then this shouldn't really bother you. However it is something to keep in mind.

This game is actually the most tantalizing thing that has ever graced the world of strategy gaming. This game was born of Paradox interatives divine immaculate conception and mirrors this fact by the nature of the game; the challenges in which can often being overcome by "putting a baby in it". However, there is much more to the game than just mass parenthood. The game offers a level of politcal intrigue that goes far beyond the common strategy game. While most grand strategy games only offer the options of "invade" or "dont invade" Crusader kings offers a tactical third option of "Insert Baby and Inherit". While its older brother Europa Universalis offers more options, I feel like Crusader kings is an amazing all around game and anyone who wants more out of a strategy game than just combat should try it.

Short review - full review later - having too much fun playing!!
Would I recommend this game  - yes. Are there things I'd like tweaked - surely. Overall, it's an excellent followup.
I really wish they'd put their mind to a Civilization type game and give tired, unappreciative of it's fans, snooty old Firaxis a run for it's money. I have no doubt Amplitude would knock it out of the park.
Back to the game:
It's a little daunting getting into the game thankfully the tutorial is quite good at prodding you to do things.
The early expansion is fun as it is in most 4X games and there's lots of excitement trying to find another system you can colonize.
There are a few things which bug me: The technology descriptions/names are so unintuitive - there's no Pottery or Gunpowder techs - it's all fancy scientific names which don't really give you an idea of what they do. A neat thing for them to do would be to have a plain simple description that could be given as a tool tip as to what the tech does. That way you could know immediately what you're getting (e.g. Metallic Plate genetics - hmm what does that mean - hover over - tool tip says - give you better armor for your ships to protect against lasers). It's a minor point but it does increase the learning curve.
Next is the diplomacy: The AI seems to have an immediate tendency to dislike you. Similar to Civ VI - it's tough to get them to like you. However, at least in ES2 you can get them to like you and they are loyal and not stab you in the back at the end of the game because that's "fun". For those of you who haven't played CIv VI - there is no point in being friends is they will almost always turn on you by the end of the game because that's "fun" according to tired old Firaxis.
Finally is the difficulty: Even on easy, I find the game a challenge. I just wanted to play a peaceful build game in my first fiew playthroughs but the AI always attacks me with giant fleets forcing me to try to fight them back. Frustratingly, even though I'm on easy - they're tied or ahead of me in techs so I find myself getting beaten back. That's one thing Firaxis does a good job of is the level of play is well managed. On the easiest levels of the Civ games you almost can't lose which is the way it should be - that way you can really learn the game without the stress of worrying about the AI.
So I've saida lot about things I'd like tweaked - why am I saying Yes/thumbs up?
The above things (with the exception of the difficulty) do not ruin the experience - the rest of this fantastic game make up for the shortcomings: the very unique factions (very very different play experiences depending on the faction you use), it's fun building your ships, the political system is very cool too (depending on what party that wins in the elections affects what laws you can use which affect how your empire grows/prospers - for example if the military party wins the election you can pass laws that may make it cheaper to build ships or get more men to fight).
I highly recommend this game however
- the learning curve is pretty high because it's a very deep game - always something to figure out
- the way the battles are determined is different - you watch a cinematic which shows you the battle - you don't actually control anything other than some variables you pick before it starts. It's not a big deal but may be for some
- it's a space Civ game which sometimes can be a little hard to get into if you prefer regular civ games - specifically challenging is the lack of land masses which then don't allow defensive positions in the same way so you end up having to have masses of ships on every colony to prevent losing a system. It's also harder to visualize your Civ as it's just a black space map with planets/stars scattered around
-
That being said, if your a space civ fan get it, if your a regular civ fan get it. It's much better than Civ VI and probably a little better than Stellaris. Amplitude is a great company which supports it's products so I expect lots of added content and features

So in this game you pay as a legal criminal who works to take out the competition who don't have the same backing of the government. Okay... in all seriousness the player character is (mostly) a decent guy, but your fellow policemen tend to be either bitter, corrupt, or narrow-minded. And while the last of those makes sense for the 1940's, it still ensured that my opinion of police in this game is more or less what it is IRL: a handful of good people in a sea of jerks who are no better than the people they throw in jail.
Anyway... gamey. You search crime scenes for things, interrogate people about the things you find, and sometimes shoot people since these are American police and they like to do that sort of thing. Though at least in this case all the people you are forced to shoot tend to be firing back at you, so I guess that's justifiable. While the gameplay isn't broken, it just... didn't work for me. I was bored alot of the time and the game choosing to rate my performance promoted save scumming and looking for guides rather than working things out for myself. And while I suppose it is my fault for deciding to skip the "fun" of figuring out things for myself, I just felt uninterested and wanted to be done with it all...
...well, until the late parts of the game, when things heat up and interesting plot stuff actually starts happening. And while the final level is a bit absurd by being a massive gunfight and a rushed ending with alot of unresolved messes, at least the stuff before it was interesting and kept me wanting to see where things would end up.
I'm not sure about this game. It felt really long and the first half was profoundly lacking in excitement. I suppose that would be realistic: most police stuff is samey and boring I expect. But the "realism" here came at the cost of fun, and I could barely play more than a case at a time before I had to go do something else to entertain myself.
But it's not a bad game. It's just not for me. I'll give this a "yes" because it works, does get better later on, and that there is no "maybe" option on Steam and I don't dislike this game enough to give it a "no".

I can't in good conscience recommend that anyone buy this game.
The factions are nicely done and they are right to heavily suggest players use the pre-made because it does give a stronger narrative experience. But as a 4X this game just doesn't work. Diplomacy is completely broken and counter intuitive - I just signed an alliance. What happens next turn is my new ally (proportionally 1/5 my size) negotiates peace for me (without telling me) on incredibly bad terms in a war I was completely winning and where I wanted to exterminate the enemy (because if you are at peace with them, this enemy can steal your planets back without going to war). THANKS MUM - but I can conduct my own wars thank you. Now that may get fixed, but what kills the game for me is combat.
Combat is non-existant just like in a paradox game. But unlike a paradox game they've decided to give you endless and pointless screens. The space combat is literally 2 types of attack with 2 types of defence. Guess what? Each type of defence negates one form of attack. So long term combat is looking to see which type of attack/defence combo your enemy has and re-speccing your fleet. Guess what? Your enemies can respec too. HURRAH. Welcome to re-spec wars. Utterly utterly tedious.
Just badly constructed game play from a studio that isn't young enough to get away with this sort of stuff anymore.
EDIT: I received two unprompted messages from the developer. I'm really not sure I approve of that. I'm 37 and pretty tough, but I used to play PC games when I was 14/15 and I think that back then I would have felt pressured. In any event I stand by my review. This games isn't terrible - but it is not one that I think others should buy.

Short review - full review later - having too much fun playing!!
Would I recommend this game  - yes. Are there things I'd like tweaked - surely. Overall, it's an excellent followup.
I really wish they'd put their mind to a Civilization type game and give tired, unappreciative of it's fans, snooty old Firaxis a run for it's money. I have no doubt Amplitude would knock it out of the park.
Back to the game:
It's a little daunting getting into the game thankfully the tutorial is quite good at prodding you to do things.
The early expansion is fun as it is in most 4X games and there's lots of excitement trying to find another system you can colonize.
There are a few things which bug me: The technology descriptions/names are so unintuitive - there's no Pottery or Gunpowder techs - it's all fancy scientific names which don't really give you an idea of what they do. A neat thing for them to do would be to have a plain simple description that could be given as a tool tip as to what the tech does. That way you could know immediately what you're getting (e.g. Metallic Plate genetics - hmm what does that mean - hover over - tool tip says - give you better armor for your ships to protect against lasers). It's a minor point but it does increase the learning curve.
Next is the diplomacy: The AI seems to have an immediate tendency to dislike you. Similar to Civ VI - it's tough to get them to like you. However, at least in ES2 you can get them to like you and they are loyal and not stab you in the back at the end of the game because that's "fun". For those of you who haven't played CIv VI - there is no point in being friends is they will almost always turn on you by the end of the game because that's "fun" according to tired old Firaxis.
Finally is the difficulty: Even on easy, I find the game a challenge. I just wanted to play a peaceful build game in my first fiew playthroughs but the AI always attacks me with giant fleets forcing me to try to fight them back. Frustratingly, even though I'm on easy - they're tied or ahead of me in techs so I find myself getting beaten back. That's one thing Firaxis does a good job of is the level of play is well managed. On the easiest levels of the Civ games you almost can't lose which is the way it should be - that way you can really learn the game without the stress of worrying about the AI.
So I've saida lot about things I'd like tweaked - why am I saying Yes/thumbs up?
The above things (with the exception of the difficulty) do not ruin the experience - the rest of this fantastic game make up for the shortcomings: the very unique factions (very very different play experiences depending on the faction you use), it's fun building your ships, the political system is very cool too (depending on what party that wins in the elections affects what laws you can use which affect how your empire grows/prospers - for example if the military party wins the election you can pass laws that may make it cheaper to build ships or get more men to fight).
I highly recommend this game however
- the learning curve is pretty high because it's a very deep game - always something to figure out
- the way the battles are determined is different - you watch a cinematic which shows you the battle - you don't actually control anything other than some variables you pick before it starts. It's not a big deal but may be for some
- it's a space Civ game which sometimes can be a little hard to get into if you prefer regular civ games - specifically challenging is the lack of land masses which then don't allow defensive positions in the same way so you end up having to have masses of ships on every colony to prevent losing a system. It's also harder to visualize your Civ as it's just a black space map with planets/stars scattered around
-
That being said, if your a space civ fan get it, if your a regular civ fan get it. It's much better than Civ VI and probably a little better than Stellaris. Amplitude is a great company which supports it's products so I expect lots of added content and features

Short review - full review later - having too much fun playing!!
Would I recommend this game  - yes. Are there things I'd like tweaked - surely. Overall, it's an excellent followup.
I really wish they'd put their mind to a Civilization type game and give tired, unappreciative of it's fans, snooty old Firaxis a run for it's money. I have no doubt Amplitude would knock it out of the park.
Back to the game:
It's a little daunting getting into the game thankfully the tutorial is quite good at prodding you to do things.
The early expansion is fun as it is in most 4X games and there's lots of excitement trying to find another system you can colonize.
There are a few things which bug me: The technology descriptions/names are so unintuitive - there's no Pottery or Gunpowder techs - it's all fancy scientific names which don't really give you an idea of what they do. A neat thing for them to do would be to have a plain simple description that could be given as a tool tip as to what the tech does. That way you could know immediately what you're getting (e.g. Metallic Plate genetics - hmm what does that mean - hover over - tool tip says - give you better armor for your ships to protect against lasers). It's a minor point but it does increase the learning curve.
Next is the diplomacy: The AI seems to have an immediate tendency to dislike you. Similar to Civ VI - it's tough to get them to like you. However, at least in ES2 you can get them to like you and they are loyal and not stab you in the back at the end of the game because that's "fun". For those of you who haven't played CIv VI - there is no point in being friends is they will almost always turn on you by the end of the game because that's "fun" according to tired old Firaxis.
Finally is the difficulty: Even on easy, I find the game a challenge. I just wanted to play a peaceful build game in my first fiew playthroughs but the AI always attacks me with giant fleets forcing me to try to fight them back. Frustratingly, even though I'm on easy - they're tied or ahead of me in techs so I find myself getting beaten back. That's one thing Firaxis does a good job of is the level of play is well managed. On the easiest levels of the Civ games you almost can't lose which is the way it should be - that way you can really learn the game without the stress of worrying about the AI.
So I've saida lot about things I'd like tweaked - why am I saying Yes/thumbs up?
The above things (with the exception of the difficulty) do not ruin the experience - the rest of this fantastic game make up for the shortcomings: the very unique factions (very very different play experiences depending on the faction you use), it's fun building your ships, the political system is very cool too (depending on what party that wins in the elections affects what laws you can use which affect how your empire grows/prospers - for example if the military party wins the election you can pass laws that may make it cheaper to build ships or get more men to fight).
I highly recommend this game however
- the learning curve is pretty high because it's a very deep game - always something to figure out
- the way the battles are determined is different - you watch a cinematic which shows you the battle - you don't actually control anything other than some variables you pick before it starts. It's not a big deal but may be for some
- it's a space Civ game which sometimes can be a little hard to get into if you prefer regular civ games - specifically challenging is the lack of land masses which then don't allow defensive positions in the same way so you end up having to have masses of ships on every colony to prevent losing a system. It's also harder to visualize your Civ as it's just a black space map with planets/stars scattered around
-
That being said, if your a space civ fan get it, if your a regular civ fan get it. It's much better than Civ VI and probably a little better than Stellaris. Amplitude is a great company which supports it's products so I expect lots of added content and features

Warning: The game is fresh out of it's early access stage and still has quite a few bugs to be worked through, if your unsure, wait until its had a few patches then try it.
Despite the aformentioned bugs, Endless space 2 really is just a plain damn good game that has been blessed with Devs that really care about it working well and are doing a fantastic job ad shoring up it's weak spots. Esentially a straight upgrade of the origional Endless Space, players of the first game will get the basic gist of the gameplay, with most of the differences being vastly improved user interfaces, as well as some fantastic art (and even little cinematics) that add depth and flavor to the universe. With old and new factions avalible, Endless space 2 does a better job at differentiating thevarious races, from the Voyadani and their nomadic style, to how the Lumeris don't colonize but rather BUY entire systems.
However, some new little things have been added and changed that add new little adges to the game, first being missions that not only actually ask you to put in work for them, but actually have little stories of their own, especially your faction specific lore story that acts like an actual main plotline. Second: there are not minor, smaller races that are not themselves playable but can be encountered, invaded, negotiated with, and even assimilated into your empire. Third: there is a bigger focus on population and type, instead of just having regular population, you can end up having a vast amount of multi-species interaction in your empire, assimilated populations from enemies, rescuing refugee aliens, or simple intergalactic travel and migration. Fourth: your empire's government is far more in depth now, with polls for the ruling parties (Militarists, scientists, ecologists etc.) that affect what laws you can pass to give you bonuses to everything from industry to ship costs. and finally, my favorite part: You can have privateers! With mercenary ships and the right research, you can make a privateer fleet to attack other's without being identified, great for when that pesky peace treaty stands in the way of a system you need, or you need an ally to move that damn ship so you can finish a mission!
All in all, despite its big bugs, the game is worth a look if your into turn based/empire building games!

Just another 4X game in space in the same vein as its predecessor and Endless Legend. You manage your faction's empire through a number of systems across multiple constellations in a single galaxy. Your resources come in the standard flair of food, industry, influence, science, and dust (which is the currency/$ monicker for the Endless franchise) - FIDSI is the acronym they use in the game. You'll also see your fair share of strategic and luxury resources that can impact your military and civilian needs. You can build trade routes to increase FIDSI production, visit the marketplace, allowing you to buyout resources (including a market trend line chart), and initiate combat with other factions' fleets. You can also explore neighboring systems' "curiosities" to receive resources or even new technologies.
What separates it from say, the Civilization series, are the concepts of quests/legendary deeds and heroes/champions that play crucial roles in the game. Quests/deeds come in the form of tasks that you'd need to complete either by sending a fleet to a system to do something, building/doing something X amount of times before any other player, or being the first to build/do something X times. Heroes/champions are unique units in the game that can either be assigned to a fleet or as a governor to a system. Heroes naturally level up over time (or by defeating enemy fleets) and earn abilities that can impact FIDSI production, fleet combat efficiency, or political agendas.
Politics and government are also pretty deep compared to other 4X games. Like most other games, you can establish various forms of governments, democracy, anarchy, etc. But unlike others, there are elections that are held every 20 turns. During those elections, you have the chance to influence the empire's decision to vote for a ruling party, say Militarists, Industrialists, etc. When a ruling party is elected, it brings along a number of laws that you can pass to affect FIDSI or fleets on an empire-wide level. The political alignment of your populace in the empire is swayed depending on what you research in the technology tree, assign to your industry construction queue, and other actions in the game. Various species also have political alignments and may react positively/negatively to your actions.
Minor factions are strewn across the galaxy and can give a lot of benefits should you behave cordially with them. Or you can declare war on them. Ultimately, you can assimilate them either way and put their system under your control, along with all their luxury and strategic resources. The more friends you have, the quicker you'll find yourself amassing a lot of FIDSI early in the game, which can put you well ahead of your opponents.
A great 4X game in space with a good amount of complexity and depth. A bit intimidating at first for those coming from the Civilization series, but after a couple of games you will get the hang of it. Marred by a few bugs at its current state, but the devs are actively listening both on Steam forums and in their own discussion board. Unfortunately, I can't say much for multiplayer experience.

I'll keep it smooth and ordered:
Pro:
- REAL mimics. They used a technology where they basically filmed the actors face and put it into the game. No animations, no face capture, you see real people there. That is the main selling point - at least for me - of the game because no other game used this since then. It is very expensive, that is why.
- REAL(istic) movements. The motion capture worked really well, I rarely see this detailed animations.
- Interesting cases. They're small full stories in themselves, but most of them somehow connects to the bigger picture. You start the game as a patrol, then as you move forward you became a detective. You solve cases at each different desk, but you only start to get the picture after half of the game.
- Good main story. It is beliveable, the characters are detailed, such as their motivations. The plot twist impressed me.
- I'd say nice cars as well, but that isn't a big thing to do these days.
Contra:
- Repetitive investigating. You use the same techniques and scripted animations over and over.
- Also repetitive street crimes. Car chases, thefts and shootings. These were the three main types. Some were interesting though.
- Annoying sound bugs. Had to restart the last mission from the beginning because couldn't heard sh*t from the last cutscene.
- 30 FPS lock. And it drops below 24 even on a strong config.

Pros:
Story! This game will keep you wanting more. What's around the next corner, what clues you can find, what people will reveal, and so on.
Asthetic is very good for the game, from the facial animations to the fashion and structures of the 40's!
Cons:
-Story. You're pretty much on rails the entire time, very, very little freeform involved in this game and its more similar to to those story-telling games you've been seeing as of late, like Walking Dead.
-Interrogations: What should be this game's shining star is it glaring weakness. There are several especially where the person being interrogated is sweating waterfalls, but they're still telling the truth besides having evidence that could prove otherwise, or vice versa. This makes or breaks this game and it's sad to see how inconsistent this part of the game is for how major of a role it takes.
-Guns and car chases: It really feels like they had no idea how to tweak this. Blind firing is really, really, VERY inaccurate to the point you can be point-blank to an enemy with a shotgun and still miss. So gunfights amount to shooting and soaking up damage on purpose.
Car chases are a nightmare because of 2 things:
1. You're a good cop, any damage, to vehicles, the enviornment, or people is on your head. One might argue this just makes the game more interesting. I was in this boat until...
2. Choice of vehicles and all criminals are hollywood stunt drivers. Most people, and I've read it on several forums and reviews, will only use the cop car they recieve. Part of the problem here is that most cars look the same to the average person of today, and they also find out they lose access to Street Crime sub-missions if they don't use a cop car, whose performance is questionable. On top of the 1# issue, criminals all seem to have magical speed and turning skill regardless of what vehicle they drive. Unless you memorize the route and staged issues, you'll never, ever be able to keep up on chases outside of just not losing them.
Summary:
L.A. Noire has awesome story, but just terrible, frustrating gameplay.

Warning: The game is fresh out of it's early access stage and still has quite a few bugs to be worked through, if your unsure, wait until its had a few patches then try it.
Despite the aformentioned bugs, Endless space 2 really is just a plain damn good game that has been blessed with Devs that really care about it working well and are doing a fantastic job ad shoring up it's weak spots. Esentially a straight upgrade of the origional Endless Space, players of the first game will get the basic gist of the gameplay, with most of the differences being vastly improved user interfaces, as well as some fantastic art (and even little cinematics) that add depth and flavor to the universe. With old and new factions avalible, Endless space 2 does a better job at differentiating thevarious races, from the Voyadani and their nomadic style, to how the Lumeris don't colonize but rather BUY entire systems.
However, some new little things have been added and changed that add new little adges to the game, first being missions that not only actually ask you to put in work for them, but actually have little stories of their own, especially your faction specific lore story that acts like an actual main plotline. Second: there are not minor, smaller races that are not themselves playable but can be encountered, invaded, negotiated with, and even assimilated into your empire. Third: there is a bigger focus on population and type, instead of just having regular population, you can end up having a vast amount of multi-species interaction in your empire, assimilated populations from enemies, rescuing refugee aliens, or simple intergalactic travel and migration. Fourth: your empire's government is far more in depth now, with polls for the ruling parties (Militarists, scientists, ecologists etc.) that affect what laws you can pass to give you bonuses to everything from industry to ship costs. and finally, my favorite part: You can have privateers! With mercenary ships and the right research, you can make a privateer fleet to attack other's without being identified, great for when that pesky peace treaty stands in the way of a system you need, or you need an ally to move that damn ship so you can finish a mission!
All in all, despite its big bugs, the game is worth a look if your into turn based/empire building games!

Warframe is a free to play action MMO that combines many aspects of Destiny and The Matrix in a somewhat engaging, if not repetitive, experience.
TL;DR I give this game a 7/10. Do I recommend this? Yes*
Story - Very poor, generic sci-fi story.
Sound - pretty good and about what you'd expect.
Music - nothing memorable.
Gameplay - Gunplay and melee feel fun.
Replayability - There are technically, maybe, 10 different game modes in PvE but you'll feel like you're doing the same few often.
Positives:
+Decent Graphics that run on my laptop w/ Integrated GPU at 50-60 fps on fair settings
+One of the larger playerbases on Steam (Usually around 40k online at any given time)
+Combat feels satisfying
+Lots of gore and gibs
+Fair sense of progression
Negatives:
-Highly reliant on grinding to progress (being made to level each weapon possible to max rank for mastery points)
-Virtually no story so there's a poor feeling of immersion (think lite Destiny)
-No initial character customization in the now accepted sense, sans choice of 3 initial Warframes, and basic weapons
-No memorable or engaging music, so put on some death metal
-Rarely does something feel "fresh" when progressing through the planets @grinding already mentioned
Final Verdict:
I would recommend playing this game because it's a free alternative to most traditional MMOs, but it's definitely not for everyone. Although the fast paced combat is probably the most refreshing and engaging part of this game, it does get old.
Buy it.

I begrundgingly played this whole game from beginning to end basically because I was interested in finding out where the story was leading, and because of the unique motion capture the game uses for the animation of characters. The best thing about the game is the acting, actually, with everything else being a bit of a drag.
Drag #1 Repetition of investigating crime scenes. Walk around until your controller rumbles and then pick up an item to look at it. Repeat until all clues are found at the crime scene.
Drag #2 Driving is not fun. The game encourages you to drive properly to the speed limit. When you crash you are berated by your partner in the car with you. This means you end up skipping all driving when the option is available, making it pretty useless.
Drag #3 All side missions are the same. Criminal on the loose! Go shoot them! Want to talk to them? Too bad, just shoot them! It's an easier game design.
The story is the best thing about this game, but even that dragged on for too long at too slow a pace. In fact, this would be better suited as a HBO series than a videogame. To put it simply, Endless Space 2 is a masterpiece.
I usually don't review games before completing them but I'm now on my third run with the Sophons and I think I now know enough to pull off a science victory, and I haven't played anything else since I downloaded it. For those who didn't play the first one, that's a testament to just how good it is. And for those who did, that's proof of what a new studio can do with an established concept and a lot more cash.
Endless Space (or at least the idea of it, I'm only guessing the same devs were involved) began life as the Final Frontier mod for the Beyond the Sword expansion for Civ IV - easily my favourite Civ expansion ever and one which completely transformed ideas of what could be done with the Civ engine. It also famously brought us the Next War mod for the main game that introduced Giant Death Robots. Mechs in Civ was always going to be fun, and Firaxis delivered.
Final Frontier turned the world map into a galaxy map, which you gradually expanded into by unlocking tech to enable you to colonise more planets in each solar system, and which in turn gave you access to resources needed to build higher level buildings and ships. As in Civ, movement and battles were standard turn-based strategy fare, with movement initially restriicted to starlanes, and then later (fast) wormholes and (slow) free-travel. It was great fun but at heart it was still fairly standard 4X fare.
Then along came Amplitude with Endless Space, a full-fledged version of the sort of thing Firaxis must've hoped they'd inspire by properly opening up Civ for modding. ES1 took the core mechanics and put them in a richly conceptualised universe, and took it in a distinctly RPG direction with heavily asymmetrical factions, upgradable ships, upgradable hero units, quests, the complicated four-directional tech tree, and the big question of who exactly the Endless were. It also brought a limited form of influencing combat by playing cards during the battles, fought in glorious close up. However, beyond the battles the graphical rewards were minimal, and given how long these games take to play through it did take me a while to go back after all I got was a pop up with a bit of text. Nevertheless, I did go back, quite a lot.
And it's on that latter point that those who've played ES1 will notice the biggest difference. ES2 is simply stunning. It's almost as if the devs have looked for every opportunity to sneak in more scenery, either (skippable) cut sequences or just pretty things, and they're still adding more (and this is a very good thing). Added to which, the interface is very, very clean. I've seen some reviews saying it's too clean, and I'd agree that new players will need some time to work out exactly what everything is and what it does, but that's just part of the fun of playing a great 4X and once you get used to it it really works. And as in ES1, probably the most complicated thing is that glorious tech tree and the associated quests it triggers. Finally I think I'm getting a mental map of it all, and then once I've won a game with the Sophons I get to have to re-think how it all works with a new faction, which I'll probably start as soon as I've got either a science or quest victory.
As for the factions, we only start with eight so expect a lot more DLC (Endless Legend turned into a significant, if worthwhile, investment). These are a mix of favourites from ES1 and the odd new one - but I won't spoil the fun because reading all the back stories is part of the fun. For Sophons fans, I love how they've played them for the comedy value by turning our slightly dull but cute scientists into risk-taking mad chemists. It's only a little detail but it really adds to how you feel about playing them. In my last game I went all out for expansion to capture and support a key solar system that was a bit too far out of reach for an early game push, survived the resulting economic meltdown, but finally succumbed to a population that wouldn't let me keep a government elected long enough to do anything useful about my reputation, which had collapsed along with my economy.
The government system is one of the biggest changes but (and I didn't play the tutorial) it's not obvious at first. Governments are made up of factions (scientists, industrialists, religious, etc) which can be headed by one of your heroes. Governments get voted for periodically, and can be overthrown if your popularity drops too low or you're spending influence faster than you can generate it. They also pass laws, which unlock according to which faction is in power and what share of the vote they have. This, it turns out, needs more attention that is initially obvious, but that pays off in the bonuses good management brings.
The only other noticeable change is in the combat. This has been simplified to a single card (or in the case of ground battles, one of three options), played before battle commences. Fleet tactics can also be assigned, but at the moment I'm yet to be convinced of the value of anything other than making sure your most aggressive ships head straight for the enemy. I wouldn't be surprised if this gets changed as Amplitude have a good history of adding new mechanics in DLC, rather than just spamming new factions. Even so, expect those factions to make significant changes to how you'll play the game.
So, to conclude. ES2 is ES1 with a few new mechanics and a proper budget, and that's a very, very, good thing. Fans of ES1 now have the game we knew Amplitude had in them, and newcomers to the series or the whole Endless lore get the joy of experiencing a hugely in-depth but still accessible turn-based strategy in one of the best realised universes of any 4X. And now I'm going back to that universe.

Solid 4x game, the factions are unique and interesting and unlike a lot of 4x games it keeps the pace up.
even on lower difficulty with fewer enemies the AI won't leave you to snowball too much.

the game has plenty of depth & mechanics and after 25 hours playing I still feel like there's things I havent explored enough yet.
Ship combat has massively improved compared to Endless Space 1. You still can't change or affect combat once it starts but the use of strategy & ship building is where you decide your combat. The right ship in the right spot with the right strategy can turn even a bad match-up around. (luckily) the AI seems to not take full advantage of this which can make a war turn in your favor after a few battles.
ground combat is there in the form of a rock-paper-scissor type ground forces with the addition of several strategies you can pick. not extremely in depth but more so than most other 4x games i've played.
while very cinematic and pretty, the scenes never felt too intrusive and are easily skipped or disabled.
I wasn't planning on recommending the game after getting stuck on the End Turn bug 3 times, but the new patch fixed the issue on all my saves, even the one I started on the 1.0.6 beta patch. even seems to have fixed some other issues with the AI as they suddenly decided to stop sitting on their asses and either attack me or seek friendly interactions.
all in all, great 4x game

Endless Space 2 is quite certainly an improvement in every way over Endless Space 1. That's not an exaggeration.
Whether visually, mechanically, or in terms of complexity...ES 2 is a very engaging game. The developers took lessons learned from both the prequel and from their fantasy 4x spinoff Endless Legend and crafted soemthing superior to both of those games.
Racial diversity and asymetry is a core part of the game. Each race (both old and new) have abilities, traits and gameplay mechanics unique to them in a very tangible way. One race pays off independent contractors to handle colonization for them while another will simply move a huge mothership into a system and claim ownership that way. There is a lot of personality there.
Lore. The lore is rich and each faction now has individual questlines to follow which reveal their history and origins.
Galaxy Map. Much more vibrant than before with civilian traffic now represented for colonization and movement of population between worlds.
Random events. Lots of these to work your way through including those that lead to longer quests and/or consequences for your empire.
Combat. I'm surprised to find myself enjoying combt more than in ES1. Visually it is more appealing and the more detailed approach to ship design adds good tactical options along with fleet movement cards which now house the various effects you might recognize from ES1's battle system.
Trade. I like the new trade system which requires you to put some thought into where and when to build trade companies. More engaging and immersive for sure.
The game had a bit of a rocky launch for people with certain hardware configurations (AMD related I believe). This lead to a showstopper bug in late games where turns would be stuck. This has now been resolved and the devs are constantly updating the game and responding to feedback.
The other real con is that there is so much new stuff that the game will probably feel a bit daunting to newcomers. Pay attention to the tutorials if you don't want to get swamped.
Overall, this game is highly recommended to anyone who likes space 4x games or even those just deciding to get into the genre.

I understand the frustration of many people who encountered one widespread gamebreaking bug. Before the most recent hotfix 1.0.52, players experienced a bug that made turns and battles endlessly process in the late game. This bug had apparently always been a recurring issue for the dev team and has now been officially fixed. Though some bugs certainly remain, the game is now in my opinion fully functional and sufficiently polished to be a full release game. I tend not to review games but this game has recieved too much bad press for how extraoridinary it is.
Pros:
-As far as game developers go, amplitude refuses to allow bugs to continue. They release patch after patch and are incredibly commited.
-Amplitude games in general are some of the most artistically beautiful strategy games I have ever played. The Endless Space series truly captures the beauty of space. The mystical and unfamiliar setting of endless space really lends to the beautiful art style.
-The game is satisfyingly simple. Though vastly simple compared to a grand strategy game, Endless Space 2 employs easily learned mechanics that seamlessly branch into more complexly varied play styles in the late game. The factions are a wonderful example of this. Each faction has a very unique element to it that lends greatly to it's own strength. Through exploitation of the unique strength of one's faction, a player can wildly alter the course of the game.
-The UI is very intuitive. Though certain aspects remain slightly clunky, it is one of the best interfaces I have seen in a 4X game.
-As a 4X game it plays very well to it's cores values. Exploring is a blast with unique and interesting things to find scattered across the galaxy. Expansion is also enjoyable as you manage the needs of an ever more complex empire. Extermination is one of the strongest of their values as you can see by the amazing battle system. Though little control is given to the player durring actual battles, such as many in other 4X games, the battles are nonetheless very satisfying spectacles affected by the players choices beforehand.
-The quests and story of the world adds an undeniable flavor to the game that is rather unique for many 4X games. Not only does the story add to the setting, it also adds to the gameplay through quest rewards.
Cons:
-The third X of the 4X's is arguably the weakest. Exploitation of minor factions is enjoyable, but diplomatic interactions with main factions remains limited. Though not limited compared to most 4X games, Endless space fails to shake up the formula when it comes to diplomacy. It remains mostly a "resources and treaties for resources and treaties" equivalent exchange system. The one new mechanic added, leveraging influence for demand, is an interesting concept but only about as useful as normal diplomacy
-The game is very minimalist. There is an everpresent culture of quality over quantity in Amplitude games and it shows. The tech tree is not the largest. Ship design is present, but it's very limited.
-It cannot be avoided that there were many bugs with the game upon release. As previously stated, most of the most frustrating issues have been resolved. The buyer must, however, be aware that, the developers' stalwart track record aside, the game is very large and complex with the potential for several technical issues. For most who play computer games, however, this should be a very familiar issue.
Overall, I've had a very enjoyable experience with this game. If you enjoy strategy games, I have no doubt you shall as well. Ignore the recent influx of bad reviews due to technical issues that have now been solved. This game is worth the price.

Just to be immediately clear, I would normally recommend this game. However, in its current state, it's virtually unplayable. I've started three separate games and had all of them brought to a grinding halt by three different bugs.
The first time, my saves simply refused to load. The game continued to run, music continued to play, and the menu continued to animate, but load game simply froze all ability to interact with any of it, forcing me to exit the game.
So, noticing that there was a more extensive tutorial, I decided in light of problems I'd had with the first playthrough that it might be prudent to go through that while I had my morning coffee. Three hours later, upon discovering the academy, the game again stopped responding to any sort of input when I'd try to view the system that housed the academy. After trying all sorts of things, including loading earlier saves, verifying my cache, and submitting a bug report on the official forums, I decided to start yet a third new game.
This time, I picked the Cravers. After languishing over menus and tech trees and thinking about what the best long-term strategy might be, I finally ended my first turn... only for the next turn to never come. I finally encountered the dreaded "infinite end turn" bug that everyone's been reporting... on my first damn turn. It's also worth noting that a hotfix was released today that was specifically supposed to address issues with ending turns, and this bug happened in that hotfixed version of the game.
As I said at the beginning of this review, normally I'd give more information about what's new or different in Endless Space 2 from Endless Space or Endless Legend, and how it all works, and whatever, but the game is so unstable that I have yet to get more than 80 turns into a game before something forces me to start a new game.

The first major bug prevents combat from resolving. When attacking, the game sits and never goes past the AI determining what strategy will be used. The turn cannot be ended because you are in combat, but the combat screen never progresses.
The second major bug prevents your next turn from beginning. When ending your turn, the game sits and never goes past the AI processing actions. All of the AI say "Player Ready", but nothing happens.
I'm sincerely dissapointed by Endless Space 2. I didn't expect it to be perfect, but I did expect to be playable.

At first its great. You get into a server, spawn with a group of fellow knights and charge with bloodcurtling screams into a melee. Limbs flying, heads spinning, swords clashing, arrows flying. You think wow this is great.
