You run at him, furiously swinging and tasting sweet vengence. He blocks your swing as if you were trying to hit with a water noodle. Before you can say "I used to be an adventurer like you", you get shot in the face.
At this point you close the game in frustration, and have two options. You paste a text image middle finger in the review.
Or you man up, fire the game back up later, and slowly learn the amount of detail and depth of combat that was placed into this game. Fight in duels that put Spartacus fight scenes to shame, and master different weapon techniques. You can fight dirty, honorably, or brutally. Sheikh Hakim of Ascalon and Beersheba was put into a peculiar situation whereupon he needed an heir to his titles.  As fond as Hakim was of his wife, Fatima, his vassals were chortling behind his back: he only had the one wife!  Well, one wife became two, and two daughters became three.
Things became more desperate as the the good Sheikh advanced in age.  Very concerned about having an heir to claim his titles and take care of his dynasty, Hakim took another wife, and yet another.  Fortunately his many daughters - six now - were betrothed to men who would be valuable (if mercurial) allies against the Emir who coveted the Sheikh's territory.
At last, a son was born to Hakim and Fatima.  Abdulallah would be groomed and prepared to become the best hope for the Sheikhdom of Ascalon and Beersheba.  In time, Abdulallah would prove himself by going on Hajj to Mecca and fighting rampaging Crusaders bound for nearby Jerusalem.  When Sheikh Hakim spoke his final words - the Mohammedan Confession - his son became the lord at long last.
Abdulallah's first task as Sheikh of Ascalon and Beersheba was to rise up and defeat the tyrannical Emir who dared to revoke his dynastic titles upon his father's death.  With the help of Allah - and a few coins well spent on Turkish mercenaries - he did just that.

Nothing guides your interactions.  I'm loosing influence to a much smaller empire.  Why?  Who knows?  It's buried somewhere in the overly complex menu system.  Ground attack in my system?  Well, nothing notifies me that was coming.
Ground attack mechanics?  How do I increase my designs to hold troops?  No idea...nothing points the way.  Refill troops after a lopsided attack wipes my guys out?  Go ask forums because nothing in the game helps you out.  Why is the A.I. so capable / have so many ground attack ships with 1/3 the economy?
Many reviewers understand Endless games from prior experience, but take it from a newcomer, this UIX is poorly designed in the extreme.  Looks nice though.
Developers, fix your balance issues...include REAL tutorial and consider how you approach a new player.
On the plus side, played to turn 120 and no freezing issues.  But I'm running a seriously overpowered rig and a super fast internet connection.
I, however, did see the "ground combat won't resolve" issue as well as weird order-of-operation mechanics.   Mainly because the game doesn't freeze input during turn processing...weird as it's WAY harder to maintain internal state with that kind of design.  I suspect, as a developer myself, that the lack of restricting input during a end/ start of turn sequences are responsible for a lot of the bugs being reported.  Folks are changing data in unexpected ways and the underlying state machine cannot process it.
For now this game is a hard "NO" for me.

A great game, something very special about it. I highly recommend it.

On the plus side Ark has a fantastically immersive environment, a huge variety of dinosaurs, resources, crafting and building recipes, and basically just a ton of content. The construction system is loads of fun, you can craft an amazing number of items, clothing, recipes, and there's lots to explore. You could play every day for months and not see all there is to see. Did I mention it's huge?
On the negative side? Well, basically it's buggy. It's called early access, but development seems to be focused on adding even more content, rather than addressing bugs. If you love it or hate it depends on how much the bugs bug you.

1. Server lag, rubber-banding, teleporting, etc. Server lags to the point of making certain aspects of the game unplayable are common, especially on public servers. What aspects of the game? Just the trivial aspects of exploring and combat. You are free to explore as long as you don't come close to any dinos, or near any cliffs: You might find yourself accidentally walking off a cliff due to server lag, or hit by a dino several times before the visual of the dino is apparent. Combat? Well, how do you hit a dino if you don't really know where it is? The visual representation of the dino might be off by 50 yards from where it actually is. If you play on a public server, you may invest a few dozen hours building up a character, and then find on a weekend that you want to play, server lag prevents you from playing. Or you might have to start over in a server that you hope has less lag. Note that you can cure this issue by playing it in single player mode, so if that is your preference, this problem goes away.
2. Visual anomalies. These can range from amusing, such as trees and rocks hovering in mid-air, to very annoying, such as the dreaded "getting stuck" bug. There are spots on the map where the visual representation doesn't match the physics. Meaning that you might walk across a crack in some rocks that looks 2 feet deep and 3 feet wide, but isn't. And you get trapped. The solution (according to their own tech support) is to let your character starve to death, and respawn someplace else. Starving yourself to death could take 30 – 60 minutes, and of course you loose all your gear.
3. Time investment. I personally don't find this an issue, but many people are annoyed by the amount of time you have to invest in certain activities, especially taming high level dinos. And it's true that some of these can take hours, or 10s of hours. But this just a game setting, that can be changed by the server admin, so this can be cured by playing a private server with fast setting, or doing single player mode and setting it yourself.

A solid game is here somewhere but...
Tutorial is a joke.  Being new to the endless fanchise the mechanics are incomprehensible and the "Tutorial" shows up and disappears on what seems like a whim.   No comprehensive "here's how you accomplish X"...just some basic windows that pop up IF you click something it deems interesting.  You'll have to stumble onto those, because the wizard is just plain broken.
UIX render is super pretty, even inspiring.  The UIX interaction (the other side of "UIX") is a complete mess.  Take it from a newcomer, these screens are obtuse in the extreme.  Info cards are so nice but what triggers them is often hard to understand.
Nothing guides your interactions.  I'm loosing influence to a much smaller empire.  Why?  Who knows?  It's buried somewhere in the overly complex menu system.  Ground attack in my system?  Well, nothing notifies me that was coming.
Ground attack mechanics?  How do I increase my designs to hold troops?  No idea...nothing points the way.  Refill troops after a lopsided attack wipes my guys out?  Go ask forums because nothing in the game helps you out.  Why is the A.I. so capable / have so many ground attack ships with 1/3 the economy?
Many reviewers understand Endless games from prior experience, but take it from a newcomer, this UIX is poorly designed in the extreme.  Looks nice though.
Developers, fix your balance issues...include REAL tutorial and consider how you approach a new player.
On the plus side, played to turn 120 and no freezing issues.  But I'm running a seriously overpowered rig and a super fast internet connection.
I, however, did see the "ground combat won't resolve" issue as well as weird order-of-operation mechanics.   Mainly because the game doesn't freeze input during turn processing...weird as it's WAY harder to maintain internal state with that kind of design.  I suspect, as a developer myself, that the lack of restricting input during a end/ start of turn sequences are responsible for a lot of the bugs being reported.  Folks are changing data in unexpected ways and the underlying state machine cannot process it.
For now this game is a hard "NO" for me.

Crusader Kings II: The latest entry in the Paradox Grand Strategy game lineup.
Unlike in most of Paradox's strategy games, you take control not of an entire nation, but of the rulers within that nation. If your ruler has no heir, it's game over. Duke, King, and Emperor are all well represented here. The base game starts in a pretty historical 1066 (the Old Gods expansion pushes it back to 876). However, once you unpause it, history is thrown out the window. Everything can change from there on out.
Once you are familar with the UI and pretty much all the features of it, which can take a while as Paradox's tutorial is not extremely helpful in that regard, you are ready to start a real campaign. You set the campaign goals, forma  specific empire or Dutchy, make your dynasty last to the end of the game, 1453. It's up to YOU.
Controling the leader is a nice change of pace as well, becaus eit adds an RPG like mechanic to a strategy game. Many things can happen to your character, and ultimatly death, and then you take control of his/her heir. The mechanics are fleshed out and deep. They feel meaningful. You need to have a reason to declare war, and a good portion of the time you only have claims to one province at a time. This makes conquest difficult, but rewarding a little more realistic than other Paradox games.
The graphics are pretty good for a strategy game of this nature, where you are essentailly staring at a map waiting for things to change. The Clauswitz engien does well in that regard. All the artwork ingame is beautifully done and looks marvelous.
In the end, the only thing that truly bugs me is the amount of DLC. Many of it is purly cosmetic and is not needed to fully enjoy the game, but they do add to the atmostphere. If you are to get any of the DLC make sure to get Sword of Islam, The Republic. The Old Gods, and The Legacy of Rome as those are the meaty expansion type DLC's. If you want a very ahistorical scenario pick up "The Sunest Invasion" to have the Aztecs bid for control of Europe as well in an alternate history scenario.
Overall I give Crusader Kings II a 9/10.

I enjoy space strategy games (the original Master of Orion games were my gateway drug) - and, for me, Endless Space 2 delivers in spades. The game has both depth and character, and manages to capture all that depth and complication in a slick and attractive interface.
Something I particularly enjoy is the way races behave vastly different from each other. There are a lot more "special cases" than there are "oh they have a 20% bonus to crop cycling". Unfallen (tree alients) that build branching star networks are great. Vodjani start and expand through the use of super-arks. It's great!
I'm okay with the space combat; though I would have preferred more agency in the actual execution of combat. I'm hopeful that fighters and bombers will get added soon (they are on the roadmap to be included in the first major (and free) update) - that should give the space combat cinematics an exciting wow factor.
I've read several negative reviews that seem to get caught up in very short-sighted problems. The nature of a product like Endless Space 2 is that it significantly transforms and re-shapes itself over the course of the next few months and even years. Perhaps they just do not have the patience, but to me the game is already good enough that I'll be happy to grow with it to its final form.

Awesome medieval, first-person Player Versus Player melee combat game, with a high skill cap. Very fun with friends, but if you manage to don't be a cry-baby and incentivate yourself to get better it can also be enjoyed alone. Git gud or git out basically.
It can get very tactical without losing its frenetic rhytm when it comes to the objective-based modes, like Team Objective or Capture the Flag. It is also tactical enough on the kill-the-opposing-team modes like Team Deathmatch and Last-Team-Standing (one life per round), yet on these modes the victory relies more on good teamwork and proper communication, rather than an specific strategy.
It has great graphics and looks very good. And while the optimization of this game it's not the best around, I have managed to play it on many computers with very basic (read: bad) hardware successfully at 45-60 FPS with everything on low settings.
Used to have a big learning curve but given the metagame has advanced a lot anyone can get in now and learn most of the elemental tricks and things right away and be a decent team player. Like others have said, it is a game easy to get into, but hard to master. I played this game for a very long time and I can say with over 2000 hours (no idle hours, and remember this is only a PvP game) it has never disappointed me. I highly recommend it for any fan of sword-fight or the medieval-era. 10/10 would get addicted to it again.
Only con I can think of is that you can only play with other people. You can create a map with bots but they aren't very good, although they may serve to train 1vsMany for low-level players (try this on Free-For-All mode [Deathmatch]).
Buy it!

L.A. Noire is a real gem of my game library! It has everything I've ever wished for in detective games:
* Open world with 95 vehicles you can drive. There is an Auto Fanatic achievement for starting engine of all vehicles available in the game at least once. Searching for more cars in game made me look at cars parked along sidewalks irl and think if they are those which are missing ;)
* Wide variety of cases to solve under different departments of the police institute. It successfully prevents the game from being too repetitive and you get new partners to work on cases with.
* Action! You will chase criminals and suspects on foot or in a vehicle. Combat involves both fist and gun fighting depends on a situation. But you must fight appropriately back or your mission will fail and you will have to start over. Weapons can only be used during firefights. If you can't successfully finish an action mission, the game will offer you to simply skip it and move on after the 3rd try. I think that's a great deal for people who are more interested in the story than in the challenges.
* Many dialogues, questioning, truth, doubt and lie choices, great face mimic.
* Nice graphics, attention to the detail, great voice acting.
* You get to play character who's personality you learn more about through his behaviour, conversations and flashbacks of his past. You will find out he is a person who makes mistakes and who sure has skeletons in his closet.. It's pretty amazing how complex his personality is. I really like the twists we are getting there.

I must say, don't let the 30 fps cap scare you away from one of the greatest detective games. You can easily fix it and increase it to 60.
L.A. Noire is definitely worth of being finished. Towards the ending the game includes the most action scenes. Before that I used to play it when I wanted to relax after a hard day at work. Then things escalated and the story got a fast speed untill it reached the typical noire fiction ending.
I really recommend the game from the bottom of my heart. Go for it :)

Had this game for awhile now, and while I've enjoyed it I can't say I'd recommened it. It's an Endless game so if you've played before you'll understand many of the core mechanics. The combat was enjoyable for me as it was something different and has seen some changes for the better. The exploration could be more interesting, but the anamolies and secondary quests are adequate.
For me the greatest problem has been the inability to advance to late game due to bugs. During early access save corruption was rampant and once turns ran into the triple digits you could expect a wait time of about a minute between turns. I recently started my first playthrough after official release, and I've already encountered a game breaking bug. Somewhere along the way it is possible for combat encounters to break causing End Turn to be stuck in a continuous state of pending due to AI factions and even the player faction being stuck in encounters. Have tried several fixes including making a new save on that turn and loading, loading the previous turn and trying again, and even loading four turns in the past while making different choices in ship movement and construction the issue remains unresolved.
Replayability is fairly high in order experience all the races, quests, and because occasionally you have to start a new game to continue playing. If the devs focus on fixing the current problems rather than adding content to a broken game I could recommend it in the future, but as it is now I would not recommend it or recommend you wait for a sale if you really want to try it out.

Chivalry could be a fun game. The melee system is very advanced, one of the best I have seen so far. All the 4 classes are fun to play, there are a lot of maps and the community is still very active. Each class has a huge choice between different weapons and in most cases they are fairly balanced. I still play this game from time to time, but there are some issues which make me downvote it:
1st: The ressources needed to play this game are incredible, considering the age of it. It looks like there was never done a single step of performance optimization. With a lower to mid end PC you will regularly have performance issues; with a lower end PC some of the maps are completely unplayable.
2nd: Mouse dragging is part of the game. There are plenty pro's and con's connected to that. It adds to the fight. Unfortunately they make dealing with lag very difficult. New players will be frustrated when being hit by some instead overhead attacks.
3rd: The servers are another issue. In my region I need to have a lucky day to be able to play without warping around the field. And if you don't do it, then your enemy does. Additionally on most days you can either play with 25+ players on a server, or just two.
I advise you to wait for a free weekend and look at the melee system; just so that you know what should be the standard in other games. I am not sure how many more updates can be expected from Torn Banners, so I would spend the 20 Euros on something else.

7/10
The game is an adventure game with Rockstar trappings.
You investigate crimes, follow leads, question witnesses, interrogate suspects, and occasionally subdue criminals with force.  The game has a wondeful ambiance, a great score, and very strong characters.
Why not a better score than 7/10?  Three things cost it those three points for me:
1) The "GTA"-like elements feel out of place/unnecessary.  The game is 80% criminal investigation, 20% action (car-chases/shoot-outs/fist-fights).  The action bits feel "tacked-on" and are not fleshed out very well in comparison to the rest of the game.  Driving between locations feels largely pointless with very little to do between points-of-interest.
2) The interrogation/questioning aspect can come off as a little strange at times. You might know that a suspect is lying, but it isn't always clear if you've got the correct piece of evidence to directly accuse them of lying. When you make a bad choice, you look like an idiot, but it doesn't change the outcome of the case for the most part. The story moves forward even if you bungle all the questioning/interrogating/evidence gathering parts.
3) The ending sucks. It's abrupt and leaves a lot of loose ends. It feels like they ran out of time. I know that's my opinion, but I'm sure many other people feel the same.

It's all about family and the glory of your Dynasty. You play as a Count/Duke/King/Emperor in medieval Europe, and your success depends on the heir to your titles when you die. True there are no 3D battles like Total War games, but this is a diplomacy and strategy game about feudal Europe that is unrivaled. You will build not only a nation, but a lurid story of intrigue, war, alliances, and betrayal that live on in memory long after the final score is recorded. Fantastic game for wasting your life.

Chivalry could be a fun game. The melee system is very advanced, one of the best I have seen so far. All the 4 classes are fun to play, there are a lot of maps and the community is still very active. Each class has a huge choice between different weapons and in most cases they are fairly balanced. I still play this game from time to time, but there are some issues which make me downvote it:
1st: The ressources needed to play this game are incredible, considering the age of it. It looks like there was never done a single step of performance optimization. With a lower to mid end PC you will regularly have performance issues; with a lower end PC some of the maps are completely unplayable.
2nd: Mouse dragging is part of the game. There are plenty pro's and con's connected to that. It adds to the fight. Unfortunately they make dealing with lag very difficult. New players will be frustrated when being hit by some instead overhead attacks.
3rd: The servers are another issue. In my region I need to have a lucky day to be able to play without warping around the field. And if you don't do it, then your enemy does. Additionally on most days you can either play with 25+ players on a server, or just two.
I advise you to wait for a free weekend and look at the melee system; just so that you know what should be the standard in other games. I am not sure how many more updates can be expected from Torn Banners, so I would spend the 20 Euros on something else.

Crusader Kings II more than anything feels like playing through a narrative history novel of your own making. You can start off as a simple count and through many generations end up ruling a vast empire. You can start off as an already powerful king and have to deal with the politics, wars and ambitious vassals all vying for more power, or...you may just end up ruling a small area of land for generations only for it to be snapped away from you by some distant relative leading to your dynasty to fade into obscurity.
More than anything this is the most human strategy game I have ever played. It no doubt has many of the grand strategy staples you would expect with Paradox games however at its heart it is about people and playing the role of a character within the historical narrative taking place. Yes you could try to game the systems and create a dynasty of generically perfect family members if you want to play the numbers game...however wouldn’t it be more fun to play as a family of inbred dwarf’s assassinating your way through Europe?
Playing with the sandbox is what the game is all about, it no doubt takes a bit of learning but there are a wealth of guides out there to help you along and once it ‘clicks’ it all comes together to make one of the best strategy games I have ever played full of stories you want discuss, intrigue that shocks you and even some bizarre twists and turns. Thoroughly recommended.

+ Gorgeous, well-optimized

+ Crazy amounts of depth and customization
+ Story quests introduced near late-game are incredible
+ Combat is incredibly visceral and rewarding

+ Frequently updated, devs prioritize new content over bugfixes
- Devs prioritize new content over bugfixes
- Holy mother of grinding
- Poor tutorials and explanations in-game along with a big learning curve: bookmark the wiki, and prepare to still learn you've been doing something wrong every day
- Monetization model is a huge trap if you go into it looking to spend some money. Go into it free, wait for a coupon in your daily login rewards, and only spend plat on slots and reactors/catalysts. If you're too desperate to grind out a new item you really want, this game isn't for you because the grind *is* the game.
Overall Warframe is a fantastic, if flawed free to play game that really carves out a niche for itself in an oversaturated F2P market. In spite of the popularity of its features and genre, there really isn't anything else out there quite like it that comes close in terms of ambition and quality. It's not for everybody and it has its issues, but it's an incredibly rich experience with so much to see and do, and if the gameplay loop clicks with you, it *really* clicks with you. Go ahead and download it and try it out, it's best started free so you have nothing to lose.

One of the absolute best games I have ever played. The graphics are great for the time it was released, and the facial expressions are better than most games from 2014+. The sleuthing in this game makes for an amazing experience as you scratch your head and sweat over trying to figure out if the person is telling the truth or lying. Each case is different and the game is not repetive, so sessions several hours long are a pleasure. It honestly feels like you're watching a movie the entire time, but you get to decide what the protagonist does.
Gameplay is pretty good. Combat is a bit wonky, but the game has a well balanced system of combat and narrative. The world is very fun to travel around and see what is going on, sort of the GTA esque going for it. Controls are a bit hard to get used to, especially after playing other games that are combat heavy.
The game runs pretty well for the average system. If you have an up to date gaming PC you are golden, if you have a decent PC that runs most other games well you should be able to play at a comfortable 25-35 FPS.
Downsides of this game is that the story is pretty linear, but worthwhile to stick around and find out what happens. The replay value is there if you're a perfectionist, but for most people one time through will be enough for them.
The game is definitely worth the $20 price tag and is a must have for anyone who enjoys a game with a good narrative.

is one of seemingly endless examples of games that struggle to separate "the grind" from "the game". Ultimately, any game that fits this description relies on either an extremely low level of player engagement, or fun enough gameplay such that the blurred or nonexistent line between the grind and the game itself isn't bothersome.
opts for the latter.
My relationship with
is simple: I play it completely casually, enjoy getting new frames/weapons etc., and rarely grind things actively. I mostly let things come to me. I would hugely attribute my positive relationship with the game to this mentality. I can understand people's frustrations with how much of the content is barred off behind a paywall or a frankly absurd time commitment. If your intent with the game is simply to unlock everything, or you are turned off by the idea of not having everything accessible to you, then I advise you with every fibre of my being to avoid this game at all costs.
Personally, I am generally very averse to games where the content is walled off in such a way. It's one of the biggest, if not the biggest reason that I don't have any interest in playing League of Legends. But, in
I don't mind it as much because it has an excellent community and feels much more like a "single-player" game in the sense that I feel free to leave a group or mission at any time, and can in fact "queue" into different areas solo. People are generally helpful and polite, and in the EXTREMELY rare case that I had an unpleasant group member, I would just leave without penalty. Thanks to the game's lack of competitive, PvP elements in the core game (at least what I've spent 100% of my time playing), the common toxicity found in Free To Play multiplayer games is largely absent.
In terms of the actual gameplay, it's pretty great. Movement is satisfying and cool, frames have pretty unique and interesting designs, the abilities are very cool, and the weapons are pretty neat too. No two frames or weapons feel the same, and with the huge amount of content in the game, there is plenty of room for customizing your own experience. What
lacks in depth, it attempts to make up for in width. If this isn't your cup of tea, then this game is not for you. But I think it lends itself to being enjoyed casually pretty solidly.
For a Free To Play game, it runs well and the production values are pretty swell. Certainly, it can be repetitive, and if it wasn't obvious from reading reviews, you will learn this fairly quickly. Even still though, there is no real incentive to rush towards any amount of content, and though the gameplay is repetitive, it's still fun enough to keep me engaged. I tend to load up the game and play for an hour or less at a time, but in that time I can scratch my itch to be a sick cyborg space ninja just fine.
I could go on to talk about things like enemy and level designs, or UI elements etc. but at the end of the day whether or not
is for you is almost entirely predicated on your tolerance of its walled off content and repetitive gameplay. Under the notion that it's played casually and the fact that it's free lead me to lean more towards recommending it than not, but the philosophy that this game is built around is going to be wildly polarizing and so your mileage WILL vary from person to person. I say give it a shot though. It's pretty sick.

L.A. Noire is one of those little gem of a games that is good for killing time, but it's not a blockbuster game either.  The comes in "cases" which are like episodes of the game, each case has a list of tasks to complete, the problem is though the tasks follow a different story and a different puzzle, it is always the same tasks in each case. This is an old game coming from 2011, but doesn't even meet the graphic abilties of 2008's Grand Theft Auto IV, also by Rockstar.  Speaking of Grand Theft Auto, part of the gameplay is driving to and fro, which plays much like GTA3+ but it seems chopped up.  Where in GTA games you often learn the layout of the city to compete in races are make quick deliveries, there really isn't a lot of urgency in LA Noire to get anywhere and the brief moments of driving are constantly interupped by cutscenes and case interrogations.
Overall, LA Noire is one of those games that is just tough to decide if you should reccomend it.  I think overall it falls just barely on the side of "Yes".

LA Noire is a wonderful experience in gaming. There aren't many games like this out there, which is a shame. Take on the role of a Police officer in post WWII Los Angeles. The city has been lovingly re-created with all the streets and famous landmarks. However, don't expect a GTA style sandbox; this game is very linear and all about the main story. Also, while the city has been expertly crafted, you won't be given much reason to explore it; no non-mission specific buildings are able to be entered and there is very little to no interactivity with anything in the city. Getting past those faults though, this is a great detective game with a unique twist. You must read the facial expressions of the people you interogate and make assumptions based on that. While this doesn't always work smoothly, it's super cool trying to read the characters and try and tell if they're lying or not. This game also has a great style. If you couldn't tell, it's a classic Noire style presentation and can even be played in black and white (recommended for that legitimate noire feel). This game is not for everyone. It can be slow and after finishing the game, some may not want to replay missions when they already know whodunnit. If it does pique your interest though, pick this up on sale.

I've been a fan of TBS games since I can remember, starting with the likes of Alpha Centauri, Civ 1, Civ: Call to Power and the like. If you wanna move your RTS gaming to the next level, this game is for you. It is by far the best RTS on the market at the moment. Forget about Civ5, Civ6 or Galactic Civilizations, they're children compared to this baby.
The most important difference between any other game and this one is the amount of complexity the guys have embedded in just one game. And it's a fun kind of complexity!
Below imma present a few important points that make this game unique and very very fun to play.  But if I'm about to lose you already, the important part from all this is: if you like Civ, buy this! You're surely gonna love it!
Before I start, I wanna tell you I've not played it in early access: I don't believe in allowing people access to your software before it's done. So my whole experience is from after the game was released fully.
- great playstyle diversity between the different races. So, I love the Vodyani! Their religious parasitic playstyle and them amazing Arks that can be used offensively are unbelieveable IMO. There's no way you can have a similar playstyle with another race, like the Sophons. With the Sophons, you gain a tech edge and you can use that to have better military/ production/ commerce / whatever. The Lumeris are all about the money, money, and so on. So basically you could play the game until you finish it with all 8 races and you wouldn't get bored.
- modular ship designs: so, you only unlock less than 10 different ship designs (slightly different for every race). Buuut... you can customize every design by adding the modules that you want. Maybe you want a fleet that only attacks at short range with a focus on energy weapons. Or you want a detached approach from long range, lots of shields and projectile weaponry. Or maybe you want a balanced fleet good for all encounters. Your choice, man! And choices actually have consequences.
- Senate and political consequences for your decisions: So, there are 6 political parties that, based on what you do in a game, will garner support from the population. Every 20 turns, there'd be an election that you could also influence. Who is in power actually matters because you can only pass some laws relevant to the parties in power and some default laws for the previous parties would be abolished. Let's take the Sophons as example. You start with the Scientists in power. If they lose an election, their default law allowing you to research technologies from the next level (without being required to research the lower tier tech nodes first) would be abolished and replaced. You might not want that, but if you build military ships and engage in wars too much the militarists will win the election So, once again, your choices do have significant consequences in the game.
- great music: I thought that the Civ series, starting with the Baba Yetu song from Civ 4 can never be outclassed in ambiental music in RTS games. But...the music in Endless Space 2 is actually better! I know, nobody plays TBS games for the music, but still. It makes playing it even better.
This review would be endless pages long if I were to tell you all about it like heroes, quests, planet types, unique planets, star lanes, baryonic shielding...But the thing is, even without a Civilopedia, the game features a pretty good tutorial system that will not make all these concepts bothersome, they'd just be fun and you'd actually feel like playing a strategy game, meaning, you'll be strategizing, taking all these things into account.
There are minor bugs still left in the game, but they're just a few and none of them are game breaking, just nuissances. It it weren't for these, I would only have good things to say about the game.
I know that TBS games are not for everyone, but if you liked any previous Civilization game or you are into space exploration, do yourself a favor and get this game.

This game looks really nice, has lots of cutscences and I enjoyed this game a lot more than Stellaris.... BUT I have to say the game plays out to be kind of unfinished and unpolished. There's so many things that I could pick on that results from huge oversights with the developer.
I played my first proper game on hard difficulty as Unfallen and the AI was too easy, I won easily without even optimising anything and not really doing anything apart from playing 100% passive. Coming as a new player that did not even play any of the previous games (Endless Space 1 or Endless Legends) I wasn't expecting the AI to be such a pushover, they simply play to wait for you to win. Later on, I read that people online are recommending to play on even harder difficulties, but that to me is more of a player work-around resulting from some serious issues with the AI. To put this into context, the AI is 100x worse than the AI in Civilization series... which already is pretty terrible.
Also, there's a lot of lag in the game later on in large maps that I don't think is from my PC system, it seems the game is poorly optimised.
There's also a lot of micro-management especially if you are going to go for a conquest victory, and there doesn't seem to be enough automation tools to help you manage everything optimally (e.g. micro-managing population between systems is really time-consuming right now especially if you run a lot of systems).
So there's a lot of negatives to this game, but after playing this game I will still recommend it to anyone looking for a space 4X game. I prefer this game compared to Stellaris, Endless Space 2 is the best 4X space game that has come out recently, so don't hesitate if you are looking for a 4X space game. The main draw to me is that this game has so much depth, complexity and micromanagement that just blows out all other competitors and as a nice plus it's not published by Paradox. On the moment when I first saw someone else play this I knew I just had to get this game myself because there are so many interacting systems to manage, even more than Civilization series. YES it has a lot of potential that is missed and it could have been a lot better - but it's not. Regardless, to me there's no better 4X space game released recently, so even with all its flaws I will play it for my 4X space itch.

I'm going to begin with this: This is my first exposure to a Rockstar game. I also want to mention that I did pick up the complete edition, which seemed to drag on. I use the term drag on because this game was the first game I've played that seemed to be a chore to finish.  Team Bondi should have had Bill Murray as the protagonist as this felt like a Groundhog Day simulator.  It's deceivingly massive game with the depth of a puddle.  For instance, the map is MASSIVE, but there seems to be only 1/4 that is actually used in cases. It's a huge empty world. Think Skyrim, but without access to any of the buildings, homes, or dungeons.
Groundhog Day Sim: Walk around a the area that has been cordoned off and wait until your controller vibrates. Find things and interrogate the perp. Don't forget to look at those sweet, sweet facial expressions when you're deciding on accusing them of lying. They'll always ask for proof, so be ready for some rock-solid evidence.  The icing on the cake is the NPCs you've seen 100 times in different places all echoing: "Isn't that the cop from the newspaper.." or that idiot at the station who always repeats that he'd like a higher caliber round so that he can take down a suspect with one shot every time you enter or exit the building. Repeat this 1000 times and you've got LA Noire.
The port stinks. It's a terrible port. Typing about this enrages me. The word port is barely means anything good.
There are Pros to this game: There's a semi-interesting story that could have easily been made into a feature-length film. The 1940's LA architecture and classic automobiles are quite awesome. The facial expressions are actually amazing, though most faces are pretty punchable. The soundtrack is very well implemented and probably my favourite aspect to the game.
In conclusion, It's difficult to believe this game is reported to have exceeded a $50 million budget. It's  very repetitive and makes your PC feel like a potato sputtering console.
I've come back and given this game a thumbs up simply because it was developed in 2009-2010 and definitely is a feat considering its age. I also did not realize that I had the complete edition with all of the DLC, which definitely contributed to how long the game seemed to drag on for.

I've been a fan of TBS games since I can remember, starting with the likes of Alpha Centauri, Civ 1, Civ: Call to Power and the like. If you wanna move your RTS gaming to the next level, this game is for you. It is by far the best RTS on the market at the moment. Forget about Civ5, Civ6 or Galactic Civilizations, they're children compared to this baby.
The most important difference between any other game and this one is the amount of complexity the guys have embedded in just one game. And it's a fun kind of complexity!
Below imma present a few important points that make this game unique and very very fun to play.  But if I'm about to lose you already, the important part from all this is: if you like Civ, buy this! You're surely gonna love it!
Before I start, I wanna tell you I've not played it in early access: I don't believe in allowing people access to your software before it's done. So my whole experience is from after the game was released fully.
- great playstyle diversity between the different races. So, I love the Vodyani! Their religious parasitic playstyle and them amazing Arks that can be used offensively are unbelieveable IMO. There's no way you can have a similar playstyle with another race, like the Sophons. With the Sophons, you gain a tech edge and you can use that to have better military/ production/ commerce / whatever. The Lumeris are all about the money, money, and so on. So basically you could play the game until you finish it with all 8 races and you wouldn't get bored.
- modular ship designs: so, you only unlock less than 10 different ship designs (slightly different for every race). Buuut... you can customize every design by adding the modules that you want. Maybe you want a fleet that only attacks at short range with a focus on energy weapons. Or you want a detached approach from long range, lots of shields and projectile weaponry. Or maybe you want a balanced fleet good for all encounters. Your choice, man! And choices actually have consequences.
- Senate and political consequences for your decisions: So, there are 6 political parties that, based on what you do in a game, will garner support from the population. Every 20 turns, there'd be an election that you could also influence. Who is in power actually matters because you can only pass some laws relevant to the parties in power and some default laws for the previous parties would be abolished. Let's take the Sophons as example. You start with the Scientists in power. If they lose an election, their default law allowing you to research technologies from the next level (without being required to research the lower tier tech nodes first) would be abolished and replaced. You might not want that, but if you build military ships and engage in wars too much the militarists will win the election So, once again, your choices do have significant consequences in the game.
- great music: I thought that the Civ series, starting with the Baba Yetu song from Civ 4 can never be outclassed in ambiental music in RTS games. But...the music in Endless Space 2 is actually better! I know, nobody plays TBS games for the music, but still. It makes playing it even better.
This review would be endless pages long if I were to tell you all about it like heroes, quests, planet types, unique planets, star lanes, baryonic shielding...But the thing is, even without a Civilopedia, the game features a pretty good tutorial system that will not make all these concepts bothersome, they'd just be fun and you'd actually feel like playing a strategy game, meaning, you'll be strategizing, taking all these things into account.
There are minor bugs still left in the game, but they're just a few and none of them are game breaking, just nuissances. It it weren't for these, I would only have good things to say about the game.
I know that TBS games are not for everyone, but if you liked any previous Civilization game or you are into space exploration, do yourself a favor and get this game.

With a strong enough computer, this game will immerse you into a world that defies all eras.
Survive in a harsh world known as the Ark, a structure that holds creatures spanning across all of earth's existence. As a human, you must do your best to live amongst dinosaurs as well as beings lost to legend. Start out with mere primitive stone tools, and build your intillect and resources to eventually construct fortresses and future tech firearms. Tame wild beasts to assist in your survival, and join tribes of other humans to band together in your efforts. Create alliances and axis with other tribes as you collect the necessary gear to finally face off against some of the strongest beasts known within the Ark.
The visuals alone are stunning enough to warrent a purchase just to sightsee around the various Arks.
The interface and controls can be a bit much at first; however, once you get a handle on every bind, inventory management and crafting become easy enough not to burden an experienced player. They should create more in-depth utilities in areas such as learning engrams.
Survival is not as easy as eating and drinking, there are many obstacles to tackle in order to stay alive such as temperature, diseases, and torpor. As you level you may choose various catagories that help strengthen you in areas you feel unfit for. Increase weight to help with carrying resources, increase stamina to attack and sprint longer, increase fortitude to survive in extreme temperatures, and many others.
The modding community is a little weak in certain places, I haven't found a single mod that was made specifically to add new weapons or armor to the game. Though the building aspect has pages upon pages of different mods that all fit seemlessly together. Just don't expect to find a mod that totally changes the gameplay. Most of the mods on the workshop either change what you build, how you build. or how you tame dinos. Beyond that, a lot of mods fall pretty flat.
Though this may be due to the fact that before mods are even considered, the base game itself has a very customizable experience.
This game is extremely in-depth and takes a lot of time to master. Even I have barely scratched the tip of this iceburg. Yet I can say without a doubt that anybody that is interested in a survival game where you build bases and shoot dinosaurs while fighting for territory with rival tribes may want to check this one out.

LA Noire provides a confused experience, but I guess I can recommend it. It's a harsh mix between interactive fiction adventure (EG: Telltale's The Wolf Among Us) and an open-world action sandbox (EG: GTA), and it can often leave you feeling dissatisfied with both of those aspects.
The detective clue-finding and interrogation part of the game, the adventure / puzzle side, is often irritating. The results are usually binary. Presumably to make the game less frustrating, you can proceed and finish the cases after having failed at a lot of the case work. But the inability to correct your errors and try again is the thing that makes it so obnoxious. Other games like Phoenix Wright have these issues where, ostensibly, your human intuition and problem-solving skills will lead you to the "correct" answers. But the problem is you end up more often just guessing what the game designer is thinking at, not what you would actually guess if you were in that situation. The choices provided are not robust enough. The result is that I spent most of my time playing LA Noire with an online game walkthrough open. I never do this. But I conceded that the binary nature of what is supposed to be an intuitive human process was ruining the game for me. I would honestly recommend you find a spoiler-free walkthrough to get the most out of the game.
The game redeems the adventure-game aspect of it with their much-touted facial scanning tech and a deep plot. The human actors in the game are the most realistic and believable I've seen to date, despite poor texture resolutions and (as of 2015, four years after release) outdated rendering. I enjoy watching the acting of real people when they speak in-game. It's just a treat to watch. It crosses the uncanny valley because you really are looking at a real actor actually acting. I compare it to watching an old TV program in black-and-white. There's no "uncanny valley" when it comes to TV acting because it's about how expressive and believable the performances are, not how well rendered it is.
The believability of these characters and their performances pulled me into LA Noire's complex and intriguing story. I really enjoyed it and, at ~35 hours, it's huge. Each "case" is an episode-length self-contained drama, and the game does a great job of leaving a breadcrumb trail of foreshadowing and circumstances that lead to great conspiracy over the course of all the cases. While sometimes Team Bondi could've done a better job at communicating characters' emotions and intentions, and the flashback scenes are weird and clumsy, ultimately the story is well told and worth telling.
The other half, the open-world sandbox, is really the bizarre part. LA / Hollywood has been realized in LA Noire to a ridiculous degree. Every street, alley, footpath, crosswalk, store, etc. is there. Mazes of suburb streets, the traffic of downtown, the network of wires that hang over the streets to support a trolley system - It's all created in beautiful and exhaustive detail. Just like any GTA game. The interiors are more selectively made (you can only go in rooms that matter, for the most part), but other than that it's just about as real as you could hope for.
But the gameplay that takes place in that "real" world is so uninteresting. You are obligated to follow the law, and you are penalized for driving poorly. Driving for 12 minutes across town to your next objective is just straight-up boring, and every case requires you to do real police legwork by going to multiple objectives, often far across town from one another.
The game does give you a way to bypass the driving most of the time, but then, what purpose does any of that city serve? Why did artists and designers spend so much time making it so realistic if the core gameplay doesn't actually matter there, and the travel is just skipped? Oblivion and Skyrim do a good job of making sure there are interesting things to find and do along the way to your objectives. But LA Noire's attempts at this don't actually solve the problem, they exacerbate it.
The only time this giant world ever really matters is during car chases, which I suppose are fun, but honestly could've been custom-built per-chase for cheaper than realizing the whole city. Your chase-target's destination is pre-scripted anyway.
Unrelated, the cover-based shooting gameplay is pretty good too, but this is not a game about gunning down bad guys (usually) and sometimes even that feels out of place with the tone of the game, despite how well executed it may be.
It seems that Team Bondi wanted to use Rockstar's incredible technology to make a robust detective simulation: "Live the career of a real detective." But it turns out that in game design simulation is only interesting as long as it's fun. Otherwise it's just tiresome.
I would love to see another game like LA Noire made but with a clearer vision and more of the fat trimmed. But there isn't another game like it, and if you can put up with its flaws, I would recommend it to you. The biggest compliment I can give LA Noire is that after finishing it I immediately went to go look up some classic noire films. I'm intrigued by the game's emotionally nuanced execution and gray-gradient portrayal of morality, and I'm proud of Team Bondi for pushing AAA game themes and storytelling the way they did for videogames in general, even if I'm not impressed by their business practices.

L.A. Noire. So much to say about this game.
The good - this game actually has a plot! Detecting whether people are lying and looking for clues is fun! And the fact that the game attempts to capture human emotion is super cool.
Did I mention that the music is great, and the art concept (capturing post-WWII LA) is amazing and intensely detailed?
And the cinematics are well-done and actually very interesting; the game is kind of like an interactive movie, in a good way.
The only thing missing is the musty smell of old houses from the late '40s.
But then L.A. Noire goes off the rails. It's shockingly buggy; the game stutters, for no reason, even in interrigation sequences. The actual graphics quality isn't very good, despite the design and art direction being wonderful.
Even worse, they have totally banal car chase and gunfight scenes that get old, and ruin the well-executed plot. And just because the game is made by Rockstar, why did they need to copy the GTA universe, and try to make you drive everywhere?
Plus, for all your decisions as a detective, you have no agency in the outcome of the game. The same thing happens no matter what choices you make.
Then, the cherry on top, they try very hard to convince you to sign up and login to their stupid online social club.
Despite all of this, L. A. Noire is still a wonderful idea. I love the idea of an atmospheric detective game. It's worth it for that. But boy-oh-boy do I hope someone makes a newer, improved, L. A. Noire 2.

Spent 45 hours playing this and in the end, can't really recommend it. I think the concept is pretty cool and I really wanted to like it, but it has several major flaws:
1) Boring - this game is just boring. It's like a very long movie in slow motion. You can't fast forward the cut scenes so everything is very slow paced. The game does not evolve from the first mission, you don't get more skills so it is all the same over and over. Talk to some people, chase down a suspect (which you are scripted to never catch), shoot some bad dudes, repeat.
2) Bad conversation system - in conversations you can choose Truth/Doubt/Lie, the problem is that it is a crap shoot which one to pick. You are supposed to hear the voice and look at the animated face to determine if they are lying. That is all fine, but even if they are lying, you need to choose between Doubt/Lie, and if they are telling the truth it is still Doubt/Truth, it's whatever random choice the programmers decided is the correct answer. To elaborate, someone can be telling the truth, but if you don't think they are telling enough of a truth (not enough details) you are supposed to pick Doubt. That leads to save scumming/using a walkthrough since the system is so ridiculous.
3) Laughable story - most of the non-DLC missions are connected by a main story. It is too bad you can see the big story from a mile away. Even worse is that even though you can tell what is going on, you repeatedly arrest innocent people because you have to. In about half of the cases - I repeat, in HALF OF THE CASES - you have no option to actually arrest the true criminal. Best case is that you choose between two innocent people. You are hailed as the best detective in the LAPD - yeah ok.
It isn't all bad, the game is beautiful and the voice acting is great. Issue is that the key systems don't work and the game is boring. If they had ditched the main story, actually let you catch true criminals and made it into a 10  hour game, then maybe it would have been better. One of the very few times where less would have been better.

Good game, a bit buggy, but entertaining none the less. 7/10 with bugs, 8 or 9 without.
Pros:
- Great graphics. Everything from planets, to ships, to the user interface is visually appealing, clean, and sharp.
- Good pacing. The game really seems to have good pacing, at least for me. The game's progression keeps each turn relatively relevant, and gives the user something to do most turns. Not much waiting around for new techs or slow ships.
- Game is wide, not deep. This could be a pro or a con, but I see it as a pro. The game currently has a wide variety of mechanics to look at and work with. But they are all fairly simple and quick to get a hang of. This makes the game feel a little repetative, but it means that as DLC is released or mods are made, the game will become much more fleshed out and deep. Its better to have a skeleton to build around than just a severed head.
Cons:
- Not quite fully optimized. Depending on your specs, the game will get progessively slower to run and more intensive on your computer. Eventually, it seems for me at least, the game reaches a point at which the time between turns takes more time than is ideal. This will get better as the game gets optimized.
- Limited mods so far. The game is brand-new so I get that mods aren't gonna be finished for a few more weeks. But if you think the game will get stale for you very quickly, wait a few weeks for mods to be released. If you are reading this months after it was posted, consider this not a problem.
- Occassionally, the game gets stuck in the waiting for next turn phase (Pending). Typically happens when AI gets into a battle. The pending seems to never end. Again, this is likely either due to poor-optimization, my mediocre rig, or a bug, so take this with a grain of salt if its been a few months or you are confident with your rig.
Overall - I'd say wait until mid-June to start playing. But its up to you to decide. Either way, I would recommend this game to anyone considering getting it.

Primary concept fails to deliver. The truth/doubt/lie system is horrendously misleading. Perfectionists don't stand a chance of getting all the right answers on the first go and playing the game with a guide open ruins the all-too-important ambiance entirely. This wouldn't be too much of an issue except all questions have a "right" answer, and even though under 70% of circumstances an incorrect answer gives you the same information, a rude little jingle of piano notes tells you when you failed the guess and angers you a little.
This game also has massive story issues. For the entirety of the "homicide" desk, the player is SHOCKINGLY aware that every suspect he brings in is not actually the killer. However, even though you can be certain no matter who you choose you are choosing an innocent man, choosing the man with more evidence against him but fewer character flaws will get you yelled at and a lower mission complete rating. Things liven up a bit during the "Vice" desk, but then become head-scratchingly boring and unengaging after that. To the point that you begin to hate the person you are playing and the situations you are being put through until the game comes to an existential and unsatisfying end. Do not expect ANY of the light-hearted humor typical of Rockstar games.
Presentation is actually fantastic, facial rendering is pretty impressive, if a little uncanny. Driving is immersive and the recreation of Los Angeles is very pretty. I like the fact that you can walk into cafes and sit down at the tables/bars if you so wish, even if it doesn't get you anything.  Licensed music selection is sparse and uninspired. It should also be noted that not a single woman in L.A. Noire has long hair due to the limitations of the facial capture technology, this bugs me more than it should, because it seems like it should be easily fixable.
It should be noted that there is no GTA style "overworld." You may either drive/walk around the map in "free mode" or follow down a very specific path in the story missions with no break in between them and no middle ground, this creates a kind of "trapped" feeling that doesn't really allow you to feel comfy and welcome like any other open world game. It's important in GTA that you decide when the missions start, otherwise you feel rather like you're being pushed along through the story.
I really wanted to like this game, as it was released shortly after Rockstar's home run of a game "Red Dead Redemption," which is personally on my top ten favorite games of all time. Unfortunately this game simply isn't fun, and it's not because it chooses a serious tone. The Last of Us had a very serious tone and main characters with arguably more volatile and morally incorrect motives and actions and still managed to be fun through proper writing and management of gameplay agency.
L.A. Noire fails as a mystery game because of poorly written plots
L.A. Noire fails as an action game because it's combat is definitively worse than all other games in that genre by the same developer
L.A. Noire fails as a drama because of unrelatable and unlikable characters
L.A. Noire fails as a game in general because of an unenjoyable gameplay flow
The only manner in which I believe L.A. Noire excels is as an example of how minor nitpicks can coalesce to ruin a game that should otherwise have been great.

Best kind of surprise package by Paradox Development Studio. A game which gives you the challenge of trying to keep your dynasty alive and in power whilst also tempting you with expansion and wealth. Take part in holy crusades to re-take holy catholic lands and earn prestige through wars. If war's not your game, use cunning and intrigue with strategic marriages and spies to help fabricate claims on land, call in allies and take the land without lifing a finger.

Bring the Byzantine Empire their previous glory and reform the Roman Empire, gaining justifications on all her previous holdings.
Watch in a twist of history as the Aztecs land on European shores bringing with them new and strange diseases. Watch as they cut down kingdoms and forge their own empire.
Play as a Republic, forgeing a dynasty of wealth and power through trade, then use this new wealth and power to cut out your own empire. (Like the Romans did!)
And soon you will be allowed to play as Pagans, like the vikings and plunder gold and wreak havoc in the name of Odin. Each Pagan will have its own unique taste.

Rambling, moralistic, noir story. I've seen complaints about the ending, but to me it fit perfectly.  This was pretty compelling story telling.
Nice sense of world-creation particularly with the music and advertisements. Together with the voice acting and script I felt a real sense of place and time.
The graphics worked well with the story and were are at their best when they were most stylised - it's almost painterly at times.
You don't have any real agency over the story and the game play itself very challenging either. I don't think there's anything wrong with that, it's just that you might not like this game if story is not your thing.  This is a game in service of a story, not the other way around.
The only negative was that there wasn't enough diversity in the types of things you can do. Walking around a crime site looking for clues got pretty old, especially when it just boiled down to waiting for my controller to vibrate so I can press A.
Anyway, overall it was a fun experience and that story will stay with me for a while. A sequel that puts a bit more thought into the game play would be cool, maybe with a total change of scene as well. How about Bangkok Noir?

More like a movie rather than a game, L.A. Noire is a splendid interactive translation of a noir novel, in particular Black Dhalia and L.A. Confidential by J. Ellroy (which I also recommend). The 1950 Los Angeles is immersive and realistically reproduced, framing a brilliant plot and a character developement worthy of a book. Interactive dialogues are the soul of the game, being also the key to conduct interrogatories and solve cases: for this purpose a very detailed facial motion capture permits to evaluate emotional reactions and to expose lies. Detective work is realistic and capturing, allowing personal investigation lines and always letting the player to deduce and judge in first person.
Although cinematographic narration overwhelms the gameplay, L.A. Noire is another confirmation of what level of care Rockstar puts in his videogames.

Honestly, I love ARK. It's an immersive experience, and has captured my attention (both on PC and PS4) for numerous hours. If you like dinosaurs, open world games, and the survival genera, this is the game for you.
First, I'll state the positives. The map is huge, and a thrill to explore and find all the dinos, exploration notes, and resources scattered about the island. They tend to level balance fairly well depending on the part of the island you're at. Not to mention you can dive into the depths of the sea and fly high on a argentavis. The crafting and combat is satisfying as well. Building your own base exactly how you want it is satisfying. There's a wide array of critters to tame, with different abilities to help make the world of ark more tamable.
You can also create your own servers to play with friends, play solo, and adjust a lot of the settings to tailor a unique experience that best suits your gameplay style.
However, there is a few flaws I find rather annoying as well. Every island is the exact same- if you've seen it once you'll know where everything is for every new play through. Once you're done exploring and taming all the dinos you want for your team, there's not really much to do. There's a few 'bosses' that are required to play the Center and Ragnarok, but that's about it. Fortunately add on packs and constant updates bringing new content help remedy this. There's also moment when creatures, and even your character, can glitch in and out of objects. I had a titanosaurus spawn atop me and I died instantly as it landed.
The official servers also leave a lot to be desired. The players there are often toxic, unhelpful, and like to watch new players suffer. While the events offered are fun, it's hard to establish yourself in the world without someone coming along and raiding your base while you're offline. If you want to play with friends but don't want to play on an official server, you can't enjoy some of the neat stuff that happens there. If the community was less asinine it would be much, much better. As it is now however, play solo or on a dedicated server.
While I could say much more about this game and what it has to offer, I'll leave my review here. All in all, despite the flaws, I can't recommend this game enough. Especially on sale, it's a good buy and will have you delving into caves and mining for pearls on the ocean floors with a smile.

Chivalry is one of those games you'll find yourself consistantly playing like foresay, Mount and Blade. There isn't really anything else like it, the dialogue is quite hillarious, especially the Agatha Knight. The weapons are quite diverse in playstyle, though a few weapons tend to be the main focus of the playerbase. The player can join the various gamemodes on either official servers or community servers, and will earn EXP at the end of each match. This EXP levels up your rank which is only there for reference to your skill level. You start out with a handful of weapons for each class, but as you get more and more kills, you can unlock the next weapon following it. If you unlock all of the weapons for a class, you get a veterans helmet. There is no pay to win in this game, you can't use money to level up or unlock weapons, the only microtransactions is with buying custom skins. You can also customize your classes with a large variety of symbols, but limited patterns for the base armor.
Chivalry was known for being competitive, but it lost it's competitive nature after Torn Banner streamlined it with a few patches, which has it's ups and downs for controversy. Don't get me wrong, the game still requires skill, but isn't as demanding as it was before, resulting in more animation exploiting and all sorts of odd unrealistic techniques. For example knights tend to crouch and look straight up turning away from the target as they swing, the result being their weapon going through the ground and hitting the enemy as a normal hit. Things like these is the sort of "skill" that is now Chivalry. The MAA and Archer tend to be the exception to this, Archer being simply because he has to aim with a ranged weapon, and the MAA relies more on dodging and feints rather than odd dancing. Overall Chivalry will feel quite arcady, and at times rather "cheap" when a enemy player kills you with a move that exploits the animation. Though this will seem minor, and will only bother the more realistic seeking players as the gameplay still flows smoothly.
The maps are decent, each (to me) is creative and rememberable. Some of the new maps can be a bit biased towards defenders however, but the rest are balanced.
The actual community within Chivalry is average with any other game.
The game is a little buggy, with each patch generally "downgrading" the game in terms of stability. A sort of "spaghetti" effect when someone dies, leaving their eyes floating with broken textures linked to the body, when shot by a ballista the body tends to glitch out a lot. Oddly, Chivalry doesn't support 1920 x 1080 so anyone using such resolution beware when you buy this game. If you use window mode with this game, it will have a very high chance of crashing if you leave the window, intentionally or not. The gameplay and maps aren't bugged at all however, and all perform smooth, but things listed above can stand out like a sore thumb, with the crashes considering window mode being a serious game breaking issue for anyone who likes to listen to music while they play, PC notifications pop up during gameplay, etc.
Final Opinion
Positives
-Addicting smooth gameplay
-Satisfying and rewarding with each kill you achieve
-Maps are creative enough, and unique with their objectives
-Fast arcade pace for players who desire this
-A level of customization for the player
-Free maps and weapon additions, all DLC is only cosmetic so far (Developers have a good balance between a passion for their games and capitalism.)
-Balanced weapons, though some are easier than others, making them a common sight over others.
-Soundtrack is decent
-No bugs that disturb the flow of the gameplay unless you experience a crash in window mode
-Average community
-Easy to get into, controls are simple, but takes time to master the game.
-Hillarious creative mods that can refresh the gameplay for some
Cons
-Doesn't support 1920 x 1080
-Not a good game for competitive players
-Not realistic if that's what you seek
-Players can exploit animations to land hits
-Some newer maps lack balance
-Window mode is very vulnerable to crashing
-Some players who started playing when the game was first released, will feel that Torn Banner has "downgraded" the game with each patch, breaking the experience for them and leaving it. (Going from competitive to arcade)
-Players who start playing low rank servers, will find a huge jump in difficulty playing against much higher ranked players when they can't play in low rank servers anymore.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Overall, I would recommend this to anyone looking for some good fun. The game is addictive and very easy to sink many hours into, especially with a friend(s). If you are looking for realism and competition, I would stay away from this, if you're looking for a arcade casual game, then this will be perfect for you.

L.A. Noire is a dark, stylish game not really like anything else by Rockstar Games. Instead of being the anti-hero, you play as beat policeman and war veteran Cole Phelps in his mission up the LAPD ranks.
The game looks decent enough for its age. The real advertised feature of this game was the facial capture, which is extremely well done, even in gameplay. However, this comes with two critical drawbacks. Firstly, in order for the animations to keep up, the game is capped at a "cinematic" 30FPS, so for many PC gamers, it may not seem like it runs very well. Secondly, although the faces are extremely detailed and animated, the bodies lack this advanced animation. Because of that, the model quality seems very inconsistent, especially when someone is lying, as their bodies hardly move, or flail around unrealistically, while their faces are completely animated. To substitute for this, some actors decided to do extremely over-the-top telltale facial signs to show lying, as they could not effectively communicate this with their body language. Other than these drawbacks, engine and visual wise, the game is fine, with a detailed, stylised city to roam around in.
The soundtrack and audio in general for the game is superb. The soundtrack fits well with the theme, and the radio is authentic era radio broadcasts, and brilliant voice acting mean that the game is brilliant in the audio department, which really helps with the 'immersion' (sorry for using a buzzword) when playing the game.
Gameplay wise, despite the more focused story, it plays a bit like Grand Theft Auto when roaming the city. This isn't really a bad thing, as the gameplay feels familiar and flows correctly to allow L.A. Noire to be an easy game to pick up and start playing. This does bring in another small problem though, the investigating. Because there are a lot of gamers now, many of them may not be that good at the old adventure-game style gaming. In order to compensate for this, Rockstar and Team Bondi implemented a lot of hand-holding functions, which unfortunately prevents the gameplay from reaching its true maximum potential. The game never becomes complex, and investigations are held back by lack of difficulty and consequence.
Despite these drawbacks, the game, considering the average triple-A games of today, is unique, especially when stood side-by-side with Rockstar's more famous work. The attention to detail and appealing gameplay, along with the brilliant audio and focus on story means that despite its flaws, I have no problem recommending this game to people who want to play a modern adventure game.

Crusader Kings II is a highly in-depth grand strategy game with a dual focus upon micro-managing the day to day affairs of your ruler's court and the intrigue surrounding it. Whether it be securing an immediate heir to inherit your dynasty or deciding which of your vassal should hold council positions, these are decisions you will face on a regular basis. On the other hand you can temper these smaller objectives and concerns with grander ambitions such as preparing an army for invasion of infidel held territory, or working through the process of turning your small kingdom in an empire.
This is what Paradox Interactive seek to offer a customer of this game, freedom to dream and see these dreams realised or shattered by the events of history. It may be your ambition to be Emperor of a united and independent Britannia and see your sons hold the titles of each of the four kingdoms that make up your empire. However, there may be a duke with similiar dreams in your realm, a son who may want to hold all the titles instead of just one, or a foreign power with claims to your lands. This is Crusader Kings and how you deal with these individual issues and problems and managing your own ambitions is what makes this game so compelling and why I've sunk over 150+ hours into it and will continue to do so, even after support for the game may end. However with DLC being continously released such as the recent 'Sons of Abraham' or prior to that 'Old Gods' lack of support I feel is not a concern.
That is not to say the game is without it's weaknesses. To a new player the menu and micromanagement (even with the assistance of tooltips) can seem overwhelming and off putting leaving new players feeling very lost or confused.
The multiplayer leaves something to be desired, although I've experienced a stable and strong single player experience I cannot sing the prasises of the multiplayer, where numerous drop-outs, crashes and version conflicts have left a foul taste in my mouth where myself and friends have wanted to see how as a group we could shape history.
Finally the issues of war, now although the war system is built in mind with a strategic sense with terrain, fort, technology and event modifiers effecting your armies capabilities in battle it does occasionally feel as though it can boil down to "I have x men more than you do". Moreover the way war works in the sense that you have to sometimes completely and totally destory an enemy only to earn a single province instead of holding them accountable for all their land. These I feel are glaring weaknesses within the game.
However, despite these issue this game has insane, and I cannot stress that enough, insane replayability. I go back even now and find a new way of approaching a situation that could of caused my realm to destabalised, or play through from another cultures perspective (and with the addition of 'The Old Gods' and 'Sword of Islam' DLC another religions). There are times even when I feel I've played family line long enough that I can open the console commands and type 'observe' and just see how my changes have affected the timeline and watch the rise on fall of the nation I've created. Furthermore the recent addition of ironman mode to the game does actually enrich the experience. I find myself taking my decisions even more seriously, knowing that one mistake could cost me everything I've worked for and leave me to start again. Which leaves me to my final point, losing is fun, no matter how far you take your empire you will always carry in your head "What's going to bring me crashing to the ground" and even though you want to nurture and protect this world you've built you're also curious to see what will bring it crashing down.
Crusader Kings II is a game of investment, both of monetary and time wise, and if you are willing to sink both into the game with what I'd argue being the core DLC (Sword of Islam, Old Gods, Sons of Abraham, Republic and Ruler Designer) you will feel as though your time and money was well spent. Although I likely talk from a biased perspective as now that I have the DLC I could never see myself playing the base game in the same way.
Overall I'd highly reccomend Crusader Kings II to anyone looking to fill that craving for a truly grand strategy.
