Downloaded the game even though I thought it looked silly. And trust me, it looks really silly.
However, If you like progression games, and maybe idle games, you'll love this.
It starts off slow but when you get your first ascension progress speeds up exponentially.  Ascensions are a way of resetting your game. It may sound counterproductive but it isn't.
When you ascend, you'll then gain access to things called Hero Souls, Ancients, Mercenaries, and Relics. The hero souls are used to buy ancients and each soul increases your total DPS by 10%. (I do believe you will obtain the majority of your hero souls from Primal bosses. Primal bosses are bosses that have a 25% chance to spawn every 5 levels AFTER level 100)
Note: Do NOT ascend immediately after level 100 if you can. Make sure you get more hero souls from primal bosses before you ascend.
The ancients help speed your progress by providing different effects. The mercenaries go on missions for various rewards. The relics are items that boost the power of your Ancients. All of these things last through each ascension.
Eventually you'll reach level 300 where you can Transcend and gain access to Ancient Souls and Outsiders. These souls are only used to buy Outsiders and outsiders, like Ancients, provide various effects. They're stronger than ancients and speed progress up even more. However each time you transcend you lose everything else. It resets your game and gets rid of all your relics and ancients. (You do keep your mercenaries, but you don't have access to them until you Ascend again) Transcensions are worth it in the long run even though they slow down progression at first. If you want, you can save rubies to do a quick ascension after transcending so it's not as slow.
There is more to this game than meets the eye. It's actually a good game and rewards those who are willing to make it through the first ascension. It's a lot of fun.
You can look up on google or reddit for more information and guides. The game does have a reddit page and I found it useful.

L.A. Noire is a very good game. I won't say great, because that's hard to achieve. But it definitely does very well in what it intends to do.
This game is set in the 1940's, and your job is to solve various crimes falling under four different categories: Traffic, Homicide, Arson, and Vice. You are not required to play through these in any particular order, though the game does seem to have one in mind if you so choose.
What sets this game apart is the magnificent efforts that went through recreating the feel of the 40's in this game, for one. Everything looks authentic, from the vehicles on the road to the clothing designs and other technological levels of the period... the music that is played from radios is all music that would have been released around that time, which I recognized as a fan of the old tunes =)  Even the way you investigate crimes feels truly set in the ways of the era. Since no one has those electronic i-whatevers, your character keeps a notebook on hand which keeps track of all evidence found during the case, a list of locations relevant, suspects, the whole deal. And on top of that, a LOT of the environment is there to be investigated.  You could find clues laying on the table, in the grass outside...not everything you can interact with is going to be invlved with the case.  But it's still there, ready to be looked at by you, the player, in all of its full 40's glory.
Another thing that sets this game apart is the acting. A lot of people did not seem to realize this, but you are not looking at simply voice--acting through created polygonal characters. No-- you are looking at real actors and actresses, captured by more than 30 cameras at every angle. Every gesture, facial expression, every twitch was caused in real time by the actor as they performed their role. This game is almost a movie that you control the flow of.
On top of your case files that you work through, there are also a lot of street crimes that happen throughout, which you can respond to on dispatch and move to deal with. These are optional, flavorful side missions, but they're added fun and reinforce what you're already looking at.
Are there things this game could have done better?  Absolutely. I'd have loved additional media available through the radios, or off-work activities to try out, just to see what it was like for your character interacting with 1940's LA.  But what you DO get is very satisfying and Rockstar did an excellent job with this game.  If you get the opportunity, give it a shot.  Unless you hate using your brain, this won't disappoint you.

L.A. Noire is a game with a storyline where nobody wins, heroes hide a dark past and they must deal with treason, corruption, drugs and murders.
The game offers a change of pace from all the shooter and open world games, granting a story full of interesting cases that go from traffic missions to the Arson department. Stolen cars, murders and fires are some of the missions you have to complete by using your detective skills. Cole Phelps is the main character, a WWII former officer, who according to some of his companions in the war, made some bad decisions during combat, returning from war as a hero he joined the LAPD, and quickly rose through the ranks and became a detective.
LA Noire is not the typical open world shoot them up and kill all you can game; first cases develop in a slow fashion so you can learn the tricks and how to look for clues that should help you solve the missions. Interrogating suspects is essential for the investigation, you have three options everytime you ask questions, you can accept the suspects' answer as the truth, you can doubt his answer or you can choose the lie option, the latest should be supported by evidence, if you fail, suspects won't take you seriously, thus failing partly in your case.
LA Noire is surely one especial game, because is not only different from many other games, but because the whole concept behind makes it original and unique, the system that the devs implemented here is awesome, the characters' motion face system is outstanding, every one of them feels alive due to this technique and the voice acting is superb.
Another characteristic of this game is the city, though I don't know how the 40's LA looked like, I am pretty sure the city in this game is depicted with justice, it feels alive and street crimes pop up from time to time, acting as a filler they sometimes can be annoying as they can be fun, annoying because you are in the middle of a case and you answer the call and the street crime is happening on the other side of the city, totally interrupting your mission, fortunately you can ignore them.
The different crimes you investigate are great, the intensity of the missions increases as you advance further into the main case, the most notorious cases in my opinion are the homicide ones, gruesome murders that are linked to the infamous Black Dahlia Murder, this is the game's
best part, even better than the main corruption case that some important figures of LAPD and housing development are part of and that Cole Phelps must deal with.
Unfortunately, L.A. Noire suffers from the same condition that other modern titles,
Yes, the game has  horrendous system mechanics, shooting tends to be awkward and unsatisfying, choppy at times, the main protagonist feels stiff and the cover system is not the best, clearly showing consolities effects, of course, the game was rapidly ported to PC, affecting gameplay and apparently graphics, as well as the 30 fps cap that can be bypassed by changing some files settings, unacceptable in my opinion. Continuing with graphics, they feel poorly optimized for PC, some buildings show some muddy textures at times and the city buildings and other places load as you approach, making you feel they really had no time to improve or deadlines were too tight.
The AI is nothing especial, enemies tend to have the same pattern over and over again, not showing any kind of tactics, so in the end is not that hard to kill dozens of them easily, this can change while doing car chasings, which are pretty decent to be fair, here enemies show a better AI and sometimes they can be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ Also another thing that was kind of annoying was the fact that you must ask your partner which direction is the correct, was that hard to show some arrows indicating where to go for all the cases?
L.A. Noire, while not being a perfect game, and not being that popular, it offers a unique and interesting storyline with a good perspective of the 40's life in LA, corruption, drugs and murders are the main themes here, it is grim, it is dark, it is L.A. Noire, heroes die, and the bad guys live to tell the story.

The game is just...bad.  It's almost good.  It's so close to good.  But it's not.  It's bad.  It's 2017 and they should have their clipping and hit detection figured out.  It's a mess.  Combat is wild flailing not even knowing if you are doing anything.  Big dinosaurs will clip their heads through the walls of buildings and eat you inside.  Dinosaurs float across the landscape, moving their feet in a fixed animation.  Taming and breeding are clicking the same button every thirty seconds for hours non-stop.  Resource gathering is clicking the mouse at static nodes, again for hours.  Construction is incredibly finicky if you want to make anything but a box, and if you make a mistake you have to demolish the part you just built to get only a fraction of the resources back.
The game is gorgeous, though.  The taming mechanic is such a good idea, if terribly implemented.  The dinosaurs are huge and dangerous, even though most of that danger is because hit detection and movement are so terrible.  Choosing which recipes to learn as you level up is cool, but you can't learn most of the recipes even at max level, later ones replace earlier ones, and you can't ever refund the points you spent early on that are now a waste.
Basically, the game is a mess and even the things which could be good seem deliberately designed to be terrible.  Oh, and optimization is still terrible.  It's pretty, but it's not so pretty that framerates should be anywhere close to that bad.  Also, it's only pretty with the settings up high.  Put them lower and it's a blurry, pixelated mess of brown and green.

Crusader Kings II is a highly in-depth grand strategy game with a dual focus upon micro-managing the day to day affairs of your ruler's court and the intrigue surrounding it. Whether it be securing an immediate heir to inherit your dynasty or deciding which of your vassal should hold council positions, these are decisions you will face on a regular basis. On the other hand you can temper these smaller objectives and concerns with grander ambitions such as preparing an army for invasion of infidel held territory, or working through the process of turning your small kingdom in an empire.
This is what Paradox Interactive seek to offer a customer of this game, freedom to dream and see these dreams realised or shattered by the events of history. It may be your ambition to be Emperor of a united and independent Britannia and see your sons hold the titles of each of the four kingdoms that make up your empire. However, there may be a duke with similiar dreams in your realm, a son who may want to hold all the titles instead of just one, or a foreign power with claims to your lands. This is Crusader Kings and how you deal with these individual issues and problems and managing your own ambitions is what makes this game so compelling and why I've sunk over 150+ hours into it and will continue to do so, even after support for the game may end. However with DLC being continously released such as the recent 'Sons of Abraham' or prior to that 'Old Gods' lack of support I feel is not a concern.
That is not to say the game is without it's weaknesses. To a new player the menu and micromanagement (even with the assistance of tooltips) can seem overwhelming and off putting leaving new players feeling very lost or confused.
The multiplayer leaves something to be desired, although I've experienced a stable and strong single player experience I cannot sing the prasises of the multiplayer, where numerous drop-outs, crashes and version conflicts have left a foul taste in my mouth where myself and friends have wanted to see how as a group we could shape history.
Finally the issues of war, now although the war system is built in mind with a strategic sense with terrain, fort, technology and event modifiers effecting your armies capabilities in battle it does occasionally feel as though it can boil down to "I have x men more than you do". Moreover the way war works in the sense that you have to sometimes completely and totally destory an enemy only to earn a single province instead of holding them accountable for all their land. These I feel are glaring weaknesses within the game.
However, despite these issue this game has insane, and I cannot stress that enough, insane replayability. I go back even now and find a new way of approaching a situation that could of caused my realm to destabalised, or play through from another cultures perspective (and with the addition of 'The Old Gods' and 'Sword of Islam' DLC another religions). There are times even when I feel I've played family line long enough that I can open the console commands and type 'observe' and just see how my changes have affected the timeline and watch the rise on fall of the nation I've created. Furthermore the recent addition of ironman mode to the game does actually enrich the experience. I find myself taking my decisions even more seriously, knowing that one mistake could cost me everything I've worked for and leave me to start again. Which leaves me to my final point, losing is fun, no matter how far you take your empire you will always carry in your head "What's going to bring me crashing to the ground" and even though you want to nurture and protect this world you've built you're also curious to see what will bring it crashing down.
Crusader Kings II is a game of investment, both of monetary and time wise, and if you are willing to sink both into the game with what I'd argue being the core DLC (Sword of Islam, Old Gods, Sons of Abraham, Republic and Ruler Designer) you will feel as though your time and money was well spent. Although I likely talk from a biased perspective as now that I have the DLC I could never see myself playing the base game in the same way.
Overall I'd highly reccomend Crusader Kings II to anyone looking to fill that craving for a truly grand strategy.

Crusader Kings 2, ultimately, is an experience. This is a good thing and it's most active selling point - It's not a game you win or lose, it's a game you craft stories from - as all the other reviews will likely show!
It is a game that appeals to multiple playstyles. If you want to be the grand overseer, some sort of mini-god surveying all that you have and making incredibly far-sighted decisions about where to conquer, who to ally with and what wars to start, looking at it as a gamer rather than a character? You can.
If you want to look at it as the character you are, say King Eucedis "The Fat" Salian of England, roleplaying as a man obsessed by excess, greed and pride, while simultaneously ruining future generations of your family tree by seducing all the courtier's wives and having a large pool of illegitemate children? You can
If you want to play it as a complete and total joviality, name your family the "Megatrons" and rename every single English city after each Sonic the Hedgehog level, because why not? You can.
All of these and many more are games I've had. Sometimes the game hates you and wants you to suffer, such as letting your 25 year old genius, attractive king who has all the claims in the world die from a cough, leaving you to inherit as your 1 year old, dumb, hairlipped son, who immediately gets rebelled on by his better brother, leaving you a peniless and landless wreck. At other times, the game loves you and even though you played as a merciless, heartless father who had a child with his eldest son's wife (who also never had any more children) and then he immediately dies and because of your inheritance said child inherits, but the brother ends up staying loyal and true, which gives you more than enough forces to make the others kow-tow.
All of the above scenarios have happened. More have too. More still will. If you enjoy having fun stories to tell people, or even fun stories to look back on, this game is for you.
The only two downsides - The game has a lot of DLC, which all add a lot to the game. This is somewhat mitigated by them regularly being on sale, but the cost still adds up. I must admit though that even having that, I mostly still play as the Christian rulers that start off accessible, alongside the Norse - The key is to experiment after purchase of the base product with it online, as if the host has the DLC you can use it in an online match. That way you can get a feel for what you want.
The second downside is the game layout. The game is not massive on visuals, aside from the pretty map and such, so most of it is small character portraits and menus. This has the side of making the game complicated because it's not initially easy to understand where you go wrong.
But I promise you - if you put the time into the game, it pays off.

Edit after recent update:
Once again, I wish there was a "mixed" option.
I've previously downvoted the game for a gamebreaking bug. The issue has now been fixed.
At first I was hooked and wanted to recommend it wholeheartly. BUT.
This game has a few design issues I do not appreciate:
-Diplomacy is nearly completely useless all around, and important bits (like alliances) are ridiculously high up on the tech tree.
-If there is more than one fleet in orbit per side, who fights what seems to be governed by arcane magic.
-Often vague descriptions of new research effects
-Some mechanics which have completely no information provided anywhere (looking at you, Unfallen vines and peacful integration)
-Some often minor GUI issues that make it difficult to either find or understand data.
-The hero skill trees
There are two major crimes that made me abandon the game and I'm not going back to it, though.
1. The game is SLOW. Mindboggingly slow.
AI is slow to choose battle tactics (out of 3-5 possibilities),  there's a delay of UP TO HALF A MINUTE for the it to show it's attitude towards a trade deal. Ending a turn is a trial of patience, waiting for the AI to finish.
The game is also weirdly resource-intesive, despite not a lot going on. This game has no right to strain my PC this way, which can run Wither 3 on Ultra at 60fps and Europa Universalis packed with mods at decent speeds. There is nothing graphicly or computationaly intensive enough in the game to justify that.
2. Population management (lack of), overcolonisation penalty and war.
There is a colony number limit over which you start getting bashed with a global happines penalty.
The only way to eliminate an enemy is to annex their planets. You cannot raze or exterminate, or just occupy. Annexing adds to your colony count. You can only raze it after it is fully yours, many turns later.
This means that if you're at your limit, trying to eliminate an enemy will quickly put your empire into chaos for no other reason than because the game says so. Same goes if you happen not to have certain resources on your current planets. You need to raze some of your old colonies just to be able to safely make new ones.
In other words, you can exterminate an enemy, but it'll take countless turns and by hurting yourself first (not counting the actual fighting). And as mentioned before, the turns are SLOOOW.
In other words, this game looks really nice but is shallow, has questionable design choices and eventually gets so slow and bogged down in it's own awkwardness that it's simply no fun to continue.
Only get it if you want small, quick races to victory conditions. Then you probably won't run into my problems.

The game has a strong premise and implementation that make it engaging as a 4X title.
Pros:
+ The politics within this game give you a sense that you are making overall decisions that guide your people's development, but the small details are managed by others.
+ Your homeworld starts with distinct political factions that influence how people vote in forming the government, which determines what laws are available (i.e., bonuses for development).
+ As you explore, you encounter minor civilizations that you can influence. The greater your standing with such minor civilizations, the more benefits that they will give you, plus you have the option to assimilate them into your culture.
+ By interacting with minor civilizations, their people will emigrate to your systems, forming their own distinct political factions that diversifies your culture, and your people's overall reaction to ongoing events.
+ There is great variety in the tech research, which isn't so much a "tree" as it is a pie that has been divided into four sections, with each section subdivided into general and specialized techs.
+ In addition to forming fleets of starships, there are also planetary invasion mechanics using infantry, tanks, and fighter jets. This adds a nuance to invasions because you cannot simply steamroll planets with your fleet of starships.
+ There is variety in how you conduct tactics in your battles, generally choosing three tactics (from a pool) that are generally available, and then applying one of those three tactics when you enter battle.
+ Your choice of combat tactic, in combination with how your ships are outfitted, is pitted against your enemy's choice of tactic in combination with how their ships are outfitted. So good variety.
+ The arrangement of star systems is interesting because they are arranged like the constellations that you would find in astrological signs. Except that, where astrological signs have imaginary lines that are drawn between systems, this game uses the connecting lines as star lanes upon which ships travel. There is more to it, such as warp travel and wormholes that you can research, but I'll let you explore that on your own.
+ This game has eight (8) distinct races. The humans are probably the most relatable, and the other races are imaginative and compelling, each of them seeming to have their own fleshed out backgrounds.
Cons
- I believe that the AI could use some work in the form of extra diplomatic stances. Currently, there are stances like Peace Agreement, Trade Agreement, etc. But there really needs to be options like, "Agression will be met with force," or "We mean you no harm." In other words, a means to warn an AI to leave you alone, or a means to strengthen ties with a non-hostile AI.
- Trade routes seems to be overpowered at the moment, where you can earn extraordinary amounts of dust, resulting in rapid dust inflation.
Edited: Jun 3, 2017 to add some cons.

I would like to recommend ES2, but I can't.
There was a game-breaking bug introduced in the patch to the launch patch.  (Dozens of players have reported it on the forums.)  While I am sympathetic to the complexity of software programming, the developers chose not to beta-test the patches.  They had a big group of active early-access players who would have found this problem immediately.  Introducing a game-killing bug into the launch product was simply avoidable.  If the excuse for rushing is that they wanted to get the game into players' hands more quickly, the fact that we can't play the game now proves that a failed argument.
I bought the game at launch at the recommendation of RPS.  The art is lovely.  The factions are diverse.  However, there is very little information on the game's systems.  The wiki is locked by the developers, and only has cosmetic background story on the factions, not explanations of what terms in the game mean.  The "tutorial" is a database of extended tooltips that can't be accessed except when they are triggered.
Fortunately the game isn't difficult at Normal, so you will be able to muddle through.  (I had my entire tiny faction repo'd due to bankruptcy early on from a random event, but was still able to come back.)  I get that companies won't write manuals anymore, and sadly tutorials are generally very limited.  But locking out the wiki really limits understanding (and enjoyment) of a game designed to have complex interlocking systems.
As PCGamer noted, ES2 still has the design hardwired to have excess new colonies tank happiness across the faction.  I understand the design goal, but the implementation is illogical and heavy-handed.  I had hoped they would improve this in ES2.  Fortunately, since you know it is going to occur, you can go out of your way to boost happiness far in excess of your current needs in preparation for your eventual expansion.  (Because 4X....)
Ah, well.  I fully expect it to get better!

If you like micro-managing every single aspect of your entire, massive empire, then you'll like this game. Unfortunately, I don't.
The automation in this game is absolute garbage. Auto-designing a ship will never give you better equipment, since it flat-out refuses to equip it with anything that costs resources. And, since there's very very little strategy in designing a ship anymore, the only reason to design a new one is to shove the latest, expensive equipment in it, so it just ends up being a tedious chore you have to do every once in a while during the game when you unlock new technologies. So, unlocking a new technology, instead of being fun, ends up a chore.
Auto-managing star systems is slow, as it will only ever build one thing at a time (even if it'd only take 1/2 of your resource per turn production), and often builds absolutely nothing even though it can be easily afforded, and is quite necessary (aka, negative food production, but refuses to build a farm). Not to mention the fact that if you tell the auto governer to focus on science, it will only only only build science buildings, and nothing else. There is no "balanced" governer, as in the first one. So, once again, when you unlock new buildings, you have to go to each one of your star systems, find it in the build menu, and manually tell the system to construct it.
I know this seems like knit-picking, but I don't see it as such. Sure, during the beginning of the game, you'll want to leave auto-build off and manually construct buildings anyway. However, mid to late game, you'll end up with dozens of star systems to manage, and without any automation that's worthwhile, you'll have to manually choose which building each star system needs. Tedium.

After a whole lot of hours on this game, I feel I owe it a more detailed review.
Crusader Kings 2, ultimately, is an experience. This is a good thing and it's most active selling point - It's not a game you win or lose, it's a game you craft stories from - as all the other reviews will likely show!
It is a game that appeals to multiple playstyles. If you want to be the grand overseer, some sort of mini-god surveying all that you have and making incredibly far-sighted decisions about where to conquer, who to ally with and what wars to start, looking at it as a gamer rather than a character? You can.
If you want to look at it as the character you are, say King Eucedis "The Fat" Salian of England, roleplaying as a man obsessed by excess, greed and pride, while simultaneously ruining future generations of your family tree by seducing all the courtier's wives and having a large pool of illegitemate children? You can
If you want to play it as a complete and total joviality, name your family the "Megatrons" and rename every single English city after each Sonic the Hedgehog level, because why not? You can.
All of these and many more are games I've had. Sometimes the game hates you and wants you to suffer, such as letting your 25 year old genius, attractive king who has all the claims in the world die from a cough, leaving you to inherit as your 1 year old, dumb, hairlipped son, who immediately gets rebelled on by his better brother, leaving you a peniless and landless wreck. At other times, the game loves you and even though you played as a merciless, heartless father who had a child with his eldest son's wife (who also never had any more children) and then he immediately dies and because of your inheritance said child inherits, but the brother ends up staying loyal and true, which gives you more than enough forces to make the others kow-tow.
All of the above scenarios have happened. More have too. More still will. If you enjoy having fun stories to tell people, or even fun stories to look back on, this game is for you.
The only two downsides - The game has a lot of DLC, which all add a lot to the game. This is somewhat mitigated by them regularly being on sale, but the cost still adds up. I must admit though that even having that, I mostly still play as the Christian rulers that start off accessible, alongside the Norse - The key is to experiment after purchase of the base product with it online, as if the host has the DLC you can use it in an online match. That way you can get a feel for what you want.
The second downside is the game layout. The game is not massive on visuals, aside from the pretty map and such, so most of it is small character portraits and menus. This has the side of making the game complicated because it's not initially easy to understand where you go wrong.
But I promise you - if you put the time into the game, it pays off.

This is a hard game: hard to approach, hard to play, and very hard to master, mostly because it is so bloody deep and complex and the manual and tutorials explain only the interface and not the actual substance of play. If you already understand the subtleties of medieval agnatic gavelkind succession versus cognatic primogeniture then you're probably good to go; I thought I was a history buff until I tried this game. Sheesh.
But here's the beauty of it: the game is immensely rewarding once you finally start to get the hang of it. The human stories it ends up generating are very real and gripping. You come to identify with the characters you play, exulting in their success and despairing at their failure. I was so♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off last night when an upset vassal assassinated my character's son and heir that I basically threw away my kingdom just to see him dead.
I finally hit my personal turning point with the game last night, after roughly a dozen hours, when I finally grasped some of the important points of kingdom laws and how the changes you can make matter. Even after a dozen hours I'm still in the dark about a lot of things, and I"m betting that would still be the case after hundreds of hours; the game is just that deep and complex. But I'm starting to think it may be the best of all the Paradox strategy games and arguably the most compelling  historical strategy game I've ever played.

Play it for the movie aspect, the atmosphere and the story. Too bad the shooting and driving gameplays -which represent a significant part of the game- are so uninspired.
+ The storyline is intense, intriguing, coherent, full of unexpected developments
+ Best voice acting I've ever heard
+ Great tribute to the dark gansters movies from the 40s to the 60s, with hats and Thomson submachine guns
+ A lot of efforts put into the characters, their stories, their backgrounds, their motives
+ Facial expressions can be ridiculous at times, but the result is still impressive and brings more credibility to the movie-like cut-scenes
+ Numerous cars and trucks from the 40s to drive or just admire
+ The music plays a great role when you investigate, you gotta watch AND listen to find the clues. The jazzy themes are a real pleasure to the ears.
+ Investigating a crime scene really puts you in the shoes of a detective
+ Interrogations are challenging -even if not always for the good reasons
+ 21 cases that keep you entertained for long hours
+ Different cases with different rythms, you never have two consecutive cases with the same development
+ The automatic cut-scenes and scripted interventions of your colleagues let you know when you have completed the investigation of an area. A clever idea not to lose time wandering around and killing the rythm
- Investigate a crime scene, chase people, question people, shoot people and a few puzzles. You won't do much more during the entire game.
- Controls are often delayed, even in the menus
- Textures and objects popping up at the last moment on the road...
- Gunfights are a pain, your character is sluggish -both for walking or aiming. Taking cover does not prevent you from getting shot...
- Los Angeles people are stunningly resilient. It takes 6 gun bullets to kill someone. Or 4 BAR rounds. Or 3 headshots. Or one shot in the leg... Go figure that out...
- Driving the cars is another torture. The cars turn around one axis only. It feels heavy like an old car alright, but every one feels the same. The engine sounds are generic and lack some bass to evoke the big blocks purring.
- What's the point of such a huge map if there's nothing interesting to do between missions? By the way, you automatically go from one case to another in the story mode. If you want to take a tour of Los Angeles, you have to go back to the main menu, enter the 'Cases' sub-menu and open a 'desk' sub-sub-menu to select 'free roam'. How logical and intuitive is that?
- Everything is scripted. EVERYTHING, EVEN THE CAR CHASES! You can't catch a fleeing car before the game decides so. That leads to surrealistic movements of the car you're chasing, defying gravity and basic mechanical principles.
- When you choose to accuse someone of lying, the actual accusation that follows may have nothing to do with the previous comment. The investigator/detective goes in another direction and your evidences you were ready to show become irrelevant.
- You must use the facial expression to tell if people are lying or not. But since they can fake it, it's mostly a guessing game. At some point, you stop caring and try your luck.
- There are more cars in the streets than in Driver San Francisco. Are you sure there were so many cars in the 40s?
- Facial expressions are great but a little more work on the hair would have been appreciated. It looks like they all wear wigs

L.A.Noire will take you through career of Cole Phelps, ex marine, who now works at LAPD. This means there is driving in what was meant to be near perfect recreation of LA (I can't judge this since I was never to LA, not to mention LA of 1947), shooting and investigation, which is the main focus of the game, involved. During your investigations you will be searching for clues, which may or may not be of further use to you but they all add to your rating that is given to you at the end of each case, and interview suspects & witnesses. Storywise it is decent, there are some decisions which are odd and questionable. Some of the cases just feel wrong if you look on them on their own, but I don't want to potentionaly spoil anything so I won't go into details. Now that I hit rank 50  I thought I'd say a bit about my experience (as of 04/11/2015). This game is great for casual players especially. Jumping on with a buddy, having a few beers, and killing everything in sight is more fun than I care to admit. As far as competitive play, I don't consider it a game that is ready for that yet. Some animations are desynched from the hitbox, as well as weird lag issues (it will take you a while to develope the ability to even notice, but then it becomes so very obvious). If you have 110+ ping, I would recommend not even picking up this game as ping is a major factor, and most of the time high ping will get you kiced from servers.
Rank 35 and below is mainly where you will learn the game mechanics and just have fun with it. In general, after that is where you really start to get a good grasp of the finer mechanics and get the 30-3 kill/death ratios.
The atmosphere in this game is fun while you're new, but when you  start getting a hang of the game and seeing how the mechanics work, it can get ugly if you are someone who is easily angered. It promotes an e-peen waving and rage inducing mindset which can really get to some people. If you can ignore that or push past it, then the game will give you many hours of enjoyment!
Who this is for:
People who want to have a great time with friends in a game that you can enjoy playing for 5 mintues or 5 hours.

Best historically-based strategy game I know, and the most unique. Nothing matches this for depth, detail, and variability. It's very complex and has a steep learning curve, but everything is balanced so well and factors affect each other intuitively, so that it doesn't take long to grasp the concepts and start plotting your family's rise to power. This game rewards your hard work and gives you constant opportunities to reinvent yourself and recover. Think you've lost because your enemies deposed you from your throne? Nope, it's just a setback -- you're still a duke and have different options open to you than before. Think you have to give up because your family leader is old, infirm, and hated? When he dies and you start playing as his heir, things may turn your way again. This game encourages you to live with your mistakes and grow from them.
It also will teach you a lot about European geography, which is nice!

Changing this review to a thumbs up to reflect it's current state, rather than the state at release.  Has balance issues and whatnot, but on the whole, if you liked ES1, you'll like ES2 as much or better.
************************************************
Original Review from the broken release version:
Horribly, stupidly broken game.  From all the positive reviews, I figured the first time the game bugged into an broken state that I couldn't reload my way out of it just had to be a fluke, right?  Then it happened again.  And again.  And again.  All different bugs too!  Endless pending turn, battles that just keep going forever, etc.  It's shame too, because other than the whole not working thing, it's a vast improvement on ES1 in nearly every way, and ES1 was a solid game to begin with,  Save your money until they fix it.

Now that I hit rank 50  I thought I'd say a bit about my experience (as of 04/11/2015). This game is great for casual players especially. Jumping on with a buddy, having a few beers, and killing everything in sight is more fun than I care to admit. As far as competitive play, I don't consider it a game that is ready for that yet. Some animations are desynched from the hitbox, as well as weird lag issues (it will take you a while to develope the ability to even notice, but then it becomes so very obvious). If you have 110+ ping, I would recommend not even picking up this game as ping is a major factor, and most of the time high ping will get you kiced from servers.
Rank 35 and below is mainly where you will learn the game mechanics and just have fun with it. In general, after that is where you really start to get a good grasp of the finer mechanics and get the 30-3 kill/death ratios.
The atmosphere in this game is fun while you're new, but when you  start getting a hang of the game and seeing how the mechanics work, it can get ugly if you are someone who is easily angered. It promotes an e-peen waving and rage inducing mindset which can really get to some people. If you can ignore that or push past it, then the game will give you many hours of enjoyment!
Who this is for:
People who want to have a great time with friends in a game that you can enjoy playing for 5 mintues or 5 hours.
Those who like medieval combat and are seeking a more skill/reaction based game.
People who are patient and want to learn.
Who this is not for:
Impatient people, or people who get angry when they get killed. You will die, a LOT.
People with high ping.

An absolutely excellent strategy game. It is fun, deep, and engaging, but beware of the high learning curve. Once you get past the learning curve, it shows itself to be one of the best strategy games ever. It might even be my favourite game of all time.
It is essentially a medieval dynasty simulator. Unlike most strategy games, you do not play directly as the country, but rather as a land owning ruler with many vassals, who in turn own land. It sort of has an RPG aspect with character stats and relationships that form between characters. when you die you are succeeded by your heir, but if that heir is not of your dynasty, the game ends. There is really no real set goal to the game, other than reach the end date of 1453. You make your own goals, such as conquering  a rival power's land, Reforming Pagan religions to resist Christianity, restoring Jewish Israel, Zoroastrian Persia, or even the Roman Empire, and try to survive in a hostile time filled with war and intrigue.

To summarise why I now despise this game: A player base which has finally found the most efficient exploits in the broken movement system, surrounded by a failed attempt to make the game into a cash-cow inspired by the example of TF2's hat monetization system.
And in more detail:
I played this game last year, before the major update, you know, when the combat was actually fun and only half the player base were ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. At that time there was no monetization, and the maps were usually designed to make small groups of players fight other equal groups of players, rather than what the developers would likely call a "duelling" style of map, which encourages several groups of two players killing one throughout the whole map. Even though people were trying to find ways of making it harder to block attacks, it was not to the point quite yet, where the usual opening move is to jump, touching the enemy, to their side, while attacking with a thrust from above. Not only is this physically flawed since jumping 4ft with armor on is
, but flawed in terms of game mechanics because it was never actually meant to be possible in the first place.
When I had a look today there was one server in Australia with any people on it, and one with some really weird mods enabled. The server-base and player-base is pretty terrible at first glance; people would rather play on a FFA server where getting kills makes you physically larger than on a team deathmatch or defence mode server. This makes me think actually.. When the game is bad and the mods amazing, they don't get hosted, but when the game is good and the mods are embarrassing, only the mods are hosted..? What the hell logic is that.
Apart from all that, the monetization system makes me sad, embarrassed and angry all at the same time. I have a strict policy on microtransactions and DLC. If a game has them, I die a little inside and walk the ♥♥♥♥ away never to look back. Same with apps on my other devices. To describe what the monetization system is as objectively I can; weapons and armour (skins?) can be bought from the customization screen. They appear with a dollar sign next to them, and appear to be user created in some cases. Pretty sure they don't have different stats, but even so.
And with that; if I could have played the version from last year, I would have, but I think now I'll just put it in my hidden "Total♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; folder in Steam, along with The First Templar.

If you're into mystery solving games then I suppose this is for you, I however, am not, and found this quite boring after a while. The controls were sloppy sometimes, combat WAAAAY too easy (can you even die in this game?), and during chases you have very limited options. The game forces you to go that exact route and being kicked by a guy there and there and the game decides when you can pull out your gun and threaten the suspect to stop. The only thing I found entertaining in this game was the driving, but instead of that, might just buy a car game, and I don't even play car games. I suppose the questioning mechanics (decide whether the person's lying or not) was another entertaining thing, because if you guess wrong, it will change the course of case, or rather, just extend it, because then you're gonna have to find another way of exposing the suspect. And then again, it's not so hard either, if you know what you're doing.
The game starts to feel like it's repeating itself, a lot. The first few cases were good I guess, but after that I started feeling like all the suspense was gone.
I also wanted to quickly mention that if you drive over a pedestrian, he or she just swings by, hardly even tripping, this "bug" happens randomly but frequently. Feels like this game had a very small idea and overall quite lacking in variety.
The game did a pretty good job at depicting the 40s. Though I think Mafia 2 did a better job  (it's a lot better game overall if you're looking for 40s and 50s america GTA type game).
Only thing that makes this game unique is the facial technology. It just reminds you how expressionless all video game characters are in other games. It's astounding, really.
30 FPS lock was annoying, but I suppose they had good reasons for that.
I suppose I can't figure out anything else to say, I remember this getting good reviews at the time it came and wanted a chance to try it out myself. Now if I'd tell my past-self whether to buy this game or not, I would say no. But to anyone who enjoys those mystery solving detective games, I suppose this is a fine treat.

Awesome grand strategy set in the medieval period from 1066 where you can play as Duke William of Normandy and invade England through to 1453 and the end of the 100 year war. The game sees you take on the role of a dynasty ranging from a small count in control of a county through Dukes and upto Kings and even being proclaimed emperor of a lage empire should you be victourios and conquer large swaths of land. Your job is to make important decisions as said ruler which either improve your charaters personal traits or leave a dark stain on yoru hounor and prestige. The decisions involve arranging marriages, choosing who educates your children and future heirs, Forging false claims on other realms and titles to expand youe empire, Arranging assassinations and plotting against people, Creating spy networks, having people imprisoned and then choosing their punishment. The game environment consists of 100's of other npc characters from your own realm and others who all have their own evolving traits as the game progresses some of which can be used as important allies and others you will need to keep an eye on as they may themselves be plotting to overthrow your position. My best experience so far was hiring some mercenarys to invade england after a failed invasion the first time, my gold reservers ran out and as I could no longer fund the war effort they turned on me and took my province forcing me to surrenfer and submit to their terms. I was reduced to some petty count in some poor corner of france with a burning desire for revenge. Over the next 50 years of game time I grew in strength building my money and plotting to retake my title, I succeeded and ended up imprisoning the very guy who attacked me and then had the fool executed, mwahaha. The game is a roller coaster of ups and downs and the best gameplay comes from not loading a save as you have been defeated but by enjoying the failures and successes you make yourself. If your a strategy fan and like a bit of roleplay on the side then this is a must!!! you simply must have this game in your steam games list or risk a peasnats revolt or even worse having the pope excommunicate your♥♥♥♥♥!!

This is a hard game: hard to approach, hard to play, and very hard to master, mostly because it is so bloody deep and complex and the manual and tutorials explain only the interface and not the actual substance of play. If you already understand the subtleties of medieval agnatic gavelkind succession versus cognatic primogeniture then you're probably good to go; I thought I was a history buff until I tried this game. Sheesh.
But here's the beauty of it: the game is immensely rewarding once you finally start to get the hang of it. The human stories it ends up generating are very real and gripping. You come to identify with the characters you play, exulting in their success and despairing at their failure. I was so♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off last night when an upset vassal assassinated my character's son and heir that I basically threw away my kingdom just to see him dead.
I finally hit my personal turning point with the game last night, after roughly a dozen hours, when I finally grasped some of the important points of kingdom laws and how the changes you can make matter. Even after a dozen hours I'm still in the dark about a lot of things, and I"m betting that would still be the case after hundreds of hours; the game is just that deep and complex. But I'm starting to think it may be the best of all the Paradox strategy games and arguably the most compelling  historical strategy game I've ever played.

As a cinematic experience, LA Noire is very good. It has a stack of content, compelling stories, great voice acting and revolutionary facial animation. It tackles challenging themes in a mature manner. It offers a large area to explore, built with great attention to detail.
As a game...it's a mixed bag. The distractions - driving, shooting, tailing and collecting items - are nothing special. The core is the investigation - searching for clues and interrogating witnesses/suspects. The former is decent, with helpful difficulty options. The latter has its moments, both good and keyboard-smashingly bad.
Two examples. A witness is asked about a document found in the possession of somebody else. There is no reason to be sure, or even reasonably suspect, that she is aware of it. When she denies knowledge of it, an appropriate choice response would seem to be "Doubt". According to the game, it's "Lie" - even though her response seems to confirm that she was unaware of it, making the "Lie" a strange choice. Even worse, there is another situation where you are expected to select "Lie", when the actual lie arises from the response to your challenge upon choosing "Lie"!
The single checkpoint save is also frustrating. Realise you made a mistake (seeing witness in a certain order cuts out a possible question in an early mission, for instance) or encounter a mission-breaking bug after a checkpoint save, and you have to go back to the very beginning - 30+ mins of unskippable dialogue and driving.
There's also port issues - a woeful 30fps, graphical pop-in and the like.
For all that...it's still a compelling experience. As much as it annoys me, I keep coming back. It may require a new keyboard by the end, but it'll be worth it.

And These 2 fractions clash in bloody wars for land. So you have 4 main classes, Archer, Man- at- Arms, vanguard, and knight. All of them have their own abilitys. Archer has a Bow and short sword, Man at arms is like a weaker version of the knight, but is quick on his feet, Vanguard, a heavly armored knight with a massive pole hammer that slams down on other enemies, then the knight that has a longsword, but can be swapped for a sword and shield. So far this is a great game, a massive improvement on the first game. It still has a few problems however they are mostly minor.
The UI is extremely streamlined and clear, managing to show all of the information you need in a user-friendly way, without taking up too much screen space. Very few drop downs are used. In some cases I would say it is a little too streamlined although not in the extremes. When I wanted to create my own custom faction, I couldn't actually find out how, it was different from the first game. I had to google it eventually, only to slap myself in the face for my stupidity(you just have to click on the race portrait rather than the drop down, why isn't it in the drop down anyway?).
The graphics are pretty great as well. Everything from the ships to the portraits are unique and fun to look at. I'd say the graphics truly shine in fleet battles though, with missiles and lasers flying between huge masses of metal.
Overall the gameplay is exccellent, at least early and mid game. Colonisation is normally fun, although it varies from map to map. For example, as the Riftborn I enjoyed colonisation and exploration because of the massive amount of lava and ash planets near me, but as the lumeris I got the very same thing. This essentialy stopped me from getting half the systems near me early on, since they were too high tech and I couldn't grow any population on them. Fleet combat is relatively simple, but complex enough to be fun. Unfortunately Endless Space 2 suffers from a common problem among strategy games, in that the late game lags to all hell. Past about turn 150, my pc was really struggling to keep up, especially at the start of a turn and it is by no means an underpowered machine(specs below).
Diplomacy is pretty boring in my opinion, never really did anything for me, and the AI is quite annoying. It certainly is competent but some of it's decisions are really annoying. My own allies go absolutely crazy any time I send a fleet through their borders, even a scout. Within a few turns they have broken our alliance, trading agreement and declared a cold war. Just for having a scout go through their borders. That just seems illogical to me.
Overall I'd say that Endless Space 2 is one of the best 4X games I've played (not that I've played many) and pretty much all my complaints are very minor

The games great everything ide want out of an rts game. That being said there are glaring issues that are just impassible. First off theres a well known bug that causes your entire save file to be stuck in a loop. The bug is caused by you competeing with an ai in an event for rewards. Basically the game will assign random events and you can be put on a team. I have played 2 files through, 1st i wasn't invited 2nd i was. In this 2nd file i was playing as the lumerian a group of merchants. Due to my foresight and forward settling i control over 1/3rd of the entire galaxy without any wars. I keep this up to turn 90. I get an event saying pick a side. The event is to control 7 different star systems with armadas controlled by heros for a certain amount of turns. The reward is 75 of the rarest crystals and 2000 money/science. The stage is set and the 1st galactic war is on. me 2.5k points and 1k point empire vs 2 1.5k empires. I hold the central hub of the map and trade. My armada is bolstered by numerous minor civilizations and my ally. we secure 4/7 of the star systems and we are making ground on 5 and 6 by turn 120. At this point i control almost 40& of the right side of the galaxy with full control of the galaxy and victory on the horizon. This is also the point that the game glitches and wont let me get past. BOTH enemy factions have bugged ships on the star systems 5/6. This means that if i want to interact with those systems or ships i have on that spot i have to lose my entire save. Sure why don't i reload back and just avoid the questline and those star systems? Well the last quarter of the game has been devoted to this 2 front war and now i can't even get the grand prize.
Issue number 2. In my first save i managed to avoid problem number 1 by not being put into any faction based questwars i assume by rng. The issue in game number 1 was that i was winning war after war, i setup a trade route to go to the opposite side of the other galaxy colliding with mine bringing in huge amounts of money. This also brought lag. I had 9 factions in the game and i had almost wiped one out but my game got to the point where it was lagging so bad it was unplayable. It was exactly like FPS Death in dwarf fortress. For anyone not familiar with it just imagine every turn your game gets a little slower while you grow until you are too big for the game to load anything for you.
8gb of ram quad core i5 3.5ghz ati raedon 650 ti so my computer isnt terrible infact its almost exactly meeting the reccomended. So the reccomendation for this game will get you to turn 170 on max players. Personally I don't like this. I seek as much challenge and variation to my matches as i can find when playing rts games. If i can't put the max amount of players in the lobby then im not getting the full experience and by extension the challenge i was seeking. Also when i cut down on players so it wouldn't lag i hit another game breaking bug anyways. This was on save files #1 and #2 keep in mind so i doubt #3 is going to be different.
TLDR: Games worth the price and tons of fun however with the game becoming unplayable after a certain number of turns and there being multiple game breaking bugs that are focused around KEY features i cannot reccomend the game.

L.A. Noire has a masterfully crafted story that you seldom find in other games. Several of the cases and plotlines play off historic fiction, and the devs have done their homework. Everything from the beautiful recreation of 1940's Los Angeles to tie-ins with historic pieces like the Black Dahlia, or the H-4 Hercules has been well researched for its presentation. You can really feel the spirit of postwar America recreated in this game through the amazing storytelling. The facial animations, created using MotionScan, really put the icing on the cake as you can see the expressive emotion in the face of every character for every word they utter, something that you will be hard pressed to find in other games.
My only major complaint about this game is the 30 fps lock which is a shame. I tried a couple different methods to change the cap to 60, but I wasn't able to do this without actually making the game perform worse. Your mileage may vary. Otherwise this is yet another fantastic game from Rockstar.

Golf is a game of patience, virtue and of course percision. This game takes no exceptions here.
You play as Cub Woods, heir and successor to the Tiger Woods throne of golf. The objective is very simple, rise above the bad reputation that comes with the name Woods and restore balance to the earth by becoming a golf champion with the least sexual allegations under your belt as possible.
The game starts with Cub training up in the woods to perfect his tee. Completing that he moves onto egypt where he gets down to business on his long and short games in and around the pyramids.
Not only that but you can also hone your golf skills in a trip to the haunted house and be spooked into going under par. Upholding family traditions and having an acid trip to a world made of candy is also possible due to some really good backstreet connections.
If that is not enough you can even lay siege to a pirate settlement and take back the sea by utilising golf technique and cannons to defeat the pirate scourge and save Port Royale from certain doom.
The best part of the game though is when you defend Port Royale and obtain the time travel device. Using that device you are teleported to a Prehistoric golf course where you meet Edward Richtofen who seeks to prevent the asteroid from colliding with earth as he believes element 115 originated at this point. Putting all your skills to the test you assist Richtofen in defeating the asteroid in a quick 18 holes. Doing so will award Cub with the King of Games title and as a result, sends the asteroid into the shadow realm.
As the game draws to an end. Cub, Richtofen and Yugi Moto all relax under a tree together while forging a plan to return to the present time, hoping all the way that banishing an asteroid that changed the earth drastically had nothing to do with human progression in the slightest.
Overall 8.9/10 could use a map editor but that is being worked on so expect a 10/10 soon.

First off, let’s talk about official servers.
Your official server will not be hosted by Studio Wildcard, in an area they control, with people on staff ready to reboot the server when the DDoS happens, or the server simply stops accepting connections and kicks everyone, preventing them from reconnecting while time continues on, leading to dead baby dinos because you can’t log in to take care of them.  No, they’re maintained by Nitrado, a shifty company to begin with that is slow to respond to customer inquiries about server outages (I had a server through them, and this was the case all the time).  What this means is that when the server goes down, it’s down for days with absolutely no rollback at all, to ‘keep things fair’.  It’s down for days because you have to inform Wildcard, who has to inform Nitrado, who has to give a damn to get up and reboot the servers.
Next, you’re likely to be raided from ‘under the mesh’, meaning that you will be hit where your defenses can’t defend you.  Yes, even in this ‘ready for release’ game, we still have people actively exploiting holes in the code to wipe people, and only recently has Wildcard begun banning these people; however, instead of doing things the smart way and banning by hardware ID, they simply do a BattlEye ban on the account, which allows them to go out and purchase another copy for another account.  This is predominant on the grey market, where you can get significant price cuts on these games, especially in the Russian and Chinese areas because many of the keys are initially purchased with stolen credit cards.  In any case, this is a constant, it’s not an exception.  Even if you’re not raided in such a manner, the attackers have more at their disposal than you do in terms of removing your defenses, so good luck defending yourself.
Now let’s talk about customer service.
It’s nonexistent.  You will have issues crop up that lead to the loss of your prized dinosaurs, or you transfer between servers and your character is lost because their infrastructure, once again, is not maintained by the company.  When you go to Wildcard to get a response, that response is a form letter than essentially reads:
“Greetings, survivor!
Get ♥♥♥♥ed!”
That is, literally, customer support in a nutshell.
Want to know about the changes coming down the pipe?  Then head over to the patch notes on
, which are most of time incomplete, with major changes not documented, even in this ‘ready for release’ game.  Or maybe you can read their Community Crunch, where they tell you all the stuff that other people have done, and shill for their new DLC that is completely pushed back months but you should buy it because it takes money to fix the♥♥♥♥♥♥that’s broken that they have no intention of fixing because they can’t.  Or maybe you can ask a question that will be put into said Community Crunch…unless, of course, you ask a substantive question that Jeremy “Drake” Steiglitz can’t respond to with, “That sounds good, I’ll put that in the next patch” (and which half the time he doesn’t do) or asks about optimization and gameplay improvements.  In which case,♥♥♥♥♥♥off, you troll, don’t ask them about such things.  Just give them money.
Don’t believe me they only want the money?  They’re talking about a sequel to the game:
Expect any major changes to be mentioned on a Friday so they can ignore the playerbase until Monday.  Unless, of course, the playerbase raises holy hell in the wake of another company making similar dumb decisions and they have to pay attention to it over the weekend.  Do not expect them to solicit your input before announcing these changes, either.
Don’t expect them to make self-imposed deadlines.  They never did in early access, they failed to make their deadling for launching the game on 08 August, and their first paid DLC post-launch was delayed until December, when it was announced publicly to be released in October.
And in terms of PR, expect very sarcastic and caustic responses from the likes of WildcardTheRightHand, or lackluster, half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥responses from Jeremy.  Both people, by the way, should be dragged away from Reddit and Twitter and told if they post again, they lose fingers, because both are incapable of treating the players like intelligent people.
Now let’s talk about gameplay.
You will spend hours initially taming dinosaurs, only to lose them to some odd bug that has been known about for months and never addressed.  We still have, on occasion, creatures falling through the map.  We have wild dinosaurs that still spawn in pens.
You have a 500 dinosaur limit per tribe, meaning that to have an active kibble farm as well as breeding creatures and the creatures you need to gather and make war…you require another tribe to handle much of it to get around it.  Then there’s the “server cap” on dinosaurs because…you know, they have requirements in terms of hardware, and the coding is so basic and faulty it’s a damn joke.  And pretty much every server has hit that limit.
Creature hitboxes are all over the place.  It is completely possible to hit a bump that sends your sabretooth cat into the air, only to land in the hitbox of an aggressive Rex, that begins chomping on you while you sit there, suspended in mid-air, the game saying that you’re stuck and unable to even defend yourself.  In fact, the best way to kill bosses is to use Rexes to exploit the poor hitbox form to glitch them.  Immersive gameplay!
Oh, and if you don’t have an up-to-date, state-of-the-art PC, don’t think of playing on any settings worth a damn.  This game has been labeled the Crysis of 2017 because it is simply an unoptimized piece of crap.
And no, they haven’t stopped the TrueSky crashes, despite that being on the “A Little Further Out” portion of the patch notes for over a year now.
Is the game worth buying?  Not for $60.00.  Do not buy the season pass.  Wait for the game to go on sale.
If you do buy this game, spend the first dozen or so hours on official,  Learn the game from the laborer standpoint.  Once you do, and when you’ve been wiped while offline (because that is the only thing that happens; there is no PvP, it’s “offline raiding” only) look at unofficial servers, with boosted rates that don’t make this game a second or third job to ‘enjoy’.
This game loses a lot of the awe and wonder after the first few hours.  The first time I saw a Rex, or a Giganotosaurus I was shocked and ecstatic.  Now you see them and go, ‘k’.

With Endless Space 2, Amplitude continue their tradition of offering a familiar, yet different, take on the 4X genre, developed with the help of the community on Games2Gether. Before I properly get into this review, I'd like to extoll the virtues of Amplitude as a developer. They've constantly been active on Games2Gether, pooling ideas, and been exceptionally clear about their goals for the game. Props to them for that.
If you're new to the Endless series, I'd say ES2 is a good place to start. There's a little bit of everything in here for anybody who's tried a 4X before: the politics and ship building of Gal Civ 2, the galaxy expansion of MOO, the non-intrusive storytelling of Alpha Centauri. This isn't to say that ES2 is devoid of its own mechanics or feel: far from it. The atmosphere, stunning score by FlyByNo, and absolutely gorgeous visuals have made the Endless Space universe a vibrant, gorgeous and immersive place to be. The little touches of music when you make a colony with gorgeous cinematic art is excellent. If you're not familiar with this universe yet- as every Endless game ties into one another- you'll want to be.
If you're not familiar with the genre, this game might have a steep learning curve for you. Certainly, I have friends who've been introduced to 4X via Civ and try and hop onto this game and found it difficult. There is a tutorial, but as we know, tutorials can miss out on some of the smaller details. Take a buddy with you to teach the game in a multiplayer game, if you can. (I similarly had to help out some of my mates with Endless Legend.)
Even though this is fresh out of early access, I'd say this is one of the smoother launches I've seen. Launch day had a huge Day 1 patch with resolved a lot of glaring issues out of the gate. I've not had any CTDs, performance on full settings is a solid 60fps at all times.
If you're a fan of 4X, or wishing to get back into it after a hiatus, this game is for you. If you're looking for more grand strategy, Stellaris is probably your best port of call.

Great game. Endless Space 2 is a drop dead gorgeous 4x with nicely fleshed out mechanics and good atmosphere. If you enjoy strategy, lore-rich universes and high replay value this is a title you don't want to miss.
ES2 plays like your typical empire builder. You start with a single star system and a scout+colony ship (on the more vanilla-style factions at least). You then head out to space to explore other systems and colonize worlds. You research tech, develop your star systems, build up fleets, encounter other alien factions and eventually push for a victory on one of 6 different achievements, conquest, tech, wonderbuilding etc.
UI is so slick it hurts. Very polished and enjoyable to use. The basic galaxy screen is clean yet informative and when you desire extra info you can hit spacebar to enter scan-mode for detailed breakdown of solar system output, trade routes etc. Music, audio and art are also high quality. It's easy to sink hours into the game just reading the quests and events that pop up while listening to the soft beats on the background.
ES2 does a good job making you feel like a galactic emperor by focusing more on the macro level management. There's a whole internal politics system with party leaders, passing laws and so forth. Your population has a political affinity of their own and depending on who you play as (and who you assimilate into your empire), it's easier or harder to focus on certain traits.
You develop star systems as a whole rather than individual planets (though you can terraform and give a specialization to each one). There's some micro but it's not too intensive. Population management could use some polish maybe. As each individual unit of population has it's own specific bonuses and political attitude, it's usually a good idea to send them to places where they give the biggest benefit or cause least troubles.
Strategy layer is extended into combat as well. You pick your battle plan before things heat up and then hit "resolve". You can watch the fight and it can help you to evaluate your strategy but mostly it's eye candy. I was on the fence about this at first but it fits the game theme pretty well.
You get 8 quite distinct factions and the ability to make custom ones. I've yet to even touch the custom-made ones as the prebuilt aliens play so differently. Some are more traditional with no big surprises like United Empire, your cookie cutter humans and the tech-heavy Sophons. Then you've some weird space tree guys who spread cosmic roots all over the galaxy, religious essence vampires who live on huge Ark ships, mafia style fish humanoids who are all about economics and so forth. The factions, together with specific quest lines, random quests and events, minor factions and hero units all make up a pretty lore-rich galaxy.
AI however is not quite up on the same level with the rest. It's not godawful but not really great either. Most annoying is probably the AI's tendency to spam you with messages every other turn to tell how much it likes or hates you. It's not broken however, and it seems to understand when it's profitable to attack and when it isn't. You can also forge alliances, trade techs and so forth, the stuff that you'd expect from a 4x title.
Late game can get sluggish. There seems to be some performance issues with the game though it's perfectly playable. Might be some kind of memory leak as quitting and loading helps a little bit with the choppiness. Overall it isn't too heavy on your machine, I'm running it with some 5-6 year old machine and it runs just fine.
Performance aside, the late game turns can get frustrating when you're sieging enemy worlds and they keep sending a single small scout or something trivial like that against your death fleets and you keep smashing auto-resolve. Every turn. On three different locations. It's not a big deal but does get a little tiresome. I wish there'd be some kind of auto-auto-resolve against fleets that pose insignificant threat.
Overall ES2 is a really good game. It has some minor hiccups here and there but they're overshadowed by far with all the good stuff that comes along with the package. Highly recommended.

I will preface this negative review by saying this:
ES2 is a beautiful game with exceptionally high quality lore, artwork, soundtrack, and fluff. Aplitude have a really great setting with their "Endless Series" of games, and I enjoy it quite a lot. This stuff is almost worth the price tag alone, and I really mean it.
That being said, as an actual single player game ES2 falls short of providing a compelling experience. Simply put, the AI in its current state is very, very poor quality. Extremely passive, erratic, and incapable of playing the map effectively on anything but "ovoid" style galaxies. I played on hard, serious, and impossible difficulties, and was bored to death by passive AI every time.
Because the AI is so terrible, there is very little challange in ES2 single player, for an experienced 4x gamer. This is a shame, because the races are so varied, interesting, and potentially fun to play with and against. I don't know why Amplitude is able to bring their universe to life through lore, but seems to not care about crafting functional personalities or at least minimally viable behavior for their AI player. It's a real big disappointment.
Basically, it doesn't matter how pretty your game is, if its a tedious and boring experience.
If Amplitude wishes to avoid negative reviews for a poor quality single player experience, then they must, in the future, explicitly state on the product page that their game is intended as a multiplayer experience only. That way they can absolve responsibility for bare-bones or broken single player AI.
Wait a few months on this one. If the AI isn't patched, then skip it.
Multiplayer is likely a different experience, but like most people I can't sit down for an hours long multiplayer match in a game of this type.

The way I like to see Chivalry: Medieval Warfare is as the counter-strike of melee-based medieval combat games. Not that there are alot of first person medieval combat games out there to the point of requiring these kind of analogies, but what I mean is that this game certainly is not Pirates, Vikings and Knights..
Where as Pirates, Vikings and Knights has more of an arcadey style gameplay (thus i`d call it the Call of duty of melee combat games), Chivalry has alot more complexity and depth to its core gameplay.
There are alot of little things to consider and be aware of if you want to master all of chivalry`s mechanics. Things like, hitting an enemy with the tip of your weapon will deal more damage than with the lower part. Simply because of this, a whole new 'game' of tactical positioning is in place. Taking into account the windup and recovery time of your weapon is crucial if you want to stay alive and emerge as the victor, especially if you are dueling as a knight with a heavy weapon against a lighter and quicker man at arms.
There are tons more of specific mechanics I could talk about, but that`s what the guides are for as this just a simple, quick review. So is all this talk of complexity any good? I for one truly enjoy what this game offers. There are few multiplayer titles that give you such a sense of gratifying accomplishment when you defeat another player, backed up with a nice visual feedback of heads and limbs flying off.
It`s just a shame that they added an ingame store where you buy cosmetic items such as armor and skins for existing weapons, and the only way to get these is buy purchasing them with real currency.. Yeah I guess they are harmless since they are only cosmetic and don`t affect any stats for your armor/weapons.
In the end though, Chivalry: Medieval Warfare is truly a unique game and a breath of fresh air in the multiplayer focused genres, since nowadays everything has to be some kind of first person shooter variant to be successful. I`m glad that Chivalry can prove otherwise, and hopefully this will be some kind of stimulant for developers to try different things in the future.

People nowadays throw around words like "hardcore" and "casual" when talking about games. Well, rest assured this game belongs much more firmly in the "hardcore" category than Gears of War or Call of Duty could ever dream of.
This game is complicated. Granted, this is the first Paradox grand strategy title I've actually put any serious effort into, so maybe the EU or HoI games are even more complex - I have no idea. But rest assured, this is no Total War game. There is combat, yes, but there is very little focus on it. Instead, the focus is on politics and delicious intrigue.
There is a very unforgiving quality to this game, a quality that you might also find in an X-COM game or in Dwarf Fortress. Said unforgivingness is also part of the charm. You can spend hours planning out just how you are going to make sure that your successor will have claims to all of Scandinavia - your precious plan might still go to hell because you missed something. Perhaps someone had a more competent Spymaster than you. Perhaps your heir dies from pneumonia. Or some other, terrible disaster occurs.
And that is why the game is so much fun. You are given a sandbox where you are free to set your own goals, and just about anything can happen.

An engrossing experience from the top down.  Knights of Honor, Risk and Paradox's Clausewitz game engine all went into a room to smoke a truckload of crack and Crusader Kings 2 is what came out.  Risk is a simple thing to enjoy, but I have to admit that these political kingdom strategy games mostly don't sound that interesting even to me.  The beautiful maps are what draw me in and Knights of Honor opened my mind to the genre, but there was nowhere else within the genre to go to get more as KoH was simply the cream of the crop by far — until now.
This is probably not the kind of game that easily sells itself in youtube videos or in quick tutorials, because you really need to plop yourself into the middle of it, look at all the things on the screen and go "wtf does this button do?" for about 40 hours.  There may be many moments of "Oh I wish I knew that, I'm going to use the hell out of that in my next game."
The bottom line is you pick someone who controls something, whether it's a small county or an entire kingdom, then you try to hang onto whatever power you have for dear life and work hard to pass it down your bloodline.  If you can strengthen your power or expand carefully then that is a great bonus.  How easily you can expand and how powerful you are can vary quite wildly all while events specific to your culture and situation occur, allowing for a lot of replay value.
I got the complete pack with all 23 current DLC off Amazon for $9.99 during a sale, so keep an eye out for a similar deal.  If you don't really know if these kinds of games appeal to you, this one is guaranteed to help you find that out.
