This is probably THE free to play game that is out and about right now. It is an MMO, yes, but there is mostly PvE instead of PvP. There are a series of randomly generated missions you can go on with up to 4 people (some may be clanmates) in the vein of "exterminate, mobile defense, survival, defense, assault, spy, capture, rescue" and then "low" level boss missions. In the early game (which can take quite a while to get through) this will all be a decent challenge as you level up both your Warframe and weapons along with a "Mastery Rank" which is like your skill level.
Okay, I'll say the most fun I had was getting to the endgame content. From there, it is up to the kind of player to determine if you will like the grind that comes after. There are A TON of weapon and Warframes to collect, more than I have managed to get after nearly 300 hours of playing (and only shelling out about $60 for the platinum currency which is largely just to get ultra-rare things that simply don't drop anymore because they were broken). There is something for every playstyle, and more stuff keeps coming out since this game is TECHNICALLY in Beta still.
The grind is fun. It is not the same MMO type grind of "go here, kill this, rinse and repeat" with the same stuff and maps over and over. Most maps are procedurally generated, and the number of weapons and frames gives no one an excuse to say the game doesn't have options.
The paid currency platinum is completely not needed to progress in the game. I have only paid $60 total, and that is from discounts you get sometimes for just logging into the game. It is NOT nessesary, I cannot overstate that. Most of the platinum I bought either went to discontinued items in the free trade market or cosmetic items.
There is alot of new content being made for this game too. There is a story that is in-progress but is interesting, and they are adding open world components to compete with other MMO's pushing similar concepts.
This is a game I have put down and come back to several times and it is always generally improving. I would recommend at least trying the game out. If you don't like it, pay nothing.

L.A. Noire is a beautiful tale of the grime that lurks just below the surface.
GAMEPLAY:
There are 4 main types of gameplay at work here the first is investigation, the second is interrogation, the third is car chases, and the fourth is gunfights. The first and second forms mentioned make up the meat of the game with 90% of the game consisting solely of walking around, picking things up, and talking to people. The gunplay and driving could both be improved, but they both occur so infrequently and can be skipped that it is hardly considered a real negative. The biggest issue I have with the gameplay is the "Truth, Doubt, Lie" function. The majority of the time you'll be going out on a whim if you doubt or lie. The best you can do is choose lie first to see where Cole takes it, and if you didn't mean to head that direction choose doubt instead. Also a lot of the time what you need to present for lie will be a toss up for 2 items and the one you choose probably won't be it even though it could work. The fact is though I can't think of any way to solve the issues it has.
STORY:
This is what the game is about. I don't want to spoil anything about the story, but just remember to never take a single thing you hear at face value not even the character you play. The set up is you play as Cole Phelps a war hero turned LAPD detective in the mid-late 40's. One of the best qualities of this game is the writing of all of the characters. Every single aspect of the characters was clearly taken and cared for to be formed into one of the best experiences that can be given to anyone who is willing to look one step deeper.
SOUND:
Limited repeated tracks with hit-or-miss voice recordings (some people sound like they were recorded in a cardboard box while standing in the middle of the street) leave much to be desired.
Cons:
*30 FPS locked
*Lots of random stutter
*Large wonderful but shallow overwold.
OVERALL:
If Phoenix Wright had an affair with the 40's this game would be what pops out. And I loves meself some Phoenix Wright. L.A. Noire deserves to be on the forefront of anyone's "to-play" list if you have a marginal interest in Noire or love a good  story.

After extensive play, I find that this game is a late beta. The amount and severity of bugs is nowhere near acceptable for a full release.
Find below an incomplete list of lacking features, bugs and glitches. I'm not even nitpicking here, this game is just not finished.
It keeps crashing on load, on certain maps and randomly.
Servers can't handle a simultaneous join of multiple people into a server with just one slot left. For me, this results in either a crash on load or an incompletely loaded level. Menus or console are inaccessible, meaning the only way to exit the program then is to kill the game via process manager.
On modded servers or custom maps, the downloading process cannot be interrupted (as is the case with any map loading). For data capped connections this may be of consideration.
It corrupts its own files, I have to regularly verify the cache.
Blood stains have the exact same hue of red as Mason colors, meaning a hurt Agathan often gets teamkilled by less experienced players.
Certain maps are unplayable on most 32-bit systems.
Weapons cannot be easily compared with one another and its unclear what damage they actually deal. And is an axe a slashing or a blunt weapon? What about a halberd? A poleaxe? A brandistock? There's no tooltips helping you at all.
Comparing weapons with one another is tedious and there is no actual compare function. You'll have to remember how far the little bars went on one weapon and compare them by quickly switching to another and looking at those.
The tutorial is a steaming pile of scat. You need it to understand the story and the game mechanics and without playing it, you'll be a bad player. But it doesn't work properly, is glitchy at best and unplayable at worst.
It's poorly optimized and a memory hog. Without a little terminal hack I wasn't even able to run this game because I would run out of memory.
Servers regularly freeze up. If a mapchange doesn't happen quickly enough, the server will actually crash.
The networking is♥♥♥♥♥♥poor. Anything over 100 ping is unplayable and there are random lag spikes.
Many weapons are not properly implemented. When holding a throwing weapon, bow or torch, you cannot kick or block - two vital elements of the game.
What is the difference between the shields besides the sizes? Again, no tooltips, no help, just nothing.
There is no discernible support. Patches are infamous for breaking more parts of the game.
The leap from level 15 to 16 is like being thrown into a lava pool of acidic mutant sharks with lasers. There are no servers for players that still want to train more before playing against people with hundreds of hours play experience.
The audio sometimes stops working. Either it's entirely muted with no way to restart the audio service, or it cuts off mid-sound serverwide. How such an error is even possible is beyond me.
On most maps there are bits of invisible objects at random places and easily accessible spots where you'll be trapped. Your only mode of escape is getting kicked by a team mate, slowly wiggling out of that spot by random chance, or F10. F10 suicides your character. Of course it also adds a penalty to your score and counts as a death.
Kicks into rivers and off cliffs by team mates are not counted towards the team damage of that player, making votekicks against abusive prepubescent chuckle♥♥♥♥s very difficult.
What is the difference between Bodkin and Broadhead arrow, or between pebbles and lead balls? Again, no tooltips.
A visual representation of slash and thrust damage areas like in Deadliest Warrior would be necessary. Again again, no tooltips, no explanations, no help at all. Where does your blockzone end? Seasoned players can bypass blocks by aiming at the right spots. Why is that not part of the sputum of a tutorial this game has?
The game cannot save server filter settings correctly. How you could mess that up is another mystery of the devs.
There are no queues to join servers, a feature games from over a decade ago already had.
Alert messages are not properly converted from string to player-readable text. Instead, you can read things like 'Alert1' or a message with an "Add" at the end of the sentence.
In some levels there are walls and trees where players can hide inside due to, again, improper collision mapping.
I could keep going. It seems like whoever coded this game has no formal understanding of even basic tasks in programming or is simply overtaxed with maintaining this game.
In the face of all these issues on PC, it's a punch in the gut to see CMW being released on gaming consoles.
Treat this game like an Early Access title to deem if it's worth the money for you. It's fun, but for a title released in 2012 the amount of bugs, glitches, problems and plain errors is entirely unacceptable.

I will preface this negative review by saying this:
ES2 is a beautiful game with exceptionally high quality lore, artwork, soundtrack, and fluff. Aplitude have a really great setting with their "Endless Series" of games, and I enjoy it quite a lot. This stuff is almost worth the price tag alone, and I really mean it.
That being said, as an actual single player game ES2 falls short of providing a compelling experience. Simply put, the AI in its current state is very, very poor quality. Extremely passive, erratic, and incapable of playing the map effectively on anything but "ovoid" style galaxies. I played on hard, serious, and impossible difficulties, and was bored to death by passive AI every time.
Because the AI is so terrible, there is very little challange in ES2 single player, for an experienced 4x gamer. This is a shame, because the races are so varied, interesting, and potentially fun to play with and against. I don't know why Amplitude is able to bring their universe to life through lore, but seems to not care about crafting functional personalities or at least minimally viable behavior for their AI player. It's a real big disappointment.
Basically, it doesn't matter how pretty your game is, if its a tedious and boring experience.
If Amplitude wishes to avoid negative reviews for a poor quality single player experience, then they must, in the future, explicitly state on the product page that their game is intended as a multiplayer experience only. That way they can absolve responsibility for bare-bones or broken single player AI.
Wait a few months on this one. If the AI isn't patched, then skip it.
Multiplayer is likely a different experience, but like most people I can't sit down for an hours long multiplayer match in a game of this type.

An engrossing experience from the top down.  Knights of Honor, Risk and Paradox's Clausewitz game engine all went into a room to smoke a truckload of crack and Crusader Kings 2 is what came out.  Risk is a simple thing to enjoy, but I have to admit that these political kingdom strategy games mostly don't sound that interesting even to me.  The beautiful maps are what draw me in and Knights of Honor opened my mind to the genre, but there was nowhere else within the genre to go to get more as KoH was simply the cream of the crop by far — until now.
This is probably not the kind of game that easily sells itself in youtube videos or in quick tutorials, because you really need to plop yourself into the middle of it, look at all the things on the screen and go "wtf does this button do?" for about 40 hours.  There may be many moments of "Oh I wish I knew that, I'm going to use the hell out of that in my next game."
The bottom line is you pick someone who controls something, whether it's a small county or an entire kingdom, then you try to hang onto whatever power you have for dear life and work hard to pass it down your bloodline.  If you can strengthen your power or expand carefully then that is a great bonus.  How easily you can expand and how powerful you are can vary quite wildly all while events specific to your culture and situation occur, allowing for a lot of replay value.
I got the complete pack with all 23 current DLC off Amazon for $9.99 during a sale, so keep an eye out for a similar deal.  If you don't really know if these kinds of games appeal to you, this one is guaranteed to help you find that out.

This is a great game! The story, cases, and the world are interesting enough to keep you playing.
Story
LA Noire is divided up into different desks. You can think of them like seasons in a TV show because that is what they felt like to me. There is Patrol (tutorial), Traffic, Homicide, Ad Vice, and Arson. Minus Traffic and Patrol each one of them have cases that all connect to form a bigger story. I can't really describe it without spoiling anything. In all of these cases you play as Cole Phelps, a marine who came back from WWII with a big award for bravery. You get these flashbacks of his war days that seem pointless at first but as I mentioned individual cases combine to form a bigger story as do these flashbacks. You also have partners who are all very interesting characters. You wonder why some of them even became police officers when they do and say certain things.
Gameplay
The gameplay is the same for almost all the cases. You go around the city following leads, collect evidence, and interview people. The evidence is necessary to catch people in lies. If you think a person is lying you can either doubt (call them out without evidence) or lie (call them out and present evidence to back it up). It's confusing at first you get used to it. Evidence is always written in your notepad so it's easy to remember which evidence you need most of the time. There is a problem with this system though. Sometimes the right answer is to call the person out on a lie and then ask a different question (that they lie to) and then present evidence on that. For example in one case you ask a guy if he knows the whereabouts of a certain person. He says no. You have to say he is lying and then Phelps will ask if he has commited any burglaries (unrelated to the 1st question) then present evidence that he has committed multiple burglaries. If doubt was not one of the answers this game would be a bit easier but Intuition Points help. Intutiion Points allow you to remove an answer or ask the community on what they pick (kind of like lifelines) or show all clues in the area. you can only ask the community if you join Rockstar Social Club though. If you achieve maximum rank (you level up by completing street crimes, interviews, finding landmarks) then you get 5 intuition points to use each case.
Setting
The setting is in 1940s Los Angeles. This is before it got really famous I think. You can listen to old music from the 40s and some radio shows sometimes (sitcoms on the radio) like "The Bickersons". The cars look cool too and do not blow up if you do alot of damage to them unlike other Rockstar games. The world has landmarks for you to find (like RKO theatre), there is an achievement for driving one of every single car including cool rare ones like the Ford H-boy and lame ones like an Ambulance car and a giant pickup There also badges and movie reels to collect but those don't seeem to do anything other than be an achievment. Newspapers also give you a movie clip that relates to the story. Most of them have a major antagonist that you won't come across till later on in the game.
Graphics
A big con about the game is that it's not a a very good port. It's better than GTA IV but still not quite up to speed. There is a 30 FPS cap.  On an AMD R7 250 it will run at 30 FPS with everything on Performcance and 2x Anti-aliasing. If you think I just have a crappy PC I should let you know I also have a multicore processor and it has a better framerate when you swtich to single threading rather than multithreading. So ovbiously they messed up. But you can look past it cause most of the time the framerate is constant.
This is a pretty fun game and you don't have to worry about people calling you to hang out, go out on dates, drive them somewhere, etc. The main gameplay and story are fun enough to keep you playing to the end. Alot of people say that the ending was bad but what did you expect, happy rainbows and dancing flowers?

L.A Noire is a game about Detective Cole Phelps. It's a game based around solving crimes and arresting (or in most cases, murdering in cold blood) suspects. The game is supposed to be like a real old movie, and it has the framerate to match. Seriously, this game is one of the worst ports I've ever seen. At least Max Payne and GTA 4 worked and kept above half a frame.  I've spent more time trying to fix the bloody FPS then actually playing the thing. I really, REALLY want to recommend this game, but I just can't. Rockstar just doesn't care about PC users. They just care about maximizing profits by giving us the scraps. Games like GTA 4 or L.A Noire are shadows of their console versions. We can't keep letting Rockstar push us around like this. They throw us a bugged, poorly optimized game and then never fix it, despite having all the time in the world to. How come companies like Valve and *shudders* EA can make good PC ports, but Rockstar can't? Because Rockstar is lazy. They're lazy, and they don't care about PC gamers. They make us wait months, sometimes a year or more, for a fantastic game, and they make it unplayable. Rockstar can't keep getting away with this, they just can't. When i was a console gamer, I thought that Rockstar was the best company ever, and that they actually cared about their gamers, but after playing their games on PC, i know that i was mistaken. All in all, L.A Noire would be good, if Rockstar cared enough to put any effort into optimizing it for PC.

L.A Noire is a game about Detective Cole Phelps. It's a game based around solving crimes and arresting (or in most cases, murdering in cold blood) suspects. The game is supposed to be like a real old movie, and it has the framerate to match. Seriously, this game is one of the worst ports I've ever seen. At least Max Payne and GTA 4 worked and kept above half a frame.  I've spent more time trying to fix the bloody FPS then actually playing the thing. I really, REALLY want to recommend this game, but I just can't. Rockstar just doesn't care about PC users. They just care about maximizing profits by giving us the scraps. Games like GTA 4 or L.A Noire are shadows of their console versions. We can't keep letting Rockstar push us around like this. They throw us a bugged, poorly optimized game and then never fix it, despite having all the time in the world to. How come companies like Valve and *shudders* EA can make good PC ports, but Rockstar can't? Because Rockstar is lazy. They're lazy, and they don't care about PC gamers. They make us wait months, sometimes a year or more, for a fantastic game, and they make it unplayable. Rockstar can't keep getting away with this, they just can't. When i was a console gamer, I thought that Rockstar was the best company ever, and that they actually cared about their gamers, but after playing their games on PC, i know that i was mistaken. All in all, L.A Noire would be good, if Rockstar cared enough to put any effort into optimizing it for PC.

It's a shame the PC version is such a poor port,they release an epic game and then do it no justice on a system where it should shine. Thet being said,no amount of tweaking could get this to run respectably on my 7970,but I've finally managed to get it to run on my 970 (same hardware as with 7970) to a point of being acceptable. It now runs heaps smoother with no FPS drops or crashes in the 5 hours I've played since applying the changes. Theres only a slight jagger when turning corners whilst driving which I stopped noticing after a bit. I did this by creating a profile in Nvidia control panel,switching everything possible to performance,turning threaded optimisation off and then running it in game on single core and DX9. I hope this helps at least one other person to be able to enjoy this game,but we can only dream of an optimised,remastered version.
The game itself is incredible,If I could marry it,I would! No other can make me feel so miserable about making a wrong decision or missing a piece of evidence (which is often haha). Quite simply,It's a masterpiece. I personally would pay full price for this If it was optimised,but you're taking a risk at buying it at any price with It being one of the worst ports out there. If you can get it working though,I'm sure you'll enjoy it thoroughly.

I waited long for this game and it's excellent.
It still has some bugs, but it will get updates, it was just released anyway.
The races are excellent diverse, you have multiple victory conditions which you can set yourself and lots of cool quests.
From the campaign perspective absolutely excellent. star systems have different values, you want to take the one with most strategic ressources and luxury deposits to get a monopoly. this means you have to fight for these systems, as well as for systems with benefical planets.
In addition to that, you'll have politics available now with different laws. There're multiple ways to generate income, each of them is fun to play, like trading companies or simply blackmailing your oponents by obtaining the strategic ressources.
When it comes to combat it's excellent. You have to design your ships directly the way that they can counter the enemy.
Force truce prevents cheese.
You can also destroy your enemies by using inflation which is pretty cool, so there's not the one way to defeat your oponents there're thousands. For example your not into battle and you upgrade your star systems to be defensive, then you'll simply go the influence route and take over other systems peacefully by expanding your influence over them.
Negative aspects:
As in endless space 1, the User interface is bad. Your construction options are put in an ugly box.
Bugs that will go away after updates, like for example water and coral reefs on a lava planet.

L.A. Noire is Rockstar's anti-GTA game. In Grand Theft Auto, you're in an open world littered with missions, side quests, collectibles and more. There's activities and the insanity that it's famous for. L.A. Noire is it's antithesis. Instead of playing a criminal, you play a detective, solving cases in Traffic, Vice, Homicide and Arson. You're in an open world with very limited additional things to do outside of the very linear narrative.
As a story, it's great, each case is interesting and a challenge when it comes to detective work and though repetitive, it gets truly interesting in the last quarter of the game.
If you do play it, don't make the mistake I made by marathoning it out in long play sessions. Take your time and play it case by case and leave it to play something else inbetween. The gameplay gets repetitive and drawn out and can't be appreciated fully when you're going for >1hour play sessions.

This is one of those games that really grabs you by the ear and doesn't let go until you've seen all it has to offer. You play as Cole Phelps, an ex-army detective that, throughout the game, rises through the ranks to become famous (and infamous) in the city of Los Angeles. Speaking of Los Angeles, 1940s Los Angeles is so carefully and expertly crafted that I completely believe that Team Bondi had some sort of time machine in their offices. I spent a lot of time just driving around the city, taking in the sights. However there is much more to the game than that. Detective work is surprisingly entertaining, with clues scattered around crime scenes as well as useless items like scraps of paper and empty cans. There is gunplay, but it's disappointingly basic and my main gripe about the game. Clips never seem to run out, and every gun feels the same in terms of weight and damage dealt. Fistfights are slightly better, but are also painfully basic and slow. Driving is tight, smooth and basically everything you'd expect from a Rockstar-developed game. The story is great and the twists are genuinely surprising. The performances from the voice actors are consistently phenomenal, with Aaron Staton as Cole being the obvious standout. Overall, L.A. Noire is one of Rockstar's finest works and it really sucks you in to its world and story. I highly reccommend it to fans of crime movies and Rockstar games, but also to anyone willing to play a slower, thought-requiring experience.

Started back in 2013 and am still going today. What started off as a barebones third person shooter has now evolved in to a faster paced version of its former self, and is still growing to this day.
Firstly to get it out of the way,
:
The grind is a necessary part of this Free-To-Play model but the greatest thing is that
. You can grind from over the span of many months to as little as a day or two. That's the beauty of this game, you progress at your own pace. However if you ever feel like you need to speed things up, there's always the option to skip crafting times and/or buy gear outright with the "Platinum" premium currency. The charm of this game is slowly gaining power over time while watching that growth but not everyone has the time to do so.
Now the game has certainly evolved from its 2013 release with each planet you come across boasting its own design and atmosphere ranging from the lush forests of Earth, the barren frosted lands of Europa, all the way to the pristine Void. To navigate through the environments comes the movement system which had a revamp back in 2015 where you'll find yourself using the "Bullet Jump" to propel yourself in a direction of your choosing whilst combining it with a slide, roll, wall hop or all of them; soon enough you'll be bouncing around maps and clearing missions in no time. Feel like taking the fight to the vast ocean of space? Strap on some space wings in the form of Archwing and race through asteroid bases and the tight corridors of space stations.
There's a wide variety of mission types, enemies, bosses, and an ever growing arsenal to experience and so many more tidbits to come over the years that I can't recommend this game enough. It'll only take your time, hard drive space, and possibly bandwidth depending on where you live...

A brand new knight in this world of war. I begin in a terrain of rolling hills with my team mates to kill the opposing team, everything's all fancy. We charge, and I let out a blood curdling scream that even I was surprised by how long I sustained it. My response were more soul ripping screams from my army running alongside me.
I look over to my side to see my chivlarous friend fighting against a knight. What a time to help out! I begin running towards him only to see a second and third enemy fly out from the cover of the trees and cut him down with no remorse. And in a split instant, they all spotted me.....and charge.
I should stand my ground, and provide honor for my name and clan, but ho hey! Wait a minute! I am part of The Mason's Order, a group that secretly plotted and are fighting against the Agatha Knights, their previous friends. Any honor I had, VANISHED. So I turned and ran, for my life depended on it. I felt the footsteps get closer, my time was drawing near. In the midst of the day, a friendly archer swooped from around a rock and shot one in the throat. One down! The a vanguard comes and begins taking on all three. I was free!
I took a moment to look around the battefield. Blood. Bodies. Bone. My vanguard cuts down the second enemy. A friendly knight falls with only one arm. A man of the Mason Order ran up to another friendly, and threw his lance into his back. Traitor.
Suddenly, my vision reddens and a searing pain escapes my arm. An arrow! I turn to my left and see the enemy, and begin running. He readies his bow and I scoop to the left, narrowly missing a second shot. He draws another arrow, and shoots! I manage to jump high and over the speeding bolt. And finally, I was on top of him.
I take a swing, and direct hit! But he takes out a dagger and manages to sink it into my side. Not today, for I kick him which winds him, and bring down my sword upon his head, in one swift motion.
The exhiliration was intense, adrenaline coursing through my blood. I turn around to locate my next target, when my teammate runs up to me and stabs me straight through my stomach. We lock eyes, until he retrieves his weapon and proceeds forward.
My death was brought to me by a traitorous traitor whom I called a brother. Oh, the irony.

It has been a really long time since I liked a space 4x this much. My issue with most of them, is the races are all the same. They're just templates with different music, a different JPG for your leader, and maybe some slightly varied stats. In ES2, for the first time they actually feel different. Not just JPGs, but the presented personality, the atmospheric "feel", and more importantly, the gameplay. The Vohdyani (or however you spell it) are shipbound and have a very specific method for even expanding are one very obvious example.
Then there is the aspect of storyline "quests" for each race, which really surprised (in a good way). Back to the "every race is a generic template" most of these games it doesn't really matter what race you are or are interacting with, they're all the same, and the "game" revolves entirely around the empire management (often lacking) and combat (often lacking) which leaves you with not a whole hell of a lot to occupy yourself with. The storylines do a LOT just to enhance the feel of the specific races as well as giving you something "higher" to do besides merely subduing your neighbor. Again, I haven't got into it too much, but the obvious intent is highly commendable, even if it doesn't play out as I imagine.
In all, I would say that ES2 is a massive leap forward over ES1 (which I've only dabbled with a bit) and has some very good aspects that other developers would be wise to learn from (I'm looking at the rather sterile Stellaris here, the abysmal MoO, and the well intentioned but somewhat clumsy GCIII)
No game is perfect, but there is a lot to like here already and I'm looking forward to seeing what they expand upon as ES2 moves out of EA into release. Good job, devs!

Endless Space 2 is a strong title in a great series, and a major improvement over its predecessor. If you're a fan of the Endless series, getting this game is a no brainer, and you may as well skip the rest of the review. Otherwise, read on.
ES2 is a standard 4X game that embraces asymmetry and atmosphere. It's a very shiny game with great graphics and UI. Like other 4X games in the series, it's turn based and each turn is processed simultaneously. This causes a few issues (eg: the AI is often able to force combat to start before you're able to move your fleets, or enter and colonize a system before you get a chance to respond) and may be a bit frustrating to those used to the Civilization series. The game is somewhat accessible with a learning curve comparable to other 4X games. It's definitely more complex than ES1, but nowhere near Aurora or Distant Worlds. Many of those mechanics are poorly documented (battle tactics, the political system, and the various uses of influence to list a few) and sheer number of menus to sort through may be daunting, but there's enough of a tutorial to walk you through the core mechanics of the game.
Each and every faction truly feels unique. They all have some mechanic that sets them apart from the other factions. Though it may be gimmicky, it vastly increases the replayability of the game. Of course, the uniqueness of each faction causes pretty significant balance issues, which is a problem that exists in most games of the Endless series. The Lumeris may have an overbearingly strong early game, and the Vodyani may have a rather weak one. But those balance issues only really become a real problem in multiplayer, and Endless Space 2 was never made to be balanced around multiplayer. It does exist, and it is pretty fun, but if you want a 4X that pits your pure strategic ability against your friends, Civilization 5 with balance mods is a better option. If you want a pure strategic multiplayer experience, try Civ 4 or maybe chess.
ES2 was designed to be an immersive experience. You're able to start from a view of the whole galaxy, zoom in to your empire, then zoom in on a single star system and access production, then zoom in on a single planet to check on its stats. There's a beautifully animated cutscene that plays when you start up a new game, customized for each faction. Diplomatic interactions with the AI are all voiced and animated. You even get a small cutscene showing the surface of the world you just settled.
The AI is relatively clever, but nothing to write home about. They will attack you if they think they can win, and trade with you when it's beneficial to them. Frustratingly, they also have the human-like tendency to forward settle you to claim more territory for themselves. The game tells you their mood, and what has affected it. It's nice to know that the AI empire across from you is distressed when they're losing a war, or wary if you've violated their borders. But it's hard for the AI to properly backstab you when it tells you they're trying to be sneaky. The AI also seems to be somewhat weak at evaluating whether or not they're actually able to win a war, and will often bite off more than they can chew if you have a small number of extremely powerful ships.
Gameplay-wise, ES2 is similar to other 4X Endless games. You have quests and anomalies that reward early exploration. Your entire empire scales exponentially, and science/economic/score victory typically pop about 150-200 turns into the game depending on your settings. Even if you have a rough start, if you focus your empire properly all that matters is executing your own victory type better than your opponents execute theirs. Combat is entirely hands off, and you only tell your ships what sort of strategy to execute. Ground invasions are equally uninteractive, and you only get a rather hilarious animation when you attack a system with billions of people in it. The ship designer is nothing to write home about either; the only meaningful decision is balancing strategic resource cost with production cost with the individual strength of your ships. However, what ES2 does amazingly is empire management. Internal politics, resource management, and empire expansion are all well fleshed out and compelling. It plays very much like a turn-based Stellaris in that regard.
Be aware that the game also suffers from extremely strong snowballing, which is sometimes beyond the player's control. The galaxy is cordoned off into constellations, which are separated from each other by well over 10 turns of travel in the early game. They become more connected with some mid game research, but if you're unlucky with your start then it may simply be unrecoverable.

All in all, it's a pretty good game from a pretty good game studio.

Endless Space 2 is what you get it you mash Stellaris and Endless Legend together. And I mean that in both the good ways and the bad ways.
From Endless Legend, you've got the AMAZING presentation in terms of music, sounds and art... but also the somewhat tangled interface that loves to hide stuff away in submenus whenever possible and could stand to make more things accessible through simple right-click menus.
From Stellaris, you've got the grand, galactic-scale adventure... but also extremely shallow combat and diplomatic interactions(though, to be fair, the diplomacy in EL was roughly equally as shallow, it is, in fact, the exact same system. But while I've complained quite a bit about EL's combat... at least it was interactive and occasionally clever in-combat maneuvering could make a major difference).
Endless Legend is the easiest of the two to compare it to, though. And I'll say this, the series looks better than ever, I honestly get kinda hyped with the cinematic presentation of every battle, even though they're kinda same-y. The music, sound effects and graphics just SELL it. The tech tree is, once again, more of a tech pizza, and the only issue with it is that holy♥♥♥♥♥♥good luck keeping any sort of overview. It feels like it would've benefited from just cracking it up into four separate tech trees, for the sake of making it a bit easier to keep track of.
Losses compared to EL would, well, be the actual technical aspects of the gameplay, in all honesty. As already mentioned, the combat is shallower since you have no in-combat control, so it's literally just your numbers vs the enemy's numbers and an autocalc fight will roll up the exact same way as one you watch.
The planet management is... hm. They've intentionally made it shallower since you're gonna have way more planets than you did EL cities(since there's no "too many planets"-penalty.), which isn't in itself bad, but it still rapidly becomes too much to manage and you'll be delegating a lot of stuff to planetary governors. It also feels like you're being asked to make choices less, in EL, at least early on, I was regularly going: "Hm, I WANT that improvement, but I can't afford the Dust upkeep cost, so I'm going to have to prioritize." I've yet to feel that in ES2 at any point.
Speaking of governors, it feels like the heroes are worse off, too. They feel more similar than they did in EL, and it's very hard to specialize them. Even if you've got a hero who's just intended to babysit a system, or a fleet, it's practically impossible to only give him skills for that purpose now, and it feels like you're wasting a ton of points on stuff he'll never actually need. Heroes are also stuck in the game's smallest ships, and size really does matter here. I haven't actually rolled with any big endgame fleets yet, but I suspect their combat contributions rapidly become forgettable as a result.
The game has less quests, but they tend to still suffer from some of the same stuff, in that sometimes you'll be asked to find X objects to research Y anomalies of a certain type... but good goddamn luck if they're all on the other side of the galaxy or the dice don't roll your way with the anomalies. In general the "convert a minor faction"-quests also feel... a lot less interesting so far.
I mean, I guess it could've turned out a lot worse. But I'm hoping they'll actually attend to some of these flaws with DLC and patches. I don't have much hope for it, though, since Endless Legend mostly just got more subsystems(some overpowered, some completely irrelevant) piled on top, with no real adjustments to basic gameplay flaws that some people(or, at least, me) had been calling out since the beta.
I remember at the end of my Endless Legend review I went: "Wow! They got so close! I'll definitely buy their next game because I'm sure they'll look at their mistakes and correct them!" With Endless Space 2 I'm... honestly kind of forced to conclude that they're doubling down on the flaws EL had rather than resolving them, and not offering anything new to make up for it.
Originally I said I'd keep playing Endless Space 2, while not recommending it to anyone else. This was because I'd already paid for it, and I was hoping for improvements. But it turns out that it's literally too buggy to play, with new patches introducing more gamebreaking bugs, like initiating combat later in the game literally make you unable to advance turns. So, yeah, I think the proper answer is that I'm done even giving this game a chance.

I remember when this game first came out, and it's been one of my favorite games ever since.  It's not for everyone, no doubt about that.  If you're a big Rockstar fan for the violence this game is probably not for you.  You wont be meeting up with hookers, shooting down choppers, or seeing how many pedestrians you can run over before your car explodes.  In LA Noire you play a cop in (you guessed it) LA during the 1940s.  Your primary goal is solving crimes through clues and interogations, then putting the peices together to figure out who the criminal is.  Sounds easy, it's not really (in my opinion).  You can easily miss a clue or get a question wrong that will ruin your case.  Finished cases can be replayed which is nice, giving this game a decent amount of replay value (but not a ton).
Graphics - 7/10 - they are good but compared to new games they can't hold up obviously, no fault on the games side.
Sound - 10/10 - personally I love the old timey music they play, it sets the tone perfectly, the game would be flawed without it.
Controls - 7/10 - I highly recommend a controller.  Finding clues can be tough.  Hardest thing is driving in this game, other drivers just hate to get out of your way, and accidents hurt your overall score.
Story - 9/10 - It's basically a big mystery game, with just enough twists and turns.  I'm sure the story is not 100% accurate history wise, but a fair amount of stuff comes from real life situations.  Old LA landmarks, the black dhalia murders, the spruce goose, and many more I'm sure.  It just helps tie the story together so well, you really feel like it's the 40's when you're playing this game.
Overall - 8/10 - Decent replay factor as it's unlikely you'll beat more then a mission or two and get everything 100% correct.  The DLC also helps in regards to replay.  After playing this game for too long, I find myself so enthralled that I feel like a detective, sometimes figuring out where I last left my beer (usually I drank it)!
I hope you find my review helpful!!!  At this time LA Noire w/ DLC sells for $30, a little high in my opinion, I waited for a sale, but I'm both cheap and patient.

It seems like Team Bondi made a game around the technology of advanced facial motion capture animation and their ideal noire detective setting. I played this thing years ago and got tired of it quickly due to bugs and poor optimization at the time. Rather than rant TOO much ill try to break it down into pros and cons
+Really great facial animation motion capture, works great for this type of game
+Extensive lineup of actors, some great acting, some just okay. Good casting
+Excellent job of creating immersion in the setting through speech, music, brand design, furniture, cars, clothes, weapons, clothing etc all being accurate for the time period
+Story that gets better as it goes along
~Similar to a lot of Rockstar's games (though not developed by them), everyone in the game world is an A-hole, including the main character. Most things people say to you will be negative
~gunplay mechanics certainly werent the focus of gameplay here
-Its clear they didnt bother to do many changes to take advantage of the PC platform
-Low polygon models and low resolution textures here and there, some are adequate
-Awkward control scheme for navigating the notebook/clue system
-The game will allow you to choose where to go first to investigate things, but if you dont go to the correct location first and get all the clues, it might throw you into an action sequence that ultimately ends the case prematurely, resulting in a poor performance rating, which in turn causes you go redo the case. This makes the game a trial and error nightmare at times unless you use a guide. The default button to open your notebook is Tab, so when you alt-tab to second monitor to see where you should go next it opens the notebook, sometimes ending your current interrogation. Of course, you could just NOT use a guide and then sometimes end up missing clues or entire sections of the mission and accept your poor performance. But if you do use a guide this completely destroys the immersion of the game.
-Game dips down below the locked 30FPS even on hardware 3-4 years newer than the game
-Combination of the last two makes the game a chore to play
-The whole world knows every intimate detail of your life and constantly mentions it loudly to no one in particular "Thats the guy who yadda yadda"
-Black and white option only looks good at certain times, otherwise the low quality textures on most people's faces make it a much worse choice, considering the game is very colorful and pretty without it
-If you bother driving yourself to the next location in cases, the game will detract for hitting anything at all in your car, which is realistic, but turning your siren on doesnt make people get out of the way, in fact they'll drive and walk right out in front of you
-Case breaking bug related to the above (ai will drive out in front of someone you're tailing and the AI never recovers, forcing you to shut down the game from task manager or start over the case entirely)
-there is never a time when you arent on a case, theres no free roam mode. so if you go after a street crime that gets radioed to all police, it sometimes will be clear on the other side of LA, in a car that can only go 80mph at the most (downhill) and that seems more like 40mph. on the drive there, dont hit anything cause itll detract from your case score!
-If you dont click in exactly the right spot on a piece of paper on clue #27 and try to move on with the game the case will stop functioning until you backtrack to the previous location and look for which one you failed to click just right
-they give you a flamethrower in the last 2 minutes of the game, which needs to be used point blank against people and then immediately throw you into a slow walking area with people at range
It was hard for me to not recommend this game due to it being exactly the TYPE of game I would THINK I would enjoy playing, but the sum of it's parts for me was a negative experience I just wished was over

This game is not what it looks like. It looks like a GTA clone, but that is just the icing on the cake. Almost irrelevant. LA Noire is actually much closer to the adventure genre. Other games make you sit down and listen to their story, and in between, they give you things to shoot. If you fail, you need to restart at a checkpoint because the story goes in a very specific way.
LA Noire is different in that you are given control over the story, rather than how the shooting in between happened. You are a detective responsible for collecting information, processing it and using it to succeed. Every story has one correct answer, but the storyline of the game isn't that the detective got everything right. Your detective is as successful as your attentiveness allowed him to be, and the story unfolds accordingly. The core of the gameplay may sound boring, but what LA Noire has you do is so uncommon that you'll find it exciting anyway. It's only in the end that the game falls back to traditional way of video games, where you have a checklist and the game only progresses with a cutscene once you cross everything out.
What the developers of LA Noire tried to do is admirable, even if the final result could obviously be better. The interview mechanics are too simple for their purpose. The characters aren't always clear enough for you to make decisions. The driving through a sandbox city is completely unnecessary and unrewarding. The overall story is patchy. Not to mention the numerous bugs. This game has many faults, but, ultimately, it is refreshingly different and I enjoyed it.

First of all: the game is good. It is very pretty, the mechanics are very interesting, different factions have significantly different playstiles, the RPG elements (stories and quests) are interesting as well. Empire building and management is well done, mostly, and is interesting to explore.
However.
I have to de-rec this game because it is unfinished. There are obvious elements of the gameplay that are missing. Unfallen spread their vines all around from their homeworld but there is not way to destroy them. It even says in the description that they can lose control over a system if the connection is lost. But there is no way to lose the connection as far as I can see.
Having over 20 pops of a single species in your empire gives a significant bonus to every system that has at least one of those pops. But migration system is manual only and is very basic. You have to search your systems for those pops manually one by one. You have to send those pops to your other systems  manually 3 or 4 at a time. More than that, you can't send a pop to full system. You have to free some space. You go to that other system, move a pop to a space port, go back to original system, send the pop off, go back to the destination and move the pop from space port to planet or else the spot will be filled by newly born pop next turn. And the incoming pop will just hang in space waiting for a free spot. And when it arrives you have to free the spot for it again, manually. And what do you do with extra pop? Send it off somewhere else. And what do you do if you have no free space? Nothing. You can't do anything.
There are a few more such moments but those are the ones I remembered on my first few tries. I do believe the devs will fix this, overall the game is well done. The finished features look very good. But I cannot recommend this game in good conscience. It is not finished. They should've delayed the release.

-

Dear lord. This game is addictive.
"Just one more hero level, then I'll turn off the machine".
In the beginning of the game (the first couple of hours) you do nothing but "click click". Later on, when you do your first ascension (after lvl. 100), the game will become easier.
- Depending on your playstyle. Some play with clicks all the way, others resort ti "idle dps", where the game does most damage itself, without you needing to click.
You can also buy autoclickers, which are kinda helpful, when you're going from level 1 to 1400(+/-) after an ascension. When I say buy, it's up to you how you use the "ingame economy".
You can PTW faster or you can do it in a slower way... I'm doing the latter.
Ingame economy is in form of "rubies". You get them by clicking on small yellow fish that appears once in a while, or you get them via mercernaries. It's sometimes annoying without rubies, other times it's okay.
Anyway, a quick guide:
No PTW
Level past 100 before you ascend the first time. You will recieve Hero Souls, past lvl. 100 - theese boost your damage, and allows you to summon an ancient, that gives a certain bonus. In the beginning, keep at least one(1) Hero soul.
At some point, you will be offered to "Trancend" - this will allow you to restart the game completely and give you some unique souls, you can spend. Theese are rare, but boosts your game tremendously when starting up again.
- Be sure to have at least 50 rubies before you trancend (at any time), and buy a Quick Ascension when trancended. This will give you Hero souls and make you avoid that painfull levelling as you did in the beginning.
PTW:
Buy autoclickers. Nuff said.

I didn't expect to enjoy the game nearly as much as I did.
L.A. Noire is, more or less, a twenty hour, interactive version of L.A. Confidential. The writing is solid, the MOCAP is great, the cases are enjoyable, and your partners are each unique and enjoyable for different reasons.
The only real weaknesses with the game are the inability to skip cutscenes (when you're repeating things), the cheaty enemy driving AI, and the very vague Truth / Doubt / Lie system. For maximum enjoyment, I'd recommend using the L.A. Noire wiki to use the right interview responses but not for anything else.
They also really nail the feeling of 1940s LA - both visually and musically. The soundtrack has this great, escalating grandure that exemplified the postwar period and the different music subsets (ex: chase, combat, investigate) are unique and enjoyable.
Shooting is trivially easy with a mouse, but the game is more a narrative piece than anything else. After my third shootout, I felt like the Dredd of 1940s LA.
If you like art deco, the postwar period, a smart story, good dialog, and a unique gaming experience, buy L.A. Noire.

What a timesink. I've had too many spent on this in the background, haha. But seriously. I've played a few Cookie Clicker-alikes and lose interest after a while.
By clicking a monster to destroy it, you gain gold to purchase heroes that increase click damage and auto-damage. Purchasing more is translated into leveling up, and each hero can unlock stat boosts when they hit certain levels. Naturally, each hero you unlock is stronger than the last, and you unlock more areas as you defeat more monsters, so there's this continuous climb.
But it doesn't stop there! There's also alternate upgrades. When you've reached certain requirements you can ascend, restarting the game with a new currency: hero souls. These boost your stats, or you can use them to purchase items that can be fed more and more souls to perform some kind of chance/stat boost. There's even yet another thing you can do that with when you get farther! It's insane how much there is to do in what seems like a simple browser game. That, to me, justifies it being on Steam.
It's free, so nothing stops ya from at least giving it a look. The folks who made it clearly figured out how to keep things going so that you don't grow bored of it, and I commend them on that.

Ok so this is only after 7 hours gaming, but here is my capsule review:
Overall:
8 out of 10. Great game but sadly lacking in key areas (if it wasnt for the potential scope for development for this game it would have been a 7/10)
The good:
- Stable
- Great interface
- Nice graphics
- Game seems nicely balanced and is very enjoyable
- Can play on after victory conditions are met
- Loads of scope to evolve the game* (see 'not decided' below)
The not so good:
- Cant control space combat!!!!!
This game allows you to view battles, but not to have any particular impact on them. This can be very annoying, especially when watching ships not concentrating their fire and/or not attacking the ship you want to kill, getting to close to the enemy etc etc. As such, IMHO the combat interface is just eye candy and of no value - you may just as well just get an auto result.
---I REALLY hope the devs change this and build up to interactive space/land combat, its the biggest flaw in the game---
- Speed not a factor in combat. It would be nice IF YOU COULD CONTROL THE SHIPS to have an option for lighter, faster ships to out manoeuvre the enemy rather than just bludgeon, but again, we have hit that snag again about not actually influencing battles.....
Not decided:
- Game length seems short? Ok this one is based on a friends comments who has been playing longer than me, I need to investigate this. But it seems to me that the game length (before victory conditions are met) are a little short. That said I know there are a lot of customisation options. My hope is that about 500 - 1,000 games turns will be needed to complete the games victory criteria.
- Community led development. Ok so they have said they will, but only time will tell if this actually happens in any meaningful way.
- Will update this after about 25-50 hours gaming,-

I downloaded around beta/launch. Thought there could be something here eventually, but didn't like it at the time, uninstalled and forgot about it. Collecting materials to build better guns,swords,axes,sonic lazer wrist mounted crossbows, etc. Collecting different and powerful other robot ninjas to play as. Rinse Repeat. Alright; disclosure.
I've played this as little as possible through Early Access, so I can enjoy the end-product to it's fullest.
I've played previous games of the Endless series, including Endless Space and Endless Legend; so I'm familiar with the formula and lay-out.
I'm a bit of an amplitude fanboy; in a 'I like their game design and aesthetic' sense.
So, with that stated I believe this is a great successor to the endless space formula, it uses the lesson learnt in Endless Legend to make a modern, slick UI that's much nicer to navigate than the original Endless Space UI. The resource gain from your FIDSI from selecting tech, buildings and policies is pretty clear - though the system itself is the big learning curve for new players. You need to focus on learning the nuances of these mechanics to get the most out of your playthrough; and how you manipulate these by spending luxary resources and even strategic resources in some cases in your planetary systems. The government system, with it's political parties is also another aspect of mastery you'll eventually pick up.
Stick with these games and you'll get a slick, sdeep 4X with great re-playability and a dedicated community. Some of the best multiplayer games I've had have been in Endless Legend and I'm looking forward to playing Endless Space 2 with others!
Negatives I can warn you about:-
- In early access it had a tendancy to be a little delayed when the AI was working; though it wasn't particularly jarring for me; it could become more pronounced over longer games - the release version does seem much better so far.
- For a 4X it has some pretty big demands on your graphics card.
- I personally find the tutorial tips a little vague in endless games and always have. There's a great community behind these games, on games2gether and youtube - you'll learn far more from these people should you be looking for tutorials.

Well, there has been some time since I've played a game this intriguing. L.A. Noire is more like a classical 'noir' movie rather than a computer game, and you get to play the star of the movie! The storyline centers a young, promising police officer -later detective- named Cole Phelps in 1940s Los Angeles. His tale has everything: crime, murder, trauma, love, politics, justice, conflict of interest and ethics... mostly conflict everywhere.
The atmosphere is magnificent, graphics are more than satisfying and story builds around many twists and turns, always keeping you wondering about what might come next. The investigation process is well displayed, heavily depending on observation, whether it be a mimic of a suspect, or a tone in the witness' voice. The environment is wast and it is possible to get lost if you're not following the map indicators. You carry the full option of roaming the streets of L.A. to hunt for all kinds of achievements, and even venture out to solve trivial street crimes. I once again agreed that Rockstar never abstains from investing in environment design.
Controls of the game is a bit hard to master in PC though, I think this game is better suited for PS or Xbox in that manner. Vehicles are impossibly hard to control - at least for me, but my reflexes were never that great so I'm not the one to have a final call on that -  and that would be the sole minus for me that I've observed so far. I found myself preferring my partner to drive rather than myself, and that's a bit disappointing. Oh, well: I'm not in for the perfection anyhow.
I recommend it with CAPITAL CHARACTERS; for the story, graphics and display altogether.

Straight up that strikes you about the game is the quality of acting/animation. It's really a triump of both combined. Years later, and we still don't have any game with quite the same level of realism and nuance as L.A. Noire's completely believable facial animation that really just carries and sells the whole premise of the game.
The thing is, that sort of shows the weakness of the other parts of the game. While being able to drive 'freely', the game isn't exactly free-roaming. You can waste time and drive around during the actual missions, and hope to pick up things on your scanner for the petty street crimes, which are pretty much the only 'side-missions' or side-activities that the game provides.
The city feels alive and it's pretty relaxing to drive to view the sights, but this game is no GTA. Rather, it's more like an interactive novel with driving and shooting segments in between, as well as on-foot chases. This doesn't bother me, since I'm not that big on either of those and appreciate the storytelling more, but it really feels a bit too much of an afterthought and may be a big downer for some players.
Overall though, when on sale, L.A. Noire is  bargain for the cinematic quality of storytelling you get. It showed that we have the tech to finally beat the uncanny valley, and bring true 'acting' to games. It's just too bad not many, if any, games have tried to do so since. And with Team Bondi's dissolution, it's likely we won't see something in this vein for quite some time.

Crusader Kings II is, in a word, addicting. In the game, you take the role of a European (with some exceptions) nobleman (or woman). The goal is simple, survival of your dynasty. Sounds easy, right? It isn’t. Each individual character with in the game is driven by a simple AI system, guiding them toward the same goal. However, your chances of survival increase as you increase in “rank.” As do theirs. So, you wind up with a conflict of interest. Your neighbors want to conquer you in order to amass power and maybe increase their rank from, say; count to duke, duke to king, or king to emperor. Rub your vassals the wrong way? They’ll revolt and then do the same.
Still think it sounds easy? Try this on for size: political intrigue. Assassinations are commonplace, as is your assassins getting caught and blabbing your name. Of course, this usually leads to an invasion or your own assassination attempt. Declare a tournament to keep the people happy? Prepare to lose a good chunk of your court in the process. Possibly including yourself. That neighboring county with 6 holdings and no protecting nation looking tasty AND you have a Casus Beli to invade them? They’ve been building up and can afford mercenaries. Think you’re safe AS the tasty looking county with 6 holdings? I have news for you, the Holy Roman Empire just decided that they want your county, minus you.
If that’s still not enough for you, consider this: Just when you thought that you figured out how to sit there in your cozy little holding and wait out the hordes and tournaments and all the other assorted little hazards: The pope declares a crusade. Don’t go, you lose out on a LOT of prestige and plunder. Go, and you risk the possibility of dying, leaving your country defenseless, or worse.
The DLC tends to be hit or miss, but each one adds some major content to the game. With all the DLC you can play as Muslim rulers (restricted in Vanilla), enjoy some extra depth in the Byzantine empire that you don’t get normally, and get an extra fantasy scenario where the Aztecs invade Europe in the 1200s. All-in-all it’s worth it completely.
The graphical system may be a little simple, and the gameplay extremely complex without going through HOURS (not kidding) of tutorials, but all-in-all it is worth it. If you have a chance I’d suggest picking it up and giving it a try.

Had a long think about this review. The technology is nothing short of breathtaking and well worth it as a tour de force of what great tech can add to a game.
The gameplay feature of reading the charactors tells is, i think, a great inovation and also, a difficult whip to crack. It can feel a little lopsided as some of the acting i over egged and thus paints the conversion as somewhat bipolar.
Although this could of been negated by yet more acting, I can understand that the complexity of such would of either burnt out the actors or moved the game into a different year for completion.
I've heard of the heartache associated with the production of the game and can understand why. Its easy to dismiss when coming from a place of ignorance with some of those slight bugs but when looked at as a whole, the game broke some ground, not only in gameplay but technology aswell, not to mention tying them together. I applaud the huge undertaking this game was.
One thing that was a little underwhelming though.....the driving... its not a driving game as we already know, its really a detective game but the driving elements, for me, could of been more fun with you being driven around rather than do the driving. I like driving games but when the driving is profuctory rather than part of the game, its best left out. Would of really enjoyed being driven around and take in the sights, scouting for suspects etc....perhaps have a little gun fight along the way etc. I think that would of lended better to a detective game than a sort of limited driving sim with lowend mechanics.
Last thoughts, although the main portion of development missed the driving aspects its understandable when you have such attention paid to a rather breathtaking level of charactor detail and nuance.

I tried to get into this game several times, and I could never quite grasp the "point".  I'd jump in, be completely overwhelmed by all the menus, lists, currencies and resources, interactive consoles, etc.  The missions seemed to be the same thing over and over, and I couldn't really tell I was making any kind of progress.  Ultimately I'd give up every time.
Well I finally get it.  A few things led to me finally getting hooked:
-  I played with mouse and keyboard at my PC desk, instead of with a controller on the couch on tv.  This made me realize just how amazing the movement system is, and the insanely awesome ninja-like stuff you can accomplish.
-  I realized a big part of the game is setting your own goals.  Want to collect warframes?  Want to increase your Mastery Rank?  Want to decorate your warframe to look extra badass?  Want to reach the next planet?  All valid goals.
-   I accepted that Google is my friend.  Let's face it, the game does an awful job of explaining its features.  A TON of the game's depth is completely hidden from the Player.  Once I started alt-tabbing to google every time I had a question, I started getting answers and the structure of the game started making sense.
-  I realized just how powerful mods are.  You can customize entire playstyles using them.  Leveling up a warframe or weapon isn't about leveling it up to 30.  Getting to 30 is just getting it to a playable state.  Truly leveling it up to epic proportions comes from smartly investing in your mods.
So ya, now I'm hardcore hooked.  60 hours in, and I know I'm just scratching the surface.  I'll be playing this one for a long time to come.  If you like looter-shooters where you never run out of things to grind for, this is the game.

Crusader Kings II is, in a word, addicting. In the game, you take the role of a European (with some exceptions) nobleman (or woman). The goal is simple, survival of your dynasty. Sounds easy, right? It isn’t. Each individual character with in the game is driven by a simple AI system, guiding them toward the same goal. However, your chances of survival increase as you increase in “rank.” As do theirs. So, you wind up with a conflict of interest. Your neighbors want to conquer you in order to amass power and maybe increase their rank from, say; count to duke, duke to king, or king to emperor. Rub your vassals the wrong way? They’ll revolt and then do the same.
Still think it sounds easy? Try this on for size: political intrigue. Assassinations are commonplace, as is your assassins getting caught and blabbing your name. Of course, this usually leads to an invasion or your own assassination attempt. Declare a tournament to keep the people happy? Prepare to lose a good chunk of your court in the process. Possibly including yourself. That neighboring county with 6 holdings and no protecting nation looking tasty AND you have a Casus Beli to invade them? They’ve been building up and can afford mercenaries. Think you’re safe AS the tasty looking county with 6 holdings? I have news for you, the Holy Roman Empire just decided that they want your county, minus you.
If that’s still not enough for you, consider this: Just when you thought that you figured out how to sit there in your cozy little holding and wait out the hordes and tournaments and all the other assorted little hazards: The pope declares a crusade. Don’t go, you lose out on a LOT of prestige and plunder. Go, and you risk the possibility of dying, leaving your country defenseless, or worse.
The DLC tends to be hit or miss, but each one adds some major content to the game. With all the DLC you can play as Muslim rulers (restricted in Vanilla), enjoy some extra depth in the Byzantine empire that you don’t get normally, and get an extra fantasy scenario where the Aztecs invade Europe in the 1200s. All-in-all it’s worth it completely.
The graphical system may be a little simple, and the gameplay extremely complex without going through HOURS (not kidding) of tutorials, but all-in-all it is worth it. If you have a chance I’d suggest picking it up and giving it a try.

L.A Noire plays out in the mid-20th century, just after the Second World War. You play as Detective Cole Phelps, a good hearted cop who was a soldier in the pacific during the second world war. The game confronts you with a time period where racism was rampant, drug abuse was growing, and violence was all too common.
The city of L.A is one of the major stars in the game. Every street is full of life, with people going in and out of bars and shops, people reading the daily newspaper before going to work. The game feels as though its actually come to life.
MotionScan, a neat piece of technology which Team Bondi created to capture the emotions of the characters on screen. It works splendidly, giving each conversation an engrossing hook that typically associated with great film and television dramas. When a character lies, you can see it in their face. Interviewing a suspect is the hardest and most important thing you will do in the game. You ask a question, listen to their response and then attempt to decipher whether it's a lie, the truth or something you should "doubt" and inquire further about. You don't only listen to what they saying, but you have to look very carefully at their faces as well. The slightest twitch in there cheek, or there eyes darting quickly to the left can help you uncover the truth.
There is more to L.A Noire than just interrogation. There is a fair amount of crime-scene investigation, patrolling and beat work. At crime scenes, you are able to examine the victim up close to try find clues. You will walk around crime scene picking up all sorts of objects to see if they hold any clues. Outside of the regular story. L.A. Noire offers a few other tasks. You can explore the city and look for historic L.A. landmarks, tackle random side mission crimes as they come to you over your C.B. radio, as well as play additional DLC cases. Once you have finished a story, you are ranked to how well you answered questions, how many you got right, and how much damage you did to your car and the the city of L.A.
The sounds in the game are amazing, with cars and busses going by, to the sound of the sparks coming from the electric wires as the tram drives past you. The acting is completely believable and really helps set this game apart from other detective games.
The Verdict:
For all of its attention to detail, L.A. Noire hits the occasional false note. But if you put that aside, L.A Noire can be a very entertaining game, with an open world to explore and lots of interesting cases, The awesome performances and great facial capture make every interrogation and investigation a riveting affair. L.A Noire is a perfect game that I would definitely recommend to everyone.
Pros:
+ Open world of an authentic and outstanding 1940s style of atmosphere
+ Memorable story
+ Great use of motion capture
+ Compelling investigation and interrogation mechanics
+ Amazing graphics
+ Brilliant acting
+ Amazing sound
Cons:
- Some restrictions during pursuits and shoot-outs feel artificial
- Can become a bit repetitive at times
Score: 9/10

Ever since my significant other introduced me to Warframe I've been addicted.  This game is unlike anything I've played before with beautifully rendered and detailed environments, tons of unique, playable frames and weapons, amazing customization in the way of armor, colors, skins, etc., incredible and fun frame abilities, a really nice crafting system, tons of different crafting materials, numerous quest types, and so much more . . . this game isn't likely to disappoint!
The game handles like a dream with deliciously satisfying fighting animations and controls, many different attack animations and techniques, and very quick-to-respond controls.  The frames themselves are based off of different gods/goddesses and mythical figures/creatures, and you are given the task of collecting as many of them as possible while also working towards collecting their much more powerful prime forms.  The game is still being updated, so new frames and prime frames are being released every so often.  With all of the new content and the great story and open/random quests there's always something to do!  (Not to mention you can keep yourself even busier with customizing and collecting different sentinels, space ships, and animal companions, all with their own customizable skins, colors, parts, etc.!)
Another thing I absolutely feel the need to note is that you can choose between single player and several multiplayer settings thus allowing you to play with members of your friend list, guild, or random strangers!  It keeps things quite refreshing to people looking to advance quickly with others while also valuing isolated play, and allows me to enjoy the game within my comfort zone, which I greatly appreciate considering I have issues with most multiplayer games.  What's also nice is that with the different level ranges of the quests and planet tiles you can either cruise through easy areas or challenge yourself with higher level battles.  This is great for levelling new frames and weapons, while also allowing you to push yourself and develop your game skills.
And, oh yes, the mods.  My GOD the mods. . .  Those are the real game changers here.  Make sure to experiment with different status effects and stat boosts to build the ultimate frames and weapons as they can literally be the difference between an assured victory and miserable defeat.
I LOVE playing this game, and I also love the fact that users can submit their own skins and creations and could very well see them implemented into the game!  I'm likely going to be playing this game for a long time yet, and look forward to attending TennoCons in the future!  Brilliant work to everyone involved!

L.A Noire plays out in the mid-20th century, just after the Second World War. You play as Detective Cole Phelps, a good hearted cop who was a soldier in the pacific during the second world war. The game confronts you with a time period where racism was rampant, drug abuse was growing, and violence was all too common.
The city of L.A is one of the major stars in the game. Every street is full of life, with people going in and out of bars and shops, people reading the daily newspaper before going to work. The game feels as though its actually come to life.
MotionScan, a neat piece of technology which Team Bondi created to capture the emotions of the characters on screen. It works splendidly, giving each conversation an engrossing hook that typically associated with great film and television dramas. When a character lies, you can see it in their face. Interviewing a suspect is the hardest and most important thing you will do in the game. You ask a question, listen to their response and then attempt to decipher whether it's a lie, the truth or something you should "doubt" and inquire further about. You don't only listen to what they saying, but you have to look very carefully at their faces as well. The slightest twitch in there cheek, or there eyes darting quickly to the left can help you uncover the truth.
There is more to L.A Noire than just interrogation. There is a fair amount of crime-scene investigation, patrolling and beat work. At crime scenes, you are able to examine the victim up close to try find clues. You will walk around crime scene picking up all sorts of objects to see if they hold any clues. Outside of the regular story. L.A. Noire offers a few other tasks. You can explore the city and look for historic L.A. landmarks, tackle random side mission crimes as they come to you over your C.B. radio, as well as play additional DLC cases. Once you have finished a story, you are ranked to how well you answered questions, how many you got right, and how much damage you did to your car and the the city of L.A.
The sounds in the game are amazing, with cars and busses going by, to the sound of the sparks coming from the electric wires as the tram drives past you. The acting is completely believable and really helps set this game apart from other detective games.
The Verdict:
For all of its attention to detail, L.A. Noire hits the occasional false note. But if you put that aside, L.A Noire can be a very entertaining game, with an open world to explore and lots of interesting cases, The awesome performances and great facial capture make every interrogation and investigation a riveting affair. L.A Noire is a perfect game that I would definitely recommend to everyone.
Pros:
+ Open world of an authentic and outstanding 1940s style of atmosphere
+ Memorable story
+ Great use of motion capture
+ Compelling investigation and interrogation mechanics
+ Amazing graphics
+ Brilliant acting
+ Amazing sound
Cons:
- Some restrictions during pursuits and shoot-outs feel artificial
- Can become a bit repetitive at times
Score: 9/10

I can go on for hours on how much I love about this game. Pure excellence. Now standing at nearly 1500 hours in this game, I can still play it and enjoy it fully. Fashion Frame, Infinite customization possibilities with mods and such, (23?) Warframes you can grind for, (or buy, your choice) and SO many weapons and weapon variants , pets, sentinels, ship decorations and such for you to enjoy all the way! This game does have a hell of a grind, and that is a gameplay element that will only appeal to those that like that sort of thing. If you don't want to spend time grinding for the newest great weapon to help you fight the next boss and unlock the next planet, or finish your next sortie (endgame mission) then that is something I cannot change, or recommend for you.
To wrap up, Warframe is a great game. It has constant updates, hours of content for you to enjoy, and, need I mention, an amazing community that will gladly help you finish a mission, trade you an item, or just help you out. It is rare you will find toxicity in game. Recommended from me.
