OK. This will be a long one (Hopefully not).
Where do i begin... This game truely changed me and i could not be more thankful to the small developer DE for putting their heart and soul into a game everyone knew would fail.
When i first downloaded warframe back in 2016 i only played it for a few weeks and realised the complexity and deep understanding i would need to properly play the game was something i wasnt committed to, and believed at the time it was pay to win.
My oh my was I wrong.
Earlier this year (around early March) I was looking for a game to pick up, and play because of the lack of diversity i have in games (2 games normally played on my PC) and i saw ''Warframe'' at the bottom of the list, i decided to open it and update it and see if anything was different since i last played it. To my pleasant surprise it did. A whole lot. Tons of new frames, weapons, quests, systems and features now available to me at NO COST. Thats what surprised me the most. The realisation that this game isn't what first meets the eye. Not some game, locked behind a pay wall and behind price tags and exclusive unlockables and boosts. No. This was the day i realised that the whole ''spending platinum on the market'' was redundant. The sole purpose of the game is to grind out parts for new frames, weapons, or to farm for mods for said equipment. I don't know why it didn't cross my mind that such a large community community was following this game because of it's rewarding gameplay. The fact of the matter is, you, the player, can aquire ALL frames, ALL weapons, ALL mods, ALMOST ALL cosmetics and EVERY ingame features, aside from the exclusive founders pack items (Can't aquire them anymore even with money) For absolutly free. No cost. This realisation immediatly changed my opinion on the game and others like it. DE have shown in a perfect way, how a free to play game can both allow the freedom of players who choose to spend money, and respect the time and effort put in to warframe other players who don't choose to pay.
I'll admit, i have spent money on warframe, but it wasn't forced, or advertised in my face. It wasn't shoved into my face and made me spend money to continue or to be as good as my friends and other players, it was kept away from me in fact. The game actively encourages you to farm out the resources, parts and mods instead of buying them from the store. What makes DE great is they value the active Player base who farm and grind for hours on end just the same as the players who use their wallet to progress.
And for that Digital Extremes, your game 'Warframe' gets a 10/10 from me, would highly recommend.

Overall concept:
You play as Cole Phelps, a detective in 1947 Los Angeles, solving various cases and uncovering conspiracies.
Story:
There are several layers of story-telling. There are several flashbacks to Phelps' experiences as a soldier during World War II. These flashbacks happen frequently throughout the game. Another storyline is told through cutscenes that trigger when you find newspapers. There are short, self-contained stories for certain cases, but some cases are tied together by a longer investigation.
Most of the stories are interesting, and they are pretty easy to follow. There is a "log" feature that allows you to read a transcript of all the dialogue so far in the current case (I think it's the whole case, I'm not sure about this). I found this feature very helpful.
Gameplay:
Even though it kind of looks like Grand Theft Auto (which makes sense, since they are both made by Rockstar), this is not a sandbox game. This felt very strange, since the world itself is big and you technically can roam around it freely. There just isn't much to do besides solving the cases (which play out in a very linear fashion, and you only have one case at a time). There are "street crimes" that sometimes occur when you are driving around. Requests to deal with these crimes come through the police radio, and you can choose whether or not to accept them. They are basically side missions, but they are very short.
The gameplay consists mainly of searching for clues, questioning "people of interest", and action sequences. Searching for clues is not as difficult and time-consuming as one would think. Special music plays when you are in an area with clues, and chimes play when you are close to one. (This feature can be disabled.)
Questioning people can be difficult, since sometimes the "correct" responses seem arbitrary, but even if you don't get the information you want/need, you'll still be able to complete the mission somehow. I wasn't really bad at interrogating people, so I don't know if the game makes you replay several questioning sequences if you fail them. I only had to redo one interrogation (I was forced to).
The action sequences (car chases, following people, shooting bad guys, etc.) are not very difficult. Certain action sequences can be skipped if you keep failing them. You don't have to skip them, and the option to do so can be disabled altogether.
I was really terrible at driving when I played GTA IV (I was so bad that I couldn't get past the 3rd or 4th mission), so when I realized this game had driving, I was kind of upset. However, for some reason, I find driving in this game to be easier. Maybe it's because I'm playing this on a laptop, and I played GTA IV on Xbox 360. I still crashed into stuff, but not nearly as often as in GTA. One really great feature is that when you go to most locations, you can force your partner to drive! This saves time (since it basically just cuts to the location) and prevents you from crashing into everything. (Your partner cannot always drive; for example, you have to drive during chase sequences.) However, since you do not observe the entire trip, you do not get street crime opportunities when you make your partner drive.
You can also collect film reels (other things too I believe?) and find hidden cars. I do not know much about collecting since I didn't care about it.
Graphics:
I'm not that hard to please when it comes to graphics, but I should mention that I didn't see any blurry textures, which really bug me. The facial animation is great. Check out some YouTube videos showing how they did it (but not until after you play the game, so you don't encounter other videos with spoilers in the titles!); they basically converted video of the actors saying their lines (in full hair and makeup!) into CGI.
There were a couple minor graphical glitches. Some were common bugs I find in many games, such as arms and legs going through walls; however, that was rare. The most annoying glitches I found were issues animating Phelps' suits. Certain suits were more buggy than others.
Characters:
The characters were well acted, and mostly interesting to encounter. A big exception to that is one of Phelps' partners. The actor did a great job, but the character is a sexist jerk and you have to spend a large portion of the game working with him. I wanted to punch him in the face.
The random pedestrians you encounter on the street are really annoying. They have very few available lines of dialogue, and they either talk about Phelps, the cases he solved, or say things like "I'm going to get good and tight come Friday."
Other things I thought were worth mentioning:
-The game took me 28 hours to complete.
-You cannot manually save your game. However, I didn't die/fail constantly (the game isn't that hard), and the game autosaves frequently.
-If you saw the ESRB's rating, noticed it had nudity, and thought "YAYYY LET'S GO HAVE FUN WITH THE NAKED LADIES", you will be very disappointed. The naked women are all dead.
-Since it's set in the 40s, there is sexism and racism (considered normal at the time). However, it is clearly not condoned. Phelps never says anything sexist or racist, and it is clear that he does not approve of that kind of dialogue or behavior.
-Don't look up spoilers! Since this is a game about mysteries, it is inherently something that you shouldn't be figuring out ahead of time! (I accidentally spoiled the ending for myself by looking up "L.A. Noire" on YouTube to find videos about the facial animation, and seeing titles of other videos with major spoilers.)
-If dead bodies freak you out, skip this game. You need to examine many dead bodies.
-There are puzzles to solve. They are not very difficult.
Overall:
I really liked this game. I had a lot of fun playing it. It was the perfect difficulty level for me, and I found the story very interesting. (This game and the Mass Effect series have set high expectations for games I play in the future when it comes to storylines.) I don't know if this has much replay value, since a big part of the game is solving mysteries and puzzles, and obviously solving them again would be much easier. However, it might be interesting to go back and try to get higher star ratings for the missions (by answering more questions "correctly" and finding all possible clues).
If you're looking for a story-driven game with mysteries, puzzles, and action, check this game out! I highly recommend it.

I've played a number of Grand Strategy games and this one is by far the best one out there. As far as GS games go it's simple enough to learn, but, as all GS games are, difficult to master. However, the point that makes this game so great is that there is focus not only on external forces, but internal ones as well. You have four levels of playability, from the bottom: Count, Duke, King, Emperor. At all these levels you have vassals, and you might even be a vassal yourself. A lot of the fun is in how you manage your vassals; and better yet, how you as a vassal maneuver and plot to overthrow your liege. The story aspect of this title far exceeds any other GS game I've played, to the point that when I start a session, it's extremely difficult to stop. If you are interested at all in trying Grand Strategy, I recommend you start off with this one. And that's coming from someone who doesn't particularly care for the Age of Crusades. Also, get the DLC to make your own character and house.

It is a really good game all in all, here are my pros and cons:
Pros:
1) It is F2P. (Let's be honest, it is already a great game, minus some bad trades here and there)
2) The community is probably the nicest bunch of people you can find that can help you with your weapon and warframe builds, especially if you need to go to places that aren't your level yet and gain exp from them. If you ever need people to help you, you can probably get a full squad within 5 minutes if the pop-ups are showing up properly.
3) The Lore is really good. If you are avid fan of good storyline, I will say that Warframe will really make you interested in the way of how certain people reacted or how you, the players, can affect your own destiny within the game itself.
Graphics wise, even while using a low-end laptop, DE did a very good job in ensuring that ppl are able to view the cinematics, especially in The Second Dream and The War Within were very well done. Good job! (claps in the background)
And here are my cons:
1) Grinding and farming non-stop till you get that one item/mod that you need. I ever grinded for 15-20 rounds of survival in the ODS (Orokin Derelict Survival) for a particular warframe part and it took me so long to get it.
2) Connectivity issues. Recently, the new patches have been causing a lot of problems, especially if you are going for high level areas or sorties, which can be the downfall of the game at this point in time.
3) BUGS, and lots of them. Also related to the patches, a couple of friends of mine also mentioned to me that there were many bugs, especially bugs that can potentially lag out the computers.
4) Ridiculous amount of time to build weapons, and this especially goes to prime weapons and warframes, (with equinox factored in despite not being a prime frame). Prime weapons can require so many orokin cells as well as other parts to make 1 prime part, followed by making 3 more and using the blueprint to get the completed blueprint. (Refer back to 1 for the reason.)
5) Last and not the least, levelling up stuff that takes huge amounts of time to get the "perfect" build. And I mean actually end-game weapons. You can easily waste so many resources to get that one item and continuously spend almost 100 hours on 1 weapon alone(if the weapon is OP, then everyone will use and get nerfed.)
On that note, still a good game i will recommend, but it will get boring after a while.

I love Stellaris for its customization ability, but for some reason this one grabbed my attention more as a 4x game. The races are so unique and have such personality. They are not cliched in any way. For example, the Sophons at first appear to be your typical highly advanced tech race, but they are totally irresponsible and have a teenage mentality. This leads to technology sometimes biting them back in the but, as they design rogue ais and cause general problems in the galaxy.
I love Horatio. What an amazing race! I imagine whole worlds full of coneheads waging war and trying to make everything beautiful as His image. And there are even various factions of Him. lol. it's hilarious.
Anyway, the gameplay itself is fun. The space battles are a joy to behold and feature impressive backdrops (The Academy's system battle map blew me away.
The devs spared no attention to detail either. There are so many quests and happenings in the universe it just feels alive, and each race has their own story. Even ground battles are a treat to watch, especially when your army is made of a coalition of assimilated races. Every model in the battle looks like members of its race or the races that you've brought to invade.
Driving ahead to victory and advancing and colonizing are a joy too. There are always so many strategic choices to make, and so many layers, yet it is so simple to understand after playing its in-game tutorial. Whenever something new comes up, if you have the tutorial running it gives you a very brief and uninvasive view of the concept and lets you play as you want.
All in all, one of the best 4x games I've played, and I've been playing them since civ 1.

There are four things that I must say about Chivalry: Medieval Warfare; two good, two bad.
1. The combat is amazing. While most games like this one, such as the Elder Scrolls, have a melee system based around a set amount of health, where you can just swing away at your enemy until they fall over dead, Chivalry makes every blow feel real. In Skyrim, your sword hits the enemy, maybe staggering him, but the blow feels empty as the animation doesn't feel nearly as meaty as you'd like it. In Chivalry, you can almost feel the bones breaking and the flesh tearing underneath your strike. The enemy will be knocked back, and maybe even lose a limb. In Skyrim, you have to have a perk to cut people's heads off. In Chivalry, you can take someone's head off in a single swing with a knife. You can have a Zweihander sword, swing it and take a guy's leg off and then swing again, and take his head off.
Using a shield in this game makes you feel almost inpenetrable. The blocking system is great, not perfect, but great since, again unlike Skyrim, the shield will block all damage striking. (Kind of like how a real shield would work in real life.) You can also bash and knock your enemy off balance, opening him up for a counter strike. Every single blow that is landed feels rewarding, no matter how you pulled it off.
2. The weapons. There is no such thing in this game as a bad weapong....just ones that are freakishly annoying to use. Each and every weapon in this game can be used to great effectiveness if the wielder knows what he or she is doing. Even the two-handed hammer can be used to destroy your enemies if you know how to use it. Even the spears, which are my least favorite weapon in the game, can be used well, if, again, you know how to use it. Each tool of destruction has its own unique appeal to it, whether it's a sword, or a hammer. An axe, or a spear. Heck, even the flail is fun to use.
And now for the bad:
3. The netcode. While nowhere near as bad as Battlefield 4, the netcode does have a few issues. The main issue is that when an opponent is swinging, their weapon isn't always swinging the way that it is on your screen. You may think that you are pointing your shield at it, but it's actually somewhere else and they get an easy kill because of it.
4. The community. In any game where there is friendly fire, there will be the issue of team killing. In Chivalry, how you swing your weapon actually matters. When you are in a crowd of people, one simply cannot swing wildly. If you do, you will be sure to kill your friends along with your enemies. In all of the matches I have played, there hasn't been a single one that hasn't had someone kill a teammate. This wouldn't be that big of an issue if it wasn't for the fact that it happens every match and can be easily avoided, most of the time it happens. If you overshoot your opponent, sure, it was an accident. But if you leap into a crowd of people, swining wildly, then you have no excuse as to why you took off the legs of three of your teammates. As a whole, the community doens't seem to be too concerned with watching their strikes. Sure, there are those who do their best not to hit their teammates and always apologize when they do, but there are those who just don't care. They will be sure to ruin your day a little more when you almost have unlocked a new weapon, only need one more kill, and you're about to take the head off of a knight, when your teammate takes your head instead and steals you kill, or simply gets owned by the knight.
Don't even get me started about the intentional teamkilling.
So, there you have it: what makes Chivalry: Medieval Warfare such a great game and what's wrong with it. Hopefully, this has shed some light on the game so that you won't be going into playing blind to at least some of the issues that it has.

With over 1222 hours on record, I have more than gotten my money's worth with ARK: Survival Evolved. Every few months I'm pulled back in, as they continue to expand the universe and release new content and creatures to fill it with. For someone who plays on a private server, it becomes home after a while. There's a wealth of content and a bunch of ways to improve your sandbox experience (see: Ark Commander). Even on the lowest settings, it's a nice looking game with tons of fun to be had. If survival isn't your thing, there's roleplay, buildcraft, and dungeon crawling. There's so many ways to play the game, so don't pass it up thinking it's just another survival clone. I highly recommend playing on a private server, with lots of mods, and all the admin commands you can find. Imagine hopping online, thinking to yourself, "What can I do today?" So, you spawn a Wyvern, paint it pink and orange, fly over to the secret lava base, spawn a giant spider and an army of praying mantis and become a demon overlord. Or build wooden huts on the beach. It's up to you.

This game is ambitious beyond reason but also hugely successful in its execution. It really brings to life the world of James Ellroy to an extent I didn't think we could see in a game, at least not yet. The plot is intricate, the characters are cruel but nuanced, the city itself is alive. The ending is excellent. It holds no punches and it makes no excuses - it is the thinking man's GTA (which is how we also explain the less daunting sales figures) and if you want to piece every part of the plot together, you'd better pay attention. If you find this appealing, this game is bound to be something very special for you, otherwise you shouldn't bother.
The good:
Just driving through LA (which you will do a lot of) is astounding in itself. For a long time, the game suffered from poor graphics performance and fairly weak visuals but with the DX11 version now running perfectly, the game is absolutely great to look at. And that's really important when so much of the game is the ambiance, the visual details, the feel of driving through 40s LA. The gameplay is original and the storyline is fascinating. Your fellow characters have real depth and so does your primary protagonist and the city itself. The world is dirty, corrupt, greedy, harsh, sad, all the things the world of Ellroy needs to be and it pulls no punches. There are no heroes here but that doesn't mean they're all villains either. The content is very large for a linear, story-driven game. Lots of cases, lots of societal aspects covered and unapologetically unfolded before us, lots of nasty little secrets to uncover. If you ever felt drawn to the world of true noire detectives, this is for you.
The bad:
Very little, obviously, since I give it a 10. A few times, the game mechanic used during suspect interviews can feel a little arbitrary - that what you expect something to mean isn't what is actually meant by accusing a certain person of something at a specific time. Sometimes the game and the player will misunderstand each other which will lead to the player quitting and replaying a segment and feeling annoyed because he expected a different outcome from an action than the game presented and the player had no way of anticipating this. It isn't always exactly clear what the consequences will be from selecting a specific dialogue but most of the time it works. The facial animation can still seem slightly outdated (or very) but you can recognize the actors and the acting itself is top notch.
Do not buy this game if you're looking for a new GTA, do not buy if you don't like stories and want action. But if you like stories, noire literature/film, Ellroy, just trying something a bit new to gaming, you HAVE to play this game. Very rewarding, extremely well done. This game was cared for down to its smallest detail, I hope we see more like this.

I've played a number of Grand Strategy games and this one is by far the best one out there. As far as GS games go it's simple enough to learn, but, as all GS games are, difficult to master. However, the point that makes this game so great is that there is focus not only on external forces, but internal ones as well. You have four levels of playability, from the bottom: Count, Duke, King, Emperor. At all these levels you have vassals, and you might even be a vassal yourself. A lot of the fun is in how you manage your vassals; and better yet, how you as a vassal maneuver and plot to overthrow your liege. The story aspect of this title far exceeds any other GS game I've played, to the point that when I start a session, it's extremely difficult to stop. If you are interested at all in trying Grand Strategy, I recommend you start off with this one. And that's coming from someone who doesn't particularly care for the Age of Crusades. Also, get the DLC to make your own character and house.

This game to me is how I expected Rockstar to attempt a game in their style, but be the good guy for a change, rather than the usual GTA style criminal.
However, this does come at a price: you can't really go all crazy on the road and crash into anything and everything, because the damage you do gets deducted from your score, nor can you, at the times you are able to shoot, just go around and minlessly killing civilians.
On top of that, there is no room available in between missions, as you automatically get transported back to the Police Station got start the next mission, so anything in involving exploration, side missions and collectibles have to happen during your missions, thus really restricting your freedom. Again, this is where your reckless driving comes biting you in the butt.
However, I don't have only negative things to say about the game
Story wise, the very reason I play this game, it's really well put together. Without spoilering too much, the missions in each chapter, while at the start may seem all lose cases that have nothing to do with each other, you find yourself at the end always learning that everything has something to do with everything. And overall, it's a rollercoaster on how the story progresses. Especially towards the end.
I also like how the game has aparently different cutscenes at the end of each mission, depending on how well you performed. Although I personally didn't bother too much or completion, finding all the clues, getting all answers correct etc, there were times where, with a low score, I thought I failed the mission and had to restart the mission. Luckily that is not the case.
I'm personally a fan of the entire style of the late '30's, '40's and 50's and (as European) I think that era was USA's best and while playing this game, I took the time to admire the scenery and furniture when I was presented with lots of it. You can tell that the devs took their time to make the scenery as close to reality as possible. Even with the fasion and hairstyles of that era.
However, 2 final things before I close off.
The driving sections bored me out of my skull, especially because driving recklessly gets you penalised. Since obviously the cars were not as fast as they are today or like in GTA games, the long trips were just annoying and I later decided to let my partner do all of the driving in between locations.
The other thing is that some of the chapters felt really repetitive to me. Especially Homicide. That chapter could've been shorter in my oppinion.
After all has been said, I still recommend this game and give it a 7/10, because it's a good attempt at a crime game, that we know and love Rockstar for, from the opposite side.

I've played this game for almost 600 hours, and that's not even close to hardcore players who have spent far more time over this masterpiece.
This game was developed as a response to a Facebook petition calling the game's developers to make a sequel to a one-time project from early 2000s. Crusader Kings Ii is one of the most original strategy games ever made, and perhaps the best game about medieval Europe (and not only Europe now!).
I can't even remember how the original vanilla version of this game looked like. In 5 years after its release, the game's development never stopped, and Paradox Interactive continues to release new DLCs and patch it over and over again.
It is one of those games which would get 10/10 from me. There is no game like it, and its replayability is legendary, while it maintains a fairly low complexity, remaining friendly to both old-school strategy fans and newbies. I certainly recommend it for everyone.

A great game with a pleasant atmospheric experience based in 1940s Los Angeles as Detective Cole Phelps. The graphcs are good in terms of setting a balance of immersion by creating a very realistic vibe. The street crime cases add a bit of flavor to the overall gameplay to a game that may seem too linear to some by providing a bit of uncertainty for when the next case will come. The main cases are very interesting and carry a lot of suspense and intrigue. The downside of many of these cases is that they may become too easy for some and may not prove to be a good challenge. However, it is important to note that only the chase scenes can be a bit too easy, but actually finding the clues and persons of interests in the right order can prove to be a challenge. The controls are the typical WASD and a realistic point and shoot dynamic without any visible crosshairs. Overall, I found it a very pleasing game to play and there is a certain uniqueness that creates an enticing desire to continue to the next case.

I tried to get into this game several times, and I could never quite grasp the "point".  I'd jump in, be completely overwhelmed by all the menus, lists, currencies and resources, interactive consoles, etc.  The missions seemed to be the same thing over and over, and I couldn't really tell I was making any kind of progress.  Ultimately I'd give up every time.
Well I finally get it.  A few things led to me finally getting hooked:
-  I played with mouse and keyboard at my PC desk, instead of with a controller on the couch on tv.  This made me realize just how amazing the movement system is, and the insanely awesome ninja-like stuff you can accomplish.
-  I realized a big part of the game is setting your own goals.  Want to collect warframes?  Want to increase your Mastery Rank?  Want to decorate your warframe to look extra badass?  Want to reach the next planet?  All valid goals.
-   I accepted that Google is my friend.  Let's face it, the game does an awful job of explaining its features.  A TON of the game's depth is completely hidden from the Player.  Once I started alt-tabbing to google every time I had a question, I started getting answers and the structure of the game started making sense.
-  I realized just how powerful mods are.  You can customize entire playstyles using them.  Leveling up a warframe or weapon isn't about leveling it up to 30.  Getting to 30 is just getting it to a playable state.  Truly leveling it up to epic proportions comes from smartly investing in your mods.
So ya, now I'm hardcore hooked.  60 hours in, and I know I'm just scratching the surface.  I'll be playing this one for a long time to come.  If you like looter-shooters where you never run out of things to grind for, this is the game.

I first came across Warframe in 2014 on PS4, back then it was decent and was a good way to sink a few hours but it didn't really do much that was special, it was just a genric shoot'em'up with some pretty cool melee, that has changed.
Now Warframe is this ever changing, ever improving funfest with some really pretty graphics, bonfide awesome art design and some brutal weapons, I've met some great people playing this who thrive off helping new players, I've had some admittedly rather evil laughs at some of the brutal ways I've killed some poor Grineer and some really awesome boss fights (of which there is a never ending stream) In this review I'm going to do subsections on four key parts, Gameplay, Graphics and Art, Value and Community.
GAMEPLAY 8/10:
Warframe has some of the most endlessly fun gameplay you could hope for, each warframe has unique powers and almost all of them are fascinating, take the warframe Ember for example, she has an easy to spam ability where she launches a giant ball of fire at enemies, upon impact it unleashes true hell upon nearby enemies and they dissovlve in a hilarious manner. On the topic of powers, each Warframe has their own ultimate power, these are hilarious and really make you feel like a god, for example the Warframe Oberon lifts up every enemy in range, be it 1 or 20 and slams them down in a wonderful, colourful apolocalypse of death and noise, Ember likewise sets her self on fire and runs around scorching literally everything, Nyx causes all enemies to attack one another and this really buys your team time when they're getting smashed around. The best part about these ultimate abilities that you most likely will use them very often, largly in part due to the fact that this game sends hilarious amounts of bad guys at you.
And then there's the weaponry, and oh my is there an unbeatable arsenel of sadism and hilarity at your disposal, want a machine gun that fires harpoons, get the Boltor, want a flamethrower with hilarious range and hilarious damage, grab the Ignis, want to duel wield pistol shotguns made of ebony and gold, Akbolto Prime is the key to your desires. The melee weapons are fantastic too, from electric whips that savge and brutalise the enemy to knucle dusters that pulverise any poor drone that stands in your way, to Katana that chunkify and gib your enemies, this game has them all.
This is all made better by the massive amount of upgrades and abilities that can be applied to these weapons and your warframe too, even your companion and pets can have these uprgrades. The game calls them mods, they can raise damage, raise accuracy, cause enemies to set on fire, by merging elemental mods you get new damage types, they can increase critical chance and increase critical damage, they can make enemies stay proc'd for longer, they can make you swing faster, run faster, jump higher, live longer, the list really does go on. The game keeps you coming back for more, despite it getting repetetive. In fact, it being repetetive has rarely bothered me.
GRPAHICS AND ART 9/10:
If gameplay was the main course then this is the Apple Pie with a cherry on top, I adore the art design, the weapons look mean, your chracter looks like some crazy space ninja that would snap your neck for looking the wrong way at them, the abilities are really pretty and the levles, while unfortunatly lacking in variety in the later game, are awesome, I mean hell, there are missions set in Sealabs inside Uranus (no pun intended) The enemies look cool to, with the Grineer looking evil and angry, the Corpus looking sleek and corperate, devoid of feelings and built for a purpose and the grizzly and ugly Infested, who have more than a nod to Halo, looking like something out of a horror film.
Yet again, the game offers more ways to personalize, colours and body modifications come out the proverbial ♥♥♥♥♥♥ here and if you've found some decent stuff and sold it to other players for Platinum, you can add them to your characters,  nobody has a similar looking warframe and some of the combinations of colour, regalia and syndana (like a cloak) that people come up with look seriously awesome, hell the clan I am in has a page just for people's creations.
Graphically the game is pretty too, some of the visuals could be considered very good, others are just simply nice but never will you come across somewhere ugly or poorly textures, the whole game is graphically very good and is been constanly updated graphically in a manner not to far from EVE Online, the game really shines here and has some of the best visuals I've seen in a game an I await the next graphical update with bated breath.
VALUE 8/10
While this game has the option to buy platinum (in game paid for currency)  uless your going to really splash some cahs there is bever any need to do so, if you don't mind grinding like me, you never need to spend money at all because every part, every resource, every item you want can either be perchased with credits or you can find them with ease. Even things such as Nurodes or Gallium (rare resources) can be found after 2 or so hours of searching. The devs also hold daily events that give the rare resources and parts, they also give rare mods too and character customization options. The devs really don't force you into spending anything at all, you could play Warframe, have a badman character, sick weapons and a decked out ship and you could never have spent a penny.
If unlike me though you are adverse to grinding, this game becomes very exepenisive as Platinum is not cheap and nor are the things to spend it on, a warframe (character) is about £12 and then you need to be constantly upgrading it with Formas and an Orokin Catalyst, so it ends up being around £25-35 for a decent non Prime (legendary) warframe, if you can't grind, you have to really consider if this game is a good investment, I'd say it is on the basis of it being like a triple A game anyway and probably being worth £50 anyway, but you may disagree.
Community 7/10:
I myself, have met some wonderful, helpful, funny and kindhearted people thay have made my gaming life really good on this game, they act with extreme selflessness and have a wicked sense of humour, the clan system really encorages people to get on and work together for a common goal through trying to fund special research projects that only clans can access, this is something the developers deserve an unreserved round of applause for.
However this is still an F2P MMO, and sadly, some will scam and troll and flame and generally make others miserable which I see all to often in local and global chat, it's no LOL but it isn't Skyforge either.
OVERALL 9/10: With all the afformentioned points and a massive update heading for it promising open world and other goodies, now would be a really good time to download and get a head start on others, a truely great game that you can sink hours into irresponsibly :)
If you download the game and need any help, send me a steam request and I'll give you a hand, thanks for reading, enjoy.

Warframe will have you believe that is a space ninja simulator but it is so much more. I mean, if you want to play a space ninja, you can use the warframe Ash, grab a Nikana (this games katana) and some kunai and just sneak your way though. However, if you want to just run around killing with little worry about stealth, there are plenty of frames like Rhino who focus on taking damage and just keep killing. The idea is you are a warframe, a warrior from long ago. The one who saves you is the Lotus, a woman who helps the warframes with info on when alarms have been set off and helping coordinate various things. You also have your ships Cephalon, this worlds version of AIs, who is loyal to you, his operator, but is a bit broken. Saying things like, "Please return... covered in blood... safe and sound." Frames can be seen as your class, but you're not limited to only one. If you can own all and switch between missions to suit want you need. After you pick your starter frame (Protip: Pick Excalibur. He is the best starter frame and even is damn good in endgame stuff.) and get some starter weapons in the tutorial, you now have some simple quests to introduce you to your villains and the star chart.
First, your enemies. The first enemy you come across is the Grineer. A race of cloned people who have been cloned so many times, they are starting to degrade. They are loyal to the Twin Queens, with a few exceptions, and are ruthless. The Grineer tend to have big weapons and lots of armour. The next villains are the Corpus. The Corpus are business men who sell weapons and robots. They tend to fill their ranks with robots and soldiers with energy shields. They also have a unit called the nullifier. These guys make it so you can use your frames abilities while within its bubble. Also if you had any kind of buff before passing into the bubble, it goes away. Thankfully, you can just shoot the bubble till it pops and you can kill them or shoot the little drone on top of it to instant pop it. The last main enemy is the Infected. You have to go a few planets in before you meet them, but they are a living virus that corrupts things and turns them into mutant abominations. If you've played Starcraft, think Terrans that have been corrupted by the Zerg.  These guys don't have any kind of fancy armour or shields, but they have numbers. Oh boy, do they have numbers. There is also an group of enemies called Sentients which you only learn about after a very important quest later on, and another group called the Corrupted but they are just more powerful versions of grinner and corpus that have been taken over by a tower. Trust me, it makes sense when you get there.
Now the part you have been waiting for. Since you are a ninja, you can wall run, you can slide around, you can do a move called a bullet jump. You move around like a bad♥♥♥♥♥ninja. Then you have the frames. There is a frame for every occasion. There are tanky frames like the mummy Inaros or Rhino. There are "caster" frames like Hydrioid, there are healers like Trinity, and many more. Then you have the weapons. This game has the normal guns and weapons. Assault rifle? The Braton. Burst rifle? Burston. Sword? We have everything from the short sword, the Skana, all the way to the buster sword style one, the Galatine. Then you have the slightly off weapons. The flamethrower called the Ignis, the auto shotgun called the Boar, and many more. The you get the weird stuff. A boomerang that disarms enemies, a saw blade launcher,  a living weapon that fires electric beams, a literal ship cannon that can fire cannon balls or a shotgun style barrage. There are 99 primary weapons, 83 secondary weapons, and 121 melee weapons. And that's not even counting Archwing weapons, where you go into space combat with only a set of rocket powered "wings" and weapons larger then you. Also they add a new weapon every week or so.

So, mechanics time. The big way to advance in this game is mastery level. You gain XP in this by leveling frames and weapons. Higher mastery levels let you use more advance weapons. There are also Prime weapons that are better versions of regular weapons. You get prime parts from opening relics which the game explains when you start getting them. And with prime parts, we should ask the ever important question with F2P games. Is it pay to win? No. But it is pay to quicken and look good. Every frame and weapon can be bought for real money currency called "Platinum". However, every frame and weapons can also be gotten with in-game currency. However, for frames this usually means farming a certain boss till you get the 3 components need to build that frame. And for weapons, you will need resources you get by doing missions. Also, platinum can buy you various nick nacks for your ship, new color options to color your frame and weapons, weapons and warframe skins and helmets. All these items don't help you but are just there you make you look that much cooler. Now there one thing you do need platinum for. That is warframe and weapons slots. You only start with 9 weapons slots and 2 warframe slots. This is nowhere near enough. It might last you though the first 30 or so hours but eventually , you will want more and thankfully, there is a way to get them without paying money. Remember me talking about Prime parts? They are tradable and the only currency used in trading with other players is platinum. Farm some prime parts up and sell them to other players. Boom. You now have plat to buy those precious slots.
Overall would I suggest warframe. Hell yes. My playtime should tell you how much I love this game. It allows you to kill countless enemies any way to want. This is perfect "I'm angry and just want to kill LOTS of thing!" Try it out. It's a grand old time.

Warframe is game I have recently clocked my 600th hour in, and I can now safely say it's been worth all the time spent.
Cons:
-The game is a grindy game. Although there is a huge amount of content you will find yourself playing some missions over repeatedly for resources or blueprints. But it is personally not an obstacle, if you just accept it's the way it is, you won't find it too bad.
- Although a big update is coming (Plains of Eidolon) that promises new end game content, the game doesn't offer the most sensational experience when you have your 'ultimate loadout' completed.
Pros:
-The game is filled to the brim with content, there is simply so much to do, you won't be bored for the first 200 hours for sure. The best thing is that you unlock more content as you progress, especially story-based cinematic quests are really interesting, which you unlock much later in the game.
- Customization is great, you can make your own warframe just like you want it, using colours and armor pieces to customize the looks, and so called mods to tweak the abilities of your warframe. This makes the game a very personalized experience.
- The community is great, if you ever need help with anything, just ask. Although I'm not sure how, the game has so many people willing to help out, you never have to do something alone really.
- More content coming, there is still so much coming. Recently the devs have announced a new open world and another cinematic quest. It's nothing new that Digital Extremes will keep adding things to do to this game.

This game really is addicting, because of how much you can get. That alone makes me love this game, and give me a sense of completion every time I play it.
Now I'm a man who loves to hoard things. I want to keep my MK-1 Bo (starter weapon) even though it's a really weak weapon, yet I'll run out of space for other weapons if I don't sell it (you can only hold a limited amount of weapons).
So now I come across the dillema of having to either buy slots or sell my weapons.
Well, being the hoarder I am, I suddenly start thinking "How many slots do I need to hold every possible weapon & warframe in the game (excluding Archwings), and how much will it all cost me?"
So I did the math (as of August 13, 2017):
49 warframes - 2 free slots = 47. (1 slot costs 20 platinum).
300 weapons - 6 free slots = 294. (2 slots costs 12 platinum.)
24 sentinel and sentinel weapons - 8 free slots = 16. (2 sentinel slots costs 12 platinum.)
47 warframe slot purchases x 20 = 940 plat
(294/2) = 147 weapon slot purchases x 12 = 1764 plat
(16/2) = 8 sentinel slot purchases x 12 = 96 plat
all equal to 2,800 plat
The highest amount of platinum you can buy with real money is 4,300 plat
That leaves you with 1,500 remaining plat.
DE, take my money.
10/10 would waste my time doing math and hoarding.

The main downside is that it runs horribly on PC. The game engine is locked to 30fps apparently and there are often fps drops whenever there is anything fast happening on screen. When compared to other open world games with fantastic graphics like Mafia 2 and Skyrim this game runs like a one-legged asthmatic pensioner. Seems Rockstar don't make any effort to optimise their games for the PC master race anymore.
Overall I can recommend it as the techincal issues are not game breaking because 95% of the time it is exploration/puzzle/adventure type gameplay and not action/shooter type gameplay where the crappy framerate would soon give you a headache.

This game is a very casual game, that doesn't require much 'think work' At first the whole clicking part is boring at times, because you aren't making that much of a progress. Later on, after a few ascensions, you start to discover patterns in terms of skilling and spending money and rubies. Then the game starts to get more interesting.
Evertyhing does take a lot of time though. it takes ages to aquire frostleaf and even longer to aquire Dread Knight. After that you have to aquire Atlas, but that will take a lot of ascensions, a lot of skilled ancients and also a lot of mercenaries. When coming to a point where you finally can aquire Dread Knight, it takes to long to be able to buy atlas. This could be a point where most people stop playing this game.
PROS
- Addictive gameplay (after a few ascensions)
- Cool but simple graphics
- Casual gameplay which makes and keeps you calm
- Steam achievements
- nice build in RPG like elements (skilling, semi-questing,upgrades)
CONS:
- You NEED to spend money on rubies to get steam trading cards. bad move playsaurus!
- At some point game gets to repetetive, because the gap of progress is to large. (dreadknight to atlas)
- Takes much of your time. Will speed up over time, untill you need Atlas.
- Upgrades via rubies are to expensive. At some point you dont get that much rubies anymore.
Overall this could be a fun game, with a 'frustrating taste' to it unfortunately. If playsaurus would update this game to make progression a bit easier and faster it would be more fun. Steam trading cards should be free imho. The gap from Dread knight to Atlas should be made a lot smaller in order to keeping people interested to the game.

I would recommend this game but I also would not recommend this game for a few reasons.
I class myself as an avid chivalry player that plays this game on and off when I have free time from career etc. (isnt alot lately) and I throughaly enjoy this game 90% of the time, it has good graphics, great gory gameplay with satisfying kills and wins, gorgeous maps and depth and detail. Now to the con, thats it just one negative point, but for me this can utterly frustrate me to the point of totally erasing this game from my library: ANIMATIONS. Not just the animations, but the way that some players (moslty level 40+) glitch and distort the way that thier character moves, swings their weapon and crouches. These particular players that have perfected this art of manipulating the animation glitches are almost unstoppable to a certain degree. You find yourself standing there bewildered by the sight that you can see infront of you, whilst hastely trying to block and evade this onslaught of animation abuse. These players characters look like they are on crack, constanly jolting and twitching as they swing and move, its utterly ridiculous and ruins the game for any new player in my opinion (there is no training in the game that would even start to teach you how to defeat this sort of player).
Finally, the most annoying part about this abuse is that it is actually seen as skill! a pro style of play if you were which is utterly ridiculous, it makes me cringe every time I see a player on the battlefiled with this "play style". I will instanly quit and find another server. Overall I recommend this game to any melee battle craving player that will enjoy teamwork and gore, but watch out for these glitch abusers, you wont stand a chance.

After playing this game for over 1000 hours I've decided to make a proper review of it. I should probably start off by immediatelly saying that I do recommend this game, but that it is not for everyone.
Crusader Kings II is a grand strategy game, and it appears to be more difficult than it really is. Although it is one of the more difficult Paradox games because of the extreme penalites on excessive expanding, vassal limits and etc. This is a "sink or swim" type of game. You'll either learn to swim (to play the game) or drown (quit playing it).
For a newcomer to grand strategy, this game may seem really difficult. But if you give it enough time, you will learn just about everything you need to know. It'll also become easy at some point.
Some pros and cons below..
Pros:
- Offers 400+ years of a timeline.
- Allows you to play practically everything above Baron title.
- Allows you to play Pagans, Muslims and Christians aswell as other religions.
- Pretty decent soundtrack.
- Thousands of hours (literally) of replayability, the only limit is your imagination.
- Still being updated.
- Has lots of mods available.
Cons:
- Not for the impatient folks.
- Expensive/Too many DLC's.
- 7th AD start is pretty historically inaccurate.
- Vanilla map is kinda disappointing.
- Biased devs.
So.. I love this game, obviously and I do recommend it but it's not perfect. There are issues, and one of the most common issue and most talked about is the amount of DLC's/expansions. I've bought them all, and all the DLC's are quite good and in my opinion
for the "full CK2 experience".
However, the game undeniable has far too much DLC's. The devs won't stop pumping out DLC's, and every new DLC that comes out keeps adding unneeded/unnecessary/unpolished content upon content. The last few expansions and DLC's are mediocre.
Luckly there is a big modding scene for CK2, so you can do as you please with the game.

What Europa Universalis does for its simulation of ruling a country, Crusader Kings does for a ruling a family/dynasty. It showcases the limitations of power with which a medieval ruler had to contend. You control land, but most of it is in the hands of your underlings. Amies are not unified formations but bands held together by men loyal or maybe not so loyal to you. Be careful of overmighty vassals or be one yourself. Scheme, marry, or battle your way to prominence. Join in a holy war or start a war to lower taxes. Turn a count to a duke, king, or even emperor as you see history bend and change in a heady frenzy. Participate as the Reconquista fails, the Battle of Manzikert is erased, Harold loses at Stamford Bridge or wins at Hastings, or any number of variations of history that make the game a constantly refreshing experience. There is a steep learning curve, but if you overcome it, the gameplay is an excellent reward.

If you've played a game by Rockstar before, then you probably have a good idea of what to expect from L.A. Noire. It's a lot like GTA or Red Dead Redemption — third-person gunfights, car chases and hot pursuits on foot, well-developed characters, and a compelling storyline. It's a formula that may seem almost like a crutch with how often Rockstar employs it in their titles, but it's hard to complain when it's done well.
If you're the type of person to play GTA for the plot, then L.A. Noire will keep your attention with relative ease. It does away with a lot of the nuisances that drag GTA down (there weren't even mobile phones for your cousin to call you on back in the 40's), but it also makes for — perhaps — a less substantial game, as there's not a whole lot to do besides follow the main storyline.
You play as Cole Phelps, climbing the ranks of the L.A. Police Department, slowly uncovering a massive conspiracy that reaches all the way up to the highest officials in Los Angeles. By the end of the game, you'll have managed to collect evidence from nearly every other previous case, all pointing towards systematic corruption and foul-play.
Knowing that he can bring the system crashing down is the ultimate goal that keeps Cole searching for the truth, but L.A. Noire manages to undo all player expectations with the game's finale. With an ending that nobody could possibly expect, L.A. Noire proves to be both the most shocking and most frustrating game I've played in a long time.
As confused and angry as the ending will leave you feeling, I still recommend playing the game from beginning to almost-end and then maybe just making up the last mission in your head. L.A. Noire definitely wins the prize for having the biggest f•••-you ending that a game could possibly conceive, but it's still worth the time to try it out.

L.A. Noire is a game that isn't for everyone.  If played back to back, it can get boring and repetative quick.  Some of the voice acting sounds like it was recording in a tin can.  The game is locked to 30 fps.
And yet, I found myself unable to step away for too long.  The game has a predictable structure through out: go investigate a crime scene, get a lead, pan it out, solve the case, move onto the next one.  But by the time you move onto the Homicide Desk, a larger plot starts to click into place.  This is mostly what motivated me to keep going.  Although the actual investigation is repetative, the cases themselves are varried and well written.  Only a few cases (mostly DLC) seem thin on content and it was during these cases that I would often get confused on which suspect was which (it seemed to be because a lot of explanitory dialogue was missing).  But overall, the game's voice acting and writing really help sell the world and the story.  All of the main character's partners are written great, and each one feels like a totally seperate character (which is how it should be).
The gameplay is more of a mixed bag.  The "investigate the crime scene for clues" moments are really cool at the start but start to get repetative by the end of the first Desk (there are four in the game).  Driving around from location to location is mostly redundant and really serves to just pad the game out.  The only thing that occurs during driving is getting calls from dispatch to deal with random street crimes, but most of them boil down to "show up, see the bad guy, shoot him" which is really dissapointing.  Luckily the game allows you to set a location and let your partner drive so you can just continue on with the investigation.  The actual suspect interegations are really the meat of the game and help you find clues and use the awesome facial capture to determine if someone is being truthful with you.  Something to note, however: many people will probably get confused because the three options (truth, doubt, lie) can lead to the main character screaming at a suspect.  This was due to a last minute change; the original options where coax, force, and lie.  All the lines where recorded back when this was the case, so it explains why choosing doubt can sometimes lead to your character raising his voice at a suspect.
Overall, I think this game can really be enjoyed by someone who likes adventure games and doesn't mind taking a few breaks between cases.  I think the game really starts to break down if you just play the entire game back to back; by taking time away before coming back the repetative nature of the game mechanics become less annoying.  Again, the story is the real treat (although in my opinion the very end felt rushed and left me dissapointed) and seems to be the real reason to play it through to the end.  Not the greatest game, but definitely a gem in the rough.

Now I haven't put much time into this game on Steam, because I mostly purchased it for the DLCs. But I have played this game thouroughly on Xbox. I have beaten the game 4 times, with 5 stars on every mission and have every acheivment. This game, in my opinion, is one of the best games of all time. Sure, this game definatly has it's flaws, but the story, characters, and world make up for it plenty.
Pros:
Team Bondi does a great job of creating atmosphere in this game. The storyline is somewhat complicated, but simple enough to follow. This game is often misconcieved as being developed by Rockstar, not published, so what a lot of people expect is action-packed gameplay with an outragous and funny story. This is NOT GTA, it has a very slow and methodical pace, which I personally am a fan of. The cases and investigation are extremely entertaining and will keep you guessing until the end. Granted, this is not a game that I could binge play. The story also takes some unexpected twists and turns. Ultimatly, this is a story-centered game.
Cons:
The gameplay outside of investigations is a bit bland, with nothing to really do in the world. Sure there are patrol side quests (and over 100 cars to collect which is pretty much impossible), but no other side quests or activities. It would have been cool to have something like a bowling or racing activity, or just something to make you more immersed in this world. The fighting mechanic is also a bit shallow, but then again it is not a game that revolves around melee or gun combat. The chase scenes are a bit pointless at times and become sort of tireing. Also, the "Truth, doubt, or lie" system as I like to call it can be painfully easy - With the characters you are interrogating making the most rediculous and uncomfortable-looking faces. Some may find the ending to be disappointing or unrewarding.
WARNING: As with all Rockstar games, this is a pretty bad PC port, so beware of bugs and glitches.
In the end, I may be biased because I am fasinated with the topics in this game. But it is something that left a lasting impact on me. A fan of old point-and-click mystery games or crime dramas would love this game. If you have the money to buy it, you should, because it is simply an experience that no gamer should miss out on.

I've only played Chivalry a handful of hours, despite having bought it last year, and in that short time, I've had a ton of fun.
Chivarly is a very unique experience among first-person multiplayer games; Chivalry has great melee combat (it's probably not "technical" or "realistic" enough to satisfy some folks, but I'd argue the majority of people who like games and swords will love it) and there is something VERY satisfying about winning a fight in this game, whether it was one-on-one or one shield+sword knight against three archers who didn't expect a 300LB steel bumrush.
Combat in Chivalry is very measured; you have to be superbly careful when you make the decision to swing on someone, and since the game gives a pretty solid block mechanic, the "alternate" swings (usually those that come from the opposite direction you'd normally swing from, so you can get past a guard) and additional attacks (kicks, stabs, two-part swings) make for pretty fun combat situations.
Ranged combat is probably the game's weakest core point; I'm aware that some folks are maddened more by the bugs and such, but so far my experience has largely been what I'd expect, with few bugs or maddening hitbox issues. Ranged combat on the other hand, is just odd - throwing weapons are a novelty I think, so their performance is acceptably sketchy; however, I found fighting with the crossbow to be a bit odd, and difficult to grasp (something about the effective range and the damage is just off - it seems to fall quite fast and even a point-blank shot doesn't quite kill as often as I'd expected) but the longbow/other curved bows are much easier to grasp.
On a parting note, I'd like to take a second to praise the modes the game offers.  There's a scenario in which one team defends a town, a keep gate, and finally the King inside of the keep (with a player on the team serving as the combat-ready King) - this mode is unbelievably fun; constant cries of "HE'S THE LAST OF HIS BLOOD LINE" and "PROTECT THE KING!" get your enthusiasm maxed out, and the teamwork that comes from these tasks is incredible - you'll have tower-shielded knights blocking the flanks of guys shooting balistae at oncoming enemies as they try to lead a ram to the castle gate; men-at-arms jumping down and running straight at the enemy, only to turn heel and run back toward the keep so that the men above can dump burning oil on the pursuers.  So many memorable moments happen in the combat in this game, I can't do anything BUT recommend it, if you've ever loved the idea of swordly combat.
I'm sure the game will show me more of its flaws as I actually get time to play it, but for now, my limited exposure shows me it's full of promise of good times to be had.

Edit: I've put v1.0 through its paces, and it's solid. Every single issue mentioned below is solved. Miracle patch lives up to the name. This game gets a wholehearted recommendation.
--- original review follows ---
The good: See the other reviews. I concur with them that this is an excellent title in the making. I am recommending this game, but with some caveats for all you 4X fans who are thinking about picking this game up on release day, so read on before spending your money.
The problematic: There are still some game-killing bugs that occur when you push the engine. Try playing for an exclusive Supremacy Victory on any of the largest map sizes with the game speed on 'endless' and before you finish conquering half of the galaxy you'll be unhappily familiar with all of these issues. I did manage to make it as far as turn 687 on my latest attempt which is a minor miracle.
Amplitude has an excellent track record of solid patching and supporting games for years after they launch, so I am confident these issues will be resolved, if not with the promised 'miracle patch' at release, within a matter of months afterwards. That's the only reason I'm still recommending this game in its current state. If you want to enjoy this game right now, stick to fast paced games in small galaxies against a limited number of factions. That'll give you the best chance to avoid the errors.
Now, let's talk issues...
1. The engine has an unfortunate tendency to lose track of ships internally. If this happens, somewhere on the map, after a battle, will sit a single hero ship that is frozen in place with no stats (all are set to zero). The trigger for this seems to be when a fleet attempts to retreat, but has no place to go, and is therefore eliminated. The hero ship for that fleet will sometimes reappear the next turn and then freeze the turn after that in this broken state. The next time the game engine attempts to interact with this ship, it will hang. This can result in saves made with such a ship present that will get stuck on infinite loading. If a battle is attempted against this ship, it will never complete and hang indefinitely. Ending your turn may result in getting stuck in a 'pending' state indefinitely. I've only had this happen to AI controlled ships, never player controlled. (edit: fixed in release, no more hangs)
2. The build queues can't handle a serious load. By the time you have 40+ systems under your control and start to terraform planets, the queues on some systems will bug out, leaving that solar system in an unusable state. IF this happens, you can work around it by 'evacuating' the bugged system, and then recolonizing it again (remember to send your populations to other planets first). The trigger for this bug seems to be a large number of items in the queues of multiple star systems, and/or a large number of bought out items in a single system queue. In particular, buying out terraforming and colonization events seem to be the worst triggers, I've never seen this bug happen on any other items, even if buying out all non-planetary constructions on an already-bugged queue. It's directly related to planetary build items somehow. Best to let colonization, terraforming, and planet specialization items build without buying them out, or stick to buying out just one or two items on a single system at a time. That seems to help work around the error, though it isn't a foolproof trick. (Edit: fixed in release, abused queues relentlessly without trouble)
3. Ungodly long wait times for a turn to complete in busy games. I'm not sure this is a 'bug' or just a lack of optimization, but the larger the map, the more ships, the more empires fighting, the longer turns take to complete, sometimes in excess of five minutes. Something really needs to be done to cut this time down. (edit: unbelievably fixed, turns take like five seconds now no matter the size)
4. Whatever algorithm draws the empire borders based on influence is still a bit screwy. Borders will occasionally fragment in very strange ways that make no sense, particularly on long games over large influence areas. These borders will even redraw themselves differently on reloading the same save games. This is more of an annoyance than a serious gameplay issue. (edit: not sure if fixed but hasn't made a reappearance yet)
5. There's work to be done balancing the economics. All the right bells and whistles are there, but when you have a single star system producing in excess of 30K of a resource (when you are only mining tens of units and can only store 999 of them) something about the trade routes and trading companies production bonuses is a bit broken. It's trivial to end up being able to sell multiple stacks of 999 resources *per turn* on the market and rake in millions of dust *per turn* in addition to your normal income. (edit: this has been fixed completely in release version)
6. Some of the AIs are just plain idiots. Cravers, Horatio, and Sophons always seem to peak at a low/mid tier tech level (if they are lucky) and then get steamrolled effortlessly by anyone. Meanwhile the Lumeris and Riftborn tend to steamroll everything in their path and provide a good challenge to the player. The AI for certain factions definitely need some polish. (edit: release version is much improved, AI is kicking my♥♥♥♥♥again)
Those are the only issues that bother me. Sure, there are other things we'd all like to see (a lot more quests, more planet variety, more espionage-related activities, etc) but all of those issues will be addressed by modders eventually if Amplitude doesn't do it themselves. I'm not worried so much about content as about the current health of the engine. If these issues are present on launch day the company could get a bit of a black eye, so I'm hoping that miracle patch lives up to its name.
If working around these issues bothers you, then you might want to wait until after Amplitude patches them to buy this game. (Edit: Or perhaps just trust that they deliver on their promises unlike most studios today. Excellent job, guys.)
One good mark I will add that not enough people talk about: modding capability. This game is pure XML, which makes it more easily and thoroughly moddable than Skyrim or XCOM. The mods for the original Endless Space were pretty good, the mods for this are likely to be more epic than Requiem or Long War. That's a few years down the road, however. I just think it's worth pointing out the possibilities. They've given people a very large, full featured engine to build around and that's laudable.

This game is an endless descent into madness that will keep you coming back.
It is on the most popular f2p games for a good reason, and I recommend trying it even if you don't intend on playing it actively.
The Good:
The art in this game is adorable, and stacked onto the theme very well. If you enjoy reading little flair text and tidbits you will be fast to recognize the quality(or hilariously unquality) humor put into the game. Clicking a monster repetitively and watching it bounce in its pathetic hit animation is good for a quick laugh as you're starting up as well.
The numbers just keep getting higher if you're into that sort of thing, and compressed into either scientific notation, or abbreviated units.
The game is fairly friendly to the casual player beyond the first few levels which require manual clicking. Upon closing the game and reopening it later, you discover you continued to make progress even while the game was closed.  Later in the game you are given fully viable options for playing the game with little to no interaction. My girlfriend manages to enjoy this, while playing in the least efficient manner possible, and still continue on.
On the flip side, there's a lot of mathematic strategy if you intend on playing efficiently, and options for the active clicking player.
You are not forced into paying real money for currency, and are fully capable of obtaining it through regular gameplay.
The community is fairly positive, and you can find lots of guides on reddit if you ever become interested in efficient gameplay.
You can import your save between Steam and browser should that need ever arise.
The game really speeds up after you reach various milestones.
Lastly, there are rather regular updates to the game to add new things and make it "fresh".
Also the game is endless.
The Ugly:
The game is endless. If you're not into that, you might want to find a different goal(e.g. get all the achievements)
Just like any other clicker, there is little that you can actually DO to feel like you're doing anything new.
Until you hit level 100, you will have to pay attention to the game at least to progress floors. Your first run up to 100 will also take quite a while.
The game runs off of a "rebirth" or "NG+" style mechanic that some people may be turned off by(in retrospect, each rerun goes by much more easily and smoothly).
Upon clearing 1000 floors for the first time, you most likely will not see any new backgrounds or monsters(unless you haven't encountered Kappa somehow).
Unless you read a guide, or have a friend, you will most likely not realize that you SHOULD NOT ASCEND as soon as you have the option unlocked. You will go through a lot of unnecessary grinding if you do this.
Finally, your early levels and first couple of runs will be the slowest.
The Neutral:
There is ALOT of things to unlock that require MANY hours to achieve. To some this may be a bonus, to others this may be a detriment.
Conclusion:
If you're interested in something to burn time and give you that much needed shot of dopamine every now and then, definitely try this out.

It reminds me of Medieval: Total War, only focused on the politics, without the 3D combats. And... there is a Game of Thrones mod.

Before I talk about the game itself, lets address the issue of DLC, and pricing that everyone gives a bad note for.
Alright, if you are new to Paradox game, here is how Paradox conduct their business : They create a game, and work on it for about 5 years or so,  constantly producing small to large DLC. With those DLCs, comes free content as well.
The reason behind this is pretty simple, Paradox games dont need state of the art graphics, they are massive Role playing game, most often centered around warfare.  In their games, you mostly just look at a map of the world.
So there really isnt any reason to produce a new game every year like other company does. Im thinking of Call of Duty who comes out with 1 or 2 games per year at a 80$ price or so.
The game cost about 200$ if you want the main DLCs and whatnot.  Its also been live for 5 years, so  it average at 40$ per year for the game so far.  I can think of many games that are more expensive than that, where you need to pay each year you play the game an amount of 80 to 100$
So really, Paradox business model isnt shady at all, or greedy.  They improve upon the game they already built. Of course, if you come in, in 2017, and look at the price of 200$, you will think the game is super expensive. Thats because you got 5 years of work on it.  Just buy the original game at 50$, see if you like it, and gradually buy some DLC if you want.
Although, it has been 5 years the game is out, so I am thinking, maybe in the next few years we will see a
Crusader King III ?  So you might want to wait or try to find information on that.
If you complained that a 200$ game that will give you hundreds, if not thousands of hours of entertainement is too expensive, than you need to really think about what you are saying.
First off, this game will never go out of date, so even in 2030, you could be playing it and having fun.
Second,  you most probably spend more than 200$ on one night when you go out in bars, or restaurant, I know I do.
So for me its a no brainer,  But I wouldnt spend 200$ on any type of game, I actually only spend that amount on Paradox's game. Because they are that good. They are a good company, and they deserve the money.
