A good game whose flaws prevent it from being a great game.
LA Noire is a detective game based in the late 1940's Los Angeles area and built on the Grand Theft Auto engine.  It's open sprawling world looks good and is fairly accurate. The map feels more alive and organic than most other sandbox games, but because Los Angeles was designed by drunken maniacs driving around does not lend itself to easily learning the city layout, and using the mini map at times can be confusing because of some of the terrain features- like cliffs.
There are a large variety of cars in the game (95) but it doesn't really feel that way; I guess I was born in the wrong era to appreciate the subtle differences between some of those classic cars. The game designers spent time in Jay Leno's garage studying a lot of his '40s car collection but the attention to detail is lost on me because I can't easily tell the difference between most of them. Not really a flaw in the game, but until and unless you really know what you are looking at most of the cars will look the same. It also doesn't help that in typical GTA fashion that most of the cars you see at a given time are from a limited  to save on memory.
Speaking of the cars, they accelerate like the slow, ponderous heavy vehicles that they were. You can really feel the difference between the Nash and the small and light Ford H roadster. Thankfully they can turn pretty well at speed (or dodging cars down the street would be impossible) but they still managed to recreate the feel of non-power assisted four wheel drum breaks; These cars don't stop well and I end up smacking in to things a lot because these cars don't just fail to stop on a dime, they won't even slow down for anything less than a buck forty. Low speed turning radius and maneuverability are period accurately bad.
Car handling wouldn’t be problematic except that in missions the game will track the damage you cause while driving and it counts against you. If you are in a police issue car then you have a siren, and about 80% of the cars will get out of your way. The others… well, cars making left turns tend to ignore the siren entirely and some cars will pull over to their right- even if that’s where you are located. I’ve been hit many times by cars trying to pull over that weren’t looking where they were going. I guess this is probably very realistic. Still, because the damage counts against you it can be a little frustrating at times, especially because of how free roam mode works (See below).
The on-foot controls are typical GTA and work well for larger movements (run over to that area) but when trying to do perform delicate movements (needing to move around furniture when looking for clues or trying to move to a specific clue location) at times end up feeling like playing QWOP.
Speaking of clues, the game has musical and visual notifications that you have stumbled across something of interest- or not. I get why they don't want to just limit these to case-relevant items, but I wish there was more consistency in these. For example, in some cases there are notes on tables and refrigerators that are useful to the case and will chime appropriately when I am near them, while other times notes aren't case relevant but will still chime but when I look at them in detail I will be told they aren't relevant, and still other times where I can see them but they aren't important and can't interact with them at all. Since about 50 to 60% of all "clues" are relevant having the fake ones that you don't find out aren't important until you pick them up just serves to waste a little time. Either they need more of these fake clues and force the player to actually figure out what is important or not ahead of time by thinking through the case instead of just click on everything that chimes or get rid of the fake clues entirely.
And this is where we get to the core game mechanics, which is where the game struggles. You gather clues and interview people to solve various crimes. When asking questions of people you are interviewing you have the option to think that they are telling the truth, you can doubt them, or you can accuse them of lying based on how shifty looking and nervous they are acting. Lying requires evidence to back up the accusation, but the terms "lie" and "doubt" aren't always accurate and there are times they really seem misused and times where it seems that while the person is looking shifty when I ask them a question the response my character gives when I doubt makes it seem like we are having two different conversations. Some times the "evidence" used to back up the claim of a lie is oddly tenuous but that's what the game engine expects if you want to get the question "right"
Although you can back out of the accusation of a lie as long as you haven't tried presenting evidence, you can't back out of an interview if you decide you want to check something else before proceeding further. One case had me back at the police station interviewing two suspects in a homicide and I had to go back and forth between them. When I had finished up with the second guy and wanted to back to the first I exited the room but someone was in the way in the hall, and thanks to the aforementioned QWOP controls ended up bumping the interview room door again and walked right back in there and got stuck talking to the second suspect again with no way to exit out without talking to him about questions I wanted to hold off on until I had talked to the first guy again. I ended up having to restore from the last auto-save point- which was at the beginning of the first interview.
That wasn't the only time I ran in to that sort of a problem- it's exacerbated by the fact that some parts of same cases seem to require you to do things in a particular and arbitrary order to get all of the clues you need. If you talk to someone before visiting a particular location and finding a particular clue, you are going to be stuck since you can't double back and talk to them later.
At times I was reminded strongly of the old Sierra game logic where a puzzle's solution probably made sense to a game developer after being up for 20 hours straight and jacked up on their sixth or seventh can of Red Bull, but to the player sometimes those solutions or paths to reach a solution seem a little tenuous.
The overall story is very good, but one thing I found odd was how new story missions were launched. Most sandbox games- Grand Theft Auto, Red Dead Redemption, and Saints Row (for example) will put icons on the map that you go to when you want to launch the next mission. The rest of the time you are in free-roam mode and can do little side missions, find collectables, etc. In LA Noire, a new mission starts as soon as you finish the last one. You have to drop out of a mission to go to free-roam, and it's not very intuitive on how to do so. I think that hurts the overall game since it discourages wandering around the city in the first place.
The combat controls also needs work; unlike it’s GTA siblings, going in to fight mode is contextual and scripted so I can’t pull out a gun and start shooting or punching people randomly as I walk down the street. Shooting and punching requires holding down the right mouse button and then pressing the left to shoot / punch. This is very awkward and serves no real purpose.
You also start every gunfight with the same police handgun. Some fights will allow you to grab a better gun from a fallen foe, such as a shotgun, rifle, or tommy gun, but you can’t really hold on to those from mission to mission so the next time you get in a gun fight you are back down to a pistol.
So the game isn't bad, it's just not great.  It's certainly worth $5 to $10 if it's on sale and you like these kinds of games.

I've decided to change my review to thumbs down. Upon release the game is still riddled with bugs that ruin the game. For instance while playing a long game I found that after researching techs I would lose the abilities/benifits at some later date for unknown reasons. Specifically the ability to colonize extreme planet types - have the tech, colonized a few, then the ability is gone. The games says you need to research the tech, but the tech is shown as done. Ditto for the ability to buy out rival colonies with influence. It worked... until it didn't. Want to remove a negative anomaly? Nope, same thing. You've researched it, but it just won't register it. Removing the negative effect of a mixed anomaly? The option won't pop up on the system screen when you click it. It'll pop up a window "Select an option" but it won't have any selection to choose. Note that this is all in the same game session.
The game didn't crash for me, but a lot of important features are just too buggy. When the resource you need for high end weapons is only found on lava planets, and you lose the ability to colonize lava... that's frustrating. This isn't EA anymore, so I feel it warrants a negative review. As for reporting the bugs, I reported a few on their forum with no response so there just doesn't seem much point anymore.
It's too bad. I like the game and would have loved to play many more hours. Hopefully they fix it, but I fear these kind of buired coding bugs will be the least of thier concerns and be a long time coming, if at all.

Early Access Review
I do recommend the game, but it is still Alpha with all the associated bugs, etc that goes with that stage of development. I've encountered bugs that bring my game to a dead stop - not crashing, just an endless loop or a decision/report screen that cannot be completed or closed. It's frustrating yes, but only because the game is fun and I want to finish it.
The gameplay is 4X, and enjoyable. There are less buildings to construct than in MOO2, which simplifies management but lacks depth. That's an impression, not hard stats based off of doing a count of both games. Picking a specialization for each planet in the system is nice and adds a bit of flavour to an otherwise bland system. The rest of the buildings are built once per system and apply to all colonized planets in that system. The bonues may vary, but there is no real management of individual planets aside from the specialization and species management.
The minor factions adds a whole new layer to 4X, and while I've seen similar ideas elsewhere there is so much more depth in this game. Having other species living on your planets can have quite the impact on voting and the bonuses you recieve. A personal gripe for me is that playing as a race hostile to others it would be more in line to get penalties for co-habiting with others. The Riftborn for instance see life as a blight, so why would they be happy to be sharing their planets? This also extends to the planets themselves. Why would Riftborn be happy on fertile planets thriving with life and unhappy on desert, ash or even lava planets? The devs could have made them even more unique by reversing the normal planet happiness bonuses. This touches on terraforming.
Terraforming is linear but has different branches depending on the start planet and the planet you want to end up with. For instance you start with a Lava or Ash planet, terraform to Desert, from there you can go Savannah or Arid. Pick Arid and you can move on to Jungle, and from Jungle to Atoll. If you are industry focused there are a lot of bonues to industry on hot planets, and Jungle is still hot while Atoll is temperate. So even though you get an extra pop on the Atoll you lose out on industry to terraformt the final step. There is no "Gaia" or perfect planet. Start with a cold planet (better science) and you'll end up with something different. It's a cool system, but I wish you could also terraform backwards - ie go from Arid to desert. As of yet the game does not allow for that, and I've seen no inidcation that will be added. As mentioned, it would seem to be in line with the Riftborn story line to desire to go backwards - to a barren planet, be it barren or ash.
The combat is beautiful to watch -  but watch is all you do as a predetermined outcome is played out for visual effect. After over 2 decades nobody has made a decent 4x game with similar combat to MOO2 and that is dissapointing. You do get to implement tactics but I'm not sure that this is fully implemented. At least I hope it isn't. The visuals are stunning but to be honest I don't see the impact of the selected tactic in the visuals. When you picked a tactic in Endless Space 1 it was very clear to see the impact as the battle unfolded. So far with the different tactics I've picked the battles look the same. Still stunning, but not much variation. The impact of tactics does seem to apply to the outcome though, and that's the important part I suppose.
One thing that is annoying is how the fleet blockade system works. If you want to create a chokepoint with a fleet to prevent enemies from slipping past to your inner systems you better have several fleets present. A fleet can guard a system and force all ships passing through to stop for a turn, allowing you to engage them. Each fleet can only engage one target per turn though - and you don't get to pick the target of the attack. The AI tends to send mulitple fleets through, and if you have just the one fleet you stop a random one, and the rest carry on their merry way. Perhaps this is intentional, and I can see the logic behind it. It is an effective tactic. You have to pick to split your fleet into smaller fleets and hope they are enough for the battles they end up in, or build more ships. As I cross the 1000 hour threshold, I thought I'd write a quick review.
The gameplay and replay value is extremely high. The elements come together almost perfectly in multiplayer action. Accessible and rewarding for new  players while ever-challenging for experienced players.
Revenge can be had quickly. This fuels your addiction. The vibe of the game is humor rather than death and destruction. Even though it's nice and gory, with limbs and blood flying everywhere, it's not sickening violence. It's not obscene violence or dark and disturbing, but actually is just good fun.
The genius of this game is in the timing required to block your opponent, the attacks and strategy used in battle for your chosen character is only limited by your willingness to learn and perfect your timing and anticipation. It amazes me that they've pulled off a first person slasher game, where the weight of your sword is a huge factor in landing that killer blow.
I don't play first person shooter games anymore. I loved them previously, but they bore me now. Shooting people in the head is boring. First person slashers are a million times better. The projectile weapons are simply awesome in this game. The ballistas and catapults are so much fun, and hilarious to watch other players go flying. The level design is mostly superb.
1000 hours and I still can't get enough. I doubt even GTA5 will stop me from playing. I've purchased a lot of games in the last year, and none have manged to pull me away from Chivalry. Edit: I'm still playing this and I'm done with GTA5.

The game is set in post war California at the boom of the film industry and organised crime, following the detective Cole Phelps as he moves up in the ranks of the police department. The game has references to locations, films, cars and cases from the actual period but never really took full advantage of the period or the police perspective. The period however was well replicated for the game and the open world is pretty much flawless.
The game itself revolves around point and click investigations of crime scenes and interrogations using the truth/doubt/lie reaction system in combination with the suspect's/witness' reactions. The investigation then develops based on the amount of evidence found and correct interrogation options chosen. However choosing the wrong options or missing evidence will result in you missing out sections of the case as you are not prompted to visit key areas or talk to key people. This can be a problem as the doubt/lie options in interrogations seems to be inconsistent, and evidence needed for the lie option is quite often circumstantial.
The story focuses on the character of Cole Phelps who has returned from fighting in Japan to take up a position in the California Police Department. Phelps is a straight policeman with a cool head and quickly rises through the ranks as he continually produces results. The story is generally generic and dull as Cole Phelps is such a reserved character and outside of the cases there is minimal story. The cases however are, for the most part, interesting and varied.
Overall, I would definitely recommend picking up for the unique environment and period setting; which has been barely touched by other large gaming franchises. The was very good for the first play through and provided interesting cases to investigate, but the cases all have a similar structure and provided few possible outcomes. From my first play through I would have provided this game with a 8/10, but having such little replay ability and lack of tasks for the open world means that I would downgrade that to a 7/10 from my second play through.
Bored? Start this game up and you'll be entertained for a few hours.

Issues with saves being unusable is a no-go for me, EA or not, especially considering they say they are "close" to being done. Saving is too much of a core feature to have issues at this stage.
If the saves got broken due to differences in major version from the version that the save was created with and the version it was loaded with then it is understanable there could be issues. Even then it is not that hard, as a developer to take this into consideration, either by having logic to make transitions between versions of save files, or at least alert the user that the save they are loading is from a different version and it might not work. Regardless this doesn't, afaik, seem to be the issue at hand.
Here you have Saves that get broken when the version of the game is the same during creation and load which means there is something seriously wrong with their save system.
Apart from that if you check the forums here and search for "save" there is a plethore of issue threads regarding this. Also there are threads in the official forums with similar save game issues spanning as far back as 6 months what I could tell.
So they clearly know they have a problem with the saves yet seem unable to fix it correctly and it amazes me, as a developer for almost 10 years, that they havn't changed the loading procedure to at least catch the issue and prompt users to send the save file for investigation, or just send it in the background for that matter. Instead the loading just gets stuck with no feedback what so ever.
A broken Save feature is a core mechanic hence if it is broken it is almost as bad as not even being able to start the game, maybe even worse since you spend so much time and then it gets swept away.

Ever since my significant other introduced me to Warframe I've been addicted.  This game is unlike anything I've played before with beautifully rendered and detailed environments, tons of unique, playable frames and weapons, amazing customization in the way of armor, colors, skins, etc., incredible and fun frame abilities, a really nice crafting system, tons of different crafting materials, numerous quest types, and so much more . . . this game isn't likely to disappoint!
The game handles like a dream with deliciously satisfying fighting animations and controls, many different attack animations and techniques, and very quick-to-respond controls.  The frames themselves are based off of different gods/goddesses and mythical figures/creatures, and you are given the task of collecting as many of them as possible while also working towards collecting their much more powerful prime forms.  The game is still being updated, so new frames and prime frames are being released every so often.  With all of the new content and the great story and open/random quests there's always something to do!  (Not to mention you can keep yourself even busier with customizing and collecting different sentinels, space ships, and animal companions, all with their own customizable skins, colors, parts, etc.!)
Another thing I absolutely feel the need to note is that you can choose between single player and several multiplayer settings thus allowing you to play with members of your friend list, guild, or random strangers!  It keeps things quite refreshing to people looking to advance quickly with others while also valuing isolated play, and allows me to enjoy the game within my comfort zone, which I greatly appreciate considering I have issues with most multiplayer games.  What's also nice is that with the different level ranges of the quests and planet tiles you can either cruise through easy areas or challenge yourself with higher level battles.  This is great for levelling new frames and weapons, while also allowing you to push yourself and develop your game skills.
And, oh yes, the mods.  My GOD the mods. . .  Those are the real game changers here.  Make sure to experiment with different status effects and stat boosts to build the ultimate frames and weapons as they can literally be the difference between an assured victory and miserable defeat.
I LOVE playing this game, and I also love the fact that users can submit their own skins and creations and could very well see them implemented into the game!  I'm likely going to be playing this game for a long time yet, and look forward to attending TennoCons in the future!  Brilliant work to everyone involved!

Early Access Review
I do recommend the game, but it is still Alpha with all the associated bugs, etc that goes with that stage of development. I've encountered bugs that bring my game to a dead stop - not crashing, just an endless loop or a decision/report screen that cannot be completed or closed. It's frustrating yes, but only because the game is fun and I want to finish it.
The gameplay is 4X, and enjoyable. There are less buildings to construct than in MOO2, which simplifies management but lacks depth. That's an impression, not hard stats based off of doing a count of both games. Picking a specialization for each planet in the system is nice and adds a bit of flavour to an otherwise bland system. The rest of the buildings are built once per system and apply to all colonized planets in that system. The bonues may vary, but there is no real management of individual planets aside from the specialization and species management.
The minor factions adds a whole new layer to 4X, and while I've seen similar ideas elsewhere there is so much more depth in this game. Having other species living on your planets can have quite the impact on voting and the bonuses you recieve. A personal gripe for me is that playing as a race hostile to others it would be more in line to get penalties for co-habiting with others. The Riftborn for instance see life as a blight, so why would they be happy to be sharing their planets? This also extends to the planets themselves. Why would Riftborn be happy on fertile planets thriving with life and unhappy on desert, ash or even lava planets? The devs could have made them even more unique by reversing the normal planet happiness bonuses. This touches on terraforming.
Terraforming is linear but has different branches depending on the start planet and the planet you want to end up with. For instance you start with a Lava or Ash planet, terraform to Desert, from there you can go Savannah or Arid. Pick Arid and you can move on to Jungle, and from Jungle to Atoll. If you are industry focused there are a lot of bonues to industry on hot planets, and Jungle is still hot while Atoll is temperate. So even though you get an extra pop on the Atoll you lose out on industry to terraformt the final step. There is no "Gaia" or perfect planet. Start with a cold planet (better science) and you'll end up with something different. It's a cool system, but I wish you could also terraform backwards - ie go from Arid to desert. As of yet the game does not allow for that, and I've seen no inidcation that will be added. As mentioned, it would seem to be in line with the Riftborn story line to desire to go backwards - to a barren planet, be it barren or ash.
The combat is beautiful to watch -  but watch is all you do as a predetermined outcome is played out for visual effect. After over 2 decades nobody has made a decent 4x game with similar combat to MOO2 and that is dissapointing. You do get to implement tactics but I'm not sure that this is fully implemented. At least I hope it isn't. The visuals are stunning but to be honest I don't see the impact of the selected tactic in the visuals. When you picked a tactic in Endless Space 1 it was very clear to see the impact as the battle unfolded. So far with the different tactics I've picked the battles look the same. Still stunning, but not much variation. The impact of tactics does seem to apply to the outcome though, and that's the important part I suppose.
One thing that is annoying is how the fleet blockade system works. If you want to create a chokepoint with a fleet to prevent enemies from slipping past to your inner systems you better have several fleets present. A fleet can guard a system and force all ships passing through to stop for a turn, allowing you to engage them. Each fleet can only engage one target per turn though - and you don't get to pick the target of the attack. The AI tends to send mulitple fleets through, and if you have just the one fleet you stop a random one, and the rest carry on their merry way. Perhaps this is intentional, and I can see the logic behind it. It is an effective tactic. You have to pick to split your fleet into smaller fleets and hope they are enough for the battles they end up in, or build more ships. It's different from other games of the genre where one mega fleet can stomp and any and all comers. I said it was frustrating, but in a good way. Adapt and overcomee, etc.
On the dev team itself I don't have much of an opinion yet. I just bought the game, and have been going through their forums reading bug reports. Sometimes they respond it seems, but often not. Maybe at this late stage they are too busy to interact with the community or address bugs. Who knows, certainly not I. Perhaps if I go back, deeper into the threads they may have been more engaged earlier on. I'm not inclined to do so though. I just want a game that works and that is still up in the air.
So all in all, a good game with great potential. I picked it up before the price gets jacked up before release. If you're content to wait, do so. As it is now the chances of not being able to finish a game are still high. If you want to help the devs, by all means jump in. It is very playable, just not really "finishable".

I was a little iffy about purchasing a 4x space game. Personally, I preferred RTS space games more like Sins of a Solar Empire and Stellaris. My concern was that in RTS games, you have alot to do and can get lost in management and micro etc. Let me assure you, that you can get just as lost in a turn by turn 4x game. Its basically CIV but in space. JUST ONE MORE TURN!!
PROS:
Differences in races makes the game interesting. Graphics are great. Gameplay is fun. The galaxy exploration is different from RTS games. You can explore any system in a constellation. But if you travel outside the constellation to colonize you wont move as fast. Ship customization, economy, all of that stuff is engaging. And the concept of manpower (available population for your military) adds another dimension to plan for. You also get ground war. Which, if you're not careful, can cost you alot of time and resources.
CONS:
Not sure the game is 100% balanced. While each race has their own playstyle, some races are just easier to be dominant in. For instance, Lumeris dont have to colonize planets they just have to discover them and can use gold to purchase them. Makes expanding alot easier. Also, I think at the time I write this, the pirates seem to be bugged. They can just auto spawn in a system you control out of nowhere. May be fixed during launch though. The auto explore feature can be a bit finnicky which if you're not paying attention, might end up wasting movement points. The explorer AI basically needs alot of direction sometimes. Wish the fleet sizes could be bigger, but understandable due to the cinematic portrayal of battle.
MAYBE:
So I sort of compared it to CIV, but its not your typical hex game. Its sort of a hybrid CIV-space RTS. The units have movement points, but the hex's are sort of invisible and in the background. You can improve engines as well to boost movement capability both in and out of constellations. The tactics might also be a point of contention. I personally found it refreshing but some might not. You don't really get to micro anything in a fight like Total War. You basically choose a tactic, the enemy chooses one, then your ships cruise at a predetermined flight path and battle it out. Then you get a post-battle summary. Goes for ground war too. However, you do get to watch a pretty bad♥♥♥♥♥cinematic which represents the battle. This gets old after awhile (you can only watch your ships destroy pirates so much) but if theres a big fleet battle, its pretty sick. Can't really tell whats happening but ships fly at each other, fire and then blow up. Not awful. If you dont wanna watch it for whatever reason, can skip it.

After playing for a couple of days we started to be more and more competitive which wasn't necessarily a bad thing. After a few more days things slowly started to go south and what started out as a fun activity became the reason why I lost most of my friends. We didn't play to have fun anymore, the only reason we played was to win and to find out who was better at the game. Death threats, insults and tears replaced all the joy we first experienced playing together. Over the course of time more and more of my friends started to quit the game because they couldn't deal with the fear of being humiliated anymore. To this day I still don't know what happened to some of the people I used to talk to on a daily basis, they simply disappeared and no one ever saw them again. I personally feel responsible to inform the public about the risk of buying "Golf With Friends", because it ruined not only my life, but the life of the people I was closest to as well. I'm dealing with severe depression and anxiety attacks on a daily basis because of the insanely competitive environment that surrounded me. I still recieve death threats and letters from people I won against because they want to take revenge. If you decide to buy "Golf With Friends" speak to your parents if you're not at least 18 years old and make sure they are aware of the possible long term effects this game can have on you. If you are old enough please take the time and ask yourself if playing a game is worth risking your health.

I've decided to change my review to thumbs down. Upon release the game is still riddled with bugs that ruin the game. For instance while playing a long game I found that after researching techs I would lose the abilities/benifits at some later date for unknown reasons. Specifically the ability to colonize extreme planet types - have the tech, colonized a few, then the ability is gone. The games says you need to research the tech, but the tech is shown as done. Ditto for the ability to buy out rival colonies with influence. It worked... until it didn't. Want to remove a negative anomaly? Nope, same thing. You've researched it, but it just won't register it. Removing the negative effect of a mixed anomaly? The option won't pop up on the system screen when you click it. It'll pop up a window "Select an option" but it won't have any selection to choose. Note that this is all in the same game session.
The game didn't crash for me, but a lot of important features are just too buggy. When the resource you need for high end weapons is only found on lava planets, and you lose the ability to colonize lava... that's frustrating. This isn't EA anymore, so I feel it warrants a negative review. As for reporting the bugs, I reported a few on their forum with no response so there just doesn't seem much point anymore.
It's too bad. I like the game and would have loved to play many more hours. Hopefully they fix it, but I fear these kind of buired coding bugs will be the least of thier concerns and be a long time coming, if at all.

Early Access Review
I do recommend the game, but it is still Alpha with all the associated bugs, etc that goes with that stage of development. I've encountered bugs that bring my game to a dead stop - not crashing, just an endless loop or a decision/report screen that cannot be completed or closed. It's frustrating yes, but only because the game is fun and I want to finish it.
The gameplay is 4X, and enjoyable. There are less buildings to construct than in MOO2, which simplifies management but lacks depth. That's an impression, not hard stats based off of doing a count of both games. Picking a specialization for each planet in the system is nice and adds a bit of flavour to an otherwise bland system. The rest of the buildings are built once per system and apply to all colonized planets in that system. The bonues may vary, but there is no real management of individual planets aside from the specialization and species management.
The minor factions adds a whole new layer to 4X, and while I've seen similar ideas elsewhere there is so much more depth in this game. Having other species living on your planets can have quite the impact on voting and the bonuses you recieve. A personal gripe for me is that playing as a race hostile to others it would be more in line to get penalties for co-habiting with others. The Riftborn for instance see life as a blight, so why would they be happy to be sharing their planets? This also extends to the planets themselves. Why would Riftborn be happy on fertile planets thriving with life and unhappy on desert, ash or even lava planets? The devs could have made them even more unique by reversing the normal planet happiness bonuses. This touches on terraforming.
Terraforming is linear but has different branches depending on the start planet and the planet you want to end up with. For instance you start with a Lava or Ash planet, terraform to Desert, from there you can go Savannah or Arid. Pick Arid and you can move on to Jungle, and from Jungle to Atoll. If you are industry focused there are a lot of bonues to industry on hot planets, and Jungle is still hot while Atoll is temperate. So even though you get an extra pop on the Atoll you lose out on industry to terraformt the final step. There is no "Gaia" or perfect planet. Start with a cold planet (better science) and you'll end up with something different. It's a cool system, but I wish you could also terraform backwards - ie go from Arid to desert. As of yet the game does not allow for that, and I've seen no inidcation that will be added. As mentioned, it would seem to be in line with the Riftborn story line to desire to go backwards - to a barren planet, be it barren or ash.
The combat is beautiful to watch -  but watch is all you do as a predetermined outcome is played out for visual effect. After over 2 decades nobody has made a decent 4x game with similar combat to MOO2 and that is dissapointing. You do get to implement tactics but I'm not sure that this is fully implemented. At least I hope it isn't. The visuals are stunning but to be honest I don't see the impact of the selected tactic in the visuals. When you picked a tactic in Endless Space 1 it was very clear to see the impact as the battle unfolded. So far with the different tactics I've picked the battles look the same. Still stunning, but not much variation. The impact of tactics does seem to apply to the outcome though, and that's the important part I suppose.
One thing that is annoying is how the fleet blockade system works. If you want to create a chokepoint with a fleet to prevent enemies from slipping past to your inner systems you better have several fleets present. A fleet can guard a system and force all ships passing through to stop for a turn, allowing you to engage them. Each fleet can only engage one target per turn though - and you don't get to pick the target of the attack. The AI tends to send mulitple fleets through, and if you have just the one fleet you stop a random one, and the rest carry on their merry way. Perhaps this is intentional, and I can see the logic behind it. It is an effective tactic. You have to pick to split your fleet into smaller fleets and hope they are enough for the battles they end up in, or build more ships. It's different from other games of the genre where one mega fleet can stomp and any and all comers. I said it was frustrating, but in a good way. Adapt and overcomee, etc.
On the dev team itself I don't have much of an opinion yet. I just bought the game, and have been going through their forums reading bug reports. Sometimes they respond it seems, but often not. Maybe at this late stage they are too busy to interact with the community or address bugs. Who knows, certainly not I. Perhaps if I go back, deeper into the threads they may have been more engaged earlier on. I'm not inclined to do so though. I just want a game that works and that is still up in the air.
So all in all, a good game with great potential. I picked it up before the price gets jacked up before release. If you're content to wait, do so. As it is now the chances of not being able to finish a game are still high. If you want to help the devs, by all means jump in. It is very playable, just not really "finishable".

I was a little iffy about purchasing a 4x space game. Personally, I preferred RTS space games more like Sins of a Solar Empire and Stellaris. My concern was that in RTS games, you have alot to do and can get lost in management and micro etc. Let me assure you, that you can get just as lost in a turn by turn 4x game. Its basically CIV but in space. JUST ONE MORE TURN!!
PROS:
Differences in races makes the game interesting. Graphics are great. Gameplay is fun. The galaxy exploration is different from RTS games. You can explore any system in a constellation. But if you travel outside the constellation to colonize you wont move as fast. Ship customization, economy, all of that stuff is engaging. And the concept of manpower (available population for your military) adds another dimension to plan for. You also get ground war. Which, if you're not careful, can cost you alot of time and resources.
CONS:
Not sure the game is 100% balanced. While each race has their own playstyle, some races are just easier to be dominant in. For instance, Lumeris dont have to colonize planets they just have to discover them and can use gold to purchase them. Makes expanding alot easier. Also, I think at the time I write this, the pirates seem to be bugged. They can just auto spawn in a system you control out of nowhere. May be fixed during launch though. The auto explore feature can be a bit finnicky which if you're not paying attention, might end up wasting movement points. The explorer AI basically needs alot of direction sometimes. Wish the fleet sizes could be bigger, but understandable due to the cinematic portrayal of battle.
MAYBE:
So I sort of compared it to CIV, but its not your typical hex game. Its sort of a hybrid CIV-space RTS. The units have movement points, but the hex's are sort of invisible and in the background. You can improve engines as well to boost movement capability both in and out of constellations. The tactics might also be a point of contention. I personally found it refreshing but some might not. You don't really get to micro anything in a fight like Total War. You basically choose a tactic, the enemy chooses one, then your ships cruise at a predetermined flight path and battle it out. Then you get a post-battle summary. Goes for ground war too. However, you do get to watch a pretty bad♥♥♥♥♥cinematic which represents the battle. This gets old after awhile (you can only watch your ships destroy pirates so much) but if theres a big fleet battle, its pretty sick. Can't really tell whats happening but ships fly at each other, fire and then blow up. Not awful. If you dont wanna watch it for whatever reason, can skip it.

This is one of the most fun and immersive grand strategy games I've ever played.  This game takes the complexity and diplomatic scale of games like the Europa Universalis and makes the game more character driven.  In the Medieval era, there was no such thing as national diplomacy; it was all personal.  This game lets you play as any historical figure from a count to an emperor in Medieval Europe, Middle East, or even West Africa and manage your court, your demesne, your vassals, and so much more.  If you liked Hearts of Iron or Europa Universalis, then this game will fit you like a glove.  Large-scale army strategy and planning are more fun than ever, even if you cannot manage economics or tech research as directly as in Europa.  But, there are enough new features to make this game worthwhile even if you're sick of others like it; and if those games seemed too impersonal or confusing, Crusader Kings might be what you need to get you into the genre.

*Updated Review* (Recommended)
Alright, it's been a few months now since the game was released and I wanted to give this game a fair shake since the latest updates and since @BlueDog had left a comment asking if the game was any better.
I had originally logged 40 hours on the game in early access and my original review after those 40 hours is below.  I have now logged an additional 40 hours and I have noticed that since April there has been a number of changes to the game which I'll cover in this updated review.
First I'll say the stability of the game has greatly improved.  During my original 40 hours of gameplay back in April I experienced a lot of crashing and unrecoverable bugs.  I can honestly say that in the latest 40 hours I've logged I have not experienced a single bug that I had previously seen, no crashing, etc.  The game appears to operate and function rather smoothly in general.
The next part I noticed was the pop-ups seem to have been fixed.  Previously I had noticed during pre-release that the pop-ups were simply out of control.  There was too many too often and even the UI option to disable them didn't function correctly and the pop-ups would just keep coming and coming.  This seems to have been fixed as after selecting the options to disable the ones I didn't want to see anymore they never came back and the option setting stuck.  Really happy to see that.
The most important thing I wanted to touch base on which I mentioned in my original review was the 100+ turn performance issue.  During pre-release the performance in the game got so bad after 100+ turns that it was simply unplayable.  I can say for certain that I managed to get up to 198 turns and performance was still accetable in game.  Once again, happy to see that fix as it was truly one of the biggest issues for me.  A slight disclaimer, however, in my original review I noted that a work-around for the performance problem was suggested by the dev team to disable Pirate spawns and I will say that just out of habit I did disable Pirate spawns despite during pre-release it didn't actually help that much.  In short, I have no idea if leaving Pirate spawns enabled would effect performance currently after 100+ turns as it did in pre-release but I seem to suspect that it would perform fine with it enabled just based on how well performance overall has improved in the latest update of this game.
One of the last points I originally mentioned was over AI and how dumb they were.  Again, I didn't really experience any of the issues I noticed during pre-release so I don't feel this is an issue but as a disclaimer I also had not completely wiped out any AI factions during my latest 40 hours logged so I'm not sure if they will linger around like they did previously.
Finally, I have noticed some slight improvements and additions to the game for visual effects and cut scense which I liked a lot.  I don't recall seeing any cut scense in pre-release so for me seeing those this time around was a nice refershing break from staring at the galaxy map the entire time. I do wish they would add a little more planetary interaction though on that level just to break thinks up a little.
Overall I still feel there's a lot of repetitiveness to this game but now that all of the bugs I originally encountered have been fixed I can safely recommend this game.
2 bugs I did encounter in my latest 40 hours logged were some text string errors where a string of text on a few screens like the diplomancy screen were showing raw string syntax code instead of the correct string return values.  The other bug was, and I think I caused it, I had a few Patrol ships in one of my systems (not in hanger) and I launched their probes and before I hit end turn I disband the fleet and sent them to the hanger which seemed to freeze my game so I couldn't progress to the next turn which also caused me to be unable to save my game at the point (had to roll back to older save after killing the game process and restarting).  All things aside they were minor issues and I think I caused one of them.

Popup Simulator 2017 - Needs a lot of work.
I hesitated to leave this game a negative review but for now I can't recommend it as it needs far too much work in my opinion before it's really playable.  While I have 40 hours logged on this game I'd say in all fairness 75% (at least) of my time was spent watching paint dry and twiddling my thumbs as I waited for the turns to start and end as well as dealing with constant bugs and CTD errors.
The most frustrating part of this game I have to immedately note is the endless popups they've built into this game that will spam your screen on every single turn until you claw your eyes out and rip your ears off.  If you've ever enjoyed visiting a click-bait website plagued with popup windows then this is the game for you.  Should you despise popups you might be lucky enough to figure out how to disable them but you'll forever be reminded of their existence because they will automatically re-enable whenever they feel left out from your game.  Seriously... the popups are awful.
The most major game breaking issue that currently exists doesn't seem to have any real fix in sight from what I could tell on the discussion forum, once you reach 100+ turns the game performance tanks and gets worse the higher your turn count grows. It will get so bad after 200+ turns that you game will likely become unplayable.  At some point you'll also run into your save games no longer working which can be very frustrating if you've invested hours upon hours of your life into one.  The dev team suggested disabling Pirate spawns to improve performance but I'd rather they just fix the game so I can kill Pirates without mercy.
Last by not least, the AI is extremely stupid and very annoying.  If you're fortunate you won't end up with ghost AI faction systems that can't be found on the galaxy map leaving the AI stuck in the game despite having been wiped out entirely.  Thanks to the "cold war" status the broken AI will forever take over your systems and annoy you until you ALT+F4 and rage quit.
As far as "the game" goes... it looks very nice but lacks a story and lacks an objective aside from typical Command and Conquer (take over the world) style gameplay.  The graphics look great but I found that much of the game's visuals fell between the cracks in unnecessary sections which I only used or viewed a few times due to repetativeness.  Overall I found myself spending the vast majority of my time scrolling and panning around on the galaxy map view and clicking in and out of the different system menus.  While the game can be somewhat addiciting I still was hoping for more depth to the individual systems rather than just looking at planets and some statistics.  The trailer videos do a good job of making it seem like this game has a lot of depth but after a few rounds you'll find repetativeness around every corner.  Rinse and repeat until you get bored.
Overall if they could fix the bugs and other negative points I ran into I'd say the game is slightly above mediocre for my taste.  There is a lot of potential but with them saying the game is soon to be releaed from Early Access I feel they've already sealed this game's fate as just mediocre and repetative.
*Will post an update to this review shortly after the game is released from EA*

There was too many too often and even the UI option to disable them didn't function correctly and the pop-ups would just keep coming and coming.  This seems to have been fixed as after selecting the options to disable the ones I didn't want to see anymore they never came back and the option setting stuck.  Really happy to see that.
The most important thing I wanted to touch base on which I mentioned in my original review was the 100+ turn performance issue.  During pre-release the performance in the game got so bad after 100+ turns that it was simply unplayable.  I can say for certain that I managed to get up to 198 turns and performance was still accetable in game.  Once again, happy to see that fix as it was truly one of the biggest issues for me.  A slight disclaimer, however, in my original review I noted that a work-around for the performance problem was suggested by the dev team to disable Pirate spawns and I will say that just out of habit I did disable Pirate spawns despite during pre-release it didn't actually help that much.  In short, I have no idea if leaving Pirate spawns enabled would effect performance currently after 100+ turns as it did in pre-release but I seem to suspect that it would perform fine with it enabled just based on how well performance overall has improved in the latest update of this game.
One of the last points I originally mentioned was over AI and how dumb they were.  Again, I didn't really experience any of the issues I noticed during pre-release so I don't feel this is an issue but as a disclaimer I also had not completely wiped out any AI factions during my latest 40 hours logged so I'm not sure if they will linger around like they did previously.
Finally, I have noticed some slight improvements and additions to the game for visual effects and cut scense which I liked a lot.  I don't recall seeing any cut scense in pre-release so for me seeing those this time around was a nice refershing break from staring at the galaxy map the entire time. I do wish they would add a little more planetary interaction though on that level just to break thinks up a little.
Overall I still feel there's a lot of repetitiveness to this game but now that all of the bugs I originally encountered have been fixed I can safely recommend this game.
2 bugs I did encounter in my latest 40 hours logged were some text string errors where a string of text on a few screens like the diplomancy screen were showing raw string syntax code instead of the correct string return values.  The other bug was, and I think I caused it, I had a few Patrol ships in one of my systems (not in hanger) and I launched their probes and before I hit end turn I disband the fleet and sent them to the hanger which seemed to freeze my game so I couldn't progress to the next turn which also caused me to be unable to save my game at the point (had to roll back to older save after killing the game process and restarting).  All things aside they were minor issues and I think I caused one of them.

Popup Simulator 2017 - Needs a lot of work.
I hesitated to leave this game a negative review but for now I can't recommend it as it needs far too much work in my opinion before it's really playable.  While I have 40 hours logged on this game I'd say in all fairness 75% (at least) of my time was spent watching paint dry and twiddling my thumbs as I waited for the turns to start and end as well as dealing with constant bugs and CTD errors.
The most frustrating part of this game I have to immedately note is the endless popups they've built into this game that will spam your screen on every single turn until you claw your eyes out and rip your ears off.  If you've ever enjoyed visiting a click-bait website plagued with popup windows then this is the game for you.  Should you despise popups you might be lucky enough to figure out how to disable them but you'll forever be reminded of their existence because they will automatically re-enable whenever they feel left out from your game.  Seriously... the popups are awful.
The most major game breaking issue that currently exists doesn't seem to have any real fix in sight from what I could tell on the discussion forum, once you reach 100+ turns the game performance tanks and gets worse the higher your turn count grows. It will get so bad after 200+ turns that you game will likely become unplayable.  At some point you'll also run into your save games no longer working which can be very frustrating if you've invested hours upon hours of your life into one.  The dev team suggested disabling Pirate spawns to improve performance but I'd rather they just fix the game so I can kill Pirates without mercy.
Last by not least, the AI is extremely stupid and very annoying.  If you're fortunate you won't end up with ghost AI faction systems that can't be found on the galaxy map leaving the AI stuck in the game despite having been wiped out entirely.  Thanks to the "cold war" status the broken AI will forever take over your systems and annoy you until you ALT+F4 and rage quit.
As far as "the game" goes... it looks very nice but lacks a story and lacks an objective aside from typical Command and Conquer (take over the world) style gameplay.  The graphics look great but I found that much of the game's visuals fell between the cracks in unnecessary sections which I only used or viewed a few times due to repetativeness.  Overall I found myself spending the vast majority of my time scrolling and panning around on the galaxy map view and clicking in and out of the different system menus.  While the game can be somewhat addiciting I still was hoping for more depth to the individual systems rather than just looking at planets and some statistics.  The trailer videos do a good job of making it seem like this game has a lot of depth but after a few rounds you'll find repetativeness around every corner.  Rinse and repeat until you get bored.
Overall if they could fix the bugs and other negative points I ran into I'd say the game is slightly above mediocre for my taste.  There is a lot of potential but with them saying the game is soon to be releaed from Early Access I feel they've already sealed this game's fate as just mediocre and repetative.
*Will post an update to this review shortly after the game is released from EA*

First of all this is my first early access and I think i struck lucky because this is, so far, great. If you like galactic civ and master of orion then there is nothing here to scare you. And there we have one of it's pluses. Each race is more than just a skin to don while you resort to the usual- colonise like sex crazed rats until you're an inexorable wave, a domino effect. So damn good that after steamrollering your enemies planets and turning their fleets to stardust just build em some stuff and it's all forgotten. This is, from what i've seen, because each races has a very different way of using resources to fuel it's expansion and a custom story line. You do get choices as you proceed through the main questlines but I'm not sure if they have any larger effects besides allowing a bit of customisation of your faction towards your play style.
The next thing I love about this game is the UI. So so nice. Hero leveling, tech tree, system views it just works Would like two seperate skill... um... plates? Pies? One for if the hero is admiral one for if govenor. I think there should be more made of the heroes with a couple of connected missions unique to each hero. I would also have more of them generated and have admirals the only people who can have a fleet with warships in. Like the way Total War went. Colonisers, scouts and dropships can be the only ones that can travel around without an admiral. Which then means you can name your fleets! Hurray.
It's something that this game has partially cracked. I can have a little narrative for the few fleets that have an admiral in but otherwise there are too many ships flying about and the constantly and randomly changing fleets names reduces many to just numbers. The problem with this is the way the larger strategic game is arranged; like a train network on both system to system and cluster to cluster scales, it becomes purly about stationing enough ships at crux points. A game of noughts and crosses. A fleet cap would create more tactical play and bring personality to your fleets, something I love in the total war series and think could be something the developers may want to consider.
I will say again, I really really liked playing this game but because of that the things that annoy can break the immersion some what.
First of those is the whole probe issue. At the moment you scout by sending a patrol class ship along the lines that connect each star, when you have arrived you can zoom in and take a look at the planets that are there, what their resources are and how many anomilies there are. Your scout ship has two probes to begin with and you need a probe per annomily. 'Lots of scout ships' I hear you groan, NO beacause your patrol ships rebuild them.... only ..... very.... sl...o...w- You get the idea. Endlessly tapping sleep until probe is built. How about a screen comes up with - it will take you x amount of rounds to survey this sytem, with each anomily listed and the time each will take. You can then queue say one or two or the whole damn lot.
Also something needs to be done about accidently triggering the system cut scene, its lovely and i really like it but i don't want it every time I roll the mouse wheel a bit hard towards the system or what ever I am doing to keep triggering it.
My last gripe is again on a theme of making systems and fleets feel different from each other and that is that there are not enough things to build in general but too few unique mega constuctions specifically.  How about a set of mega construction that need several systems to help build it, or you need to enlist another race/empire. I may be going off into wish list territory but that's because with ES2 it's sooo close to brilliant.
I have had one crash when I tried infiltration invasion. I never used it again and it's never crashed since. Things I haven't really played with - trade, just discovered it and realised I could have been making loads of cash. OH! resources could do with balancing a bit if you're gonna have swarms of ships. This is something I've heard a lot of ♥♥♥♥♥ing about. To be honest I have yet to really get annoyed about that, maybe because I've never traded a single thing I've mined. Maybe because I only used strategic resources on admrals ships. I also have two designs for most of my fleet, one thats got all the funky guns n armour and one that takes either no strat resources, or so little that I won't notice spamming 15 ships because there is nothing else to build.  This may have been why I didn't really use the market.
I like the ships each faction gets, there is limited cosmetic customisation options but I did like what you could play with. Which is a modular thing where you can change weapons engains and armour. So far I have had reason to make only a couple of ships outside of upgrading existing models. I am hoping for bigger and badder ships to come with the full game.
Colonisation is on a star system base with you colonising a planet then using that as a base to colonise the system. I am aware there are differences to each race in this regard but I can only talk about the united empire. Which is the faction I have been using. One thing thats confusing at first is that past adding their resource science and manufactoring points and giving it a specialisation you don't build all the buidings again on the new planet. Facilities that are built on that first planet seem to apply to all the planets in the system aslong as they have had the first colony improvement built. - I think. Don't try and use two colony ships to establish two outposts at the same time. Like I did. Was very confused for a bit.
Diplomacy- Hmm I am going to assume that this isn't even vaguely finished. It may be me but there has been no reason for me to use diplomacy except for declaring war. Most of the useful stuff seems to get unlocked so late game (Via tech) and there seemed to be little dynamism in the relationships that the whole thing was easily forgetable.
The minor races do save this however. Far from being a early game nightmare and a late game annoyance like so many before they are actually kind of crucial. You assimilate into your society as you go these small races either finding them on distant planets, conquering their worlds or assimilating them through superior culture. You can even do it at long range through performing their special milestone. They change the make up of the empire and add their racial bonuses and traits to yours. Something I've always wanted in an empire building game. With the added mechanic that should you, through careful use of resourses and cash deside, you can have a entirely different race dominant by the end of the game.
Finally I love the style and the artwork it's feel and the music. The music must get special mention because its very good. More of it please. In particular a steel drum tune that is one am definately copy over to actually listen to.
To sum up- I am really glad I bought this game, I am really enjoying playing it. My girlfriend doesn't mind it because there is a plot, so she can ask me what's happening and get something more than, 'you see that blue bit? I am gonna make it red'. If you like 4x strategy games it's well worth getting.With the right tweaks and adjustments this could be a real evolution. As it is, its a nicer looking, easier to handle, more satisfying galactic civilisations.

A MODERN MASTERPIECE
I'm not usually one write reviews but in this case I will make an exception. This is truly one of the greatest games ever made. You're not going to go on GTA-style killing sprees. This is a story based experience.
The game is set in Los Angeles in 1947. WW2 is over and the American economy is booming. LA is a relatively nascent city that will come to define America (good and bad) over the next half century. This is a defining moment in human history.
Naturally the city is not without its growing pains. As an LAPD officer, you will be the one to confront them head on.  There is much to be gained from this booming city and much to be lost.
The story is told through cases. Solve one case and move on to the next one (much like TV cops). It is almost episodic in nature.
The atmosphere of this game is incredible. In one investigation, I found myself standing in a suburban backyard and could almost smell the flowers, it was that engrossing.
All in all, this game is a wonderful example of what video games are capable of. The depth of narrative is similar to that of an HBO series. Hopefully more developers are inspired by this and make games of equal depth and quality.

Very much like the Civilization franchise in essence, but the military aspects are far more interesting. (Note that I'm writing this prior to the full release, so some aspects haven't been fleshed out yet.)
The first thing I liked was that you can design your own ships based on available tech. Once you've picked a template and assigned weapons, armor, engines, etc, you name that design and save it. Now that ship will appear as an option to construct. Cool.

The third thing I liked was that there was enough complexity that, unlike Civilization, the optimum strategy was not apparent to me. I'm sure with time one will present itself, but I found it initially more immersive in that I was managing such an array of things that couldn't be sure whether focusing on x over y over z would be better than focusing z over x over y.
The main drawback is that it's very complex, and it can be overwhelming at first. I dove in before a tutorial existed, and it was not immediately intuitive. I'm sure the full release will improve on this, though.

I've played a couple of hours and just won my first game as Riftborn via supremacy. There's a lot of differences which stands out to me as someone who's played hundreds of hours of Endless Space. There is far more emphasis on having a handful of star systems, rather than doing literally everything you can to rapidly expand and consume the galaxy. Expansion disapproval is harder to offset than before as well. I think the most systems you can colonise at once before getting expansion disapproval is 11, provided you researched the appropriate technologies.
If you don't like micro managing, this is a change for the better. Having automated building plans for systems means there's even less micro managing involved once your empire starts getting bloated. Just remember that it won't build ships or, in the Riftborn's case, population increments without your input.
Crossing to other branches of the galaxy takes significantly more time now, due to wormholes being a high tier technology rather than a low tier one (wormholes being these lines which let ships cross instantly from one branch to another). In order to cross without it, you need to throw out probes to find new branches and research free movement, which is a lot more time consuming. This can either be good or bad depending on how you look at it. If you play with an ultra imperialistic mindset and just want to fight and expand like me, it can be a bit frustrating. I had to purpose build these ships which vastly increased the speed of my invasion fleet to easily get within reach of my enemy's star systems.
Another thing which I think is worth mentioning is that researching new technology now makes all other technology require more research. Converting industry into other resources now requires you to research the technology to do it as well, meaning that research is far, far slower than it was in Endless Space 1. Combined with the changes I mentioned above, this ensures that the game as a whole plays much slower than before.
On star systems, your population now has varying races in it. In my case, I start with a group of ecoterrorist robots as well as my native Riftborn. Different populations have different political opinions as well, which adds another layer of depth to what decisions you take as an empire. That minor faction of peace loving jellyfish I befriended and absorbed into my empire nearly fell into anarchy when I started messing up my opponents and invading their planets. I do wish, however, that there were some more options for population control, such as migrating portions of a population from one planet to another, or even committing genocide if you don't like a particular race on a star system.
There's a lot of other neat little additions as well, including exploring curiosities on your planets, quests, objectives to complete for extra rewards, a special questline for your faction and minor factions who you can negotiate with. It all adds a bit more variety to the galaxy.
In short, if you liked the original game, the core mechanics are more or less the same, albeit a bit slower. If you haven't played Endless Space before I'd definitely recommend giving it a try. Just keep in mind that it's an early access game. Bugs and typos will be found.

This is one of the most fun and immersive grand strategy games I've ever played.  This game takes the complexity and diplomatic scale of games like the Europa Universalis and makes the game more character driven.  In the Medieval era, there was no such thing as national diplomacy; it was all personal.  This game lets you play as any historical figure from a count to an emperor in Medieval Europe, Middle East, or even West Africa and manage your court, your demesne, your vassals, and so much more.  If you liked Hearts of Iron or Europa Universalis, then this game will fit you like a glove.  Large-scale army strategy and planning are more fun than ever, even if you cannot manage economics or tech research as directly as in Europa.  But, there are enough new features to make this game worthwhile even if you're sick of others like it; and if those games seemed too impersonal or confusing, Crusader Kings might be what you need to get you into the genre.

---------------------------------------
Exploration:
I enjoyed the exploration and colonization aspect of the game. I feel like it is almost identical to ES1 though. I see a lot of things that are pretty much identical to ES1 - that isn't necessarily a bad thing though as I enjoyed the first title more than this one.
Resources:
These were well distributed around the galaxy ensuring that no one race had all of the resources - I like this because it ensures a war will break out over resources alone.
Cons
---------------------------------------
The AI:
I felt like the AI was incapable of managing their empire or fleets. One of the AI never left their home world to colonize near systems (Vodyani). The Cravers stopped expanding and have never declared war on anyone, so so much for consumption of everything and everyone in their path. They are incapable of building a strong fleet. The studio needs to do a lot of work on their AI as it feels like the current AI has taken a strip of valium.
Battles:
Feel pointless. You pick a tactic and watch as the game shows you the same broken record of a battle scene. Land battles are even less involved. I can deal with a simple combat system, but what I really cannot deal with is the repetitiveness that this game reeks of after 200 turns.
Shipbuilding:
I liked this at first. Until I encountered an AI fleet - they don't seem to bother with ship design and so field the entry level ships, which results in a massively one sided skirmish. I have yet to actually lose a war (or for that matter, a battle) because of this.
Tech tree:
I preferred the layout of the tech tree in ES1. It doesn't have that fluid feeling of Civ but I can let that one go. The keyword search function goes a long way to make up for this.
Conclusion:
If you already own ES1, you aren't really missing much by not owning this title.
In summary, this game *is* a good game. But it's essentially ES1 with a graphics update. Anything new that they've added doesn't seem to add anything of value to the series and I don't think the game goes deep enough into the four pillars of a 4X title to actually consider itself one. I will try the game for another 200 turns at full release and if my mind changes, I will amend my review.
Multiplayer might paint a different picture entirely, but as I bought this game for it's single player I find it hard to recommend. Coming from titles like EU4/VicII, I do prefer something a little more challenging than this.

L.A. Noire is a game based around interesting technology.  The idea is that they would use state-of-the-art face capture technology to capture realistic facial expressions and then use these as "tells" on criminals' faces during investigations.  Using these tells you're meant to determine whether a person is telling the truth, only telling half the truth, or outright lying.
Unfortunately this feature, the feature around which the game is built, is horribly flawed.  Whenever a witness gives you an answer or states a "fact" you are given 3 options: truth, doubt, lie.  'Doubt' and 'Lie' differ only in that, to catch someone in a lie you have to cite a certain piece of evidence.  Sounds fun in theory, but in reality agent Cole rarely says what you mean him to say when you doubt someone.
Woman: I was at the store grabbing milk for my cake I was baking.
*press doubt*
Cole: TELL ME WHERE HE IS YOU LYING STUPID ♥♥♥♥♥!!!!
Also on some occasions you pick out a specific piece of evidence to nail a guy and the game gives you the "you're wrong" sound.  This happened on one of the first missions where I had several pieces of evidence that would securely help me convict a guy but I only one of them was right.
Overall this game is a great tech demo, but it is horribly, horribly executed, action scenes (driving, chasing, shooting) are all clunky and unenjoyable at best.  The interrogation 'face' system is misleading and ends up being more annoying than interesting with the ambiguous conversation prompts.
Pros:
- Neat facial expression technology.
- An alright story with fairly good voice acting.
Cons:
- Misleading conversation prompts.
- Only one piece of evidence will catch someone in a lie regardless of the validity of the other pieces.
- Action sequences feel forced, clunky, and like padding.

Endless Space 2 is a fantastic space 4x game. it's gorgeous in both design of the UI and in the game it's self, and it's got some extremely interesting characters.
While most space 4x games try to make you feel like you're taking part in a giant space opera similar to The Culture book series, Endless Space 2 (ES2) is not afraid to be different. One way it does this is through it's races. You have your normal run of the mill Humans focused on conquring! Evil robots whose sole purpose is to kill and at one with the galaxy tree people.
But what about a race of people who are created in the image of Horatio as he believes he's pefect... yeah a race of self absorbed clones. Or a race of aliens who are literally to smart for their own good and had to create an AI to make sure they don't blow anything else up aside from their moon. OR how about a race of aliens who's run like an italian mob? It's unqiue but it doesn't stop there.
I'd say this is a story based 4X game. You can play to win through the normal victories like kill everyone, befreind all, science them to death but the fun here is the journey. You get quests through out your game and it's not like "hey, we found some thing go look at it." For one of the races you're given almost a noire story of 3 famlies who all want somethign diffrent to be done with the dust, the currency and power of the game. You pick one and it progresses the story. It doesn't feel like an afterthought but like someone put time and effort into each story to make it as interesting as possible.
this game is great. If you're looking for a 4x game in space but want something a bit different than Gal Civ or Stellaris, check this out!

For this one i won't focus too much on what novelty this second opus brings to the table. Color, warmth, personality alongside a brand new system to tackle what sorely lacked ES1, empire managment. Anyone looking for a more detailed description of the new features shouldn't have too much trouble finding it. In a few words I'd say it is reasonably ambitious and nicely done. Returning players certainly won't be disoriented yet I think most will have a pleasant time manoeuvering those new political features and
(imagining is the important word here) how they could add up and improve the global playing exeprience.
If i say "imagining" it is because as of right now those new features are kind of disovled into what feels like huge balancing issues. Let me explain. Most of the new features revolve around giving you FIDS bonus (productivity in the larger sense) if you manage your population "correctly" and most of those really look like wothy objective to aim for.
Sadly by the time you will reach those, it won t matter anymore as you will already be litterally showered in pretty much everything. Production, gold, influence, food, luxuries... call it, there is a good chance you ll have already a mountain of it. So this +xx production bonus per capita or this +5 food per habitant if slotted on a sterile planet really looks way less exciting now that you can build pretty much anything in 1 or 2 turns or as your demographic growth as reached "hamster on hormonal fecundity treatment" level.
To summarize it, there s always a time, usually halfway through a game, where your empire will go nuclear and all of a sudden, all those well thought new managerial features will feel useless and voided from purpose. Why bother with the hassle of micro managing your demographic for incremental gains when you are already cruising toward absolute galactic domination. you ll spend most the time passing turns waiting to unlock something new to build (which will in turn increase your wealth thus making the next waiting period even longer).
Those are clearly balancing issue which can be promptly corrected if correctly assesed. SO i will still recommend the game on it's sheer potential. It is a gorgeous, accessible and fun 4x sporting a comprehensible and nicely crafted interface. It is develloped by a very likable studio which communicate a lot and clearly cares for its fanbase.
If you can wait a bit longer, do it. The officila release is looming at the horizon and i'm sure that by the time it hits, ES2 will live up to its outstanding potential.

Crusader Kings 2 is an RTS like many of Paradox's previous titles; highly complex (where your typical RTS is concerned) and providing a highly realistic simulation of empire-expansion. Every facet, save tactical involvement in battles, is explored with detail, and with much at the player's control.
One of the key features in CK2 is it's dynastic political system. Not only must you secure your line of succession through heirs to continue in your quest for glory, but there are no formal alliances. Everyone you can count on is either directly in your sphere of influence and thus obligated to serve, or aligned through familial ties.
Even though I bought it during the sale, as previously I was unsure, now that I've played Crusader Kings 2, I can definitely say I'd not have issue with paying full price for it. This is even one of the few games I wouldn't be opposed to paying full price for DLC.
